label: H.R. 4930
title: To expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
short_title: Customs IP Information Sharing Bill
one: Lets U.S. Customs and Border Protection share more information, including nonpublic data from online marketplaces and shippers, with trademark and copyright owners and other interested parties when it reasonably suspects imported goods are counterfeit or pirated.
summary: This bill changes a section of the Tariff Act of 1930 that covers how U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) handles goods it thinks may violate trademark or copyright law. Today, if CBP suspects an import is a violation, it can ask certain parties, such as the rights holder, for help and can share details that appear on the item, its packaging and its labels. The bill raises the bar a bit by requiring "reasonable suspicion" instead of simple suspicion. It also widens what CBP can share to include images and information about packing materials and containers. It lets CBP ask for help from "any other party with an interest in the merchandise," as the CBP Commissioner decides. Most notably, CBP could share nonpublic information about the goods that came from online marketplaces, express shipping companies, freight forwarders, or other businesses involved in selling or importing them, if CBP received or obtained it. When CBP shares that kind of information, it must notify the person receiving it, following rules set by the Homeland Security Secretary. The bill spends no money directly. Its main effects would be more help for intellectual property owners in policing counterfeits. It could also raise questions about the privacy of business data and how broadly "interested party" is read. The bill has been sent to the President for signature.
does: Changes the trigger for CBP to seek help from 'suspects' to 'has a reasonable suspicion' that imported goods violate certain trademark and copyright laws.
Expands what CBP can share with the helping party to include information and images of packing materials and containers, not just the item, its packaging and labels.

Allows CBP to share nonpublic information about the goods that was generated by online marketplaces, express consignment operators, freight forwarders, or any other entity involved in selling, importing or facilitating the import, if CBP has received or obtained it.
Requires CBP to notify the recipient of the nonpublic information transmitted, under regulations the Secretary of Homeland Security may set.
Adds 'any other party with an interest in the merchandise, as determined appropriate by the Commissioner' to the list of people CBP may ask for help.
who: Trademark and copyright owners who want to stop counterfeit and pirated imports
U.S. Customs and Border Protection staff
Online marketplaces, express shipping companies and freight forwarders whose nonpublic data could be shared
Importers and sellers of goods suspected of infringement
Consumers who may buy counterfeit or unsafe goods

benefits: May help stop counterfeit goods, some of which are unsafe, such as fake medicine, electronics or toys, from reaching consumers.
Gives rights holders better information to confirm whether goods are fake, which could speed enforcement.
Raises the standard from suspicion to 'reasonable suspicion,' which may limit careless requests.
Requires notification when nonpublic information is shared.
concerns: Nonpublic business information from marketplaces and shippers could be shared with private parties, raising privacy and trade-secret questions.
'Any other party with an interest' is broad and left to the Commissioner's judgment.
Mainly benefits intellectual property owners, often large companies.
Notification goes to the recipient of the data, not clearly to the businesses whose data is shared, and the bill does not spell out a way for wrongly accused importers to contest it.
Small sellers or importers could face delays or seizures of lawful goods based on shared information.
imp.cost: No funding or cost estimate is given in the bill text. It appears to create no new spending, though CBP would need staff time to implement the changes and to write rules.
unknowns: What regulations the Homeland Security Secretary would set for notification and for protecting sensitive data.
How the Commissioner would decide who is an 'other party with an interest.'
How often the new sharing authority would be used and its effect on lawful importers.
Whether any privacy or trade-secret protections apply to shared data beyond what the text shows.

stage.stage_label: Sent to the President for signature
stage.last_action: Presented to President.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to expand the sharing of information about suspected intellectual property rights violations in trade, so that U.S. Customs and Border Protection can get help from rights holders and other interested parties in deciding whether imported goods infringe trademark or copyright laws. Based on the CRS summary, it does this by changing the standard for seeking help to "reasonable suspicion," widening the information CBP can share, and allowing CBP to share certain nonpublic data from marketplaces, shippers, and other businesses involved in importing goods.

oppose: The bill allows CBP to share nonpublic business information from online marketplaces, express shippers, and freight forwarders with private parties. Opponents could ask whether that data needs stronger privacy and trade-secret protections.
The phrase "any other party with an interest in the merchandise" is broad and left to the CBP Commissioner to decide. Opponents could ask Congress to define who qualifies more narrowly.

The bill notifies the recipient of shared data, but it does not clearly notify the businesses whose data is shared or set out a clear way for importers wrongly accused to challenge a decision. Opponents could ask for those protections.
Small sellers and importers could face delays or seizures of lawful goods based on shared information. Opponents could ask how the bill protects legitimate businesses from these costs.
support: The bill helps stop counterfeit goods, some of which are unsafe, such as fake medicine, electronics, or toys, from reaching consumers. Supporters could say better information sharing helps protect public safety.
Rights holders would get better information to confirm whether goods are fake, which could speed up enforcement. Supporters could say this helps honest businesses that own trademarks and copyrights.
Raising the trigger from "suspects" to "reasonable suspicion" sets a higher bar before CBP asks for outside help, which may limit careless requests. Supporters could point to this as a safeguard.
The bill requires CBP to notify the recipient whenever nonpublic information is shared, which adds a record of what was transmitted. Supporters could say this improves accountability.

crs:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade. 
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels. 
This bill (1) expands the definition of 
person
 to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP. CBP must provide the person with notification of the transmitted information.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. (expanded sharing provision) lets CBP share nonpublic business data from marketplaces and shippers with rights holders, and notice goes only to the recipient, not the businesses whose data is shared, so the public and affected firms have less visibility into who receives their information.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly strengthens enforcement tools for intellectual property owners, often large companies, and the nonpublic data sharing benefits those rights holders while the burden of possible seizures or delays falls on importers and sellers.

equality.reason: Expanding the 'interested party' category at the Commissioner's discretion lets some private parties get CBP information and help that others, including smaller importers, do not get, creating unequal access to enforcement tools.

justice.reason: The bill sets no process for importers wrongly accused to contest a referral or seizure, and the Commissioner's broad discretion over who qualifies as an interested party is not bounded by standards, which weakens accountability; the notification requirement partly offsets this.

news.overall: Coverage in both groups does not directly report on the bill, which is about sharing information on suspected IP rights violations in trade. Lean Left outlets place the IP issue within the U.S.-China trade fight and new tariffs, with a strategic and policy framing. Center outlets lean on specific enforcement and legal events, such as the Huawei verdict and a trademark case, and report tariffs as separate news. The evidence is thin: three Lean Left headlines and five Center headlines, with only brief descriptions, so this reflects headline-level framing only.

label: H.R. 8552
title: Veterans’ Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
short_title: Veterans' Disability Compensation Cost-of-Living Increase 2026
one: Raises veterans' disability pay, dependent add-ons, clothing allowances, and survivor benefits on December 1, 2026, by the same percentage as the Social Security cost-of-living increase.
summary: This bill gives disabled veterans and the survivors of some veterans a yearly raise so their benefits keep up with rising prices. On December 1, 2026, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) must raise several payments by the same percentage that Social Security benefits go up that same day. The payments covered are: disability compensation for veterans with service-connected disabilities, extra pay for veterans with dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC), a monthly benefit paid to surviving spouses and children of certain veterans. The bill also lets the VA make matching adjustments for certain people covered under an older law (Public Law 85-857) who have not received compensation under the main veterans' disability chapter. The VA must publish the new payment amounts in the Federal Register, the government's official daily notice, by the date the Social Security increase figures must be published. The bill does not name a percentage because it depends on the Social Security calculation, which was not given in the material. It also does not give a cost estimate. This kind of bill is passed most years. The latest action listed is a message on Senate action sent to the House, so the final steps may still be pending.
does: Requires the VA to raise listed disability compensation rates on December 1, 2026.
Ties the raise to the same percentage as the Social Security cost-of-living increase effective that date.
Covers wartime disability compensation, extra pay for dependents, the clothing allowance, and survivor benefits (DIC) for spouses and children.
Lets the VA adjust rates for certain people under Public Law 85-857 who have not received compensation under the main disability chapter.
Requires the VA to publish the new amounts in the Federal Register by the Social Security publication deadline.
who: Veterans with service-connected disabilities
Veterans with dependents who receive extra compensation
Surviving spouses and children receiving DIC
Certain disabled veterans who get the clothing allowance
The VA, which must pay and publish the new rates
Federal taxpayers, who fund the benefits

benefits: If enacted, recipients' payments would likely rise each year with the Social Security cost-of-living adjustment, which may help benefits keep pace with rising prices.
Tying the increase to an existing federal formula may make the process predictable and automatic each year.
concerns: The bill does not set a fixed percentage, so the size of any increase cannot be known from the text alone.
Because the increase depends on the Social Security figure, benefits could rise by more or less in a given year depending on that calculation.
imp.cost: ["The material does not include a cost estimate or a total dollar figure for this bill. The total cost would depend on the Social Security percentage for December 1, 2026, which is not stated in the material. The bill does not describe a separate funding source."]
unknowns: The exact percentage increase for December 1, 2026 is not stated in the material.
The total cost to the federal government is not given.
The bill's status is unclear from the material: the latest listed action is that it was sent to the President for signature, so it may or may not be signed into law.
The material does not say which specific Public Law 85-857 recipients would be covered or how many people that would affect.
The material does not explain how the VA would handle the increases administratively beyond publishing the amounts in the Federal Register.

stage.stage_label: Sent to the President for signature
stage.last_action: Presented to President.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give disabled veterans and certain survivors a yearly cost-of-living increase so their benefits keep pace with rising prices. It ties the raise to the percentage increase in Social Security benefits effective December 1, 2026, and requires the VA to publish the new amounts in the Federal Register.

oppose: The bill does not set a fixed percentage. The size of the increase depends on the Social Security calculation, so the cost and the benefit change cannot be known from the text alone.
The bill does not include a cost estimate, so Congress and the public do not yet have a figure for how much the annual increases would add to federal spending.
Automatic yearly increases are set by formula rather than by a fresh review each year. Some constituents may prefer that Congress review veterans' benefit levels case by case.
support: The bill would help veterans and survivors keep up with rising prices by matching the Social Security cost-of-living increase each year.
Linking the raise to an existing federal formula makes the process predictable, so veterans can plan around a known method instead of waiting for a new vote each year.
The bill covers several benefit types at once, including disability compensation, extra pay for dependents, the clothing allowance, and survivor benefits (DIC) for spouses and children.

crs:
Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill requires the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to increase the amounts payable for wartime disability compensation, additional compensation for dependents, the clothing allowance for certain disabled veterans, and dependency and indemnity compensation for surviving spouses and children. Specifically, the VA must increase the amounts by the same percentage as the cost-of-living increase in benefits for Social Security recipients that is effective on December 1, 2026. The act requires the VA to publish the amounts payable, as increased, in the Federal Register.
The VA is authorized to make a similar adjustment to the rates of disability compensation payable to persons who have not received compensation for service-connected disability or death.

transparency_kindness.reason: Requires the VA to publish the new payment amounts in the Federal Register, a public official notice, so the adjusted rates are openly available.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill concerns veterans' benefit payments and does not involve bailing out corporations or shifting utility or ratepayer costs.

equality.reason: Sec. 1 applies one uniform rule, the Social Security COLA percentage, to all covered compensation and DIC recipients, so benefit increases are tied to the same measure for everyone covered.

justice.reason: Automatic annual adjustment tied to a published federal formula makes benefit amounts more predictable and consistent for recipients, though it does not add new remedies or review rights.

label: H.R. 2302
title: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025
short_title: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act
one: Moves federal land and tribe-owned land in El Dorado County, California, into trust as part of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians' reservation, and bans casino-style gaming on it.
summary: This bill would give the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians, in El Dorado County, California, more land to add to its reservation. First, it cancels an old 1964 federal order (Public Land Order 3309) that set aside certain land. The CRS summary says the order reserved the land as a Forest Service experiment station. The bill then moves control of that land to the Secretary of the Interior. Within 180 days of becoming law, the Secretary must put two areas of land "into trust" for the tribe. Trust means the U.S. government holds the legal title for the tribe's benefit. One area is federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The other is land called Indian Creek Ranch, which the CRS says the tribe already owns. Both areas become part of the tribe's reservation. The Secretary must check whether a land survey is needed. If one is done, it must be kept on file where the public can view it. The bill also bans all gaming on this land, including casino-style gaming. The bill text gives the acreage as about 80 and 185 acres. The CRS summary gives about 85.3 and 118.84 acres, 204.14 in total. The bill relies on a map dated May 2, 2025, which I could not see. The bill says nothing about costs, environmental review, or local government input.
does: Revokes Public Land Order 3309 (from 1964) and transfers jurisdiction over that land to the Secretary of the Interior.
Requires the Secretary to place two parcels into trust for the tribe within 180 days, subject to valid existing rights.
Declares the trust land part of the tribe's reservation, managed under the usual rules for tribal trust land.
Requires a review of whether a survey is needed, and allows minor fixes to clerical or surveying errors.
Requires any survey to be kept on file for public inspection at the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
Bans Class II and Class III gaming on the land under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.
who: Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians
Residents and local governments in El Dorado County, California
Department of the Interior, Bureau of Land Management, and Bureau of Indian Affairs
Forest Service (if it currently manages the land, as the CRS describes)
Anyone holding existing rights on the land, such as easements

benefits: The tribe would gain a larger reservation land base, which may support tribal housing, governance, or cultural uses. The bill does not say what uses are planned.
Placing the land in trust may give the tribe the legal protections that come with trust status.
The gaming ban is stated clearly, which may reduce questions about future casino use of the land.
concerns: Removing BLM and Forest Service land from federal public management and placing it in trust may reduce public access or public uses of that land.

The acreage figures differ between the bill text (about 80 and 185 acres) and the CRS summary (about 85.3 and 118.84 acres, 204.14 total), which could cause confusion about exactly what land is covered.
The bill relies on a map dated May 2, 2025, that was not available for this analysis, so the exact boundaries cannot be confirmed here.
Local government input, environmental review, and effects on county services or tax revenue are not addressed in the material provided.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not state any cost, appropriation, or funding amount. The material provided does not give a cost estimate."]
unknowns: The exact acreage and boundaries, because the bill text and CRS summary give different figures and the referenced map was not reviewed.
Whether the land has existing uses, leases, or rights that would be affected by the transfer.
How the transfer may affect county property tax revenue, local services, or land-use rules.
Whether an environmental review will be required before or after the land is taken into trust.
What the tribe plans to do with the land.
How the cancellation of the 1964 order will affect any other claims or uses of the land.

stage.stage_label: Sent to the President for signature
stage.last_action: Presented to President.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to place about 204 acres of land in El Dorado County, California, into trust for the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians and make that land part of the tribe's reservation. It first revokes a 1964 public land order that reserved the land as a Forest Service experiment station and moves control of that land to the Secretary of the Interior. The bill's material does not state the sponsor's specific reasons beyond these land transfer goals.

oppose: Public access concern: The bill moves about 85 acres of BLM and former Forest Service land out of federal public management and into trust. You could ask your member how the public will keep access to recreation or other uses the land now supports.

Unclear acreage: The bill text gives about 80 and 185 acres, while the CRS summary gives about 85.3 and 118.84 acres, totaling 204.14. You could ask for a single, confirmed acreage and a copy of the May 2, 2025 map before a vote.

Missing local input and review: The material provided does not address environmental review, county services, or tax revenue effects, or whether local governments were consulted. You could ask your member what analysis was done and how El Dorado County residents were included.
support: Tribal land base: The bill would give the Shingle Springs Band about 204 acres to add to its reservation. You could say this supports the tribe's governance, housing, and cultural uses, which the bill's supporters may see as a long-standing goal.

Trust status: Placing land in trust means the U.S. government holds legal title for the tribe's benefit. You could say this gives the tribe the legal protections that come with trust status for land it already owns in part.

Clear gaming limit: The bill explicitly bans Class II and Class III gaming on the land. You could say this gives clarity about how the land will be used and answers concerns about future casino development.

crs:
Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025
This bill takes approximately 204.14 acres of specified lands in El Dorado County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians.
The bill revokes a specified public land order and administratively transfers the land from the Forest Service to the Department of the Interior. (In the public land order, the land was designated for use by the Forest Service as an experiment station.)
The bill directs Interior to take the following lands into trust for the benefit of the tribe: (1) approximately 85.3 acres of federal land managed by Interior's Bureau of Land Management (which includes the land transferred from the Forest Service), and (2) approximately 118.84 acres of fee land held by the tribe. These combined lands, approximately 204.14 acres, shall be part of the tribe's reservation. Further, the bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

transparency_kindness.reason: Survey under the bill is only kept on file at BIA if one is done, and the bill's acreage figures conflict with the CRS summary and rely on a map not publicly described in the text, so the public has less clear information about the land covered (Sec. on survey and map references).

local_say.reason: The bill moves federal public land into trust and declares it reservation land without providing for county or local government input, reducing local say over land use on that parcel.

news.overall: Only one outlet perspective was provided, with two headlines, and neither appears to cover the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians Land Transfer Act of 2025. The evidence is too thin and off-topic to compare how coverage of this bill is framed across perspectives. Coverage of the bill itself would need to be supplied to make a meaningful comparison.

label: H.R. 2400
title: Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026
short_title: Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026
one: The bill moves about 557 acres of national forest land in Shasta County, California, to the Department of the Interior to be held in trust for the Pit River Tribe as part of its reservation, and it bans casino-style gaming on that land.
summary: This bill would move a piece of federal land called the Four Corners Property out of the Forest Service's care and give it to the Pit River Tribe. The land is about 557 acres in Shasta County, California. First, the Department of Agriculture (which oversees the Forest Service) would hand control of the land to the Department of the Interior. Interior would then hold the land "in trust" for the Tribe. Trust means the United States government holds legal title, and the Tribe gets the benefit and use of the land. Once in trust, the land becomes part of the Tribe's reservation. Any rights that other people already legally hold on the land would stay in place. About 87 acres of roads, highways, public rights-of-way, easements and special use permit areas are excluded from the transfer. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, Interior must complete a survey of the land. Interior, Agriculture and the Tribe may agree to make small fixes to the boundaries or survey. The bill also bans all casino-style gaming (the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act's "class II" and "class III" gaming) on this land. The bill text does not describe any rules on public access, environmental review, or how the Tribe would manage the land. This version is the Senate's amendment. The latest recorded action is a message sent back to the House about that Senate action.
does: Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to transfer administrative control of the Four Corners land to the Secretary of the Interior.
Requires the land to be taken into trust for the Pit River Tribe, subject to valid existing rights.
Makes the land part of the Tribe's reservation and puts it under the laws that apply to Indian trust land.
Requires a full survey within 180 days of enactment.
Lets Interior, Agriculture and the Tribe agree to minor corrections to the land boundaries and survey.
Bans class II and class III gaming on the land.
Excludes about 87 acres of roads, rights-of-way, easements and special use permit areas shown on the map.
Ties the land description to a Forest Service map titled 'Proposed Land Conveyance to the Pit River Tribe,' dated June 30, 2026.
who: The Pit River Tribe, including the XL Ranch, Big Bend, Likely, Lookout, Montgomery Creek and Roaring Creek Rancherias
Residents and neighbors near the Four Corners Property in Shasta County
People or groups who currently use the land through permits or easements
The Forest Service and the Department of the Interior, which would handle the transfer and survey
Members of the public who now use this national forest land for recreation

benefits: The Tribe could gain a land base tied to its reservation, which may support its governance, cultural, or land-use goals.
Holding land in trust may give the Tribe a stable legal status for the property, based on the bill's description.
Existing rights and excluded roads and permit areas are said to stay unchanged, which may reduce disruption for current users.
concerns: The bill does not describe public access rules, so people who use the land now may face unknown changes in access.
The material does not describe environmental review or how the land would be managed, which may leave questions about land care.
Moving federal land out of Forest Service management may affect how the land is used for recreation, timber, or other purposes, though the bill does not say what those uses are.
The gaming ban is stated, but the bill does not explain other uses the Tribe might choose for the land.
imp.cost: ["The material does not state any cost, funding amount, or budget effect for the transfer, the survey, or ongoing management."]
unknowns: The bill text does not say how the Tribe would manage the land or what uses would be allowed.
It is not stated whether the public could continue to access the land.
The material does not describe environmental review requirements before or after the transfer.
The specific existing rights held by others on the land are not listed in the material.
The survey results, and whether any boundary fixes would be made, are not known.
The material does not say whether the bill will become law, since the latest action is a message about the Senate amendment.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to transfer about 557 acres of federal land in Shasta County, California, known as the Four Corners Property, into trust for the Pit River Tribe and make it part of the Tribe's reservation. The bill's materials describe this as moving the land from Forest Service administration to the Department of the Interior, which would hold it in trust for the Tribe.

oppose: The bill does not describe public access rules, so people who hike, hunt, or use the land now may not know whether that access will continue.
The bill text does not describe environmental review or land management plans, which may leave open questions about how the land will be cared for after the transfer.
Moving the land out of Forest Service management could change how it is used for recreation or other purposes, and the bill does not say what those uses would be.
Taking federal land into trust removes it from federal public land status, and a constituent could ask their representative how much public input was part of the process.
support: The bill would give the Pit River Tribe a land base tied to its existing reservation, which may support its governance, cultural, and land-use goals.
Placing the land in trust may give the Tribe a stable legal status for the property, based on the bill's description.
The bill says existing valid rights are kept in place, and about 87 acres of roads, rights-of-way, easements, and special use permit areas are excluded, which may reduce disruption for current users.

crs:
Pit River Land Transfer Act of 2026
This bill takes approximately 557 acres of specified federal land in Shasta County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Pit River Tribe.
The land, known as the Four Corners Property, is currently administered and managed by the Forest Service. Administrative jurisdiction over the land must be transferred to the Department of the Interior. Interior must then take the land into trust for the benefit of the Tribe. The land taken into trust shall be part of the Tribe's reservation.
The bill also prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

environment.reason: Sec. 3 moves about 557 acres of national forest land out of Forest Service management into trust with no environmental review or land-care standards stated, so federal environmental safeguards that apply to national forest land may no longer clearly apply.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill sets no public access, comment, or disclosure rules for the land after transfer, so the public would have less visibility into how the land is used and managed.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill does not involve corporate profit or shareholder gains; it transfers federal land to a tribe and bans casino-style gaming.

local_say.reason: Sec. 3 moves land from federal forest management into federal trust status for a tribe, which removes the land from the national forest planning and public-land decision processes that local residents and the public currently take part in, though the bill does not itself create a local approval step.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no bailout or ratepayer provisions; the material states no cost or funding amount.

equality.reason: The bill applies to one specific tribe and parcel, and it is a land transfer to a sovereign tribe rather than a difference in treatment of individuals under the law; effects on equality are unclear.

justice.reason: The bill sets a survey deadline and preserves valid existing rights, but it creates no new remedies or accountability mechanisms, so its effect on legal fairness is unclear.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not change what individuals may do on the land in a clear way; it bans gaming on the land but does not otherwise restrict personal choices, and the public-use effects are not described.

news.overall: Evidence is limited: each group is represented by one headline with no article description, so conclusions are tentative. The Lean Left headline frames the bill as a Democratic move to restrict data centers on public lands, while the Lean Right headline frames the issue as public demand for input on data centers without naming the bill. Neither piece shows how the outlet views the bill's land transfer provisions, so a fuller comparison would need article text.

label: H.R. 5254
title: Gateway Partnership Act
short_title: Gateway Partnership Act
one: Lets the National Park Service sign a one-time, up-to-five-year deal with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events at Gateway Arch National Park and its buildings, with fees to cover costs and a required report to Congress.
summary:
This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior, who oversees the National Park Service, make a single agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation. The Foundation is a nonprofit that serves as the park's official philanthropic partner. The agreement could last up to five years. It would let the Foundation host private events, such as receptions, at Gateway Arch National Park in St. Louis. Events could use buildings such as the Arch Visitor Center and the Old Courthouse.

The agreement must set dates and times when the Foundation can be the only group holding a special event in certain buildings. It must also cap the number of events per month and set the National Park Service staffing needed for safety and resource protection. The Foundation must carry liability insurance that names the United States as an additional insured. The agreement must also say the federal government and its employees are not liable for injuries or deaths from the Foundation's use of the buildings.

Events must fit the park's purposes and must not harm its appearance or block public access. The Park Service must charge a fee for wear and tear. It may also recover its other costs, including utilities, security, and staff time. The authority ends seven years after enactment. Within four years, the Secretary must report to Congress on visitor access, security, staffing, and finances.
does: Allows one agreement of up to five years between the Interior Secretary and the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events at the park.
Requires the agreement to set exclusive-use dates and times, a monthly cap on events, and Park Service staffing levels for safety.
Requires liability insurance that lists the United States as additionally insured.
Requires a clause saying the federal government and its employees are not liable for injuries or deaths from the Foundation's use of the buildings.
Bars events that harm the park's integrity or appearance, or that block or disrupt public access.
Requires a fee for wear and tear and lets the Park Service recover all event-related costs.
Keeps the Park Service's ability to host its own events and issue other permits.

Gateway Partnership Act
This bill authorizes the National Park Service (NPS) to enter into a one-time agreement with the Gateway Arch Park Foundation to host private events at the Gateway Arch National Park and its buildings for a period of up to five years. label: H.R. 7834
title: Safe Cloud Storage Act
short_title: Safe Cloud Storage Act
one: Protects cloud companies hired by law enforcement to store child sexual abuse material as evidence from most lawsuits and criminal charges, as long as they meet strict security, reporting, and U.S.-storage rules.
summary: Police and prosecutors investigating child sexual exploitation often need to store huge amounts of illegal images and videos as evidence. Current law protects companies that store this material for the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, but not companies hired directly by law enforcement. This bill closes that gap. A cloud company hired by a federal, state, tribal, or local law enforcement or prosecution agency to store this material, make it available on request, and provide technical and forensic support becomes an "approved vendor." Approved vendors cannot be sued or criminally charged over that work. That protection ends if the vendor acted with intentional misconduct, negligence, actual malice, reckless disregard, or for a purpose unrelated to its contract duties. To qualify, vendors must follow federal cybersecurity standards, use end-to-end encryption, limit and log employee access, get an independent audit every year, fix problems the audit finds, and keep the data in the U.S. unless the agency approves a transfer for an investigation. Vendors must notify the Justice Department within 30 days of signing a contract, and must report contract breaches, such as non-payment, and keep preserving the evidence until it is lawfully transferred. Agencies must keep the evidence under FBI security policy and retain it for required periods. The bill does not limit lawful investigative use of the material or victims' rights, and it does not authorize audits of government systems.
does: Creates a new section 202 in the PROTECT Our Children Act of 2008 covering storage of child pornography, child obscenity, and intimate images of minors (including digital forgeries) by law enforcement contractors.

Defines an 'approved vendor' as a cloud service provider that meets the security requirements and is contracted by a federal, state, tribal, or local law enforcement or prosecutorial agency to store the material, make it available on request, and give maintenance, technical, and forensic support.
Bars civil claims and criminal charges in federal or state court against an approved vendor for work under its contract.

Keeps liability in place if the vendor engaged in intentional misconduct or negligent conduct, acted with actual malice or reckless disregard of a substantial risk of injury, or acted for a purpose unrelated to its contract duties.

Requires vendors to follow the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, access the material only with agency consent and for support purposes, minimize and log employee access, use end-to-end encryption, undergo an independent annual audit (assessing NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5), and promptly fix audit findings.

Requires agencies to store evidence in line with the FBI Criminal Justice Information Services security policy and keep it for the period required by applicable law or policy, or at least the statute of limitations or sentence length including post-conviction review.
Requires data to stay in the U.S. unless the contracting agency expressly consents to a transfer it deems necessary for investigation.

Requires vendors to file a notification letter with DOJ's Criminal Division within 30 days of a contract, and to report agency non-payment, material breach, or termination without lawful evidence transfer within 30 days, while continuing to preserve the evidence until lawful transfer.

Rule of construction: does not limit lawful agency use of the material, agencies' legal and court obligations or victim requests under 18 U.S.C. 3509(m)(3), and does not authorize audits of government entities or systems.

Federal, state, tribal, and local police and prosecutors

Investigators and prosecutors of online child exploitation
The Department of Justice Criminal Division and state attorneys general

Carve-outs for negligence, malice, and reckless conduct keep vendors accountable for bad behavior.
Vendors must keep preserving evidence even if an agency stops paying, which helps protect cases.

Vendor protections apply to a wide range of agencies, and oversight depends on DOJ and state attorneys general.

Total cost to agencies and vendors.
Whether audit results will be shared with the public or Congress.
How strongly DOJ will oversee compliance and the notification letters.
How the bill's 'digital forgery' coverage will be applied to AI-generated images.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to protect cloud vendors hired by law enforcement agencies from civil and criminal liability when they store, maintain, and process child sexual abuse material as evidence in investigations of online child sexual exploitation. The bill's stated aim is to extend to these contractors the liability protections that already cover vendors working directly with the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, while requiring cybersecurity and evidence-storage standards.

Audit results are not required to be made public, and the bill does not authorize audits of government systems, so outside parties may have limited ability to verify that security rules are being followed.

The bill sets strong security rules, including NIST-based cybersecurity standards, end-to-end encryption, limited and logged employee access, and an independent audit every year, which can help protect victims from further exposure.

crs:
Safe Cloud Storage Act
This bill limits the civil and criminal liability of vendors that contract with law enforcement agencies to provide digital storage services (e.g., cloud-based storage) for storing, maintaining, and processing child sexual abuse material (CSAM) in investigations of online child sexual exploitation.
Under current law, the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) receives reports of online child sexual exploitation via its CyberTipline, evaluates and prioritizes the reports, and refers the reports to law enforcement agencies to investigate. Currently, federal law limits the liability of vendors that contract directly with the NCMEC to store and transfer CSAM. However, federal law does not limit the liability of vendors that contract with law enforcement agencies to assist in investigations.
This bill establishes liability protections for vendors that contract with federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies to store, maintain, and process CSAM in investigations of online child sexual exploitation. Specifically, the bill prohibits a civil claim or criminal charge in federal or state court against such a vendor, so long as the vendor has not engaged in intentional misconduct or negligent conduct, acted with malice or reckless disregard, or acted for a purpose unrelated to its contractual duties.
The bill requires vendors to comply with cybersecurity requirements for CSAM that is stored, maintained, or processed. The bill also requires vendors to comply with storage requirements for CSAM that is retained as evidence.

environment.reason: The bill concerns storage of evidence in cloud systems and does not address water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Audit results are not required to be public (possible concerns) and the bill does not authorize audits of government systems, which limits public visibility into how evidence is stored; the bill also protects victims' data from exposure through encryption and limited access (Sec. 202 security requirements), which partly offsets this.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 202 shields private cloud vendors from civil suits and criminal charges for their contract work, which reduces the financial exposure of companies and shifts the risk of harm onto those affected by data handling failures.

local_say.reason: The bill sets federal rules for vendors and does not change how state or local communities make land-use, facility, or permit decisions; the vendor contracting remains with agencies.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill creates no spending or appropriation and does not transfer corporate losses to taxpayers; vendor costs for audits are borne by vendors or passed to agencies through contracts, which is not a bailout or ratepayer tax break in itself.

equality.reason: The liability shield applies to all approved vendors on the same terms and does not treat groups of people differently under the law.

justice.reason: Sec. 202 bars civil claims and criminal charges against approved vendors, which limits victims' remedies for data-handling harm; the negligence and misconduct carve-outs preserve some accountability, so the score is not more severe.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill regulates vendors and agencies handling evidence and does not expand or restrict what individuals may legally do with their own lives.

news.overall: Coverage provided is thin: two Lean Left headlines and four Center headlines, with no article text beyond short fragments, so the evidence for each group is limited. Neither group's headlines directly describe the Safe Cloud Storage Act itself, so framing of the bill is inferred only loosely from related topics like data preservation, AI liability, hacking, and online safety. The Deseret News sentencing story appears unrelated to the bill's subject and offers little framing signal.

label: H.R. 8454
title: To provide for the transfer of administrative jurisdiction over certain Federal land in the State of California, and for other purposes.
short_title: Ackerson Meadow Land Swap (Yosemite / Stanislaus)
one: Swaps management of about 160 acres of Forest Service land (to Yosemite National Park) and about 170 acres of Park Service land (to Stanislaus National Forest) at Ackerson Meadow in Tuolumne County, California.
summary:
This bill trades management of two small pieces of federal land near Ackerson Meadow in California. About 160 acres now run by the Forest Service as part of Stanislaus National Forest would move to the Department of the Interior and become part of Yosemite National Park. About 170 acres now run by the National Park Service would move to the Department of Agriculture and become part of Stanislaus National Forest. The land stays public. Only the agency in charge changes.

According to the Congressional Research Service, cattle graze on the parcel now managed by the Park Service. Grazing happens mostly on Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management land. The Forest Service uses a "multiple-use" approach that fits with grazing. So the swap would let that land be managed under rules that allow it.

The bill lets the two agencies make minor fixes and survey corrections by mutual agreement. Those fixes take effect when a notice is published in the Federal Register, the government's public journal. The bill says it does not erase valid existing rights, permits, leases, easements or similar authorizations. The new managing agency would take over administering them. The bill does not mention money. It passed the House on September 14, 2026, and the Senate passed it without changes by unanimous consent on November 17, 2026.

label: H.R. 1520
title: Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act
short_title: Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act
one: Bans hospitals, transplant programs and the national organ network from denying organ transplants or related care because of a disability, unless an individualized assessment finds the disability medically relevant, and requires reasonable accommodations.
summary: This bill would make it illegal for organ transplant programs and related health providers to turn someone away from a transplant just because they have a physical or mental disability. It covers any program that gets federal money and any public entity covered by the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Protected steps include being found eligible, being referred to a transplant center, being put on the waiting list, and receiving the transplant and follow-up care. A provider may still consider a disability, but only after an individualized assessment, in line with existing disability-rights rules. If a person could follow post-transplant health requirements with reasonable changes or support, such as aids, services or "supported decision-making" (help from trusted people in making choices), then their inability to do so alone cannot be held against them. Providers must make reasonable changes to policies unless doing so would fundamentally change the program, and must supply aids and services unless that would be an undue burden. The bill also changes the law governing the national organ network (OPTN) so its medical criteria for allocating organs cannot discriminate based on disability. People who face discrimination can complain to the Office for Civil Rights at the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which must consider fast or early resolution and may require a remedy. HHS must report to Congress each year on complaints, results and the resources needed. The bill keeps existing rights under the ADA, Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, and state laws, and does not change health-privacy rules. The bill passed the Senate with an amendment on Nov. 19, 2026, and goes back to the House.
does: Defines key terms by reference to existing disability law, including 'covered entity' (programs receiving federal funds that involve transplants, and public entities under ADA Title II), 'related services' (evaluation, waiting-list listing, counseling, treatment, postoperative care, information, and other physician-recommended services).

Amends the Public Health Service Act so the national organ network (OPTN) cannot use medical criteria for allocating organs that discriminate on the basis of disability, and keeps a public comment opportunity on those criteria.

Bars covered entities from finding a qualified person with a disability ineligible, denying a transplant or related services, refusing to refer them to a transplant center or specialist, or refusing to put them on waiting lists because of disability.
Allows disability to be taken into account only after an individualized assessment, consistent with the ADA, Section 504 and 45 CFR 84.56.
Says a person's inability to independently follow post-transplant requirements cannot be counted against them if reasonable modifications or auxiliary aids and services would let them comply.

Requires reasonable modifications to policies (which may include supported decision-making) unless they would fundamentally alter the program, and requires auxiliary aids and services unless doing so would fundamentally alter the program or be an undue burden.
Leaves existing federal health-privacy, security and substance-use-record confidentiality rules unchanged.
Directs HHS's Office for Civil Rights to consider complaints for expedited or early resolution and allows it to require remedies consistent with Section 504 and ADA enforcement.
Requires an HHS report to Congress within one year and annually after, covering complaint counts, process, results, resources needed, and recommendations to improve enforcement.
States that the Act does not limit rights or remedies under the ADA, Section 504, or other federal or state laws giving additional protection.

Provides a federal complaint route with possible fast resolution.
Annual public reporting to Congress improves oversight.
Does not weaken existing ADA, Section 504 or state protections.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to prohibit health care providers and organ-matching entities from denying or restricting access to organ transplants solely because of an individual's disability. It aims to make transplants and related care more available to people with disabilities, and to give them a federal complaint route through HHS's Office for Civil Rights.

oppose: The bill allows disability to be considered in transplant decisions only after an individualized physician assessment, but the 'individualized assessment' exception and the 'undue burden' and 'fundamentally alter' limits leave room for disputes over how they are applied.

Organs are scarce, so you could ask how the bill would affect fairness among patients already waiting, and whether medical criteria for allocating organs should stay with medical experts.
support: The bill would bar transplant programs from turning someone away solely because of a physical or mental disability, covering evaluation, waiting-list placement, the transplant itself, and follow-up care.

crs:
Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act
This bill expressly prohibits health care providers and other entities involved in matching donated organs with recipients from denying or restricting an individual's access to organ transplants solely on the basis of the individual's disability, except in limited circumstances.
Specifically, these entities may consider an individual's disability when making decisions about transplants only if a physician finds, based on an individualized evaluation, that the individual's physical or mental disability is medically significant to the provision of the transplant. A disability shall not be considered medically significant if the individual has an adequate support system in place to comply with transplant-related medical requirements.
These entities must also make reasonable changes to their policies to make transplants and related care more available to individuals with disabilities.
Aggrieved individuals may bring claims of discrimination to the Office of Civil Rights of the Department of Health and Human Services. The bill provides for expedited resolutions of these claims.
In addition, the board of directors of the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network may not issue policies that prohibit or hinder access to an organ transplant based solely on the individual's disability. This network is a public-private partnership linking professionals involved in the U.S. organ donation and transplantation system.

transparency_kindness.reason: Requires HHS to report to Congress annually on complaint counts, results and resources, and OPTN must keep a public comment opportunity on allocation criteria; the bill also bars disability-based denials of transplant care, which is humane treatment of people.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill regulates transplant providers and the OPTN on access for people with disabilities; it does not shift costs or favor corporate profit margins in a clear way, and compliance costs are not specified in the text.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no bailout or ratepayer provisions; no cost-shifting mechanism is described in the text.

equality.reason: Sec. (bars finding a qualified person with a disability ineligible or denying transplant, referral, or waiting-list access because of disability) gives people with disabilities equal access to transplant evaluation and care, and the OPTN criteria cannot discriminate on disability.

justice.reason: Creates a federal complaint route at HHS OCR with expedited resolution and authority to require remedies, plus a reporting requirement, though the bill does not create a direct private right to sue.

personal_freedom.reason: Protects an individual's ability to choose a transplant and related services without disability-based denial, and allows supported decision-making to count toward compliance, expanding what people can choose about their own medical care.

news.overall: None of the eight headlines names the Charlotte Woodward Organ Transplant Discrimination Prevention Act or describes its provisions, so the evidence on how this bill is framed is very limited. The Lean Left headlines concern broader health policy fights and a workplace discrimination suit, while the two Center headlines are unrelated to transplant policy. Based on these headlines alone, no group's coverage can be characterized as taking a position on the bill itself.

label: H.R. 2478
title: Financial Exploitation Prevention Act of 2025
short_title: Financial Exploitation Prevention Act of 2025
one: Lets mutual funds and their transfer agents temporarily hold back withdrawals when they reasonably suspect someone 65+ or an impaired adult is being financially exploited, and asks the SEC for recommendations.
summary: This bill changes the Investment Company Act of 1940 to give mutual funds (open-end investment companies) and the transfer agents that serve them a new tool against elder financial abuse. If a fund or agent reasonably believes a withdrawal (redemption) by a "specified adult" is tied to financial exploitation, it may delay payment beyond the usual seven days. A specified adult is anyone 65 or older, or anyone 18 or older the company reasonably believes has a mental or physical impairment that keeps them from protecting their own interests. The first delay can last up to 15 business days. If the company finds exploitation likely, it can add 10 more business days, but it must tell the account holder's trusted contact in writing within two days (unless that contact is suspected of the abuse), start an internal review, and keep the money in a demand deposit account. State regulators, agencies or courts can extend the hold further. Participation is voluntary: a fund and transfer agent opt in by notifying the SEC. Those that opt in must ask account holders for a trusted adult contact, keep that information, and tell customers in writing that the contact may be reached. Funds must set internal procedures, name employees with authority to delay, disclose the policy in their prospectus, and keep records for the SEC. Within one year, the SEC must report to Congress on further regulatory or legislative changes, after consulting other financial regulators.

who: see items

benefits: May stop or slow theft from seniors and impaired adults before money is gone.
Trusted-contact system lets firms reach a family member or other person if something looks wrong.
Records, internal reviews, and prospectus disclosure add accountability.
SEC report may lead to better protections later.
concerns: Account holders could be unable to reach their own money for up to 25 business days or longer if a regulator or court extends it, even when no abuse occurred.
The 'reasonable belief' standard is subjective, and the 65+ age line could lead to age-based treatment of capable seniors.
Participation is voluntary, so protection will vary by fund.
No explicit appeal process for the account holder is stated, and notice goes only to the named contacts, not necessarily the holder, in the extension step.
Held money sits in a demand deposit account; the text does not say who bears any loss or earns interest.
imp.cost: No spending or appropriation is in the bill. Funds and transfer agents would bear compliance costs if they opt in, and the SEC would bear the cost of the report and reviewing records. No cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: How many funds and transfer agents will opt in.
Whether the text gives legal immunity to firms that delay; none is stated in the text provided.
How the SEC will oversee the use of holds and what its report will recommend.
Whether account holders will be told directly of a hold and how they can challenge it.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give mutual funds and their transfer agents a way to pause certain withdrawals when they reasonably believe an older adult (65 or older) or an impaired adult (18 or older) is being financially exploited. It aims to stop or slow theft before the money is gone. It also directs the SEC to report recommendations on addressing financial exploitation of these adults.

oppose: The 'reasonable belief' standard is subjective, and the bill does not spell out a clear test for when a firm must act. Critics could argue this gives firms broad discretion over customers' own money.
The 65-and-older line could lead to age-based treatment of capable seniors. Some people may be delayed from accessing their funds even when no abuse is occurring.
Account holders could be unable to reach their money for up to 25 business days, or longer if a state regulator, agency, or court extends the hold, even if no exploitation took place.

The bill does not state an explicit appeal process for the account holder, and in the extension step notice goes to named contacts rather than necessarily the holder. Some constituents may want stronger protections for the account holder's rights.
support: The bill gives mutual funds and transfer agents a tool to pause a suspicious withdrawal before money is gone, which may help stop or slow theft from seniors and impaired adults.
A trusted-contact system lets firms reach a family member or another named person if something looks wrong, adding a safety check beyond the account holder alone.
The bill adds accountability through required internal review procedures, recordkeeping for the SEC, and disclosure in the fund's prospectus.
The bill requires the SEC to report to Congress with recommendations within one year, which could lead to stronger protections later.

crs:
Financial Exploitation Prevention Act of 2025
This bill establishes procedures for delaying the redemption of certain securities if an investment company or agent believes that an older individual or an individual with certain impairments has been financially exploited.
Specifically, the bill allows for the delay of the redemption of a security issued by an open-end investment management company and serviced by a transfer agent if the company or agent reasonably believes the redemption involves the financial exploitation of an individual (1) age 65 or older, or (2) age 18 or older who is unable to protect his or her own interests due to a mental or physical impairment. (Open-end investment management companies offer securities in pooled investment vehicles such as mutual funds. Transfer agents facilitate certain transactions for corporations and investment companies, including dividend distribution and change of securities ownership.)
The company may initially delay the redemption for up to 15 days and, upon making a determination of exploitation, may delay the redemption an additional 10 days. A state regulator, appropriate administrative agency, or court may extend this period. In the event of delay, the company must hold the amounts related to the redemption in a demand deposit account. The bill also establishes notification requirements. 
The bill requires the registered open-end investment company and transfer agent to notify the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) if they elect to comply with the procedures established under this bill. 
Additionally, the SEC must make recommendations to address the financial exploitation of these adults.

environment.reason: The bill concerns mutual fund redemptions and elder financial abuse; it does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on trusted contacts requires firms to tell customers in writing that the contact may be reached, and to disclose the policy in the prospectus, while the SEC must report to Congress; however, the extension step may notify only named contacts rather than the holder, which limits transparency to the account holder.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill lets funds and agents delay withdrawals to protect people from exploitation, though it also imposes compliance costs on firms and the held money's interest and loss treatment is unaddressed.

local_say.reason: The bill sets federal SEC-level procedures and does not give states or communities a new role in decisions, although state regulators may extend holds, which is a small state role.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill involves no taxpayer bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks; it creates no spending or appropriation.

equality.reason: Sec. defining 'specified adult' applies the withdrawal delay based on age 65 or older or impairment, so account holders in those groups face different treatment than other holders, though the stated purpose is protection.

justice.reason: Sec. on delayed redemption allows up to 25 or more business days of hold without a stated appeal process for the account holder, and the extension step may not notify the holder, reducing due process and remedies.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. on delay authority lets firms restrict an account holder's access to their own money for up to 15 business days, extendable further, based on a subjective belief, which restricts what these individuals may choose to do with their funds.

label: H.R. 4624
title: Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act of 2026
short_title: Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act of 2026
one: The bill lets private "unified boxing organizations" run boxing leagues under federal rules and raises health, safety, drug-testing, insurance and minimum-pay standards for professional boxers.
summary:
This bill changes the Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996. It creates a new kind of private group called a "unified boxing organization" (UBO). A UBO is a league-style company that signs boxers to contracts, runs matches under one set of rules, and sets up title belts. A boxer can choose to take part in this system instead of the older promoter-based one. UBOs still have to follow state or tribal boxing commissions.

A UBO must meet extra safety rules. It must provide a second ambulance and a second ringside doctor at each match. It must require extra brain-health exams after a knockout. Boxers age 40 or older need a supplemental exam, which includes a chest X-ray, blood panel and urinalysis. A UBO must also run an anti-doping program. An independent third party must test both boxers in at least half of its matches, and no-notice testing is allowed. Boxers get notice, a chance to defend themselves, review by an impartial decision-maker, and an appeal before they are penalized. Each UBO must also give boxers access to training and rehab facilities, injury insurance during training, and a medical coordinator.

The bill sets rules for contracts. A UBO contract can last no more than 4 years, or 3 years for a boxer's first deal. A boxer can talk to other promoters during the last 90 days. Boxers must be paid at least $200 per scheduled round. The UBO must offer at least 2 matches a year or pay a minimum guarantee. The contract-length and negotiation protections also apply to ordinary promoter contracts. A UBO cannot manage boxers, take payments tied to rankings, or pay boxing commission officials. Betting on matches and sharing inside information for betting are banned. UBOs must give boxers itemized pay statements. They must file basic information, and rating details, with the Federal Trade Commission or post it on a public website.

For all professional boxing, not just UBOs, the bill requires a fuller set of medical exams. These include an eye exam, heart tests, brain scans (MRI and MRA for boxers 40 and over), infectious disease tests, and a pregnancy test for women. Ringside doctors must hold a certification after 2 years. The minimum health insurance is $50,000 for injuries and $15,000 for accidental death, and boxers do not pay the premium. Promoters and UBOs must pay at least $200 per round. State commissions must set up drug testing for title matches and random testing for other matches.

A UBO officer or employee who knowingly violates the rules could face up to 1 year in prison and a $100,000 fine. The fine rises for matches with revenue over $2 million. The rules take effect on enactment and apply to matches starting 240 days later. Groups that show good-faith progress can get up to 1 more year to comply.
does: Defines a 'unified boxing organization' (UBO) as a private league or association that organizes matches between boxers under contract with it, under unified rules, with a title-belt system. It may use titles and rankings from independent groups.

Treats a UBO as compliant with the federal boxing law if it meets the basic safety rules plus new conditions. Matches must still happen under state or tribal boxing commissions, and states can add stricter rules.
Requires UBOs to provide one extra ambulance and one extra licensed ringside physician at each match. It also requires extra brain-health exams after a knockout before a boxer can fight again.
Requires a supplemental fitness exam each year for boxers 40 or older. It includes a urinalysis and blood panel, plus a chest X-ray at least every 6 years.
Requires UBOs to provide training and rehab access at reasonable cost, insurance for training injuries, and a medical coordinator for each boxer.

Requires a UBO anti-doping program. An independent third party tests both boxers in at least half of matches, no-notice testing is allowed, and a public annual list of tested substances and penalties is required. Boxers get notice, a chance to defend themselves, impartial review and an appeal.

Sets contract rules. Contracts are capped at 4 years, or 3 years for a first deal. Boxers can talk to others in the final 90 days. Pay is at least $200 per scheduled round. UBOs must offer 2 matches a year or pay a guarantee of 10 times the per-round minimum. The cap and negotiation protections also apply to promoter contracts.

Bans betting on matches and sharing inside information to help bets. It bars UBOs from managing boxers, taking ranking-related payments, or paying or contracting with boxing commission officials. It requires itemized pay disclosures to boxers.

Requires UBOs to file basic company information and annual ratings information with the FTC and the Association of Boxing Commissions, or post it on a free public website. The FTC may charge a fee. Independent ratings groups tied financially to a UBO must also file.

Expands the baseline rules for all professional boxing. They add required exams (physical with blood work, eye, heart, infectious disease, brain imaging or neurological exam, pregnancy test) and require certified ringside physicians after 2 years. Boxers do not pay insurance premiums. The minimum coverage is $50,000 for injuries and $15,000 for accidental death.
Sets a $200-per-round minimum pay for every boxer in any match run by a promoter or UBO.

Requires state boxing commissions to set up drug-testing procedures for title matches and random testing for other matches. It lets commissions accept independent testing or medical procedures that meet or exceed the rules. Independent sanctioning bodies may nominate judges and referees for title fights, but commissions need not accept them.

Allows UBOs to pay independent sanctioning organizations fees and to hire third parties for administrative work. Financial terms are excluded from any required disclosure. Payments directly to those groups' officers or employees are barred.
Sets criminal penalties of up to 1 year in prison and a $100,000 fine for UBO officers or employees who knowingly violate the rules. Fines rise in proportion to revenue over $2 million.
Takes effect on enactment and applies to matches 240 days later. Groups making good-faith progress may get up to 1 more year. It also updates a citation to a tribal law.
who: Professional boxers, especially older boxers, women boxers, and those early in their careers
Boxing promoters and any new unified boxing organizations
State and tribal boxing commissions
Ringside physicians and medical providers
Sanctioning bodies such as the WBC
Federal Trade Commission and the Association of Boxing Commissions
Boxing fans and event venues
Insurers that cover boxing injuries

benefits: More thorough medical screening, including brain imaging, may catch dangerous conditions earlier.
Extra ambulances and ringside doctors could improve emergency response.
Boxers would get a $200-per-round minimum, and insurance premiums would not be charged to them.
Contract caps, the 90-day talk window, and the ban on manager conflicts and ranking payments may reduce exploitation.
Public filings and itemized pay statements add transparency.
Drug-test penalties require notice, a defense, impartial review and an appeal.
Anti-betting rules protect the integrity of matches.
concerns: UBOs are private groups that get a separate compliance path, and critics might see that as weakening oversight of existing promoters.
UBOs must test in only half of matches, and no-notice testing is optional.
Boxers still pay the deductible on health insurance.
The $50,000 injury coverage might not cover serious injuries.
Financial terms of agreements with third parties are excluded from required disclosure.
Higher costs could discourage small promoters or fewer events, and boxers might lose fights.
Brain exams and imaging could be costly and hard to access in some places.
imp.cost: No federal spending is specified. UBOs must pay for the extra safety conditions, with the boxer paying only the insurance deductible. The FTC may charge fees to cover the cost of processing filings. Compliance costs for promoters and state commissions are not estimated in the material provided.
unknowns: How many UBOs will form, and whether they'll attract boxers.
How much extra compliance work falls on state and tribal commissions without new federal funding.
Whether the insurance minimums are enough for serious injuries.
How the FTC will use or enforce the filings.
Whether the final House vote will match the Senate version. The latest action is a Senate message sent to the House.
