purpose: The bill says its goal is to revive American professional boxing by creating a new kind of private, league-style group called a "unified boxing organization" (UBO) that can sign boxers, run matches under one set of rules, and offer title belts, while adding new safety, health, contract, and transparency rules for boxing. It also expands baseline medical, insurance, and minimum-pay rules for all professional boxers under the Professional Boxing Safety Act of 1996.

oppose: The bill creates a separate compliance path for private UBOs. A constituent could ask whether this weakens oversight of existing promoters, which already operate under the 1996 Professional Boxing Safety Act.
Drug testing for UBOs applies to at least half of matches, and no-notice testing is allowed but not required. A constituent could ask why testing is not required for every match.
Boxers still pay the deductible on health insurance, and the required $50,000 injury coverage may not fully cover serious injuries. A constituent could ask whether these minimums are high enough.
support: The bill adds stronger medical screening for all professional boxers, including eye, heart, infectious disease, and brain imaging exams, which could catch dangerous conditions earlier. A constituent could ask the member to support these added protections.

UBOs must provide an extra ambulance and an extra ringside physician at each match, and boxers would get a $200-per-round minimum pay with insurance premiums not charged to them. A constituent could say these changes protect fighters' safety and pay.

The bill adds contract limits, a 90-day window to talk with other promoters, itemized pay statements, and bans on betting and conflicts of interest. A constituent could say these rules add transparency and may reduce exploitation of boxers.

cost_flag: No federal spending is specified. UBOs must pay for the extra safety conditions, with the boxer paying only the insurance deductible. The FTC may charge fees to cover the cost of processing filings. Compliance costs for promoters and state commissions are not estimated in the material provided.
crs:
Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act of 2026
This bill authorizes the establishment of private-sector Unified Boxing Organizations (UBOs) and otherwise expands the regulatory framework for professional boxing. (See 
CRS Report IF12982
 for an overview of the federal regulation of professional boxing in the United States.)
Under the bill, UBOs may organize matches involving boxers contracted with the UBO and must comply with other regulations with respect to such matches (e.g., conduct matches under the authority of a state boxing commission). UBOs also operate alongside existing professional boxing organizations (e.g., World Boxing Council (WBC)).
UBOs must meet certain additional requirements, for example
the UBO must implement an anti-doping program that includes drug testing in advance of matches,
boxers age 40 or older must receive supplemental physical examinations,
each match must have at least two ambulances on site, and
boxers must have access to equipment and facilities that are operated by the UBO for training and rehabilitation.
The bill also expands the required health insurance coverage and minimum pay for all professional boxers.
Further, the bill requires state boxing commissions to establish procedures to ensure that drug tests are administered for title matches and at random for all other matches.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on UBO filings requires basic company information and annual ratings details to be filed with the FTC and ABC or posted publicly, and itemized pay statements go to boxers; however, financial terms of third-party sanctioning arrangements are excluded from required disclosure, which limits openness.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. on minimum pay of $200 per scheduled round, the 4-year contract cap with a 3-year first-deal limit, the 90-day negotiation window, and the ban on UBO ranking-related payments favor boxers' pay and bargaining position; however, boxers still pay insurance deductibles and UBOs bear compliance costs that may be passed on to consumers or reduce events.

local_say.reason: Matches still must be held under state or tribal commissions, which keep their authority and may add stricter rules, but commissions may decline sanctioning-body nominees and the bill does not clearly expand local input on decisions.

justice.reason: Sec. on anti-doping penalties requires notice, a chance to defend, impartial review and an appeal, and criminal penalties apply to knowing violations by UBO officers; however, UBOs get a separate compliance path and the injury coverage remains capped at $50,000.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill adds some restrictions on UBOs and betting while allowing boxers to choose the UBO system instead of promoters, and these effects roughly offset.

news.overall: None of the provided headlines directly covers the Muhammad Ali American Boxing Revival Act, so this analysis can only describe adjacent coverage. The Center group has the most related material, but it is mostly about college sports legislation and a boxing film, and the Lean Left and Lean Right groups each have headlines on unrelated topics (sports betting, CTE research, MLB labor). Because the evidence is thin and off-topic across all three groups, it cannot show how each perspective frames the bill itself; coverage specifically about the bill would be needed for a meaningful comparison.

label: H.R. 9496
title: End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
short_title: End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
one: The bill pauses tax deadlines, penalties and interest for Americans held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad (and their spouses) and sets up refunds for penalties charged since 2021.
summary:
This bill changes the tax code so Americans who are held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad don't get punished by the IRS for missing tax deadlines while they are held. The time they are detained does not count when figuring out filing and payment deadlines, refund or credit claims, or when the IRS can assess and collect more tax. Penalties and interest that would normally build up during that time stop. The same relief applies to their spouses.

To work, the State Department (for people found to be wrongfully detained) and the Justice Department's Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell (for hostages) must give the Treasury lists of qualifying people each year, starting by January 1, 2027. The Treasury must update its computer systems so collection activity and penalty buildup are paused for these people.

If a person was already charged penalties or interest and is later identified as a hostage or wrongfully detained, the IRS must cancel them and refund anything collected. The bill also creates a program, due by January 1, 2027, for refunds of penalties and interest paid for tax years ending from January 1, 2021 until the bill becomes law. Those people, their spouses or dependents can apply. The IRS must notify those identified within 90 days of enactment or release, and the usual refund time limits are extended. Interest on overpayments is not affected by the pause. The bill's text does not give a cost estimate.
does: Adds a new tax code section (7511) that ignores the time a U.S. national is unlawfully or wrongfully detained or held hostage abroad when judging tax filing and payment deadlines, refund and credit claims, and penalty and interest amounts.
Extends the same relief to the spouse of a qualifying individual.
Defines qualifying people as U.S. nationals found wrongfully detained under the Levinson Act (State Department determination) or held hostage under findings of the Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell.
Requires the State Department and the Attorney General (through the Fusion Cell) to send the Treasury annual lists of qualifying people, starting by January 1, 2027.
Says the pause does not apply to interest on overpayments, and limits some interest rules on timely returns.
Requires Treasury to update its databases so statute-of-limitations dates, interest and penalty buildup, and collection actions are suspended for these people.
Requires abatement (cancellation) and refund of penalties and interest assessed or collected for tax years ending during detention once a person is identified as qualifying.

Creates, by January 1, 2027, a program letting eligible individuals, spouses or dependents claim refunds of penalties and interest paid for periods from January 1, 2021 to enactment, with notice to people within 90 days and extended refund deadlines.
The forward-looking rules apply to tax years ending after enactment; the refund program applies to tax years ending on or before enactment.
who: U.S. nationals held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad, and their spouses and dependents
Internal Revenue Service and Treasury Department, which must build systems and a refund program
State Department and Justice Department (Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell), which must compile lists
Federal taxpayers generally, through small lost revenue from abated penalties

benefits: Stops penalties and interest from piling up on people who cannot deal with taxes while detained.
Refunds past penalties paid since 2021, easing hardship for families.
Requires notice to eligible people so they don't have to find the program on their own.
Spouses and dependents are covered.
concerns: Eligibility depends on government determinations, so people not formally recognized as wrongfully detained or hostages may be left out.
The refund program only covers 2021 onward, so earlier cases are not covered.
The IRS and agencies take on new work and system changes with tight deadlines.
imp.cost: No cost estimate is given in the text. Costs would likely come from forgone penalties and interest and agency administration, probably small given the number of people affected.
unknowns: How many people would qualify and how much revenue would be forgone.
Whether the agencies get extra funding to run the program.
How quickly the State and Justice lists will be produced and how disputes over eligibility are handled.
Exact final status: metadata says it passed both chambers, with a Senate message sent to the House, so any amendments are unclear.

stage.last_action: Message on Senate action sent to the House.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep Americans who are held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad from being penalized by the IRS for missing tax deadlines while they are detained. It would pause the running of certain tax deadlines, penalties, and interest during detention, extend that relief to their spouses, and create a refund program for penalties and interest already paid for tax years from 2021 until enactment.

oppose: Eligibility depends on formal government determinations (a State Department finding under the Levinson Act or a Hostage Recovery Fusion Cell finding), so some people who were detained or held could be left out if they are not formally recognized.
The refund program covers only tax years ending from January 1, 2021 onward, so earlier cases would not be eligible for refunds under this bill.

The bill gives the IRS and the State and Justice Departments new reporting, system-update, and notice tasks with tight deadlines, such as lists due by January 1, 2027, and notices within 90 days, which may strain agency resources. The bill text does not include a cost estimate.
support: The bill stops penalties and interest from building up on Americans who cannot manage their taxes while they are held hostage or wrongfully detained abroad.
The bill refunds penalties and interest already paid since 2021, which could ease financial hardship for detainees' families.
The bill requires the IRS to notify eligible people, so they do not have to find out about the program on their own, and it covers spouses and dependents too.

crs:
End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act
This bill extends certain federal tax deadlines for U.S. nationals who are unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or held hostage abroad and their spouses. The bill also allows for an abatement and refund of additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed to such individuals for failing to meet a federal tax deadline during a period of detention.
Specifically, under the bill, the time period during which a U.S. national is unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or held hostage abroad is disregarded in determining certain federal tax deadlines, including deadlines for
filing a return for and paying federal income, estate, gift, employment, or excise taxes;
a tax credit or refund claim; and
the determination, assessment, and collection of additional taxes, interest, or penalties.
The bill requires the Department of State and the Department of Justice to annually provide the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) with lists to identify U.S. nationals who qualify for an extension.
The bill also requires the IRS to (1) abate and refund additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed for any tax year ending during a period of detention for which an extension of a federal tax deadline is permitted; and (2) establish a program allowing U.S. nationals unlawfully or wrongfully detained abroad or taken hostage abroad (or their spouse or dependent) to claim a refund of additional taxes, interest, and penalties assessed for any tax year ending during a period of detention from 2021 to the bill’s enactment date.

transparency_kindness.reason: Requires agencies to send Treasury lists and IRS to notify eligible people within 90 days, and stops penalties on people who cannot manage taxes while held, which is a humane outcome.

equality.reason: Sec. 7511 extends the same deadline relief to spouses and provides refunds to spouses and dependents, though eligibility turns on formal government determinations that may leave some detainees out.

justice.reason: The abatement and refund requirement and the 90-day notice duty give affected people a real remedy and clearer process, though eligibility depends on determinations that may exclude some people.

news.overall: The supplied coverage does not frame the End Tax Penalties on American Hostages Act at all. The Center headlines are about a Colombia hostage incident, North Korea at the U.N., and Senate business, and the Lean Right item is a Thanksgiving greeting with no description. The evidence is too thin to compare perspectives on this bill, so I can't say how outlets differ in their treatment of it.

label: H.R. 973
title: Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act
short_title: Setting Consumer Standards for Lithium-Ion Batteries Act
one: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to make existing industry fire-safety standards for e-bike and e-scooter batteries and electrical systems mandatory within 180 days, and to report on battery fires after five years.
summary:
This bill would turn voluntary safety standards for lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes, e-scooters and similar devices into mandatory federal rules. Today, many of these standards (known as UL 2271, UL 2849 and UL 2272) are optional, and some products on the market do not meet them. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) would have to adopt them as official consumer product safety rules. The rules would apply only to consumer products, not commercial or industrial equipment.

If the groups that write these standards update them later, the update would automatically become a federal rule 180 days after the CPSC is notified. The CPSC would have 90 days to block an update if it decides the change does not improve safety. Once adopted, the standards would be treated like any other CPSC safety rule, so they could be enforced against makers and sellers.

Within five years, the CPSC must give Congress a report on fires, explosions and other hazards from these batteries. It must include where the information came from, the make and model, whether the battery met the standard, and the manufacturer and country of manufacture, if known. The text does not give a cost or new funding. Some details, like enforcement costs and the effect on small sellers and prices, are not addressed.
does: Within 180 days of enactment, the CPSC must adopt three standards as final mandatory consumer product safety standards: ANSI/CAN/UL 2271 (batteries for light electric vehicles), UL 2849 (e-bike electrical systems), and UL 2272 (personal e-mobility devices), as they exist on the date of enactment.
Limits the standards to 'consumer products' as defined in the Consumer Product Safety Act, so commercial and industrial uses are outside the scope.

If a standards organization revises one of these standards later, it must notify the CPSC; the revision becomes a federal safety standard 180 days later (or a later date the CPSC sets), unless the CPSC says within 90 days that the revision does not improve safety and keeps the existing standard.
Treats the standards, and later revisions, as consumer product safety rules under section 9 of the Consumer Product Safety Act, which makes them enforceable.

Within 5 years, the CPSC must report to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee on fires, explosions and other hazards from lithium-ion batteries in micromobility products.
The report must cover the source of the information, make and model, whether the battery met the standard, and the manufacturer and country of manufacture, where known.
who: Manufacturers, importers, distributors and retailers of e-bikes, e-scooters and similar devices and their batteries
Consumers who buy and charge these devices
Residents of apartment buildings and dense housing where battery fires are especially dangerous
Firefighters and first responders
Delivery workers who rely on e-bikes
The Consumer Product Safety Commission
Standards organizations such as UL Solutions, ANSI and the Standards Council of Canada

benefits: Could reduce fires, injuries and deaths from e-bike and e-scooter batteries.
Creates a uniform national baseline instead of a patchwork of local rules.
Gives CPSC enforcement tools against noncompliant products.
The report will give Congress and the public data on hazards, makers and countries of origin.
Keeps standards current automatically, while letting the CPSC block changes that do not improve safety.
concerns: Compliance and certification testing could raise prices or burden small manufacturers and sellers.

How the rule will affect prices and availability of e-bikes and scooters.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make safety standards for rechargeable lithium-ion batteries in micromobility devices such as e-bikes and e-scooters mandatory federal consumer product safety rules, rather than voluntary standards. It also requires a report to Congress on fires, explosions and other hazards from these batteries within five years.

oppose: Compliance and certification testing could raise prices for e-bikes and e-scooters, and small manufacturers and sellers may find the testing costs hard to absorb.
The bill adopts standards written by private organizations and applies future revisions automatically, which gives those groups significant influence and limits public comment on changes.
Locking in the standards as they exist on the date of enactment could leave newer safety needs unaddressed until Congress or the CPSC acts again, and the CPSC gets only 90 days to block a revision.
support: The bill would turn standards that many e-bike and e-scooter batteries currently follow only voluntarily into mandatory federal rules, so noncompliant products could be enforced against.
Fires from lithium-ion batteries are a safety concern, and a single national baseline could replace a patchwork of differing local rules.

The bill requires a five-year CPSC report on fires, injuries and deaths, including the make, model, manufacturer and country of manufacture where known, which would give Congress and the public better data.

label: H.R. 2347
title: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
short_title: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026
one: A large Senate-amended package that speeds up and narrows federal environmental and energy permitting, limits court challenges and state and tribal review powers, adds data-center ratepayer protections, brownfields and wildfire-smoke funding, and also gives sexual-assault survivors a tax exclusion on damages they receive.
summary:
This bill began in the House as a short measure, the Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act. The Senate replaced all of its text with a three-division package. The survivor tax provision is now Division C. The digest I was given has gaps. It skips the end of Sec. 1204 and everything through the start of Sec. 1403, including the Endangered Species Act and "project certainty" sections. It also skips much of Division B between Sec. 2111 and Sec. 2215, and it cuts off at Sec. 2222 and the start of Sec. 2301. I could not review those parts.

Division A, Title I rewrites the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA). NEPA requires agencies to study the environmental effects of major projects. The bill says NEPA is only an information process and does not require any particular outcome. It narrows what counts as a "major Federal action," which exempts many projects. It sets hard deadlines of 1 year for environmental assessments and 2 years for full impact statements. It lets project sponsors push disputes to the Council on Environmental Quality chairman, whose binding decision cannot be appealed in court. Agencies that miss deadlines face penalties, such as limits on the agency head's travel. Courts could only send a flawed approval back to the agency, with no cancellation or injunction. Lawsuits must be filed within 150 days, and challengers must have filed detailed comments and show direct personal harm. The bill also builds a federal permitting data portal that uses automation and AI. The public can see non-sensitive data and Congress can see performance data. It creates a public tracker for major projects and a $20 million per year Permitting Improvement Fund. FAST-41 project lawsuit windows shrink from 2 years to 150 days.

Clean Water Act changes make EPA set water quality criteria by formal rulemaking. State and tribal Section 401 water-quality certification of federal permits becomes harder. A state could deny certification or add conditions only if it proves by "clear and convincing evidence" that they are needed and least burdensome. The review time is capped at one year. Special rules with a 9-month cap apply to gas pipelines and interstate power lines. State-issued discharge permits can last 10 years instead of 5. EPA could block a dredge-and-fill disposal site only before the Corps issues a permit. The bill treats discharges into under 2 acres of waters as minimal harm, and it requires nationwide permits for certain activity types.

The permitting-litigation sections let an applicant who proves bad-faith denial or unreasonable federal delay recover attorney fees, economic damages, and an extra 50 to 100 percent of expected construction cost. Taxpayers' Judgment Fund pays this. Federal agencies would also face a one-year deadline for decisions on permits that do not need NEPA review, enforceable in court.

For nuclear power, the NRC could issue licenses without hearings if no one requests one, and it must use informal procedures. Uranium enrichment plants could start construction before licensing. Some nuclear approvals are exempt from the new deadlines. The NRC chairman could pay career executives up to 110 percent of the normal Senior Executive Service maximum.

Other environmental provisions help communities in some ways. Prescribed burns can count as "exceptional events" under the Clean Air Act. This could keep smoke from them from counting against a state's air-quality compliance. EPA also gets a grant program for smoke protection in schools and community buildings. Brownfields cleanup funding rises to $200 million per year through FY2031. Grant caps go up, and small and disadvantaged communities get cost-share waivers. There are new audits and public site inventories.

Division B covers energy. It reshapes federal power-line siting. FERC gets more authority and states' eminent-domain role is removed. Landowners get formal input. A new rule on data centers says other customers cannot be charged the costs of serving a large computing site. Developers must post financial assurances, and states may set tougher terms. FERC must also open wholesale markets to small behind-the-meter batteries and generators, require advanced grid technology when benefits exceed costs, speed interconnection with automation, and require grid data sharing. A voluntary rooftop-solar and EV-charger permitting program gets $20 million per year. Mining changes allow extra mill sites for a $400 annual fee and apply hardrock leasing to acquired lands. Part of the fee and lease money goes to an Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund for cleaning up old mines. Geothermal "observation test" wells of up to 10 acres each would get a categorical exclusion from NEPA review. Historic preservation review gets firm timelines, with automatic proceeding if state, tribal, or local offices do not respond. Court remedies are also limited, with a 150-day filing window. The Historic Preservation Fund gets $200 million per year, and tribal officers get $20 million per year for a database.

Division C gives survivors a tax benefit. Damages received because of any sexual act or contact, with or without medical records or visible injury, are excluded from taxable income. A settlement or judgment that says the damages are for such acts counts as credible evidence in a tax dispute. Treasury must run a public-awareness program. The text I saw does not clearly exclude punitive damages, even though the title says "other than punitive damages." This applies to payments under decisions or agreements made after enactment.
does: Division C, Sec. 3001: Excludes from taxable income damages received on account of any sexual act or sexual contact, whether or not there are medical records or visible injuries. The IRS currently generally requires observable bodily harm.

Division C: If a judgment or settlement says damages are for a sexual act or contact, that statement counts as credible evidence in a tax dispute. This effectively shifts the burden of proof to the IRS. It applies to decisions and agreements made after enactment, and replacement agreements for older ones do not count.

Division C: Treasury, working with the Justice Department's Office on Violence Against Women, must run a public-awareness program about the exclusion. The title says 'other than punitive damages,' but the text I saw does not clearly state that limit.
NEPA Sec. 1101: Redefines NEPA as an information process for considering foreseeable environmental effects. It states that NEPA does not mandate any particular outcome.

NEPA Sec. 1102: Adds a long definitions section. It narrows 'major Federal action' to exclude many projects, including minimal-federal-involvement projects, loan-only projects, routine administrative actions up to $10 million, and some infrastructure repairs that add no more than 20 percent capacity. It also excludes projects funded by Army Corps programs where the federal share is $50 million or less.
Sec. 1103: Gives every agency 180 days to revise its NEPA procedures. The CEQ chairman must standardize them.

Sec. 1105: Lets agencies stack multiple categorical exclusions and use state or tribal reviews as a substitute. A project sponsor can force an environmental assessment to be converted into a full impact statement. Once one agency decides no document is needed, no other agency may prepare one.

Sec. 1106: Sets deadlines of 1 year for environmental assessments and 2 years for impact statements, with a record of decision 45 days after the impact statement. Outstanding permits are due 90 to 120 days later. Sponsors approve extensions.

Sec. 1106: Gives the CEQ chairman power to resolve disputes with a binding decision that is not judicially reviewable. Agencies missing deadlines face penalties, including senior staff time requirements and a 25-mile travel limit for the agency head. Sponsors can sue to enforce deadlines. Excuses must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

Sec. 1106: Agencies need not consider scientific research made public after the notice of intent. They may not delay a decision to wait for new research or another agency's comments. Impact statement comment periods are 45 to 60 days, extendable to a maximum of 75.

Secs. 1107-1109: Programmatic reviews last 10 years instead of 5. Agencies must publish and share categorical exclusions. Agencies must act on applications within 60 days to declare them complete and 60 days after that to choose a review level. Sponsors must provide a stakeholder-engagement record of up to 20 pages.

Sec. 1110: Limits NEPA lawsuits. Claims must be filed within 150 days, and the claimant must have filed a detailed comment and show direct personal harm. Cases go to the court of appeals, with a rule of substantial deference to the agency. The only remedy is remand without vacatur or injunction, with a 180-day schedule. The project can continue during remand. Tribal trust-land actions are largely shielded from NEPA suits except by the owning tribe.

Sec. 1121 and following: Creates an 'eNEPA' system. It sets data standards, automated screening, AI-assisted comment analysis, and a cloud-based authorization portal hosted by GSA. The public and Congress get access to non-sensitive and performance data. A pilot begins within a year, and the full system is due by December 1, 2028. Authorizes $5 million per year.

Subtitle C, Secs. 1131-1133: Creates a public Environmental Review and Permitting Tracker for impact-statement projects and long-delayed assessments. Updates are posted within 7 days, and delays and litigation status are listed. Establishes a Permitting Improvement Fund of $20 million per year for FY2027-2033, for training, detailees, and process standardization.
Sec. 1134: Cuts the lawsuit window for FAST-41 covered projects from 2 years to 150 days.

Sec. 1201: Requires EPA to use formal rulemaking when setting water quality criteria. It sends challenges to final criteria and to the 'waters of the United States' definition to the courts of appeals.

Sec. 1202: Rewrites Clean Water Act Sec. 401. Certification is limited to water quality requirements. Denials and conditions require the state or tribe to prove its case by clear and convincing evidence, and conditions must be the least burdensome. The state or tribe must meet application-completeness deadlines, review time is capped at one year, and applicants can sue. Special 9-month rules apply to gas pipelines and interstate transmission lines.
Sec. 1203: Extends state-issued discharge (NPDES) permits from 5 years to 10 years.

Sec. 1204: Limits EPA's veto of dredge-and-fill disposal sites to the period before the Corps issues a permit. General permits last 10 years. Discharges into under 2 acres count as minimal harm. The Corps must maintain certain nationwide permits (12, 14, 27, 43, 57, 58). The text for the rest of this section and the intervening sections through the start of Sec. 1403, including Endangered Species Act and 'project certainty' provisions, was not provided.

Permitting litigation sections (headings missing): Applicants who prove bad-faith denial or unreasonable delay of federal permits may get an injunction, attorney fees, economic damages, and an additional 50 to 100 percent of expected construction cost. These payments come from the taxpayer-funded Judgment Fund. Class actions are barred, and recipients must build the project or repay.
Sec. 1403: Gives agencies one year to decide permit applications that do not need NEPA review. Applicants can sue, courts must rule in 120 days, and any injunction must require a decision in 60 days.
Sec. 1501: Lets the NRC issue licenses and amendments without a hearing if no one asks for one, and requires informal procedures for hearings. This applies to pending cases.

Secs. 1502-1504: Allows uranium enrichment plants to start construction before licensing, with 15 days' notice to the state, local governments, and tribes. Exempts nuclear facility licensing from the new NEPA and one-year deadlines. Allows the NRC to pay career executives up to 110 percent of the Senior Executive Service maximum.

Sec. 1601: Counts prescribed fire, including tribal cultural burning, as an 'exceptional event' under the Clean Air Act. It orders EPA rule revisions, deems state petitions approved if EPA does not act within a year, and creates 'Smoke Ready Communities' grants for schools and community buildings, subject to appropriations.

Sec. 1602: Expands brownfields cleanup. It raises remediation grants to $1 million and multipurpose grants to $2 million, allows 10 percent for demolition, and waives cost share for small and disadvantaged communities. It also adds technical-assistance grants, audits, a public site inventory, and studies. It authorizes $200 million per year for FY2027-2031, plus $60 to $80 million per year for state and tribal programs.

Secs. 2101-2105 (transmission): Changes federal power-line siting. FERC permits facilities of at least 230 kV 'necessary in the national interest' after a 45-day comment period. It must consider landowner input, and state eminent-domain authority is removed. Utilities must file cost-allocation tariffs. Part of the text on this section was cut off.
Sec. 2106: Directs FERC to revise transmission pricing to assign costs to 'computational load' (data center) customers, possibly as a separate class.

Sec. 2107: Adds a federal 'ratepayer protection' rule for data centers. Other customers cannot be charged the retail incremental cost of serving a computing site, and utilities must obtain financial assurances before building for it. States may set tougher terms, use competitive solicitations, and treat computing loads less favorably than other industrial loads.

Sec. 2108: Opens wholesale electricity markets to small behind-the-meter batteries and generators and their aggregations. It bars double compensation, with disgorgement and penalties of up to 3 times the amount. It requires annual public reports. It also creates a voluntary DOE streamlined local permitting program for solar, storage, and EV charging, funded at $20 million per year for FY2026-2031.

Secs. 2109-2111: Requires public utilities to use grid-enhancing technologies and the best conductors when benefits exceed costs. Penalties can include a lower return on equity. FERC must also speed interconnection with automation and AI, and require grid data sharing within 15 days, with penalties. An automated study specification is due within a year.

Sec. 2215: Allows extra mining mill sites for a $400 per year fee, with no patenting. It extends hardrock mineral leasing to acquired lands. Part of the fees and lease receipts go to a new Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund to cover reclamation, with up to 5 percent for administration. Existing withdrawals and the government's authority to examine claims are preserved.

Sec. 2221: Creates a geothermal 'observation test project' category. These are test wells of up to 10 acres each and 100 acres in total. The Secretary must create a NEPA categorical exclusion within a year, and casual-use activity is not a major federal action. Sec. 2222 and later (royalties, hydropower, offshore, FERC staffing, DOE nuclear announcements) were not included in the digest.

Sec. 2301 (historic preservation review): Sets deadlines for consultation. A state, tribal, or local party that does not respond in 30 days is bypassed, and objections get 45 days. Agencies must develop program alternatives. Court review gets substantial deference, remand-only remedies, a 150-day filing window, and a comment requirement. Non-signers cannot challenge programmatic agreements. Listing a property late does not force a review to be reopened.

Sec. 2302: Authorizes $200 million per year for FY2027-2036 for the Historic Preservation Fund. Creates a $20 million per year tribal grant program (FY2027-2030) for tribal historic preservation officers to build records databases. Location information can be withheld from the public to protect sacred sites, and shared data is exempt from FOIA.
who: Survivors of sexual assault or abuse who receive settlements or court awards
Project developers and sponsors (energy, pipelines, mining, transmission, nuclear, data centers)
Communities, landowners, and neighbors near federal-permitted projects
State, local, and tribal governments, including their water-quality agencies and historic preservation offices
Environmental, conservation, and historic preservation groups that comment on and sue over projects
Electric ratepayers and utilities, including those serving data centers
Federal agencies (CEQ, EPA, Army Corps, NRC, FERC, Interior, DOE) and their senior staff
Taxpayers, who fund the Judgment Fund and the authorized programs
Brownfield communities, small towns, schools, and people exposed to wildfire smoke
Native American tribes, including those with sacred sites or trust lands

benefits: Survivors of sexual assault could keep more of a settlement or award, even without medical records or visible injury. They would also face a lighter burden in a tax dispute.
Data-center costs would be kept off other ratepayers' bills, with required financial assurances and strong state authority.
Brownfields funding of $200 million per year and larger grants could clean up polluted sites in small and disadvantaged communities.
Smoke Ready Communities grants could improve indoor air in schools. Prescribed burning could reduce wildfire smoke risk.
The Abandoned Hardrock Mine Fund and Historic Preservation Fund provide dedicated cleanup and preservation money.
Public permitting trackers and portals could make project status, delays, and litigation easier to see.
Faster, more predictable permitting could speed clean energy, transmission, and grid upgrades. Rooftop-solar permitting support and market access for small batteries could also lower costs.
concerns: Narrowing NEPA, exempting many projects, ignoring late-arriving science, and treating NEPA as information-only could allow harmful projects to go forward with less scrutiny.
Limits on standing, a 150-day filing window, comment prerequisites, and remand-only remedies could make it much harder for communities to challenge bad approvals.

Section 401 limits and the 'clear and convincing evidence' burden could weaken state and tribal power to protect their water. EPA's dredge-and-fill veto, 10-year permits, and the 2-acre minimal-effect rule could also reduce water protection.
Developer damages of 50 to 100 percent of construction cost, paid from the Judgment Fund, could shift costs to taxpayers.
A binding, unreviewable CEQ chairman decision on interagency disputes and penalties for agencies could pressure staff to approve quickly.
Optional NRC hearings, construction before licensing, and exemptions from deadlines for nuclear approvals could reduce public participation and oversight in nuclear safety.
Removing the state eminent-domain role and giving FERC more siting power could limit local say. Historic and tribal review gets bypass rules and weaker remedies.
Hardrock leasing, extra mill sites, and geothermal exclusions could increase mining and drilling impacts on public land.
The bill is bundled, so a survivor-support provision comes with major rollbacks. The Division C text also does not clearly exclude punitive damages despite its title.
imp.cost: Authorizations seen: $5 million per year for eNEPA technologies; $20 million per year for the Permitting Improvement Fund (FY2027-2033); $200 million per year for brownfields (FY2027-2031); $60-80 million per year for state and tribal brownfields programs; $20 million per year for DOE distributed-energy permitting (FY2026-2031); $200 million per year for the Historic Preservation Fund (FY2027-2036); $20 million per year for tribal databases (FY2027-2030). Developer damages come from the open-ended Judgment Fund. The mill-site fee is $400 per year per site. The tax exclusion would reduce federal revenue by an unknown amount. Many authorizations are subject to appropriations, so actual spending is not guaranteed.
unknowns: The digest omits the end of Sec. 1204 through the start of Sec. 1403, including Endangered Species Act and 'project certainty' provisions, so I could not assess them.

It also omits Division B sections between 2111 and 2215, Sec. 2222 and later items (geothermal royalties, hydropower, offshore, FERC staffing, DOE nuclear announcements), and the start of Sec. 2301, so those are not assessed.
It is unclear how much the survivor tax exclusion would cost in lost revenue.
It is unclear whether the Division C text intentionally omits the 'other than punitive damages' limit.
It is unclear how courts and agencies would apply terms like 'clear and convincing evidence' for state water-quality decisions.
The total long-term cost of Judgment Fund payments is unknown.
The Senate-amended version may need House agreement, and the final form could differ.

crs:
Survivor Justice Tax Prevention Act
This bill excludes from gross income certain damages received by an individual due to any sexual act or sexual contact and establishes the applicable burden of proof in court proceedings regarding the characterization of such damages for federal tax purposes. 
Under current law, amounts received as damages (other than punitive damages) from a judgment, award, or settlement of a claim may be excluded from gross income and, thus, are not subject to federal income tax, if attributable to a personal physical injury or physical sickness. The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) generally interprets 
personal physical injury
 to require observable bodily harm (e.g., bruising, cuts, swelling, or bleeding).
Under the bill, amounts received as damages (other than punitive damages) from a judgment, award, or settlement due to any sexual act or sexual conduct, whether or not there are medical records or observable injuries of such act or contact, may be excluded from gross income.
Further, if a judgment, award, or settlement states that damages are due to any sexual act or sexual conduct, then the IRS has the burden of proving otherwise in court proceedings related to the tax liability associated with such damages. 
Finally, the bill requires the IRS to promote public awareness of the exclusion from gross income of damages related to any sexual act or sexual contact.

environment.reason: Sec. 1101-1110 narrow NEPA, limit lawsuits to remand-only remedies, and exempt many projects; Sec. 1201-1204 weaken state Section 401 review, lengthen permits to 10 years, and treat discharges under 2 acres as minimal, reducing water protection; partly offset by brownfields cleanup funding (Sec. 1602) and smoke-related grants (Sec. 1601).

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2302 lets location data on sacred sites be withheld and exempts shared data from FOIA, and Sec. 1110 limits public challenges; partly offset by the public permitting tracker (Sec. 1131) and public eNEPA data access (Sec. 1121 and following).

people_over_profit.reason: Permitting litigation sections give developers attorney fees, economic damages, and 50-100 percent of construction cost from the Judgment Fund, and Sec. 2107 limits data-center cost shifts only partly while Sec. 1102 exempts many projects from review, favoring project sponsors over public interests.

local_say.reason: Sec. 2101-2105 remove the state eminent-domain role and give FERC siting power after a 45-day comment period; Sec. 1501 makes NRC hearings optional when no one requests one; Sec. 1110 and Sec. 1202 limit challenges and state Section 401 authority, though Sec. 2101-2105 do require landowner input and Sec. 2107 lets states set tougher data-center terms.

no_bailouts.reason: The permitting litigation sections pay developer damages of 50-100 percent of construction cost from the taxpayer-funded Judgment Fund, shifting project-delay costs to taxpayers.

equality.reason: Sec. 1110 shields tribal trust-land actions from NEPA suits except by the owning tribe and limits standing to those showing direct personal harm, while Division C's tax exclusion applies to survivors of sexual acts broadly and Sec. 2107 treats computing loads differently; net effect is unequal access to challenge decisions.

justice.reason: Sec. 1110 and Sec. 2301 cut the filing window to 150 days, limit remedies to remand without vacatur, and require detailed comments before suit; Sec. 1106 makes the CEQ chairman's decision unreviewable, while Division C's burden-shifting and the damages remedy in the permitting sections add some accountability for agencies and survivors.

personal_freedom.reason: Division C expands what survivors may exclude from income, but the permitting and NEPA provisions mainly govern agencies and project sponsors, and the effects on individual choices are mixed and unclear.

label: S. 2677
title: A bill to expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade.
short_title: Customs IP Information Sharing Bill (S. 2677)
one: Lets U.S. Customs and Border Protection share more information, including nonpublic data from online marketplaces and shippers, with trademark and copyright owners and other interested parties when it reasonably suspects imported goods are counterfeit or pirated.
summary: This bill changes one section of the Tariff Act of 1930 about how U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) deals with imported goods it thinks may violate trademark or copyright laws, such as counterfeits. Today, CBP can ask certain parties, like the trademark or copyright owner, for help checking the goods, and it must give them information about the goods and their packaging and labels. The bill raises the bar for starting this process from simply "suspects" to "has a reasonable suspicion." It also widens what CBP can share to include photos and information about packing materials and shipping containers. The bill also lets CBP share nonpublic information that online marketplaces, express shipping companies, freight forwarders, or other companies in the import chain have given to CBP or that CBP has obtained. When CBP shares that kind of information, it must notify the person receiving it, following rules the Secretary of Homeland Security may set. Finally, CBP can ask for help from "any other party with an interest in the merchandise," as decided by the CBP Commissioner. The bill text does not say how privacy, trade secrets, or the business information of the companies whose data is shared would be protected, other than the notification requirement. It also does not provide any new funding. The bill is described as scheduled for further action in the House after Senate action.
does: Changes the trigger for CBP's involvement from when it 'suspects' a violation to when it 'has a reasonable suspicion' that imported goods violate certain trademark or copyright laws.
Expands the information CBP must give to the helping party to include images and information on packing materials and containers, not just the goods, packaging, and labels.

Allows CBP to share nonpublic information about the goods that was generated by online marketplaces, express consignment operators, freight forwarders, or any other entity involved in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the goods, if CBP received or obtained it.
Requires CBP, when it shares such nonpublic information, to notify the recipient of what information was transmitted, following regulations the Secretary may set.
Adds 'any other party with an interest in the merchandise, as determined appropriate by the Commissioner' to the list of parties CBP may ask for help and share information with.
who: Trademark and copyright owners, who would get more information to identify counterfeits and pirated goods
Online marketplaces, express shipping companies, freight forwarders, and other import-chain businesses whose nonpublic data could be shared
Importers and sellers, including small online sellers, whose goods may be examined or whose shipping data may be passed on
U.S. Customs and Border Protection staff
Consumers who could encounter counterfeit or unsafe goods

benefits: Could help rights holders spot counterfeit goods faster, which may protect consumers from fake or unsafe products such as counterfeit medicine, electronics, or car parts.
Moving from 'suspects' to 'reasonable suspicion' sets a somewhat firmer standard before information is shared.
The notification requirement creates a record of what nonpublic information was passed along.
Could support honest businesses and workers harmed by counterfeiters.
concerns: Nonpublic business data from marketplaces and shippers could be shared with outside parties, which could raise privacy or trade-secret concerns.
'Any other party with an interest in the merchandise' is broad and left to the CBP Commissioner's judgment.
Small sellers or importers could be wrongly flagged, delayed, or have goods held based on a rights holder's view.
The bill benefits mostly corporate intellectual property owners and includes no public reporting or oversight requirements.
imp.cost: No funding or cost estimate is given in the bill text. Any implementation costs would fall on CBP and DHS through regular appropriations.
unknowns: What regulations the Secretary would write on notifications and on safeguards for shared data.
Who the Commissioner would treat as an 'other party with an interest' in goods.
How often the sharing would happen and whether it would increase seizures of legitimate goods.
Whether the information would be protected from further disclosure by the recipients.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to expand the sharing of information with respect to suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade. According to the CRS summary, it lets U.S. Customs and Border Protection share more information with trademark owners, copyright owners, and other interested parties when it has a reasonable suspicion that imported goods violate certain trademark or copyright laws, so those parties can help determine whether the goods are infringing.

oppose: Nonpublic business data from online marketplaces, express shippers, and freight forwarders could be shared with outside parties. The bill text does not spell out privacy or trade-secret protections beyond a notification requirement, so you could ask your member how those businesses' information would be safeguarded.
The phrase 'any other party with an interest in the merchandise' is broad and is left to the CBP Commissioner to decide. You could ask who would qualify and what limits would apply.

Legitimate small sellers or importers could be wrongly flagged or have shipments delayed based on a rights holder's view. You could ask what steps would protect them if goods are held, and whether the bill includes public reporting or oversight.
support: The bill could help rights holders spot counterfeit goods faster. Fake medicine, electronics, and car parts can put consumers at risk, so faster information sharing could help protect them.
Changing the standard from 'suspects' to 'has a reasonable suspicion' sets a somewhat firmer threshold before CBP shares information with outside parties.

The bill requires CBP to notify the recipient of what nonpublic information was shared, which creates a record of what was passed along. Honest businesses and workers harmed by counterfeiters could also benefit from better tools to catch fakes.

crs:
This bill expands the authority of U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to provide information to certain persons (e.g., trademark or copyright owners) regarding suspected violations of intellectual property rights in trade. 
Under current law, if CBP suspects that merchandise is being imported in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws, it may request assistance from specified persons when determining whether the merchandise is imported in violation of these laws. To permit the party to conduct examination and testing, CBP must provide them with specified information that appears on the merchandise and its packaging and labels. 
This bill (1) expands the definition of 
person
 to allow CBP to request assistance from any other appropriate party with an interest in the imported merchandise, and (2) expands the scope of information that CBP is authorized to share with others to include information on and images of packing materials and shipping containers.
The bill allows CBP to request this assistance if it has a reasonable suspicion (currently, suspects) that the merchandise being imported is in violation of certain trademark and copyright laws.
Additionally, CBP may provide a person with nonpublic information about the imported merchandise that was generated by an online marketplace or similar market platform, express consignment operator, freight forwarder, or any other entity that plays a role in the sale, importation, or facilitation of the merchandise into the United States and has been provided to, shared with, or obtained by CBP.

environment.reason: The bill concerns information sharing about imported goods suspected of IP violations and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 1 allows CBP to share nonpublic data from marketplaces and shippers with outside parties, and the bill has no public reporting or oversight requirement, though the notification requirement gives some record of what was shared.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 1 lets CBP share nonpublic business data and examine goods to help private IP owners, mainly benefiting corporate rights holders rather than the public, though it may also protect consumers from counterfeit goods.

local_say.reason: The bill concerns federal CBP authority and does not change state or community decision-making power.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no bailout or ratepayer cost-shifting provisions, and it provides no new funding.

equality.reason: Sec. 1 lets CBP share nonpublic data from some import-chain businesses and gives rights holders and an open-ended 'any other party' category access to examination, which may treat importers and rights holders unequally.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 lowers the bar from 'suspects' to a 'reasonable suspicion' threshold that is somewhat firmer, but the bill gives no due process or remedy for importers wrongly flagged and leaves the 'any other party' designation to the Commissioner's discretion.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill affects government enforcement and information sharing about goods and does not expand or restrict what individuals may do with their own lives.

news.overall: None of the six headlines names the bill, so coverage addresses its subject only indirectly. Lean Left and Center pieces link the topic to U.S.-China trade, tariffs, and the Huawei trade-secret case, while Lean Right pieces focus on surveillance and tech regulation. Evidence is thin for every group, with only two Lean Right headlines and no direct coverage of the bill's provisions.

label: S. 3977
title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
short_title: Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
one: Raises the debt limits that let small businesses use Subchapter V bankruptcy (to $7.5 million) and let individuals use Chapter 13 repayment-plan bankruptcy (to $2.75 million total debt), restoring higher limits that expired in 2024.
summary: This bill changes who can use two kinds of bankruptcy that are meant to be simpler and cheaper than the standard routes. The first is Subchapter V, a streamlined way for small businesses to reorganize their debts and keep operating. The bill sets the debt cap at $7.5 million. Today it is about $3.4 million, after a higher limit expired in 2024. The second is Chapter 13, where a person with regular income pays back debts over time through a court-approved plan. Today there are separate caps for secured debt (backed by property, like a mortgage) and unsecured debt (like credit cards), totaling roughly $2.1 million. The bill replaces them with one combined cap of $2.75 million. Public companies, their affiliates, and businesses whose main activity is owning a single piece of real estate stay excluded from Subchapter V. Affiliated groups are judged by their combined debt. The change would apply only to bankruptcy cases filed on or after the date the bill becomes law. It does not forgive debt, spend money, or change the rules of the bankruptcy process beyond who is eligible. The text does not say whether the higher limits are permanent. The CRS summary says the bill restores the limits that lapsed in 2024. The Senate passed the bill on August 3, 2026, and it was held at the desk on August 10, 2026, which is a procedural step in the House.
does: Raises the Subchapter V (small business) debt limit to $7,500,000 from about $3.4 million.
who: Small and mid-sized businesses with debts between about $3.4 million and $7.5 million

benefits: Businesses and individuals with larger debts may be able to use the simpler and lower-cost routes, which could help them reorganize and keep operating.
Using one combined Chapter 13 limit may make eligibility easier to understand and apply than separate secured and unsecured caps.
concerns: Creditors may face longer or more difficult repayment processes if more debtors qualify for these routes.
Because the limits are higher, more cases might be handled under these streamlined procedures, which could affect how much creditors recover.
Because the bill does not say whether the limits are permanent, debtors and creditors may face uncertainty about future rules.
imp.cost: ["The bill text does not state any cost, funding, or budget effect. The material says it does not forgive debt or spend money."]
unknowns: Whether the higher limits are permanent or temporary is not stated in the bill text.
How many additional cases would qualify under the new limits is not stated.
What effect the change would have on creditor recoveries or court workloads is not stated.
The exact current Chapter 13 secured and unsecured limits are described only as roughly $2.1 million combined.

stage.stage_label: Scheduled for House floor vote (second chamber)
stage.last_action: Held at the desk.

purpose: The bill says it restores debt limits for Subchapter V (small business reorganization) and Chapter 13 bankruptcy that expired in 2024. Per the CRS summary, it raises the Subchapter V limit from about $3.4 million to $7.5 million and sets a combined Chapter 13 limit of $2.75 million for secured and unsecured debt, replacing separate caps totaling about $2.1 million. The stated aim, based on the title and CRS summary, is to restore these higher limits so that more debtors can use these streamlined reorganization routes.

oppose: The bill raises the Subchapter V debt cap to $7.5 million, so larger businesses could use a faster, lower-cost process that may limit creditors' ability to shape the outcome.
Creditors could face longer or more difficult repayment processes if more debtors qualify, which may reduce how much they recover.
The bill does not say whether the higher limits are permanent, so creditors and debtors may face uncertainty about future rules.
support: The bill restores Subchapter V limits that expired in 2024, which could help small businesses with larger debts reorganize and keep operating instead of closing.
Subchapter V is designed to be simpler and cheaper than standard bankruptcy routes, so the higher cap could lower costs for eligible businesses.
Combining secured and unsecured debt into one Chapter 13 limit of $2.75 million may make eligibility easier to understand and apply for individuals with regular income.

crs:
Bankruptcy Threshold Adjustment Act of 2026
This bill restores changes that expired in 2024 applicable to debt limits for Subchapter V (small business reorganization) and Chapter 13 (the wage earner's plan) bankruptcies.
Specifically, the bill increases the debt limit under Subchapter V from approximately $3.4 million to $7.5 million and increases the cumulative debt limit under Chapter 13 from approximately $2.1 million to $2.75 million.
The bill also applies both secured and unsecured debt towards the Chapter 13 limit. (Currently, separate limits apply to secured and unsecured debt under Chapter 13 bankruptcy.)

equality.reason: Expanded access to Chapter 13 and Subchapter V extends a debt-relief option to more debtors, and the single combined Chapter 13 cap is simpler to apply evenly.

justice.reason: Restoring debt-relief eligibility that lapsed in 2024 gives more debtors a fair path to repay and reorganize rather than face liquidation.

personal_freedom.reason: Debtors gain a broader option to choose a court-supervised reorganization that keeps their businesses and assets running.

people_over_profit.reason: Raising the Subchapter V cap lets larger businesses use a cheaper, streamlined reorganization route, which mainly benefits businesses and their creditors and owners rather than ordinary people, though it also helps keep workers' jobs in place.

label: S. 911
title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
short_title: Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
one: The bill would let certain retired law enforcement officers, or their families, get federal Public Safety Officers' Benefits if the officer is killed or permanently disabled in a targeted attack because of their police service.
summary: Right now, a federal program called the Public Safety Officers' Benefits (PSOB) program pays money to families of officers who die in the line of duty, and to officers who are permanently disabled on duty. This bill would widen that program to cover some retired law enforcement officers. To qualify, the person must have left their job in good standing at a public agency. They must also have died or become permanently and totally disabled as the direct result of an injury from a targeted attack. The attack must have happened because of the person's past work as a law enforcement officer. In other words, this is about retired officers who are singled out and attacked in revenge or retaliation for their service, not about general injuries or crimes. The bill would take effect once signed into law. It would apply to cases still pending at the Bureau of Justice Assistance, and to new claims. It also reaches back to cover events on or after January 1, 2012. The bill is named for Chief Herbert D. Proffitt. The text does not say who he was or give the case behind the name. It does not include a cost estimate or new funding amounts.
does: Adds a new subsection (p) to the federal public safety officers' benefits law (34 U.S.C. 10281).
Defines a "retired law enforcement officer" as someone who left service in good standing at a public agency, with or without pay.
Makes such a retiree eligible for benefits if they die or become permanently and totally disabled as the direct result of a targeted attack because of their law enforcement service.
Takes effect on enactment and applies to pending matters before the Bureau of Justice Assistance and to later claims.
Applies to qualifying actions taken against retired officers on or after January 1, 2012.
who: Retired law enforcement officers who are targeted because of their service
Surviving families of retired officers killed in such attacks
Bureau of Justice Assistance, which runs the PSOB program
Federal taxpayers, who fund the program
Public safety agencies and the families of past qualifying victims since 2012

benefits: Could provide financial support to families of retired officers killed in retaliatory attacks.
Could provide support to retired officers who become permanently and totally disabled from such attacks.
The retroactive start date could allow past cases from 2012 onward to be considered.
concerns: The bill's limits (targeted attack, link to past service, good standing) may be hard to apply, which could lead to disputes over individual claims.
Retroactive coverage to 2012 could increase the number of claims the Bureau of Justice Assistance must review.
imp.cost: ["The bill text does not include a cost estimate or new funding amounts. The total cost to the PSOB program is not stated."]
unknowns: The total number of retired officers who might qualify is not stated.
The cost to the PSOB program is not stated, and no cost estimate is included.
How 'targeted attack' and 'good standing' will be defined and applied is not described in the material provided.
The material does not say who Chief Herbert D. Proffitt was or what case inspired the bill.
The bill's status in the second chamber is listed only as scheduled for a House floor vote; whether it will pass is not known.

stage.stage_label: Scheduled for House floor vote (second chamber)
stage.last_action: Held at the desk.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to extend Public Safety Officers' Benefits (PSOB) death and disability benefits to certain retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled from a personal injury caused by a targeted attack based on their past law enforcement service. Under the bill, the retiree must have retired in good standing, and the change applies to events on or after January 1, 2012.

oppose: The bill expands a federal benefits program to a new group, retired officers, which could add costs to the PSOB program. The bill does not include a cost estimate or new funding amounts, so the financial impact is unknown.
Retroactive coverage back to January 1, 2012 could increase the number of claims the Bureau of Justice Assistance must review, adding to its workload.
Key terms such as 'targeted attack,' 'direct and proximate result,' and 'good standing' may be hard to apply consistently, which could lead to disputes over individual claims.
support: The bill would give families of retired officers killed in retaliatory attacks, and retirees who become permanently and totally disabled from them, financial support similar to what the PSOB program already offers to active officers.
The bill limits coverage to targeted attacks based on past law enforcement service and to retirees who left in good standing, which narrows who qualifies.

The retroactive start date of January 1, 2012 could allow past cases to be considered, so eligible families and retirees would not be excluded only because the event happened before the law took effect.

crs:
Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025
This bill extends death and disability benefits under the Public Safety Officers’ Benefits (PSOB) program to certain retired law enforcement officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled as a direct and proximate result of a personal injury from a targeted attack based on the retired officer’s law enforcement service.
To be eligible for PSOB benefits under the bill, a retired law enforcement officer must have retired in good standing.
The bill applies retroactively to retired officers who die or become permanently and totally disabled on or after January 1, 2012.

equality.reason: Retired officers who are attacked for their service become eligible for the same benefits that active officers' families already receive, closing a gap in coverage.

justice.reason: It provides financial redress to victims of retaliatory attacks based on their past service and reaches back to 2012 to cover past cases.

life.reason: It extends survivor death benefits and disability benefits to families and retirees harmed by targeted attacks tied to their law enforcement service, which helps protect and support people harmed by violence.

no_bailouts.reason: It adds new federal benefit payments from taxpayer funds without any cost estimate or funding limits, though the payments go to individuals rather than corporations.

honesty_kindness.reason: It compassionately provides financial support to families and disabled retirees who were singled out for attack because of their service.

news.overall: The Center group provides only three headlines with no descriptions, and none names the Chief Herbert D. Proffitt Act of 2025. Only the Government Executive piece about House veterans' benefits votes plausibly touches on federal legislation, so I can't say how this coverage frames the bill itself. A fuller set of articles that name the bill would be needed for a meaningful comparison.

label: S. 97
title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act
short_title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department's SelectUSA program to gather input from state economic development groups and report to Congress on how to attract more foreign investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, using no new money.
summary: This bill tells SelectUSA, a Commerce Department program that tries to attract business investment to the United States, to study how to bring more foreign investment into making computer chips (semiconductors) here. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, SelectUSA's leader must ask state-level economic development organizations for comments. They would be asked what the federal government can do, what barriers exist, what opportunities states have found, and what resource gaps hold them back. They would also be asked for ideas on how SelectUSA can help and how to work with allied countries so that "foreign adversaries" do not benefit from the effort. Within two years, SelectUSA must send a report to the Senate and House commerce committees. The report would review the comments, describe what SelectUSA is already doing, and assess strategies it could use. The bill does not create new grants, tax breaks, or rules, and it does not authorize new money. SelectUSA must do the work with funds it already has. The bill passed the Senate on May 20, 2025, and is now waiting in the House. The text does not say anything about environmental, water, or air standards, or about public input beyond state organizations.
does: Defines SelectUSA as the Commerce Department program created by Executive Order 13577.
who: SelectUSA staff and the Commerce Department

benefits: Could give Congress better information about barriers and gaps that states face when trying to attract chip-related investment.
Could help identify ways the federal government can support chip manufacturing investment in the United States.
Could encourage coordination with allied countries, which may strengthen supply chain security.
Costs no new federal money and creates no new mandates, so it may be a low-impact step.
concerns: Because the bill only requires a study and report, it may not lead to any direct change in chip investment or supply chain security.
Input is limited to state economic development organizations, so views from other groups, such as workers, local communities, or industry, may not be gathered under this bill.
Relying on existing SelectUSA funds may limit how much work can be done, which could affect the quality of the study.

unknowns: The text does not say what specific strategies SelectUSA would recommend or whether Congress would act on them.
The text does not say how many state organizations would respond or how comments would be weighted.
The text does not address environmental, water, or air standards for chip plants.
The text does not describe public input beyond state economic development organizations.
The bill passed the Senate on May 20, 2025, and is scheduled for a House floor vote. Whether the House will pass it, or change it, is not stated.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help the U.S. secure its semiconductor (computer chip) supply chain by studying how to bring more foreign direct investment into chip-related manufacturing and production in the United States. It requires the SelectUSA program, a Commerce Department effort to attract business investment, to gather comments from state economic development organizations and report those comments to Congress, along with strategies SelectUSA could use.

oppose: The bill is a study and reporting requirement only, so it may not produce any direct change in chip investment or supply chain security, and Congress may be asked to spend time on a report with limited practical effect.
Public input is limited to state economic development organizations, so workers, local communities, and industry groups may not be heard under this bill.
SelectUSA must do the work with funds it already has, which could limit how thorough the review is and could affect the quality of the report.
support: The bill would give Congress better information about the barriers and resource gaps states face when trying to attract chip manufacturing investment.
It could help identify ways the federal government can support chip production in the United States, which may strengthen supply chain security.
It encourages coordination with allied countries so that foreign adversaries do not benefit from efforts to build chip supply chains, and it costs no new federal money and creates no new mandates.

crs:
Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act
This bill requires the SelectUSA program to solicit comments from state economic development organizations regarding federal efforts to increase foreign direct investment in semiconductor-related manufacturing and production. SelectUSA must then report to Congress on such comments and the strategies that SelectUSA may employ to increase such investment and to secure the U.S. semiconductor supply chain.
SelectUSA is a Department of Commerce program established to coordinate federal efforts to attract and retain business investment in the United States.

environmental_protection.reason: The bill does not address environmental standards or impacts of chip manufacturing.

transparency.reason: The bill requires SelectUSA to solicit comments from states and report its findings to Congress committees, which modestly increases government reporting to the public's representatives.

local_say.reason: State-level economic development organizations are asked for their views on barriers and opportunities, giving states a formal channel to shape federal investment strategy, though it is consultative only.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill creates no grants, tax breaks, or subsidies and authorizes no new money, so it neither adds nor removes bailouts or ratepayer-funded breaks.

label: S. 99
title: Strengthening Support for American Manufacturing Act
short_title: Strengthening Support for American Manufacturing Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department to hire an outside expert group to review its manufacturing and supply-chain offices and recommend ways to make them work better, with a report to Congress.
summary: This bill is a study bill. It does not create new programs, give out money, or change any rules for businesses. It tells the Secretary of Commerce to produce a report within one year of the bill becoming law. The report must list which Commerce Department offices and bureaus work on two things: keeping key supply chains strong (for example in defense, health, communications, energy, transportation, and farm supplies), and helping U.S. manufacturers and manufacturing workers with research, resources, or policy. For each office, the report must describe its duties and programs, its legal authority, and how well and how efficiently it works. It must also point out overlap or gaps between offices doing similar work. Finally, it must recommend ways to improve operations and coordination, including with other federal agencies. The Secretary must work with the National Academy of Public Administration, an independent, congressionally chartered group, to produce the report. Within 180 days after finishing the report, the Secretary must send it to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The Secretary must also send suggested legislative changes and the Department's own response to the recommendations. The bill text does not say how much the study would cost or where the money would come from.
does: Requires Commerce to produce a report within 1 year of enactment on its offices working on supply chain resilience and manufacturing and industrial innovation.
who: Department of Commerce offices and bureaus involved in manufacturing and supply chains

benefits: A review could show which Commerce offices overlap, which may help Congress and the Department reduce duplicated work.
Identifying gaps could help show where manufacturers or supply chains may be under-served.
Recommendations on coordination with other agencies could lead to clearer roles across government.
concerns: The bill does not require any follow-up action, so the report's recommendations may not be carried out.
Because the report is due to Congress and not the public in the text provided, outside observers may have limited visibility into its findings.
imp.cost: ["The bill text does not say how much the study would cost or where the money would come from."]
unknowns: The total cost of the contract with the National Academy of Public Administration is not stated.
The source of funding for the study is not stated.
It is not stated whether the report will be made available to the public.
It is not stated what changes, if any, would follow from the report's recommendations.
The latest action is listed as a scheduled House floor vote in the second chamber; the material does not say whether the bill will pass.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to get a clear picture of the Department of Commerce offices and bureaus that work on keeping critical supply chains resilient and on helping American manufacturing and industrial innovation. It requires an independent review of what each office does, its legal authority, how well it works, and where its work overlaps or has gaps, with recommendations to improve effectiveness and coordination. The bill is a study only and does not create new programs or change rules for businesses.
