Commerce already has many offices in this area, and the report may repeat reviews that have already been done. You could ask whether existing oversight, such as GAO reports or agency reviews, already covers these offices.
support: The bill would give Congress an independent, detailed look at Commerce offices that work on supply chains and manufacturing, which could help it make better-informed decisions.
The review would look for overlap and gaps between offices doing similar work, which could help the government use its resources more efficiently and serve manufacturers and workers better.
The bill asks for recommendations on coordination with other federal agencies, which could lead to clearer roles and fewer gaps across government in supply chain and manufacturing work.

crs:
Strengthening Support for American Manufacturing Act
This bill requires the Department of Commerce to contract with the National Academy of Public Administration to study and report on the offices and bureaus of the department that are relevant to critical supply chain resilience and manufacturing and industrial innovation.
The report must evaluate the purpose, statutory authority, effectiveness, efficiency, and limitations of each such office and bureau and provide recommendations to improve their effectiveness, efficiency, and impact.

transparency.reason: The bill requires a public-facing report on Commerce offices' duties, authority, effectiveness, and overlaps, and sends it plus the Department's response to Congress.

label: S. 1353
title: A bill to extend the authority for modifications to the Second Division Memorial in the District of Columbia.
short_title: Second Division Memorial Extension
one: Gives more time for additions or engravings to be made to the Second Division Memorial in Washington, DC, which honors Second Infantry Division members who died in service.
summary:
The Second Division Memorial is in President's Park in Washington, DC. It honors members of the Army's Second Infantry Division who died serving the country. A 2017 defense law (section 352 of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2018) gave permission for changes to the memorial. That permission has a time limit. According to the Congressional Research Service (CRS), the permission lets a veterans' group, the Second Indianhead Division Association, Inc., Scholarship and Memorials Foundation, add commemorative elements or engravings on the memorial's raised platform or stonework.

This bill is very short. It says the 2017 permission keeps applying, even though a general rule in federal law (40 U.S.C. 8903(e)) would normally end it. The bill's text sets the new end date as September 30, 2033. The CRS summary says September 30, 2032. The two sources disagree, and the bill text is what would become law. The bill does not create new spending, new rules, or new powers beyond extending the existing deadline. The text I was given does not say who pays for the changes or what the approval process is. Those details would be in the earlier 2017 law, which I could not see.
does: Extends the existing authority from section 352 of the 2018 defense law to modify the Second Division Memorial.
Overrides the normal time limit in 40 U.S.C. 8903(e) for this authority.
Sets the new end date as September 30, 2033 in the bill text (the CRS summary says 2032).
Per CRS, lets the foundation keep adding commemorative elements or engravings on the platform or stonework honoring fallen Second Infantry Division members.
who: Second Indianhead Division Association, Inc., Scholarship and Memorials Foundation
Families and veterans of the Second Infantry Division
Visitors to President's Park in Washington, DC
National Park Service and other federal bodies that oversee memorials in DC (their role is not described in the text provided)

benefits: Lets the memorial be updated to honor more fallen service members over a longer period.
Keeps a long-planned, veteran-led project from lapsing because of a deadline.
Very small change with little risk.
concerns: The CRS summary (2032) and the bill text (2033) give different end dates, which could cause confusion.
The text provided does not describe approval steps or public review for changes to the memorial.
imp.cost: The bill text does not provide funding or give a cost estimate. It only extends an existing authority. How the modifications are paid for is set in the earlier 2017 law, which I could not see.
unknowns: Who pays for the additions and engravings.
What review or approval process applies to design changes.
Whether the end date is meant to be 2032 or 2033.
How many additions are planned.

label: S. 2887
title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
short_title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
one: Adds Route 66, about 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, to the National Trails System as a National Historic Trail, with strong limits on land acquisition, buffer zones, new permits, and any interference with energy projects.
summary:
This bill would officially name Route 66 a National Historic Trail. The trail would include every path U.S. Highway 66 followed between 1926 and 1985. It runs about 2,400 miles from Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California. The Secretary of the Interior would run the trail in a way that keeps its quirky, one-of-a-kind character. Before taking actions that would strongly affect Indian Tribes, the Secretary would have to consult with them.

The bill also sets many limits. The federal government could not take land by eminent domain, which is the power to force a sale. Outside federal areas, it could only get land from owners who agree. It could not acquire land more than an average of a quarter mile on either side of the trail. The bill says the trail creates no "buffer zone." Activities that can be seen or heard from the trail could not be limited because of it. Nothing about the trail could block, hinder, or disrupt energy development or transport, such as pipelines and power lines. The designation would not add new permit requirements and would not change who can grant easements or rights-of-way (permission to cross land). It would also keep the trail from being treated as National Park System land under a pipeline law.

The text does not list any money amounts. It passed the Senate on November 12, 2026, and now goes to the House. The text does not say whether Congress would set aside money, and a CRS summary was not available.

title: Improving Access to Workers’ Compensation for Injured Federal Workers Act of 2025
short_title: Improving Access to Workers' Compensation for Injured Federal Workers Act
one: The bill would let nurse practitioners and physician assistants treat injured federal employees and make decisions in the federal workers' compensation system, roles now limited mostly to physicians.
summary: Federal employees hurt on the job can get benefits through a program called the Federal Employees' Compensation Act (FECA). Right now, the law mostly counts doctors (physicians and similar practitioners) as the providers whose care and opinions count in that program. This bill adds nurse practitioners and physician assistants, called "other eligible providers," to the law. They would count only for what they are allowed to do under their own state's law. The bill changes several sections so that these providers can be used where the law now says "physician." For example, an injured worker could choose one of them for treatment. Their reports could also count when deciding a claim. One change involves disputes. If the government's doctor and the worker's doctor disagree, a "third physician" now settles it. The bill changes that to "an additional physician." The bill gives the Secretary of Labor six months after it becomes law to finish the rules needed to carry it out. The bill text does not include a cost estimate or new funding. The Senate passed it without changes by unanimous consent. The House has not yet acted, based on the information provided.

label: S. 3493
title: Carson City Public Land Correction Act
short_title: Carson City Public Land Correction Act
one: The bill gives Carson City, Nevada about 1,270 acres and a small road parcel of federal land for free, orders the sale of other federal parcels to bidders, and updates a 2009 land law, with sale money going into a local account for costs and buying sensitive land.
summary: This bill adjusts how federal land around Carson City, Nevada, is handled under a 2009 law. First, the federal government would give Carson City about 1,270 acres for free. The city must use it for public purposes such as recreation and flood control, and the land can go back to the federal government if it stops being used that way. Second, about half an acre would go to the city for free to build a street connector. The city must add a crosswalk on South Curry Street near the Forest Service office within 2 years. Third, the Bureau of Land Management would sell about 356 acres to qualified bidders. The city would keep certain water line, drainage, and other existing rights. Fourth, the city could offer back about 45 acres to the federal government, which must accept. About 21 of those acres would then be sold. Sale money would go into a Carson City Special Account. It could pay for sale-related costs, including environmental reviews, and for buying environmentally sensitive land in the city. The bill also lets the city make agreements with outside parties, including for-profit ones, to run places like the Capitol City Gun Club, Centennial Park, and Eagle Valley Golf Course, without an appraisal. It sets a one-year deadline to offer certain lands for sale if there is a qualified bidder. The bill does not require the federal government or the city to clean up existing contamination on the conveyed lands.

label: S. 3589
title: RISE Act
short_title: RISE Act (Respond, Innovate, Succeed, and Empower Act)
one: Requires colleges that take federal student aid to accept common disability records as proof of disability, publish how they decide on accommodations, and report anonymized counts of students with disabilities, and authorizes $10 million for a national technical-assistance center.
summary: This bill changes the Higher Education Act, the main federal law covering colleges that receive federal student aid. First, colleges would have to accept several kinds of existing paperwork as enough proof that a student has a disability. These include a high school IEP (a special education plan) or a Section 504 plan used at any point in high school, a record from another college, a record from a licensed professional, a service record under the Americans with Disabilities Act, or documentation of a disability from military service. Colleges could still choose rules that are easier than these. Second, colleges would have to clearly explain how they decide who gets accommodations. They would need to share this with students, parents, and faculty, including at orientation and on a public website. Third, colleges would report yearly numbers to the federal data system (IPEDS): how many students are registered with disability services, how many get accommodations, what share of students that is, and how many degrees or certificates they earn. Colleges would not report numbers when doing so could identify a single student. Fourth, it authorizes up to $10 million over fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for a national center that helps colleges support students with disabilities. Authorizing money does not itself spend it; Congress must still appropriate it. The bill says it does not change the meaning of rights under the ADA or Section 504.

label: S. 3923
title: Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Renews and greatly expands NOAA's weather, tsunami, hurricane, tornado, wildfire, heat, drought and alert programs for fiscal years 2027–2031, with new reporting rules, more use of private-sector data, and several new spending authorizations.
summary:
This bill renews and expands a 2017 law that guides how the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) researches and forecasts weather. It authorizes about $167–174 million a year for weather research. It also sets up or renews programs for tornadoes, hurricanes, tsunamis, precipitation, atmospheric rivers, coastal flooding, extreme heat, drought, and wildfire weather.

The bill pushes NOAA to improve how warnings reach people. It would modernize NOAA Weather Radio, with $100 million for upgrades in 2027 and $25 million a year for operations. It bars buying upgrade equipment from companies based in foreign countries of concern. It orders studies of how people understand and act on alerts, with extra attention to rural areas, Tribes, older adults, people with disabilities, and non-English speakers.

It also leans more on commercial data, such as private satellites, radar, aircraft and ocean vessels. It adds rules for open data sharing, cost comparisons, and reports to Congress. It creates a "Fire Ready Nation" program with incident meteorologists, a fire weather testbed, and a temporary premium-pay waiver for wildland fire workers in 2027. It also lets NOAA transfer excess satellites to other agencies and keep the reimbursements. Finally, it requires annual unfunded-priority lists and capital plans. These are authorizations, meaning they allow spending but don't provide the money. Congress would still have to appropriate it.

Expands the Commercial Data Program and pushes NOAA to buy private weather data, use multiyear contracts, and share data with the weather enterprise.
Sets up heat-health programs ($2.7M a year), aviation weather ($10M a year), aerial snow surveys, and drought and subseasonal forecasting ($40M and $15–17M a year).

Waives premium pay caps for certain wildland fire employees for 2027 and requires a hiring plan.
Lets NOAA transfer excess satellites to other agencies outside normal property rules, keep reimbursements in a special account, and notify Congress 60 days ahead.
Requires annual unfunded priorities lists, capital investment plans, and public stock assessment schedules.
Allows Arctic observation networks, Pacific Island technical help, and international weather partnerships.

label: S. 432
title: Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Establishment Act
short_title: Fort Ontario Holocaust Refugee Shelter National Historical Park Act
one: The bill would create a new National Park Service site at Fort Ontario in Oswego, New York, to preserve and tell the story of 982 World War II refugees housed there from 1944 to 1946, once enough land has been acquired.
summary:
This bill would set up a new national historical park in New York State at Fort Ontario. During World War II, 982 refugees, mostly Jewish people who had fled the Holocaust, were housed there from August 1944 to February 1946. The park's purpose is to preserve and teach about their stories for future generations.

The park would not start right away. The Secretary of the Interior must first decide that enough land, or interests in land, has been acquired inside the "Proposed Boundary" on a September 2024 map to make a manageable park. Within 30 days after that decision, the Secretary must announce the park in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice.

The National Park Service could get land by donation, by purchase with donated or taxpayer-appropriated money, or by exchange. Land owned by the State or a local government could be obtained only by donation. The Secretary could sign agreements with the State and with public or private groups to provide education and interpretation. The Secretary could also make agreements to restore important historic resources on non-federal land in or near the park. Any such agreement that helps non-federal land must allow reasonable public access. Within 3 fiscal years after funding becomes available, the Secretary must finish a general management plan in consultation with the State. The bill text does not give a dollar amount or say how much land is involved.

label: S. 433
title: National Manufacturing Advisory Council Act
short_title: National Manufacturing Advisory Council Act
one: Creates a Commerce Department advisory council of up to 30 industry, labor and academic members to advise on manufacturing policy and send Congress a yearly strategic plan, with no new money.
summary: This bill would set up a National Manufacturing Advisory Council inside the Department of Commerce within 180 days of becoming law. The council would have up to 30 members chosen by the Commerce Secretary. They would come from private industry (including small and mid-sized makers), colleges and universities, and labor unions. The Secretary must also take public suggestions for who to appoint, when practical. It would take over the work of the existing U.S. Manufacturing Council. The council would meet at least every 180 days under federal open-advisory-committee rules. It would advise Commerce on things like worker training, apprenticeships, new technology, supply chain problems, jobs for low-income people and new workers, and employee ownership of companies. It would collect input from rural areas, economically distressed areas, and places hit by factory layoffs. It would also look for federal, state or other regulations that cause unnecessary supply chain disruption, higher prices or costly burdens, and suggest fixes. Every year it would send a national strategic plan and a report of its activities to the Secretary and congressional committees. The bill gives it no new funding. The council would end on September 30 of the fifth year after its first meeting. The council only gives advice; it cannot make rules or spend money.

label: S. 1872
title: Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act
short_title: Critical Infrastructure Manufacturing Feasibility Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department to study which imported products that critical infrastructure depends on could be made in the U.S. (including in rural areas and industrial parks) and to publish a report with recommendations.
summary: This bill orders a study. It does not create new programs, spending, or rules. Within one year of becoming law, the Secretary of Commerce would study the 16 critical infrastructure sectors listed in a 2013 presidential directive. These include areas like energy, water, transportation, health care, and communications. The study would look for products these sectors need to build, run, maintain, or restore themselves that are in high demand and are being imported because of U.S. manufacturing, material, or supply chain limits. The Department would then weigh the costs and benefits of making those products in the U.S., including effects on jobs, labor conditions, and prices. It would pick out the products that could realistically be made here. It would also ask whether they could be made in rural areas, industrial parks, or industrial parks in rural areas, and what stands in the way. Finally, it would identify existing federal policies, regulations, or guidance that may block or raise the cost of domestic manufacturing. Within 18 months, Commerce must send Congress an unclassified report, which may have a classified annex, with recommendations. The report must also be posted publicly on the Commerce website. The bill says it does not give Commerce power to force anyone to hand over information, so the study depends on voluntary cooperation. The bill does not say how much the study would cost or where the money would come from.

title: Historic Greenwood District—Black Wall Street National Monument Establishment Act
short_title: Black Wall Street National Monument Act
one: Creates a National Park System unit in Tulsa, Oklahoma, to preserve and teach the history of the Greenwood District, Black Wall Street, and the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, with a mostly descendant-led advisory commission.
summary: This bill would create the Historic Greenwood District–Black Wall Street National Monument in Tulsa, Oklahoma, as part of the National Park System. Its purpose is to preserve and explain the history of the Greenwood District, the thriving Black business community known as Black Wall Street, and the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre. The monument would not officially exist until the Interior Secretary decides enough land has been acquired to make a manageable park. The Secretary could get land inside the mapped boundary only by donation, by buying from a willing seller, or by swapping land. The bill says it does not affect the rights of private property owners inside or next to the monument. The Secretary could also sign agreements with public or private groups for education, interpretation, and technical help. The National Park Service would run the site under normal park laws and write a management plan within 3 years after money is first made available. The bill also creates an 11-member advisory commission. Seven members would be descendants of people who lived or worked in Greenwood in 1921, three would have historic preservation expertise, and one would be recommended by Tulsa's mayor. Members serve without pay, though travel costs are covered. The commission would end 10 years after the monument is established. The bill exempts the commission from a federal advisory committee law (FACA), which normally sets open-meeting and record rules. It does not give a dollar amount.

label: S. 1092
title: WIPPES Act
short_title: WIPPES Act (Do Not Flush wipe labels)
one: Requires clear "Do Not Flush" words and a symbol on baby, cleaning, and personal care wipes that people might flush, bans claiming they're flushable, and has the FTC enforce it with one national standard.
summary: This bill would make companies that package or sell certain wet wipes put a clear "Do Not Flush" message and symbol on the package. It covers baby and diapering wipes, plus household and personal care wipes (disinfecting, cleaning, makeup removal, feminine and adult hygiene, and similar) that contain petrochemical-derived fibers (plastic-based fibers) and are likely to be flushed. The bill spells out where the label must go for tubs, flexible packs, bulk packs, and combined products. The words and symbol must each cover at least 2 percent of the front panel and stand out with high contrast. Companies could not say or imply that these wipes can or should be flushed. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) would enforce the rule as an unfair or deceptive practice and would issue guidance within 180 days, working with the EPA, FDA, and Consumer Product Safety Commission. That guidance could not be used as the sole basis for enforcement. The rules would start one year after enactment and would not apply to products packaged or sold before then. The bill also blocks states and local governments from setting "Do Not Flush" labeling rules that differ from the federal ones. The aim is to cut sewer clogs and pollution caused by wipes in wastewater systems. The text does not set a dollar amount or create a new grant program.

label: S. 1377
title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
short_title: Theodore Roosevelt National Park Wild Horses Protection Act
one: Requires the Interior Department to keep a genetically diverse herd of at least 150 horses in the South Unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, limits when horses can be removed, and requires yearly public reporting on the herd.
summary:
This bill would change the 1947 law that governs Theodore Roosevelt National Park in North Dakota. It would require the Secretary of the Interior to keep a herd of horses in the park's South Unit. The herd must be genetically diverse, meaning varied enough to stay healthy over time, and must have at least 150 horses.

Within 120 days of becoming law, Interior must write a plan for managing the horses. The plan must be cost-effective and must make sure the park's natural resources, such as grasslands and wildlife habitat, are not harmed.

The bill also limits removing horses from federal land in the park. Removal is allowed only as part of a plan to keep the herd genetically diverse, in an emergency, or to protect public health and safety. As written, the text joins these conditions in a slightly unusual way, so how they fit together could be a question for the agency or courts.

Finally, each year Interior must monitor the herd and publish what it finds about the herd's size, makeup, and health. The bill does not add money. It does not say how many horses is too many, or what happens if the herd and the park's plants and wildlife come into conflict. The bill passed the Senate on June 11, 2026, and is now in the House Natural Resources Committee.

label: S. 1437
title: ASCEND Act
short_title: ASCEND Act (NASA Commercial Satellite Data Program)
one: The bill makes NASA's program for buying commercial Earth-imaging satellite data a permanent, formal program in law, with rules protecting scientific publication, favoring U.S. vendors, and requiring yearly reports to Congress.
summary:
The ASCEND Act would write into federal law a NASA program that buys Earth-observation data and images from commercial satellite companies. NASA has run this as the Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition pilot since 2019 and has called it a success. The bill would rename it the Commercial Satellite Data Acquisition Program and place it in NASA's Earth Science Division. NASA would use it to get data cost-effectively for its own science needs and, where appropriate, for other federal agencies and researchers.

The bill sets several rules. Contracts with vendors cannot block scientists from publishing the commercial data or images in academic or scientific papers. They also cannot block publishing information derived from or built on that data. NASA may write or change license terms so that people outside NASA-funded projects can use the data as widely as possible. NASA must buy from U.S. vendors (companies or nonprofits incorporated in the U.S.) as much as practical.

NASA must report to Congress within 180 days of enactment and then every year. The reports must list vendors, describe license terms, explain how each vendor advances science (including National Academies priorities), and say whether agreements allow use by federal employees, contractors, or non-federal users. The bill does not give a specific dollar amount. It does not create new spending on its own, so costs would come from NASA's regular budget.

Accessing Satellite Capabilities to Enable New Discoveries Act or the ASCEND Act
This bill provides statutory authority for the Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition (CSDA) program run by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Through the CSDA program, NASA acquires remote sensing data and imagery from commercial satellites to support its Earth science research. (
Remote sensing
 generally refers to the collection of data by instruments in Earth’s orbit, such as satellites, that can be processed into imagery of Earth’s surface.)
Under the bill, NASA may establish or modify end-use agreements to allow for broad use of data and imagery acquired under the program, including by individuals outside of NASA (e.g., other federal agencies). The terms of any data or imagery acquisition may not prevent the publication of such data or imagery for scientific purposes or the publication of information derived from it. To the extent practicable, NASA must acquire such data and imagery from U.S. vendors.

environment.reason: The bill sets up a data purchasing program and does not directly protect or harm water, air, land, or ecosystems; any environmental benefit depends on later use of the data.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on publication rules bars vendor contract terms from blocking publication of data-based scientific papers, and the annual reports list vendors, license terms, and who may use the data, which adds some public visibility; however, the reports go to Congress without a public-release requirement.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill directs federal purchases from commercial vendors and allows steady government revenue for companies, but it also sets broad public-use license terms and publication protections, so the effects on the balance between people and profit are mixed.

local_say.reason: The bill concerns a federal NASA program and does not change how states, localities, or communities make land use, facility, or permit decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill authorizes data purchases paid from NASA's regular budget and does not involve rescuing failing companies or shifting costs to ratepayers.

equality.reason: Under the license-term provision, NASA may set terms allowing use by people outside NASA-funded projects as widely as possible, and the reports track non-federal access, which broadens equal access to the data; the U.S.-vendor preference is a counterweight, so the net effect is modest.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal remedies or due process; its reporting requirement adds some oversight but does not create new enforceable rights.

personal_freedom.reason: The publication protections in the bill bar contract terms that would prevent scientists from publishing results and derived information, expanding what researchers may legally say and publish.

label: S. 282
title: Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument Access Act
short_title: Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument Access Act
one: Lets the Interior Secretary add land to Maine's Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument from willing sellers only, protects hunting, fishing and fiddlehead picking, and sets rules for logging-road safety and public education.
summary:
This bill covers the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument in Maine. It keeps the monument's current boundaries but lets the Secretary of the Interior add land in a mapped area next to it. The land can be bought from willing sellers, donated, or swapped. The bill clearly bans the use of eminent domain, which is the government's power to force a land sale. Any land added becomes part of the monument.

The monument would be run under this bill, the 2016 presidential proclamation that created it, and the laws for National Park System units. On newly acquired land, hunting, fishing and other outdoor recreation that already happened before the purchase must continue, in line with the proclamation. People may gather fiddlehead ferns by hand for personal use, though the Secretary can limit this if it could harm monument resources. The Park Service must work with local communities and Tribal governments to teach the public about the area's natural and human history, including Native land use and past timber management. The Secretary may do non-commercial timber harvests when needed under the management plan. Existing rights, including access through the monument for timber removal outside it, are protected. The Secretary must also provide safety information and work with stakeholders so visitors and logging trucks can share roads safely. Finally, the Secretary may acquire up to 10 acres near the monument for offices and visitor services, and may make agreements with Maine, local or Tribal governments, or private groups, including to build a shared information center.

National Park Service and Department of the Interior

Keeps traditional uses such as hunting, fishing and fiddlehead picking.

Safety measures could reduce conflicts between visitors and logging trucks.
A shared information center could improve visitor access.
concerns: Allowing hunting and recreation to continue on acquired land could limit some conservation protections.
Noncommercial timber harvests are allowed inside a national monument, which some conservation supporters may dislike.
Protecting existing timber access rights means logging traffic continues near the monument.
Some local residents may oppose expanding federal land ownership even with willing sellers.
imp.cost: The text gives no dollar amounts. Land purchases, the 10-acre site and the safety and education work would need federal funding, likely through appropriations (money Congress approves separately). Donations and agreements with outside partners could offset some costs.
unknowns: Total cost of buying land and building facilities is not stated.

What counts as 'necessary' timber harvest is left to the Secretary.
How the Secretary would decide to limit fiddlehead gathering is not detailed.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to set rules for the Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument in Maine, keep its current boundaries, and let the Secretary of the Interior add nearby land from willing sellers, donations, or land swaps, with no eminent domain. It also aims to keep existing uses such as hunting, fishing, and fiddlehead gathering, add public education and visitor safety measures, and allow shared visitor facilities.

oppose: The bill allows hunting, fishing, and other recreation to continue on newly acquired land, which could limit some conservation protections there.

support: The bill can only add land from willing sellers, through purchase, donation, or swap. It bans eminent domain, so landowners are not forced to sell.
The bill could protect more forest, river, and wildlife habitat near the monument, which may help the region's natural resources over time.
The bill keeps traditional uses such as hunting, fishing, and fiddlehead picking, and it lets the Park Service limit fiddlehead gathering if it could harm monument resources.

The bill requires public education developed with local communities and Tribal governments about the area's natural and human history, including Native land use. It also requires safety information so visitors and logging trucks can share roads more safely.

environment.reason: Sec. on boundary expansion lets the Secretary add land next to the monument from willing sellers, donations or swaps, and added land becomes part of the monument, which can protect forest, river and wildlife habitat; noncommercial timber harvests and continued hunting on new land partly offset this.

transparency_kindness.reason: The education provision requires the Park Service to work with local communities and Tribal governments to present natural and human history, including Native land use and past timber management, giving a fuller account; the bill also requires safety information for visitors and logging trucks.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill protects existing timber access for logging operations and allows noncommercial harvests, but it does not clearly shift costs to consumers or favor corporate gains beyond that; effects are mixed.

local_say.reason: Sec. bans eminent domain and relies on willing sellers, and the Secretary must work with local communities, Tribal governments, Maine and local governments on agreements and stakeholder safety work, giving local input more weight.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts or ratepayer rate shifts; federal land purchases would be funded through appropriations, which is not a bailout.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same willing-seller and no-eminent-domain rules to all landowners and gives the public the same access; it does not create unequal treatment for any group.

justice.reason: The bill bans eminent domain for the added land, which protects landowners from forced sale, and requires safety information and stakeholder coordination for visitors and logging traffic.

personal_freedom.reason: The fiddlehead gathering provision lets people gather ferns by hand for personal use, and hunting, fishing and recreation on newly acquired land must continue, though the Secretary may limit fiddlehead gathering if it could harm monument resources.

label: H.R. 3174
title: Made in America Manufacturing Finance Act
short_title: Made in America Manufacturing Finance Act
one: Raises the maximum government-backed loan sizes for small U.S. manufacturers under the SBA's 7(a) and 504 loan programs.
summary:
This bill would let small manufacturers borrow more through two Small Business Administration (SBA) loan programs. These programs don't lend money directly. Instead, the government guarantees part of a loan made by a bank or lender, so the lender takes less risk.

First, the bill defines a "small manufacturer." It must be a small business whose main business is manufacturing (industry sectors 31, 32 or 33) and whose production facilities are all in the United States.

Second, in the 7(a) program, which covers working capital and operating needs, the bill raises the cap on the guaranteed portion of a loan for small manufacturers from $3.75 million to $7.5 million. It raises the cap for certain loans from $4.5 million to $9 million. The cap for export-related loans goes from $5 million to $10 million. The bill also sets the gross loan amount at $10 million. That is the total loan size.

Third, in the 504 program, which pays for big fixed assets like buildings and equipment, the maximum for small manufacturers goes from $5.5 million to $10 million.

The bill gives no new money, no spending amount, and no changes to environmental, labor or oversight rules. It says nothing about who pays if loans default. Federal loan guarantees carry some risk of taxpayer losses. SBA loans usually charge borrowers fees meant to offset those costs. The bill text doesn't say how this change would affect those fees or the program's overall cost.

Raises the 7(a) cap for the related higher-limit category from $4.5 million to $9 million for small manufacturers, with no more than $8 million used for working capital, supplies, or export financing.
Raises the cap on 7(a) export-related loans (paragraph 14) for small manufacturers from $5 million to $10 million.
Raises the maximum 504 loan (Small Business Investment Act section 502) for small manufacturers from $5.5 million to $10 million.
Makes no changes to appropriations, fees, or environmental or labor standards in the text provided.

No new environmental or safety conditions are attached, so larger loans could fund more polluting facilities.
Loans of up to $10 million are big for 'small' businesses and could favor larger firms within the small-business category.
Only manufacturers benefit, not other small businesses.
imp.cost: The text has no appropriation and no cost estimate. The guaranteed loans are backed by the federal government, so costs depend on defaults and on fees borrowers pay. I did not see a Congressional Budget Office estimate.
unknowns: Official cost estimate and effect on SBA loan subsidy rates or fees.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help small manufacturers get more financing by raising the maximum loan amounts under two Small Business Administration programs: the 7(a) program, which covers working capital and operating needs, and the 504 program, which covers major fixed assets such as new facilities. The bill defines a small manufacturer as a small business whose primary business is in manufacturing sectors (NAICS 31, 32, 33) and whose production facilities are all in the United States.

oppose: The bill roughly doubles federal loan guarantee limits for 7(a) and 504 loans. Larger guarantees could mean bigger taxpayer losses if borrowers default, and the bill does not say how this would affect fees or the program's overall cost.

Loans of up to $10 million are large for a 'small' business. Critics could argue that the benefit may go mostly to bigger firms within the small-business category rather than the smallest manufacturers.
The bill helps only manufacturers. Other small businesses that do not make goods would not receive the higher limits, which some could see as unfair.

Made in America Manufacturing Finance Act
This bill increases the maximum loan amounts available to small manufacturers under the Small Business Administration's 7(a) and 504 loan programs.

label: S. 1055
title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
short_title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
one: Gives American Indian and Alaska Native patients, or their providers, 15 days instead of 72 hours to notify the Indian Health Service of emergency care received outside IHS facilities so the care can be paid for.
summary: The Indian Health Service (IHS) runs a program called Purchased/Referred Care (PRC). It pays for medical care that American Indian and Alaska Native patients get from outside providers when IHS or tribal facilities can't provide it. Today, if a patient has an emergency and goes to a non-IHS hospital or provider, someone must tell the PRC program within 72 hours after treatment starts or the patient is admitted. If no one does, payment can be denied. This bill changes that deadline to 15 days. People who are elderly or disabled already have a 30-day deadline, and that would stay the same. The bill is very short. It amends Section 406 of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act by adding a general 15-day rule and keeping the existing special rule for elderly or disabled Indians. The patient, someone acting for the patient, or the medical provider can send the notice. The bill does not add money or create a new program. It changes only a paperwork deadline that is a condition of payment. The CRS summary does not give a cost estimate. The deadline change could reduce denied claims, which can leave patients with large bills after an emergency.

Adds a new subsection (a) to Section 406 of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act (25 U.S.C. 1646) and renames the existing text as subsection (b).

IHS Purchased/Referred Care program staff and authorizing officials
Tribal health programs and rural communities with few IHS facilities nearby
Elderly or disabled Indians, whose 30-day deadline stays the same

benefits: Fewer emergency claims could be denied for late notice.
Patients may avoid large unexpected medical bills.
Providers outside IHS have more time to find out a patient's eligibility and file notice.
Could help patients in rural or remote areas, where emergency care often happens far from IHS facilities.
concerns: The 15-day deadline is still shorter than the 30 days for elderly or disabled patients, and a deadline can still cause denials.
Longer notice windows could slightly increase PRC program costs or make budget planning harder, though no estimate is given.
The bill does not fix the larger problem of PRC funding shortfalls.

unknowns: Cost estimate: none was provided.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give more time to notify the Indian Health Service's Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program about emergency care that American Indian and Alaska Native patients receive from non-IHS providers or facilities. Under current law, the notice deadline is 72 hours, and missing it can lead to payment being denied. The bill extends that deadline to 15 days, while keeping the 30-day deadline for elderly or disabled Indians.

oppose: The bill lengthens the notice window for emergency claims, which could increase PRC program costs or make budget planning harder. The summary does not include a cost estimate, so the size of this effect is unknown.

crs:
Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
This bill extends from 72 hours to 15 days the time period to notify the Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program of emergency medical care received from a non-Indian Health Service (IHS) medical provider or at a non-IHS medical facility. This bill does not apply to individuals who are elderly or disabled, who continue to have a 30-day notification requirement for emergency services.
The IHS provides medical and dental services directly to American Indian and Alaska Native patients whenever possible. The PRC program pays for medical or dental care that is provided away from an IHS or tribal health care facility. The PRC program must be notified of requests for authorization of payment for health care services from a non-IHS provider.
Currently in emergency cases, the patient, an individual on behalf of the patient, or the medical care provider must, within 72 hours after the beginning of treatment for the condition or after admission to a health care facility, notify a PRC authorizing official of the need for the emergency medical care. This bill instead allows the patient, other individual, or provider to notify PRC within 15 days of the treatment or admission.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. (a) extends the notice window from 72 hours to 15 days, giving patients and providers more time to provide truthful eligibility and treatment information before a claim can be denied, which reduces the chance a patient is left with an unexpected bill.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. (a) makes it less likely that a late-notice technicality causes non-IHS providers to lose payment, which shifts some burden away from providers' revenue and toward the PRC program, and the bill directs the benefit toward patients facing large bills.

no_bailouts.reason: Sec. (a) makes more emergency claims payable from existing PRC funds that would otherwise be denied for late notice, which could shift costs to the federal program and its funding base, though the bill adds no new money and no estimate is given.

equality.reason: The 15-day rule applies to all American Indian and Alaska Native patients who use emergency care from non-IHS providers, and the existing 30-day rule for elderly or disabled Indians is kept in new subsection (b), so the change applies uniformly within each group.

justice.reason: Sec. (a) reduces the chance that a payment is denied on a procedural timing condition alone, giving patients and providers a longer and more workable window to obtain a remedy for emergency care.

label: S. 1514
title: Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act
short_title: Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act
one: Moves about 72 acres of Washington land from the U.S. Forest Service to the Interior Department, places it in trust for the Quinault Indian Nation as part of its reservation, and bars casino-style gaming there.
summary:
This short bill would take about 72 acres of land in Washington State, known in the bill as Allotment 1157, away from the U.S. Forest Service and hand it to the Department of the Interior. The Interior Department would then hold the land in trust (meaning the federal government holds legal title for the benefit of the tribe) for the Quinault Indian Nation. Once in trust, the land would become part of the Quinault Indian Reservation and would be managed under the rules that generally apply to tribal trust land.

The bill keeps in place any existing rights on the land, such as easements (permission to cross or use land), rights-of-way, permits, utility corridors, and access rights. These would continue after the transfer unless they are changed or ended under federal law.

The bill bans gaming on the new trust land. That means the tribe could not open a casino or other gaming operation there under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, which is the federal law that governs tribal gaming.

The bill also deals with contamination. Before taking the land into trust, Interior must meet the disclosure requirements for hazardous substances (dangerous materials) under a federal cleanup law called CERCLA. However, Interior is not required to clean up or reduce any contamination that is found.

The bill states that nothing in it affects the tribe's treaty rights under the 1855-1856 Treaty of Olympia. The Congressional Research Service summary describes the transfer as administrative, meaning it is handled by agency action rather than a new program with new spending. The bill text does not list any cost or funding amount.

The bill was introduced April 29, 2025 by Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA), with one cosponsor. Its latest recorded action is "Held at the desk," and the metadata lists it as scheduled for a House floor vote.
does: Transfers about 72 acres in Washington (Allotment 1157, shown on a map dated February 2, 2024) from the U.S. Forest Service to the Department of the Interior, subject to existing valid rights.
Requires Interior to take the land into trust for the Quinault Indian Nation, and makes it part of the Quinault Indian Reservation.
Keeps existing easements, rights-of-way, permits, utility corridors, and access rights in effect unless changed or ended under federal law.
Requires the land to be administered under the rules generally applied to federal trust land held for tribes.
Prohibits gaming on the land under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.
Requires Interior to meet hazardous-substance disclosure rules under CERCLA section 120(h) for the transfer, but does not require cleanup or abatement of any contamination.
States that the bill does not affect the tribe's treaty rights under the Treaty of Olympia (1855-1856).
who: Quinault Indian Nation, which gains trust land within its reservation.
U.S. Forest Service, which gives up the land.
Department of the Interior, which takes on the land in trust.
Current holders of easements, rights-of-way, permits, or access rights on the land, whose rights carry over.
Nearby residents and visitors who use the area, and anyone concerned about possible contamination on the parcel.

benefits: Gives the Quinault Indian Nation trust land inside its reservation, which can support tribal self-determination over the land.
Keeps existing easements, permits, and access rights in place, so current users are not cut off by the transfer.
Bars gaming on the parcel, which the bill states directly.
concerns: The bill does not require cleanup of any hazardous substances or contamination found on the land, so pollution could remain.
Because only disclosure is required, the public may not learn about contamination unless it is reported through that process.
imp.cost: The bill text does not state any dollar amount or funding source. The CRS summary describes the transfer as administrative, meaning it is done through agency action rather than new spending.
unknowns: The bill text does not say what contamination exists on the parcel or how severe it is.
The bill does not say whether the Forest Service or Interior would pay for any future cleanup.
The bill text does not describe the land's current uses beyond the rights it preserves, so its effect on local recreation or water is unclear.
The latest action is 'Held at the desk,' so it is unclear when or whether a vote will occur.

crs:
Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act
This bill administratively transfers approximately 72 acres of specified lands in Washington from the U.S. Forest Service to the Department of the Interior. environment.reason: Sec. on CERCLA: Interior must meet hazardous-substance disclosure rules but is not required to clean up or abate any contamination found, so existing pollution could remain on the parcel.

transparency_kindness.reason: The CERCLA section 120(h) disclosure requirement means hazardous-substance information about the parcel must be disclosed before the land is taken into trust.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill transfers land between federal agencies to trust status for a tribe and does not clearly shift costs to corporations or consumers or favor corporate profit either way.

local_say.reason: The bill moves land to tribal trust and reservation status without a clear new public comment or local decision-making process, and it neither clearly adds nor removes local or state input.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no bailout or ratepayer provisions; the CRS summary describes the transfer as administrative with no funding amount.

equality.reason: The bill applies to a specific parcel for one tribe; it does not clearly create unequal treatment of individuals, and the gaming ban applies to this land only under existing federal gaming law.

justice.reason: The bill keeps existing easements and rights and sets a disclosure step, but provides no clear new remedy or accountability mechanism for contamination harm.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill keeps existing access rights and does not clearly expand or restrict what individuals may do; the gaming ban restricts only the tribe's option on this parcel.

title: Secure Space Act of 2026
short_title: Secure Space Act of 2026
one: Bars the FCC from granting satellite licenses, U.S. market access, or earth station authorizations to companies on its national-security "Covered List" (like Huawei and ZTE) or their affiliates.
summary: This bill would add a new section to the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019. It would stop the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from approving satellite licenses, permission for foreign-licensed satellites to serve the U.S. market, or ground-station (earth station) authorizations when the holder or controller is on the FCC's "Covered List." That list names companies whose equipment or services are judged to pose an unacceptable national security risk. Huawei and ZTE are examples. The ban also covers "affiliates," meaning companies that own, control, are controlled by, or share a parent with a listed company. Owning 10 percent or more counts as ownership. The bill also lets, but does not require, the FCC to publish a report on supply chain security risks. That report would look at satellite and earth station licensees that use equipment made by listed companies. The bill says this does not expand or shrink the FCC's existing powers. The ban would apply only to licenses, petitions, and authorizations granted after the bill becomes law. It would not undo existing ones. The FCC would have one year after enactment to write rules to carry this out. The bill does not authorize new spending. Its stated focus is national security in satellite communications, not environmental, consumer pricing, or local-control issues.
does: Prohibits the FCC from granting satellite system licenses (geostationary or non-geostationary orbit) to entities on its Covered List or their affiliates.
Prohibits the FCC from granting petitions for U.S. market access for foreign-licensed satellite systems if held or controlled by a listed entity or affiliate.
Prohibits the FCC from authorizing individually licensed or blanket-licensed earth stations (including gateway stations) held or controlled by listed entities or affiliates.

Defines 'affiliate' as any entity that directly or indirectly owns, controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with another entity, with ownership meaning at least a 10 percent equity interest.
Allows, but does not require, the FCC to issue a report assessing supply chain security risks for licensees that use equipment from listed companies; this does not expand or reduce FCC authority.
Applies only to licenses, petitions, and authorizations granted on or after the date of enactment, so existing ones are not covered.
Requires the FCC to issue implementing rules within one year of enactment.
who: Companies on the FCC Covered List (e.g., Huawei, ZTE) and their affiliates seeking satellite or ground station approvals
Satellite operators and foreign-licensed satellite companies seeking U.S. market access
Earth station operators and companies that buy equipment from listed vendors
The FCC, which must write rules within a year
U.S. consumers and businesses relying on satellite communications

benefits: Could lower the risk that equipment or services judged a national security threat end up in U.S. satellite networks.
Gives a clear statutory rule instead of leaving the decision to FCC discretion.
Applies only going forward, so it avoids sudden disruption to existing services.
concerns: The optional supply chain report may not produce any public transparency.
The 10 percent ownership affiliate test could sweep in companies with minor or indirect ties.
Compliance could add costs for operators that may be passed to customers.
Existing licenses held by listed entities are not covered.
imp.cost: No spending or funding is authorized in the bill. The FCC would bear rulemaking costs from its existing budget. No cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: How many pending or future applicants are affected.
How the FCC will treat affiliate relationships in practice.
Whether the FCC will choose to publish the optional report.
Effects on satellite service prices or availability.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to protect U.S. national security in satellite communications by barring the FCC from granting satellite licenses, market access for foreign-licensed satellites, or earth station authorizations to entities on the FCC's Covered List (such as Huawei and ZTE) or their affiliates. The bill's official title is the Secure Space Act of 2026, and its CRS summary describes it as adding a new section to the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019.

oppose: The bill applies a 10 percent ownership threshold to define 'affiliate,' which could reach companies with only minor or indirect ties to a listed company, possibly blocking firms that pose no real security risk.
Compliance work and possible added costs for satellite and ground-station operators could be passed on to customers, and the bill does not include any funding to offset them.

The bill covers only licenses and authorizations granted after it becomes law, so existing licenses held by listed entities are not affected. Critics could argue this leaves a gap in the protection it claims to provide.
The supply chain risk report is optional, so the FCC is not required to publish public information about which licensees use equipment from listed companies, which limits transparency.
support: The bill would stop the FCC from licensing satellites or ground stations tied to companies its own Covered List identifies as national security risks, such as Huawei and ZTE.
By writing the rule into law, the bill would give a clear, consistent standard rather than leaving each decision to FCC discretion.
Applying the rule only to new licenses and authorizations avoids sudden disruption to services that already operate in the U.S.
The ban extends to affiliates, so a listed company cannot avoid the rule simply by working through a related company that owns or controls it.

crs:
Secure Space Act of 2025
This bill prohibits the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from granting satellite licenses or earth station authorizations, including U.S. market access for foreign-licensed satellites, to specified foreign entities of concern and their affiliates. (Earth stations, also commonly known as ground stations, are earth-based radio stations that communicate with satellites. A grant of U.S. market access permits one or more foreign-licensed satellites to communicate with one or more U.S.-licensed earth stations.)
Specifically, the FCC may not grant a satellite license, an earth station authorization, or market access to any entity, or an affiliate thereof, that produces or provides communications equipment or services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. (The FCC maintains a list of such equipment and services, known as the Covered List. Providers of such equipment and services include, for example, Huawei Technologies Company and ZTE Corporation.)

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill's optional FCC supply chain report could add some public information, but it is discretionary and the bill does not require public release, so the net effect on transparency is unclear.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill restricts certain listed companies from FCC approvals for national security reasons; any compliance costs passed to customers are speculative and not directly required by the text, so the effect is unclear.

local_say.reason: The bill concerns federal FCC licensing decisions and does not create new roles for state or local governments or communities in siting or permitting.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no provisions about bailouts, subsidies, or shifting costs to ratepayers, and authorizes no spending.

equality.reason: The bill applies one rule to all entities on the Covered List and their affiliates based on national security grounds rather than treating groups differently by identity; the 10 percent affiliate test applies uniformly.

justice.reason: The bill creates a clear statutory standard for FCC decisions, but it does not add due process, appeal, or remedy rights for affected companies, so the net effect on legal fairness is unclear.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill restricts which companies may obtain satellite licenses, not what individuals may do, say, or choose about their own lives.

label: S. 3219
title: Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2026
short_title: Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2026
one: Moves about 9.89 acres of federal land in Albuquerque, once part of the Albuquerque Indian School, into trust for the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico, gives the buildings to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, and bans gaming on the land.
summary: This bill would return three pieces of federal land in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico. The land is about 9.89 acres and was once part of the Albuquerque Indian School, a boarding school for Native children that operated until 1981. The General Services Administration (GSA), which manages federal property, would have 90 days after the bill becomes law to hand control of the land to the Department of the Interior. Interior would then have another 90 days to take the land "into trust" for the Pueblos. Trust land is owned by the United States but held for a tribe's benefit and is covered by federal Indian trust law. The bill says the land must be used for the Pueblos' education, health, culture, business and economic development. It stays subject to existing private and city rights-of-way, easements and utility agreements. Interior would also give all buildings and improvements on the land to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a nonprofit owned and run by the 19 Pueblos. Federal agencies now on Tract 2 could stay under a lease of up to 24 months. That lease could be extended if both sides agree, and tenants could leave early. A new survey and all encumbrance records would be filed in the public records of Bernalillo County and with the Bureau of Indian Affairs. Gaming, such as casinos, would be banned on the land. The bill gives no cost estimate in its text.
does: Within 90 days of enactment, requires GSA to transfer administrative control of three tracts (about 9.89 acres total: 3.57, 5.78 and 0.54 acres) in Albuquerque to the Interior Secretary.
Within 90 days after that transfer, requires Interior to take all U.S. right, title and interest in the land into trust for the 19 named New Mexico Pueblos.
Requires land use for educational, health, cultural, business and economic development of the Pueblos, under federal Indian trust land laws.
Keeps the land subject to existing private or municipal encumbrances, rights-of-way, easements of record and utility service agreements.

Requires Interior to obtain a survey and a copy of all encumbrances from GSA, allows minor clerical or survey corrections, and requires the records be filed with the Bernalillo County Clerk and the Bureau of Indian Affairs land titles office.
Requires Interior to convey federal ownership of all buildings and improvements on the land to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, to own outright (in fee), within 90 days of the transfer.
Requires a lease letting current federal tenants stay on Tract 2 for an initial term of up to 24 months, extendable by mutual written agreement, with tenants able to end it early.
Prohibits Class II and Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act on the land.
who: The 19 Pueblos of New Mexico, which would gain trust land
The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, which would receive the buildings
Federal agencies and tenants now using the land, especially on Tract 2
GSA and the Department of the Interior, which carry out the transfers
Albuquerque residents and neighbors, and utilities or others holding easements
Descendants of Albuquerque Indian School students and Native communities

benefits: Returns land tied to a painful boarding school history to the Pueblos' control.
Lets the Pueblos use the land for education, health, culture and economic development.
Gives buildings to a nonprofit owned by the 19 Pueblos rather than selling them.
Records the survey and encumbrances in public records.
Protects existing easements and utility agreements, and bars gaming.
concerns: Trust land generally leaves local property tax and city regulation, so neighbors may have less say.
Federal tenants might need to move, which could disrupt services if timing is tight.
The gaming ban limits one way the Pueblos could earn money from the land.
The CRS summary and bill text differ on some provisions, which may cause confusion.
imp.cost: The bill text states no appropriation or cost. Costs would include federal administrative work, the survey, and possibly the loss of federal property value or tenant relocation. No official estimate was provided.
unknowns: No cost estimate or value of the land and buildings is given.
Whether environmental conditions on the old school site have been assessed or who pays for any cleanup.
How Albuquerque would be affected by lost tax revenue or changed land-use authority.
Where federal tenants would go and what relocation would cost.
Which version of the bill the CRS summary describes, since it differs from the text.

stage.last_action: Held at the desk.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to return about 9.89 acres of federal land in Albuquerque, New Mexico, that was once part of the Albuquerque Indian School to the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico. It would place the land into trust for the Pueblos' educational, health, cultural, business, and economic development. The bill's summary describes the land's history as a boarding school that operated until 1981.

oppose: Taking the land into federal trust generally removes it from local property tax rolls and city zoning control, so neighbors and local governments may have less say over future uses.

The bill moves federal tenants off Tract 2 and requires a warehouse relocation, which could disrupt government services if the timeline proves too tight. A constituent could ask how the agencies will be supported during the move.
The bill bans Class II and Class III gaming on the land. Some constituents may see this as a limit on a tool the Pueblos could use to raise revenue, and may ask whether the ban is needed.
support: The land is tied to the Albuquerque Indian School, a boarding school that operated until 1981. Returning it to the Pueblos can be seen as a step toward addressing that history.
The bill limits use of the land to education, health, cultural, business, and economic development for the Pueblos, which gives a clear public purpose for the site.

The bill transfers buildings to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, a nonprofit owned by the 19 Pueblos, and keeps existing easements and utility agreements in place. It also requires the survey and encumbrance records to be filed in public records.

crs:
Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2025
This bill takes three tracts of specified federal land (approximately 9.89 acres) in Albuquerque, New Mexico, into trust for the benefit of the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico. (These three tracts of land were historically part of the Albuquerque Indian School, which was an Indian boarding school until 1981.)
The land is currently administered by the General Services Administration (GSA). Within 90 days of this bill's enactment and the relocation of all federal tenants, the bill requires (1) the GSA to transfer administrative jurisdiction over the land to the Department of the Interior, and (2) Interior to take the land into trust for the benefit of the 19 Pueblos.
The land taken into trust must be subject to a right-of-way easement, as determined by the GSA, on the federal land located within Tract 1 for purposes of retrieving or relocating federal property from the land to another location. (Tract 1, which is approximately 3.57 acres, contains a warehouse that is 76,682 square feet.)
The bill requires the land taken into trust to be used for the educational, health, cultural, business, and economic development of the 19 Pueblos. Further, the land must remain subject to existing private and municipal encumbrances, rights-of-way, restrictions, easements of record, and utility service agreements.
The bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

environment.reason: The bill does not address water, air, or land cleanliness or environmental review; it transfers land with existing use and no stated environmental provisions.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on survey and records requires the new survey and all encumbrance records to be filed in Bernalillo County public records and with the Bureau of Indian Affairs, making land records more visible to the public.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. on buildings transfers all buildings and improvements to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center rather than selling them, and the land is held for Pueblo education, health, and economic development rather than sold to private buyers.

local_say.reason: Trust status generally removes land from local property tax and city land-use regulation, so Albuquerque and neighbors would have less say, though the Pueblos (a tribal government) gain control of the land.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill involves transferring federal land and buildings without any corporate bailout or ratepayer cost shift; it has no cost estimate, but nothing in it shifts costs to taxpayers or ratepayers in a clear way.

equality.reason: The bill applies to a specific set of tribes and tracts; it grants land to named Pueblos as a federal trust remedy, which is a targeted action but is not clearly an unequal treatment of people under the law.

justice.reason: Sec. on return of land addresses a boarding school history by returning land to the Pueblos and provides defined deadlines and remedies for transfer, making the process more accountable.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not meaningfully expand or restrict what individuals may do about their own lives, aside from banning gaming on the land, which is a limit on tribal and business activity there.

news.overall: The evidence is thin: each group has only two headlines, truncated in the input, and none of them mention the Albuquerque Indian School Act. Lean Left coverage in these samples leans toward culture and criminal investigation, while Center coverage leans toward federal resource policy and a law enforcement search. Because the bill itself is absent from every item, this analysis cannot compare how outlets framed the legislation, and it would need articles that cover the bill directly.

label: S. 3257
title: John A. Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act
short_title: John A. Hauser Mental Health in Aviation Act
one: The bill directs the FAA to make it easier and less stigmatized for pilots and air traffic controllers to seek mental health care and still get medical clearance to work, and it authorizes up to $15 million per year for three years to support that work.
summary: This bill aims to help pilots and air traffic controllers get mental health care without fearing they will lose their jobs. Within 18 months, the head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) must update its medical rules and guidance to encourage people to seek help and to disclose mental health conditions or symptoms. The FAA must also carry out the recommendations of a 2024 expert committee on mental health and medical clearances within two years. If it declines any recommendation, it must explain why to Congress. The bill requires regular reviews of the "special issuance" process. This is the way pilots with certain medical conditions can still get cleared to fly. The reviews would consider approving more medications and treatments and giving doctors who do aviation medical exams more mental health training. Congress would authorize up to $15 million a year for fiscal years 2026 to 2028 to hire and train more aviation medical examiners, including psychiatrists, and to clear a backlog of cases. The FAA must also run a public education campaign through 2028 to reduce stigma, publicize support services, and build trust between the FAA and aviation workers. It would work with airlines, flight schools and airports. The bill expands the groups the FAA must consult, including unions and flight schools. It also requires reports and briefings to Congress. The text does not change safety standards directly. How much the FAA loosens or tightens rules depends on its later decisions.
does: Within 18 months, requires the FAA Administrator to update medical regulations (including 14 CFR part 67) and guidance to encourage pilots and controllers to seek help for, and disclose, mental health conditions or symptoms.

Amends the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 so the mental health task group must get feedback from airline, charter and general aviation professionals, air traffic controller and pilot unions, accredited aviation universities, and flight schools. Its report must also review National Transportation Safety Board recommendations and cite the clinical research and protocols it relied on.

Says the Administrator 'may' act on the task group's recommendations within 180 days of the bill's enactment and of each report. If the Administrator declines a recommendation, the Administrator must send Congress a justification within 90 days.

Requires reviews of the mental health 'special issuance' process (medical clearance with conditions), starting 180 days after the first task group report. Reviews are yearly for two years, then every three years. They consider approving more medications and treatments, more mental health training for aviation medical examiners, possibly letting trained examiners issue more certificates, and improving the process overall.

Authorizes up to $15 million per year for fiscal years 2026-2028 for the FAA Office of Aerospace Medicine. The money would recruit and train more aviation medical examiners (including psychiatrists), expand oversight, clear the backlog of special issuance cases, provide mental health training, and support related activities.

Within two years, requires the FAA to implement, as appropriate, the recommendations of the 2024 Mental Health & Aviation Medical Clearances Aviation Rulemaking Committee. It must consult the listed stakeholders and cite clinical evidence for recommendation 6. It may commission studies to fill data gaps, to be finished within one year. It must explain to Congress any refusal to implement a recommendation.

Requires a public information campaign for fiscal years 2026-2028 to reduce stigma, publicize support services, and improve trust between the FAA and aviation workers. It includes online information, postings at medical examiner offices, and outreach to airlines, flight schools and airports.
Requires a briefing to Congress within 90 days of launching the campaign, and a report within two years of implementation on outreach results and stakeholder feedback.
who: Pilots and student pilots
Air traffic controllers
FAA Office of Aerospace Medicine and aviation medical examiners
Airlines, flight schools, and airports (asked to share information)
Aviation unions and professional groups consulted by the FAA
The flying public, through possible effects on aviation safety
Federal taxpayers (up to $15 million per year for three years)

benefits: Could make aviation workers more willing to seek mental health care early, which may help them and the public.
May cut the backlog and delays in medical certification.
Requires the FAA to justify refusing expert recommendations, which adds accountability.
Calls for evidence-based review of medications and treatments.
Gives unions, flight schools, and workers a formal role through consultation.
concerns: The FAA 'may' act on task group recommendations, so results depend on agency discretion.
Loosening medical standards could raise safety questions if it isn't backed by strong evidence, though the bill requires citing clinical research.
It authorizes up to $15 million per year, but the money must still be appropriated.
Disclosure encouragement may not remove workers' fear of losing certification if the FAA process stays burdensome.
imp.cost: Authorizes up to $15,000,000 per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2028 (up to $45 million total) for the FAA Office of Aerospace Medicine. Congress would still have to appropriate the money. The bill doesn't state a separate cost for the public information campaign.
unknowns: Which changes the FAA will actually adopt from the 2024 committee recommendations.
Which medications or treatments might be newly approved for pilots and controllers.
Whether Congress will appropriate the full $15 million per year.
How much the public campaign will cost and where that money comes from.
Whether the stated deadlines will be met.
