purpose: The bill says its goal is to help pilots and air traffic controllers get mental health care without fearing they will lose their jobs or certification. It aims to encourage people to seek help and disclose mental health conditions, to speed up and improve the FAA's "special issuance" medical clearance process, and to build trust between the FAA and aviation workers. The bill does not change safety standards directly; how rules change depends on later FAA decisions.

oppose: act on the expert task group's recommendations, so the bill's effects depend on agency discretion and could be limited in practice.

Loosening or changing medical standards for pilots and controllers could raise safety questions if the changes are not backed by strong evidence, and the bill does not set specific safety requirements itself.
The bill authorizes up to $15 million a year, but that money still has to be approved through the appropriations process, so the added staffing and backlog relief are not guaranteed.
support: The bill aims to encourage pilots and controllers to seek mental health care early without fearing they will lose their jobs, which could help both workers and the public.
It requires the FAA to explain to Congress in writing if it declines a recommendation from its 2024 expert committee, which adds accountability to the process.

It authorizes funding to hire and train more aviation medical examiners, including psychiatrists, and to reduce the backlog of special issuance cases, which could shorten delays in medical certification.

cost_flag: Authorizes up to $15,000,000 per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2028 (up to $45 million total) for the FAA Office of Aerospace Medicine. Congress would still have to appropriate the money. The bill doesn't state a separate cost for the public information campaign.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2 public education campaign and the requirement to explain to Congress any declined task group recommendation (plus reports and briefings) make FAA decisions more visible, and the campaign aims to reduce stigma around mental health care.

local_say.reason: The bill expands required consultation to aviation unions, flight schools, and accredited universities, giving these groups a formal role in the task group's work.

equality.reason: Sec. on disclosure encouragement aims to reduce the fear of losing certification for pilots and controllers who seek mental health care, giving them more equal footing to get help without career penalty.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 and the explanation-to-Congress requirement add accountability for FAA decisions on expert recommendations, and the special issuance reviews add a structured evidence-based review process, though the FAA 'may' act on recommendations limits this.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. 1 and the medical-rule updates encourage pilots and controllers to disclose mental health conditions without fearing loss of certification, which expands their ability to seek care and speak openly about their health.

label: S. 3258
title: Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2026
short_title: Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2026
one: Requires the FAA to publish and keep updated a public, user-friendly list of medications that pilots and air traffic controllers may use, along with the "Do Not Issue" and "Do Not Fly" lists.
summary: This bill would make the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) publish a clear list of medications that pilots, air traffic controllers, and people training for those jobs can safely take, whether prescribed or bought over the counter, and still qualify for medical certification. Today the FAA keeps lists of "Do Not Issue" and "Do Not Fly" drugs for its medical examiners but has no public list of approved drugs. Within one year of the bill becoming law, the FAA must post the list on its website and make it available in MedXPress, the online system people use when they first apply for a medical certificate. The list must also include the banned lists, side effects and warnings (contra-indications), whether the FAA must review the use of a drug, and, where practical, how long someone must stay off or limit duty while adjusting to a new medication. It must include a way for doctors to contact the FAA with questions. Before release, the FAA must consult groups such as pilot and controller unions, flight schools, aviation universities, the Civil Aviation Medical Association, general aviation groups, and an existing aeromedical working group. The FAA must update the list at least yearly and whenever its medical examiner guide or policy changes. A savings clause says publishing the list does not make the FAA legally liable if someone relies on it and has a bad reaction, causes harm, or is denied certification.
does: Requires the FAA, within 1 year of enactment, to publish and maintain on a public website a list of medications (prescription and over-the-counter) it has determined can be safely used and approved for medical certification of pilots (airmen) and air traffic controllers.
Requires the list to include the Do Not Issue and Do Not Fly medication lists, contra-indications, and whether FAA review is needed.
Requires the list to be user-friendly and available in MedXPress when people first seek medical certification or clearance, including trainees.
Requires, if practicable, the minimum time someone must have limited or no duties to stabilize on an allowed medication.

Requires consultation before release with the Aeromedical Innovation and Modernization Working Group, pilot and air traffic controller union representatives, accredited aviation colleges, Part 141 flight schools, the Civil Aviation Medical Association, general aviation groups, and others the FAA chooses.
Requires contact information or a mechanism for doctors and medical providers to ask the FAA questions about the list.
Requires updates within 1 year of first publication and whenever the Guide for Aviation Medical Examiners or related FAA policy changes.
Includes a savings clause stating that publishing the list does not assign liability to the FAA if someone relies on it and suffers a reaction, causes harm, or is found ineligible.
who: Pilots and student pilots seeking FAA medical certificates
Air traffic controllers and trainees
Aviation medical examiners and doctors treating aviation workers
The FAA, which must create and maintain the list
Flight schools, aviation universities, and unions consulted
Air travelers, indirectly, through aviation safety and workforce health

benefits: Applicants could avoid unknowingly taking disqualifying medications or being denied certification.
Pilots and controllers might seek needed treatment sooner, including for mental health, if rules are clear and less feared.
Doctors would get a contact point and clearer information.
Consultation with unions and training schools gives affected workers a voice.
Could improve aviation safety by clarifying wait times to stabilize on a medication.
concerns: The savings clause means the FAA would not be liable if someone relies on an incorrect or outdated list.
A list could become outdated if updates are slow, since the bill requires updates only about yearly or when guidance changes.
The FAA may use 'as appropriate' discretion to leave out details.
May create a false sense that listed drugs are safe for every individual.
imp.cost: No funding amount is specified and no CBO estimate was provided. Costs would be FAA staff time to build, consult on, and maintain the list, likely paid from existing FAA appropriations.
unknowns: How many medications would be included and how detailed the entries would be.
How much it would cost the FAA and whether new funding is needed.
Whether the bill will pass, since the metadata shows 'held at the desk' status.
How the savings clause would work in legal disputes.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to have the FAA publish a clear, public list of medications that pilots, air traffic controllers, and people training for those jobs can take and still qualify for medical certification. The bill notes that the FAA currently keeps "Do Not Issue" and "Do Not Fly" lists for its medical examiners but has no public list of approved medications. It aims to give applicants clearer information before they apply.

oppose: The savings clause says the FAA would not be legally liable if someone relies on the list and suffers a reaction, causes harm, or is denied certification. Opponents could ask how individuals would be protected if they follow an incorrect or outdated list.

The bill lets the FAA use discretion, 'as appropriate,' to leave out details. Opponents could ask Congress to require the full set of wait times, warnings, and review requirements instead of leaving them to agency judgment.
support: Applicants could check medications in advance and avoid unknowingly taking a drug that could lead to a denied certification. The list would appear in MedXPress, where people first apply.
Clear, public rules may encourage pilots and controllers to seek needed treatment sooner, including for mental health, instead of fearing that disclosure will end their careers.

The bill requires consultation with pilot and controller unions, flight schools, aviation universities, and the Civil Aviation Medical Association before release, giving affected workers and experts a voice. It also gives doctors a contact point for questions.

crs:
Aviation Medication Transparency Act of 2025
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to compile, publish, and annually update a list of medications that may be safely prescribed to pilots and air traffic controllers for the purposes of issuing a medical certification. The list must be publicly available on the FAA website and distributed to those seeking a license and medical certification.
Currently, the FAA does not have a list of approved medications. However, the FAA does have lists for Aviation Medical Examiners of 
Do Not Issue
 medications and 
Do Not Fly
 medications.

environment.reason: The bill concerns aviation medical certification and does not touch water, air quality, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2 requires the FAA to publish the medication list publicly on its website and in MedXPress, including banned lists and warnings, and to provide a contact channel for doctors, which makes FAA medical decisions more visible and answerable.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill does not address corporate profits or shift costs from corporations to the public; its effects on profit are not clear.

local_say.reason: The required consultation with pilot and controller unions, flight schools, aviation universities, and general aviation groups gives affected workers and organizations a formal voice before the list is released.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has nothing to do with bailouts or ratepayer charges; its costs are FAA staff time paid from existing appropriations.

equality.reason: The list applies the same medication standards to all pilots and controllers and gives everyone the same access to it, so no group is treated unequally and equal access improves only slightly.

justice.reason: Sec. 2 gives applicants a clear, published standard and a way for doctors to ask questions, which makes certification decisions more consistent; however, the savings clause removes FAA liability when someone relies on an incorrect list, which limits real remedies for harm.

personal_freedom.reason: Publishing which prescription and over-the-counter medications are acceptable lets pilots and controllers make informed choices about their own treatment without guessing whether they will lose certification.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage (two headlines) ties the bill's subject to safety and accountability, crediting investigative reporting for FDA drug-testing action and questioning FAA leadership during the ground stop. Center coverage (three PBS headlines, one unrelated to aviation) focuses on the ground stop's unexplained cause, a dispute over blame, and the administration's funding request. Neither group's headlines mention the bill by name, and the evidence is thin, with only one or two articles per group, so these comparisons are tentative.

label: S. 4822
title: Saving the OOI Act of 2026
short_title: Saving the OOI Act of 2026
one: Bars the National Science Foundation from using federal money to shut down or scale back Ocean Observatories Initiative instruments off Oregon, Washington, Alaska, North Carolina, and in the Irminger Sea until a thorough review with scientist and coastal community input is done.
summary: The Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI) is a network of underwater instruments that collect physical, chemical, geological, and biological data about the ocean. According to the Congressional Research Service, on May 21, 2026, the National Science Foundation (NSF) announced it would remove all in-water equipment from four of the five active OOI arrays. This bill would stop that. It says NSF cannot use any federal money to decommission (shut down and remove) or descope (scale back) OOI instruments off Oregon, Washington, Alaska, and North Carolina, or in the Irminger Sea, until NSF finishes a thorough review of the program and the national assets it provides. That review must include real input from the scientific community and coastal communities. The bill also directs the NSF Director to keep the OOI running with full and consistent operations, including monitoring in every state where instruments were already decommissioned, until the review is finished. The bill does not give a dollar amount, does not set a deadline for the review, and does not say where the money to keep operations going would come from. It overrides other laws that might conflict ("notwithstanding any other provision of law"). It was introduced by Sen. Murkowski (R-AK) with 11 cosponsors.
does: Prohibits NSF from using any federal funds to decommission or descope OOI instruments off Oregon, Washington, Alaska, and North Carolina, and in the Irminger Sea, until a review is complete.
Requires NSF to first conduct a thorough review of the OOI and the national assets it provides, with robust engagement from the scientific and coastal communities.

Directs the NSF Director to maintain OOI with full and consistent operations, including monitoring in all states that had instruments decommissioned, until the review is done (effectively requiring restoration).
Applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' so it overrides conflicting laws.
Sets no deadline for the review, no new funding amount, and no specific funding source.

Coastal communities and states (Oregon, Washington, Alaska, North Carolina) that rely on ocean monitoring for fisheries, weather, and safety
The National Science Foundation and its budget
Fishing and maritime industries that use ocean data
Taxpayers, who fund NSF operations

benefits: Preserves continuous ocean data on physical, chemical, geological, and biological conditions.
Gives scientists and coastal communities a formal voice before decisions are made.
Avoids gaps in long-term records that are costly or impossible to recover.
Bipartisan-looking support, with a Republican sponsor and 11 cosponsors.
concerns: No new money is provided, so keeping OOI running could force NSF to cut other research.
No deadline for the review, so the pause could be open-ended.
Limits NSF's discretion to manage its own budget and priorities.
It is unclear how and when already-removed equipment would be restored.
imp.cost: No dollar amount or funding source specified. Costs would come out of NSF's existing federal funds unless Congress appropriates more.
unknowns: How much it would cost to maintain or restore the instruments.
How long the NSF review would take.
Why NSF proposed the removal (budget or other reasons) is not stated in the material provided.

crs:
Saving the OOI Act of 2026
This bill prohibits the National Science Foundation (NSF) from using federal funds to decommission or descope Ocean Observatories Initiative (OOI) instruments until a thorough review of OOI is completed.
OOI measures and observes ocean conditions using a series of in-water instruments that gather physical, chemical, geological, and biological data. On May 21, 2026, NSF announced that it would remove all in-water infrastructure from four of the five active OOI arrays.
Under the bill, NSF must conduct a thorough review of OOI with engagement from the scientific and coastal communities before decommissioning or descoping specified OOI instruments. This includes OOI instruments anchored off of Oregon, Washington, Alaska, and North Carolina, as well as instruments anchored in the Irminger Sea. NSF is required to maintain full and consistent OOI operations, including monitoring in states where instruments have already been decommissioned, until the review is complete.

transparency.reason: Requires a review with stakeholder engagement before decisions are made, and preserves public scientific data.

local_say.reason: Requires engagement from coastal communities before instruments off their shores are removed.

environmental_protection.reason: Keeps in-water instruments that monitor ocean ecosystems and conditions operating instead of being removed.

label: S. 850
title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
short_title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
one: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to study threats at the U.S.-Canada border every three years, update its northern border strategy, brief Congress in a classified setting, and set performance measures for its air and marine patrols.
summary: This bill updates an existing 2016 law that asks the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to review security along the U.S.-Canada border. Under the bill, DHS must do a new threat analysis of that border and repeat it every three years. The analysis must now also look at recent changes in the number and demographics (such as who is being caught) of people apprehended at the border, including sector-by-sector changes. Within 18 months of the bill becoming law, DHS must update its Northern Border strategy, then update it every five years, using the latest threat analysis. Within 30 days after each analysis is submitted, DHS must give a classified (secret) briefing to the relevant congressional committees. The bill also tells DHS, through the head of Customs and Border Protection's Air and Marine Operations, to create performance measures within 180 days. These would show how well air and maritime patrols secure the northern border between official ports of entry. This follows recommendations from the Government Accountability Office, Congress's watchdog agency. The bill does not authorize any new money; DHS would have to do this work with funds it already has. Overall it is a reporting and oversight bill. It does not add agents, build barriers, or change immigration rules.

Requires a classified briefing to the appropriate congressional committees within 30 days after each threat analysis is submitted.

Directs DHS, through the Executive Assistant Commissioner of CBP Air and Marine Operations, to develop performance measures within 180 days to assess how effectively it secures the northern border between ports of entry by air and sea (implementing GAO recommendations).
Authorizes no additional funds to carry out the Act.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to update a 2016 law on northern border security by requiring DHS to regularly analyze threats along the U.S.-Canada border, including terrorist and criminal threats and recent changes in apprehensions. It also requires regular updates to the Northern Border strategy and asks CBP's Air and Marine Operations to create performance measures for air and marine patrols between ports of entry, following GAO recommendations.

oppose: The bill adds new recurring reporting duties for DHS, such as threat analyses every three years and strategy updates every five years, which could take staff time away from other priorities since no new funding is authorized.
The main briefings to Congress are classified, and the bill does not require public release of the threat analysis or strategy, so residents of border communities may see little of the results.
The bill does not require DHS to gather input from border communities, tribes, or local officials before writing the analysis and strategy.
The bill's focus on apprehension demographics could raise equity concerns, and the bill does not explain how that data would be used.
support: The bill requires regular, data-based threat reviews of the northern border, which could help keep security strategy current instead of relying on old assessments.
Performance measures for air and marine patrols between ports of entry could show whether existing spending is working, which supports responsible use of taxpayer money.
Regular classified briefings give appropriate congressional committees ongoing oversight of northern border security.
The bill authorizes no new funds and does not add agents, barriers, or immigration changes, so it carries no added direct cost and is a focused oversight measure that follows GAO recommendations.

crs:
Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to regularly perform a threat analysis of the northern U.S. border.
The analysis must be performed every three years and include terroristic and criminal threats, recent changes in apprehensions, and improvements needed to prevent terrorism and reduce criminal activity.
DHS must update its northern border strategy not later than September 2, 2026, and every five years thereafter, incorporating the results from the latest threat analysis. DHS must also provide a classified briefing to the appropriate congressional committees.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Air and Marine Operations (AMO) must develop performance metrics to assess the AMO’s effectiveness at securing the northern border between ports of entry in air and maritime environments.

transparency.reason: It adds regular reporting and briefings to Congress and performance measures, though the briefings are classified and no public release is required.

news.overall: None of the 8 headlines names the Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act, so this analysis cannot show how any outlet frames the bill itself. The coverage instead concerns U.S.-Canada trade and defense tensions, U.S.-China tariff relations, FAA and DHS-related hearings, and a seasonal weather story. The Lean Right group has only one article, and the Lean Left group's pieces are truncated, so the evidence is thin for both; the Center group has the most volume but is also unrelated to the bill on the headlines shown.

label: H.R. 8469
title: Making appropriations for military construction, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2027, and for other purposes.
short_title: Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2027
one: Funds military construction, family housing, the Department of Veterans Affairs, and related agencies for fiscal year 2027, with spending rules, oversight requirements, and policy riders.
summary:
This is the yearly spending bill for military building projects, the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA), and a few related agencies. It covers the budget year that ends September 30, 2027.

Title I – Military construction (Department of Defense). The bill pays for building and fixing military bases and facilities. The largest amounts are about $2.1 billion for the Army, $5.5 billion for the Navy and Marine Corps, $3.7 billion for the Air Force, and $3.8 billion for Defense-wide agencies. Smaller amounts go to National Guard and Reserve facilities. It also pays about $482 million for the U.S. share of NATO's facility program and $465 million into the Base Closure Account. Family housing gets roughly $1.9 billion for construction and operation. Extra money is added for projects on the services' unfunded priority lists, and for design work on barracks, child development centers, base resilience, and demolition. The bill sets many rules. Cost-plus contracts over $25,000 need approval. Steel purchases must give American producers a chance to compete. Large foreign contracts are limited. Congress must be notified before new overseas installations or major transfers. Maintenance spending on generals' and admirals' quarters is capped at $20,000 per unit without notice. No money may be used to close Guantánamo Bay Naval Station, and no money may be used for planning or construction at Arlington National Cemetery under this title.

Title II – Veterans Affairs. The VA gets very large amounts. These include about $10.6 billion in added 2026 money and $283.8 billion in advance money for compensation and pensions, and $23.6 billion for readjustment benefits such as education and rehabilitation. Health care gets about $70.7 billion for medical services, $42 billion for community care, $12 billion for medical support, and $13.5 billion for facilities. Medical research gets $900 million. There is $3.4 billion for the electronic health record rollout, and part of that is held back until the VA gives Congress an updated cost and schedule plan. The Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund (care for veterans exposed to burn pits and similar hazards) gets $54.6 billion now and $53.7 billion available October 2027. The bill rescinds (takes back) about $1.65 billion and $754 million in earlier medical funds. Construction gets about $661 million for major projects and $318 million for minor projects. There are also state nursing home and veterans cemetery grants. Many provisions set minimum spending: $1.444 billion for women veterans' care, $700 million for suicide prevention outreach, $3.5 billion for caregivers, about $3.46 billion for homelessness programs, $6.4 billion for telehealth, about $710 million for opioid programs, and others. Policy rules include: limits on VA research on dogs, cats, and monkeys unless the Secretary personally approves it for combat-related needs, with reports and inspections; a ban on cutting Veterans Crisis Line staffing or hours; fertility treatment and adoption help for certain disabled veterans; a ban on buying computers and similar gear from listed Chinese military-linked or forced-labor-linked companies; a phase-out of Social Security numbers for logging in by September 30, 2027; protection for VA workers and patients speaking to Congress; guaranteed inspector general access to records; rural care reports before any clinic closures; and blocking a rule on VA special transportation rates for one year. It also requires a Bakersfield, California clinic to move forward and bars closing the Port Charlotte, Florida clinic.

Title III – Related agencies. This funds the American Battle Monuments Commission ($107.9 million), the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims ($50 million), Arlington and Soldiers' and Airmen's Home cemeteries ($118 million), and the Armed Forces Retirement Home ($77 million).

Title IV – General provisions. These include standard rules: funds expire at year-end unless stated; no projects named after sitting House members; agencies may post required reports online; computer networks must block pornography; limits on first-class travel; no lobbying with funds; a bar on reporting veterans as "mental defectives" for gun-purchase background checks without a judge's finding; and a limit on repeated environmental impact statements for the same military project. It also bars VA from enforcing a rule that stops VA providers from filling out state medical-marijuana forms, and bars money for detention facilities in the U.S. for Guantánamo detainees.

The bill was reported as awaiting a Senate vote. The text shows many offsetting "increase/reduce" amendments with net zero effect.
does: Appropriates roughly $15.7 billion for military construction across the Army ($2.13B), Navy/Marine Corps ($5.51B), Air Force ($3.71B), and Defense-wide ($3.76B), available until September 30, 2031.
Funds National Guard and Reserve facilities: Army Guard $198M, Air Guard $291M, Army Reserve $42M, Navy Reserve $2.3M, Air Force Reserve $60M.
Provides $482M for the U.S. share of the NATO Security Investment Program and $465M for the Base Closure Account.
Provides about $1.9 billion for Army, Navy/Marine Corps, Air Force and Defense-wide family housing construction and operations, plus small housing improvement fund amounts.

Adds $500M for projects on service unfunded priority lists, and $15M/$15M/$15M for barracks design and child development center design, $5M each for resilience design, and $20M each for demolition, requiring expenditure plans within 60 days.

Sets military construction guardrails: written approval for large cost-plus contracts, Buy-American steel competition, limits on foreign contractors and land-purchase prices, no property taxes paid abroad, notifications for new overseas installations and large exercises.
Caps repairs to general/flag officer quarters at $20,000 per unit per year without 30 days' notice and requires annual reporting of each such quarters' costs.

Bars funds for Arlington National Cemetery projects within the military construction title, bars closing or realigning Guantánamo Bay Naval Station, and bars building U.S. facilities to house Guantánamo detainees.

Provides VA benefits money: about $10.56B extra for FY2026 and $283.8B in advance for FY2028 for compensation and pensions; $23.6B for readjustment benefits; $90.9M for insurance and indemnities; and funds housing loan, vocational rehab loan, and Native American veteran housing loan programs.

Provides VA health care: $70.7B medical services, $42B community care, $12B medical support and compliance, $13.5B medical facilities, and $900M medical and prosthetic research, with priority for service-connected, low-income and special-needs veterans and funding for prosthetics designed for women.
Rescinds $1.65B from prior Medical Support and Compliance funds and $754M from prior Medical Facilities funds.

Funds VA administration: $425M general administration (25% withheld until the Secretary testifies on the budget), $268M Board of Veterans Appeals, $5.45B IT (reduced by $100M), $3.4B electronic health record (25% withheld until a plan with cost, schedule, performance certification and staffing is delivered), $290M Inspector General, $500M National Cemetery Administration.

Funds VA construction: $661M major projects, $318M minor projects, $173M state extended care facility grants, $62M veterans cemetery grants; requires construction contracts be awarded on deadlines and Congress be told of bid savings and scope changes.
Provides $54.6B (plus $53.7B available October 2027) to the Cost of War Toxic Exposures Fund for care, benefits and research for veterans exposed to environmental hazards.

Requires minimum VA spending: $1.444B women veterans, $700M suicide prevention outreach, $3.5B caregivers, $42M PTSD center, $80M neurology centers, about $354M rural health, $3.46B homelessness, $6.365B telehealth, $710M opioid programs, $32M intimate partner violence program.

Limits VA research using dogs, cats and non-human primates started after July 1, 2025 to cases personally approved by the Secretary as necessary, combat-related and with ethical review, with reporting, USDA inspections, and violation reports.

Protects the Veterans Crisis Line (no staffing/hours cuts, immediate trained response, hiring freeze exemption), directs staffing to meet the 125-day claims goal, and bars actions that increase veteran wait times.
Allows VA fertility counseling/treatment and adoption reimbursement for veterans with service-connected disabilities preventing procreation; funds childcare program expansion.

Bars VA from buying computers, printers and videoconferencing gear from companies on specified Chinese military, forced-labor and export-control lists; bars paying award fees to poorly performing contractors.
Requires VA to stop using Social Security numbers to authenticate people by September 30, 2027, with exceptions (fraud, law, outside systems, no substitute).
Protects oversight: bars VA settlements that stop people speaking to Congress, guarantees Inspector General access to records, and requires frequent reports to Appropriations Committees.

Requires a report on rural access impacts before any VA hospital or clinic closure or service cuts, bars closing the Port Charlotte, Florida clinic, and directs the Bakersfield, California clinic to start construction or temporary services by September 30, 2027.
Blocks for FY2027 a VA rule on rates paid for special modes of transportation, and bars enforcement of VA directive prohibiting providers from completing state medical marijuana program forms.
Funds related agencies: American Battle Monuments Commission $107.9M, Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims $50M, Army cemeteries including Arlington $118M, and Armed Forces Retirement Home $77M.

Adds general provisions: no lobbying with funds, no first-class travel contrary to rules, no named projects for sitting House members, pornography blocking on networks, VA gun-background-check reporting limit requiring a judicial finding, and one environmental impact statement per military construction project number.
who: Veterans receiving VA health care, disability compensation, pensions, education, housing loans and caregiver support
Women veterans, rural veterans, homeless veterans, and veterans exposed to burn pits and other toxins
Active-duty service members and military families using barracks, family housing and child development centers
VA employees, contractors, and crisis line staff
National Guard and Reserve units
Communities near military bases and VA facilities, including Bakersfield, CA and Port Charlotte, FL
Rural Alaska veterans and Tribal health providers
Animals used in VA research (dogs, cats, primates)
U.S. taxpayers who fund the spending
Defense and construction contractors and U.S. steel producers

benefits: Funds veterans' health care, disability benefits, caregivers, homelessness, telehealth, and suicide prevention at stated minimums.
Protects the Veterans Crisis Line from cuts and requires immediate trained response.
Adds oversight: inspector general access, quarterly reports, protections for speaking with Congress, and a plan requirement before releasing electronic health record funds.
Restricts VA animal research on dogs, cats and primates and requires inspections and reporting.
Supports fertility treatment and adoption help for severely disabled veterans, and funds barracks, child care centers, and family housing.
Bars procurement of IT gear from listed Chinese military-linked companies; requires rural impact analysis before clinic closures.
concerns: Very large federal spending, with no stated offsets in the text.
Rescinds about $2.4 billion in prior VA medical support and facilities funds, which could strain operations.
Rider limiting enforcement of a VA rule on special transportation rates could affect veterans needing medical transport.
Rider limiting repeated environmental impact statements for military projects could reduce environmental review.
Rider on gun-background-check reporting and the marijuana-form directive are policy choices some may disagree with; effects on veterans' safety and care are debated.
Military construction at large scale with no stated environmental, water, or air safeguards; defense contractors benefit from spending.
Earmark-like directives (Bakersfield, Port Charlotte) are specific local spending decisions that may bypass normal priority-setting.
imp.cost: Discretionary and mandatory-style appropriations totaling several hundred billion dollars, including about $283.8B in advance VA benefits money for FY2028, $54.6B plus $53.7B for toxic exposures, roughly $70.7B for VA medical services, and about $15.7B for military construction. Funded from the general Treasury; it also includes rescissions of about $2.4 billion in earlier VA funds.
unknowns: Which specific military construction projects are funded, since project lists are in the committee report, not the bill text.
Final amounts after the many offsetting amendment adjustments shown in the text.
How the rescissions will affect VA services and wait times.
Environmental effects of construction projects and any water or air impacts, which are not described.
Whether the Senate will change the bill before passage.

environment.reason: The bill funds military construction and VA facilities but its provisions do not directly add or remove water, air, or land protections; the Title IV limit on repeated environmental impact statements for military projects could reduce environmental review, which is a modest negative, but the text is limited and the effect is uncertain.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on VA Inspector General access, reports to Appropriations Committees, protections for staff and patients speaking to Congress, rural impact reports before clinic closures, and gun-background-check reporting limits add transparency and humane protections, though the EIS limit and withheld funds pending plans are partial offsets.

people_over_profit.reason: Title I contract provisions and the bar on award fees to poorly performing contractors are mixed, but the bill funds large defense and construction contracts and limits oversight of repeated environmental reviews that benefit project sponsors, and it rescinds $2.4B in VA funds that shifts operating strain onto veterans.

local_say.reason: Title IV limits repeated environmental impact statements for the same military project, reducing public and local review, and Title II directs specific clinic decisions (Bakersfield, Port Charlotte) from Washington, though the rural-impact report before clinic closures gives some local input.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide bailouts to corporations; it is an appropriation for government operations and does not clearly shift private losses to taxpayers.

equality.reason: Title II sets minimum funding for women veterans' care, prosthetics designed for women, and fertility and adoption help for certain disabled veterans, expanding equal access to care, though the Guantanamo and specific-clinic provisions treat some locations differently.

justice.reason: Sec. guaranteeing Inspector General access to records, bars on settlements that prevent speaking to Congress, and a requirement that a judicial finding precede veterans being reported as mental defectives make VA processes more accountable and protect due process.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill expands veterans' access to fertility treatment and adoption help but restricts VA research on dogs, cats and primates and bars the VA from enforcing the marijuana-form directive, which roughly offset in its effect on individual choices.

label: S. 1135
title: A bill to amend the National Trails System Act to direct the Secretary of Agriculture to conduct a study on the feasibility of designating the Bonneville Shoreline Trail.
short_title: Bonneville Shoreline Trail Feasibility Study
one: Directs the Secretary of Agriculture to study whether the roughly 280-mile Bonneville Shoreline Trail in Utah could be designated as part of the National Trails System.
summary: This short bill adds the Bonneville Shoreline Trail to the list of routes that the National Trails System Act says should be studied for possible national designation. The trail is a system of existing and potential trails, about 280 miles long, running from the Idaho-Utah border to Nephi, Utah. It follows the old shoreline "bench" left by ancient Lake Bonneville. The bill says the Secretary of Agriculture, whose department includes the Forest Service, would carry out the study. A feasibility study only asks whether designation makes sense. It does not create a national trail, buy land, change who owns land, or set any rules for land use. The text we have does not give a deadline, a budget, or details on what the study must cover, such as public input, land ownership, or environmental effects. label: S. 1157
title: Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025
short_title: Women and Lung Cancer Research and Preventive Services Act of 2025
one: Requires HHS, with Defense and Veterans Affairs, to review and update federal lung cancer research, screening, and treatment efforts, especially for women and people with few known risk factors, and report to Congress within 2 years.
summary: This bill tells the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), working with the Departments of Defense and Veterans Affairs, to take a close look at what the federal government is doing about lung cancer. The focus is on women and people who have few known risk factors, such as those who never smoked. A second goal is to get more people to take lung cancer screening tests, specifically those the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (an independent expert panel) recommends screening for. The review must look at what research already exists, what research is underway, and what we still don't know. It must also look for new research that could be done across agencies, including studies of environmental and genetic factors that may cause lung cancer in women, and new technology such as biomarker testing (tests that look for signs of disease in the body). It must also check current public health strategies for screening and diagnosis, consider other evidence-based approaches, and decide whether more public awareness and education are needed. Where appropriate, agencies must update their programs and plans. Within two years of enactment, HHS must send a report to key House and Senate committees. The report must summarize findings, describe any changes already made, and recommend further changes, including any legal barriers. The bill does not give any specific amount of money and does not create new benefits or mandates on private parties.

one: Creates a Finger Lakes National Heritage Area covering 14 New York counties, run locally by the Finger Lakes Tourism Alliance, with federal help for 15 years.
summary: This bill would officially create the Finger Lakes National Heritage Area in New York. A National Heritage Area is a region recognized by Congress for its shared history, culture, and natural features. It is not a national park, and the land stays under its current owners. The area would cover 14 counties: Cayuga, Chemung, Cortland, Livingston, Monroe, Onondaga, Ontario, Schuyler, Seneca, Steuben, Tioga, Tompkins, Wayne, and Yates. The Finger Lakes Tourism Alliance would be the local group in charge of coordinating the area. Within 3 years of the bill becoming law, that group would have to send the Secretary of the Interior a proposed management plan for approval. The bill adds the area to the existing National Heritage Area System, which was set up in a 2019 law, the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act. That law sets the rules for how heritage areas work and what help they can get. Under this bill, the Interior Secretary's authority to give federal help to this area would end 15 years after enactment. The bill text does not give a dollar amount. No Congressional Research Service summary was available. Whether the bill limits federal control over private land comes from the existing 2019 law, which this bill text does not repeat.

label: S. 2479
title: Reserve Organization of America Charter Amendments Act of 2026
short_title: Reserve Organization of America Charter Update
one: The bill renames the federally chartered Reserve Officers Association of the United States as the Reserve Organization of America and rewrites its charter in federal law with updated rules and restrictions.
summary: This bill updates the federal charter of a nonprofit group for military reservists. The group is now called the Reserve Officers Association of the United States. The bill renames it the Reserve Organization of America and replaces its chapter in Title 36 of the U.S. Code with a new one. The group's purpose stays the same: to support and promote a military policy that gives the country adequate national security. Who can be a member, and how the group is governed, would follow the group's own constitution and bylaws. The group must hold an annual meeting. It keeps perpetual (permanent) existence and the exclusive right to use its name, seals, emblems and badges. The charter bars the group from operating for profit, issuing stock, paying out income or assets to members, or lending money to officers or governing-body members. Officials who approve such a loan would be personally liable for it. The group and its members acting for it cannot give money or help to political parties or candidates. The group must keep accurate financial records, meeting minutes and a member list. Voting members can inspect those records for a proper purpose. It must have a registered agent in Washington, D.C. to receive legal papers, and it is legally responsible for acts of its officers and agents within their authority. Any older legal reference to the old name would count as a reference to the new name. The bill does not provide money. It is mainly a housekeeping and governance update.

label: S. 3321
title: FAIR Leave Act
short_title: FAIR Leave Act
one: The bill would end a rule that lets employers cap the combined family and medical leave of married couples who work for the same employer.
summary:
Under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), eligible workers can take unpaid, job-protected leave for things like a new child, a serious health condition, or caring for a sick family member. Right now, there is one exception. If a husband and wife both work for the same employer, the employer may limit their combined leave to 12 weeks in a year for certain reasons. Those reasons are bonding with a new child (birth, adoption, or foster placement) and caring for a parent with a serious health condition. A similar combined cap applies to leave taken to care for an injured service member. Married coworkers can lose leave that couples at different employers would get.

The FAIR Leave Act is very short. It repeals, or deletes, that section of the FMLA (Section 102(f)). If it becomes law, each spouse who qualifies for FMLA leave could take their own full amount, even if both work for the same employer. The bill does not create paid leave. It does not change who qualifies for FMLA, and it does not change the usual amounts of leave. It also does not spend federal money. Costs would fall on employers, who may have to cover two employees being out at once. The bill text does not give a start date. The metadata says the Senate passed it and sent it to the House. No CRS summary was available, so this analysis relies on the bill text and my understanding of the existing law.

As a result, married couples who both work for the same employer could each take their full FMLA leave for a new child or for a parent's serious health condition, instead of sharing 12 weeks. This is based on how current law works, not on text in the bill.
Would likewise end the combined cap that can apply to spouses taking military caregiver leave (for a covered service member with a serious injury or illness). This is also based on existing law.

label: S. 4035
title: DEATH BETS Act
short_title: DEATH BETS Act
one: Bars federally registered trading exchanges from listing event-betting contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, war, U.S. military operations, or contracts expected to resolve mainly on someone's death.
summary: This bill changes the Commodity Exchange Act, the law that governs futures and event-contract markets. It would stop registered exchanges (called "registered entities") from listing or clearing certain "event contracts," which are bets on whether a real-world event will happen. Specifically, it covers contracts in a category the law calls "excluded commodities" (the part about events or outcomes beyond anyone's control). Contracts that expressly refer to terrorism, assassination, war, or U.S. military operations would be banned. So would any similar activity the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), the federal regulator, decides by rule is covered. A second ban applies to contracts that, when listed, are reasonably expected to be settled mainly by a person's death. The bill also includes a rule of construction, which is a clarification. It says the bill does not change the legal status of other contracts involving activities already described in a different part of the law (section 5c(c)(5)(C)(i)), such as gaming or unlawful activity. Those stay as they are. The bill has no spending and does not create new penalties of its own. It relies on the existing rules for registered exchanges. The text does not say when it takes effect, so it would likely start when signed. Supporters would say it prevents profiting from, or creating incentives for, violence and death. Critics could raise questions about how "principally based on a death" would be interpreted and about the CFTC's discretion to widen the list.
does: Adds a new subsection (d) to Section 5c of the Commodity Exchange Act that bars registered entities (such as futures exchanges) from listing for trading or accepting for clearing certain contracts.
Bans event contracts, based on "excluded commodities" under section 1a(19)(iv), that expressly reference terrorism, assassination, war, or U.S. Armed Forces military operations.
Lets the CFTC extend the ban by rule or regulation to any "similar activity" it finds necessary and appropriate to achieve the Act's purposes.
Bans event contracts that, at the time of listing, are reasonably expected to resolve principally based on the death of an individual.

Includes a rule of construction saying the bill does not change whether other contracts involving activities named in section 5c(c)(5)(C)(i) are permitted, beyond the specific activities in the new subsection.
Sets the short title as the Discouraging Exploitative Assassination, Tragedy, and Harm Betting in Event Trading Systems Act (DEATH BETS Act).
who: Prediction-market and event-contract platforms and futures exchanges registered with the CFTC
Traders and bettors who use event-contract markets
The CFTC, which would enforce the ban and could define "similar activity"
The general public, including potential targets of violence and military families

label: S. 4631
title: Expanding Whistleblower Protections for Contractors Act of 2026
short_title: Expanding Whistleblower Protections for Contractors Act of 2026
one: Expands whistleblower protections for people working under federal defense, NASA, and other federal contracts and grants, including protection for refusing an unlawful order, and bars waiving those protections through forced arbitration.
summary:
This bill updates two existing whistleblower laws: one covering Department of Defense (DoD) and NASA contractors (Title 10, section 4701) and one covering other federal contractors and grant recipients (Title 41, section 4712). Today, these laws protect employees from being fired, demoted, or otherwise punished for reporting things like gross mismanagement, waste of federal money, abuse of authority, legal violations tied to contracts or grants, or a serious danger to public health or safety.

The bill adds protection for refusing to follow an order that would require breaking a law, rule, or regulation related to a contract or grant. It creates a new term, "protected individual," that covers contractors, subcontractors, grantees, and subgrantees, their current employees, former employees whose protected act happened before they left, and people working under personal services contracts. It expressly includes state, local, tribal, and territorial governments and their employees, and members of the intelligence community.

The bill says protections can't be signed away by any agreement or condition of employment, including predispute arbitration agreements (agreements to use private arbitration instead of court before any dispute happens). It also says executive branch officials have no authority to ask a contractor or grantee to retaliate against a whistleblower, and it lets agencies propose discipline for officials who do so. I could not see any funding amounts or start date in the text.

Expanding Whistleblower Protections for Contractors Act of 2026
This bill expands whistleblower protections for employees of federal contractors and grant recipients to include the act of refusing to obey an unlawful order and to apply these protections to members of the intelligence community and other governmental employees.
Current law protects employees of federal contractors or grant recipients from a reprisal (i.e., discharge, demotion, or discrimination) for disclosing evidence to Congress or another appropriate official of certain misconduct involving federal contracts, grants, or funds. The bill expands these protections to include an employee's refusal to obey an order that would require the employee to violate a law, rule, or regulation related to any contract, subcontract, grant, or subgrant. The bill also specifies that these protections apply to employees of federal contractors or grant recipients who are current or former members of the intelligence community or employees of state, local, or tribal governments. 
Further, the bill specifies that these protections may not be waived in a predispute arbitration agreement.
The bill specifies that an executive branch official may not request a federal contractor or grant recipient to engage in a reprisal against a protected employee, and it authorizes federal agencies to propose disciplinary action against officials that do so.

label: S. 5600
title: Dennis John Benigno Traumatic Brain Injury Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Traumatic Brain Injury Program Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Renews federal traumatic brain injury (TBI) tracking, prevention, and state grant programs through fiscal year 2031, adds a focus on higher-risk groups, requires more public data sharing, and orders two reports to Congress.
summary:
This bill renews the federal government's traumatic brain injury (TBI) programs. Those programs track how many people have brain injuries, study what causes them, and give money to states and tribes for TBI services. The current funding authority covers 2020 through 2024. The bill extends it to 2027 through 2031. "Authorizing" funding means Congress allows the money to be spent. A separate spending law still has to provide the actual dollars.

The bill also updates how the programs work. The CDC would collect more data on groups at higher risk, such as people whose jobs raise their risk. It would also look at causes, risk factors, and long-term outcomes, which may include related mental health conditions. The CDC would have to post summary (aggregated) TBI and concussion information on its website, including prevention tips for higher-risk groups. The surveillance program would be renamed for the late Rep. Bill Pascrell, Jr.

State grants would explicitly include tribal governments and American Indian consortia. The bill also updates the legal definition of TBI. It lets the HHS Secretary revise that definition after talking with states and other groups.

Within two years, HHS must send Congress a report on higher-risk groups, such as survivors of domestic violence or sexual assault and public safety officers. HHS must also complete a study of long-term effects of TBI, including links to dementia and mental health conditions. If HHS does that study itself, it must post the report publicly.

Requires the CDC to publish aggregated TBI and concussion information online, including prevention strategies tailored to higher-risk groups where feasible.
Renames the surveillance and registries program after Bill Pascrell, Jr.
Explicitly includes Tribal governments in state grant outreach language and updates the TBI definition, letting the HHS Secretary revise it after consulting states and others.

label: S. 4448
title: Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026
short_title: Accelerating Broadband Permits Act of 2026
one: The bill would add public tracking tools and reports for federal broadband grant spending and federal permitting, and would add mid-size broadband construction projects to the federal permitting-coordination program.
summary: This bill is about getting rural and unserved areas online faster by improving how the federal government tracks broadband money and permits. First, it requires the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to run a public website dashboard showing how much money each state or territory has spent from the BEAD program (the $42.5 billion broadband grant program from the 2021 infrastructure law) and how many locations now have service. NTIA must also post the states' semiannual progress reports within 90 days, with business-secret information blacked out. Second, NTIA must build a tool so states can see where each of their subgrantees stands on federal permits. Third, for applications to use federal property for communications equipment, NTIA must set up data controls and an alert system within 120 days, study what causes delays, work to fix them, and report each year to four congressional committees. Federal agencies already have a 270-day deadline for these applications. Fourth, the bill adds broadband construction projects that need a NEPA environmental review and cost more than $5 million to the projects eligible for FAST-41, a federal program that sets schedules and posts public timelines for permit reviews. The bill does not repeal NEPA or any environmental rule. It does not appropriate new money. The text does not say how much the new NTIA duties would cost.

Requires NTIA to create a tool that helps states track the federal permit requirements, submissions, and progress of each subgrantee. States must use it starting 90 days after their final proposal is approved and subgrant agreements are signed.

Requires NTIA, within 120 days of enactment, to develop data controls so federal agencies can accurately track processing time for applications to use federal property for communications facilities (the existing 270-day deadline applies to these).

Requires NTIA to analyze the causes of delay in those applications as they happen, take action to address them, and send an annual report to four congressional committees (Senate Commerce and Senate Energy, House Energy and Commerce and House Natural Resources).
Requires NTIA, within 120 days, to set up a way to alert federal agency staff when an application is at risk of missing the 270-day deadline.

Amends the FAST-41 permitting law so broadband infrastructure construction projects that are subject to NEPA and likely to need more than $5 million in total investment count as 'covered projects.' That would bring them into the program's coordinated schedules and public tracking.

label: H.R. 1013
title: Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act of 2025
short_title: Retirement Fairness for Charities and Educational Institutions Act
one: The bill changes federal securities laws so 403(b) retirement plans, used by public school staff, charity workers, and church employees, can invest in pooled bank trust funds and insurance company separate accounts, as 401(k) plans already can.
summary:
Many teachers, nurses at nonprofit hospitals, charity workers, and church employees save for retirement in 403(b) plans. Today, federal securities rules mostly limit these plans to mutual funds and annuities. Larger 401(k) plans can also use other pooled investment options, such as collective investment trusts (CITs). A CIT is a pooled fund run by a bank or trust company. 401(k) plans can also use insurance company "separate accounts," which are investment accounts an insurer keeps apart from its other money. These options often have lower fees.

This bill would update three securities laws: the Investment Company Act of 1940, the Securities Act of 1933, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. After that, 403(b) plans could invest in CITs and insurance company separate accounts without those products having to follow the full registration and disclosure rules that apply to mutual funds.

The bill sets conditions. A plan must be covered by ERISA (the main federal private-pension law), or the employer must agree to act as a fiduciary for choosing the plan's investment options. A fiduciary has a legal duty to act in participants' best interest. Government plans would need the employer or another responsible person to review and approve each investment option before it is offered. The bill does not say when it would take effect. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Banking Committee.

Treats qualifying 403(b) plans like 401(k) and governmental plans for purposes of securities law exemptions.
Requires the plan to be under ERISA, or the employer to agree to be a fiduciary for choosing investment options, or the plan to be a governmental plan.
For governmental 403(b) plans, requires the employer, a fiduciary, or someone acting for the employer to review and approve each investment option before it is offered.
Makes matching changes in the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, including broker and registration rules.

These options often have lower fees, which could help savers keep more of their returns.
Reduced registration and disclosure requirements could make these products easier and cheaper for providers to offer.
concerns: Products that do not follow mutual fund registration and disclosure rules may give workers less standardized information to compare options.
Employers acting as fiduciaries may face legal responsibility for investment choices, which could be hard for smaller organizations to manage.
Plans not covered by ERISA rely on the employer's fiduciary role, so protections may vary from plan to plan.

Whether the Senate will pass the bill is not yet known; it is currently in the Senate Banking Committee.

label: H.R. 10238
title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
short_title: Cybersecurity for Small Businesses Act of 2026
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to create and share cybersecurity guidance with small businesses, including information on Defense Department cybersecurity certification for federal contractors, and to report yearly to Congress.
summary:
This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to help small businesses protect themselves from hackers and online threats. The SBA would work with two other federal agencies that focus on cybersecurity, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Together they would develop and share guides and resources on good cybersecurity habits.

The bill also covers small businesses that want to work as contractors or subcontractors for the federal government. The SBA, working with the Department of Defense and other agencies, would give them information about the Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC). This is a set of cybersecurity standards for Defense Department contractors. The SBA would draw on existing Defense Department resources, including a small business office, a program created in the 2026 defense bill, and the APEX Accelerator program. The SBA would post this information on its website and in its outreach.

Each year the SBA would also consult its Office of Advocacy on the best ways to share other cybersecurity information. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, and every year after that, the SBA would send Congress a report. The report would give the number and a description of small businesses that contacted the SBA about cybersecurity. The bill does not set aside new money, and it does not create new penalties or requirements for businesses.

one: Requires the Small Business Administration to create, share, and yearly update educational materials that help small businesses spot and protect themselves from harmful conduct by foreign adversaries, such as hacking, IP theft, forced labor, and fraud.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to build and share guides that teach small businesses about harm that can come from foreign adversaries, meaning governments or companies tied to countries the U.S. treats as threats. The SBA must work with other agencies, including Homeland Security, State, the FBI, Treasury, Commerce, and the Trade Representative. The guides must explain what this harmful conduct looks like and how it hurts small businesses. Examples in the bill are stealing trade secrets, hacking, forced labor in supply chains, counterfeit goods and customs fraud, and unfair investment practices. The guides must also give best practices for protecting intellectual property, private business information, and supply chains. They must give cybersecurity and data protection tips, warn about risks in foreign investments, joint ventures, and licensing deals with adversary-linked entities, and point to federal help. They must also advise on protecting business interests abroad without needlessly limiting lawful business. The SBA would share the materials through its district offices and other programs. Starting October 1, 2027, it must review and update them every year. If the SBA decides a new type of activity poses a significant national or economic security risk, it must tell the House and Senate small business committees what the activity is and why. The bill creates no new penalties, rules, or grants. It does not give a cost estimate, and I could not see one in the text.

label: H.R. 10375
title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act of 2026
short_title: 504 Modernization and Small Manufacturer Enhancement Act
one: Updates the SBA 504 small business loan program by adding new goals (job training, disaster recovery, tiny businesses), easing loan closing and building-leasing rules, and dropping the "credit elsewhere" test for these loans.
summary: The SBA 504 program helps small businesses buy or improve buildings and equipment. Loans go through nonprofit-style local groups called certified development companies (CDCs). This bill changes the program in several ways. First, it adds new public-policy goals that can qualify a project: workforce training (a company with a 12-week in-house training program, or a contract to hire people with 12 weeks of relevant training), helping a disaster-declared area recover for five years (extendable a year at a time), and expanding businesses with 10 or fewer employees. Second, it lets top-rated CDCs make fixes at loan closing, such as correcting typos, moving up to 10% of project costs, and adding or changing guarantors. It also shifts file-review duties from SBA district counsels to the SBA's credit risk office for certain loans and sets requirements for the attorneys who close loans. Third, it sets leasing rules: a new facility may lease out up to 20% of space, and small manufacturers need to occupy only 50% instead of 60%. For existing buildings, a business may lease up to 50%, or up to 66% with conditions, including 12 months of prior occupancy and yearly checks that it is not a real estate developer. Fourth, the SBA must create a marketing and outreach plan. Fifth, 504 loans and loans to CDCs would no longer need proof that the borrower could not get credit elsewhere. The SBA must report to Congress within 5 years. The changes apply to loans made on or after October 1, 2027. The bill does not state a cost.
does: Adds three new qualifying public-policy goals to the 504 program: workforce training (12-week in-house program or contract for 12-week-trained applicants), disaster-area revitalization (five years from the declaration, extendable by the SBA one year at a time), and expansion of businesses with 10 or fewer employees.

Lets accredited-lender CDCs make closing changes: shift up to 10% of project cost, fix typos in names and addresses, add eligible passive companies and operating companies, swap guarantor/co-borrower roles, add guarantors with no ownership stake, and reduce debt or project cost.

Moves responsibility for file reviews of loans closed by designated attorneys to the SBA Office of Credit Risk Management, and removes district counsels' review of those closing packages, starting 180 days after enactment.
Defines designated attorneys for Priority CDCs: they must be licensed and in good standing in the state, carry malpractice insurance, and complete SBA-approved training.
Requires the SBA to develop a marketing and outreach plan for 504 loans, possibly with resource partners.

Sets leasing limits: new facilities may lease up to 20% (business must occupy at least 60%, or 50% for small manufacturers, with plans to reach 80% occupancy within 10 years); existing buildings may lease up to 50%, or up to 66% with 12 months prior occupancy, annual CDC examinations and anti-investor certifications, and lease terms capped at 1 year (residential) or 5 years (commercial).
Exempts 504 loans, other Small Business Investment Act financings, and SBA loans to CDCs from the 'credit elsewhere' requirement.
Requires an SBA report to Congress within 5 years on how the leasing changes affect small business access to capital.
Applies to loans made or guaranteed on or after October 1, 2027.

imp.cost: No cost estimate or new appropriation is stated in the bill text. Costs could come from added SBA administration work and the risk of losses on guaranteed loans; the 504 program is generally financed by fees paid by borrowers. Exact effects are not stated.

The program provides a small business with SBA financing—through a certified development company intermediary—for expansion or modernization.
Specifically, the bill expands the public policy goals that allow an intermediary to qualify for assistance to include additional objectives. These include (1) workforce development through work-based or work-integrated training, and (2) aiding the revitalization of an area for which a disaster has been declared or determined.
The bill also authorizes an intermediary to take specified actions to facilitate the closing of 504 loans, such as correcting borrower or lender information on loan documents or reallocating up to 10% of the cost of a project.
Further, the bill allows small businesses to lease a larger portion of renovated buildings that are financed with 504 loans to other tenants in certain circumstances. In the case of a project to renovate or reconstruct an existing building, a small business may lease a maximum of 66% of the building to commercial or residential tenants if certain conditions are met. For example, the small business must have occupied the building for 12 consecutive months prior to the project.
Additionally, the bill exempts intermediaries from the requirement to demonstrate they are unable to obtain credit elsewhere to receive 504 loans.

environment.reason: The bill concerns SBA loan programs, leasing and closing rules, and does not address water, air, land protection or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on closing changes lets CDCs correct and reallocate loan terms and add guarantors at closing, and shifts file review from district counsels to the credit risk office, which may reduce public visibility into loan decisions; the required 5-year report and new marketing plan partly offset this.

people_over_profit.reason: Dropping the credit-elsewhere test and allowing leasing up to 50-66% of existing buildings lets borrowers earn rental income from financed property, and the bill's reallocation and guarantor changes shift risk toward the public guarantee, though the loan-fee structure and small-business focus partly offset this.

local_say.reason: The bill neither clearly expands nor reduces community or state input on land use or facilities; disaster-area revitalization is a federal program goal with no local approval mechanism either way.

no_bailouts.reason: Exempting 504 loans from the credit-elsewhere requirement (Sec. on credit-elsewhere exemption) can place more SBA-guaranteed, taxpayer-backed risk on loans borrowers could obtain privately, with no stated cost estimate.

equality.reason: The new goals for expanding businesses with 10 or fewer employees and the required marketing and outreach plan broaden access to 504 financing for smaller firms.

justice.reason: Moving file review away from district counsels and letting designated attorneys close loans under varied rules, with closing changes made without a full new review, may weaken oversight and consistency, though designated-attorney licensing, insurance and training requirements add some accountability.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill mainly changes program rules for businesses and CDCs and does not meaningfully expand or restrict individuals' personal choices.

news.overall: Evidence is extremely limited: only one Lean Left article (NPR) was provided, and its headline does not explicitly reference the bill. No comparison across perspectives is possible from this input. Coverage from other outlet groups would be needed to assess how the bill itself is framed.
