label: H.R. 1047
title: GRID Power Act
short_title: GRID Power Act
one: Directs FERC to write a rule letting grid operators move "dispatchable" power plants (like gas, coal, or nuclear plants that can run on demand) up the line to connect to the grid, with FERC deciding each request within 60 days.
summary: New power plants have to wait in a line, called the interconnection queue, to hook up to the high-voltage electric grid. This bill tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to change the rules for that line so "dispatchable" power plants can connect faster. Dispatchable means a plant whose output can be predicted and called on when needed. The bill does not name fuels in its text, but the Congressional Research Service says fossil fuel plants are the main example. Within 90 days of becoming law, FERC must start a rulemaking. It must finish within 180 days. The rule must let grid operators (utilities, ISOs and RTOs) ask FERC to move certain dispatchable projects higher in the queue. Each request must show why the move is needed and how it would improve grid reliability or resilience. Operators must also hold a public comment and stakeholder process before they file a request, and they must report regularly to FERC on grid reliability. FERC must approve or deny each request within 60 days. FERC must review the rule at least every five years. The bill doesn't spend money. It does not say what happens to renewable or battery projects that get pushed back, and it does not set environmental conditions on projects that get priority. The bill has passed the House and is now in a Senate committee.
does: Requires FERC to begin a rulemaking within 90 days of enactment and issue a final rule within 180 days.

Directs FERC to fix inefficiencies in how interconnection requests are processed so new dispatchable projects that improve reliability and resource adequacy can connect quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably.
Changes FERC's standard large-generator interconnection procedures and agreement so transmission providers (utilities, ISOs, RTOs) may propose moving new dispatchable projects higher in their queue.
Requires each proposal to show a demonstrated need and explain how prioritization would improve grid reliability or resilience.
Requires a public comment and stakeholder engagement process before a proposal goes to FERC.
Requires transmission providers to report regularly to FERC on grid reliability and resilience and on actions taken under the Act.
Requires FERC to approve or deny each proposal within 60 days of submission.
Requires FERC to review, and update if needed, the rule at least every five years.
Defines 'dispatchable power' broadly as generation providing known and forecastable supply when needed for reliability. It does not list fuel types in the bill text.
who: Developers of new power plants waiting in interconnection queues, especially renewable and storage developers who could be moved back
Developers of gas, coal, nuclear, and other dispatchable plants who could move up
Utilities, ISOs, and RTOs that run interconnection queues
FERC, which would face tight deadlines
Electricity customers and ratepayers, whose bills and reliability could be affected
Communities near new plants, and people affected by air and water pollution from them

benefits: Could help speed up new generation that can run on demand, which may reduce blackout risk during peak demand or extreme weather.
Requires operators to show need and explain the reliability benefit before getting priority.
Requires public comment and stakeholder engagement before a proposal is filed, and regular reporting to FERC.
Proposals are optional for operators and need FERC approval, and the rule is reviewed every five years.
concerns: Priority could go mainly to fossil-fuel plants, which could add air and water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.
Wind, solar, and battery projects could be pushed back in the queue, which could slow cleaner and often cheaper power.
The 60-day FERC deadline is short and may limit careful review or public input.
The bill has no environmental review or ratepayer cost protections.
The public comment step happens before filing, and the bill does not give communities a say at FERC or in local siting.
imp.cost: No spending is authorized. FERC would bear the administrative work. The bill does not say who would pay for grid upgrades or higher costs, so ratepayers could be affected through normal utility rates.
unknowns: Which projects would count as dispatchable, since the bill text sets no fuel limits.
How many projects would be moved ahead, and how far renewable and storage projects would be delayed.
How FERC and grid operators would write and use the rule.
Effects on electricity prices and emissions.
Whether the Senate will act on it.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make sure new dispatchable power projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can connect to the high-voltage grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably. It addresses the problem of long waits in the interconnection queue by directing FERC to revise its rules so transmission providers can propose moving those projects higher in the line. The Congressional Research Service describes fossil fuel plants as the main example of dispatchable power, though the bill text does not name fuel types.

oppose: The bill could push new fossil fuel plants ahead of other projects in the queue, which may add air and water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. The bill sets no environmental review or emissions conditions for prioritized projects.
Wind, solar, and battery projects could be moved back in the queue. Those projects can often be built faster and at lower cost, so this could slow cleaner power.
The bill has no ratepayer cost protections, and the 60-day FERC review deadline is short, which may limit careful review and public input before a decision is made.
support: The bill aims to help new power plants that can run on demand connect to the grid sooner, which could reduce blackout risk during peak demand or extreme weather.
Grid operators must show a demonstrated need and explain how priority would improve reliability or resilience before FERC can approve it, which adds a check on how the priority is used.
The bill requires public comment and stakeholder input before a proposal is filed, regular reporting to FERC on reliability, and a rule review at least every five years.

crs:
Guaranteeing Reliability through the Interconnection of Dispatchable Power Act or the GRID Power Act

This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to issue and periodically review a rule that revises the approval process for interconnection requests of generating units that produce electricity to prioritize dispatchable power projects (e.g., certain fossil fuel projects). 
Under the bill, 
dispatchable power
 generally refers to an electric energy generation resource, such as a generating unit that produces electricity from fossil fuels, capable of providing known and forecastable electric supply in time intervals necessary to ensure grid reliability. Currently, FERC receives interconnection requests from those projects and other generating units, such as units that produce electricity from renewable energy. Interconnection requests are requests from generating units to connect to the high voltage transmission lines of the electric grid.
First, the rule must address the efficiency and effectiveness of the existing procedures for processing interconnection requests to ensure that new dispatchable power projects that improve grid reliability and resource adequacy can interconnect to the electric grid quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably. 
Second, the rule must revise the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Procedures, and the pro forma Large Generator Interconnection Agreement as appropriate, to authorize transmission providers to submit proposals to FERC to prioritize new dispatchable power projects that will improve grid reliability and resource adequacy by assigning those projects higher positions in the interconnection queue of the provider. FERC must review and approve or deny such proposals within 60 days after the proposal is submitted.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 (rulemaking) moves dispatchable projects, which the CRS summary says include fossil fuel plants, up the queue without any environmental conditions or review, which could increase air and water pollution from those plants.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires a public comment and stakeholder process and regular reporting to FERC, which helps transparency, but comment happens before filing and the 60-day FERC deadline limits review, roughly offsetting.

people_over_profit.reason: Priority favors developers of dispatchable plants, which could benefit corporate interests, but the bill also aims at reliability for customers and requires showing need; the net effect is unclear.

local_say.reason: The 60-day FERC approval deadline and the lack of any community role at FERC or in local siting give communities less say over new plants, though state and local stakeholders take part in the pre-filing process.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not say who pays for grid upgrades triggered by reprioritized projects, so costs could flow to ratepayers through normal utility rates.

equality.reason: Sec. 1 prioritizes one category of generators (dispatchable, including fossil fuel) over others such as wind, solar and battery projects, which could be pushed back in the queue.

justice.reason: The 60-day FERC deadline for approving or denying priority requests may limit careful review and public input, and the bill provides no remedy for affected developers or communities.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill concerns generator interconnection procedures and does not restrict or expand what individuals may do about their own lives.

label: H.R. 1453
title: Clean Energy Demonstration Transparency Act of 2025
short_title: Clean Energy Demonstration Transparency Act
one: Requires the Department of Energy to publish, at least twice a year, contracts, milestone status, and major changes for clean energy demonstration projects it funds or manages.
summary: This bill adds a reporting rule to the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. It covers clean energy demonstration projects, which are pilot-scale projects the Department of Energy (DOE) funds to test new energy technology. Starting six months after the bill becomes law, and at least every six months after that, the Energy Secretary must send a report to key House and Senate committees. The report must also be posted online for the public. For each project, the report must include a copy of the first contracts or financial assistance agreements between DOE and the award recipient, along with related documents the Secretary thinks are appropriate. It must list technical, material, or financial milestones that were met or missed. It must also describe major changes to the project's scope, schedule, funding (including cost-share requirements, meaning the share the recipient pays), partners, or budget. DOE may combine these reports with other required reports, where practical, to avoid duplicating work. The bill does not add money, change which projects get funded, or set penalties for missing the deadlines. The bill passed the House on May 19, 2025, and is now in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
does: Requires DOE reports on clean energy demonstration projects starting six months after enactment, then at least every six months.
who: Department of Energy and its Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations (new reporting work)

benefits: Greater public and congressional visibility into how DOE demonstration projects are progressing and whether they meet their goals.
Earlier notice of missed milestones, cost changes, or schedule delays, which could help lawmakers respond sooner.
Makes project contracts and agreements available to the public, which may improve accountability for how federal money is spent.
Allowing reports to be combined with other required reports may reduce extra paperwork for DOE.
concerns: Publishing contract details and project documents may reveal information that recipients or DOE would prefer to keep private, though the material does not say how such information would be handled.
Because the bill sets no penalties for missed deadlines, DOE could submit late reports without direct consequences.
Reporting duties could add workload for DOE staff, although combining reports is allowed to reduce duplication.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not add money and does not change which projects receive funding, according to the summary provided. No cost estimate is given in the material. Any costs would likely come from DOE's existing budget for preparing and posting the reports, but the material does not state this."]
unknowns: The material does not say how much staff time or cost the reporting would require.
It is not stated whether any information in the contracts or documents could be withheld or redacted before public posting.
It is not stated which specific clean energy demonstration projects would be covered beyond the general definition.
The material does not say how 'major changes' or 'appropriate' documents would be defined.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill, and whether it would change before passage, is not stated.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to increase transparency about clean energy demonstration projects that the Department of Energy's Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations manages or supports. It does this by requiring DOE to report on each project's status, including its first contracts or agreements, milestones met or missed, and major changes to scope, schedule, funding, partners, or budget, and to post these reports online. The bill's title describes its aim as demonstration transparency.

oppose: The bill adds recurring reporting duties every six months, which could take time and staff effort away from managing the projects themselves, even though DOE may combine these reports with other required reports.

Publishing contracts, financial assistance agreements, and related project documents online could expose business or technical information that companies or DOE would prefer to keep private, and the bill does not explain how such information would be protected.
The bill sets no penalties for late reports, so the reporting requirement may not be enforced in practice, which raises questions about whether it would deliver the oversight it describes.
support: The bill requires regular reports to key House and Senate committees, which gives lawmakers earlier notice of missed milestones, cost changes, or schedule delays so they can respond sooner.
Posting the first contracts and financial assistance agreements online lets the public see how federal money for clean energy demonstration projects is being spent, which supports accountability.
The bill allows DOE to combine these reports with other required reports where practical, which the bill's text says is meant to avoid duplicated paperwork.

Clean Energy Demonstration Transparency Act of 2025
This bill directs the Department of Energy (DOE) to submit and publish online semiannual reports on the status of certain clean energy demonstration projects that are managed or supported by DOE's Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations.

transparency_kindness.reason: The report must be posted online for the public and must include copies of the first contracts or financial assistance agreements, plus milestones met or missed and major changes to scope, schedule, funding, cost-share, partners, or budget.

people_over_profit.reason: Public posting of agreements and cost-share and funding changes makes it harder for recipients to shift project costs or hide missed milestones at taxpayer expense, though the bill does not directly alter corporate profit terms.

no_bailouts.reason: The semiannual reporting of cost changes, funding changes, and cost-share requirements gives Congress and the public earlier notice of cost growth on federally funded projects, which may help identify overruns before taxpayers absorb them, though the bill sets no direct limits on funding.

justice.reason: Sec. (reporting provision) requires regular public reporting on milestones and agreements, which improves accountability for federal demonstration funding, though it provides no penalties or remedies for missed deadlines.

label: H.R. 1455
title: ITS Codification Act
short_title: ITS Codification Act
one: The bill writes into federal law the existing federal telecom research lab (the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences) and orders it to start an effort to develop tools for finding people trapped in mines, collapsed buildings, and similar places.
summary:
The Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) is a lab inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), part of the Commerce Department. It already exists, but this bill would put it into federal law so its role is official. The bill says ITS would be the main executive-branch lab for studying radio signals, how they travel, and how they interfere with each other. It would also test technology that lets federal agencies and private companies share radio spectrum (the airwaves used for phones, radar, and more), and help make federal spectrum more available to non-federal users. The bill lets ITS make research and technology agreements with outside parties under several existing laws.

The bill also requires ITS to start an initiative to help develop emergency communication and tracking tools. These would help find people trapped in places where regular radios don't work well, such as underground mines, high-rise buildings, or collapsed structures. ITS would work with private companies and federal agencies to assess needs and help develop technical standards. Within 18 months, the NTIA head would have to send Congress, and post publicly, a report on that needs assessment. The bill does not state a dollar amount or create new funding. I could not see any budget numbers in the text.
does: Adds a new section 106 to the NTIA Organization Act that makes ITS an official, permanent test center.
Names ITS the primary executive-branch lab for studying radio emissions, interference, and how signals travel.
Directs ITS to test spectrum-sharing technology and promote access to federal spectrum for non-federal users.
Lets the Assistant Secretary hand ITS other NTIA duties.
Allows ITS to enter research, technology-transfer, and interagency agreements under several listed laws.
Requires an initiative on emergency communication and tracking technology for locating trapped people in mines, high-rises, and collapsed structures.
Requires a public report to Congress on the needs assessment within 18 months.
who: Miners and others who work in hazardous confined spaces
First responders and search-and-rescue teams
NTIA and ITS staff in Boulder, Colorado, and the Commerce Department
Wireless and telecommunications companies seeking spectrum access
Federal agencies that use spectrum, such as defense
Consumers who rely on wireless services

benefits: Making ITS official in law could give its research role lasting, clear authority.
Shared-spectrum testing could help make more radio airwaves available for public and commercial use.
Work on tracking tools could help rescuers find trapped people faster where normal radio fails.
The required public report could give Congress and the public information about emergency communication needs.
concerns: The text does not state a dollar amount or new funding, so agencies may need to shift existing resources to carry out the new duties.

Broad authority to enter agreements with outside parties could raise questions about how partners are chosen and how conflicts of interest are handled, though the material does not address these points.
The material does not say how the tracking tools would be tested or regulated before use.

unknowns: How much the initiative and shared-spectrum testing would cost, and where the money would come from.
Which specific private companies or agencies would take part, and how partners would be selected.
What the needs assessment would find, and whether it would lead to later rules or funding.
How the new tracking tools would perform in real emergencies.
Whether the bill would change ITS's current work or staffing in practice.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to put the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) into federal law as the official research and engineering arm of the NTIA, and to direct ITS to start an initiative for developing emergency communication and tracking tools that can help locate trapped people where conventional radio communication is limited, such as underground mines. The bill's stated aims, based on its title and summary, are to give ITS lasting, clear authority and to strengthen work on spectrum sharing and emergency locating technology.

oppose: The bill does not state a dollar amount or new funding, so ITS and NTIA may have to shift existing resources to take on the new duties, which could affect other work.

The bill lets ITS enter research, technology-transfer, and interagency agreements under several existing laws, but the text does not say how outside partners are chosen or how conflicts of interest are handled. You could ask your member how those safeguards would work.

The bill does not explain how the tracking tools would be tested or regulated before use, so you could ask whether safety and reliability standards will be set before the technology is relied on in emergencies.
support: Writing ITS into federal law could give its research role lasting, clear authority instead of depending on administrative arrangements that can change.
The bill directs ITS to test spectrum-sharing technology and promote federal spectrum access for non-federal users, which could help make more airwaves available for public and commercial use.

The required initiative on tracking tools could help rescuers locate trapped people faster in places like mines, high-rises, and collapsed buildings where normal radio fails, and the public report to Congress within 18 months would give lawmakers and the public information on those needs.

Institute for Telecommunication Sciences Codification Act or the ITS Codification Act
This bill provides statutory authority for the Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS), which serves as the telecommunications research and engineering arm of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration.
The bill also directs ITS to establish an initiative to support the development of emergency communication and tracking technologies for use in locating trapped individuals in confined spaces (e.g., underground mines) and other environments where conventional radio communication is limited.

label: H.R. 197
title: Lake Winnibigoshish Land Exchange Act of 2025
short_title: Lake Winnibigoshish Land Exchange Act
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to swap about 17.5 acres of federal land in Chippewa National Forest for about 36.7 acres owned by Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC, if the company offers the swap.
summary:
This bill covers a small land swap in Itasca County, Minnesota, near Lake Winnibigoshish (often called Lake Winnie). The swap involves the Chippewa National Forest. If a private company, Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC (BWLT), offers to give the U.S. about 36.7 acres, the Forest Service must accept the offer within one year. In return, the Forest Service must give BWLT about 17.5 acres of federal land. The federal government would keep a right of way (an easement) so people can still reach national forest land west of the federal parcel.

The swap is supposed to be equal in value. If the federal land is worth more, BWLT pays the difference in cash. If the company's land is worth more, the government does not have to pay the difference, and the extra value counts as a donation from BWLT. Before the government accepts the company's land, the company must complete a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment. This is a records review and site check for signs of contamination. The company must also show clear title to the land. BWLT pays all closing costs, including survey, title, and environmental study costs. Land the government gets would become part of the Chippewa National Forest and be managed under normal national forest rules. The map and legal descriptions would be finalized after the bill passes and kept open for public viewing at Forest Service offices.
does: Requires the Forest Service to accept BWLT's offer of about 36.7 acres and convey about 17.5 federal acres to BWLT within one year of the offer.
Keeps a federal road-access easement to national forest land west of the federal parcel.
Requires equal value, with BWLT paying cash if the federal land is worth more.
Waives any government payment to BWLT if the company's land is worth more, treating the extra value as a donation.
Requires a satisfactory Phase I Environmental Site Assessment by BWLT before the government accepts the company's land.
Requires appraisals by an independent appraiser that both sides agree on, using federal and professional appraisal standards.
Requires BWLT to pay all closing costs and survey costs.
Adds the acquired land to the Chippewa National Forest, to be managed under national forest laws.
Requires the final map and legal descriptions to be available for public inspection, and lets the Forest Service and BWLT fix minor errors by mutual agreement.
Subjects the exchange to valid existing rights and any other terms the Secretary finds appropriate.
who: Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC, which would gain the federal parcel and give up its own land.
The Forest Service and Chippewa National Forest managers.
People who visit, fish, camp, or live near Lake Winnibigoshish in Itasca County.
Federal taxpayers, who would not pay closing costs.
Local and tribal communities with interests in the area, though the bill text does not mention them.

benefits: Could add land along the Lake Winnibigoshish shoreline to the Chippewa National Forest.
Could keep public road access to national forest land through the reserved easement.
Requiring BWLT to pay closing costs and environmental study costs could reduce costs to the government.
The environmental review requirement could help identify contamination before the government takes ownership.
concerns: If the company's land is worth more, the government would receive the extra value as a donation without paying the difference, which some may see as an uneven deal.
The bill does not state how the land values would be determined, so the fairness of the exchange is hard to judge from this summary.
Land exchanges can change how land is used, and the effects on local recreation, timber, or wildlife are not described in the material provided.

The amount of any such payment is not stated.", "The material does not say how much the exchange would cost or save overall."]
unknowns: How the land values would be appraised, and what the land is actually worth, is not stated.
What the Phase I environmental assessment might find, and what would happen if it finds contamination, is not stated.
The exception to the equal-value rule is mentioned but its details are not given in the material provided.
The exact location, map, and legal descriptions are not included in the summary and would be finalized after passage.
The bill's current status is in Senate committee, so whether it will pass is uncertain.

stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Reported by Senator Boozman without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to carry out a land exchange near Lake Winnibigoshish in Minnesota's Chippewa National Forest. The Forest Service would accept about 36.7 acres of shoreline land offered by Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC, and give the company about 17.5 acres of federal land, with the acquired land added to the national forest. The bill says the exchange must be for equal value, with cash used to balance any difference, and that a road-access easement to nearby national forest land will be kept.

oppose: The bill says the government would receive extra value from the company's land as a donation if that land is worth more, with no payment owed to the company. Some constituents may see this as an uneven trade in which the public gives up more than it gets.

The bill does not explain how land values would be set beyond requiring appraisals by an independent appraiser both sides agree on. Without a clear valuation method in the bill, it is hard to confirm the exchange is fair to taxpayers.

Land exchanges can change how public land is used. The bill summary does not describe effects on local recreation, timber, or wildlife, so a constituent could ask the member to request those details before supporting the bill.
support: The bill would add about 36.7 acres along the Lake Winnibigoshish shoreline to the Chippewa National Forest, which the bill says would then be managed under national forest rules.
The bill requires the company to pay all closing costs, including survey and environmental study costs, which could reduce costs to the government.

The bill requires a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment before the government accepts the land, which could identify contamination before the government takes ownership, and it keeps a road-access easement so people can still reach nearby national forest land.

crs:
Lake Winnibigoshish Land Exchange Act of 2025
This bill directs the Forest Service to exchange specified land along the shoreline of Lake Winnibigoshish (commonly known as Lake Winnie) in the Chippewa National Forest in Minnesota for specified land owned by Big Winnie Land and Timber, LLC (BWLT), if BWLT offers to make the exchange. The land acquired by the Forest Service must be added to and managed as part of Chippewa National Forest. 
The bill outlines requirements and conditions for the exchange. For example, the Forest Service must reserve an easement for road access to certain land in the forest. The bill also conditions the exchange on the satisfactory completion of a Phase I Environmental Site Assessment by BWLT before the nonfederal land is accepted in the exchange.
In addition, the exchange must be for equal value or the values must be equalized by a cash payment, subject to an exception.
Finally, the bill directs BWLT to pay all closing costs associated with the exchange.

label: H.R. 2600
title: ASCEND Act
short_title: ASCEND Act (NASA Commercial Satellite Data Program)
one: The bill makes NASA's program for buying Earth-imaging data from commercial satellite companies a permanent part of federal law, with rules protecting scientific publication, wider data use, a preference for U.S. vendors, and yearly reports to Congress.
summary:
This bill would write into federal law a NASA program that buys satellite pictures and data of Earth from private companies. NASA started this as a pilot in 2019 and says it worked well. Scientists use this kind of data to study land, water, weather, and climate.

Under the bill, NASA would run the program inside its Earth Science Division. NASA could buy data from commercial companies and could set or change license terms so that more people than just NASA-funded researchers can use the data. The contracts could not block scientists from publishing the data for scientific purposes, or from publishing new information made from it. NASA would have to buy from U.S. companies as much as practical.

Starting 180 days after the bill becomes law, and every year after, NASA would send Congress a report. It would list the agreements, the license terms, how each one helps science (including National Academies priorities), and whether federal workers, contractors, or the public can use the data.

The bill does not give a specific dollar amount. It does not say how much NASA must spend. The bill has passed the House and is waiting on the Senate calendar.

Places the program in NASA's Earth Science Division.
Bars contract terms that block publishing the data for scientific purposes or publishing information derived from it.
Lets NASA set or change license terms so people other than NASA-funded users can use the data as widely as possible.
Requires buying from U.S. vendors to the maximum extent practicable.
Requires a report to Congress within 180 days and every year after, covering agreements, license terms, scientific benefit, and who can use the data.

Taxpayers, who fund the purchases

Annual reports could give Congress and the public a view of how the data is being used.
concerns: The bill sets no dollar amount or spending limit, so total costs over time are unclear.
Preferring U.S. vendors 'to the extent practicable' may limit NASA's options if foreign sources offer better data or prices.
Broad use of data by people outside NASA could raise questions about who gets access and for what purposes.

Accessing Satellite Capabilities to Enable New Discoveries Act or the ASCEND Act
This bill provides statutory authority for the Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition (CSDA) program run by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA). Through the CSDA program, NASA acquires remote sensing data and imagery from commercial satellites to support its Earth science research. (
Remote sensing
 generally refers to the collection of data by instruments in Earth’s orbit, such as satellites, that can be processed into imagery of Earth’s surface.)
Under the bill, NASA may establish or modify end-use agreements to allow for broad use of data and imagery acquired under the program, including by individuals outside of NASA (e.g., other federal agencies). The terms of any data or imagery acquisition may not prevent the publication of such data or imagery for scientific purposes or the publication of information derived from it. To the extent practicable, NASA must acquire such data and imagery from U.S. vendors.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill authorizes paid data purchases from commercial vendors under the program, but it does not provide a bailout, rescue, or ratepayer tax break.

equality.reason: Under the license-term provision, data NASA pays for can be used by people beyond NASA-funded researchers, including other agencies and the public, which broadens equal access to the data.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal processes, due process, or remedies for harm.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill governs federal contracts and data licensing and does not expand or restrict what individuals may do in their own lives.

label: H.R. 2659
title: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Against State-Sponsored Threats Act
short_title: Strengthening Cyber Resilience Against State-Sponsored Threats Act
one: Creates a temporary federal task force, led by CISA with the FBI as vice chair, to coordinate agency responses to Chinese state-sponsored hackers like Volt Typhoon and to report to Congress for about seven years.
summary: This bill would require the Department of Homeland Security, working through its cyber agency (CISA), to set up a joint task force within 120 days of the bill becoming law. The task force would help federal agencies that oversee key sectors, such as energy, water, transportation and agriculture, work together to find and respond to hacking by groups tied to the Chinese government. One named group is Volt Typhoon, which has been reported to hide inside U.S. critical infrastructure networks. CISA's director would chair the task force and the FBI director would be vice chair. Members would be technical experts with proper security clearances. Agencies would have to share relevant information, audits and analyses with it. The task force would send Congress a first report within 540 days and then yearly for five more years. The reports would cover risks by sector, what resources and legal powers agencies still need, and how a crisis or conflict with China could disrupt infrastructure, the military and the economy. They would also include a one-time plan for an awareness campaign for infrastructure owners and operators. Reports would be classified, but an unclassified executive summary must be posted on a public DHS website. The task force would end 60 days after its last briefing. It would be exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act, which normally requires open meetings and public records for advisory groups, and from the Paperwork Reduction Act. The bill does not give a dollar cost or set aside new money.
does: Requires DHS, acting through CISA, to set up a joint interagency task force within 120 days of enactment to coordinate agencies' detection of, analysis of, and response to Chinese state-sponsored cyber threats, including Volt Typhoon.

Names the CISA Director as chair and the FBI Director as vice chair; members are agency representatives, ideally cybersecurity, forensics or threat-intelligence experts. It covers the Sector Risk Management Agencies named in National Security Memorandum-22.
Lets the task force coordinate with existing task forces or working groups to avoid duplicating work.

Requires a first report to congressional homeland security, judiciary and intelligence committees within 540 days, then annual reports for five more years, each followed by a classified briefing within 30 days.

Reports must assess sector risks and trends, resources and authorities agencies need, potential damage to infrastructure in a crisis or conflict with China, U.S. ability to counter the threat, effects on military mobility (rail, aviation, ports), and economic and social effects. They must also give recommendations and a one-time awareness-campaign plan for infrastructure owners.
Reports are classified, but an unclassified executive summary of each must be posted on a public DHS website.
Requires DHS, CISA, DOJ, FBI and relevant sector agencies to give the task force information, audits, and assessments it needs, handled under existing laws and with proper security clearances.
Ends the task force 60 days after its final briefing, and exempts it from the Federal Advisory Committee Act and the Paperwork Reduction Act.

Owners and operators of critical infrastructure (power, water, transportation, communications, etc.), who would get recommendations and an awareness campaign
Congressional committees on homeland security, judiciary and intelligence, which receive reports
The general public, which depends on infrastructure such as water and power and would see only unclassified summaries

The bill focuses on one country's actors and does not address other cyber threats.
Exempting the task force from the Paperwork Reduction Act removes one check on federal information-gathering burdens.

How much of each report would be public beyond the executive summary.
Whether the task force would overlap with existing CISA and FBI efforts.
Whether private infrastructure owners would be asked to take on new duties or receive federal help (the bill creates no mandates).
How the Senate committee will change the bill.

crs:
Strengthening Cyber Resilience Against State-Sponsored Threats Act
The bill creates a joint interagency task force to facilitate agency collaboration on efforts to respond to Chinese state-sponsored cyber actors, including Volt Typhoon. 
The task force must be established and led by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), an agency within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The task force must facilitate collaboration and coordination among the Sector Risk Management Agencies (SRMAs) specified in the President's National Security Memorandum- 22 (e.g., the Department of Defense, the Department of Energy, and the Department of Agriculture) to detect, analyze, and respond to Chinese state-sponsored cyber actors by ensuring that such agencies’ actions are aligned and mutually reinforcing.
The bill directs DHS, CISA, the Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and specified SRMAs to provide the task force with analysis, inspections, audits, and other relevant information necessary for the task force to carry out its responsibilities. The production and use of information must comply with all applicable statutes, regulations, and executive orders, and task force members must have appropriate security clearances to access classified information.
The task force must provide annual reports and briefings to Congress detailing its assessment of cyber threats and recommendations to improve the detection and mitigation of the cybersecurity threat posed by Chinese state-sponsored cyber actors.
The first report must be provided no later than 540 days after the establishment of the task force, and additional reports must be provided annually thereafter for six years.

title: Benton MacKaye National Scenic Trail Feasibility Study Act of 2026
short_title: Benton MacKaye National Scenic Trail Feasibility Study Act
one: Requires the Agriculture Department to study, within two years, whether the 287-mile Benton MacKaye Trail in Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina should become a national scenic trail.
summary:
This bill does not create a new national trail. It only orders a study. The Benton MacKaye Trail is a hiking-only (nonmotorized) trail about 287 miles long that runs through Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina. The bill adds the trail to the list of routes in the National Trails System Act that the government must study for possible national scenic trail status.

The Secretary of Agriculture, who oversees the U.S. Forest Service, would have two years from the date the bill becomes law to finish the study and send it to Congress. The Secretary must talk with interested groups, including the Benton MacKaye Trail Association, while doing the work.

The bill does not say what the study must examine, such as land ownership, environmental effects, or cost. It does not give money for the study, and it does not say how the public or local landowners and communities would be able to weigh in beyond the "interested organizations" the agency must consult. Making the trail a national scenic trail would need a separate act of Congress later. The bill passed the House on June 2, 2026, and is waiting on the Senate calendar.

title: University of Utah Research Park Act

one: The bill confirms that the University of Utah's use of about 593 acres of formerly federal land in Salt Lake City as a research park, including student housing and a transit hub, counts as a valid public purpose under federal law.
summary: In 1968 the federal government gave about 593.54 acres of land in Salt Lake City to the University of Utah under the Recreation and Public Purposes Act. That law lets public bodies get federal land for public uses like schools and parks. The University has used the land as a research park, and the Interior Department approved that plan in a 1970 letter. This bill says that use, and any later changes the Interior Department approved before the bill becomes law, is a valid public purpose under that 1926 law. It also says other uses are valid if they fit a research park and related university purposes. The bill names student housing and a transit hub as examples. The earlier terms and conditions in the 1970 letter and approvals still apply to the approved plan. The bill does not give out new land or spend money. It appears to clear up legal doubt about whether the land's current and future uses fit the original grant. The bill text does not say what happens if the land is used for something else. It also does not say whether private companies that lease space in the park are covered, or whether the public gets a say in future changes. The House passed it on December 15, 2025. It is now on the Senate calendar.

label: H.R. 3029
title: To amend the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act to support nucleic acid screening, and for other purposes.
short_title: Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act
one: Directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to research and help set voluntary best practices and technical standards for screening synthetic DNA/RNA orders to reduce the risk of creating dangerous biological agents, authorizing $5 million a year for 2027–2031.
summary:
This bill updates an existing science law (the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act) to focus NIST, the federal measurement and standards agency, on the safety of synthetic DNA and RNA. Companies can now make custom genetic material, which helps create medicines and farm products. But the same technology could be misused, on purpose or by accident, to make dangerous germs or toxins.

The bill tells NIST to do measurement research that supports best practices and technical standards for screening orders of synthetic genetic material. That includes testing how accurate and reliable screening is, setting security and access controls for databases of "sequences of concern," writing technical guidance, and developing ways to check that companies follow the standards. NIST must also look at how well these efforts work.

NIST must bring together a group of stakeholders, including industry, universities, nonprofits, and customers. The group will develop and update shared priorities and best practices and create roadmaps. Within 18 months of the group's first meeting, NIST must report the group's findings to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Science Committee. The bill also adds risk-management best practices and standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including risks tied to artificial intelligence. It authorizes $5 million per year from 2027 through 2031. "Authorizes" means Congress allows the spending, but a separate vote must actually provide the money. The bill does not itself create new mandates or penalties for companies.
does: Names the law the Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act.
Adds to NIST's existing duties: best practices, guidelines and technical standards for managing risks in engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including risks from artificial intelligence.

Requires NIST, consulting other federal agencies as it sees fit, to carry out measurement research supporting biosecurity standards for nucleic acid synthesis. Topics include testing screening accuracy and reliability, security and access controls for sequence-of-concern databases, technical implementation guidance, conformity-assessment standards, and methods to evaluate effectiveness.

Requires NIST to convene a consortium of industry, universities, nonprofits and customers to develop and update consensus priorities and best practices for screening synthetic nucleic acid orders and to develop roadmaps.

Requires a report summarizing the consortium's findings to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee within 18 months of the consortium's first meeting.
Authorizes $5 million per year for fiscal years 2027–2031, drawn from NIST's existing authorized laboratory research funds, to carry out this work.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help NIST support the development of best practices and technical standards for screening synthetic nucleic acid (DNA and RNA) orders, so that the technology used for medicines and agricultural products is less likely to be misused to create dangerous biological agents. crs:
Nucleic Acid Standards for Biosecurity Act
This bill explicitly requires the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to support the development of best practices and technical standards for nucleic acid synthesis.
Nucleic acids, including deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) and ribonucleic acid (RNA), carry genetic information within cells. Nucleic acid synthesis is the process of designing and creating custom nucleic acids; it is used in the development of medications and agricultural products. However, this technology also poses a risk of misuse (e.g., the intentional or unintentional creation of dangerous biological agents).
The bill requires NIST to carry out measurement research to support the development and improvement of biosecurity best practices and technical standards related to nucleic acid synthesis. This effort must address specified topics including nucleic acid synthesis screening, operational security, and conformity assessment. (A 2023 executive order titled 
Safe, Secure, and Trustworthy Development and Use of Artificial Intelligence
 directed NIST to develop and refine similar specifications and best practices for use by synthetic nucleic acid providers. NIST's work on this topic is ongoing.)
In carrying out this effort, NIST must convene stakeholders to develop and periodically update consensus priorities and best practices for synthetic nucleic acid screening mechanisms. Within a specified period, NIST must submit a summary of the stakeholder group’s findings to Congress.
NIST must also take steps to advance risk management best practices and technical standards for engineering biology and biomanufacturing, including with respect to risks associated with the use of artificial intelligence.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on consortium and report requires NIST to report findings to the Senate Commerce and House Science committees within 18 months, adding some congressional visibility into the work; the bill does not require public release or public comment on the standards.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill sets voluntary best practices and standards with no mandates or penalties on companies, and its costs fall on existing NIST research funds, so it neither clearly favors people over profit nor shifts costs to the public.

justice.reason: The bill creates no new enforcement, due process, or remedy mechanisms; it only requires research, standards development, and a report.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill imposes no new mandates or penalties on individuals or companies, so it does not expand or restrict what people may do.

news.overall: Only one outlet group was provided, with four headlines and no descriptions, so the evidence is thin and the framing is inferred from headlines alone. None of the headlines names nucleic acid screening or the bill, so any connection to this legislation is an assumption rather than something the coverage shows. Comparison across perspectives is not possible with this input.

label: H.R. 3187
title: To require the Secretary of Agriculture to convey a parcel of property of the Forest Service to Perry County, Arkansas, and for other purposes.
short_title: Perry County, Arkansas Forest Service Land Conveyance
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to give a roughly 0.81-acre parcel in Perryville, Arkansas, to Perry County for public uses like education and youth development, with the land returning to the federal government if it stops being used that way.
summary: This bill would make the U.S. Forest Service hand over a small piece of land, about 0.81 acres, to Perry County, Arkansas. The land is at 1069 Fourche Avenue in Perryville and includes any buildings on it. The county has to ask for it in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The county would not pay for the land itself, but it would have to pay all the costs of the transfer. That includes a survey, any required environmental review, and any review required by the National Historic Preservation Act. The county must use the land only for public purposes, such as education and youth development. If the county stops using it that way, the land can go back to the United States, but only if the Forest Service chooses to take it back. The land is handed over "as is" through a quitclaim deed, which means the government makes no promises about the title. The Forest Service also would not have to give the usual promise about cleaning up hazardous contamination. Existing rights, such as easements held by others, would stay in place. The House passed the bill on December 15, 2025. It is now on the Senate calendar and has not yet had a Senate vote.
does: Requires the Forest Service to convey about 0.81 acres (parcel 850-10555-001, 1069 Fourche Avenue, Perryville, AR) to Perry County if the county asks in writing within 180 days of enactment.
who: Perry County government and residents of Perryville, Arkansas

benefits: The county could gain a property of about 0.81 acres with buildings for public uses such as education and youth programs.
The Forest Service would no longer need to manage a small parcel that it may not need, and the transfer would be made at no cost to the government for the land itself.
Requiring the county to use the land for public purposes may help keep it in public service.
concerns: Because the transfer is "as is" with no title promises or contamination warranty, the county could face unknown title problems or cleanup needs after the transfer.
The county would bear all transfer costs, which could be significant depending on survey, environmental, and historic review needs; the amounts are not stated.
The reversion right depends on the Forest Service choosing to take the land back, so the enforcement of the public-use requirement is not guaranteed.
The bill does not describe the condition of the buildings or the current use of the property.

The bill does not state the amount of these costs or any federal funding. The bill does not give a cost estimate from the Congressional Budget Office."]
unknowns: The bill does not say what the land is currently used for or what condition the buildings are in.
The bill does not say whether the land has any known contamination or existing easements beyond the general statement that valid existing rights stay in place.
The total cost to the county for the survey and reviews is not stated.
It is not stated how the Forest Service would decide whether to use its option to take the land back.
The bill does not say how the land's public purpose would be monitored after the transfer.
The bill is on the Senate calendar and has not had a Senate vote; whether it will pass the Senate is unknown.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 295.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to transfer a small Forest Service parcel of about 0.81 acres (about one acre per the CRS summary), with any buildings on it, to Perry County, Arkansas, so the county can use it for public purposes such as education and youth development. The bill's official title describes it as a conveyance of Forest Service property to the county.

oppose: The bill transfers the land 'as is' by quitclaim deed with no title promises and no warranty about contamination, so the county could inherit unknown title or cleanup problems.
The county would pay all costs of the transfer, including the survey, any environmental review, and any historic preservation review. The bill does not state how much these costs could be.
The bill does not describe the condition of the buildings or the current use of the property, so Congress may lack details needed to judge whether the transfer is appropriate.
The reversion requirement depends on the Forest Service choosing to take the land back if it stops serving public purposes, so enforcement of the public-use condition is not guaranteed.
support: The Forest Service would no longer have to manage a small parcel it may not need, which could reduce federal property responsibilities.
The county would receive a property with buildings that could support public uses such as education and youth programs, at no cost for the land itself.
The bill requires the county to use the land for public purposes and allows the land to revert to the United States if that use stops, which helps keep the property in public service.
The county must request the land in writing within 180 days and pay the transfer costs, so the local government takes on the responsibility of the transfer process.

crs:
This bill directs the Forest Service to convey approximately one acre of land to Perry County, Arkansas, upon the request of the county. The county must use the land for public purposes, such as supporting education and youth development. If it ceases to be used for such purposes, then the property must, at the discretion of the Forest Service, revert to the United States.
The exact acreage of land to be conveyed must be determined by a survey satisfactory to the Forest Service.
The conveyance must be subject to valid existing rights, made without consideration, made by quitclaim deed, and subject to other terms and conditions that the Forest Service considers to be appropriate to protect the interests of the United States.
As a condition of the conveyance, the county must pay costs associated with the conveyance, including the cost of a survey, any environmental analysis or resources survey required under federal law, and any analysis required to comply with the National Historic Preservation Act.
The bill prohibits the Forest Service from having to provide any covenant or warranty for the property and improvements conveyed to the county.

local_say.reason: Sec. 1 lets Perry County decide whether to request the parcel within 180 days, giving the county a say over use of the land.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 disclaims title warranties and contamination cleanup promises, and makes reversion depend on the Forest Service's discretion, so the county has limited remedies if problems arise.

label: H.R. 331
title: To amend the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to clarify a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes.
short_title: Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act Clarification
one: The bill lets holders of existing water-transport permits on Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land use them, on their own behalf or for a State, Tribe, or public entity, to recharge underground aquifers without a new federal authorization, after giving BLM 30 days' notice.
summary:
Some ditches, canals, and pipelines cross public land run by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). The people or groups who hold permits or rights-of-way for them can already move water across that land to refill underground water supplies, called aquifer recharge, as long as they don't expand or change how the permit is used. This bill widens that rule.

Under the bill, a permit holder could use the existing permit for aquifer recharge for itself or for a State, local government, Indian Tribe, or other public entity. It would not need new approval from the Interior Department. The bill says this use cannot be treated as an expansion, change, or major departure from the permit.

There are limits. The holder must give BLM written notice at least 30 days ahead. The notice must name who will use the permit, identify the permit, describe the plan, and include a copy of the agreement between the holder and the user. The bill also says it does not excuse anyone from federal laws or BLM policies. It also does not authorize building, changing, or expanding any infrastructure.

The CRS summary also mentions an exemption from extra BLM rent for non-profit uses. I could not find that language in the bill text I was given. It may come from the existing law. The summary also says the use would not count as a "major federal action", but the bill text I saw does not use that phrase.
does: Lets holders of existing BLM rights-of-way, easements, permits, or similar authorizations use them for aquifer recharge without new Interior Department authorization.
Allows that use on behalf of the holder or of a State, local government, Indian Tribe, or public entity.
Says such use is not an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation from the existing authorization.
Requires written notice to BLM at least 30 days before the use begins.
Requires the notice to name the user, identify the authorization, describe the intended use and scope, and attach the agreement between the holder and the user.
States that the law does not waive the holder's duty to follow all applicable federal laws and BLM policies.
States that the law gives no authority to build, modify, or expand existing infrastructure.
Makes small wording fixes, changing 'Act' to 'section' in parts of the existing law.
who: Holders of water rights-of-way, ditches, and canals across BLM land, such as irrigation districts and water companies
States, local governments, Indian Tribes, and public water entities that want to recharge aquifers
The Bureau of Land Management and the Interior Department
Farmers, ranchers, and communities in the West that depend on groundwater
People living near affected canals and public lands who may want input on new uses

benefits: Could make it easier for public entities to use existing water infrastructure on BLM land to refill underground water supplies without a new federal approval process.
The 30-day notice and agreement requirement may give BLM a record of who is using each authorization and why.
Keeping federal laws and BLM policies in place may limit how far the change reaches.
concerns: Because the bill says this use is not a major federal action, some people may worry that federal environmental review would not apply to these projects. The bill text provided does not state how NEPA would apply, so this is a possible concern, not a confirmed effect.
Allowing use on behalf of other entities could shift how existing permits are used over time, which some may see as a change in scope despite the bill's wording.
The 30-day notice may give BLM limited time to review or object, depending on how the notice is handled.
imp.cost: ["The bill text provided does not state a cost or funding amount. The CRS summary says holders would not pay additional BLM rent for these uses, except for-profit uses. The CRS summary's rent exemption language was not found in the bill text provided, so its effect on federal revenue cannot be confirmed from the material given."]
unknowns: Whether the rent exemption appears in the bill text or existing law. The source material conflicts on this point.
Whether the 'not a major federal action' wording in the CRS summary appears in the bill text, since the bill text provided does not use that phrase.
How BLM would respond to notices, and whether it could object or set conditions.
How the for-profit limit would be applied in practice.
How much water could be moved, and what effects this could have on land, wildlife, or other water users.
The bill's current status: it is in Senate committee, which is the second chamber.

stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify and expand the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act so that holders of existing BLM rights-of-way and similar authorizations can move water across public land to refill underground aquifers, including on behalf of states, Indian Tribes, or public entities, without getting new approval from the Department of the Interior.

oppose: The bill says this use is not an expansion, modification, major federal action, or substantial deviation. A constituent could ask the Congressman how this affects federal environmental review under NEPA, since the bill text does not explain it.

The bill lets permit holders act for states, Tribes, or other public entities without new federal approval. A constituent could ask how BLM would track changes in who uses each permit and whether the 30-day notice gives BLM enough time to review or object.

The bill allows use of existing infrastructure for aquifer recharge but does not authorize building or expanding it. A constituent could ask how the Congressman would make sure existing permits are not used in ways that change their original scope over time.
support: The bill would let existing ditches, canals, and pipelines on BLM land be used to refill underground water supplies without a new federal approval process. A constituent could say this helps communities use infrastructure already in place.

The bill requires holders to give BLM written notice at least 30 days ahead, naming the user, the permit, the plan, and the agreement between the parties. A constituent could say this gives BLM a record of how each permit is used.
The bill says it does not waive federal laws or BLM policies and does not authorize new construction. A constituent could say these limits keep the change narrow and in line with existing rules.

crs:
This bill modifies the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to expand provisions concerning authorizations (e.g., rights-of-way) to transport water across public land administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for aquifer recharge purposes.
Under the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, the holder of existing rights-of-way, easements, permits, or other authorizations to transport water across BLM land may transport the water for aquifer recharge purposes without additional authorization from the Department of the Interior so long as the use does not expand or modify the operation of such authorizations across public land.
The bill allows the holders of such authorizations to act not only on behalf of themselves, but also on behalf of states, Indian Tribes, or public entities, to use the existing authorizations for aquifer recharge without additional authorization from the Department of the Interior. Further, the bill states that this use may not be considered an expansion, modification, major federal action, or substantial deviation.
Additionally, the bill exempts holders from paying additional rents to the BLM for any use of such authorizations; however, the exemption does not apply to for-profit uses of aquifer recharge or for-profit entities. 
Finally, holders of rights-of-way or other authorizations must provide notice to the BLM of the intended use of authorization as specified by the bill.

environment.reason: Sec. 2 lets existing ditches and canals on BLM land carry water to refill aquifers without new federal review, which can help groundwater supplies; the bill also keeps all federal laws and BLM policies in place, so the environmental effect is modest and somewhat uncertain.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires 30-day written notice naming the user, permit, plan, and agreement, which adds some public record, but it does not make notices public or give the public a chance to comment, so the net effect is unclear.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill is mixed: it spares for-profit uses from the rent exemption in the CRS summary, but the bill text provided does not contain that exemption, so the effect on corporate versus public interests cannot be confirmed.

local_say.reason: The bill removes the need for new Interior Department authorization, which lessens federal review, but it extends use to States, Tribes, and local entities, which gives those public bodies more ability to act; the effects roughly offset.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no bailout provisions; the rent exemption that could shift costs to taxpayers appears only in the CRS summary and not in the bill text provided.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same rule to all permit holders and does not create different treatment for any group.

justice.reason: The bill keeps federal laws and BLM policies in place (Sec. 2), but the 30-day notice does not clearly provide BLM review or a remedy, so the effect on accountability is unclear.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill concerns how permit holders and public entities use existing water authorizations and does not directly expand or restrict what individuals may do about their own lives.

label: H.R. 3410
title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
short_title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
one: Directs the FAA to change its rules so civil aircraft can fly faster than the speed of sound over U.S. land without special permission, as long as no sonic boom reaches the ground, and to set takeoff and landing noise limits for those aircraft.
summary: Right now, FAA rules ban civil (non-military) aircraft from flying faster than the speed of sound, called Mach 1, over U.S. land unless the FAA gives a special authorization. This bill would order the FAA to rewrite that rule within one year of the bill becoming law. Under the new rule, a civil aircraft could fly faster than Mach 1 in U.S. airspace with no special permission, as long as it is flown so that no sonic boom reaches the ground. The bill also requires the FAA to finish a rule by April 1, 2027, saying these aircraft cannot be louder at takeoff and landing than the most recent noise levels required for current subsonic (slower than sound) aircraft. The FAA must also set up a process to review and update those noise limits over time as quieter technology and related rules change. The bill does not mention fuel use, air pollution, climate effects, or public hearings. It also does not say how the "no boom reaches the ground" condition would be tested or enforced, and it doesn't give local governments or residents any role. The bill does not create new spending or subsidies. It passed the House on March 24, 2026, and is now in the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
does: Orders the FAA to issue or revise rules within 1 year of enactment so civil aircraft may fly above Mach 1 without special authorization.
Limits that permission to flights operated so that no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.
Requires a final FAA noise rule by April 1, 2027, capping takeoff and landing noise at the most recent levels required for current subsonic aircraft.
Requires the FAA to set a process for periodically reviewing and updating the noise rule as technology and regulations change, as the FAA Administrator decides.
Points to the current rule (14 CFR 91.817) as an example of a regulation to change; today it bans such flights over land without special authorization.
who: Aerospace companies developing supersonic civil aircraft
Airlines and business-jet operators and their (likely high-paying) passengers
The FAA, which must write and enforce new rules on tight deadlines
People living under flight paths or near airports, who could experience noise
Wildlife and the general public, if emissions or noise change

benefits: Could allow faster civil air travel over U.S. land without case-by-case FAA authorization, which may reduce paperwork for supersonic aircraft makers and operators.
Setting noise limits tied to subsonic standards could mean supersonic aircraft are no louder at takeoff and landing than slower jets.
A required review process could let noise limits keep up with quieter technology over time.
concerns: The bill does not say how the 'no sonic boom reaches the ground' condition would be tested or enforced, so it is unclear whether the rule would hold up in practice.
Because the bill gives no role to local governments or residents and does not require public hearings, communities may have little say in how the rules are applied.
The bill does not address fuel use, air pollution, or climate effects, so these possible impacts are not covered.
Noise limits are set only for takeoff and landing; the bill does not address noise from flight over land at supersonic speeds beyond the sonic boom condition.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not create new spending or subsidies. The material does not state what the FAA would cost to carry out the rulemaking, reviews, or enforcement."]
unknowns: It is not stated how the FAA would measure or enforce the requirement that no sonic boom reaches the ground.
It is not stated whether the FAA's rule would set specific decibel or noise numbers beyond pointing to subsonic standards.
The material does not say what effects on fuel use, air quality, or climate could follow from more supersonic flight.
The material does not say whether the Senate will take up the bill or whether it will change.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to modernize U.S. aviation rules so civil aircraft can operate faster than Mach 1 over U.S. land without a special FAA authorization, provided no sonic boom reaches the ground. It also aims to set takeoff and landing noise limits for these aircraft, tied to the noise levels required for current subsonic aircraft, with a process to update those limits over time.

oppose: The bill does not explain how the 'no sonic boom reaches the ground' condition would be tested or enforced, so it is unclear whether the limit would work in practice.
The bill gives local governments and residents no formal role and does not require public hearings, so communities may have little say in how the new rules are applied.
The bill does not address fuel use, air pollution, or climate effects of faster civil flights, so these possible impacts would not be covered by the bill.
support: The bill would remove the requirement for case-by-case FAA special authorization for supersonic civil flights over U.S. land, which could reduce paperwork for aircraft makers and operators.

The bill requires noise limits for takeoff and landing that match the most recent levels required for current subsonic aircraft, so supersonic aircraft would be no louder at those times than slower jets.
The bill requires the FAA to set a process for periodically reviewing and updating the noise rules, so limits could keep pace with quieter aircraft technology over time.

crs:
Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to allow civil aircraft to operate at speeds above Mach 1 (i.e., supersonic) over land in the United States under certain conditions. 
Specifically, the FAA must issue or revise regulations to allow for the operation of civil aircraft at speeds greater than Mach 1 in the national airspace system without a special authorization, so long as no sonic boom reaches the ground in the United States.
The FAA must also issue a final rule to establish noise standards that prohibit civil aircraft operating at speeds greater than Mach 1 from exceeding takeoff and landing noise levels required for subsonic aircraft (i.e., aircraft that operate at speeds that do not exceed Mach 1). As part of the rule, the FAA must specify a process to periodically review and update the noise standards to reflect future advances in aircraft noise reduction technology and regulatory changes.
Current regulations prohibit civil aircraft from operating above Mach 1 speeds over land in the United States without a special flight authorization issued by the FAA.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 (as summarized) lets supersonic civil aircraft fly over U.S. land without authorization and sets noise limits only for takeoff and landing, while the bill says nothing on fuel use, air pollution, or climate effects, so the existing environmental review that special authorization brings is removed without a replacement.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill removes the case-by-case FAA authorization for supersonic flights and provides no public hearing, comment, or disclosure requirement, and it does not say how the no-sonic-boom condition would be tested or verified.

people_over_profit.reason: Removing the special authorization requirement mainly reduces regulatory steps for aircraft makers and operators, and the bill places the burden of noise and boom impacts on residents below flight paths without requiring any compensation or mitigation.

local_say.reason: Under the rule the bill directs, supersonic flights over land need no special FAA authorization, and the bill gives no role to state or local governments or residents in these decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill creates no spending, subsidies, or ratepayer cost shifts, so it does not bear on bailouts.

equality.reason: The rule applies the same conditions to all civil supersonic aircraft and does not treat any group differently, though the bill notes that the passengers are likely high-paying, which does not change the legal treatment.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 removes the case-by-case FAA authorization review that currently applies to supersonic flights over land, and the bill gives no enforcement mechanism or remedy for residents harmed if the no-boom condition fails.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill affects what aircraft operators may do, not what individuals may do about their own lives, so the effect on personal freedom is unclear.

label: H.R. 4922
title: D. C. Criminal Reforms to Immediately Make Everyone Safe Act of 2025
short_title: DC CRIMES Act of 2025
one: The bill would treat DC residents aged 18 to 24 as adults instead of "youth offenders," end judges' power to go below mandatory minimum sentences for youth offenders, bar DC's local government from changing existing criminal sentences, and require a public website of juvenile crime data.
summary:
This bill changes how criminal sentencing works in Washington, DC. Today, DC's Youth Rehabilitation Act lets judges treat people up to age 24 as "youth offenders." That can mean lighter or different sentences, such as probation instead of jail. The bill would cut that age limit so only people under 18 qualify. It would also remove a rule that lets judges give a youth offender a sentence below a mandatory minimum.

The bill's title and the CRS summary say it would also block the DC Council and other DC authorities from changing any criminal sentence that is in effect when the bill becomes law. The bill text provided to me does not include a section doing this, so I could not check its exact wording.

Finally, the bill would make the DC Attorney General build a public website within 180 days. It would show juvenile arrest and prosecution data, such as age, race, sex, type of crime, repeat arrests, cases declined, and sentence lengths. It would be updated monthly, kept as an archive, and offered in downloadable machine-readable form. It could not show any juvenile's personal information. Courts and police would have to share juvenile records with the Attorney General for this purpose. The bill passed the House on September 16, 2025, and is now in the Senate.
does: unused
who: People aged 18 to 24 charged with crimes in DC
DC judges, prosecutors, and defense lawyers
DC Council and DC residents, who vote for local lawmakers but lack full congressional representation
DC Attorney General's office, which must build and run the website
Crime victims and DC communities
Researchers, journalists, and the public who would use the data

benefits: The website could give the public clear, regularly updated, downloadable data on juvenile crime and how cases are handled.
Data broken down by age, race, and sex could help people spot patterns and unfairness.
Supporters say firmer sentences and mandatory minimums may deter crime and improve public safety.
