The bill also (1) reduces the maximum age of a youth offender from 24 years to 18 years, and (2) repeals a provision that allows a DC criminal court to issue a sentence to a youth offender that is less than the mandatory minimum term otherwise required by law. label: H.R. 5549
title: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
short_title: Efficient Nuclear Licensing Hearings Act
one: The bill would let the Nuclear Regulatory Commission skip its end-of-process public hearing for nuclear power plant permits and licenses, and for uranium enrichment facility licenses, when no affected person asks for one.
summary:
Today, the Atomic Energy Act requires the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to hold a public hearing before it issues certain permits and licenses for nuclear power plants. This bill changes that. If no one whose interests may be affected asks for a hearing, the NRC could issue a construction permit, operating license, combined permit and license, or an amendment to one of these without holding a hearing. It would still have to give 30 days' notice in the Federal Register, the government's daily public notice publication. For some amendments that pose no significant safety hazard, even that notice could be skipped, which the law already allows.

If a hearing is held, the NRC would have to use informal hearing procedures. These are usually simpler and less court-like than formal ones.

The bill also changes licensing of uranium enrichment facilities, which make nuclear reactor fuel. The NRC would hold a hearing only if an affected person requests one. It would also no longer have to hold that hearing "on the record," which is a formal, court-style process.

The changes would apply to applications already pending at the NRC when the bill becomes law. I could not see the full text of the old law that is being struck, so this summary relies on the bill's wording and the CRS summary.

Applies the changes to all applications and proceedings pending at the NRC on or after the date the bill becomes law.

Could reduce NRC workload and time spent on routine or uncontested applications.
Informal hearing procedures, if used, may be simpler and less costly to run.
concerns: Members of the public may not know a licensing action is happening if they miss the Federal Register notice or if the notice is skipped for some amendments.

The bill applies to the licenses and permits if a hearing has not been requested by a person whose interest may be affected. label: H.R. 5729
title: North Rim Restoration Act
short_title: North Rim Restoration Act
one: The bill lets the National Park Service use fast-track emergency contracting to rebuild and restore the Grand Canyon North Rim after the Dragon Bravo Fire, and lets it hand some rebuilding contracts to the current North Rim concessioner without competitive bidding.
summary:
The Dragon Bravo Fire damaged parts of Grand Canyon National Park's North Rim. This bill would make it faster for the National Park Service (NPS) to hire contractors for the cleanup and rebuilding. It has two main parts.

First, it lets NPS use emergency buying rules, such as higher spending limits before full bidding rules apply, without waiting for a presidential disaster declaration. This covers forest restoration, rebuilding and designing damaged structures, improving grounds and buildings, and other recovery work in the burned area. The authority ends after 7 years or when the work is done, whichever comes first. If a new wildfire hits the area, NPS can ask Congress for a 12-month extension.

Second, it lets NPS sign contracts without competitive bidding for rebuilding or running things like employee housing, water and power systems, lodging, food service, and shops on the North Rim. NPS may do this only if it decides in writing that the current North Rim concessioner (the private company that runs visitor services there) is uniquely positioned to do the work and that skipping competition is needed for safety, resource protection, or continuity of services. These contracts cannot extend the company's existing concession contract or give it ownership-type rights. NPS may still choose to use competition.

NPS must also send Congress a report every 180 days on costs, overruns, contractors, conflicts of interest, and any waste, fraud, or abuse.
does: Allows NPS to use emergency acquisition rules (48 CFR part 18) in the burned area of Grand Canyon National Park without a presidential emergency or disaster declaration.
Covers forest restoration, rebuilding and design of fire-damaged structures, improvements to grounds and structures, and recovery work.

Lets NPS award noncompetitive (sole-source) contracts for North Rim assets such as employee housing, water, wastewater, power and communications systems, lodging, food service, retail, and transportation.
Requires a written finding by the Secretary that the current concessioner is uniquely positioned and that skipping competition is needed for safety, resource protection, or essential services.

Says these contracts do not change, extend, or add benefits (such as leasehold surrender interest) to the existing concession contract, and do not allow a concession contract to be awarded without following concession law.
Lets the Secretary still use competitive procedures if that is in the government's best interest.

Requires reports every 180 days to four congressional committees on expected cost, spending, overruns, contractors, conflicts of interest, waste, fraud, abuse, under-budget contracts, and completion timeline.

Ends both authorities after 7 years; the emergency authority ends sooner if recovery is finished. A 12-month extension can be requested if a new wildfire interferes, subject to congressional approval.

crs:
North Rim Restoration Act
This bill allows the National Park Service (NPS) to expedite the approval of contracts to restore forests, structures, and assets within areas of the Grand Canyon National Park impacted by the Dragon Bravo Fire in Arizona.
Specifically, the bill authorizes the NPS to use emergency acquisition flexibilities without a presidential emergency or disaster declaration to contract for the following services in such impacted areas: managing or restoring forests, rebuilding structures affected by the fire, improving grounds and structures, conducting recovery efforts, or other specified activities.
This authority expires on the date that is the earlier of the following: (1) seven years after the date of this bill's enactment, or (2) the date on which projects and recovery efforts within such area are completed. The NPS may request Congress extend such authority for 12 months if a new wildfire ignites within such area and impacts recovery efforts related to the Dragon Bravo Fire.
The bill also authorizes the NPS to enter into noncompetitive procurement contracts for rebuilding, rehabilitating, replacing, or operating assets, such as lodging or utilities, to support the recovery and reopening of the Grand Canyon National Park North Rim. This authority is conditioned upon the NPS making certain determinations regarding the North Rim concessioner and it terminates seven years after this bill's enactment.

no_bailouts.reason: Sec. 1 and Sec. 2 direct federal funds to rebuild and run North Rim assets through noncompetitive and emergency contracts, which could shift recovery costs to taxpayers, though the bill does not describe a direct subsidy to the company.

equality.reason: Sec. 2 gives the current North Rim concessioner a special path to contracts that other potential bidders cannot use, creating unequal access to federal work.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 removes the presidential disaster declaration prerequisite and Sec. 2 allows sole-source awards, reducing standard competition checks; the 180-day reports in the bill add some accountability, which partly offsets this.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not change what individuals may legally do or choose about their own lives.

The headlines do not clearly name the North Rim Restoration Act, so it is unclear how directly these articles address the bill. Coverage from other outlet perspectives would be needed to assess how the bill is framed across the spectrum.

label: H.R. 617
title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
short_title: American Music Tourism Act of 2025
one: Directs the Commerce Department's tourism office to identify and promote music-related places and events (and sports events for international visitors) and to report to Congress every two years.
summary:
This bill changes an existing law called the Visit America Act. It tells the Commerce Department's top tourism official (the Assistant Secretary for Travel and Tourism) to find places and events in the U.S. that matter to music tourism and to promote travel to them. That covers music museums, studios, venues of all sizes, festivals, concerts, and other live music events. The bill asks for both domestic promotion (Americans traveling within the U.S.) and international promotion (foreign visitors coming here).

The bill also rewrites the section on international business and leisure travel. It keeps the focus on large meetings and conferences and on rural and other destinations rich in cultural heritage or ecological tourism. It adds a duty to promote international travel to sports and recreation events.

Finally, the tourism official must send Congress a report one year after the bill becomes law, then every two years. The report covers activities, findings, achievements, and "vulnerabilities" tied to the tourism goals. The reports go to the Senate Commerce Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The bill adds a definition of "music tourism." It does not give a dollar amount, create new grants, or set new rules for businesses. It passed the House on April 28, 2025, and is waiting on the Senate calendar.

label: H.R. 6329
title: Information Quality Assurance Act of 2025
short_title: Information Quality Assurance Act of 2025
one: Requires the White House budget office and federal agencies to update their information-quality rules so agencies use the best available evidence for major rules and guidance, and publish the key facts they relied on and let the public comment on them.
summary: This bill changes federal law so agencies have to show their work when they write rules and guidance. Within one year of becoming law, the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which oversees how federal agencies operate, must update its existing information-quality guidelines. These cover "influential" information, meaning data an agency reasonably decides will have a clear and substantial impact on important public actions, policies, statements, or private-sector decisions. Agencies then have one year to update their own guidelines so they rely on the "best reasonably available" evidence that fits the purpose. The bill also tells OMB to direct agencies to put the critical facts they relied on into the public docket (the rule's file) or administrative record, along with citations to other sources. When an agency takes public comments on a rule or guidance, it must also let the public comment on those critical facts, and it must post any major later changes to them. Agencies can withhold material if a law bars release, and must then explain why and what they're doing to widen access. Agencies must follow the rules only "to the maximum extent feasible" considering cost. Existing ways to ask an agency to correct bad information stay available. The bill authorizes no new money.

It requires agencies to rely on the best reasonably available influential information, publish the critical factual material they used, and give the public a chance to comment on that material. The bill's findings and summary describe these steps as a way to improve the quality and openness of federal information.

oppose: The bill adds steps to rulemaking and guidance, such as public comment on critical facts and posting later changes. Opponents may say this could slow down agencies that need to act quickly on health, safety, or other urgent matters.

The phrase "to the maximum extent feasible," along with cost considerations, gives agencies room to decide how much to follow the rules. Opponents may worry this could lead to uneven application across agencies.

The term "best reasonably available" evidence is not defined in detail in the bill. Opponents may say agencies could interpret it differently, which could create uncertainty for the public and for businesses.
support: The bill requires agencies to publish the critical facts they relied on and cite other sources. Supporters may say this makes agency reasoning easier for the public and courts to check.
The public would get a chance to comment on the key facts behind a rule, not only on the final rule. Supporters may say this could improve transparency and lead to better decisions.
Posting major later changes to those facts would let people track how an agency's evidence shifts over time. Existing ways to ask an agency to correct inaccurate information would remain available.

crs:
Information Quality Assurance Act of 2025
This bill requires the Office of Management and Budget to revise the guidelines for federal agencies with respect to the dissemination or use of 
influential information or evidence
, which means information or evidence about which an agency can reasonably determine that reliance on or dissemination of has, or will have, a clear and substantial impact on important public actions, policies or statements, or on important private sector decisions.
The guidelines must ensure that federal agencies rely on the best reasonably available influential information and evidence that is appropriate for the purpose when developing, issuing, or informing the public about the rules and guidance of the agency.
An agency also must publish (1) the critical factual material relied on as part of the rulemaking or guidance development process, and (2) a citation to any other source used to inform the rulemaking or guidance development process.
The guidelines must also require an agency to provide certain opportunities for the public to comment on the critical factual material upon which the agency relied.

environment.reason: The bill concerns how agencies document and justify evidence in rules and guidance; it does not directly change pollution limits, land protections, or ecosystem safeguards.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on critical facts requires agencies to publish the critical factual material and citations in the docket or record, lets the public comment on those facts, and posts major later changes; withheld material must be explained.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill does not shift costs between corporations and the public in a clear way; its effects on regulated businesses versus public interest are mixed and not clearly directional.

local_say.reason: Opening critical facts to public comment gives members of the public and communities a further opportunity to weigh in on rules that affect them.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has nothing to do with bailouts, subsidies, or ratepayer tax shifts, and authorizes no new money.

equality.reason: The requirements apply uniformly to all agencies and all members of the public; no group is treated differently under the bill.

justice.reason: Requiring agencies to rely on the best reasonably available evidence, publish critical facts, and keep existing correction processes makes agency decisions more checkable and accountable, though the undefined standard and the 'maximum extent feasible' qualifier limit enforceability.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do, say, or choose in their own lives.

votes.question: On Motion to Suspend the Rules and Pass

Because the items do not address the bill, no comparison of how each perspective frames the bill itself can be drawn from this material.

label: H.R. 7567
title: Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026
short_title: 2026 Farm Bill (Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026)
one: A massive five-year farm bill that renews and changes USDA programs for crop and disaster aid, conservation, food aid and trade, SNAP, farm credit, rural development, research, forestry, crop insurance and animal and plant health, with a mix of conservation and water gains alongside several rollbacks of environmental review and regulation.
summary:
This is the 2026 "farm bill," a giant package that renews most USDA programs through fiscal year 2031 and rewrites many of them. The version passed by the House and received in the Senate on May 19, 2026. This summary is based on a section-by-section digest. A few sections were cut off in that digest (Title II funding amounts, parts of Title IV and Title VII, a few forestry and conservation sections, and parts of the crop insurance and later titles). I can't describe those parts.

Commodities (Title I): It extends the suspension of old "permanent" price-support law through 2031. It expands tree-loss aid, creates a framework for direct aid to specialty crop growers after market disruptions (payment cap not lower than $900,000 for farm-dependent operations), and lets USDA give disaster aid as block grants when Congress funds it. It adds dairy cost-reporting rules, extends dairy programs, allows propane storage loans, restores tobacco as an agricultural commodity for the Commodity Credit Corporation, and loosens proof rules for Mexican wolf livestock losses.

Conservation (Title II): It extends the Conservation Reserve Program and EQIP, and adds composting, wildlife habitat corridors and precision-agriculture technology (payments up to 90 percent of costs). It creates a $100 million-a-year soil health grant program for states and tribes, funds feral swine control, and raises the federal share for repairing aging watershed dams to 90 percent. It speeds disaster payments, expands use of private technical advisers, and sets up an Office of Conservation Innovation. It also creates a Forest Conservation Easement Program that replaces the Healthy Forests Reserve Program and allows some subsurface mineral development on conserved forest, and it eases rules on land easements.

Trade (Title III): Food for Peace moves from USAID to USDA, with a floor of $15 million a year for an international food relief partnership and a conditional $200 million a year for therapeutic foods. The bill raises export promotion funding, protects use of "common" food names such as feta and parmesan in foreign markets, creates an agricultural trade enforcement task force (including pressing India at the WTO), and orders reports on USMCA changes and Argentine beef imports.

Nutrition (Title IV, partly visible): SNAP states could hire private contractors for certification work in some conditions. SNAP gets permanent nationwide online purchasing, EBT card security rules, added incentive foods (animal protein), hot rotisserie chicken as an eligible food, and fuller payment-error reporting. It extends TEFAP and other food programs.

Credit (Title V): It raises farm loan limits (for example, direct farm ownership loans from $600,000 to $850,000), cuts experience requirements, expands small and fast-approval loan options, allows nonperforming guaranteed loans to be refinanced into direct USDA loans, extends heirs-property help with $60 million a year for legal services, and widens Farm Credit System powers, including lending for rural community facilities and fishing.

Rural development (Title VI): It renames and reworks the ReConnect broadband program ($350 million a year, higher speed standards, limits on overbuilding), and expands water and wastewater aid, including distressed-system loan forgiveness, a circuit rider program, and $20 million a year for household wells and septic systems. It adds childcare, rural health, a food supply chain loan guarantee (up to $40 million per loan), meat-processing grants, and a rural innovation center.

Research (Title VII): Most research and extension programs are extended through 2031, with new priorities such as precision agriculture, PFAS and microplastics, biochar, and specialty crop automation ($30 million a year reserved). It adds more centers of excellence, a new Aquaculture Advisory Committee, and more reporting by the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research.

Forestry (Title VIII): It raises project size limits and creates new exemptions from environmental review for hazard trees, utility rights-of-way and fuel reduction. It removes the need to redo Endangered Species Act consultations when new species are listed, and sets a goal of containing wildfires within 24 hours in high-risk conditions. It expands good neighbor agreements, adds white oak, giant sequoia, and tree nursery programs, and creates a land exchange in Wisconsin and a naming change for Secure Rural Schools.

Energy, horticulture, regulation (Titles IX–X): It adds waste energy recovery to REAP, a tree-planting grant program, hemp rule changes (total THC testing, reduced testing for industrial hemp), a GE microorganism movement pilot, organic oversight changes, and pesticide-law changes that give USDA a bigger voice in EPA decisions, exempt some plant-incorporated protectants and biostimulants from FIFRA, and delay registration review deadlines to 2031. It also creates a five-year Clean Water Act safe harbor for aerial fire retardant.

Crop insurance (Title XI): It adds a specialty crop advisory committee, revenue-loss coverage changes, interest limits, support for veteran farmers, and many studies on new coverage types (smoke damage, frost, hurricanes, mushrooms, swine disease).

Miscellaneous (Title XII): It adds animal disease and detector dog provisions, rules for importing dogs, a bar on states setting production standards for out-of-state livestock, Rio Grande and Colorado River water treaty reports, rollover protection grants, a seafood office, honey testing, whole milk in school breakfasts, commodity board transparency, grain standards reauthorization through 2033, and an exemption of farm tractors and some self-propelled farm equipment from Clean Air Act engine emission standards.

Total cost is not given in the material I saw.
does: Title I: Extends the suspension of permanent price-support law through 2031 and extends dairy indemnity and promotion programs to 2031.
Expands the Tree Assistance Program (pest and biennial losses, replanting different varieties, 120-day decision deadline, advance payments through FY2035).
Creates a specialty crop emergency aid framework paying a share of prior-year sales; payment caps for farm-dependent operations may not be set below $900,000.
Lets USDA deliver future disaster aid as block grants for crop, tree, poultry and livestock losses when extra funds are provided.
Requires dairy manufacturers to report production cost and yield data, with a USDA report every 2 years; exempts the action from Executive Order 12866 review.
Allows propane storage loans, treats marketing and sugar loan servicing as emergency work during funding lapses, and restores tobacco as a CCC agricultural commodity.

Makes domestic production of food-ingredient commodities a 'priority objective of the President' in federal policy and requires a study of fertilizer storage loans and electronic disaster program forms.
Title II: Extends CRP (including 8.6 million acres of continuous enrollment goal), the farmable wetland program, grassland, EQIP, CSP and private grazing land programs through 2031.

Adds composting, precision agriculture (up to 90% cost payment in EQIP), wildlife habitat connectivity, and a Southern Border Initiative to pay for repairing farmland damage near the border (no dollar amount stated).
Creates a soil health state/tribal grant program at $100 million per year (max $5 million or 50% of a state's cost per grant).
Creates a feral swine program with CCC funding ($150 million a year for FY2025-2031) and repeals the earlier provision.
Authorizes remedial work on old watershed dams, raises federal rehabilitation share from 65% to 90%, and requires public data on watershed spending.
Lets disaster-hit producers get up to 75% of emergency conservation and 75% of forest restoration payments in advance, and expands wildfire eligibility.

Expands use of certified third-party technical providers, creates a streamlined process for new conservation practice standards, an Office of Conservation Innovation, direct-hire authority for NRCS, and farmer-to-farmer networks.
Caps CRP and wetland easement enrollment at 25% of a county's cropland; requires source water protection coordinators and public reporting on source water protection.

Reworks agricultural land easements (lower-cost-share option, narrower USDA inspection rights, easier modification and exchange, exemption from adjusted gross income limits) and wetland reserve stewardship funding.
Creates a Forest Conservation Easement Program (replacing the Healthy Forests Reserve Program) that can allow limited subsurface mineral development and utility subordination.
Updates the Regional Conservation Partnership Program and Critical Conservation Areas (adding wildlife corridors and the Columbia Basin).

Title III: Moves Food for Peace from USAID to USDA, repeals minimum food aid levels, guarantees at least $15 million a year for the International Food Relief Partnership, and conditionally requires $200 million a year for therapeutic foods.

Raises export promotion funding (for example $500 million in FY2027 and $533 million a year for FY2028-2031), adds common-name protections for foreign markets, a perishable produce trade working group, and extends international programs to 2031.

Creates an international agriculture exchange program ($10 million a year), an agricultural trade enforcement task force (including a WTO plan targeting India's price supports), and reports on USMCA changes, Argentine beef imports, and shrimp trade.

Title IV: Lets states contract out SNAP certification in some conditions, makes online purchasing permanent, orders EBT card security rules, adds animal protein as an incentive food and hot rotisserie chicken as eligible, requires fuller payment error reporting, and extends TEFAP and tribal food programs (visible portions only).

Title V: Raises farm loan limits (direct ownership $850,000; guaranteed $3.5 million; direct operating $750,000; microloans $100,000), cuts experience requirements, and creates faster approval processes and a pilot.
Allows refinancing of troubled guaranteed loans into direct loans, funds heirs property legal services ($60 million a year), and extends many credit programs to 2031.

Expands Farm Credit System powers (rural community facilities, aquatic businesses, export finance, rural infrastructure) and names FCA the sole regulator; lets FCA examine low-risk institutions every 24 months.
Title VI: Rebuilds the ReConnect broadband program ($350 million a year, 50/25 Mbps minimum, caps on guarantee fees, overbuilding limits) and funds innovative and satellite broadband demonstrations.

Expands rural water and wastewater programs: circuit riders ($25 million a year), distressed system loan forgiveness, household well and septic loans up to $20,000 ($20 million a year), and extends emergency water and Alaska village programs.

Adds a food supply chain loan guarantee (up to $40 million per loan), meat processing grants, rural childcare priority, rural health facility refinancing, a Rural Development Innovation Center, and a rural energy savings program expansion.

Title VII: Extends research and extension programs to 2031, adds research priorities (PFAS, microplastics, biochar, smoke damage, invasive species), $30 million a year for specialty crop mechanization, centers of excellence, organic transition research ($7.5 million a year), and veteran farming grants.

Creates an Aquaculture Advisory Committee, requires aquaculture reports, adds transparency reporting for the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research, and requires annual state matching attestations for land-grant funds.

Title VIII: Raises acreage caps for forest projects from 3,000 to 10,000 acres, creates new categorical exclusions from NEPA review (hazard trees, utility rights-of-way, fuel reduction) and removes ESA and historic review for some utility actions.

Removes the need to reinitiate ESA consultation on forest and BLM plans when new species or information appear; sets a 24-hour wildfire containment goal in high-risk conditions; expands good neighbor agreements and stewardship contracting.
Adds white oak, giant sequoia, tree nursery, agroforestry, timber loan guarantee ($220 million cap), community wood facilities, grazing improvements, and a Wisconsin land exchange release.

Titles IX-X: Adds waste energy recovery to REAP, a second-use battery study, a tree planting grant program ($50 million a year), hemp rule changes, a GE microorganism movement pilot, organic inspection changes, specialty crop block grants through 2031, and an Office of Biotechnology Policy.

Changes pesticide law (FIFRA): exempts some plant biostimulants and plant-incorporated protectants, requires more USDA coordination and published economic analysis, and extends registration review deadlines to 2031; creates a 5-year Clean Water Act injunction safe harbor for aerial fire retardant.

Title XI: Creates a specialty crop insurance advisory committee, changes disclosure and interest rules, freezes administrative reimbursement rates, starts a late-planting pilot in Texas, and orders many research studies on new coverage types.

Title XII: Adds animal disease and detector dog provisions, live dog import rules, a federal bar on states imposing production standards on out-of-state livestock, Rio Grande and Arizona water treaty reports, rollover protection grants, a USDA Office of Seafood, fishing loans, honey standards and testing, whole milk in school breakfast, commodity board record publication, and grain standards reauthorization through 2033.

Exempts new and in-use agricultural tractors and self-propelled farm sprayers, fertilizer applicators and harvesters from Clean Air Act emission standards, and treats qualified renewable biomass as zero-carbon for USDA actions.
who: Farmers, ranchers, orchardists, dairy and specialty crop producers
Rural communities, water and broadband utilities, rural hospitals
SNAP and food assistance recipients, state SNAP agencies, retailers
Landowners, conservation districts, tribes, land trusts
Forest Service, national forest communities, timber and utility companies
Crop insurance companies, agents, Farm Credit System lenders
Pesticide makers, EPA and wildlife agencies, people living near farms and fire-retardant use
International food aid recipients and exporters
Consumers, pet owners and animals, and anyone exposed to farm equipment emissions or pesticides

benefits: Large investments in rural water, wastewater, household wells and distressed utilities could improve drinking water access.
Soil health grants, composting, wildlife corridors and watershed repair could improve land and water quality.
Heirs property help, higher cost-share for socially disadvantaged farmers and beginner/veteran support could widen access to land and credit.
More public reporting on watershed spending, commodity boards, aquaculture and the research foundation could improve transparency.
Farm and ranch stress, mental health and rollover protection provisions could protect lives.
concerns: Exempting farm tractors and self-propelled equipment from Clean Air Act engine standards could increase air pollution.
Clean Water Act safe harbor for aerial fire retardant and weaker pesticide review timing could raise water and wildlife risks.
Expanded NEPA categorical exclusions, no ESA reconsultation and exemptions from ESA and historic review for utility rights-of-way reduce public input and wildlife safeguards.
Preempting state and local production standards for livestock products limits community and state choices.
Block-grant disaster aid, larger loan limits, loan refinancing of nonperforming guaranteed loans, and Farm Credit expansion could shift risk to taxpayers.
SNAP states could contract out certification work to private contractors, and private incentives could harm service quality.
imp.cost: No total cost was provided in the material I reviewed. The bill uses a mix of mandatory CCC funding (for example feral swine at $150 million a year, soil health grants at $100 million a year, trade promotion at $500-$533 million a year) and authorizations subject to appropriations (broadband at $350 million a year, circuit riders at $25 million a year, heirs property $60 million a year). Conservation funding amounts in Title II were cut off.
unknowns: Total ten-year cost and offsets are not stated in the material provided.
Title II conservation funding levels after FY2027, and parts of Titles IV, VII, VIII, IX and XI were cut off in the digest.
How agencies would use broad discretion (specialty crop payment factors, Southern Border Initiative, block grants) is unknown.
Whether the Senate will change the bill, including controversial preemption and environmental provisions, is unknown.

label: H.R. 7618
title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act of 2026
short_title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act
one: Extends National Park Service battlefield preservation grants through 2036 and orders studies of French and Indian War and Mexican-American War sites, subject to funding.
summary: This bill keeps alive a set of National Park Service grant programs that help protect and restore American battlefields. Right now, the acquisition grants (money to buy or protect battlefield land) are approved through 2028. The bill pushes that out to 2036. It also changes the rules for the other two grant programs, which pay for updating how battlefields are explained to visitors and for restoring battlefield sites. It sets one combined spending limit of $2 million per year through 2036 for those two programs, and it removes an older subsection of the interpretation grant law. The bill also asks the National Park Service to study sites linked to important events in the French and Indian War (1754–1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846–1848). The studies would list sites, rank how important they are, look at threats to them, and suggest ways to protect them. These could include making some a national park unit. Outside groups could do the studies, and the Park Service would check them. The studies only happen if Congress provides money. Finished studies go to House and Senate natural resources committees. Authorizing money does not itself spend it. Congress must still approve funds each year.
does: placeholder
who: National Park Service
Battlefield preservation groups such as the American Battlefield Trust
State, local and Tribal governments near battlefield sites
Landowners near historic sites
Visitors, students and history researchers
Taxpayers

Could protect historic land from development, which may also preserve open space and green habitat.
Studies must consult States, Tribes, local governments and the public, and are sent to Congress, which adds openness.
Allows outside groups to do studies, which could speed work.
concerns: Uses federal tax dollars, with a $2 million yearly cap for two programs, and the money is not guaranteed.
Studies may eventually lead to proposals for new National Park units, which could affect nearby landowners and local communities.
The bill text I saw does not say whether Tribal perspectives on these wars will be given weight beyond consultation.

The bill's official title mentions changing cost-sharing rules, but the text shown only changes authorization dates and amounts. I could not see the full current law, so the cost-sharing effect is unclear.

unknowns: Total cost of the studies and acquisition grants.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep three National Park Service grant programs that help preserve, interpret, and restore American battlefields running through fiscal year 2036, instead of expiring after 2028. It also asks the Park Service to study sites tied to key events of the French and Indian War and the Mexican-American War to see which ones may be worth preserving.

oppose: The bill uses federal tax dollars to extend grant programs for about eight more years. Someone who opposes this could argue that Congress should review the cost of these programs before extending them.

The bill's funding is not guaranteed. Authorizing money does not spend it, and Congress must still approve funds each year. A constituent could ask how the programs will be paid for in a tight budget.

The studies could eventually lead to proposals for new National Park units. A constituent could ask the member how landowners and local communities would be protected from new federal land decisions, and whether their views would carry enough weight.
support: The bill keeps battlefield preservation going. Its acquisition grants, which help buy or protect battlefield land, would run through 2036 instead of ending in 2028. A constituent could say this gives communities more time to plan and protect historic sites.
Protecting battlefield land can also keep open space and green habitat from being lost to development. A constituent could point to this as a benefit for both history and nature.

The studies must consult States, Tribes, local governments, and the public, and the finished reports go to House and Senate natural resources committees. A constituent could say this builds openness into the process before any decisions are made.

cost_flag: Sets $2,000,000 per year through FY2036 for the interpretation and restoration grants combined. The acquisition grant amount is not changed in this text other than the end date. Studies are subject to appropriations, and no cost figure is given. I did not see a CBO estimate.
crs:
American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act of 2026
This bill extends through FY2036 three National Park Service (NPS) grant programs that preserve U.S. battlefields and requires the NPS to study additional sites for potential preservation.
Specifically, the bill extends through FY2036 grant programs for the acquisition, interpretation modernization, and restoration of certain U.S. battlefields. (Under current law, the grants are authorized through FY2028.)
The bill also requires the NPS to prepare or certify studies of locations tied to significant events during the French and Indian War (1754-1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846-1848) for potential preservation.

environment.reason: Sec. on acquisition grants extended to FY2036 keeps funding for buying and protecting battlefield land, which can preserve open space and green habitat; the bill does not directly address water or air.

transparency_kindness.reason: The required site studies must consult States, Tribes, local governments and the public, and finished studies go to House and Senate natural resources committees, which adds some public visibility.

people_over_profit.reason: Preservation grants for battlefield land keep historic sites from development for public benefit, and the bill does not shift costs onto ratepayers or consumers, though it does use federal taxpayer funds for these purposes.

local_say.reason: Studies consult States, local governments and the public, but they could lead to proposals for new National Park units that affect nearby communities, so the net effect on local say is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide money to corporations or shift fiscal responsibility to ratepayers; it concerns federal grants for battlefield preservation.

equality.reason: The grant and study provisions apply uniformly to battlefield sites and do not create differing legal treatment for any group.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal processes, due process, or remedies for harm.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do with their own lives; acquisition grants are voluntary government programs.

label: H.R. 8800
title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
short_title: FY2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), with SAVE America Act voting rules attached
one: A huge yearly bill that sets Pentagon and nuclear-weapons policy and funding for fiscal year 2027, adds major maritime-industry and critical-minerals programs, and carries an unrelated Division E that would require proof of citizenship to register to vote and photo ID to vote in federal elections.
summary:
H.R. 8800 is the yearly defense policy bill. It does not itself hand out money. It authorizes spending levels and sets rules, and separate appropriations bills actually pay for things. It has five divisions.

Division A (Defense) is the biggest. Procurement (Title I) approves multiyear contracts for Navy destroyers, oilers, E-2D aircraft, armored vehicles, and about 30 types of munitions and missiles. It also sets minimum inventories of fighters, P-8A aircraft, Stryker vehicles, and amphibious ships. Research (Title II) pushes drones, counter-drone systems, quantum computing, hypersonics, and AI, including an "artificial general intelligence" preparedness effort and a rewrite of the rules on autonomous weapons. Operations and Maintenance (Title III) adds nuclear energy to Defense Department energy policy, orders a transportable nuclear microreactor in the Indo-Pacific by 2030, and calls for studies of geothermal power and of old base water and wastewater systems. It also orders a pilot to recycle electronic waste. It bans single-use bag limits at commissaries, and bars Chinese-origin seafood.

Personnel (Titles IV–VII) sets troop numbers and raises the death gratuity from $100,000 to $165,000. It adds bereavement leave for pregnancy loss and stillbirth and expands fertility coverage (starting October 2028). It also adds dental coverage for junior reservists. On the other side, it bars TRICARE coverage of gender-related treatment, limits diversity-based personnel decisions, and bans hate symbols. It also strengthens military justice for sexual assault, domestic violence, and retaliation, and reverses planned cuts to 41 military hospitals and clinics. Health provisions include quicker TRICARE complaint handling, a study of missile-field cancer risks, and a ban on gain-of-function research funding.

Acquisition (Title VIII) raises many contracting thresholds. Companies would not have to submit certified cost or pricing data until $10 million, up from $2 million. It also overhauls data-rights rules, mostly in the government's favor, and sets stricter domestic-sourcing rules for magnets, tungsten, and other critical minerals. It adds rules on cloud and consumption-based buying.

Other titles: Finance (Title X) requires audit progress by cutting 0.5 percent of non-personnel Defense budgets each year the department lacks a clean audit opinion. It renames the Defense Department the "Department of War" in law. It limits hiring freezes at shipyards and depots and blocks firing child-care, school, and health workers without cause, and it blocks funds for the executive order restricting federal collective bargaining. It sets up a Navy shipyard pay demonstration project. Foreign affairs (Title XII) expands partnerships with Israel, the Abraham Accords countries, and Taiwan, and authorizes more Virginia-class submarines for Australia. Title XIV includes critical-minerals traceability and a bigger cable ship fleet. Title XVII reauthorizes the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035. It creates a UAP (UFO) records collection at the National Archives with a Review Board and strong public-disclosure rules. It also adds VA psychedelic-therapy reporting.

Division B (Military Construction) authorizes base projects, including about $14.8 billion at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard. It strengthens tenant protections in privatized housing, including bans on landlord nondisclosure agreements and retaliation, and 72-hour window-fall notices. It also removes National Historic Preservation Act coverage for most military housing, and bans speed cameras on bases. It restores earlier Army base names.

Division C (Energy and Maritime) funds Energy Department nuclear weapons work. That includes a goal of 180 plutonium pits a year by 2050, extra Hanford and Savannah River cleanup money, and a bar on applying a 2019 waste reclassification notice to Washington State waste. It also restricts foreign visitors at national laboratories. It then adds a very large maritime package, the SHIPS for America Act, a Coast Guard authorization, and Maritime Administration programs. The maritime package creates a Maritime Security Trust Fund of up to $20 billion and shipbuilding financial incentives. The incentives are exempt from NEPA review, bar stock buybacks for 5 years, and bar foreign-adversary suppliers. It raises the U.S.-flag cargo preference share for government cargo to 100 percent and sets shipper penalties of at least 10 percent of cargo value for missing U.S.-vessel targets. It rewrites the 1851 Limitation of Liability Act. It also starts a pilot for remotely crewed offshore supply vessels in the Gulf of America and sets a 10 percent domestic ship-repair target.

Division D contains the funding tables: about $337.7 billion for operations, $190.0 billion for military personnel, $28.6 billion for construction, and $41.3 billion for Energy Department national security programs. I could not see the procurement and research totals in this digest.

Division E, the SAVE America Act, is unrelated to defense. It would require documentary proof of U.S. citizenship (passport, REAL ID showing citizenship, or birth certificate plus photo ID, and similar) to register for federal elections. States would have to check their rolls against the DHS SAVE system within 30 days of enactment. It would also require photo ID to vote in person, with a provisional ballot and 3-day cure, and a photo ID copy for mail ballots. Uniformed and overseas military voters are exempt, and election officials face criminal penalties for registering people without proof.

Overall, the bill mixes real protections for service members and families, many transparency and water-infrastructure provisions, and heavy new support for defense and maritime industries, with weaker environmental review in some places and a sweeping voting-rules change.
does: Division A, Title I (Procurement): authorizes FY2027 procurement as set in funding tables and approves multiyear or incremental contracts for up to 15 Arleigh Burke destroyers, John Lewis-class oilers, 12 E-2D aircraft, armored multipurpose vehicles, submarine tenders, and amphibious ships (San Antonio/America class through 2030). It also sets minimum inventories: 1,800 fighters, 136 P-8As, 1,524 Strykers, 33 amphibious ships, and delays F-22 retirement to 2032.

Title II (Research and Development): funds many small programs by offsetting cuts, and directs work on drones, counter-drone systems, quantum computing policy, hypersonics, AI data centers, low-cost weapons, a U.S.-Israel technology cooperation initiative, and an AGI (artificial general intelligence) preparedness initiative run by the Chief Digital and AI Officer. It also repeals a facility-prototyping pilot and restructures test and evaluation offices.

Title III (Operations and Maintenance): adds nuclear energy to Defense energy policy, sets a minimum 20 MW size for the Navy installation reactor pilot, and orders a transportable nuclear microreactor in the Indo-Pacific by January 1, 2030. It also requires standard scope documents for munitions-cleanup projects, a pilot to recycle military electronic waste, geothermal and PFAS-related studies, and a report on aging base water and wastewater systems.

Title III also bans connected vehicles from foreign entities of concern on DoD property, requires mine, torpedo, and sonobuoy inventory strategies, protects DoD freight from carrier liens, requires Chinese-linked trucking firm certification and a secure carrier registry, and requires reports on property left behind after withdrawals.

Titles IV–V (Military Personnel and Policy): sets reserve and operational-support strength levels and cuts about $750 million in unobligated personnel funds. It requires prompt notice when generals are removed, bars enlisting nationals of China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea, and requires merit-only personnel actions. It also bans hate symbols, bars prediction-market trading on nonpublic information, and requires faster administrative investigations.

Military justice changes: adds a UCMJ offense for sharing intimate images (including deepfakes), allows the death penalty for child rape, creates a retaliation offense for reporting sexual harassment, and denies good-conduct credit for listed sex offenses. It also expands victim access to the military appeals court, requires a DoD victim notification system, extends Special Victims' Counsel to domestic violence victims, and creates a sexual-misconduct prevention advisory committee.

Honors and chaplains: authorizes Medals of Honor for Peralta, Lodge, and six Midway commanders, plus Distinguished-Service Crosses. It also adds sense-of-Congress review of other recipients, creates a Medal of Honor liaison, and enacts the Military Chaplains Modernization Act of 2026, including religious-protection language.

Title VI (Compensation): raises the death gratuity from $100,000 to $165,000 with annual inflation adjustments, adds a $1,000 Survivor Benefit Plan payment when a spouse dies first, and adds bereavement leave for pregnancy loss and stillbirth. It also allows a fuel discount at exchanges through 2029, bans commissary limits on single-use bags, bars Chinese-origin seafood in dining facilities and commissaries, and extends the military retirement fund to all uniformed services.

Title VII (Health): creates a no-premium dental plan for junior reservists, adds fertility treatment coverage (IVF with limits) starting October 1, 2028, and bans TRICARE coverage of gender-related treatment. It also reverses planned downgrades at 41 military treatment facilities within 30 days, requires OB-GYN or midwife and sexual assault nurse examiner coverage at every facility, and sets TRICARE site-based payment and complaint rules.

Health studies and pilots: orders a GAO audit of the TRICARE pharmacy contractor, a National Academies review of cancer risks at Minuteman III missile sites, a study of toxic exposure and fertility, suicide-prevention pilots, and a five-year wastewater drug-surveillance pilot. It also removes legal peptides from the banned-substances list and extends psychedelic therapy studies to 2033.

Title VIII (Acquisition): raises many contract thresholds (certified cost or pricing data from $2 million to $10 million; simplified acquisition from $250,000 to $500,000; micro-purchases to $25,000; major-program thresholds), broadens other-transaction authority, requires modular open systems and expands contractor trade-secret protection, and changes concession rules with retailers.

Acquisition integrity and workforce: bars contracts with employers of convicted human traffickers, bars non-tactical vehicle parts made with forced child labor, makes government purpose rights the default for technical data, creates an Intellectual Property Ombudsman and mediation, and creates acquisition talent officers and performance objectives. It also strengthens sustainment review, with public summaries within 60 days unless security prevents it.

Critical-minerals sourcing: replaces earlier sourcing bans with Tier 1 and Tier 2 domestic and non-covered-nation sourcing rules for magnets, tungsten, tantalum, gallium, germanium, and similar materials, with waivers, 10-year records, 'preferred domestic manufacturer' designations, and 12-month qualification of new sources. It restructures the Federal Acquisition Security Council in the White House.

Industrial base: authorizes multiyear munitions contracts (13 and 18 system categories), capacity-expansion reports for munitions (up to 500 percent), second-source rules for solid rocket motors, foreign-military-sale demand planning, a 'Pay-to-Print' parts program, and added uses of the Defense Industrial Base Fund. It also bars certain foreign-made tracked-vehicle drivetrains and sets new domestic content rules for ship components.

Title X (General Provisions): requires Payment Integrity Act compliance, sets a Joint Task Force Audit, and cuts non-personnel Defense budget authority 0.5 percent each March 2 when audits are missing or fail. It also adds naval vessel and shipyard rules (components from the U.S. industrial base, armament of auxiliaries, a surface-ship repair contract), bans funds for closing the Rock Island Arsenal Museum, and lengthens post-service lobbying bans to five years.

Title X, other: renames the Department of Defense the 'Department of War' in law, requires public disclosure of foreign gifts of $50,000+ to military colleges, repeals dozens of old reporting requirements, and adds counter-drone and installation-defense plans, an AI scam threat study, and a plan for border domain awareness.

Title XI (Civilian Personnel): bars FY2027 funds for Executive Order 14251 limiting collective bargaining, bars hiring freezes in many essential positions, bars firing child care, school, and health workers without misconduct, and bars shipyard hiring freezes or layoffs. It also creates pay demonstration projects (ICBM maintenance, Navy shipyards, Army depots) and new direct-hire authorities.

Title XII (Foreign Nations): raises several security-cooperation caps, creates an Inter-Pacific Air Forces Academy, authorizes sale of three Virginia-class submarines to Australia, creates U.S.-Taiwan industrial and drone programs, requires reports on Russia, Somalia, Gaza-Egypt tunnels, and Western Hemisphere threat networks, and sets quarterly reporting on military contact with Russia.

Title XIV and XV (Other Authorizations, Cyber and AI): authorizes working capital, chemical munitions destruction, counter-drug, Inspector General, and Defense Health Program funds. It also expands the cable security fleet to at least 6 ships, creates critical-minerals traceability and recovery programs, and sets AI policy updates (including autonomous weapons rules with human-control elements), a bar on IT vendors that share vulnerabilities with countries of concern, and cyber reporting requirements.

Title XVI (Space, Strategic, Intelligence): restructures Space Force acquisition, keeps Next-Gen OPIR Polar, funds wildfire-resilience satellite data, requires cost and flight-test conditions for space-based interceptors, restricts changes to Navy use of Space Launch Complex 46, and requires a solid-rocket-motor second source for major missiles. It also creates an adversary supply-chain intelligence cell.

Title XVII (Other Defense Matters): reauthorizes the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 through 2035 (adding AI), creates a U.S.-Abraham Accords Defense Cooperation Initiative, bars CCP-linked financial apps on DoD devices, creates an atomic civilians medal, and requires the Pentagon to keep its Scouting America partnership.

Title XVII, UAP subtitle: creates a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives and a nine-member independent Review Board. It requires records to be disclosed unless postponement is shown by clear and convincing evidence, bars destroying records, requires Federal Register notices, and ends the Board in September 2030.

VA and emerging therapies: requires a VA senior official for emerging therapeutic interventions (including psychedelic-assisted therapy), semiannual reports, workforce training plans, and a report on Executive Order 14401 on serious mental illness treatments.

Title XVIII (Industrial base): adds adversarial-capital monitoring, a synthetic diamond plan, a Defense Supply Chain Intelligence program with chip-level testing, counterfeit parts rules, education-requirement limits in contracts, veteran-employment 'Schedule V' disclosure for large contractors, a Berry Amendment extension to seafood, and a copper, uranium and critical minerals preference.

Division B (Military Construction): authorizes Army, Navy, Air Force, and Defense-wide projects (including about $14.76 billion at Puget Sound Naval Shipyard), and extends or modifies earlier projects. Authorizations expire October 1, 2029 (or when the next MILCON Act passes) and are capped at stated costs.

Division B, housing: requires 72-hour notice of window falls, expands reprisal protections for privatized housing tenants, bars landlord nondisclosure agreements, sets work-order timeliness standards, raises barracks reinvestment from 5 to 10 percent, and requires tenants to be told about the complaint database.

Division B, other: excludes most military housing from the National Historic Preservation Act (with limited exceptions), bans automated speed cameras on bases, restores earlier names (Fort Moore, Fort Shughart-Gordon, Fort Liberty, and others), limits school-project local match to 20 percent, requires an always-open visitor gate, and conditions Guam power-grid transfers (50 percent underground lines).

Division C, energy: authorizes NNSA, cleanup, and nuclear energy funding. It sets a goal of 180 plutonium pits per year by 2050, adds NNSA other-transaction authority, bars funds for national laboratories that admit covered foreign visitors, bars applying the 2019 high-level waste reinterpretation to Washington State waste, and authorizes $45 million for the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board and $13 million for naval petroleum reserves.

Division C, SHIPS for America and maritime: creates a Maritime Security Advisor and Board, a Maritime Security Trust Fund (capped at $20 billion, subject to appropriation), and shipbuilding financial incentives (exempt from NEPA and National Historic Preservation Act review, Buy America applies, no stock buybacks for 5 years, no foreign-adversary suppliers).

SHIPS for America cargo and shipping rules: raises the U.S.-flag share of government cargo from 50 to 100 percent, creates new cargo preference for certain commercial cargo with FMC penalties of at least 10 percent of cargo value, sets a 10 percent domestic ship-repair target rising 5 percent a year, and revises the Limitation of Liability Act (foreign owners capped at 5 times vessel value, with wage claims excluded).

Coast Guard and Maritime Administration: adds a sixth vice admiral, a Chief Prevention Officer, domestic buoy-chain sourcing, corrosion pilot, other-transaction authority, a remotely crewed offshore supply vessel pilot in the Gulf of America, a rule requiring notice and public comment before closing Coast Guard stations or changing homeports, and mariner credentialing modernization. It also provides State academy fuel funding up to $20 million per year for 2027–2036, and Merchant Marine Academy modernization.

Division D (Funding Tables): sets FY2027 amounts, including O&M about $337.7 billion (down $952 million from the request), military personnel about $190.0 billion, military construction about $28.6 billion, and Energy national security programs about $41.3 billion. Notable adds include $97 million for the Navy Energy Program, $122 million for Air Force operational energy, Israel cooperation programs, and Hanford and Savannah River cleanup. Notable cuts include Space Force Automate SAT C2 (-$719 million) and CCA (-$137 million).

Division E (SAVE America Act): requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register for federal elections (passport, REAL ID showing citizenship, birth certificate plus photo ID, etc.). It requires states to submit voter lists to DHS for SAVE checks within 30 days, adds criminal penalties for officials who register people without proof, and requires photo ID for in-person and mail voting. It exempts military and overseas voters, provides provisional ballots with a 3-day cure, and takes effect on enactment.
who: Active-duty, Guard, Reserve members, military families, retirees, and survivors (pay, health care, housing, child care, benefits)
Military health system patients and TRICARE beneficiaries, including at 41 facilities facing service changes
Defense contractors, shipbuilders, shippers, ship owners, maritime workers, and critical-minerals producers and suppliers
DoD civilian employees, including shipyard, depot, school, child care, and health workers
Residents of privatized military housing and communities near bases, Guam, Hanford-area communities, and ports
All registered and prospective voters, state and local election officials (Division E)
Taxpayers, since the bill authorizes hundreds of billions in spending
Allies and partners (Israel, Taiwan, Australia, NATO, Indo-Pacific nations)
Researchers, universities, and AI and tech companies working with DoD
Veterans, including those seeking emerging mental-health therapies

Higher death gratuity, bereavement leave for pregnancy loss, expanded fertility coverage, junior reservist dental care, and reversal of planned military clinic and hospital downgrades.
Public UAP records collection, public foreign-gift disclosure by military colleges, and public posting of many reports.

Water-related benefits: a report on aging base water and wastewater systems, a PFAS destruction report, a wastewater surveillance pilot, Pearl Harbor water treatment plant funding, and extra Hanford and Savannah River cleanup money.

label: H.R. 8880
title: Small Business Cybersecurity Assistance Evaluation Act of 2026
short_title: Small Business Cybersecurity Assistance Evaluation Act
one: Requires the Government Accountability Office to study and report on how well federal cybersecurity help for small businesses works and how to improve it, with no new money authorized.
summary: This bill asks the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's nonpartisan watchdog agency, to look at the federal programs, tools, and services meant to help small businesses with cybersecurity. The study would cover how these programs help owners spot cyber risks, check how ready they are, and plan for, limit, and recover from cyberattacks, scams, fraud, and social engineering (tricking people into giving up access or money). It would also look at programs that help owners find or get money to pay for these protections. The GAO would describe the most common attacks hitting small businesses, list the federal programs, and assess how well known and widely used they are, and why use differs. It would also assess how well the programs work together and how effective they are. It would point out basic cybersecurity ideas the programs leave out and recommend ways to make them more effective, better known, and better coordinated. The GAO would send the findings to the small business committees of the House and Senate. The bill does not create new programs, rules, or requirements for businesses. A section says no money is authorized to be appropriated for it, so the GAO would have to do the work with existing funds. The bill passed the House on June 23, 2026, and is now in a Senate committee.
does: Directs the GAO to study current federal cybersecurity programs, tools, and services for small businesses.
who: Small business owners and their employees and customers

Findings could point Congress toward better coordination among federal small business cybersecurity programs.
Because the bill imposes no new requirements on businesses, it would not add compliance duties for small firms.
concerns: The bill creates no new help for small businesses by itself; any improvements would depend on later action by Congress or agencies.
Because no funding is authorized, the study may be limited by GAO's existing budget and staff time.

label: H.R. 9613
title: Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act
short_title: Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act
one: Changes the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's independent reactor safety advisory panel so it can skip reviewing license applications it deems routine, caps its size at 15 members, and sets term limits.
summary: This bill changes the law that sets up the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards, an expert panel that advises the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) on reactor safety. Today, the law says the panel must review certain license applications for nuclear facilities. Under this bill, the panel could decline to review an application if it decides the application has nothing unique, new, or noteworthy, or does not raise issues that warrant its review. The bill caps the panel at 15 members, appointed by the NRC, who should have varied technical expertise. Members could serve up to two 4-year terms, with more allowed if the NRC finds a compelling need. This applies to members appointed after the bill becomes law. Nuclear Advisory Committee Reform Act
This bill modifies requirements governing the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC), including by allowing the committee to decline to review certain license applications (e.g., applications for commercial nuclear power plants) issued by the NRC.

summary: A 2022 law (part of the CHIPS and Science Act) bars researchers who get federal research money from joining "malign foreign talent recruitment programs." These are programs where a foreign government offers pay or other rewards in ways that create conflicts of interest or involve unauthorized activity, like sharing protected information without permission. This bill makes a small wording fix to that definition. First, it says the programs covered are those tied to a "foreign country of concern," a term already defined in federal law, and the CRS summary says this includes China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. Second, it removes the older two-part structure of the definition and folds the list of covered activities into one list. Third, it says the pay or rewards can come "directly or indirectly," which could catch money routed through middlemen. The bill adds no new money, no new agency, and no new penalties. Its effect is to define which foreign programs researchers who get federal funds must avoid. It passed the House on March 24, 2025, and is now with the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.

summary: This bill would move the Crossett Experimental Forest in Arkansas from federal ownership to the State of Arkansas. The land includes the R.R. Reynolds Research Natural Area and related buildings and facilities. The state would have to ask in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The state must keep using it for forest research, education, and demonstration, in line with its long research history. It must also work with the University of Arkansas at Monticello and the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture and give them reasonable access. If the state fails to follow these rules and doesn't fix the problem within 180 days of written notice, the Secretary of Agriculture may take back all or part of the land. The Forest Service must also give the state copies of its research plans, plot data, measurement histories, and archives. Existing legal rights on the land would stay in place. label: H.R. 1346
title: To amend the Clean Air Act with respect to the ethanol waiver for Reid Vapor Pressure under that Act, and for other purposes.
short_title: Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025 (Year-Round E15 and RFS Reform)
one: Allows gasoline with 10–15% ethanol (E15) to be sold year-round nationwide, overrides some state opt-outs, and rewrites how small oil refineries are treated under the federal renewable fuel rules.
summary:
Right now, gasoline blended with 10% ethanol (E10) gets a special allowance to be a bit more evaporative than normal in summer. Gasoline with 15% ethanol (E15) does not, so it is often barred from sale in the summer ozone season (smog season). This bill gives E15 the same allowance, so E15 could be sold year-round everywhere.

Some states asked EPA after January 1, 2022 to be left out of this allowance because of air pollution worries. The bill cancels those requests and applies the E15 allowance anyway. States could ask to be excluded again, but only with new paperwork filed after the bill becomes law.

The bill also changes the Renewable Fuel Standard, the rule that makes fuel companies blend in renewable fuel or buy credits. Starting in 2028, small refinery exemptions would end in their current form. Instead, companies making 75,000 barrels a day or less would have their obligation cut by 75%, and EPA could not shift that burden to others. Very small or at-risk refineries could ask for yearly exemptions, capped at 150 million gallons' worth of fuel, with petitions made public. Some small refineries would get back credits they used for 2016–2018. Finally, EPA must update E15 pump labeling and underground tank rules within 18 months. The bill refers to the "Farm, Food, and National Security Act of 2026," which is not defined here, so timing is somewhat unclear.

Cancels state exclusions requested after January 1, 2022, so E15 rules apply there. States may submit new exclusion notifications after enactment.
Defines a 'small refining company' as a company or affiliated group producing 75,000 barrels per day or less of obligated fuels in 2025.

Ends existing small refinery exemption extensions and petitions: none for years after 2027, none considered after July 1, 2028, and EPA must act on outstanding ones by October 1, 2028 where practicable. Existing legal remedies for past petitions are preserved.

Starting in 2028, cuts the renewable fuel obligations of small refining companies by 75%, with no later re-eligibility if they exceed the size limit; EPA may not reallocate those obligations to other parties.
Returns or re-credits renewable fuel credits to certain small refineries for 2016–2018 compliance years that had pending or denied petitions.

Creates a new yearly exemption from 2028 for 'qualifying small refineries' at imminent risk of closure, idling, or conversion caused solely by compliance costs. It requires an officer's attestation, bars confidentiality, requires public posting within 30 days, 90-day EPA decisions, and a total cap of 150 million gallons of conventional biofuel energy content (adjusted later).
Requires EPA to finalize, within 18 months, a rule updating E15 dispenser labeling and underground storage tank regulations for E15 compatibility.

crs:
Nationwide Consumer and Fuel Retailer Choice Act of 2025
This bill amends the Clean Air Act to address the limitations on Reid Vapor Pressure (a measure of gasoline's volatility) that are placed on gasoline during the summer ozone season. Specifically, the bill applies the waiver for Reid Vapor Pressure requirements that is applicable to gasoline blended with 10% ethanol (E10) to gasoline blended with up to 15% ethanol (E15). This change allows gasoline that is blended with 10% to 15% ethanol to be sold year-round.
Currently, states may be excluded from the waiver for Reid Vapor Pressure requirements by submitting documentation supporting that the waiver would increase air pollution. The bill nullifies existing state exclusions, but states may submit documentation after enactment of the bill to be excluded going forward.
The bill also modifies the Renewable Fuel Standard Program, which requires transportation fuel sold or introduced into commerce in the United States to contain minimum volumes of renewable fuel. Under the existing program, obligated parties, such as small refineries, must satisfy the volume obligations by either blending renewable fuels into their gasoline or diesel fuel products or by acquiring credits that represent the required renewable fuel volume. The bill directs the Environmental Protection Agency to return compliance credits to small refineries under certain circumstances.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 extends the summer evaporation waiver to E15 and cancels prior state exclusions, which could raise smog-forming emissions in some areas; the 75% RFS obligation cut could also reduce renewable blending.

transparency_kindness.reason: The small refinery exemption process requires officer attestation, bars confidentiality, and requires public posting of petitions within 30 days, which makes that process more open.

people_over_profit.reason: The 75% obligation cut for small refining companies and the returned credits shift compliance burden and reduce costs for refiners, with EPA barred from reallocating those obligations to other parties, which moves costs onto others in the fuel system.

local_say.reason: Sec. 1 cancels state exclusions requested after January 1, 2022, removing states' existing ability to opt out of the summer E15 waiver; new exclusions are allowed only through new filings after enactment.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide taxpayer funds to corporations; the credit return and obligation cut are regulatory relief rather than monetary bailouts, so this is unclear and scored neutral.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same fuel rules to all states and does not create unequal treatment of any group; the small refinery provisions use size-based criteria that apply uniformly.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 nullifies existing state exclusion determinations retroactively, and the 2016-2018 credit returns and cancelled small refinery petitions alter settled decisions, which reduces consistency in the legal process, though existing legal remedies for past petitions are preserved.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. 1 allows E15 to be sold year-round, expanding the fuel choices drivers and retailers may legally purchase and sell.

label: H.R. 2140
title: Diesel Emissions Reduction Act of 2025
short_title: Diesel Emissions Reduction Act of 2025
one: Extends the EPA's diesel emissions reduction grant, rebate and loan program for five more years, through fiscal year 2029.
summary: This bill is very short. It changes one year in an existing law, the Energy Policy Act of 2005, from 2024 to 2029. That law lets the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) run a program that helps pay for cleaner diesel engines. Under the program, the EPA can give grants, rebates, or loans to owners of older diesel vehicles and equipment. The money helps them replace old engines or add pollution-control equipment to them. Examples include school buses, trucks, ports, and construction equipment, though the bill itself does not list them. The bill does not change how the program works, who can qualify, or the rules. It only keeps the program's legal authority to operate going through FY2029. The bill text shown does not give a dollar amount. The extension is only an authorization, so Congress would still have to approve actual spending in separate budget bills. Without the extension, the program's authority to receive funding would stay expired. The bill has passed the House and was placed on the Senate calendar, where it awaits a possible vote.
does: Changes the end date in Section 797(a) of the Energy Policy Act of 2005 from 2024 to 2029.
Keeps the EPA's authority to fund diesel engine replacements and retrofits through FY2029.
Leaves the program's existing rules and eligibility unchanged.

People living near highways, ports, rail yards and other diesel-heavy areas
Children riding diesel school buses
Engine and pollution-control technology makers
The EPA and federal taxpayers, who fund the grants

May improve health for children and for communities near freight corridors.
Gives school districts and small fleets a way to pay for cleaner engines.
Could also lower greenhouse gas emissions from some engines.
concerns: Uses taxpayer money to help private fleet owners with upgrades.
Extending the authorization does not guarantee any money will be appropriated.
The bill text does not say how funds are split between areas or how results are measured.

unknowns: How much money Congress will actually provide each year.
Whether the Senate will vote on the bill and pass it.
How the program's rules and priorities may change under EPA management.
The exact cost, which the bill text does not state.

The program provides grants, rebates, or loans to help replace diesel engines or add pollution control technology. The bill does not change the program's rules or eligibility.

oppose: The bill uses taxpayer money to help private fleet owners pay for engine upgrades, and you may question whether that is the best use of public funds.
The bill only extends the program's legal authority to 2029. It does not provide a dollar amount, so Congress would still need to decide future spending in separate budget bills.
The bill text does not say how funds would be divided among regions or how results would be measured, so you may want to ask how success would be tracked and whether the program is cost-effective.

Children and communities near busy freight routes may benefit from cleaner engines, and this program could help reduce their exposure to diesel pollution.

School districts and small fleet owners may have a hard time paying for cleaner engines on their own, and this program offers grants, rebates, or loans to help them. Some upgrades could also lower greenhouse gas emissions.
