How many facilities would use the interim rules and how much battery volume they would store.
Whether fire and environmental incidents would rise or fall.
How states with stricter rules would respond. I could not tell from the text whether state rules are preempted.
The cost to the EPA of the rulemaking.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make it easier to recycle lithium-ion batteries and recover critical minerals (per its title, the "Battery Recycling for America's Competitive Economy Act," and the CRS summary). It does this by letting facilities that store these batteries before recycling follow the lighter large-quantity universal waste rules instead of the stricter hazardous waste storage rules, so they can store batteries without a special permit until the EPA finishes a permanent rule. The bill also gives the EPA 18 months to write that rule.

oppose: Removing the hazardous waste storage permit could mean less oversight, inspection, and public input for recycling sites that store large numbers of lithium-ion batteries.

Lithium-ion batteries can catch fire. Large storage sites could pose fire, air, and runoff risks to nearby communities, and the bill would apply the lighter rules right away, before the EPA finishes its safety review.
The bill says the EPA must only 'consider' extra safety requirements, not adopt them, so safety gaps could remain in the final rule.
support: Recycling lithium-ion batteries can be costly under current hazardous waste rules. This bill could make recycling cheaper and faster, which may keep batteries out of landfills.
Recovering minerals like lithium, cobalt, and nickel from used batteries could reduce reliance on imported materials and support domestic supply.

The bill keeps protections in place. Interim universal waste rules still require training, labeling, release response, and shipment tracking, and the EPA must write a permanent rule through public notice and comment within 18 months, while considering health, environmental, and safety requirements.

crs:
Battery Recycling for America’s Competitive Economy Act or the BRACE Act
This bill modifies the regulation of lithium-ion batteries under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act in order to facilitate the recycling of lithium-ion batteries and the recovery of critical minerals. Specifically, the bill directs certain facilities that store lithium-ion batteries prior to recycling them to follow regulations for large quantity handlers of universal waste instead of following the more stringent hazardous waste regulations that currently apply, thereby allowing these facilities to store lithium-ion batteries without needing a special permit.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 (interim rule) lets recyclers store lithium-ion batteries under the lighter universal waste rules instead of the hazardous waste storage permit, which may reduce oversight of fire, runoff and air risks, though the bill keeps training, labeling, release response and tracking duties and requires a permanent EPA rule that must consider health and environmental protection.

transparency_kindness.reason: Removing the hazardous waste storage permit under the interim rule (Sec. 1) removes a public permit process, which reduces the public's ability to see and comment on storage sites that store many batteries.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 1 removes the permit requirement for storage facilities, lowering their compliance costs and making it cheaper for recyclers, while the risks of fire and pollution from storage are borne by nearby communities and the public.

local_say.reason: Sec. 1 removes the special hazardous waste storage permit for these facilities, which eliminates a process through which local communities and neighbors could weigh in on storage sites.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 replaces the hazardous waste permit regime with lighter universal waste rules for these facilities, reducing inspection and accountability for storage sites, although the bill does require a permanent EPA rule through notice and comment.

label: H.R. 9785
title: South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act
short_title: South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act
one: Directs the Interior Department to study whether three Missouri River water supply projects serving rural and municipal areas in South Dakota and neighboring states are feasible, with the federal share of each study capped at $10 million and 50%.
summary: This bill does not build anything. It pays for studies. It tells the Secretary of the Interior to look at whether three proposed projects could bring drinking and other water from the Missouri River to communities, farms, and businesses. The three are the Western Dakota Regional Water System, an expansion of the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System (Iowa, Minnesota, South Dakota), and the Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System (South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, Minnesota). Each is run by a nonprofit group that would share the study work and costs. The federal government could pay no more than half of each study and no more than $10 million per study. For the first two projects, Interior must finish by writing a report that recommends whether Congress should approve construction and how costs should be split, with locals paying at least 25% of construction. That report goes to the House and Senate natural resources committees and must be posted publicly with the study documents. Interior must also consult federal, state, tribal, regional, and local authorities. The Dakota Mainstem study is optional ("may") and has no public-report or tribal-consultation requirement in the text. Authority for each study ends after 7 years. The bill does not approve construction or provide construction money, and it does not say where the study money would come from.
does: Orders Interior to study feasibility of a Missouri River water project for the Western Dakota Regional Water System.
Orders Interior to study feasibility of expanding the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System in Iowa, Minnesota, and South Dakota.
Allows (but does not require) Interior to study a Dakota Mainstem water supply project in South Dakota, Iowa, Nebraska, and Minnesota.
Caps the federal share of each study at $10 million and 50% of study cost.
Requires reports for the first two studies recommending whether to build and setting a local construction cost share of at least 25%.
Requires those reports and study documents to be sent to congressional committees and made public.
Requires consultation with federal, state, tribal, regional, and local authorities on the first two studies.
Ends each study authority 7 years after enactment.

The three nonprofit regional water systems named in the bill
Department of the Interior (Bureau of Reclamation)
Tribal nations and local governments in the study areas, who would be consulted on the first two studies
Federal taxpayers, who would cover up to half of study costs
Communities and ecosystems along the Missouri River

Spending is limited: $10 million and 50% federal caps per study, with a 7-year sunset.
Requires a local share of at least 25% of any later construction costs in two of the reports.
concerns: Studies could lead to large later taxpayer-funded construction projects.
Taking more water from the Missouri River could affect river ecosystems, fish and wildlife, and other users, and the text does not mention environmental review.
The Dakota Mainstem study has no public-report requirement, no stated recommendation on local cost share, and no required tribal consultation.

The bill does not say where the money comes from, and no money is appropriated in the text. Local nonprofits would cover the rest. Future construction would need separate approval, with at least 25% local share recommended for two of the projects.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to have the Department of the Interior study whether water projects drawing from the Missouri River could supply municipal, rural, and industrial water in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, and South Dakota. It names three systems: the Western Dakota Regional Water System, the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System, and the Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System. The bill does not build anything or provide construction money. It addresses the problem of communities needing reliable, good-quality water supplies, according to its findings and summary.

oppose: The bill pays for studies that could lead to large later construction projects. Since the bill does not set construction costs, you could ask your member how much taxpayers might eventually pay.

Taking more water from the Missouri River could affect river ecosystems, fish, wildlife, and other water users. The bill's text does not mention environmental review, so you could ask how these effects would be checked before any project moves forward.

The Dakota Mainstem study is optional, has no public-report requirement, and has no required tribal consultation. You could ask why the bill's transparency and consultation rules apply to only two of the three studies.
support: The bill pays for feasibility studies only. It does not build anything or provide construction money, so Congress would see the findings before any later decision.

Two of the studies must produce public reports sent to the House and Senate natural resources committees. Local, state, and tribal authorities are consulted on those studies, which gives communities a voice in the process.

The bill limits spending. Federal money is capped at 50% of each study's cost and $10 million per study, and each study authority ends after 7 years. Any later construction would require local cost sharing of at least 25% under the reports' recommendations.

cost_flag: Federal share of each of the three studies is capped at $10 million and 50% of that study's cost (up to $30 million total). The bill does not say where the money comes from, and no money is appropriated in the text. Local nonprofits would cover the rest. Future construction would need separate approval, with at least 25% local share recommended for two of the projects.
crs:
South Dakota Water Feasibility Studies Act
This bill directs the Department of the Interior to study the feasibility of constructing projects to supply municipal, rural, and industrial water from the Missouri River in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, and South Dakota. Specifically, the bill requires studies on projects to supply water to the (1) Western Dakota Regional Water System; (2) Lewis and Clark Regional Water System, Inc.; and (3) Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System.

environment.reason: The bill only orders feasibility studies and builds nothing, so it neither protects nor directly harms water or ecosystems; the text does not mention environmental review, but studies do not themselves withdraw water.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on reporting requires the first two studies' reports and study documents to be sent to House and Senate natural resources committees and posted publicly, and consultation with tribal, state, and local authorities is required for those two studies; the Dakota Mainstem study lacks these requirements.

people_over_profit.reason: The studies could inform later projects that benefit both households and industrial users, and the 25% local cost share is a recommendation for later construction, with effects that roughly balance and remain uncertain.

local_say.reason: Sec. on consultation requires Interior to consult state, tribal, regional, and local authorities on the first two studies, and the reports go to Congress for a construction decision, giving local governments more input; the optional Dakota Mainstem study has no such requirement.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill funds only feasibility studies with a federal share capped at 50% and $10 million per study, and it does not shift ratepayer costs or bail out a corporation at this stage; future construction cost splits are not yet set.

equality.reason: The bill treats the three named systems and their service areas under the same study framework, with no group singled out for different legal treatment.

justice.reason: The bill sets no new legal process for individuals or remedies for harm; it orders studies and reporting that are procedurally modest and do not clearly make legal processes fairer or less fair.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do, say, or choose about their own lives.

news.overall: Only two headlines from one outlet (Christian Science Monitor, Center) were provided, and neither addresses the South Dakota bill directly. The evidence is limited to a single perspective with no article descriptions, so no comparison across perspectives is possible. The coverage that is present concerns Western reservoir and Colorado River conditions rather than the state-level water feasibility legislation.

label: H.R. 1621
title: Entrepreneurs with Disabilities Reporting Act of 2025
short_title: Entrepreneurs with Disabilities Reporting Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to send Congress a report within 180 days on the challenges entrepreneurs with disabilities face and how well SBA serves them.
summary: This bill asks the Small Business Administration (SBA), the federal agency that helps small businesses, to study how well it serves people with disabilities who want to start or run a business. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the SBA head must send Congress a report. The report must describe the challenges and needs of these entrepreneurs, what help the SBA already gives them, and how the SBA reaches out to them through its regional offices, small business development centers, and women's business centers. It must also describe teamwork between SBA offices and other federal agencies, point out gaps in the current help, explain how entrepreneurs with disabilities use and access SBA resources, and suggest any new laws Congress may need to pass to fix the problems found. The bill creates no new programs, benefits, or rules, and it gives no new money. The agency must do the work with funds it already has. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee. Any real changes would only come from later legislation based on what the report finds.

label: H.R. 1634
title: ThinkDIFFERENTLY About Disability Employment Act
short_title: ThinkDIFFERENTLY About Disability Employment Act
one: Directs the Small Business Administration, working with the National Council on Disability, to help people with disabilities start businesses or find jobs at small businesses, and to help small businesses hire them, with no new money provided.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to do three things, working with the head of the National Council on Disability. First, help people with disabilities who want to start a business or be self-employed. Second, help people with disabilities find jobs at small businesses. Third, help small businesses hire people with disabilities and deal with accessibility issues, such as making workplaces usable for them. The SBA would carry this out through one or more formal agreements (called memoranda of understanding) with the Council or other partners. It must also do outreach and education so people and businesses know about these services. Within two years of the bill becoming law, the SBA must send Congress a report. The report must describe how the work was done, look at ways to expand the SBA's technical abilities, list achievements, and lay out plans to continue. The bill says no additional funds are authorized, so the SBA would have to pay for this out of money it already has. That could limit how much it can do, or pull resources from other SBA programs. The bill does not create new benefits, mandates on businesses, or penalties. It is a coordination, outreach, and reporting measure. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Small Business Committee.

label: H.R. 1664
title: Deploying American Blockchains Act of 2025
short_title: Deploying American Blockchains Act of 2025
one: Makes the Commerce Department the President's main adviser on blockchain technology, sets up a 7-year Blockchain Deployment Program and advisory committees, and requires public annual reports to Congress.
summary: This bill would make the Secretary of Commerce a main adviser to the President on blockchain and similar "distributed ledger" technology. That is a shared digital record kept across many computers and protected by cryptography. It also covers tokens, which are digital stand-ins for information on those systems, and tokenization, which is making them. The Secretary would work to support U.S. leadership in this area. That includes developing policy on issues such as cybersecurity, fraud reduction, identity, artificial intelligence, health care uses, and supply chains. The Secretary would also study how federal agencies could use blockchain and how to keep it secure. The bill creates a Blockchain Deployment Program that ends 7 years after enactment. Within 180 days, Commerce must set up advisory committees. They would include federal officials and outside experts: industry, developers, small businesses, academics, consumer groups, nonprofits, cybersecurity experts, rural stakeholders, and artists. Commerce would also develop voluntary best practices and shared terminology and support open-source work. Nothing in the bill forces private companies to share information, ask for help, or follow the recommendations. Starting two years after enactment, and every year after, Commerce must post a public report online and send it to Congress. The report covers its activities, suggested new laws, and emerging risks. The bill does not give a dollar amount or create new regulations or penalties. The CRS summary matches the text.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to support U.S. leadership in blockchain technology and other distributed ledger technology, tokens, and tokenization. crs:
Deploying American Blockchains Act of 2025
This bill requires the Department of Commerce to support the leadership of the United States in the use of blockchain technology and other distributed ledger technology, tokens, and tokenization. Generally, blockchain technology is a distributed digital ledger that uses cryptography to share verified information across a network of computers. Tokens refer to the transferrable, digital representation of information recorded on blockchain technology and tokenization is the process of creating a token.
Specifically, Commerce must advise the President on policies related to the deployment and use of blockchain technology and other distributed ledger technology, applications built on blockchain technology or other distributed ledger technology, tokens, and tokenization. Commerce also must establish advisory committees to support the adoption of blockchain technology to facilitate the development of best practices with respect to blockchain technology, applications built on blockchain technology, tokens, and tokenization.
Commerce must report annually on the activities under this bill and provide any recommendations for additional legislation to strengthen U.S. competitiveness with respect to blockchain technology.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on annual report requires Commerce to post a public report online and send it to Congress covering its activities, recommendations, and emerging risks, which increases public visibility into the program.

justice.reason: The bill creates no new enforcement, remedies, or due process changes; its provisions are advisory and voluntary.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill creates no new regulations or penalties and expressly does not require private entities to do anything, so it neither expands nor restricts individual choices.

label: H.R. 1764
title: Aligning SEC Regulations for the World Bank’s International Development Association Act
short_title: Aligning SEC Regulations for the World Bank's IDA Act
one: Exempts bonds and other securities issued or guaranteed by the World Bank's International Development Association (IDA) from standard U.S. securities registration laws, while letting the SEC require reports and suspend the exemption.
summary:
The International Development Association (IDA) is part of the World Bank. It gives loans and grants to the world's poorest countries. To raise money, it can issue securities, such as bonds. This bill would treat IDA's securities, and any it guarantees, as "exempted securities" under two main U.S. securities laws, the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. That means IDA would not have to go through the normal registration process that most companies face. Other World Bank institutions already get similar treatment.

The bill keeps some oversight in place. IDA would still have to file annual and other reports with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), as the SEC decides is appropriate and necessary for the public interest or to protect investors. The SEC, after consulting a federal advisory council on international monetary problems, could suspend the exemption at any time for some or all of IDA's securities. The SEC may also report to Congress on how the exemption works.

The exemption would start 30 days after the bill becomes law. It would not take effect if, before then, the Treasury Secretary tells the House Financial Services and Senate Banking committees that IDA is giving financial aid to a country the State Department has found to repeatedly support international terrorism. The text does not give a cost estimate. The bill passed the House and is now in a Senate committee.
does: Amends the International Development Association Act to treat securities issued or guaranteed by IDA (principal and interest) as "exempted securities" under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.
who: The International Development Association and the World Bank Group

benefits: May lower IDA's administrative burden and help it raise money for aid to the poorest countries.
concerns: Investors would get fewer of the standard registration protections for IDA securities.
imp.cost: The text includes no appropriation or cost estimate. It changes how securities are regulated and does not provide funding. Any effect on federal spending isn't stated.
unknowns: What reports the SEC would require from IDA.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to align SEC treatment of securities issued or guaranteed by the International Development Association (IDA), part of the World Bank, with the treatment already given to other World Bank institutions. It treats IDA securities as "exempted securities" under the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, so IDA does not have to go through the usual registration process, while IDA still files reports with the SEC and the SEC may suspend the exemption. IDA is a lender that provides loans and grants to the world's poorest countries, and the bill aims to help it raise money to do that work.

oppose: Investors would lose some standard registration protections for IDA securities, which means less standardized disclosure before they buy.

The exemption would take effect automatically 30 days after enactment, and the SEC's oversight is limited to reporting requirements it decides are appropriate, so the public has fewer built-in checks.
The bill does not include a cost estimate, so Congress and the public may not have a clear picture of the financial risks involved before the change takes effect.
support: The bill would reduce IDA's administrative burden, which could help it raise money more efficiently for loans and grants to the world's poorest countries.
Other World Bank institutions already receive similar exemptions, so this bill would bring IDA into line with that existing treatment.
IDA would still have to file annual and other reports with the SEC, and the SEC could suspend the exemption at any time, which keeps some oversight in place.

crs:
Aligning SEC Regulations for the World Bank's International Development Association Act 
This bill exempts from securities regulations any securities issued by the International Development Association (IDA) of the World Bank. The association provides loans and grants to developing countries. The Securities and Exchange Commission may suspend this exemption at any time.
The bill does not apply if, before the bill's date of enactment, the Department of the Treasury reports that IDA is providing financial support to a country whose government has repeatedly provided support for acts of international terrorism, as determined by the Department of State.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. (exemption) removes the standard SEC registration disclosures for IDA securities, so less standardized public information is available to investors, though IDA must still file annual and other SEC reports as the SEC deems necessary.

justice.reason: Exempting IDA securities from registration reduces the standard investor protections and enforcement hooks that apply to most issuers, though the SEC retains power to suspend the exemption and require reports.

label: H.R. 1804
title: 7(a) Loan Agent Oversight Act
short_title: 7(a) Loan Agent Oversight Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to send Congress a yearly report on the paid agents who help businesses get or refer 7(a) small business loans, including fraud, fees, and risk.
summary: The Small Business Administration (SBA) runs the 7(a) loan program, which guarantees loans for small businesses that can't get credit elsewhere on reasonable terms. Many borrowers and lenders use paid "agents" to prepare applications, write business plans, or broker and refer loans. This bill would require the SBA to give Congress a yearly report about those agents. The report would cover how many agents there are and what types; how many fraudulent loans involved an agent; how often the SBA had to buy back (pay on its guarantee) loans that involved an agent; and how many referral fees were paid, and how much in total, split by whether the borrower or the lender paid. It would also include a combined risk analysis of the biggest agents, those responsible for at least 1 percent of loan dollars or loan counts, without naming them. Finally, it would analyze interest rates on loans that used agents and describe how the SBA communicates with agents. The bill does not set new rules, penalties, or spending. It only adds reporting and information-sharing with Congress. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Small Business Committee.
does: Adds a new annual report requirement to Section 47 of the Small Business Act, to be sent to Congress in addition to an existing report.
Report must count 7(a) agents helping applicants, broken down by agent type as listed on the SBA's Fee Disclosure and Compensation Agreement form or later versions.
Report must state the number of fraudulent loans made where the applicant used a 7(a) agent.
Report must give the SBA's purchase rate (how often it paid out on its guarantee) for loans where an agent was used.
Report must give the number and total dollar value of referral fees paid to agents, split by whether the applicant or the lender paid.
Report must include a combined, anonymous risk analysis of agents responsible for at least 1 percent of the dollar value or number of agent-assisted loans.
Report must analyze interest rates on loans where an applicant or lender used an agent.
Report must describe how the SBA communicates with agents.

Defines a 7(a) agent as anyone providing covered services for a lender or applicant, including help with applications, business plans, financial statements, or consulting, brokering, or referral services.
who: Small business owners applying for SBA 7(a) loans
Loan agents, packagers, and brokers
7(a) lenders
The Small Business Administration, which must collect and report data
Congress and its small business committees

label: H.R. 1816
title: WOSB Accountability Act
short_title: WOSB Accountability Act
one: Requires that only certified (not self-certified) women-owned small businesses count toward federal contracting goals for such businesses, with a temporary bridge for pending applicants and quarterly SBA briefings to Congress.
summary:
The federal government has a goal of giving at least 5% of its contract dollars to women-owned small businesses. Until recently, many firms could simply say they were women-owned (self-certify) and have their contracts counted toward that goal. This bill would change that. Once it takes effect, only businesses certified by the Small Business Administration (SBA), another federal agency, a state government, or an SBA-approved national certifying group would count toward the goals.

The change would start after the end of the second full fiscal year following SBA's issuing of new rules, which the SBA must write within one year of the bill becoming law. Businesses that were self-certified, applied for formal certification before the start date, and are still waiting for a decision would be treated as certified until a decision is made. That keeps a slow application backlog from making them drop out of the count.

The SBA must brief the House and Senate small business committees within 60 days of enactment and every three months after that. Briefings cover expected applicants, pending and approved applications, processing times, costs to SBA and to applicants, outreach efforts, and any extra authority or money SBA says it needs. The bill gives no new money for any of this. The aim is to make the contracting numbers more accurate and to cut down on firms falsely claiming women-owned status, though certification could add paperwork and cost for real women-owned firms.

Treats certain self-certified firms as certified for goal-counting purposes if they applied for certification before the effective date and have not yet received a decision, until SBA or the national certifier decides.
Requires SBA to issue regulations within one year of enactment.

States that no additional funds are authorized to carry out the bill.

Congressional small business committees receiving the briefings

benefits: More accurate measurement of whether agencies meet women-owned small business goals.

Bridge provision protects firms with pending applications from losing counted status because of delays.
Quarterly briefings give Congress data on costs, backlogs and needs.
concerns: Certification may add cost, paperwork and delays for small, genuine women-owned businesses.
No additional funding is authorized, so SBA may struggle to process applications.
Firms that do not apply in time could stop counting toward goals, possibly reducing agencies' incentive to contract with them.
imp.cost: No additional funds are authorized. SBA must absorb the rulemaking, briefing and certification-processing work within existing resources. Briefings must report SBA's administrative costs and applicants' estimated certification costs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make sure only certified women-owned small businesses count toward federal women-owned small business contracting goals, so the goal numbers are more accurate. label: H.R. 2480
title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act of 2025
short_title: Securing Semiconductor Supply Chains Act of 2025
one: Requires the Commerce Department's SelectUSA program to gather input from state economic development groups and report to Congress on how to attract foreign investment in U.S. semiconductor manufacturing, with no new money.
summary: This bill is a study-and-report bill. It does not create new subsidies, tax breaks, or regulations. It tells SelectUSA, a Commerce Department program that helps attract business investment to the U.S., to do two things. First, within 180 days of the bill becoming law, SelectUSA must ask state-level economic development organizations for comments. It would ask what the federal government can do to boost foreign investment in making semiconductors (computer chips), what barriers exist, what opportunities and resource gaps the states see, and how to work with allied countries so that foreign adversaries do not benefit from these efforts. Second, within two years, SelectUSA must send a report to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee. The report must review the state comments, describe what SelectUSA is already doing, and assess strategies to increase investment and secure the chip supply chain. The bill says no additional money is authorized to carry it out, so the work would have to be paid for from existing funds. The bill's findings say that chip shortages hurt the economy and national security and that foreign and private investment could help rebuild domestic capacity. The bill does not mention environmental, water, or air standards for any resulting factories, and it does not mention public input beyond state economic development groups. It has passed the House and is now in the Senate.

label: H.R. 3422
title: Promoting Opportunities for Non-Traditional Capital Formation Act
short_title: Promoting Opportunities for Non-Traditional Capital Formation Act
one: Adds two duties to the SEC's small business advocate office: educate underrepresented, rural, and disaster-hit small businesses about ways to raise money, and meet yearly with state securities regulators.
summary: This bill changes the law that sets up the Securities and Exchange Commission's Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation. That office already helps small businesses and small investors with the process of raising money. The bill gives it two new jobs. First, it must provide educational materials and host or take part in events that explain ways to raise money. These events are for small businesses and small business investors. They must focus on three groups: underrepresented small businesses (including women-owned and minority-owned ones), businesses in rural areas, and small businesses hurt by hurricanes or other natural disasters. Second, the office must meet at least once a year with representatives of state securities commissions. These are the state agencies that oversee investments. The goal is to talk about working together to help small businesses and small investors. The bill does not create new funding, new regulations, or new rules for companies, and it does not change who can invest. It only adds duties to an existing office. The bill passed the House and is now in the Senate Banking Committee. The text does not say how much the added work would cost or whether the office would receive extra money.

label: H.R. 4491

short_title: SBA IT Modernization Reporting Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to follow a government watchdog's recommendations for managing risks in its new IT systems and to give Congress a plan and briefing on how it will do so.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to fix problems the Government Accountability Office (GAO, Congress's watchdog agency) found in a newly launched computer system. That system lets small businesses apply for and manage certifications used to win government contracts. The GAO's November 2024 report said the SBA needed to better manage risks, including cybersecurity weaknesses. Under the bill, the SBA's Administrator, working through its Chief Information Officer, must carry out the GAO's recommendations. Within 180 days of the bill becoming law, the SBA must send the House and Senate small business committees a plan. The plan must lay out new rules for handling technology projects. Those rules cover identifying and ranking risks, planning how to reduce them, including cyber risk information in purchasing and strategy plans, bringing security experts into contractor selection, and using GAO best-practice guides to build schedules and cost estimates. The plan must also name which SBA office is responsible and give deadlines for each step. Within 30 days after sending the plan, the SBA must brief the committees. The bill does not give new money and does not create new penalties. It is mainly about oversight and good project management. The text is complete, and the CRS summary matches it.
does: Directs the SBA Administrator, through the agency's Chief Information Officer, to take needed actions to carry out the recommendations in GAO report GAO-25-106963 (published Nov. 6, 2024) on SBA IT modernization risks.

Requires policies for each IT modernization project to identify risk sources, define risk parameters, set risk management strategies, document risks across all project phases, and rank risks and create risk management plans.
Requires risk-reduction measures to be tied to mitigation plans.
Requires IT acquisition and strategic plans to include the information needed to manage cyber risks, and requires a documented traceability analysis (tracking requirements through the project).
Requires security experts to take part in selecting contractors for a project.
Requires master schedules and cost estimates to follow GAO's published best-practice guides.
Requires the plan to name the responsible SBA office and give timelines for each action.
Requires a briefing to the two committees within 30 days after the plan is submitted.

SBA IT Modernization Reporting Act
This bill requires the Small Business Administration (SBA) to implement the recommendations from a Government Accountability Office (GAO) report published on November 6, 2024, related to modernizing the SBA's information technology systems.
Specifically, the SBA must address risks related to its certification project that allows small businesses to apply for and manage government contracting certifications. The GAO recommendations include developing a project risk management strategy and risk mitigation plan and managing cybersecurity vulnerabilities.
The SBA must submit to Congress an implementation plan for the modernization not later than 180 days after the enactment of this bill.

environment.reason: The bill concerns IT project management and cybersecurity and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires a written implementation plan and a committee briefing within 30 days, which adds reporting to Congress on how SBA manages its IT project; however, the plan goes to committees rather than being published to the public, so the gain is limited.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill focuses on SBA's internal IT project management and does not clearly shift costs to or from corporations versus the public.

local_say.reason: The bill gives congressional committees a plan and briefing but does not change state or local input on decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no provisions about bailouts or ratepayer cost shifts; it provides no new funding.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same IT oversight requirements to the SBA certification system and does not create unequal treatment of any group.

justice.reason: The bill requires implementation of GAO recommendations, a named responsible office, set timelines, and a congressional briefing, which adds accountability for the agency's handling of the system; it sets no penalties for noncompliance, which limits the gain.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill governs agency IT project management and does not expand or restrict what individuals may do.

label: H.R. 4549
title: Office of Rural Affairs Enhancement Act
short_title: Office of Rural Affairs Enhancement Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration's Office of Rural Affairs to be led by a competitively hired, qualified assistant administrator, to hold webinars and regional outreach events for rural small businesses, and to publish an annual public report.
summary:
This bill updates the law that created the Office of Rural Affairs inside the Small Business Administration (SBA), the federal agency that helps small businesses. Right now the office exists, but the bill sets firmer rules for how it is run.

First, the office's head, called the Assistant Administrator, would have to be a regular career (competitive service) employee. That means hired through a competitive process, not a political appointment. This person would need education, experience, or knowledge about rural affairs and small business issues, plus experience providing development help to rural small businesses.

Second, the bill requires the office to host webinars and outreach events in different regions of the country for rural small businesses. It must invite SBA district offices, partner groups (such as small business development centers, women's business centers, SCORE chapters, and Veteran Business Outreach Centers), and federal and state agencies, along with other interested people.

Third, the SBA must send Congress a report within 180 days of enactment and then once a year. It must also post the report publicly. The report covers the office's budget, staff count, the Assistant Administrator's name, its activities, the number of events, what was learned at the events, and an analysis of how well SBA lending programs serve rural small businesses.

The bill also makes small wording fixes, including updating the name of a tourism office. It does not provide new money. It does not say how much the changes would cost.
does: Requires the head of the SBA Office of Rural Affairs (the Assistant Administrator) to be an employee in the competitive service, meaning hired through a competitive process.

Requires the Assistant Administrator to have education, experience, or knowledge related to rural affairs and small business issues, and experience providing development assistance to rural small businesses.

Requires the office to host webinars and outreach events in various regions of the country for rural small businesses, and to invite SBA district offices, resource partners, federal and state agencies, and other interested people.
Defines resource partners as small business development centers, women's business centers, SCORE (Service Corps of Retired Executives) chapters, and Veteran Business Outreach Centers.
Requires an SBA report to the House and Senate small business committees within 180 days of enactment and every year after, also posted publicly on an SBA website.

Requires the report to list the office's operational details (Assistant Administrator's name, budget, staff count), its activities, number of events, an analysis of SBA lending to rural small businesses, and information gathered at events.

Makes wording changes: uses the term 'rural small business concern,' changes 'provide information' to 'promote' for agency programs, and replaces the defunct 'United States Tourism and Travel Administration' with the Commerce Department's National Travel and Tourism Office.
who: Small businesses in rural areas, which would get more outreach and information.
The SBA and its Office of Rural Affairs, which would take on new hiring, outreach, and reporting duties.
SBA resource partners and district offices, which would be invited to take part in events.
House and Senate small business committees, which would receive annual reports.
The public, which could read the annual reports.

benefits: Rural small businesses could learn about SBA and other federal programs more easily.
Public reports on budget, staffing, and lending could make the office more accountable.
Competitive hiring and required experience could mean a more qualified office head.
Information gathered at events could show rural needs to Congress.
concerns: The bill adds duties but provides no new funding, so the work could strain existing SBA resources.
Webinars and events may not reach rural areas with poor internet access.
Reports and outreach do not by themselves change loan terms or give rural communities decision-making power.
imp.cost: No funding is authorized or stated in the bill. No cost estimate was provided. Costs would likely come from existing SBA budgets.
unknowns: How much the new outreach and reporting would cost.
Whether the SBA would add staff or shift existing staff.
Whether the lending analysis would lead to any changes in SBA programs.
How the Senate will act on the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 282.

purpose: The bill says it updates the law creating the SBA Office of Rural Affairs to set firmer rules for how the office is run. Its stated goals are to have a qualified, competitively hired office head, to require outreach to rural small businesses through webinars and regional events, and to require annual public reports to Congress on the office's budget, staffing, activities, and SBA lending to rural small businesses.

oppose: The bill adds new duties to the SBA Office of Rural Affairs but provides no new funding, so the work could strain existing agency resources that are already committed to other programs.
Webinars and outreach events may not reach rural areas with poor or no internet access, so the bill's main outreach method may miss the communities it aims to serve.
Reports and events do not by themselves change loan terms or give rural communities a direct say in decisions, so you may feel the bill does too little on the problems rural businesses face.
support: The bill requires the office head to be hired through a competitive process and to have experience with rural affairs and development help for rural small businesses, which could lead to a more qualified leader.

Required webinars and regional events could help rural small business owners learn about SBA and other federal programs more easily, including through partners like SCORE chapters and small business development centers.

Annual public reports on the office's budget, staffing, and rural lending could make the office more accountable to Congress and the public, and the information gathered at events could show lawmakers what rural businesses need.

crs:
Office of Rural Affairs Enhancement Act
This bill requires the Small Business Administration (SBA) to use a competitive hiring process to select an assistant administrator for the Office of Rural Affairs. The assistant administrator must have experience (1) with rural affairs and issues relating to small businesses, and (2) providing development assistance to rural small businesses.
Additionally, the bill requires the office to host webinars and regional outreach events for rural small businesses.
The SBA must report annually about the office's activities.

transparency_kindness.reason: Annual reports on the office's budget, staffing, activities and SBA rural lending must be posted publicly (report provision requiring public posting), which makes the office's work easier to see.

local_say.reason: The required webinars and regional outreach events invite rural small businesses, district offices, and state agencies to take part, and the report records information gathered at events, giving rural communities a channel for input, though no decision-making power is added.

equality.reason: Outreach requirement targets rural small businesses across regions, giving them more equal access to SBA program information, and the competitive hiring rule applies merit-based selection to the office head.

justice.reason: Competitive-service hiring with stated qualification requirements (Sec. on Assistant Administrator) makes selection of the office head more consistent and accountable, though the bill provides no new remedies for harm.

label: H.R. 5490
title: Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
short_title: Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
one: Creates a five-year federal task force, sanctions authority, victim-support programs, and satellite-imagery access to fight Southeast Asian scam compounds that use trafficked labor to defraud Americans.
summary:
This bill targets large "scam compounds," mostly in Burma, Laos, and Cambodia. Criminal groups run them. They use trafficked workers, many forced to work, to run online fraud such as "pig butchering." That is a scam where a fraudster builds a fake relationship and pushes the victim to put money into a fake crypto investment. The bill says Americans lost at least $10 billion to these operations in 2024.

Within 30 days of becoming law, the President must set up an interagency Task Force chaired by the Secretary of State. It must include State, Justice (including the FBI), Homeland Security (including the Secret Service), and Treasury. The SEC, FTC, FCC, and other agencies may join, and intelligence agencies may help. Members must fully share relevant data and their plans. The Task Force must consult regularly with state and local law enforcement, anti-trafficking and anti-corruption groups, private companies, and regional civil society. It ends after five years.

Within 240 days, the Task Force must give Congress a strategy. The strategy covers pressuring governments that tolerate scams, investigating China's and the Burmese military's roles, training foreign police, protecting trafficking victims, imposing sanctions, pushing for Financial Action Task Force reviews, recovering stolen assets, building an allied coalition, and improving data sharing. It also lists "harnessing offensive cyber capabilities" to disrupt scam centers. The Task Force must set measurable success indicators and send annual reports for five years. The reports cover sanctioned people, estimated losses and recoveries, trafficking victim numbers, and known scam centers.

The President may, but is not required to, freeze U.S. assets and bar visas for foreign people who own, run, or significantly support scam compounds. The same applies to government officials who knowingly enable them or profit from them. Penalties follow existing emergency economic powers law. Exceptions cover humanitarian aid, food and medicine, UN obligations, intelligence and law enforcement work, trafficking victims, and imports of goods. The President can waive sanctions for national security reasons after notifying Congress 15 days ahead.

The State Department may fund trauma-informed care, shelter, and reintegration for trafficking victims in scam centers. It may also give nongovernmental groups and researchers high-resolution satellite imagery to document abuses, and it must report on who gets access. Funding comes from money already authorized under an existing foreign assistance law. The bill adds no new appropriation.
does: Requires the President to create an interagency Task Force within 30 days, chaired by the Secretary of State, with State, Justice/FBI, Homeland Security/Secret Service/HSI, and Treasury as required members.
Allows the SEC, FTC, FCC, intelligence community, and any other relevant agency to join or support the Task Force; all member agencies must fully share relevant data and their plans.
Requires the Task Force to consult quarterly with state and local law enforcement and regularly with anti-trafficking and anti-corruption NGOs, private-sector actors, and regional civil society.
Requires a comprehensive strategy to Congress within 240 days to shut down scam centers, stop their spread, dismantle criminal and trafficking networks, and hold corrupt officials accountable.

Strategy objectives include pressuring complicit governments, investigating China's and Burma's military's roles, training foreign law enforcement, protecting trafficking victims, pursuing FATF reviews, recovering stolen assets, and forming an allied coalition.

Strategy objectives also include using offensive cyber capabilities against scam centers and assessing whether existing Fusion Centers can be used for data integration across federal, state, and local agencies.
Requires measurable success indicators, such as sanctions, indictments, arrests, U.S. losses mitigated, trafficking victims rescued, and scam centers reduced.

Requires annual unclassified reports (with optional classified annex) for five years, covering sanctioned persons, Chinese entities that aid them, estimated U.S. losses and recoveries, trafficking victim counts, known scam centers, spread outside Southeast Asia, and funding recommendations.

Authorizes the President to block property and deny or revoke visas for foreign persons who own, direct, or significantly support scam compounds, and for officials who knowingly enable or profit from them.

Applies existing emergency economic powers law penalties to violations; exempts humanitarian aid, food and medicine, UN headquarters obligations, intelligence and law enforcement activities, trafficking victims, vessel crew safety, and goods imports.
Lets the President waive sanctions on national security grounds by certifying to Congress at least 15 days ahead.

Authorizes the State Department to run trauma-informed care, shelter, and reintegration programs for trafficking victims in scam centers, designed to avoid revictimization and gather evidence for prosecutions.
Authorizes State to give NGOs and research institutions access to high-resolution satellite imagery to document scam-center human rights abuses, with a report within 180 days on terms and recipients.
Directs State to use funds already authorized under Foreign Assistance Act section 481 for the strategy; creates no new appropriation.
Ends the Task Force five years after enactment.
who: Americans targeted by online investment and romance scams, and their families
Trafficking victims forced to work in scam compounds, from many countries
Foreign criminal syndicate leaders, enablers, and complicit officials in Southeast Asia and possibly China
Federal agencies (State, DOJ, DHS, Treasury, possibly SEC, FTC, FCC, intelligence agencies)
State and local law enforcement and anti-trafficking and human rights groups
Banks, crypto platforms, and tech firms that may be consulted or that handle blocked assets
Researchers and NGOs that could receive satellite imagery
Foreign governments in Burma, Laos, Cambodia, and China

benefits: Could reduce fraud losses for Americans and help recover stolen assets.
Funds and authorizes care, shelter, and reintegration for trafficking victims.
Improves coordination among federal, state, and local agencies and with foreign partners.
Requires public-facing reporting and measurable goals, with congressional oversight.
Gives NGOs and researchers satellite imagery to document abuses independently.
concerns: No new money is appropriated; the work relies on existing authorized funds, which may limit results.
Offensive cyber operations are named without detail or limits.
Required full sharing of data and plans across agencies, including with law enforcement, raises privacy questions that the bill does not address.
The President can waive sanctions for national security reasons, and the sanctions are optional.
Sanctions on officials and strained relations with China and Southeast Asian governments could have diplomatic effects.
Sanctions could affect people who are in fact victims if they are not identified correctly, though the bill exempts determined trafficking victims.
imp.cost: No new appropriation. The State Department must use amounts already authorized under section 481 of the Foreign Assistance Act (international narcotics control and law enforcement). The bill gives no cost estimate.
unknowns: How much money will actually be spent and whether it will be enough.
How aggressively the President would use the optional sanctions or waivers.
What offensive cyber activities would be used and what oversight would apply.
How effective sanctions would be against groups operating with local government protection.
How the Senate Foreign Relations Committee might change the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Foreign Relations.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to shut down criminal syndicates that run mass online scam operations against Americans, many of them large "scam compounds" in Southeast Asia that use trafficked workers. It aims to do this by creating an interagency Task Force, requiring a strategy and annual reports to Congress, authorizing optional sanctions on people who support these operations, and providing support for trafficking victims.

oppose: The bill appropriates no new money and relies on funds already authorized under Foreign Assistance Act section 481, which some may see as limiting how much the Task Force can accomplish.
The bill names offensive cyber operations against scam centers but gives no detail or limits on how they would be used, which some constituents may want clarified.
Requiring agencies to fully share relevant data and plans, including with law enforcement, raises privacy questions that the bill does not address.

Sanctions on foreign government officials and pressure on China and Southeast Asian governments could strain diplomatic relationships, and sanctions could affect people who are misidentified as perpetrators rather than victims.
support: Americans lost at least $10 billion to these operations in 2024, according to the bill's findings, and the bill creates a single federal Task Force to coordinate the response across agencies.
The bill requires a detailed strategy to Congress within 240 days and annual public reports for five years, with measurable success indicators, which supports congressional oversight.

The bill gives the President authority to freeze assets and deny visas to people who own or significantly support scam compounds, and it protects trafficking victims with care, shelter, and reintegration support.
The bill exempts determined trafficking victims from sanctions and lets State give researchers and nongovernmental groups satellite imagery to document abuses independently.

crs:
The following analysis is based on draft 
bill text
 that was made available by the House of Representatives and may differ from the bill text as introduced.
Dismantle Foreign Scam Syndicates Act
This bill establishes an interagency task force to shut down criminal syndicates perpetuating mass online scams. This bill also explicitly authorizes sanctions against foreign individuals or entities operating or providing support to scam compounds. (Scam compounds target individuals for financial fraud and are concentrated in Southeast Asia.)  
The President must establish an interagency task force to shut down transnational criminal syndicates that use large scam centers and forced labor of trafficked persons to perpetuate mass online scams against Americans. The task force must submit to Congress and oversee implementation of a strategy to combat scam centers, dismantle the criminal elements involved with them, and hold corrupt officials accountable. The task force must periodically report to Congress, including a list of foreign persons sanctioned by the United States for their involvement with online financial scams from Southeast Asia against U.S. nationals.
The President is explicitly authorized to impose visa- and property-blocking sanctions on (1) any foreign individual or entity that owns, controls, directs, or provides significant support to a significant scam compound operation or an enabling service; and (2) foreign government officials who knowingly enable or benefit from scam compound operations within their jurisdiction.
The Department of State is authorized to provide (1) trauma-informed care and other support services for trafficked persons within online scam centers, and (2) high-resolution satellite imagery to nongovernmental organizations and research institutions for the purposes of monitoring and documenting human rights abuses related to online scam centers in Southeast Asia.

environment.reason: The bill concerns scam compounds and trafficking; it does not address water, air, land, or ecosystem protection.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on annual unclassified reports and satellite imagery access for NGOs and researchers, plus State reporting on imagery recipients, makes government action on scam centers more visible; trauma-informed victim care and exemptions for trafficking victims add humane treatment, though required full data sharing and classified annexes limit openness.

people_over_profit.reason: Sanctions and asset freezes target criminal syndicates and enablers, and the strategy aims to recover stolen assets for defrauded Americans; the bill does not shift costs onto consumers or taxpayers beyond existing authorized funds.

local_say.reason: The bill adds state and local law enforcement consultation, but it does not give local communities decision-making authority over land use, facilities, or permits; federal interagency control and presidential discretion dominate.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts of corporations or shifting costs to ratepayers.

equality.reason: Sanctions and visa bans apply based on conduct across foreign persons and officials, and trafficking victims are protected regardless of nationality; no group is treated unequally by the text.

justice.reason: Sec. requiring measurable success indicators, annual reports for five years, and congressional oversight add accountability; Sec. on sanctions exceptions protects determined trafficking victims, though the broad waiver authority and optional sanctions reduce consistency.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. on sanctions and visa bans and the broad data-sharing requirement with law enforcement limit what foreign persons and officials may do, and the bill does not address privacy protections for individuals whose data is shared; the impact on Americans' own choices is limited.

label: H.R. 754
title: Investing in Main Street Act of 2025
short_title: Investing in Main Street Act of 2025
one: Lets certain banks put up to 15% of their capital and surplus into small business investment companies, up from the current 5% limit.
summary: This bill changes one federal law, the Small Business Investment Act of 1958. That law lets certain banks invest in small business investment companies (SBICs). SBICs are privately owned funds licensed by the Small Business Administration. They invest in and lend to small businesses. Today, a bank can put no more than 5% of its capital and surplus into SBICs. Capital and surplus is roughly the bank's own financial cushion. The bill raises that cap to 15%. It makes the same change in both places where the cap appears. One place covers investing directly in SBICs. The other covers investing in an entity set up only to invest in SBICs. The bill doesn't create a new program, spend new federal money, or add new rules. It also doesn't say how banks must use the extra room. Supporters would likely argue that more bank money could reach small businesses that have trouble getting capital. Critics could worry that banks would put more of their cushion into riskier, less liquid investments. Whether either happens would depend on how much banks choose to invest and how well the SBICs perform. The bill passed the House and is now in the Senate Banking Committee. The text has no start date, so it would presumably take effect when enacted.
does: Raises from 5% to 15% the share of a bank's capital and surplus that it may invest in one or more small business investment companies (SBICs).
Raises from 5% to 15% the cap on investing in any entity established to invest solely in SBICs.
Amends Section 302(b) of the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 (15 U.S.C. 682(b)) and changes nothing else in that law.
Adds no new spending, programs, reporting duties, or safeguards in the text provided.
who: Banks and other banking entities covered by Section 302(b), which could invest more in SBICs
Small business investment companies, which could draw more private bank capital
Small businesses seeking investment or loans from SBICs
Bank depositors and regulators, who have an interest in the safety of bank investments
Taxpayers, only indirectly, through SBA's role licensing SBICs

benefits: Could channel more private bank money to small businesses.
Could help small businesses that have trouble getting traditional loans.
Costs taxpayers nothing directly and creates no new program.
concerns: Tripling the cap could expose banks to more risk from less liquid investments.
The bill adds no new safeguards, reporting, or targeting toward underserved communities.
Larger banks could gain the most, and the money might not reach the neediest small businesses.
If bank investments lost value, failures could add pressure for public support, though the bill doesn't provide any.
imp.cost: No federal spending is authorized in the text. No cost estimate was provided. The investment would come from banks' own capital.
unknowns: How much more banks would actually invest.
How bank regulators would treat the larger holdings.
Whether the money would reach small businesses in underserved or local communities.
Whether SBICs would change their behavior or risk-taking with more bank capital.
Which banking entities are covered and how many would use the higher cap.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to let certain banks invest more in small business investment companies (SBICs), which are privately owned, SBA-licensed funds that invest in and lend to small businesses. It does this by raising the cap on a bank's investment from 5% to 15% of its capital and surplus, in both places the cap appears in federal law (Section 302(b) of the Small Business Investment Act of 1958).

oppose: Tripling the cap from 5% to 15% lets banks put a much larger share of their capital cushion into SBIC investments, which can be less liquid and riskier than traditional bank assets.
The bill adds no new safeguards, reporting requirements, or limits on how banks use the extra room, so there would be little public information about the added exposure.
The benefits could go mostly to larger banks with more capital to invest, and the bill does not direct funding toward underserved communities or the smallest businesses.
support: The bill could bring more private bank money into small business investment funds, which may help businesses that have trouble getting traditional loans.
The bill creates no new federal program, spends no new taxpayer money, and makes only a narrow change to one section of existing law.
Banks already participate in SBICs under current rules; raising the cap lets willing banks invest more while SBIC performance and bank decisions determine the outcome.

crs:
Investing in Main Street Act of 2025
This bill authorizes certain banking entities to invest up to 15% of their capital and surplus in one or more small business investment companies (SBICs) or in any entity established to invest solely in SBICs. The current limit is 5%.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 302(b) cap raised from 5% to 15% lets banks shift more of their own capital into SBIC investments, with no targeting or safeguards to ensure the funds reach small businesses rather than primarily benefiting bank and fund returns.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill involves no federal spending or guarantees; the text does not provide any bailout or ratepayer cost shift, though bank losses could create indirect pressure for public support, which the bill does not itself create.

label: H.R. 787
title: Plain Language in Contracting Act
short_title: Plain Language in Contracting Act
one: Requires federal contracting notices aimed at small businesses to be written clearly and include searchable key words, with the Small Business Administration writing rules within 90 days.
summary: This bill would make federal contracting notices for small businesses easier to read and find. These are the notices that federal agencies post on the government's single website for contract opportunities (the "single Government-wide point of entry" in federal law, currently SAM.gov). Under the bill, each notice about small businesses would have to be written so a small business can easily understand what the agency wants. Notices would need to be clear, short, and well organized. To the extent practical, they would also follow best practices for their subject and audience. Notices would also have to include key words, as far as practical, so small businesses searching the site can quickly find and understand them. The Administrator of the Small Business Administration (SBA) would have 90 days after the bill becomes law to issue rules putting this into effect. The bill says no new money is authorized, so agencies and the SBA would have to do this with existing funds. The bill does not change who can win contracts, how contracts are awarded, or how much is spent. It only changes how notices are written and labeled. Supporters would say it helps small firms, which often lack legal staff, compete for federal work. A possible concern is that "to the maximum extent practicable" leaves agencies room to fall short, and no enforcement method is described.
does: Requires every 'covered notice' (a small-business-related notice an agency posts on the government-wide contracting website) to be written so a small business can easily understand its intent.
Requires notices to be clear, concise, and well organized, and to follow other best practices for their subject and audience to the maximum extent practicable.
Requires notices, to the maximum extent practicable, to include key words in their description so small businesses can find and understand them when searching the government-wide site.
Directs the SBA Administrator to issue implementing rules within 90 days of enactment.
Uses the Small Business Act's definitions of 'Federal agency' and 'small business concern.'
States that no additional funds are authorized to carry out the Act.
Per the CRS summary, notices must also comply with the Plain Writing Act of 2010; the bill text provided does not itself spell out that reference.
who: Small businesses looking for federal contracts
Federal agencies that post contracting notices
Small Business Administration, which writes the rules
Contracting officers and procurement staff
Taxpayers, indirectly, through possibly broader competition for contracts

benefits: Small businesses may spend less time and money decoding notices.
Better key words could make opportunities easier to find.
Wider small-business participation could increase competition and help local firms.
Costs the government little, since no new funds are authorized.
concerns: 'Maximum extent practicable' language gives agencies flexibility and may weaken results.
The bill describes no enforcement or penalty for unclear notices.
No new funding may mean agencies and the SBA struggle to implement it well.
The 90-day deadline for rules may be tight for the SBA.
imp.cost: No additional funds authorized; implementation must come from existing agency and SBA resources. No cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: How the SBA will define and measure 'easily understand' and 'clear.'
How compliance will be checked or enforced.
How much effort agencies will need and whether staff time will be diverted from other work.
Whether the bill will receive a Senate committee vote.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make federal contracting notices for small businesses clear, concise, and easy to find, so small firms can understand what federal agencies want and compete for federal work. It would require these notices to follow plain-writing standards and include searchable key words, and it directs the Small Business Administration to issue implementing rules within 90 days.

oppose: The bill says agencies must follow its clarity and key-word requirements only "to the maximum extent practicable," which gives agencies wide flexibility and could leave the bill's goals unmet.
The bill does not describe any enforcement method or penalty if a notice is unclear, so it is unclear how the requirements would be checked.
The bill authorizes no new funding, so agencies and the SBA would have to carry out the work with existing budgets, and the 90-day deadline for SBA rules may be hard to meet.
support: The bill would require notices for small businesses to be written so a small business can easily understand what the agency wants, which could save small firms time and money decoding them.
Requiring key words in notices, where practical, could help small businesses find contracting opportunities on the government-wide website more easily.
Clearer notices could encourage more small businesses, including local firms, to compete for federal work, and the bill does not change contract awards or spending, while authorizing no new funds.

crs:
Plain Language in Contracting Act
This bill requires that notices of contracting opportunities for small businesses are written in a clear, concise, and accessible manner.
Each notice also must comply with the requirements of the Plain Writing Act of 2010, which are applicable to publications and notices by federal agencies.
The Small Business Administration must issue rules to implement these requirements.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 1 requires contracting notices for small businesses to be clear, concise, and easy to understand and searchable, which makes public contracting information more accessible to the public.

equality.reason: Sec. 1 makes federal contracting notices easier for small businesses to read and find, which may give smaller firms that lack legal staff a more equal chance to learn about and pursue federal opportunities.

label: H.R. 788
title: DOE and SBA Research Act
short_title: DOE and SBA Research Act
one: Requires the Department of Energy and the Small Business Administration to sign an agreement to do joint research, include small businesses where appropriate, and report to Congress within two years, with no new money authorized.
summary:
This bill tells two federal agencies, the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Small Business Administration (SBA), to work together on research and development. They must sign a formal agreement (a "memorandum of understanding" or similar deal) to carry out shared research that supports both agencies' goals. Small businesses must be included in this work "as appropriate."

The agencies may also make "reimbursable agreements," which means one party pays another back for work or services, with outside groups, and may team up with other federal agencies. The work must follow existing research security rules from a 2022 law (the CHIPS and Science-related Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act), which are meant to protect federally funded research from improper foreign influence.

Within two years, the agencies must send Congress a report covering how they coordinated, ways to expand their technical abilities, research achievements, future areas of shared success, and plans to keep working together. The bill authorizes no new spending, so any work must be paid for from money the agencies already have. The bill does not say what topics the research would cover, and it sets no specific environmental, energy, or safety standards. Its effects will depend on how the agencies carry it out.
does: Requires the Energy Secretary and the SBA Administrator to enter into a memorandum of understanding or similar agreement for joint, cross-cutting research and development tied to both agencies' missions.
Requires small businesses (as defined in the Small Business Act) to be included in the activities, as appropriate.
Allows reimbursable agreements (where one party repays another for services) between DOE, SBA, and appropriate entities, and allows collaboration with other federal agencies.

Requires a report to Congress within two years covering coordination, ways to expand technical capabilities, collaborative research achievements, areas of future mutual success, and continued coordination.
Requires the activities to be consistent with the research security provisions of the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act (Public Law 117-167).
Authorizes no additional appropriations (CUTGO compliance), so the work must use existing funds.
who: Department of Energy and Small Business Administration staff and leadership
Small businesses that may take part in joint research
Other federal agencies that may collaborate
Members of Congress who receive the report
Outside entities that may enter reimbursable agreements

benefits: Could help small businesses take part in federal energy research.
Could cut duplication and improve coordination between two agencies.
Requires a report to Congress that gives some oversight.
Keeps research security protections in place.
Costs no new authorized money.

label: H.R. 789
title: Transparency and Predictability in Small Business Opportunities Act
short_title: Transparency and Predictability in Small Business Opportunities Act
one: Requires federal agencies to publicly explain why they cancelled contract solicitations open to small businesses and to help affected small businesses find similar opportunities, with no new money provided.
summary: When a federal agency asks for bids on a contract that at least two small businesses could compete for, and then cancels it, small businesses that spent time and money preparing bids are often left in the dark. This bill tries to fix that. Within 180 days of becoming law, the Small Business Administration (SBA) must write rules requiring the agency to publicly explain why it cancelled the solicitation. The agency must also share whatever it knows about plans to reissue it, including timing, and about plans to fold the same work into another contract or task order. All of this must be posted on the government's single public contracting website. If the agency does not plan to reissue the solicitation, the SBA must also set up a process to refer any small business that prepared a bid to the agency's Office of Small and Disadvantaged Business Utilization. That office would be required, once notified by the business, to help it find similar contracting opportunities. The bill says no extra funds are authorized, so agencies would have to do this work with existing budgets. The bill is narrow and procedural. It does not change who can win contracts or how they are awarded. It adds a layer of public explanation and a small amount of help for businesses affected by cancellations.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make federal contract cancellations more transparent and predictable for small businesses.
