The bill requires SBA to write new rules within 180 days, which adds to federal rulemaking and administrative work, and the bill does not change how contracts are awarded or compensate businesses for bid costs.
support: The bill would require agencies to publicly explain why a small-business contract was cancelled, which could discourage arbitrary or improper cancellations and make the process fairer to bidders.
Small businesses that spent time and money preparing bids would get clearer information about whether and when work will be reissued, helping them plan and decide where to focus their efforts.

The bill would help small businesses get referred to their agency's Office of Small and Disadvantaged Business Utilization for help finding similar contracting opportunities, and it posts the information on the existing government contracting portal instead of creating a new system.

Transparency and Predictability in Small Business Opportunities Act
This bill requires the Small Business Administration (SBA) to issue rules for disclosing information about federal contract solicitations for which small businesses were eligible and that were issued and cancelled.
Under the rules for such a solicitation, an agency must provide (1) a justification for the cancellation, (2) information about any plans to reissue the solicitation and any associated time frames, and (3) information about any plans to include the requirements of the solicitation in another contract or task order of the agency.
Additionally, for such solicitations that an agency does not intend to reissue, the SBA must provide procedures for the agency to refer a small business that prepared a bid for such covered solicitation to the Office of Small and Disadvantaged Business Utilization for assistance in identifying similar contracting opportunities.

equality.reason: Sec. 2 gives small businesses that bid on cancelled solicitations a referral to agency small-business offices for help finding similar opportunities, a modest equal-access benefit for that group, though it does not change award rules.

justice.reason: Requiring public written justifications for cancellations and a referral process for affected bidders adds accountability for agency decisions, though remedies are limited to information and assistance rather than compensation.

label: H.R. 7934
title: Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
short_title: Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
one: Requires federal agencies to publish searchable public online databases of their larger or more significant legal settlement agreements, with reports on any that are withheld.
summary: When a federal agency settles a legal case, the deal is often hard for the public to find. This bill would require each agency that makes a "covered" settlement to run a public, searchable website listing those settlements within two years of enactment. A settlement is covered if it requires at least $10 million in payments, involves a court-appointed special master or monitor, involves a state, tribal, or local government, or meets extra criteria set by the White House budget office (OMB). The database would show a copy of each agreement, whether it settles civil or criminal claims, the date, the laws allegedly broken, attorney fees, payments to or from the government, penalties, expected length, and any governments named. Agencies may leave out material covered by a confidentiality clause, a court order, or Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) exemptions, and classified information. But each agency must report yearly to Congress and the public on how many agreements were fully withheld and why. Some settlements are excluded, including those about federal employee personnel matters, plea bargains and non-prosecution agreements, tax-code matters, and the U.S. Trustee Program. OMB must issue guidance within one year. The law applies to new settlements and, where practicable, to those from 2015 onward that are still in effect. The database would not change any settlement's terms or create new legal rights.
does: Adds a new section 307 to title 5 of the U.S. Code requiring each agency that has entered a covered settlement to create and maintain a public, searchable online database within 2 years of enactment.

Defines covered settlements as settlement agreements or deferred prosecution agreements with at least $10 million in explicitly obligated payments, a special master or monitor, a state/tribal/local/other non-federal government party, or designation by OMB under extra criteria (likely significant compliance costs).

Requires the database to list, where practicable: a copy of the agreement; civil/criminal nature; execution date; statutes alleged violated; attorney fees; amounts parties must pay; penalties or fines; payments made to or by the federal government; projected duration; and governments named.
Allows withholding of material under confidentiality provisions, court orders, or FOIA exemptions; nothing requires disclosure of classified information.

Excludes settlements related to the U.S. Trustee Program, federal employee personnel actions, non-prosecution agreements and plea bargains, the Internal Revenue Code, and matters under chapter 46 of title 18 (civil forfeiture).

Directs OMB, with the Attorney General, to issue guidance within 1 year: publication at least annually, common machine-readable data standards, extra criteria for covered status, a consistent web address (such as agencyname.gov/settlements), a certification process for existing databases, and rules for multi-agency settlements.

Requires annual reports to Congress and the public, starting 2 years after enactment, on how many covered settlements were fully withheld and which exemptions applied (including specific FOIA exemptions).

States that database information does not change a settlement's terms and creates no legal rights or judicial review; applies to new settlements and, where practicable, those entered since Jan. 1, 2015 and still in effect.
who: Federal agencies that enter settlements (extra reporting and web work)
Office of Management and Budget and the Department of Justice (guidance duties)
The general public, journalists, watchdog groups, and researchers who want to see settlements
Congress, which gets annual non-disclosure reports for oversight
State, tribal, and local governments named in settlements
Companies and other parties settling with the government, whose agreements may become public
Communities affected by settlements, such as environmental or consumer cases

benefits: Makes settlement terms, payments, and penalties searchable by the public, journalists, and watchdogs.
Annual reports show how many settlements are withheld and under which exemptions, aiding oversight.
Communities can more easily see agreements involving their local or state governments.
Standard data formats and web addresses make information easier to find and compare across agencies.
Could discourage quiet deals that favor large companies.
concerns: Confidentiality clauses, court orders, and FOIA exemptions could let agencies withhold many agreements.
'To the extent practicable' language gives agencies room to skip publishing, especially for older settlements.
Exclusions (plea bargains, non-prosecution agreements, tax, personnel, civil forfeiture) leave out some significant deals.
No judicial review or legal right to enforce compliance is created.
Agencies have 2 years to comply, so results are not immediate.
The $10 million threshold could leave out smaller settlements affecting individuals or communities, unless they involve a government party or OMB designation.
imp.cost: No funding is provided and no cost estimate is given in the material. Agencies would pay for building and maintaining databases from existing budgets, so costs may vary.
unknowns: What additional criteria OMB will set for covered settlements.
How many settlements will be withheld under exemptions.
How much agencies will spend to comply.
How thoroughly agencies will publish older settlements back to 2015.
Whether the 'practicable' standard will be applied loosely.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make federal settlement agreements easier for the public to find. It would require agencies to publish a searchable online database of covered settlements, including copies of the agreements, payments, attorney fees, and penalties, and to report yearly on how many settlements are withheld and why. The bill says the database would not change any settlement's terms or create new legal rights.

oppose: The bill adds a new reporting and website requirement for federal agencies, which could take staff time and money to build and maintain, especially across many agencies over a two-year deadline.

The bill does not create judicial review or a way to enforce it, and agencies may withhold material under confidentiality clauses, court orders, or FOIA exemptions, so some people may question how much new information it would actually provide.
The bill excludes several types of agreements, such as plea bargains, non-prosecution agreements, and tax matters, so some significant government deals would not appear in the database.
support: The bill would make federal settlement terms, payments, and penalties searchable by the public, journalists, and watchdog groups, which could improve transparency in how the government resolves legal cases.

The bill requires yearly reports to Congress and the public showing how many settlements were fully withheld and which exemptions were used, which would give lawmakers and citizens a way to check agency decisions.
Settlements involving state, tribal, or local governments would be listed, so residents could more easily see agreements that affect their own communities.

crs:
Settlement Agreement Information Database Act of 2026
This bill requires federal agencies to publish a searchable, online database of information about certain settlement agreements entered into by the agency. The database must include
a copy of each settlement agreement,
whether the agreement resolves a civil or criminal claim (or both),
the date the agreement was executed,
any alleged statutory violations,
the amount of attorneys fees provided by or to the United States,
any payment made to or by the federal government,
the projected duration of the agreement, and
any unit of government that is identified by the terms of the agreement.
In general, the bill applies to settlement agreements that
require at least $10 million in payments by a settling party;
involve the appointment of a special master or monitor;
involve a party that is a state, county, or local government; or
meet other criteria as determined by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
The bill excludes several types of settlement agreements from the database, including agreements related to a federal employee personnel action, a non-prosecution agreement or plea bargain, or the Internal Revenue Code.
To extent practicable, the bill also applies retroactively to covered settlement agreements that were entered into on or after January 1, 2015, and remain in effect on or after the date of enactment.
The OMB must issue guidance to implement the bill.

environment.reason: Sec. 307 database would make environmental enforcement settlements (such as cleanup consent decrees) publicly searchable, improving visibility into how they are enforced, though it does not itself set cleanup standards.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 307 requires public, searchable online databases with copies of agreements, payments, penalties, and attorney fees, and annual reports to Congress and the public on withheld settlements and the exemptions used.

people_over_profit.reason: Making payments, penalties, and deals with companies public can discourage quiet, company-favorable settlements, though the bill's exclusions and withholding options limit this effect.

local_say.reason: Sec. 307 covers settlements involving state, tribal, or local governments and lets communities see agreements affecting their area, though it does not give them a formal decision role.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide funding or bailouts and does not shift costs to taxpayers or ratepayers.

equality.reason: The disclosure rules apply uniformly to covered settlements and do not create differing treatment of groups.

justice.reason: Public visibility of federal settlements improves accountability, but the bill creates no judicial review or enforceable right and allows broad withholding, which limits the gain.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose in their own lives.

news.overall: Lean Left and Center coverage both center on the GAO nomination and the contractor directive, but Lean Left pieces frame them more as threats to oversight and as Democratic concerns, while Center pieces give more space to the nominee's own pledges and to the procedural stakes for congressional appropriations power. The Lean Right item is a single headline with no description, so its framing is only tentatively characterized as a general question about oversight effectiveness. None of the headlines mention the Settlement Agreement Information Database Act itself, so the coverage provided does not show how outlets treat the bill directly.

label: H.R. 804
title: Rural Small Business Resilience Act
short_title: Rural Small Business Resilience Act
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to make sure people in disaster-declared rural areas have full access to its disaster assistance, including through targeted outreach and marketing, within one year.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to do a better job reaching rural communities after a disaster. Within one year of the bill becoming law, the SBA Administrator must make sure the head of the SBA's Office of Disaster Recovery and Resilience takes whatever steps are needed so people in rural areas with an official disaster declaration have "full access" to SBA disaster assistance. The bill names one example of such a step: targeted outreach and marketing materials aimed at those people. It uses the existing Small Business Act definition of "rural area" and the existing disaster declaration process in section 7(b) of that Act. The bill also makes a small clean-up change: it renumbers a duplicate paragraph (16) in the Small Business Act as paragraph (17). The bill does not create a new loan program, change eligibility rules, or add money. It also does not spell out what "full access" means or how success would be measured. The text does not give a cost estimate. Any costs would probably come from the SBA's existing budget unless Congress provides more.

label: H.R. 818
title: SPUR Act
short_title: SPUR Act (Small Business Procurement and Utilization Reform Act of 2025)
one: Requires the federal small business contracting scorecard to report how many small businesses, including veteran-, HUBZone-, disadvantaged-, and women-owned ones, win their first federal prime contract each year.
summary: Federal agencies get an annual "scorecard" that grades how well they meet goals for giving contracts to small businesses. This bill adds one more item to that scorecard: the number of "new small business entrants." These are small businesses that win a federal prime contract (a contract made directly with the government, not as a subcontractor) for the first time. The count would be broken out for service-disabled veteran-owned businesses, businesses in HUBZones (federally designated areas with low income or high unemployment), businesses owned by socially and economically disadvantaged people, and women-owned businesses. The count would be reported by industry code, with a comparison to the prior year when that data exists. The bill also adds definitions of "new small business entrant" and "scorecard," and it makes a small technical fix to a cross-reference. It does not create new contracting set-asides, programs, or goals. It does not authorize any new spending. Agencies would need to track and publish more data. The possible result is better public visibility into whether federal contracting is reaching new and underrepresented small firms. The bill passed the House and is now in the Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee.

label: H.R. 825
title: Assisting Small Businesses Not Fraudsters Act
short_title: Assisting Small Businesses Not Fraudsters Act
one: Bars people finally convicted of financial crimes or false statements involving certain COVID-19 relief loans and grants, and businesses connected to them, from getting most Small Business Administration (SBA) financial help.
summary: This bill adds a new rule to the Small Business Act. If a person connected to a small business is finally convicted of a crime involving financial misconduct or a false statement tied to certain COVID-19 relief programs, that person can no longer get financial help from the SBA. The business they are connected to also loses eligibility. The covered programs are the Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) loans, COVID-19 disaster loans (the Economic Injury Disaster Loans), the Restaurant Revitalization Fund, and the Shuttered Venue Operators Grants. "Connected" is defined broadly: officers, directors, owners of more than 20% of the business, key employees, entities at least 20% owned or controlled by those people, and others who control or are controlled by the business. A "final" conviction means the appeal period has run out or all appeals are finished, so people still appealing are not affected. The ban does not block regular disaster loans under section 7(b), so disaster victims can still get that help. It also does not apply to government contracts or agreements signed before the bill becomes law. The bill does not say how long the ban lasts, which appears to make it open-ended. label: H.R. 828
title: SERV Act
short_title: SERV Act (Successful Entrepreneurship for Reservists and Veterans Act)
one: The bill requires the Small Business Administration to report yearly on its veterans task force and outreach, and the GAO to study veteran and Reservist small businesses' access to credit, with no new money authorized.
summary: This bill asks for two reports and does nothing else. First, each year when the Small Business Administration (SBA) sends its budget request to Congress, it would also have to send a report. The report must cover who has been appointed to the SBA's veterans interagency task force (a group of federal agencies that coordinates help for veteran-owned businesses) and what the task force has done. It must also lay out a plan to promote and reach out about veteran programs, such as Veteran Business Outreach Centers, Boots to Business, and several training programs for service-disabled veterans, women veterans, and procurement. Second, within one year of the bill becoming law, the Government Accountability Office (GAO, Congress's watchdog agency) must report to the House and Senate veterans' and small business committees on how easily small businesses owned by veterans, service-disabled veterans, Reservists, and their spouses (or spouses of active-duty members) can get credit. The study would look at where they get loans, default rates compared with other small businesses, available federal lending programs, unmet credit needs, obstacles, how deployments affect credit history, and how aware owners are of federal help. The bill says no additional money is authorized to carry it out, so agencies would have to pay for the reports from existing funds. The bill does not create new loans, benefits, or regulations.

The yearly report must also outline a plan for outreach and promotion of veteran programs, including Veteran Business Outreach Centers, Boots to Business, Boots to Business Reboot, the Service-Disabled Entrepreneurship Development Training Program, Veteran Institute for Procurement, Women Veteran Entrepreneurship Training Program, and Veteran Women Igniting the Spirit of Entrepreneurship.

Requires the GAO to report within one year of enactment to the House and Senate veterans' affairs and small business committees on access to credit for small businesses owned and controlled by veterans, service-disabled veterans, Reservists, and their spouses.

The GAO report must, as far as practical, analyze credit sources, default rates by source compared to small businesses generally, federal lending programs, unfilled credit gaps, obstacles, the effect of deployment on credit history, and awareness of federal programs.
Defines 'covered individual' (veteran, service-disabled veteran, Reservist, or spouse of those or of an Armed Forces member) and borrows other definitions from the Small Business Act.
States that no additional funds are authorized to be appropriated to carry out the Act.
who: Veterans, service-disabled veterans, Reservists, and their spouses who own or want to start small businesses
Small Business Administration staff who must prepare the annual report
Government Accountability Office, which must do the study
Congressional veterans' affairs and small business committees that receive the reports
Lenders serving small businesses, whose default data may be analyzed

benefits: More oversight and public information on how SBA veteran programs are run and promoted.
Could identify gaps in credit for veteran and military-family business owners and lead to better-targeted help.
Could raise awareness of existing programs among veterans.
Looks at how deployment affects credit history, which could inform fairer treatment of service members.
concerns: Reports alone do not create new help; benefits depend on Congress acting on the findings.

Adds an annual reporting duty for the SBA.
imp.cost: No new funds are authorized. The reports would be paid for out of existing SBA and GAO budgets. No cost estimate was provided in the material.
unknowns: What the GAO will find about credit gaps and default rates.
Whether Congress will act on the findings with new programs.
How much staff time the reports will take.
Whether GAO can get complete data, since the bill says 'to the extent practicable'.

label: H.R. 832
title: Small Business Advocacy Improvements Act of 2025
short_title: Small Business Advocacy Improvements Act of 2025
one: Adds international economic research and representation before foreign governments to the duties of the SBA's Office of Advocacy, and fixes two typos.
summary:
The Small Business Administration (SBA) has an independent office called the Office of Advocacy. It speaks up for small businesses inside the federal government, studies how rules affect them, and does research on their role in the economy. This bill widens that job to cover the global economy.

First, the office's research duty would include the role of small businesses in the "international economy," not only the U.S. economy. Second, the office would be told to represent small businesses' views and interests before foreign governments and international groups. The goal is to feed into rules and trade efforts that could affect small businesses.

The bill also fixes two typos in the existing law. "Complete" becomes "compete," and "serviced-disabled" becomes "service-disabled."

The bill gives no new money, no new regulatory powers, and no new requirements on private businesses. It does not say how the office would pay for the added international work, so it would likely come out of the office's existing budget. It does not say how the office would coordinate with other agencies that already handle trade, such as the U.S. Trade Representative. The bill passed the House and is now in the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.
does: Amends the Office of Advocacy's primary functions so its examination of small businesses' role in the economy also covers the international economy.

Adds a new duty: represent the views and interests of small businesses before foreign governments and international entities, to contribute to regulatory and trade initiatives that may affect small businesses.
Corrects a typo in paragraph (9), changing 'complete' to 'compete'.
Corrects a typo in paragraph (12), changing 'serviced-disabled' to 'service-disabled'.
Does not provide new funding, new enforcement powers, or new requirements for private companies.

Adds no new cost or burden on private businesses.

The office could be stretched thin if it gets no added resources.
The bill has no requirement for public reporting or consultation on its international advocacy.
Which small businesses' views get represented, and how those views are chosen, is not specified.
imp.cost: No funding is provided or authorized in the text. No cost estimate was given in the material I saw. Any added cost would likely come from the office's existing budget.
unknowns: How the office would carry out representation before foreign governments and international bodies.
Whether it would need more staff or money.

Whether the Senate will take up the bill.

label: H.R. 9640
title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends the USGS Earth Mapping Resources Initiative through 2031 with $84 million, adds water-mapping and modern sensing data, and requires contractors to disclose ownership while favoring U.S.-owned firms.
summary: This bill renews the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (Earth MRI), a U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) program that maps underground geology to find where critical minerals like lithium and titanium may be located. The program's current funding runs through fiscal year 2026. The bill adds $84 million for fiscal years 2027 through 2031. It also changes how the program works. The mapping can now use newer technology, such as airborne gravity measurements, advanced chemical analysis, and real-time data collection, and it can also help study geothermal and geologic hydrogen resources, in addition to critical minerals. The program must also pull in data from the USGS 3D Hydrography Program, which maps the nation's water features like rivers and streams. Finally, the bill sets new rules for contracts. Any company that wants a USGS contract under this program must disclose who owns the main contractor and each subcontractor. USGS must also give preference, where practicable, to U.S.-owned and U.S.-controlled companies, while still considering specialized expertise. The bill does not itself approve any mining or drilling, and it does not change environmental review rules. It is a mapping and data program, so its effects depend on how the maps are later used by others.
does: Authorizes $84,000,000 for fiscal years 2027 through 2031 for the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, which currently covers 2022 through 2026.

Allows the program's mapping to include data from modern sensing technologies: airborne gravity gradiometry, digital geochemistry, real-time or near real-time data systems, and data-driven analytical methods.
Expands the resources studied after geophysical mapping to critical minerals, geothermal, geologic hydrogen, and other subsurface resource systems.
Adds the USGS 3D Hydrography Program (water resource mapping) to the data sources the initiative must integrate.
Requires USGS, to the extent practicable, to prefer U.S.-owned and U.S.-controlled entities for contracts, while still weighing specialized expertise essential to the program.
Requires any entity seeking a contract under the initiative to disclose ownership of the primary contractor and each subcontractor expected to do part of the work.

Mining, geothermal, and energy companies that use public geologic data

Taxpayers, who fund the $84 million

Integrating water-resource mapping could improve understanding of how mineral areas relate to water supplies.
Public geologic data can help science, hazard assessment, and planning.
Preference for domestic firms could keep sensitive data and contract dollars in the U.S.
Geothermal and hydrogen mapping could support alternative energy sources.
concerns: Better mineral maps could speed up mining, which can affect water, air, land, and local communities.
The bill has no requirement for community or Tribal input.
The U.S.-owned preference could reduce competition or raise costs, though it allows for expertise.
Disclosure goes to USGS; the bill does not say it must be made public.
Spends $84 million in federal money, which would benefit industries that use the data.

unknowns: Whether disclosed ownership information would be public.
How 'to the extent practicable' will be applied in contract decisions.
How much of the money will go to mineral mapping versus water, geothermal, or hydrogen work.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reauthorize the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, a USGS program that integrates and modernizes mapping of U.S. natural resources with a focus on critical minerals such as lithium and titanium, through fiscal year 2031. According to the CRS summary, it also expands the program's data integration to include USGS 3D Hydrography Program data, allows newer sensing technologies, and sets rules for contractor ownership disclosure and domestic preference in USGS contracts.

Better mineral maps could make it easier and faster to find sites for mining. Mining can affect water, air, land, and nearby communities. A constituent could ask the member to make sure local and Tribal voices are heard before these maps lead to projects.
The bill has no requirement for community or Tribal input in the program. A constituent could ask whether the member would support adding public consultation steps.

The bill requires contractors to disclose ownership, but it does not say this information must be made public. A constituent could ask the member to require public disclosure so voters can see who is doing government-funded work.

The preference for U.S.-owned contractors could reduce competition or raise costs, although the bill still allows weight to be given to specialized expertise. A constituent could ask how the USGS will balance these goals.
support: The bill renews a USGS mapping program through fiscal year 2031, which keeps the government's work on underground geology and critical minerals like lithium and titanium going. A constituent could say this supports the nation's supply of materials used in many products.

Adding USGS 3D Hydrography data could help show how mineral areas relate to rivers, streams, and water supplies. A constituent could say this helps planners and scientists understand water resources better.
Public geologic data can help with science, natural hazard assessment, and land-use planning. A constituent could say this kind of open data benefits many people beyond mining companies.

The ownership disclosure rule and the preference for U.S.-owned, U.S.-controlled contractors could help keep sensitive government data and contract dollars in the U.S. A constituent could say this adds transparency about who is doing federal work.
The bill allows newer technologies and expands mapping to geothermal and geologic hydrogen resources. A constituent could say this could support cleaner energy options alongside critical minerals.

cost_flag: $84 million authorized for fiscal years 2027–2031 (about $16.8 million per year if spread evenly). Authorization is not actual spending; Congress must still appropriate the money.
crs:
Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
This bill reauthorizes through FY2031 the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, a U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) program charged with integrating and modernizing the mapping of U.S. natural resources, with a focus on critical mineral resources such as lithium and titanium. The bill also expands the initiative’s data integration functions and requires the USGS to give preference to U.S. contractors under the initiative.
Specifically, the bill requires entities contracting with the USGS pursuant to the initiative to disclose the ownership of the primary contractor and each subcontractor carrying out a part of the contract. To the extent practicable, the USGS must give preference to entities owned and controlled in the United States when entering contracts under the initiative, while giving appropriate consideration to specialized expertise essential to the objectives of the initiative.
Further, under current law, the initiative is required to provide certain types of integrated mapping, including geologic, geophysical, and topographical mapping. Under the bill, the initiative must include data from the USGS 3D Hydrography Program, which maps U.S. water resources. The bill also explicitly allows the initiative’s integrated mapping to include data from modern sensing technologies, including real-time data acquisition systems and data-driven analytical methods.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks; it authorizes program funding for USGS mapping.

equality.reason: The U.S.-owned preference applies only 'to the extent practicable' and is weighed against specialized expertise, so it creates a mild distinction by ownership nationality but the effect on equal access is unclear.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal processes, due process, or remedies; the ownership disclosure is a modest accountability step for contractors but its scope is limited.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose about their own lives.

label: H.R. 1343
title: Federal Broadband Deployment Tracking Act
short_title: Federal Broadband Deployment Tracking Act
one: Requires the federal telecom agency (NTIA) to give Congress, within 180 days, a plan for tracking applications to put communications equipment on certain federal lands and for letting applicants see their application status.
summary: This bill asks one federal official, the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information (who leads the NTIA, the National Telecommunications and Information Administration), to write a plan and send it to Congress. The plan must be sent within 180 days after the bill becomes law. It would cover how the agency would track Form 299 applications. Form 299 is the standard form companies use to ask permission to build or change communications equipment, such as cell towers or broadband lines, on federal land. That land includes land managed by the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Reclamation, and National Forest System land. The permission can be an easement, right-of-way, lease, or license from the Interior or Agriculture Department. The plan must explain how applications would be tracked from acceptance through processing to final decision. It must also explain how applicants would get more openness about where their application stands, how to put the plan in place as fast as possible, and any barriers the agency sees. The bill does not change who gets permits, does not change environmental or review rules, and does not give money. It only requires a planning report. The bill passed the House and is now in a Senate committee. No cost estimate was provided.
does: Requires the NTIA head (Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information) to submit a plan to Congress within 180 days of enactment.
The plan must describe how the agency would track the acceptance, processing, and disposal (final decision) of each Form 299 for communications use authorizations.
The plan must describe how applicants would get more transparency about the status of their Form 299.
The plan must describe how to carry it out as quickly as possible and identify any barriers to implementation.

Covers authorizations (easements, rights-of-way, leases, licenses) from the Interior or Agriculture Secretaries for communications facilities on BLM, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service, Bureau of Reclamation, and National Forest System land.
The plan goes to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
Does not itself create a tracking system, change permit standards, or alter environmental review.
who: Communications and broadband companies applying for permits on federal land
NTIA and the Interior and Agriculture departments

Congressional committees overseeing telecom
People and communities near federal lands, including land-management stakeholders

Could help identify delays that slow broadband in rural areas.
Low cost, because it only requires a plan.
Does not weaken any review or protection rules.
concerns: Transparency is described for applicants, not clearly for the public or affected communities.
The stated goal of 'expeditious' implementation could lead to pressure to speed reviews on public lands later.
The plan is not binding, so it may produce little change.
Doesn't say how local communities or tribes would have a say in these permits.
imp.cost: No funding is provided and no cost estimate was given. Costs would come from NTIA staff time to prepare the plan. Any later tracking system could cost more, which is not addressed.
unknowns: Whether the plan would be made public.
How NTIA, which doesn't issue these permits, would get data from Interior and Agriculture.
Whether Congress would later fund or require a tracking system.
Whether tracking would lead to faster approvals and how that would affect environmental review.

The plan would cover how applications are tracked from acceptance to final decision, how applicants can see the status of their applications, how to carry out the plan as quickly as possible, and what barriers exist. The bill does not create a tracking system itself, change permit standards, or alter environmental review.

oppose: The bill is a planning requirement only, and the plan it calls for is not binding, so it may not lead to any real change in how permits are handled.
The bill asks for 'expeditious' implementation of permit tracking, and a faster process could create pressure to shorten reviews on public lands later.

The bill's transparency provisions focus on applicants, not on the general public or on communities affected by towers or lines built on federal land, and it does not describe how local communities or tribes would have a say.
support: The bill would give Congress a clearer picture of where Form 299 applications stand and where delays happen, which could help lawmakers act on rural broadband slowdowns.
The bill is low cost because it only requires a plan, not new spending or a new system.
The bill does not change permit standards, environmental reviews, or protections for public lands, so existing safeguards stay in place.

justice.reason: The plan must describe how applications would be tracked from acceptance to final decision and how applicants can see status, which modestly increases accountability in the permit process.

news.overall: Coverage across both groups describes the same legislation as an energy permitting bill, not a broadband bill. label: H.R. 2389
title: Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act
short_title: Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act
one: H.R. 2389 would move about 72 acres of Washington land (Allotment 1157) from the U.S. Forest Service to the Interior Department, place it in trust for the Quinault Indian Nation as part of its reservation, bar gaming on it, and limit the federal government's cleanup duties for hazardous substances on it.
summary: H.R. 2389, the Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act, is a short bill about one parcel of land in Washington State. It would take roughly 72 acres, shown on a map dated February 2, 2024 as "Allotment 1157," away from the U.S. Forest Service and hand it to the Department of the Interior. The Interior Department would then hold the land in trust (a legal arrangement where the federal government holds title for the benefit of a tribe) for the Quinault Indian Nation. Once in trust, the land would become part of the Quinault Indian Reservation and would be managed under the rules that apply to other tribal trust land. The bill says the transfer is subject to "valid existing rights," meaning rights other people already hold in the land would remain in place. The land could not be used for gaming (casino-style gambling) under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act. The bill also says nothing in it changes the tribe's treaty rights under the 1855-1856 Treaty of Olympia. On contamination, the Interior Department must follow the federal disclosure rules for hazardous substances under Section 120(h) of the Superfund law (CERCLA) before taking the land into trust. However, it would not be required to clean up or reduce any hazardous substances, pollutants, or contaminants found there. The bill does not state a cost or funding source. The Senate Committee on Indian Affairs held a hearing on June 3, 2026. The bill text I reviewed is complete and not truncated.
does: Transfers about 72 acres (Allotment 1157 on a map dated Feb. 2, 2024) from the U.S. Forest Service to the Department of the Interior, subject to valid existing rights.
Requires Interior to take the land into trust for the benefit of the Quinault Indian Nation.
Makes the land part of the Quinault Indian Reservation and subject to the laws generally applied to tribal trust property.
Prohibits gaming on the land under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act.
States that nothing in the Act affects treaty rights under the 1855-1856 Treaty of Olympia.

Requires Interior, before taking the land into trust, to meet Superfund (CERCLA Section 120(h)) disclosure rules for hazardous substances, but does not require Interior to clean up or reduce those substances.
who: Quinault Indian Nation, which would gain about 72 acres of trust land within its reservation.
U.S. Forest Service, which would lose management of the parcel.
Department of the Interior, which would take on trust management and disclosure duties.
Neighbors or other holders of rights in the land, whose existing rights are preserved, and anyone who might later be affected by contamination on the parcel.

benefits: Gives the Quinault Indian Nation trust land within its reservation, which may support tribal self-government and land management.
Keeps the tribe's Treaty of Olympia rights unchanged.
Bars casino-style gaming on the parcel, which the bill's text does not otherwise address.
concerns: The bill does not require cleanup of hazardous substances, pollutants, or contaminants, so any contamination on the parcel could remain.
Moving the land out of Forest Service management may reduce federal environmental oversight of the parcel, though the bill does not say so directly.
imp.cost: The bill does not state a cost or funding source. Its text does not appropriate money.
unknowns: What hazardous substances are present on the parcel and how serious they are.
Whether the Forest Service has already studied the land or identified any cleanup needs.
What 'valid existing rights' apply to the parcel, such as easements or leases held by others.
How much the transfer and trust process would cost the federal government.
How the land will be used after it is placed in trust.

stage.last_action: Committee on Indian Affairs. Hearings held.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to transfer about 72 acres of land in Washington State (Allotment 1157) from the U.S. Forest Service to the Department of the Interior, which would hold the land in trust for the Quinault Indian Nation and make it part of the Quinault Indian Reservation. The bill's summary indicates the transfer is subject to valid existing rights and does not change the tribe's rights under the 1855-1856 Treaty of Olympia.

oppose: The bill does not require the Interior Department to clean up hazardous substances, pollutants, or contaminants on the parcel. It only requires the federal disclosure rules to be met, so any contamination could remain in place.

Moving the land out of Forest Service management could reduce federal environmental oversight of the parcel. The bill does not discuss this directly, so a constituent could ask how the land would be monitored after the transfer.
The bill does not state a cost or a funding source. A constituent could ask Congress to clarify what the transfer would cost and who would pay for any future land management or cleanup needs.

The bill states that nothing in it changes the tribe's treaty rights under the 1855-1856 Treaty of Olympia, so the transfer is described as leaving those rights intact.

crs:
Quinault Indian Nation Land Transfer Act
This bill administratively transfers approximately 72 acres of specified lands in Washington from the U.S. Forest Service to the Department of the Interior. Interior must take this land into trust for the benefit of the Quinault Indian Nation. Land taken into trust shall be part of the tribe's reservation.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires federal hazardous-substance disclosure under CERCLA Section 120(h) before the land transfer, which gives the public truthful information about contamination on the parcel.

label: H.R. 2458
title: Secure Space Act of 2025
short_title: Secure Space Act of 2025
one: Bars the FCC from granting satellite licenses, U.S. market access, or ground-station approvals to companies (or their affiliates) that make or provide equipment or services on the FCC's national-security "Covered List."
summary:
This bill would change a 2019 law about trusted communications networks. It would stop the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from approving certain satellite-related applications if the company that would hold or control the approval makes or provides equipment or services on the FCC's "Covered List." That list names products and services judged to pose an unacceptable national security risk. Huawei and ZTE are examples of providers on it. The ban also covers any affiliate of such a company. An affiliate is a company that owns, is owned by, or is under common control with another company.

The ban applies to three kinds of approvals. The first is licenses for satellite systems, both high-orbit (geostationary) and low-orbit (nongeostationary). The second is petitions to let foreign-licensed satellites serve the U.S. market. The third is authorizations for ground stations, which are the earth-based stations that talk to satellites. That includes individually licensed stations, blanket-licensed stations, and gateway stations that route satellite traffic.

The rule would apply to approvals granted on or after the date the bill becomes law. The text does not mention existing licenses. The FCC would have one year to write rules to carry this out. The bill does not provide new money. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee.
does: Adds a new Section 10 to the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 and renumbers the old Sections 10 and 11 as 11 and 12.
Bars the FCC from granting licenses for geostationary or nongeostationary satellite systems to an entity that produces or provides covered communications equipment or services, or to its affiliate.

Bars the FCC from granting petitions for a declaratory ruling that would give such an entity or affiliate access to the U.S. market for its satellite system (market access for foreign-licensed satellites).
Bars the FCC from authorizing individually licensed or blanket-licensed earth stations, including gateway stations, if they would be held or controlled by such an entity or affiliate.
Defines 'blanket-licensed earth station,' 'individually licensed earth station,' and 'gateway station.' It uses the Communications Act definition of 'affiliate.'
Applies only to licenses, petitions, or authorizations granted on or after the date the bill becomes law. The text does not address existing licenses.
Requires the FCC to issue implementing rules within one year of enactment.
who: Satellite operators and satellite internet companies seeking FCC licenses or U.S. market access
Companies and affiliates that produce or provide equipment or services on the FCC Covered List, such as Huawei and ZTE
Ground station and gateway operators
The Federal Communications Commission, which must write rules within a year
U.S. consumers and government users of satellite communications
National security agencies concerned about communications supply chains

benefits: May lower the risk of spying or sabotage through satellite networks built or run by companies on the Covered List.
Gives a clear statutory rule rather than leaving the decision to the FCC's discretion.
Closes a gap by covering satellites, market access, and ground stations, not just terrestrial networks.
Applies to affiliates, so the ban is harder to dodge through related companies.
concerns: The text does not say what happens to licenses already granted, so existing risks may remain.
The broad affiliate language could sweep in companies with only loose ties to a covered entity.
The bill sets no appeal or waiver process. It leaves those details to FCC rules.
Fewer eligible providers could reduce competition and raise prices or limit service in some places.
imp.cost: The bill provides no funding and the text gives no cost estimate. The FCC would use existing resources to write rules within a year.
unknowns: How many pending or future applicants would be affected.
Whether the FCC will review existing licenses held by covered entities.
How the FCC will define 'produces or provides' and handle affiliate disputes.
The effect on satellite service costs and competition.
How the Senate committee will act on it.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to protect U.S. communications networks from national security risks. It would stop the FCC from granting satellite licenses, market access for foreign-licensed satellites, and earth station authorizations to entities (and their affiliates) that produce or provide equipment or services on the FCC's Covered List, such as Huawei and ZTE. It amends the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 to add this rule.

oppose: The bill does not say what happens to licenses already granted, so it may not address risks that exist today while adding new limits on future approvals.
The affiliate language uses the Communications Act definition, which could reach companies with only loose ties to a covered company, even if they had no role in the risky equipment or services.
Fewer eligible providers could reduce competition in satellite service, which may raise prices or limit service in some areas. The bill sets no waiver or appeal process to address unusual cases.
support: The bill would give a clear rule in law that bars approvals for companies on the FCC's Covered List, rather than leaving the decision only to agency discretion.
Covering satellite licenses, market access, and ground stations closes a gap, since the earlier law focused on terrestrial networks and this extends the protection to space-based communications.
Applying the ban to affiliates makes it harder for covered companies to avoid the rule through related companies, which may lower the risk of spying or sabotage through satellite networks.

crs:
Secure Space Act of 2025
This bill prohibits the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from granting satellite licenses or earth station authorizations, including U.S. market access for foreign-licensed satellites, to specified foreign entities of concern and their affiliates. (Earth stations, also commonly known as ground stations, are earth-based radio stations that communicate with satellites. A grant of U.S. market access permits one or more foreign-licensed satellites to communicate with one or more U.S.-licensed earth stations.)
Specifically, the FCC may not grant a satellite license, an earth station authorization, or market access to any entity, or an affiliate thereof, that produces or provides communications equipment or services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. (The FCC maintains a list of such equipment and services, known as the Covered List. Providers of such equipment and services include, for example, Huawei Technologies Company and ZTE Corporation.)

local_say.reason: Sec. 10 (new) bars the FCC from granting satellite licenses, market access petitions, and earth station authorizations to covered entities and affiliates, removing FCC discretion in these approvals, and the summary notes no appeal or waiver process is provided, so state and local input on those decisions is not expanded.

equality.reason: Sec. 10 (new) applies a licensing bar to entities based on their affiliation with listed foreign providers, so companies with loose affiliate ties face different treatment from other applicants.

justice.reason: The bill sets no appeal or waiver process and leaves existing licenses unaddressed, and the affiliate definition could reach companies with only loose ties, which gives affected firms limited remedy for a broad categorical bar.

news.overall: Across the groups, the headlines mostly cover adjacent regulatory and export-control stories rather than the Secure Space Act itself, so the bill's framing cannot be directly assessed. The Lean Left and Center groups both report the SpaceX satellite approval and the Megaspeed export matter, with the Lean Left leaning toward skepticism and internal disputes and the Center giving more neutral regulatory descriptions. The Lean Right has only one article, so its framing is based on very limited evidence.

label: H.R. 2591
title: Mental Health in Aviation Act of 2025
short_title: Mental Health in Aviation Act of 2025
one: Directs the FAA to change its rules so pilots and air traffic controllers can seek and disclose mental health care with less fear of losing their medical clearance, and sets aside money to staff and promote that effort.
summary: This bill tells the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to change its rules so pilots and air traffic controllers are more willing to get help for mental health problems and to be honest about them. Today, many aviation workers fear that admitting to a mental health issue could end their career, so they may stay quiet. Within two years, the FAA must update its medical rules (including 14 CFR part 67) to encourage people to seek help and disclose conditions. It must also carry out, as far as practical, the recommendations of two expert groups: a mental health task group created in the 2024 FAA law and an FAA rulemaking committee that reported in April 2024. If the FAA declines any recommendation, it must explain why to Congress. Every year, the FAA must review its "special issuance" process, which lets someone with a medical condition fly with a restricted certificate. The review must look at approving more mental health medications, training medical examiners, giving examiners more authority, and improving the process. The bill sets aside $13.74 million a year for fiscal years 2026–2028 to hire and train more aviation medical examiners, including psychiatrists, and to clear a backlog of cases. It also sets aside $1.5 million a year for three years for a campaign to reduce stigma and build trust. The money comes from the FAA's existing funds, not a new tax. Labor unions and medical examiners must be consulted.
does: Within 2 years of enactment, requires the FAA to update its regulations (including 14 CFR part 67) to encourage people in aviation to seek help for mental health conditions or symptoms and to disclose them.

Expands the 2024 FAA law's mental health task group: it must review National Transportation Safety Board recommendations on aviation workforce mental health and describe the clinical studies and protocols used by licensed professionals. It must also consult air traffic controller unions, pilot union groups, aviation medical examiners, and other stakeholders.
Within 180 days after the task group's report, requires the FAA to act on its mental health recommendations. If it rejects any, it must give Congress a justification.

Requires the FAA to implement, to the greatest extent practicable and within 2 years, the recommendations the Mental Health and Aviation Medical Clearances Aviation Rulemaking Committee submitted on April 1, 2024. It must consult stakeholders and justify to Congress any recommendation it does not adopt.

Requires an annual review and update, as appropriate, of mental health special issuance rules and policies for pilots and controllers. The review must reclassify and approve more medications that can safely be prescribed to airmen, improve examiner mental health training, delegate more authority to examiners if the FAA finds it appropriate, and improve the special issuance process.

Sets aside $13.74 million per year for fiscal years 2026–2028 from existing FAA operations funds to recruit and train more aviation medical examiners (including psychiatrists), expand oversight, and clear the backlog of special issuance requests at the Office of Aerospace Medicine.

Sets aside $1.5 million per year for fiscal years 2026–2028 for a public information campaign to destigmatize mental health care in aviation, raise awareness of support services, and build trust. The FAA must report to Congress within 1 year after creating the campaign.
Defines key terms, including the congressional committees that receive reports and 'special issuance.'
who: Commercial and private pilots
FAA air traffic controllers
Aviation medical examiners and psychiatrists
The FAA and its Office of Aerospace Medicine
Pilot and controller unions
Airlines and the flying public
Pharmaceutical and mental health providers serving aviation workers

benefits: Could lead more pilots and controllers to seek treatment early, improving their health and aviation safety.
Could reduce the stigma and career fear around mental health care.
Could speed up the backlog of special issuance cases, so workers wait less to return to duty.
Requires consultation with unions and medical examiners and written justification to Congress when recommendations are rejected.
Uses existing FAA funds, with a modest set-aside of about $15.24 million per year.
concerns: Approving more medications and delegating authority to examiners could raise safety questions if not carefully implemented.
The 'to the greatest extent practicable' wording and the 'if appropriate' language leave the FAA wide discretion, so results could be limited.
The set-asides come from existing FAA funds, which could reduce money for other FAA activities.
Controllers' and pilots' medical privacy and how disclosures are used are not addressed in detail.
imp.cost: $13.74 million per year for fiscal years 2026–2028 for aviation medical examiners and backlog reduction, plus $1.5 million per year for the same years for a public information campaign. That is about $45.7 million total over three years. It is taken from amounts already made available to the FAA under 49 U.S.C. 106(k)(1), not a new tax or fee.
unknowns: What specific regulation changes the FAA would make and whether they would be adopted in time.
Which medications would be approved and how safety would be assessed.
What the task group's final recommendations will say, since the bill requires action on them.
Whether other FAA programs would lose funding because of the set-asides.
Whether the Senate Commerce Committee will take up the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to change FAA rules so pilots and air traffic controllers are more willing to seek mental health care and to disclose mental health conditions without fearing they will lose their careers. It aims to carry out recommendations from an FAA task group and a rulemaking committee, review how the FAA handles mental health special issuance cases, add medical examiners, reduce the backlog of cases, and run a public campaign to reduce stigma.

oppose: Approving more mental health medications and giving aviation medical examiners more authority could raise safety questions if the changes are not carefully tested and monitored.

The bill uses broad wording such as 'to the greatest extent practicable' and 'as appropriate,' which gives the FAA wide discretion. Some may worry that rules meant to protect safety could be weakened in practice.

The $15.24 million per year set aside would come from existing FAA funds, which could reduce money for other FAA programs. The bill does not say how the new medical rules would protect worker privacy or how disclosed information would be used.
support: Many pilots and controllers fear that admitting a mental health problem could end their careers, so they may hide problems. The bill aims to make workers more willing to get help early, which could improve safety.
The bill requires the FAA to act on recommendations from its expert task group and rulemaking committee, and to explain to Congress any recommendation it rejects. This adds accountability.

The bill would add money to hire and train more aviation medical examiners, including psychiatrists, and to reduce the backlog of special issuance cases. This could shorten the wait for workers to return to duty, and it uses existing FAA funds rather than a new tax.

cost_flag: $13.74 million per year for fiscal years 2026–2028 for aviation medical examiners and backlog reduction, plus $1.5 million per year for the same years for a public information campaign. That is about $45.7 million total over three years. It is taken from amounts already made available to the FAA under 49 U.S.C. 106(k)(1), not a new tax or fee.
crs:
Mental Health in Aviation Act of 2025
This bill requires the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to review and update its regulations and policies on mental health for pilots and air traffic controllers.
The FAA must update regulations and take any other actions necessary to implement the recommendations of (1) the Aviation Workforce Mental Health Task Group, and (2) the Mental Health and Aviation Medical Clearances Aviation Rulemaking Committee (the ARC).
The FAA must also annually review and update, as appropriate, the applicable regulations and policies on mental health-related special issuance for pilots and air traffic controllers. As background, an Authorization for Special Issuance of a Medical Certificate is a discretionary document from the FAA which allows an airman with a disqualifying medical condition to fly under a restricted medical certificate.
Among other things, the review and update must
reclassify and approve additional medications that may be safely prescribed to airmen to treat mental health conditions,
delegate additional authority to aviation medical examiners (AMEs) consistent with the ARC recommendations, and
improve the special issuance process for pilots and air traffic controllers.
 The bill authorizes the FAA to take actions to recruit and train additional AMEs.
The bill also authorizes an FAA public information campaign or education efforts to (1) destigmatize individuals in (or interested in joining) the aviation industry who seek mental health care, (2) broaden awareness of available supportive services, and (3) establish trust with pilots and air traffic controllers.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on the task group and ARC requires FAA to justify to Congress any rejected recommendation, and the bill requires consultation with unions and medical examiners, which makes FAA decisions more open to review; the stigma campaign aims to reduce needless fear around disclosure.

equality.reason: Sec. requiring FAA to update rules so aviation workers with mental health conditions can seek help and disclose without career loss, and to expand special issuance for medications, gives affected workers a more equal path back to duty, though the bill does not directly address discrimination against any group.

justice.reason: Sec. requiring annual special issuance review and written justification to Congress for rejected recommendations, plus a backlog-clearing set-aside, makes the certification process more consistent and accountable, though the 'greatest extent practicable' and 'if appropriate' language leaves FAA discretion.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. expanding special issuance and reclassifying more mental health medications would let more airmen with those conditions legally fly and keep their certificates, widening what they may do with their careers.

label: H.R. 3903
title: Chugach Alaska Land Exchange Oil Spill Recovery Act of 2025
short_title: Chugach Alaska Land Exchange Oil Spill Recovery Act of 2025
one: H.R. 3903 would require the federal government to swap about 65,374 acres of federal land in the Chugach region of Alaska for about 231,000 acres of subsurface land (mineral rights under land Chugach Alaska Corporation already owns) that Chugach would offer up, with the stated aim of consolidating federal ownership of land bought with Exxon Valdez oil spill settlement money.
summary:
H.R. 3903 is a bill that would order a land trade between the federal government and Chugach Alaska Corporation, an Alaska Native regional corporation created under the 1971 Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (ANCSA). Chugach is one of the Alaska Native regional corporations that received land and money under that law.

The bill's stated purposes are to authorize, direct, and speed up this land exchange, and to bring the surface and underground ownership of certain federal land and interests acquired under the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Habitat Protection and Acquisition Program into single federal ownership.

The exchange works in two directions. First, Chugach may offer to give the Department of the Interior all of its rights, title, and interest in about 231,000 acres of subsurface estate (the rights to minerals and resources below the ground) on land listed in the bill. These are parcels Chugach already owns, where the federal government or the State of Alaska holds the land's surface through the oil spill program. If Chugach makes this offer within one year of the bill becoming law, Interior must accept it.

Second, Interior must convey to Chugach all federal rights in about 65,374 acres of fee simple land (full ownership) in the Chugach region. These include about 63,414 acres of Forest Service land, such as the Kushtaka Lake, Snow River, Martin River and Hinchinbrook Island parcels, and about 1,960 acres of Bureau of Land Management and National Park Service land, such as the Taan Fjord, Kageet Point, and Thompson Pass parcels. Interior must make these conveyances as soon as practicable. Transfers are subject to existing third-party rights, such as rights-of-way and easements, and to public access easements required by ANCSA.

The bill also says Chugach must leave out of its offer up to 209 acres where a village corporation has kept development rights (other than timber rights) or that has been set aside for shareholder homesites. Land that Interior accepts would be managed as part of the federal unit where it sits. Both sides may fix minor map or acreage errors by mutual agreement, and if a map conflicts with the written acreage, the map controls unless both sides agree otherwise.

The bill does not state a dollar price, appraisal value, or federal payment for either side of the trade. The text and the CRS summary do not say how the swapped acreage was valued.
does: Requires Interior to accept an offer from Chugach Alaska to convey roughly 231,000 acres of subsurface estate (mineral and resource rights) if the offer is made within one year of enactment.
Requires Interior to convey to Chugach all federal rights in roughly 65,374 acres of fee simple land in the Chugach region, as soon as practicable after enactment.

Lists the specific federal Forest Service parcels to be conveyed (about 63,414 acres), including Drier Bay, Kushtaka Lake, Snow River, Hinchinbrook Island, Martin River, Johnson River, and Robinson Mountains parcels.
Lists the specific Bureau of Land Management and National Park Service parcels to be conveyed (about 1,960 acres), including Taan Fjord, Kageet Point, and Thompson Pass parcels.

Lists the non-federal subsurface parcels Chugach may offer, which include land where the United States holds surface conservation easements or where the State of Alaska holds the surface and the United States holds a conservation easement, both acquired through the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Habitat Protection and Acquisition Program.
Requires Chugach to exclude from its offer up to 209 acres where a village corporation keeps development rights (other than timber rights) or that is designated for shareholder homesites.
Makes the conveyances subject to valid existing rights, reservations, rights-of-way, and other third-party encumbrances on the land as of enactment.
Requires public easements to be reserved on the federal land conveyed, as required under Section 17(b) of ANCSA.
Treats land conveyed to Chugach as if it were land conveyed under ANCSA.
Requires that the title to the non-federal land Chugach gives up be in a form the Secretary of the Interior finds acceptable.
Requires acquired land to become part of the surrounding federal unit and be managed under that unit's rules.

Allows Interior and Chugach to correct minor errors in maps, acreage estimates, or land descriptions by mutual agreement, and says a map controls over a conflicting acreage or description unless both agree otherwise.

The State of Alaska and conservation groups connected to the Exxon Valdez Oil Spill Habitat Protection and Acquisition Program, because the bill covers land bought with oil spill settlement money.
Village corporations that hold development rights or shareholder homesite designations within the affected area.

crs:
Chugach Alaska Land Exchange Oil Spill Recovery Act of 2025
This bill authorizes a land exchange between the Chugach Alaska Corporation (also known as Chugach, an Alaska Native regional corporation in southcentral Alaska) and the federal government.
Specifically, if Chugach offers to convey to the Department of the Interior all right, title, and interest of Chugach in and to approximately 231,000 acres of subsurface estate within one year of the bill's enactment, then Interior must accept the offer and convey all right, title, and interest of the federal government in and to approximately 65,374 acres of fee simple land located in the Chugach region. (The Chugach region includes portions of land on the Kenai Peninsula and the coast of Prince William Sound in Alaska.)
The bill directs Chugach to exclude from its conveyance to Interior all right, title, and interest in any land, not to exceed a total of 209 acres, for which a village corporation has retained development rights (other than timber development rights) or that has been designated for a shareholder homesite program.

environment.reason: Sec. 3 conveys about 65,374 acres of federal Forest Service, BLM and NPS land out of public management into private Chugach ownership, and the bill sets no explicit conservation or habitat protections that would carry over, which could reduce protection of ecosystems on those parcels. transparency_kindness.reason: The bill states no dollar price, appraisal or valuation for either side of the trade, and the Chugach Region Land Study Report it references is not in the text, so the public cannot review the basis for the exchange.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 3 requires Interior to accept Chugach's subsurface offer and convey about 65,374 acres of federal land without any stated payment or appraisal, which may favor the corporation's gains over public ownership of those lands and resources.
