label: H.R. 3925
title: Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation Land Exchange Act
short_title: Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation Land Exchange Act
one: H.R. 3925 would swap about 1,460 acres owned by the San Manuel Band of Mission Indians for about 1,475 acres of San Bernardino National Forest land in California, with a cultural-preservation agreement for the Arrowhead landmark site.
summary:
This bill would authorize a land trade between the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation (also called the San Manuel Band of Mission Indians) and the federal government. The tribe is located on the San Manuel Indian Reservation near Highland and San Bernardino, California.

If the tribe offers to give the federal government about 1,460 acres of its land, the U.S. Forest Service must accept that offer. In return, the Forest Service must give the tribe about 1,475 acres of National Forest System land that is currently part of the San Bernardino National Forest. The Forest Service must complete the exchange as soon as practicable, and no later than one year after receiving the tribe's offer. The bill's text says one year; the CRS summary describes a 120-day timeline, so the exact deadline should be checked against the final text.

The Forest Service keeps an easement, or legal right of access, to portions of three Forest Service roads (1N22, 1N24, and 1N25) that cross the land being conveyed. Exact acreage will be set by surveys approved by the Forest Service and the tribe. The tribe pays for the survey of its own land. Minor boundary changes and map corrections are allowed if both sides agree.

As a condition of the trade, the tribe must sign an agreement with the Forest Service within one year of enactment to preserve the historical and cultural integrity of the Arrowhead landmark site, a site in the foothills above San Bernardino. The agreement must be recorded with San Bernardino County and the Forest Service. Land the government receives becomes part of the San Bernardino National Forest. The bill also says the exchange is not subject to a section of the Federal Land Policy Management Act of 1976 that normally governs federal land sales and exchanges.
does: Requires the Forest Service to accept the tribe's offer of about 1,460 acres of tribal land (NF-1 through NF-5 on the maps) if the tribe offers it.

Requires the Forest Service to convey about 1,475 acres of National Forest System land (F-1 and F-2 on the maps) to the tribe in return, as soon as practicable and within one year of receiving the offer.
Keeps a Forest Service easement for access to parts of Forest Service roads 1N22, 1N24, and 1N25 that cross the federal land being transferred.
Requires surveys approved by the Forest Service and the tribe to set the exact acreage and legal descriptions; the tribe pays the cost of the survey for its own land.
Allows minor boundary adjustments and error corrections only by mutual agreement, and says the official map controls if maps and acreage figures conflict.

Requires the tribe, as a condition of the trade, to sign an agreement within one year of enactment to preserve the historical and cultural integrity of the Arrowhead landmark site, and to record that agreement with San Bernardino County and the Forest Service.
Makes land the government receives part of the San Bernardino National Forest, managed under national forest laws.
Exempts this exchange from Section 206 of the Federal Land Policy Management Act of 1976, a general federal land-exchange rule.
Requires the land maps to be kept on file for public inspection at Forest Service offices.
who: The Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation (San Manuel Band of Mission Indians), which gains about 1,475 acres of national forest land and gives up about 1,460 acres.
The U.S. Forest Service and the public who use the San Bernardino National Forest, which would lose about 1,475 acres and gain about 1,460 acres.
San Bernardino County and visitors to the Arrowhead landmark site, which is subject to a cultural-preservation agreement.

benefits: Lets the tribe consolidate and reacquire ancestral land near its reservation.
Requires a formal agreement to protect the Arrowhead landmark site and records it publicly.
Acreage is roughly equal, so the national forest total changes little.
concerns: About 1,475 acres of public national forest would leave federal ownership and public management.

The bill exempts the trade from a federal land-exchange rule (FLPMA Section 206), which could reduce the usual public review or appraisal requirements; the bill text does not spell out what that rule requires.
Forest Service road access is kept only for three named roads, so public access to other parts of the transferred land is not addressed in the text.
imp.cost: The bill does not appropriate money. The tribe pays for the survey of its own land. The bill does not state the land values or whether the trade is value-equal.
unknowns: Whether the lands are of equal value, since the bill does not require an appraisal.
What the Arrowhead preservation standard ('to an extent mutually agreed upon') will require in practice.
What the public-access and recreation impact will be on the 1,475 acres leaving national forest status.
Which deadline controls: the bill text says one year, while the CRS summary says 120 days.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Indian Affairs.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to authorize a land exchange between the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation and the federal government. Under the bill, the tribe would give about 1,460 acres of its land to the Forest Service, and the Forest Service would give the tribe about 1,475 acres of National Forest System land in San Bernardino National Forest. The bill also requires the tribe to sign an agreement to preserve the historical and cultural integrity of the Arrowhead landmark site.

oppose: About 1,475 acres of public national forest land would leave federal ownership and public management under this bill, and the constituent may want to ask how the loss of that public land is weighed against the land received.

The bill exempts this exchange from Section 206 of the Federal Land Policy Management Act of 1976, which is a general federal land-exchange rule. The bill text does not spell out what that rule requires, so a constituent could ask what public review or appraisal steps would be skipped.
The bill keeps Forest Service access only for parts of three named roads (1N22, 1N24, and 1N25). A constituent could ask what public access would be kept or lost on the other transferred land.
support: The bill would let the San Manuel Nation consolidate and reacquire ancestral land near its reservation, which the bill's supporters would see as a benefit to the tribe.
The bill requires a formal, recorded agreement to protect the Arrowhead landmark site, which gives the site a public, enforceable protection that might not otherwise exist.
The acreage exchanged is roughly equal (about 1,460 acres given and 1,475 acres received), so the total size of the national forest changes very little.

crs:
Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation Land Exchange Act
This bill authorizes a land exchange between the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation (also federally recognized as the San Manuel Band of Mission Indians) and the federal government. The tribe is located on the San Manuel Indian Reservation near the cities of Highland and San Bernardino in California.
Specifically, if the tribe offers to convey to the federal government all right, title, and interest of the tribe in and to approximately 1,460 acres of land, then the Forest Service must accept the offer and convey all right, title, and interest of the federal government in and to approximately 1,475 acres of National Forest System land. The Forest Service must accept the offer and convey the land as soon as practicable within 120 days of receiving the offer.
As a condition of the land exchange, within 120 days of the bill's enactment, the tribe must enter into an agreement with the Forest Service under which the tribe agrees to preserve the historical and cultural integrity of the Arrowhead landmark site. The site is located in the foothills of the San Bernardino Mountains directly above San Bernardino, California.
Land acquired by the Forest Service shall become part of the San Bernardino National Forest.

environment.reason: The acreage is roughly equal and the land moves between federal and tribal ownership without a stated change in use, so the bill does not clearly affect water, air, or ecosystem protection.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. (map provision) requires the land maps to be kept on file for public inspection at Forest Service offices, and the cultural-preservation agreement must be recorded publicly with San Bernardino County and the Forest Service.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill involves a land trade between a tribe and the federal government and does not involve corporate profit or shareholder gains.

local_say.reason: The exchange is mandatory once the tribe makes an offer and the Forest Service 'must accept,' and the bill exempts the trade from FLPMA Section 206, which limits the usual review steps that give the public and local governments a say in federal land exchanges.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not appropriate money or involve bailouts, and the tribe pays for its own survey costs.

equality.reason: The exchange terms apply to the specific tribe and parcels involved and do not create unequal treatment of people under the law.

justice.reason: The exemption from FLPMA Section 206 may reduce the usual appraisal and public review requirements, and the bill does not state land values or whether the trade is value-equal, which weakens accountability for the exchange.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose about their own lives.

label: H.R. 4795
title: Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
short_title: Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
one: Colleges that take federal student aid would be barred from commercial boycotts of Israel, and colleges with international-education (Title VI) funding would have to certify each year that they treat academic exchanges with Israel like those with any other country.
summary:
This bill adds new conditions to federal funding for colleges and universities. First, any school that takes part in federal student aid programs (like Pell Grants and federal loans) would have to promise not to join a "nonexpressive commercial boycott" of a "major strategic partner" of the United States. The bill defines that partner by pointing to a 2014 law; the Congressional Research Service says this means Israel, along with companies licensed, regulated, or organized under Israeli law. A boycott, as defined, is a business action, such as refusing to deal or ending business ties, meant to limit commercial relations and not based on a valid business reason. Exceptions follow those in an existing anti-boycott law.

Second, schools that receive or apply for Title VI money (federal funds for foreign language and international studies) would have to certify by July 31 each year that their students and faculty may take part in academic programs in Israel on the same terms as programs in other countries. They would also have to certify that students and faculty from Israeli schools can join their programs on the same terms as those from other foreign schools. Programs include conferences, exchanges, study abroad, and joint research. A school that does not certify would lose all Title VI funds in the next fiscal year.

Finally, the bill states Congress's opinion that limits on college cooperation with Israel do not serve U.S. security and economic interests. That statement is not binding.
does: Adds a new condition to the Higher Education Act's program participation agreement: schools in federal student aid programs must not engage in a 'nonexpressive commercial boycott' of a major strategic partner of the U.S.
Defines 'major strategic partner' by reference to section 4 of Public Law 113-296 (which the CRS identifies as Israel), plus entities licensed, regulated, or organized under that country's laws.

Defines a covered boycott as a commercial action (including refusing to deal or ending business activities) intended to limit commercial relations and not based on a valid business reason; it excludes actions covered by exceptions in the Anti-Boycott Act of 2018 regulations.
Requires schools participating or applying in any Title VI program to submit an annual certification to the Education Secretary by July 31, starting the year of enactment.

The certification must state that the school will let its students and faculty join academic programs (conferences, teaching and cultural exchanges, study abroad, joint research) in Israel on the same terms as in other countries.
The certification must also state that students and faculty of Israeli postsecondary schools may join the school's academic programs on the same terms as those from other foreign schools.
A school that misses the July 31 deadline is ineligible for all Title VI funds in the next fiscal year, including money from grants awarded earlier.
Adds a non-binding 'Sense of Congress' that limits on college cooperation with Israel do not serve U.S. security, stability, and economic vitality.
who: Colleges and universities that take part in federal student aid programs
Schools that receive or apply for Title VI international education and foreign language funds
Students and faculty who study, teach, or do research in or with Israel
Students and faculty at Israeli universities seeking to join U.S. programs
Students, faculty, and campus groups that run or support boycott or divestment campaigns
Campus investment and business offices that decide contracts and vendors
The Department of Education, which would collect certifications

benefits: Could protect Israeli students, faculty, and partner institutions from being shut out of exchanges and joint research.
Could encourage academic cooperation and cultural exchange across borders.
Gives clear annual certification rules for Title VI schools.
Limits to 'nonexpressive' commercial actions and the anti-boycott exceptions mean protected speech is not directly banned.
concerns: Could discourage student-led or faculty-led divestment and boycott campaigns, chilling protest and dissent.
Singles out one country for special protection in federal education law.
Loss of Title VI funds, or student aid eligibility, could hurt schools and students who did nothing wrong.
The 'valid business reason' standard is vague and could lead to inconsistent enforcement or schools over-complying out of caution.
Could limit the say of campus communities and governing boards over institutional investments and vendor choices.
Certification for Title VI could pressure schools to continue programs in places where students and faculty face safety concerns, since terms must match other countries.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or new spending is provided in the material. The bill works by adding conditions to existing federal funds, with Title VI funding at risk for schools that do not certify.
unknowns: How the Education Department would enforce the boycott ban and judge a 'valid business reason'.
Whether the penalty for violating the boycott ban is loss of all federal student aid eligibility, and how that would be applied.
How the Anti-Boycott Act exceptions, which are in regulations, would apply to colleges.
How schools would handle safety or travel-advisory issues under the 'same terms and conditions' requirement.
Whether the bill would be challenged in court on free speech grounds.
Whether the Senate HELP Committee will take it up.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to protect economic and academic freedom in higher education by barring colleges that take federal student aid from joining certain commercial boycotts of Israel, and by requiring colleges that receive Title VI international education funds to certify that students and faculty can join academic programs in Israel and from Israeli institutions on the same terms as those in other countries. It also includes a non-binding statement from Congress that limits on college cooperation with Israel do not serve U.S. security and economic interests.

oppose: The bill's boycott ban could discourage student-led or faculty-led divestment and boycott campaigns, which some people see as lawful political speech and protest.
The bill singles out one country, Israel, for special protection in federal education law, which some critics say departs from how such policies usually work.
Losing federal student aid eligibility or all Title VI funds could hurt schools, programs, and students who had no part in any boycott.
The phrase 'valid business reason' is not clearly defined, so schools could enforce the rule unevenly or over-comply out of caution.
support: The bill aims to protect Israeli students, faculty, and partner institutions from being shut out of exchanges and joint research with U.S. schools.
Clear annual certification rules for Title VI schools would give the Education Department a straightforward way to check that academic programs are open on equal terms.
The bill limits its boycott ban to 'nonexpressive' commercial actions and keeps the existing anti-boycott law's exceptions, so it does not directly ban protected speech.
Supporters say the bill could encourage academic cooperation and cultural exchange across borders, which they see as valuable to U.S. interests.

crs:
Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act of 2026
This bill prohibits institutions of higher education (IHEs) that participate in federal student aid programs from engaging in boycotts against Israel. Specifically, IHEs may not engage in a commercial action intended to limit commercial relations with Israel, or with an entity licensed by, regulated by, or organized under the laws of Israel, that is not based on a valid business reason. 
Further, IHEs receiving, or applying to receive, Title VI funds (federal funding for foreign language and international education programs) must annually certify that (1) students and faculty are allowed to participate in academic programs located in Israel in the same manner and under the same terms and conditions as programs in other foreign countries, and (2) students and faculty at postsecondary institutions located in Israel may participate in such IHE’s academic programs in the same manner and under the same terms and conditions as students and faculty from other foreign countries.

environment.reason: The bill does not address water, air, land, or ecosystem protection.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on program participation agreement and the certification requirement create a new compliance obligation that could discourage public debate on campus, though the bill does not itself create secrecy; the 'valid business reason' standard is vague, which reduces clarity about what is prohibited.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill restricts institutional boycott actions and affects campus investment decisions, but it does not clearly shift costs to consumers, taxpayers, or the public in a way that favors corporate profit over people or the reverse.

local_say.reason: The boycott provision limits how colleges and their governing boards may make commercial and investment decisions, and the Title VI certification sets national terms for school programs, reducing campus and community say.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts or ratepayer cost shifts.

equality.reason: Sec. on the boycott condition and Title VI certification single out one country and its companies for special treatment in federal education law, creating unequal rules for a specific foreign nation and its partners compared with others.

justice.reason: Loss of all Title VI funds for missing a certification deadline, including grants awarded earlier, is a severe penalty, and the vague 'valid business reason' standard may lead to inconsistent enforcement.

personal_freedom.reason: The boycott condition restricts what schools and, through them, campus groups and staff may do in commercial dealings with Israeli entities, limiting choices about divestment and business relationships.

votes.question: On Passage

news.overall: The provided headlines mostly do not mention the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act, so no group's framing of the bill itself can be assessed; the evidence is thin, with only one Center article and two Lean Right articles. Lean Left coverage emphasizes economic harm from declining international enrollment and Israel-related political divisions, while Lean Right coverage emphasizes free speech and legal disputes over academic and Israel-related speech. The Center headline is a neutral statistical report with little framing beyond the numbers.

label: H.R. 6162
title: Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2025
short_title: Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2025
one: Transfers about 9.89 acres of federal land in Albuquerque, once part of the Albuquerque Indian School, into trust for the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico, gives the Tract 1 buildings to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, and bans gaming on the land.
summary: This bill would return about 9.89 acres of federal land in Albuquerque, New Mexico, to the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico. The land was once part of the Albuquerque Indian School, a federal Indian boarding school that operated until 1981. It is now run by the General Services Administration (GSA), the federal government's property manager. Within 90 days of the bill becoming law, the GSA must move out any federal tenants and hand control of the land to the Department of the Interior. Within another 90 days, Interior must take the land "into trust" for the 19 Pueblos. Trust land is land the federal government holds for a tribe, and it is subject to special federal rules. The Pueblos must use the land for education, health, culture, business, and economic development. It stays subject to existing private and city rights, such as easements, rights-of-way, and utility agreements. The federal government must also give its ownership of the buildings on Tract 1, including a 76,682-square-foot warehouse, to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center. Interior must get a survey and copies of the land's encumbrances (legal claims on the property) from the GSA. It may fix clerical errors in the survey. The documents must be recorded in public county and Bureau of Indian Affairs records. The bill bans casino-style gaming on this land. The bill text names no price and no funding. The cost to the government is mainly the value of the land and buildings given up, plus the cost of relocating tenants.
does: Within 90 days of enactment, requires the GSA to relocate all federal tenants from the land and transfer administrative control to the Interior Secretary.
Within 90 days after that, requires Interior to take all U.S. interest in three tracts (about 9.89 acres total: 3.57, 5.78, and 0.54 acres) into trust for the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico.

Names the 19 Pueblos: Acoma, Cochiti, Isleta, Jemez, Laguna, Nambe, Ohkay Owingeh, Picuris, Pojoaque, San Felipe, San Ildefonso, Sandia, Santa Ana, Santa Clara, Santo Domingo, Taos, Tesuque, Zia, and Zuni.
Requires the land to be used for the educational, health, cultural, business, and economic development of the 19 Pueblos, under federal laws for Indian trust land in New Mexico.
Keeps the land subject to existing private or municipal encumbrances, rights-of-way, restrictions, recorded easements, and utility service agreements.

Requires the U.S. to convey its ownership of buildings and structures on Tract 1 (including a 76,682 sq ft warehouse) to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center in fee, meaning full private ownership, within 90 days of the relocation and jurisdiction transfer.

Directs Interior to obtain a survey and copies of all encumbrances from the GSA, lets it correct clerical and survey errors, and requires recording in Bernalillo County and Bureau of Indian Affairs records.
Prohibits Class II and Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act on the land.
who: The 19 Pueblos of New Mexico, who would hold the land in trust
The Indian Pueblo Cultural Center, which would receive the Tract 1 buildings
Federal agencies now using the site, which must move out within 90 days
The General Services Administration and the Department of the Interior, who carry out the transfers
Albuquerque residents, neighbors, and utilities near the site, whose existing easements and rights stay in place
Descendants and communities connected to the Albuquerque Indian School

benefits: Returns land tied to a painful boarding school history to Native communities.
Gives the 19 Pueblos control over use of the land for education, health, culture, and economic development.
Gives the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center a building it can use, which could expand cultural and economic activity.
Moves unused or underused federal property to productive community use.
Requires public recording of the survey and transfer documents.
The gaming ban and preserved easements limit surprises for neighbors and the city.
concerns: The 90-day deadlines for moving federal tenants could be hard to meet and could disrupt agencies.
The federal government gives up land and buildings without payment, which has an opportunity cost.
The bill does not say what happens if the site has environmental contamination or building problems.
Because the land is usable for business and economic development, the specific uses are not set. Neighbors have no explicit role in decisions.
imp.cost: The bill provides no funding and does not state a cost. Costs would likely come from relocating federal tenants, survey and administrative work, and the value of the land and buildings the government gives up. The text and CRS summary give no estimate.
unknowns: The cost of relocating the federal tenants and who pays.
Whether the land or buildings have environmental contamination or need repairs.
How the 19 Pueblos will jointly govern and use the land.
What the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center plans to do with the Tract 1 warehouse.
Whether the Senate will act on the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to take about 9.89 acres of former Albuquerque Indian School land in Albuquerque, New Mexico, into federal trust for the benefit of the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico. The land was historically part of an Indian boarding school that operated until 1981, and the bill says the land is to be used for the Pueblos' education, health, cultural, business, and economic development. The bill also transfers a warehouse building on one tract to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center.

oppose: The federal government would give up about 9.89 acres and a 76,682-square-foot warehouse without payment, so taxpayers would lose the land's value and any future sale or lease income.
The 90-day deadline to move all federal tenants may be hard to meet and could disrupt federal agencies currently using the site.
The bill does not say how environmental contamination or building repair problems would be handled, which could leave costs unclear for taxpayers or the new owners.
The bill does not set specific land uses or give neighbors a formal role in decisions, so a constituent may want more local input written into the law.
support: The land is tied to the Albuquerque Indian School, a federal boarding school that operated until 1981, and returning it to the 19 Pueblos would address that painful history.
The bill would give the 19 Pueblos control over the land for education, health, culture, and economic development, rather than leaving it under federal management.
Transferring the warehouse to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center could give that institution a building it can use to expand cultural and economic activity.
The bill keeps existing easements, rights-of-way, and utility agreements in place, and it bans casino-style gaming on the land, which may reassure neighbors and the city.

crs:
Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2025
This bill takes three tracts of specified federal land (approximately 9.89 acres) in Albuquerque, New Mexico, into trust for the benefit of the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico. (These three tracts of land were historically part of the Albuquerque Indian School, which was an Indian boarding school until 1981.)
The land is currently administered by the General Services Administration (GSA). Within 90 days of this bill's enactment, the GSA must (1) relocate all federal tenants on the land, and (2) transfer administrative jurisdiction over the land to the Department of the Interior.
Within 90 days after the relocation of federal tenants and transfer of administrative jurisdiction, the bill requires (1) Interior to take the land into trust for the benefit of the 19 Pueblos, and (2) the federal government to convey its ownership interests in buildings and other structures located within Tract 1 to the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center to own in fee. (Tract 1, which is approximately 3.57 acres, contains a warehouse that is 76,682 square feet.)
The bill requires the land taken into trust to be used for the educational, health, cultural, business, and economic development of the 19 Pueblos. Further, the land must remain subject to existing private and municipal encumbrances, rights-of-way, restrictions, easements of record, and utility service agreements.
The bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

environment.reason: The bill does not address environmental cleanup or contamination; it says nothing about how contamination or building problems would be handled, so the effect is unclear.

transparency_kindness.reason: Interior must record the survey and transfer documents in county and Bureau of Indian Affairs records, which makes the transfer documents publicly available (Survey and recording provision).

people_over_profit.reason: The land and buildings go to tribes and a cultural center rather than a corporation, but no sale price or payment is set; the effects on profit and public costs are mixed and unclear.

local_say.reason: Sec. on trust transfer moves land out of local and state control into federal trust for the Pueblos, and neighbors and the city have no explicit role in later land-use decisions; existing easements and city rights are preserved, which partly offsets this.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide a bailout or shift utility or corporate costs to ratepayers; the land and building transfer is a federal property disposal without a stated payment, which is an opportunity cost rather than a bailout.

equality.reason: Returns land tied to the boarding school history to the 19 Pueblos and restores access to trust land for tribal education, health, and economic uses, though it applies only to a specific group.

justice.reason: The bill sets out deadlines, names the Pueblos, and requires recording of survey and encumbrance documents, which gives clearer and more accountable transfer procedures.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not change what individuals may do or choose about their own lives; the gaming ban applies to the land but does not restrict individual choices beyond that site.

news.overall: Evidence is very limited: three headlines, all truncated, and none explicitly about the Albuquerque Indian School Act of 2025. The Lean Left items focus on Native food culture and a criminal investigation on Menominee land, while the Center item focuses on uranium and Navajo land, so the groups do not cover the bill in a directly comparable way. No group's coverage can be reliably characterized as to how it frames the bill itself.

label: H.R. 681
title: To amend the Act of August 9, 1955 (commonly known as the “Long-Term Leasing Act”), to authorize leases of up to 99 years for land in the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation and land held in trust for the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), and for other purposes
short_title: Wampanoag Tribes 99-Year Leasing Authority
one: Lets the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) lease their trust land for up to 99 years under the federal Long-Term Leasing Act.
summary: This bill makes a one-sentence change to a 1955 federal law known as the Long-Term Leasing Act. That law normally limits leases of Native American trust land (land the federal government holds for a tribe) to shorter terms. It also lists specific tribes whose lands may be leased for up to 99 years. The bill adds two Massachusetts tribes to that list: the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, for its reservation, and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), for its trust land. If the bill becomes law, these tribes could approve leases of up to 99 years for homes, businesses, or other development on that land. Such leases still need the usual approval from the Secretary of the Interior under the existing law. The bill doesn't create new funding, doesn't change who owns the land, and doesn't spell out any new environmental or other rules. Longer leases can make it easier for tribes to attract financing and investment. Supporters see this as a way to expand tribal self-determination and economic development. The Congressional Research Service describes the bill the same way. The text doesn't say what kinds of projects might follow, so the effects depend on future tribal decisions and the federal approval process.
does: Amends subsection (a) of the Long-Term Leasing Act (Act of Aug. 9, 1955, 25 U.S.C. 415(a)) by adding the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation to the list of lands eligible for leases up to 99 years.
Also adds land held in trust for the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) to that list.
Places these lands in the same category as other named tribal lands, such as the Confederated Tribes of the Chehalis Reservation.
Does not appropriate money, change land ownership, or add new rules; leases remain subject to the existing law's requirements, including federal approval.
who: Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and its members
Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) and its members
Businesses, developers, lenders, or tenants who may lease tribal land
Neighbors and local communities near tribal trust land in Massachusetts
Department of the Interior (Bureau of Indian Affairs), which reviews and approves leases

benefits: Gives the two tribes the same long-term leasing flexibility as other listed tribes.
Longer leases may make it easier to get financing for housing, businesses, or community projects.
Supports tribal self-determination over local land use.
Doesn't spend federal money.
concerns: Very long leases (up to 99 years) could lock land into uses for generations and may limit future flexibility.
The bill doesn't add any specific environmental or community-input rules for leased projects.
Outside developers could gain much of the benefit if leases aren't structured carefully.
imp.cost: No spending or funding is provided. The CRS summary and the text mention no cost. Federal staff time to review leases would come from existing Interior Department resources.
unknowns: What kinds of projects the tribes might approve with longer leases.
Whether environmental review or other safeguards would apply to specific leases (the bill doesn't change them).
Whether the Mashpee reservation wording covers all of its trust land. The text uses the term 'Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation' without defining it.
When or whether the Senate will vote; the bill is on the Senate calendar.

stage.last_action: Committee on Indian Affairs. Reported by Senator Armstrong for Senator Murkowski without amendment. With written report No. 119-136.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to authorize leases of up to 99 years for land in the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe Reservation and for land held in trust for the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah). It does this by adding both tribes' lands to a list in the 1955 Long-Term Leasing Act, which already allows certain tribal trust lands to be leased for longer terms. The Congressional Research Service summary describes the bill the same way: it lets both tribes lease their trust land for up to 99 years.

oppose: A 99-year lease can tie up land for several generations. Opponents could argue that this limits future tribal and community choices about how the land is used.
The bill does not add new environmental review or community-input rules for leased projects. Opponents could ask Congress to require these protections before extending long leases.
Long leases could benefit outside developers more than the tribes if the lease terms are not carefully written. Opponents could ask for stronger safeguards on lease terms.
support: The bill gives the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) the same long-term leasing option that other listed tribes already have. Supporters see this as fair treatment.
Longer leases can make it easier to secure financing for housing, businesses, and community projects. Supporters say this can help the tribes build their economies.

The bill supports tribal self-determination, since the tribes would decide whether to lease their land. It also spends no federal money and does not change land ownership. Each lease would still need approval from the Secretary of the Interior under existing law.

crs: This bill authorizes the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) to lease their land held in trust for a term of up to 99 years. Both tribes are located in Massachusetts.

local_say.reason: The bill amends subsection (a) of the Long-Term Leasing Act to add the Mashpee Wampanoag Reservation and Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) trust land, letting the tribes themselves decide on up-to-99-year leases for their own land, though Interior approval is still required.

equality.reason: The amendment places the two Massachusetts tribes in the same leasing category as other named tribal lands, giving them equal access to the same long-term leasing authority.

news.overall: Evidence is extremely limited: only two Lean Left headlines were provided, neither about the bill or its subject matter, and no article descriptions were included. No Lean Left coverage of the bill itself is present in this set, so no comparison with other perspectives can be drawn from it. Coverage from other outlets would be needed to assess how the bill is framed.

label: H.R. 8658
title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
short_title: Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
one: Gives American Indian and Alaska Native patients (or their providers) at least 15 days, instead of 72 hours, to notify the Indian Health Service after emergency care at a non-IHS provider so the bill can be paid.
summary: The Indian Health Service (IHS) runs a program called Purchased/Referred Care (PRC). It pays for medical care that American Indian and Alaska Native patients get outside IHS or tribal facilities. Right now, if a patient has an emergency and goes to a non-IHS hospital or doctor, someone must notify IHS within 72 hours of treatment or admission. If they miss that window, payment can be denied. This bill changes the rule to say the notification deadline can be no shorter than 15 days. People who are elderly or disabled already have a 30-day deadline, and that stays the same. The bill does this by editing Section 406 of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act. It splits the section into two parts: a general rule with the new 15-day minimum, and the existing rule for elderly or disabled patients. The bill does not add money or create new benefits. It only changes the paperwork deadline for emergency care payment. It could mean fewer patients and providers lose coverage because of a missed short deadline. It may also affect how quickly IHS can plan and track its purchased care spending. The bill passed the House and was received in the Senate on September 15, 2026.
does: Amends Section 406 of the Indian Health Care Improvement Act (25 U.S.C. 1646), which covers emergency contract health services.

Creates a new general rule: for an Indian receiving emergency care from a non-IHS provider or facility, the deadline to notify IHS (as a condition of payment) must be at least 15 days, up from 72 hours.
Keeps the separate rule for elderly or disabled Indians, who continue to have a 30-day notification period.
Allows the patient, someone acting for the patient, or the provider to give the notice (per the CRS summary of current practice).
Does not appropriate new money or change who is eligible for PRC.
who: American Indian and Alaska Native patients who use IHS and need emergency care outside IHS or tribal facilities
Non-IHS hospitals, clinics, and doctors that treat these patients and seek payment
IHS Purchased/Referred Care program staff and authorizing officials
Elderly or disabled Native patients (their 30-day rule is unchanged)
Tribal health programs and rural communities far from IHS facilities

benefits: Fewer emergency claims could be denied for late notice.
Patients and providers get more time to file, which helps people who are very sick, far from services, or unaware of the rule.
Could lower the risk of patients facing surprise medical debt.
Could make non-IHS providers more willing to treat IHS patients in emergencies.
concerns: It does not add funding, so more approved claims could strain a PRC budget that is already limited.
The bill says 'not less than 15 days', so IHS could set a longer period, and the exact deadline is not fixed.
Does not fix broader IHS funding or access problems.
Longer notice windows could make IHS's budget tracking harder.
imp.cost: No funding is provided or authorized in the bill text. No cost estimate was given. Any added cost would come from more claims being approved within PRC's existing budget.
unknowns: Whether a CBO cost estimate exists and what it says.
How much PRC spending would rise from fewer denied claims.
How IHS would put the new deadline into practice and whether it would pick a period longer than 15 days.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give more time to notify the Indian Health Service's Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program about emergency care that American Indian and Alaska Native patients receive from non-IHS providers or facilities. Under current law the deadline is 72 hours; the bill sets it at no less than 15 days, while keeping the 30-day deadline for elderly or disabled individuals.

oppose: The bill does not add any funding to the PRC program, so approving more claims could put more strain on a budget that is already limited.
The bill sets only a minimum of 15 days, so the exact deadline is not fixed and could be longer than 15 days, which may make IHS budget tracking and planning harder.
The bill does not address broader IHS funding or access problems, so it may not solve the underlying shortage of care that leads patients to seek outside emergency treatment.
support: The current 72-hour window can be too short for patients who are very sick, far from services, or unaware of the rule, and missing it can lead to denied payment.
A 15-day minimum gives patients and providers more time to file, which could reduce surprise medical bills for people who received emergency care.
The bill keeps the existing 30-day deadline for elderly and disabled individuals and does not change who is eligible for PRC, so its change is narrow and focused on paperwork timing.

crs:
Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act
This bill extends from 72 hours to not less than 15 days the time period to notify the Purchased/Referred Care (PRC) program of emergency medical care received from a non-Indian Health Service (IHS) medical provider or at a non-IHS medical facility. This bill does not apply to individuals who are elderly or disabled, who continue to have a 30-day notification requirement for emergency services.
The IHS provides medical and dental services directly to American Indian and Alaska Native patients whenever possible. The PRC program pays for medical or dental care that is provided away from an IHS or tribal health care facility. The PRC program must be notified of requests for authorization of payment for health care services from a non-IHS provider.
Currently in emergency cases, the patient, an individual on behalf of the patient, or the medical care provider must, within 72 hours after the beginning of treatment for the condition or after admission to a health care facility, notify a PRC authorizing official of the need for the emergency medical care. This bill instead allows the patient, other individual, or provider to notify PRC not less than 15 days of the treatment or admission.

environment.reason: The bill concerns payment notification deadlines for health care and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 406 as amended gives patients and providers a longer window (at least 15 days instead of 72 hours) to notify PRC, reducing the chance that a sick patient loses payment coverage over a missed short deadline.

people_over_profit.reason: The amended Sec. 406 lets providers and patients notify PRC within at least 15 days, making it easier for non-IHS providers to get paid for emergency care, which favors patients and providers over payment denials.

local_say.reason: The bill changes a federal notification deadline and does not alter community or tribal decision-making authority over facilities, land use, or services.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide a bailout or shift costs to ratepayers; it changes a notice deadline, though it may increase PRC claims paid from existing funds, which is too speculative to score.

equality.reason: The general 15-day rule applies to all eligible Indians receiving emergency care, and the bill keeps the 30-day rule for elderly or disabled patients, so the change expands equal access to payment for emergency care across patients who previously faced the 72-hour limit.

justice.reason: Sec. 406 as amended gives a longer, more workable notice period, reducing the chance that valid emergency claims are denied for technical lateness.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill concerns payment paperwork timelines and does not expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose about their own lives.

news.overall: None of the provided coverage directly addresses the Indian Health Service Emergency Claims Parity Act. Lean Left items cover adjacent topics such as health disparities, costs, federal funding, and tribal affairs, while the Center group has only one article on global vision loss. Evidence is thin across all groups, and no perspective's framing of the bill itself can be assessed from these headlines.

label: H.R. 9332
title: Load Forecasting Enhancement Act
short_title: Load Forecasting Enhancement Act
one: Sets up temporary regional boards of federal and state regulators to study how utilities predict electricity demand, then asks states to consider adopting the resulting best practices and ties some federal energy-conservation aid to more transparent forecasting.
summary:
Electric utilities predict how much power customers will need, and those predictions drive decisions about building power plants and power lines, which in turn affect customers' bills. This bill aims to make those predictions more accurate, open, and consistent.

Within 90 days of becoming law, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) would divide the country into regions and create a joint board for each. Each board would include one FERC commissioner, who chairs it, and one representative from each state utility commission in the region. The boards would study forecasting methods, data quality, transparency, stakeholder involvement, economic development projections, and how to evaluate requests from very large power users such as big industrial or commercial sites, including whether those users have made financial commitments to the utility. They would identify best practices and report to FERC.

Within one year, FERC would publish a report for Congress with those best practices and recommendations for using them consistently across states. The boards would then end.

The bill also adds a new federal standard to a 1978 law (PURPA). State utility regulators would have to consider, within one to two years, whether to require utilities' forecasting to follow FERC's recommendations. States that already acted on a similar standard are exempt, and nonregulated utilities do not have to consider it. Finally, state energy conservation plans, a condition for certain federal aid, would have to include programs to improve the accuracy, oversight, and transparency of utility load forecasts. The bill does not state a cost.
does: Requires FERC, within 90 days of enactment, to create regions covering every state and a joint board for each region to study electric load forecasting.
Each joint board has one representative from each state utility commission in its region plus one FERC commissioner as chair.

Boards must study how forecasting affects affordability, reliability and resilience, data collection and modeling methods, transparency and accuracy, stakeholder engagement, economic development projections, best available technologies, and evaluation of service requests from large industrial or commercial users (including their financial commitments to utilities).

Boards identify best practices and report to FERC; within one year FERC must publish and send Congress a report with those practices and recommendations for consistent use across states. Boards end the day after the report is submitted.

Adds a new PURPA standard saying utility forecasting procedures should incorporate FERC's published recommendations; state regulators must begin consideration within 1 year and finish with a determination within 2 years of enactment. Considering a standard does not force adoption.

Exempts nonregulated utilities from the consideration requirement, and exempts utilities in states that already adopted, held proceedings on, or had a legislative vote in the prior 3 years on a similar standard.

Amends the Energy Policy and Conservation Act so state energy conservation plans, a condition of federal assistance, must include procedures and programs to improve the accuracy, oversight, and stakeholder transparency of utility load forecasts.
who: Electric utility customers (households and businesses), whose bills depend partly on forecast-driven investments
Investor-owned and other state-regulated electric utilities
State public utility commissions and state energy offices
FERC commissioners and staff
Large industrial and commercial power users such as data centers and factories
Consumer advocates, environmental groups, and other utility stakeholders

benefits: May improve forecast accuracy and public visibility into the data and methods utilities use.
Could reduce the risk that ratepayers pay for unneeded generation or grid buildout.
Explicitly examines whether large new loads have made financial commitments, which could protect other customers from carrying their costs.
Keeps final decisions with state regulators, who must only consider the standard.
Stakeholder engagement is a required study topic.
concerns: Boards are made up of regulators only; there is no guaranteed seat for consumer advocates, environmental groups, or the public.
Recommendations are not binding, so effects may be limited or uneven across states.
The bill does not say forecasts must account for efficiency, clean energy, or environmental impacts, and the study list includes economic development projections that could favor growth assumptions.
Adds work and possible cost for FERC and state commissions, and ties some federal conservation aid to new plan requirements, which could burden state energy offices.
Nonregulated utilities and states with prior similar actions are exempt, leaving gaps.
imp.cost: The bill does not authorize or state any funding. Costs would fall on FERC and state commissions, which would staff the boards and carry out the study, and potentially on state energy offices updating conservation plans.
unknowns: How FERC would draw the regions and whether boards would include public or consumer input.
What best practices the boards would recommend.
How many states would adopt the recommendations after considering them.
Total cost of running the boards, since none is specified.
How the conservation-plan requirement would affect states' eligibility for federal assistance.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make electric load forecasts more accurate, open, and consistent, because utilities' predictions of future power demand drive decisions about building power plants and power lines that affect customers' bills. It would have FERC set up regional joint boards to study and recommend best practices for forecasting, and would ask states to consider adopting those recommendations.

oppose: The boards would include only federal and state utility regulators. The bill does not guarantee seats for consumer advocates, environmental groups, or the public, so you could ask why those voices are left out of the process.
The recommendations are not binding. States only have to consider them, so the bill may produce uneven results across states while still adding federal work and cost for FERC and state commissions.

The study list does not explicitly require forecasts to account for energy efficiency, clean energy, or environmental impacts, and it includes economic development projections that could favor growth assumptions. You could ask that these factors be required in any forecasting standard.
support: The bill addresses a real issue: utility demand forecasts shape power plant and transmission spending, and those costs can show up on customer bills. Better forecasts could help reduce the risk that ratepayers pay for unneeded infrastructure.

The bill requires FERC to study whether large new customers, such as big industrial or commercial sites, have made financial commitments to utilities. This could help protect other customers from carrying the costs of those projects.

The bill keeps final decisions with state regulators, who only have to consider the recommendations. It also makes forecasting methods and data more transparent to the public and makes stakeholder engagement a required study topic.

crs:
Load Forecasting Enhancement Act
This bill requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to establish regional boards to study and recommend best practices for electric load forecasting, which is the process of predicting the demand for electricity at a particular time. It also requires states to consider adopting the recommendations.
Specifically, the bill directs FERC to establish regional boards to study electric load forecasting, chair the boards, and run them jointly with each state public utility commission in the regions. The boards must (1) study issues relevant to identifying best practices for electric load forecasting that enhance the reliability and affordability of electric service to customers, and (2) identify such best practices. FERC must make recommendations to Congress for the consistent use across states of such best practices by electric utilities.
The bill also modifies provisions under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act to require state public utility commissions to consider adopting those recommendations.
It also modifies the Energy Policy and Conservation Act to make federal assistance for state energy conservation plans contingent upon the plan including procedures and programs to improve the accuracy, oversight, and transparency to stakeholders of the forecasting of electric loads by electric utilities.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 3 requires the joint boards to study transparency and accuracy of forecasts and FERC to publish a report for Congress, and the EPCA amendment requires state conservation plans to include stakeholder transparency programs for load forecasts.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill studies whether large users have made financial commitments to utilities, which could protect ratepayers, but it does not directly change corporate profit or shift costs; the effects are indirect and uncertain.

local_say.reason: The PURPA standard requires state commissions to consider FERC recommendations but keeps final decisions with states, and the regional boards are made up of regulators, so state and local say is neither clearly expanded nor reduced.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no provision on bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks; it does not authorize funding.

equality.reason: The standard applies to all utilities, but exempts nonregulated utilities and states with prior similar actions, which creates some uneven treatment, though the exemptions are based on regulatory status rather than group identity.

justice.reason: The bill concerns forecasting studies and planning standards rather than legal processes, remedies, or due process.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not change what individuals may legally do, say or choose.

label: H.R. 9497
title: Water Resources Development Act of 2026
short_title: Water Resources Development Act of 2026 (WRDA 2026)
one: A large, roughly two-year Army Corps of Engineers bill that authorizes hundreds of flood, harbor, ecosystem, water supply, and water/wastewater projects and studies, sets up new Corps offices, and changes some permitting and liability rules.
summary:
This is the regular "WRDA" bill Congress passes to tell the Army Corps of Engineers what to study and build. It does not by itself provide money; it authorizes projects, and later spending bills must fund them. It passed the House and was received in the Senate on Sept. 17, 2026.

Title I (General Provisions) reorganizes the Corps. Within 180 days it must create four offices: inland navigation construction, water supply and drought resilience, technical assistance and community outreach (prioritizing rural and Tribal communities), and alternative project delivery. A new 11-member Levee Owners Board would advise the Corps and Congress. The Corps would write rules for "categorical permissions," which let certain low-impact activities near federal works skip individual permission. These must have a 30-day public comment period, be posted online, and still follow NEPA, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. Other provisions speed the electronic permit system, tighten study schedules, and let non-federal sponsors cover cost overruns without raising the federal share. One provision shields the Corps from Superfund (CERCLA) liability for contaminated-sediment cleanup done under an EPA-approved joint plan with a local sponsor. Mitigation for fish and wildlife harm must be publicly posted. Congress also expresses support for equal consideration of nonstructural flood solutions and for the Everglades reservoir schedule, and Corps district boundaries are shifted in Missouri and Arkansas.

Title II (Studies and Reports) authorizes 107 new feasibility studies and 26 changes to existing project studies. It orders 53+ studies and 12 final reports expedited. It also requires many reports and GAO and Inspector General reviews. Topics include Tribal policy, park ranger classification, beach renourishment, forecast-informed reservoir operations, floating cabins, and the emerging harbor maintenance backlog. It also directs site-specific work: a Lake Okeechobee review, Columbia Lock and Dam repairs, an Upper Missouri sedimentation study (capped at $25 million, with a bar on changing the Missouri River Master Manual), a Cochiti Lake atomic-contamination review, and Columbia River land transfer studies, including for a Tribe. Several land disposition studies cover Big Sandy Lake, Table Rock Lake, and Foster Joseph Sayers Dam. Table Rock Lake homeowners could keep structures and septic systems on federal land until abandonment or failure.

Title III (Project Authorizations and Modifications) includes the large environmental infrastructure list. It authorizes about 150 new local water, wastewater, and stormwater projects, from $60,000 to $100 million each (Tampa Bay water supply is $100 million). It raises federal spending caps on 84 earlier projects, in some cases sharply (Washington, D.C. from $1 million to $201 million; Alameda County from $20 million to $116 million). It lets the federal share be paid as reimbursement for work sponsors already did. It also adds Houston Ship Channel and Mobile Harbor changes, floodplain management and planning assistance changes, and forecast-informed reservoir operations at more dams.

Title IV adds many named small flood, navigation, ecosystem restoration, dredged-material, and stormwater projects, and expedites 17 other named projects and a Tribal irrigation project.

Title V extends National Dam Safety Program timelines by five years, changes one number from 2 to 7 (the text does not say what), and removes "low-head dams" from two list items. FEMA must study why states struggle to prioritize high-hazard dams.

Some sections of Title III's middle (before the environmental infrastructure list) and parts of Title III after Section 312 were not fully visible, so provisions there may be missing from this analysis.
does: Creates four new Corps program offices within 180 days: Inland Navigation Construction Management; Water Supply, Water Conservation, and Drought Resiliency; Technical Assistance and Community Outreach (prioritizing rural, Tribal, and disadvantaged communities); and Alternative Delivery Methods. Funded from existing Corps general expense money, with reports due in 2 years.
Establishes an 11-member Levee Owners Board of levee owner-operators to advise the Secretary and Congress on levee reliability, flood-risk budgets, and feasibility reports.

Requires a rule creating 'categorical permissions' for low-impact activities affecting federal works (Section 408), with 30-day public comment, website posting, and continued compliance with NEPA, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act. A proposed rule is due in 180 days.

Shields the Corps from Superfund (CERCLA) liability for contaminated-sediment removal under an EPA-approved joint plan with a non-federal sponsor; requires documenting contaminants, seeking responsible parties, and public comment, while preserving federal cost recovery from polluters.
Lets the Corps accept non-federal funds to cover project cost overruns above the statutory maximum, without raising the federal share.
Speeds up the Corps' electronic permit and tracking system (1-year deadline), makes final environmental review documents public, and tightens feasibility study schedules and concurrent reviews.
Requires fish and wildlife mitigation plans before project approval, allows credit-based mitigation, and requires public posting of each project's mitigation requirements and status.

Sets non-binding policies on using all Corps missions, treating nonstructural flood solutions equally, keeping recreation access during construction, and reviewing real estate minimums for flood projects.
Moves Corps district boundaries for certain Missouri and Arkansas counties within 90 days and requires notice and consultation for any other change.
Orders open information-sharing with all Members of Congress, a National Academy of Public Administration workforce review, and status reports on ten overdue Corps reports.
Adds seven projects to the 'ability to pay' list (reduced local cost share) and three to a pilot program list.
Authorizes 107 new feasibility studies and 26 modifications of existing project studies, mostly flood, coastal storm, ecosystem restoration, navigation, and water supply.
Directs expedited completion of 53+ studies, 12 final reports, and several other named studies and plans, including the New York/New Jersey Harbor and Tributaries report and Everglades-related work.

Orders reports or GAO/Inspector General reviews on topics such as Tribal policies, park ranger classification, beach renourishment, architect-engineer services, state fish and wildlife recommendations, forecast-informed reservoir operations, floating cabins, and the harbor maintenance backlog.

Directs site-specific actions: Lake Okeechobee after-action review (limited from recommending more federal control of state waters), Columbia Lock and Dam repair report, Calumet Harbor disposal facility closure plan, Brandon Road sediment cleanup plan, and Cochiti Lake atomic contamination evaluation.
Authorizes an Upper Missouri River Basin sedimentation study capped at $25 million with a 65% federal share, and bars it from considering changes to the Missouri River Master Water Control Manual.

Orders land disposition studies (Big Sandy Lake, Table Rock Lake, Foster Joseph Sayers Dam, Columbia River Tri-Cities and Tribal trust), and lets Table Rock Lake homes, structures, and septic systems stay on federal land until abandonment or failure.
Raises the Assateague Island authorization ceiling from $35 million to $45 million and orders research on dryland stream and shoreline stabilization technologies.

Authorizes about 150 new environmental infrastructure (water, wastewater, stormwater) projects in dozens of states, territories, and Tribal areas, with federal amounts from $60,000 to $100 million each.
Raises federal spending caps and expands purposes for 84 previously authorized environmental infrastructure programs and lets the federal share be paid by reimbursing sponsors' prior costs.

Adds dams to forecast-informed reservoir assessments, expands floodplain management and planning assistance, adds the Bayport East channel in Houston, and rewrites Mobile Harbor dredged-material disposal language.

Authorizes many small named flood, navigation, aquatic ecosystem, drought resiliency, dredged-material, and stormwater projects, and directs expedited completion of 17 other named projects plus a Gila River Tribal irrigation project.
Extends National Dam Safety Program deadlines to 2031, changes a number from 2 to 7, removes 'low-head dams' from two list items, and requires a FEMA study on prioritizing high-hazard dams.

purpose: The bill says it is the regular Water Resources Development Act, which authorizes and modifies water infrastructure projects, studies, and programs of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, such as ports and harbors, navigation, flood and storm damage reduction, ecosystem restoration, water supply, and dam rehabilitation. Its stated aim is to set the Corps' project list and direct changes to how it operates and delivers projects. The bill does not itself provide funding; later appropriations bills would need to fund the projects it authorizes.

oppose: The bill creates a Superfund (CERCLA) liability shield for the Corps for contaminated-sediment cleanups done under a joint plan. Someone concerned about accountability could ask how the Corps and EPA will ensure cleanups are adequate and that polluters still pay.

The bill directs the Corps to write a rule creating 'categorical permissions' for low-impact work near federal projects, which could mean less individual review. Constituents could ask how the rule will protect wetlands, fish, and wildlife, and whether it will keep full NEPA, Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act review.

The bill includes about 150 new local projects and raises spending caps on 84 earlier projects, some sharply (for example, Washington, D.C. from $1 million to $201 million). Constituents could ask whether these increases are justified and how they compare with other national priorities, since taxpayers would pay the federal share.
support: The bill authorizes about 150 new local water, wastewater, and stormwater projects, including in small rural and Tribal communities. Supporters could point to the need for safer drinking water and better wastewater and stormwater systems in their area.

The bill authorizes 107 new feasibility studies and several flood, coastal storm, and ecosystem restoration projects. Supporters could say these help reduce flood risk to homes and lives and restore wetlands, estuaries, and fish and wildlife habitat.

The bill adds public transparency requirements, including public posting of permit, mitigation, and study information, a 30-day comment period for categorical permissions, and a new office focused on rural and Tribal outreach. Supporters could say these make the Corps more open and accountable to communities.

cost_flag: Authorizes projects but does not appropriate money; later appropriations are needed. Individual authorizations range from $60,000 to $100 million, and many caps are raised by tens of millions. The Upper Missouri sedimentation study is capped at $25 million (65% federal). The new Corps offices are funded from existing general expense authority. No total cost estimate was provided.

Water Resources Development Act of 2026
This bill authorizes and modifies certain water resource infrastructure projects and programs of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and makes related requirements. For example, the bill authorizes and modifies various water resources feasibility studies and projects of the Corps of Engineers, such as studies or projects to
maintain ports and harbors,
make certain waterways more navigable,
reduce flood and storm damage,
restore aquatic ecosystems and protect fish and wildlife,
protect shorelines,
address harmful algal blooms,
rehabilitate dams,
manage recreational sites and facilities,
support water supply and storage projects, and
support other water resources infrastructure.
The bill also directs the Corps of Engineers to establish an Office on Alternative Delivery Methods in order to accelerate project delivery of infrastructure. 
In addition, the bill directs the Corps of Engineers to issue a rule that establishes categorical permissions for certain harbor or river improvements that will cause only minimal adverse environmental effects.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 categorical permissions must still comply with NEPA, the Clean Water Act, and the Endangered Species Act, and mitigation plans for fish and wildlife harm are required before approval and publicly posted; ecosystem restoration and water infrastructure authorizations also help, though the Table Rock Lake provision allowing structures and septic systems to stay on federal land until abandonment or failure could affect water quality and the Superfund shield limits federal cleanup liability for contaminated sediment, which offsets some of the gain.

transparency_kindness.reason: Categorical permission rule requires a 30-day public comment period and website posting, final environmental review documents must be made public, and fish and wildlife mitigation requirements must be publicly posted; the Limits on reports about state waters (Lake Okeechobee review) and the bar on considering Missouri River Master Manual changes restrict what analysis can recommend.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 1 Superfund shield and Sec. 2 authorizing non-federal sponsors to cover cost overruns could shift costs onto local ratepayers, while Title III raises federal caps on 84 projects, shifting costs to taxpayers; the Corps' categorical permissions also may favor development interests with less individual review.

local_say.reason: Title I's Levee Owners Board and the Sec. 408 categorical permission rule's 30-day public comment give local owners and the public input, and the Missouri and Arkansas district boundary changes require notice and consultation; however, Table Rock Lake homeowners' retention rights and the Lake Okeechobee limit on recommending federal control of state waters are mixed.

no_bailouts.reason: Title III raises federal caps on 84 earlier projects (e.g., D.C. from $1 million to $201 million, Alameda County from $20 million to $116 million) and allows reimbursement for work sponsors already did, shifting costs to federal taxpayers, and the cost-overrun provision can shift costs to local ratepayers.

equality.reason: Title I's Alternative Delivery and Technical Assistance offices prioritize rural and Tribal communities, and Title III's environmental infrastructure list authorizes projects across many states, territories and Tribal areas, expanding access to water and wastewater projects.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 Superfund (CERCLA) liability shield for the Corps for sediment cleanup under an EPA-approved joint plan reduces accountability for remedies, though the bill requires documentation, public comment, and preserved cost recovery from polluters.
