label: H.R. 9617
title: CHARM Act
short_title: CHARM Act (Critical Mineral Recovery Strategy)
one: Requires the EPA, working with other agencies, to build a national strategy for recovering critical minerals from discarded materials and to report on it publicly every two years.
summary:
This bill adds a new section to the federal Solid Waste Disposal Act. It tells the head of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to develop and carry out a "National Critical Mineral Recovery Strategy." The goal is to coordinate federal efforts to pull critical minerals, such as those the U.S. Geological Survey lists as essential to the economy or national security, out of discarded materials. Those materials include mining waste and metal processing waste.

To build the strategy, the EPA and other relevant agencies must list the programs and legal powers they already have that relate to this work. They must also identify which discarded materials might hold critical minerals, and which minerals might be in them. They must look at legal, technical and other barriers to recovery and at ways to expand it. They must also consider how recovered minerals could strengthen U.S. supply chains. One required task is to find ways to recover minerals while minimizing risks to human health and the environment.

Two years after enactment, and every two years after that, the EPA must send a report to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and post it publicly. The report covers the strategy, actions taken or planned by the EPA and other agencies, and any legislative recommendations. The bill does not set aside money, create new regulations, or create new permits. It is a planning and reporting measure. Whether it leads to more recovery, or to weaker or stronger waste rules, would depend on later decisions.
does: Adds a new Section 2009 to Subtitle B of the Solid Waste Disposal Act, creating the National Critical Mineral Recovery Strategy.

Directs the EPA Administrator, in consultation with other relevant federal agencies, to develop and carry out the strategy to coordinate federal efforts to recover critical minerals from discarded materials.
Requires identifying EPA and other agencies' existing programs and authorities relating to critical mineral recovery from discarded materials.

Requires identifying discarded materials (including mining waste, residuals and metal processing waste) and the critical minerals that may be in them, and opportunities to expand recovery and address legal, technological and other barriers.
Requires evaluating how recovered critical minerals strengthen domestic supply chains.
Requires identifying ways to recover minerals in a manner that minimizes risk to human health and the environment.

Requires a public report to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Environment and Public Works Committees within 2 years of enactment and every 2 years afterward. It must describe the strategy, past, ongoing and planned actions by the EPA and other agencies, and recommendations for legislation.
Defines 'critical mineral' by reference to the Energy Act of 2020 (U.S. Geological Survey's critical minerals list), and updates the table of contents of the Solid Waste Disposal Act.
who: Environmental Protection Agency and other federal agencies that must coordinate and report
Congressional committees receiving reports (House Energy and Commerce; Senate Environment and Public Works)
Mining, metal processing, recycling and waste management companies that may see new recovery opportunities or policies
Manufacturers that rely on critical minerals
Communities near mine waste or processing sites, and the general public who can read the reports

benefits: Could reduce waste and put discarded materials to productive use.
Could strengthen domestic supply chains for minerals used in electronics, batteries and defense.
Requires public reports, improving visibility into federal efforts.
Requires attention to human health and environmental risks when identifying recovery opportunities.
Coordinates scattered federal programs and may identify legal barriers.
concerns: The health and environment language only requires identifying opportunities that minimize risk, not a binding standard.
Focus on mining and processing waste and on 'legal barriers' could lead to later calls to loosen rules, though the bill itself does not.
Could add work for the EPA without any stated funding.
No requirement for public or local community input in developing the strategy.
imp.cost: The bill authorizes no new money and no CBO cost estimate is given here. Costs would be the EPA's staff time to develop the strategy and prepare reports every two years, paid from existing appropriations.
unknowns: How much the EPA would spend and whether it gets extra funding.
Whether the strategy would recommend changes to waste, mining or environmental laws.
Which materials and minerals would be prioritized.
Whether communities near affected sites would have a chance to weigh in.
Whether it would lead to actual increases in mineral recovery.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to coordinate federal efforts to recover critical minerals from discarded materials, such as mining waste and metal processing waste. It directs the EPA, working with other agencies, to create a National Critical Mineral Recovery Strategy that identifies existing programs, waste sources, barriers to recovery, and ways to strengthen U.S. supply chains while minimizing risks to health and the environment. It requires reports to Congress every two years.

oppose: The bill does not set a binding health or environmental standard. It only asks the EPA to identify recovery methods that minimize risk, so critics may want stronger safeguards written into law.
The bill asks the EPA to look at legal barriers to recovery. Opponents could worry this may lead to later proposals to loosen existing waste rules, although the bill itself does not change any rules.
The bill does not provide funding, yet it adds planning and reporting work for the EPA. You could ask how the agency would pay for this work without taking resources from other priorities.

The bill does not require public or local community input when the strategy is written. You could ask your member to add a requirement for community involvement, especially where mining or processing waste is located.
support: The bill aims to recover critical minerals from waste that already exists, which could reduce waste and put discarded materials to productive use.
Critical minerals used in electronics, batteries, and defense are often supplied from abroad. The bill asks the EPA to study how recovered minerals could strengthen U.S. supply chains.

The bill spreads federal efforts across agencies into one coordinated strategy. It also requires public reports every two years, which gives Congress and the public more visibility into what is happening.
The bill requires the strategy to look at ways to recover minerals while minimizing risks to human health and the environment, so safety is part of the planning from the start.

cost_flag: The bill authorizes no new money and no CBO cost estimate is given here. Costs would be the EPA's staff time to develop the strategy and prepare reports every two years, paid from existing appropriations.
crs:
Coordinating and Harnessing America’s Recovery of Minerals Act or the CHARM Act
This bill requires the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to establish and carry out a national strategy for recovering critical minerals from discarded materials. 
Critical minerals
 are defined as any mineral, element, substance, or material designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey because it is essential to U.S. economic or national security, has a vulnerable supply chain, and serves an essential function in manufacturing a product.
The EPA must report to Congress every two years on its actions, plans, and recommendations relating to the national strategy.

environment.reason: The bill only requires identifying ways to recover minerals while minimizing risks to health and the environment; it sets no binding standard and changes no waste rules, so its effect on environmental protection is unclear.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2009 requires a report to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Environment and Public Works Committees that is posted publicly every two years, which increases visibility into federal efforts.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill is a planning and reporting measure that creates no subsidies, permits, or rule changes, so it does not clearly shift costs or favor corporate or public interests.

local_say.reason: The bill requires no public or local community input in developing the strategy, but it also does not change any existing local decision-making authority, so the effect on local say is neutral.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill authorizes no new money and does not provide taxpayer support or ratepayer cost shifts to corporations.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same planning and reporting duties regardless of who is affected and does not create unequal treatment of any group.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal processes, enforcement, or remedies for harm, so its effect on justice is neutral.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill creates no new regulations, permits, or restrictions on individual choices and does not expand them, so it does not affect personal freedom.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage is larger, with seven headlines, and splits into two strands: NPR and NYT's environmental and safety reporting, and NYT and Politico's coverage of the permitting process. The Center group has only one article, about an Alabama fire, so it offers almost no basis for comparison. Most headlines do not name the CHARM Act, so any connection to the bill is inferred from topic, and the descriptions are empty, which limits what can be said about how each outlet characterizes the bill itself.

label: H.R. 9718
title: Reshoring American Manufacturing Act of 2026
short_title: RAM Act (Reshoring American Manufacturing Act of 2026)
one: Requires the Small Business Administration to run a free webpage, for four years, that helps small manufacturers move production back to the U.S.
summary: This bill tells the Small Business Administration (SBA) to build and maintain a website to help small businesses bring some or all of their manufacturing back to the United States. This is called "onshoring" or "reshoring." The SBA's Office of Manufacturing and Trade must launch the page within 60 days of the bill becoming law. The page must list contact information for SBA offices and partner groups. It must also offer a free tool that helps small businesses find companies or organizations that could help them move production home. The office may add other useful information. For four years, the office must ask the SBA's Chief Counsel for Advocacy for yearly suggestions on improving the page. Within two years of launch, the SBA must study how well the page works and report to Congress. It must then send updated reports each year until the four-year mark. After four years, the whole law expires. The bill does not give money, tax breaks, or loans to businesses, and it sets no new rules on them. It does not say how much the webpage will cost, and the text gives no new funding. The SBA would likely pay for it from its existing budget.

Requires the page to include contact information for general inquiries, relevant SBA offices, and partner organizations.

SBA Office of Manufacturing and Trade and Office of Advocacy staff

May help create or keep domestic manufacturing jobs, though this is not guaranteed.
Requires a public effectiveness review and reports to Congress.
Sunsets after four years, so Congress can decide whether to continue it.
Provides no direct money or tax breaks to companies.
concerns: The bill sets no standards for which partners or entities appear in the tool, such as environmental, labor, or safety records.
It has no community input requirement for the new facilities that reshoring could produce.
A website alone may do little to change decisions that are driven by costs.
Reshored factories could bring local pollution or water use, which the bill does not address.

unknowns: The exact cost to the SBA.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help small businesses move some or all of their manufacturing from overseas back to the United States, a process called onshoring or reshoring. It would do this by having the Small Business Administration create and maintain a webpage with resources, contact information, and a free tool to help businesses find entities that could assist with onshoring.

oppose: The bill sets no standards for which partners or entities appear in the free tool, such as environmental, labor, or safety records, so a listed partner may not have been vetted.
The bill does not address possible local effects of new factories, such as pollution or water use, and it has no community input requirement for new facilities.
A website alone may do little to change business decisions that are mainly driven by costs, so the bill may not achieve its goal of bringing manufacturing home.
support: The bill gives small businesses free, centralized information on moving production to the United States, which could be useful to owners who do not know where to start.
The bill may help create or keep domestic manufacturing jobs, although the bill does not guarantee this result.
The bill requires a public effectiveness review and reports to Congress, and it expires after four years, so Congress can decide whether to continue it based on how it works.

cost_flag: No money is authorized or appropriated in the text. The cost is likely absorbed by the SBA's existing budget, and no cost estimate was provided.
crs:
Reshoring American Manufacturing Act of 2026
This bill requires the Office of Manufacturing and Trade of the Small Business Administration (SBA) to establish and maintain a webpage with a list of resources and information related to onshoring to the United States all or part of the manufacturing capacity of small businesses. In general, onshoring involves transitioning the manufacture of goods by U.S. companies from overseas to domestic production.
The webpage must include (1) contact information for relevant offices of the SBA and partner organizations, (2) a free tool designed to help small businesses identify entities that could assist with onshoring the business's manufacturing capacity, and (3) other information the office determines is appropriate.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. (webpage requirement) creates a public, free online resource and requires a public effectiveness study and yearly reports to Congress on the page's performance.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill gives no money, tax breaks, or loans to businesses, so it does not involve bailouts or ratepayer shifts.

label: H.R. 1612
title: Flatside Wilderness Additions Act
short_title: Flatside Wilderness Additions Act
one: Adds about 2,212 acres of Ouachita National Forest in Arkansas to the Flatside Wilderness and renames it the Flatside-Bethune Wilderness.
summary: This bill would add about 2,212 acres of the Ouachita National Forest in Arkansas to the existing Flatside Wilderness. The added land is shown on a map dated November 12, 2024. Wilderness is the strongest level of federal land protection. It generally bars roads, motor vehicles and permanent buildings, and it keeps the land in a natural state. The bill also renames the whole area the Flatside-Bethune Wilderness, and any older legal reference to the Flatside Wilderness would count as a reference to the new name. The bill says it does not limit the Secretary of Agriculture's existing authority to take action against fire, insects and diseases in wilderness, as the Wilderness Act of 1964 and other current laws and rules allow. The bill does not provide new money. It has passed the House and is on the Senate calendar. The bill text does not say who Bethune is or what current uses of the added land might be affected, and I could not see the map itself.

label: H.R. 1665
title: DIGITAL Applications Act
short_title: DIGITAL Applications Act
one: Requires the Interior Department and the Forest Service to set up online portals within one year for applications to place cell towers and other communications equipment on federal public lands and national forests.
summary: This bill is about paperwork. Today, companies that want to put a cell tower, antenna, or other communications equipment on federal public lands or national forests use a standard application called Form 299. The bill would require the Department of the Interior and the Forest Service (part of the Agriculture Department) to each build an online portal within one year of the bill becoming law. The portals would accept, process, and "dispose of" (meaning finish handling, such as approving or denying) those applications. Each agency must tell the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the part of the Commerce Department that advises on telecom policy, within three business days of launching its portal. NTIA must then post a link to each portal on its website. The bill does not approve any projects, does not change the rules or environmental reviews that apply to these applications, and does not give anyone automatic permission to build. It also does not set a dollar amount or say where the money will come from. The bill passed the House and is now in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee. The main effects would likely be faster, more convenient, and more trackable applications. Some people may worry that easier applications will lead to more facilities on public land, though the bill text does not change review standards.
does: Requires the Interior Department and the Forest Service (through the Agriculture Department) to each set up an online portal within 1 year of enactment.

The portals must accept, process, and dispose of Form 299 applications for communications use authorizations (easements, rights-of-way, leases, licenses, or similar permissions for communications facilities on public lands or National Forest System land).
Each agency must notify NTIA's Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information within 3 business days of launching its portal.
Requires NTIA to publish a link to each portal on its website.
Defines key terms, including communications facility, covered land (BLM-type public lands and National Forest System land), and Form 299 (the existing standard application form or any successor).
Does not change the legal standards, environmental review, or public input requirements for these applications, and does not provide new funding.
who: Telecommunications and tower companies applying to place equipment on federal land
Interior Department (including land management agencies) and Forest Service staff who must build and run the portals
NTIA, which must post links
Rural and remote communities that may gain better wireless service
Users, local communities, and conservation groups concerned with development on public lands and national forests

benefits: Could make applications easier, faster, and more trackable for applicants.
Could improve government transparency and efficiency by moving a paper process online.
Could help expand wireless coverage in rural and remote areas.
A single NTIA page linking to the portals makes them easier to find.
concerns: Easier applications could lead to more facilities on public lands and national forests, with possible effects on wildlife, plants, and scenery.
The bill does not require the portals to be public-facing or to show application status or allow public comment.

label: H.R. 1681

short_title: Expediting Federal Broadband Deployment Reviews Act
one: Creates a federal task force to push the Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service to review requests to build or change communications facilities (like cell towers) on public lands faster.
summary: This bill would set up a federal "strike force" to speed up how quickly two land agencies, the Bureau of Land Management and the Forest Service, review requests to place or change communications equipment (such as cell towers or broadband lines) on public lands and national forests. These requests are called communications use authorizations, and they can be easements, rights-of-way, leases, or licenses. Within 180 days of becoming law, the head of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) would form the group. Members would be the NTIA head, the heads of the two land agencies, and one designee each from the Agriculture and Interior departments. The group would hold regular calls, set "objective and reasonable" goals for review times, and track whether each agency office meets them. Within 270 days of enactment, the NTIA head must report to several House and Senate committees on how well it is working. The bill does not change any environmental, historic, or public comment requirements, does not waive existing laws, and does not give money. It also does not say what happens if goals are missed. Supporters would likely say it helps rural areas get internet service. Critics might worry that pressure to hurry could reduce careful review of land impacts, though the bill text doesn't require shortcuts.

label: H.R. 1709
title: Understanding Cybersecurity of Mobile Networks Act
short_title: Understanding Cybersecurity of Mobile Networks Act
one: Requires the Commerce Department's telecom agency (NTIA) to study and report to Congress within one year on how secure U.S. mobile phone networks and devices are against hacking and spying by adversaries.
summary: This bill asks for a study, not new rules. Within one year of becoming law, the head of the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), working with the Department of Homeland Security, must send a report to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee. The report would look at how well U.S. mobile networks and phones hold up against cyberattacks and spying by "adversaries." That term covers hackers and also foreign governments or groups that act against U.S. security. The report must assess whether mobile providers have fixed known weaknesses and whether they follow security best practices. It must also cover how common and effective encryption and identity-checking technology is, what keeps providers from upgrading to stronger tools or dropping older weak ones, and whether customers weigh security when buying service or phones. It must estimate how common, how costly, and how available "cell site simulators" are, along with other tools that can intercept phone traffic. These are fake cell towers, and adversaries could use them. NTIA must consult many groups, including the FCC, intelligence agencies, researchers, small and rural providers, and device makers. The report is limited to mobile networks and leaves out 5G. It must be public in unclassified form, though it may have a classified annex. Details that could help attackers would be removed from the public version. Congress's committees would get the full version. The bill sets no money amount and creates no new requirements for companies.

title: Communications Security Act
short_title: Communications Security Act
one: Gives the FCC's communications security advisory council a permanent legal basis, sets who can serve on it, and requires its reports to be posted publicly.
summary:
This bill would turn into law an advisory council that the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) already uses to get advice on the security, reliability, and interoperability of communications networks. Interoperability means different systems and equipment working together. Within 90 days of enactment, the FCC would either create a new council or designate an existing advisory committee for the job. If it picks an existing committee, it would have to change the membership to match the bill's rules.

The FCC Chair would appoint members to 2-year terms. Where practicable, members would include communications company representatives, public interest groups or universities, and officials from federal, state, local, or tribal governments, with at least one from each level of government. The Chair could leave out any company or group deemed "not trusted." That means the Chair has publicly found it tied to a foreign adversary, or has found it a national security threat using criteria from the 2019 Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act. Each member must have relevant knowledge and experience.

Every two years, the council would send the Chair its reports, including working-group reports and recommendations. The FCC would have to post each report on its website. The council would also be exempt from the normal rule that federal advisory committees end after two years unless renewed. The bill does not appropriate any new money, and the advice would not be binding on the FCC.

crs:
Communications Security Act
This bill provides statutory authority for a council established by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to provide advice regarding the security, reliability, and interoperability of communications networks. (This advice is currently provided by the FCC’s Communications Security, Reliability, and Interoperability Council.)
The bill specifies that the FCC may designate an existing advisory committee to fulfill this role, provided the committee’s membership is modified, as necessary, to comply with membership requirements set forth in the bill. 
Specifically, the bill requires the council to include, to the extent practicable, representatives of companies in the communications industry; public interest organizations or academic institutions; and federal, state, tribal, and local governments (with at least one member representing each level of government). Members are to be selected by the FCC's chair and generally may not include representatives of entities owned or controlled by, or subject to the influence of, a foreign adversary, or otherwise deemed to pose a threat to U.S. national security. 
Under current law, federal advisory committees must generally terminate after two years unless they are renewed or a statute specifies a different termination date. However, the bill exempts the council from this requirement.

one: Adds two Colorado public water providers to the list of entities allowed to access, use, maintain, and repair the Bolts Ditch and its headgate inside the Holy Cross Wilderness.
summary: The Bolts Ditch is an old water ditch and headgate (the gate that controls how much water enters the ditch) located inside the Holy Cross Wilderness in Colorado. A 2019 public lands law, the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act, already lets certain parties access the ditch to divert water and to use, maintain, and repair it. This bill makes a one-sentence change to that law. It adds two more entities to the list: the Eagle River Water and Sanitation District, which is a Colorado special district (a local government body), and the Upper Eagle Regional Water Authority, a regional water authority organized under Colorado law. Both are public water providers. The bill does not create new water rights, does not say how much water can be taken, and does not give money. It also does not change the wilderness boundaries. Based on the text, the entities would get permission to access the site for diversion, use, maintenance, and repair, as the existing law already allows for others. The bill does not spell out what environmental review or conditions, if any, would apply. Those details come from the 2019 law and from existing water rights, and I could not see them in the material provided. The bill has passed the House and is now in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

title: To direct the Secretary of Commerce to submit to Congress a report containing an assessment of the value, cost, and feasibility of a trans-Atlantic submarine fiber optic cable connecting the contiguous United States, the United States Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria.
short_title: Trans-Atlantic Undersea Cable Study (U.S.–Virgin Islands–Ghana–Nigeria)
one: The bill orders the Commerce Department to study, and report to Congress within one year, whether a undersea internet cable linking the U.S. mainland, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria is worthwhile, affordable, and feasible.
summary: This bill does not build anything. It only asks for a study. Within one year of becoming law, the Secretary of Commerce, working through the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), must send a report to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee. The report would look at the value, cost, and feasibility of a trans-Atlantic undersea fiber optic cable connecting the contiguous U.S., the U.S. Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria, with the goal of strengthening U.S. national security. It must cover digital and national security and economic opportunities, how long the current cables to the Virgin Islands will last, how secure current communications to the islands are, whether Virgin Islands telecom infrastructure is ready, and the chance to work with "trusted" partners. It must also look at building a data center and high-security cloud facility with its own power supply in the Virgin Islands to serve U.S. Africa Command, Special Operations Command, and other national security communications. The agency cannot force any company or group to hand over data for the report. The report must be public (unclassified) but may have a classified annex. The bill does not give any money for the study or the cable, and it does not say who would pay for a cable if one were built later.
does: Requires the Secretary of Commerce (acting through NTIA) to deliver a report to the House Energy and Commerce and Senate Commerce committees within 1 year of enactment.
The report assesses the value, cost, and feasibility of a undersea fiber optic cable linking the contiguous U.S., U.S. Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria to enhance U.S. national security.

Required topics include digital security, national security, and economic opportunities; lifespan of existing cables to the Virgin Islands; current security of mainland–Virgin Islands telecommunications; and readiness of Virgin Islands infrastructure.

Also must assess working with 'trusted' entities and the geopolitical and economic benefits, connectivity opportunities to maximize U.S. economic investment, and the state of submarine cables tied to U.S. networks.

Must assess the value, cost, and feasibility of a data center and high-security cloud facility with independent power generation in the Virgin Islands for Africa Command, Special Operations Command, and national security communications.
Bars the Secretary from requiring any entity to provide data for the report.
Report must be unclassified with no dissemination restrictions, but may include a classified annex.
Defines 'not trusted' entities by reference to national security risk determinations under the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019; 'trusted' means not so determined.
who: Residents and businesses of the U.S. Virgin Islands, who could see better connectivity and possible infrastructure investment if a cable is later built
Federal agencies, especially Commerce/NTIA, which would carry out the study
Military commands (Africa Command, Special Operations Command) that could use secure communications
Telecommunications and cable companies and data center operators who may be potential partners or competitors
People and businesses in Ghana and Nigeria
Congressional committees receiving the report
Taxpayers, who would fund the study staff time

benefits: Public, unclassified report would give Congress and the public information about cable security and the aging Virgin Islands connections.
Could identify ways to improve internet reliability and economic opportunity in the U.S. Virgin Islands.
No mandatory data collection protects companies from compelled disclosure burdens.
Low cost and no commitment to build anything.
concerns: The text does not require assessing environmental effects on oceans, marine life, or local ecosystems.
It does not require input from Virgin Islands residents or the local government.
The data center with independent power generation could raise air emission or fuel questions if later pursued.
It does not address who would pay for a future cable, so private companies could later seek public subsidies.
A classified annex may limit some public visibility.
Military framing (Special Operations, Africa Command) may influence how the territory's infrastructure is used.
imp.cost: No funding is authorized or appropriated. The study would be carried out by NTIA/Commerce using existing resources; no cost estimate was provided in the material I was given. Any cable or data center cost would be assessed in the report itself.
unknowns: Actual cost of a cable and the data center, which the report would estimate.
Who would build, own, and pay for any cable.
Environmental effects of the cable and facilities.
Whether the report would lead to any legislation or funding.
How much of the report would be classified.
Whether the bill will advance in the Senate committee.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to get a report on whether a trans-Atlantic undersea fiber optic cable linking the contiguous U.S., the U.S. Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria would be worth it, how much it would cost, and whether it can be built, with the aim of strengthening U.S. national security. The bill points to the age of existing cables to the Virgin Islands and the security of current communications to the islands as reasons to study the question. It does not fund or require construction of any cable.

oppose: The bill spends federal effort on a study that does not address who would pay for a cable, so a future project could later seek public subsidies.
The report does not require assessing environmental effects on oceans, marine life, or local ecosystems, which a constituent could ask Congress to add before any project moves forward.
The bill does not require input from Virgin Islands residents or the territorial government, so local voices would not be part of the study as written.
A data center with independent power generation and a classified annex could raise questions about fuel or air emissions and about public visibility if the project is pursued later.
support: The bill asks for a public, unclassified report, giving Congress and the public information about the security and age of current cables to the U.S. Virgin Islands.
The study could identify ways to improve internet reliability and economic opportunity for Virgin Islands residents and businesses.
The bill costs little and commits the government to building nothing; it only asks for an assessment.
The bill bars the Secretary from forcing companies to hand over data, which limits the compliance burden on private firms during the study.

crs: This bill requires the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to submit a report to Congress that assesses the feasibility, value, cost, and security implications of a submarine fiber optic cable to connect the contiguous United States, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Ghana, and Nigeria. The report must include, among other topics, an assessment of the potential establishment of a data center and high-security cloud services facility in the U.S. Virgin Islands for certain national security communications.

environment.reason: The study does not build anything and the report is not required to assess environmental effects, so it neither protects nor harms water, air, or land.

transparency_kindness.reason: Report must be public and unclassified with no dissemination restrictions (Report provision), though a classified annex is allowed, which limits some visibility.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill only requests a feasibility study; it does not shift costs to consumers or taxpayers or favor corporate profit, and it does not address who would pay for a future cable.

local_say.reason: The bill does not require input from Virgin Islands residents or government, but it also does not reduce any existing local authority, so the effect is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: No funding is authorized or appropriated, and the bill does not direct any taxpayer money to corporations, so it does not touch bailouts or ratepayer shifts.

equality.reason: The bill treats the study subjects evenly and does not create unequal rights; the 'trusted' versus 'not trusted' entity distinction applies to companies by national security determination, not to people.

justice.reason: The bill neither adds nor removes due process or remedies for harm; it is a study request.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not change what individuals may legally do, say, or choose.

label: H.R. 1765
title: Promoting United States Wireless Leadership Act of 2025
short_title: Promoting U.S. Wireless Leadership Act
one: Directs the Commerce Department's NTIA to encourage and help U.S. companies and other stakeholders take part in international bodies that set 5G and future wireless standards, while excluding those deemed national security threats.
summary: This bill tells the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), part of the Commerce Department, to help the United States have a stronger voice in the groups that set technical rules for 5G and future wireless networks. These groups include the International Organization for Standardization, 3GPP, the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, and bodies accredited by ANSI or ATIS. NTIA would work with the National Institute of Standards and Technology and the State Department. It would "equitably" encourage a wide range of companies and other stakeholders to join these bodies, and offer them technical expertise to help them take part, as far as each body allows. Companies or stakeholders that NTIA finds to be a national security threat ("not trusted") are left out. NTIA may only make that finding based on specific decisions by national security interagency bodies, Commerce supply-chain determinations under Executive Order 13873, or whether the company makes equipment covered by the 2019 defense law's ban (section 889). Within 60 days of enactment, NTIA must brief key House and Senate committees on its strategy. The bill does not give new money, set new rules for the public, or create new penalties. It only directs outreach and technical help. The bill passed the House and now sits in a Senate committee.
does: Requires NTIA (the Assistant Secretary of Commerce for Communications and Information), in consultation with NIST and the State Department, to equitably encourage companies and a wide variety of stakeholders to participate in standards-setting bodies for 5G and future wireless networks, to the extent those bodies allow.
Requires NTIA to equitably offer technical expertise to those companies and stakeholders to help them participate.
Excludes any company or stakeholder NTIA determines is 'not trusted,' meaning a national security threat.

Limits that determination to specific findings by executive branch national security bodies (such as the Federal Acquisition Security Council), Commerce determinations under Executive Order 13873, or whether the company provides covered telecom equipment under section 889(f)(3) of the 2019 defense law.
Lists covered bodies: ISO, voluntary bodies such as 3GPP and IEEE, and any body accredited by ANSI or ATIS.
Requires a briefing to the House Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs Committees and Senate Commerce and Foreign Relations Committees within 60 days of enactment on NTIA's strategy.
Defines terms such as 5G network, cloud computing, communications network, and not trusted.
who: NTIA and other federal agencies (NIST, State Department)
U.S. telecommunications and technology companies and other stakeholders (such as researchers and groups) that join standards bodies
Companies deemed national security threats or making covered equipment, who would be excluded from NTIA's help
Congressional committees receiving the briefing
Consumers and the public, indirectly, through the kind of wireless technology standards that get adopted

benefits: Could give U.S. companies and other stakeholders more help taking part in global wireless standards, possibly strengthening security and interoperability.
Requires a briefing to four congressional committees, which adds some oversight.
The 'not trusted' test is limited to specific, existing national security findings, which limits arbitrary exclusions.
Calls for 'equitable' outreach to a wide variety of stakeholders, not just large firms.
concerns: Mainly supports industry participation; no explicit seats for consumer or public-interest groups.
The 'not trusted' determinations may not be public, so the process could be hard for the public to check.
Briefings go to Congress, not the public, so transparency is limited.
Could indirectly benefit large companies with the most resources to take part.
imp.cost: The bill provides no new funding and no cost estimate was given. NTIA would carry out the duties with existing resources, though costs are not specified.
unknowns: How much NTIA's outreach would cost and whether it would need extra funding.
Which companies and stakeholders would be labeled 'not trusted,' and whether those decisions would be public.
How 'equitably' will be defined and applied in practice.
Whether the standards bodies will allow added participation, since the bill applies only 'to the extent' they allow it.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help the United States have a stronger voice in the international groups that set technical standards for 5G and future wireless networks. It directs the National Telecommunications and Information Administration to encourage a wide range of companies and stakeholders to take part in those groups and to offer them technical help, while excluding entities found to be national security threats.

oppose: The bill sets no explicit seats or support for consumer and public-interest groups. Supporters could be asked how the bill ensures everyday users have a voice in standards-setting, not just industry.

Outreach and technical help may mostly benefit large companies that already have the staff and money to take part in standards bodies. Smaller firms and public-interest groups could still be left behind.
The 'not trusted' determinations may not be made public, and briefings go to Congress rather than the public. Citizens may have limited ability to check how exclusion decisions are made.
support: The bill targets a real gap: it asks NTIA to help U.S. companies and stakeholders join global wireless standards groups, which could help shape the rules for 5G and future networks.
It adds oversight by requiring NTIA to brief four congressional committees within 60 days of enactment on its strategy.

The 'not trusted' exclusion is limited to specific, existing national security findings, such as decisions by federal national security bodies or the section 889 equipment ban, which may limit arbitrary exclusions.

crs:
Promoting United States Wireless Leadership Act of 2025
This bill requires the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to encourage companies and other relevant stakeholders to participate in organizations that set standards for wireless communications networks and equipment. NTIA must also offer technical assistance to facilitate such participation. 
NTIA may not encourage or facilitate participation by companies and stakeholders determined to pose a threat to U.S. national security.

transparency_kindness.reason: Under the 'not trusted' provision, NTIA's exclusion determinations may not be public, and the only oversight is a briefing to four congressional committees rather than public reporting or comment.

equality.reason: The bill directs NTIA to encourage a wide variety of stakeholders to participate 'equitably' and to offer technical expertise, which broadens access to standards-setting, though the exclusion of 'not trusted' companies treats some firms differently.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage (four headlines) centers on the Nvidia-China national security angle and the political fallout for Commerce Secretary Lutnick, with the Megaspeed matter treated as a dispute within the administration. Center coverage (two headlines) reports the Megaspeed export ban as a regulatory fact, plus an unrelated AI safety report. Neither group's headlines mention the Promoting United States Wireless Leadership Act of 2025, and the evidence is thin (six headlines with no descriptions), so this analysis cannot establish how either side frames the bill itself.

label: H.R. 1766
title: NTIA Policy and Cybersecurity Coordination Act
short_title: NTIA Policy and Cybersecurity Coordination Act
one: Creates a formal Office of Policy Development and Cybersecurity inside the NTIA (the Commerce Department's telecom and internet policy agency) and renames its existing policy chief position to match.
summary:
This bill sets up a new office inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA). The NTIA is the part of the Commerce Department that advises the President on telephone, internet, and communications policy. The new Office of Policy Development and Cybersecurity would be led by an Associate Administrator who reports to the head of the NTIA. The person who now holds the closest existing job, Associate Administrator for Policy Analysis and Development, would be renamed and would keep working in the new role automatically.

The office would study and develop policy on the internet, phones, media, and other digital services. It would promote what the bill calls "market-based" policies for innovation, competition, consumer access, digital inclusion, and workforce development. It would run studies on how Americans use the internet and phones, when told to by the NTIA head or Congress. It would coordinate open, consensus-based, multistakeholder processes (meetings of industry, experts, and others) to write cybersecurity and privacy guidance. It would encourage security researchers to work with communications companies and software developers. It would also push for secure supply chains, help commercialize new communications technology, and give the public access to related data and research. It would pay particular attention to small businesses and rural communities and ask small and rural providers for feedback. The bill does not give the office new regulatory power, and it does not provide any new money. The text does not say how much it would cost.
does: Creates the Office of Policy Development and Cybersecurity within the NTIA, led by an Associate Administrator who reports to the Assistant Secretary (the NTIA head).

Directs the office to analyze and develop national communications and internet policy, including 'market-based' policies for innovation, competition, consumer access, digital inclusion, workforce development, and economic growth.

Requires studies, when delegated by the Assistant Secretary or required by Congress, on how people in the U.S. access and use the internet, phones, mass media, other digital services, and video services.
Directs the office to coordinate transparent, consensus-based, multistakeholder processes to create cybersecurity and privacy guidance for the internet and other communications networks.
Promotes collaboration between security researchers and communications providers and software developers, and supports policies for network security, resilience, and secure supply chains.

Lets the office assist with the program for preventing future vulnerabilities under the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019, and present cybersecurity policy before the FCC, Congress, and elsewhere at the Assistant Secretary's direction.

Directs the office to speed innovation and commercialization of communications technology, identify barriers such as access to capital, and give the public data, research, and technical help, while protecting classified information.

Requires coordination within Commerce, with state agencies, and with the FCC or other federal agencies, with a focus on small businesses and rural communities, and requires the office to seek feedback from small and rural providers.
Renames the current Associate Administrator for Policy Analysis and Development as Associate Administrator for Policy Development and Cybersecurity, and the current officeholder continues in the job.
who: NTIA staff and leadership, especially the current policy Associate Administrator
Telecommunications, internet, and software companies that would take part in cybersecurity processes
Small and rural communications providers, who would be asked for feedback
Internet and phone users, especially in rural or underserved areas
Security researchers
Congress, the FCC, and other agencies that receive NTIA policy advice

benefits: Gives cybersecurity and privacy policy a clear home and leader within the NTIA.
Requires public access to relevant data and research and open, consensus-based processes.
Focuses on digital inclusion, rural communities, and small providers.
Could improve the security of communications networks and supply chains.
concerns: The 'market-based' framing and commercialization goals could favor industry interests over consumer protection.
Multistakeholder processes can be dominated by well-resourced companies.
The office would advise and advocate but has no binding authority, so its effect could be limited.
The bill may duplicate work already done by the NTIA's existing policy office, since it mostly renames that position.
imp.cost: The bill does not authorize new funding. Costs would come from the NTIA's existing budget. No cost estimate is provided in the material given.
unknowns: Whether the NTIA would get extra staff or money for the office.
How much real change this brings, since it largely formalizes and renames an existing policy function.
Who would take part in the multistakeholder processes and how consumer groups would be included.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to create an Office of Policy Development and Cybersecurity inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), so that the agency has a dedicated office to analyze and develop policy on internet and communications technologies, including innovation, competition, cybersecurity and resilience, and commercialization of communications technology. The bill's official title and CRS summary describe this as a policy and cybersecurity coordination effort; they do not state the specific problem that prompted it.

oppose: The bill's policy goals are framed around 'market-based' approaches and commercialization. A constituent could ask the member how the office will make sure consumer protection and privacy get equal weight with industry growth.

The office would advise and advocate but has no binding authority and no new funding, and the bill does not state its cost. A constituent could ask whether this new layer would add cost or overlap with the NTIA's existing policy office, since the bill mostly renames that position.

Multistakeholder processes can be dominated by well-resourced companies. A constituent could ask what safeguards ensure that smaller companies, consumer groups, and the public have a real voice in writing cybersecurity and privacy guidance.
support: The bill gives cybersecurity and privacy policy a clear leader and home inside the NTIA, which a constituent could say is a sensible way to organize federal work on a growing set of security risks.

The bill requires public access to relevant data and research and open, consensus-based processes. A constituent could say this promotes transparency in how communications security guidance is developed.

The bill directs attention to small businesses, rural communities, and small providers, and requires the office to seek their feedback. A constituent could say this helps make sure rural areas are not left out of network security and digital access policy.

crs:
NTIA Policy and Cybersecurity Coordination Act
This bill establishes an Office of Policy Development and Cybersecurity within the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA) to analyze and develop policies related to internet and communications technologies.
Specific activities of the office include, for example, developing policies that promote (1) innovation, competition, and other elements of the communications, media, and technology markets; (2) security and resilience to cybersecurity incidents while fostering innovation; and (3) commercialization of communications technologies.
The existing Associate Administrator for Policy Analysis and Development within NTIA must be redesignated as Associate Administrator for Policy Development and Cybersecurity, and must serve as head of the office.

transparency_kindness.reason: Requires transparent, consensus-based multistakeholder processes for cybersecurity and privacy guidance and gives the public access to data and research, though the bill does not set specific public comment or disclosure rules.

people_over_profit.reason: The 'market-based' framing and commercialization goals, including identifying barriers like access to capital, lean toward industry growth, though the office also focuses on digital inclusion and rural and small providers.

local_say.reason: The bill has the office coordinate with state agencies and seek feedback from small and rural providers, but it does not give states or localities new decision-making authority.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no provisions about bailouts or ratepayer charges; it authorizes no new funding and uses existing NTIA budget.

equality.reason: Sec. on digital inclusion and attention to rural communities and small providers supports equal access to internet and phone services for underserved groups.

justice.reason: The bill creates no new legal process, remedies, or accountability mechanisms; it is advisory and has no binding authority.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do, say, or choose about their own lives.

label: H.R. 2247
title: Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act
short_title: Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act
one: Lets pilots show FAA inspectors a digital copy of their pilot or medical certificate instead of only a paper original, with the FAA required to update its rules by November 30, 2028.
summary: Right now, pilots must carry physical copies of their pilot (airman) certificates and medical certificates and show them when asked by the FAA and certain other officials. This bill would change federal aviation law so that a pilot can show an FAA inspector either a physical certificate or a digital certificate issued by the FAA. The digital version could be stored on an electronic device, or in a cloud-based system where there is enough internet connection. The digital certificate would have to be presented following authentication and verification rules (ways to prove it is real) set by the FAA. The bill also requires the FAA to issue a final rule by November 30, 2028, updating its regulations in several parts of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations (parts 61, 63, 65, 67 and 107) to carry out the change. The bill text itself speaks only of presenting certificates to FAA inspectors; the CRS summary notes that current rules also cover law enforcement, TSA, and NTSB requests, and the bill does not clearly change those. The bill does not list a cost or funding amount. It is a small, practical change that mostly reduces paperwork for pilots, including recreational drone pilots and others covered by those rule parts, though details about security and privacy depend on FAA rules yet to be written.
does: Adds a new subsection (m) to 49 U.S.C. 44703 allowing anyone issued an airman certificate, including a medical certificate, to present it to an FAA inspector in physical or digital form.
Physical option: a certificate issued by the FAA Administrator or a designee.
Digital option: a digital certificate issued by the Administrator, stored on an electronic device or, where connectivity is sufficient, a cloud-based system.
Digital certificates must be presented under authentication and verification requirements set by the FAA Administrator.
Requires the FAA to issue a final rule by November 30, 2028, updating 14 CFR parts 61, 63, 65, 67, and 107 and any related guidance and policies.
The bill text only addresses presentation to FAA inspectors; it does not explicitly change rules for presenting to law enforcement, TSA, or NTSB.
who: Pilots holding FAA airman certificates and medical certificates
Remote (drone) pilots covered by part 107
Other certificate holders under parts 63 and 65 (e.g., flight crew, mechanics, air traffic controllers)
FAA inspectors and the FAA rulemaking staff
Pilots without reliable connectivity or devices

benefits: Pilots no longer risk being unable to show proof of certification if a paper copy is lost or left behind.
Could reduce paperwork and replacement costs.
Physical certificates remain valid, so no one is forced to go digital.
FAA sets authentication standards, which could reduce fraud.
concerns: Pilots without smartphones, reliable power, or connectivity could be disadvantaged if digital becomes the norm.
Storing medical certificates digitally raises possible privacy and data security questions.
The bill only mentions FAA inspectors, so pilots might still need paper for other officials.
Rulemaking could take until late 2028, so the benefit may be slow to arrive.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is provided in the material. The FAA would bear the costs of building digital certificates and writing rules, presumably from existing appropriations.
unknowns: What authentication and verification standards the FAA will adopt.
How digital medical certificate data will be protected.
Whether other agencies (TSA, NTSB, law enforcement) will accept digital copies.
Cost to the FAA of implementing the digital system.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to let pilots show FAA inspectors a digital copy of their airman and medical certificates, in addition to the existing paper option, so that a lost or forgotten paper certificate is less of a problem. It requires the FAA to update its rules (14 CFR parts 61, 63, 65, 67 and 107) by a final rule due November 30, 2028, and says digital certificates must follow FAA authentication and verification requirements.

oppose: Digital certificates would depend on phones, batteries, and internet or cloud access. Pilots without these tools could end up at a disadvantage if digital copies become the common expectation.
Storing medical certificates digitally raises privacy and data security questions. Constituents may want to see the FAA's security and privacy rules before the change takes effect.
The bill only addresses FAA inspectors. Pilots may still need paper for law enforcement, TSA, or NTSB requests, so the bill may not reduce carrying paper as much as its title suggests.
support: The bill lets pilots show a digital certificate to an FAA inspector, so a lost, forgotten, or damaged paper card would no longer mean a problem during an inspection.
Digital certificates could reduce paperwork and the cost of replacing lost certificates for pilots, including recreational drone pilots under Part 107.
Paper certificates stay valid under the bill, so no pilot would be forced to switch to digital. The FAA must also set authentication and verification standards, which could help reduce fraud.

crs:
Pilot Certificate Accessibility Act
This bill allows a pilot to present a digital copy of certain certificates (e.g., an airman certificate or a medical certificate) when required to present such documentation by a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) inspector.
Under current FAA regulations, a pilot must present for inspection a physical copy of an airman certificate and other paperwork upon a request from the FAA; a federal, state, or local law enforcement officer; or an authorized representative of the Transportation Security Administration or the National Transportation Safety Board. This bill allows a pilot to present a certificate such as an airman certificate or a medical certificate to an FAA inspector as (1) a physical, original copy; or (2) a digital copy stored on an electronic device or cloud storage platform.
The FAA must update current regulations to implement this change.

equality.reason: New subsection (m) of 49 U.S.C. 44703 gives digital presentation rights that depend on having a device and connectivity, so pilots without smartphones or reliable internet could be disadvantaged in practice, though physical certificates remain valid.

personal_freedom.reason: New subsection (m) lets certificate holders choose between physical and digital presentation to FAA inspectors, expanding how they can meet the requirement.

label: H.R. 5663
title: ACPAC Modernization Act
short_title: ACPAC Modernization Act
one: Adds a ticket agent representative to the Department of Transportation's Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee.
summary: The Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, or ACPAC, advises the U.S. Department of Transportation on ways to improve airline customer service. Under current law, it has four required seats: one each for airlines, airport operators, state or local governments with consumer protection expertise, and nonprofit public interest groups with consumer protection expertise. This bill adds a fifth required seat for a representative of ticket agents. Ticket agents are businesses that sell airline tickets to the public, such as travel agencies and online booking sites. The bill also removes the words "ticket agents," from another part of the same section of law (subsection (i)). The bill text doesn't show what that subsection says, so it is probably a clean-up change to match the new seat, but I couldn't confirm that. The bill doesn't create new spending, new rules for airlines or ticket sellers, or new powers for the committee. It only changes who must sit on an advisory body. The bill passed the House and was sent to the Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee in March 2026. Its effect on travelers would be indirect. It would give ticket sellers a formal voice when the committee gives advice, and the Department of Transportation would not have to follow that advice.
does: Amends Section 411(b) of the FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012 to add a fifth required category of committee member: ticket agents.

Keeps the four existing member categories: air carriers, airport operators, state or local governments with consumer protection expertise, and nonprofit public interest groups with consumer protection expertise.

Strikes the words 'ticket agents,' from subsection (i) of the same section. The bill text doesn't show what that subsection says, so the exact effect is unclear, but it appears to be a conforming edit.
Does not add funding, new regulations, or new powers for the committee.
who: Ticket agents, such as travel agencies and online booking companies, who would gain a guaranteed seat on the committee
Airlines and airports, who share the committee with one more member
Consumer groups and state or local government members, whose seats would not change but who would have one more voice at the table
Air travelers, who could be affected indirectly through the committee's advice to the Department of Transportation
Department of Transportation staff who run the committee

benefits: Ticket sellers who deal with travelers every day would have a formal voice in the committee's advice.
The committee could hear a wider range of practical problems, such as refunds and fee disclosure.
There is no new cost or new regulation.
concerns: One more industry-side seat could shift the balance of the committee away from consumer advocates, though consumer seats remain.
A larger committee could make it a bit harder to reach agreement.
imp.cost: The bill provides no new funding. It changes only the makeup of an existing committee. No cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: What subsection (i) of Section 411 says and why 'ticket agents,' is being removed from it.
How ticket agents would be chosen for the seat and whether the committee's size or voting rules would change.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill.

stage.last_action: Received in the Senate and Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.

purpose: The bill says it adds a required seat for a ticket agent representative on the Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee (ACPAC), which advises the Department of Transportation on airline customer service improvements. According to the CRS summary, the change expands the committee's membership to include ticket sellers, who deal directly with travelers. The bill does not add funding, new regulations, or new powers for the committee.

oppose: The committee already has four required seats, and the bill adds a fifth for an industry group. Some people may feel this gives the seller side more weight in advice meant to protect travelers.
The bill does not add funding or rules, but a larger committee could be harder to organize and could take longer to reach agreement on advice.

Consumer seats stay in place, but you could ask your representative whether consumer and public interest voices should be given extra weight, or whether the balance of seats should be reviewed as a whole.
support: Ticket agents, such as travel agencies and online booking sites, handle refunds, fees, and changes for many travelers every day. Giving them a required seat would bring that practical experience into the committee's advice.
The bill is low-cost. It does not add spending, new rules for airlines or ticket sellers, or new powers for the committee.
The committee would gain a wider range of views on customer service problems, such as refunds and fee disclosure, which could lead to more useful advice to the Department of Transportation.

label: H.R. 2102
title: Major Richard Star Act
short_title: Major Richard Star Act
one: The bill would let certain medically retired veterans with combat-related disabilities and fewer than 20 years of service keep their full military retired pay while also receiving their VA disability compensation, instead of having one reduced by the other.
summary:
Today, many veterans who retire from the military and also get VA disability pay see their military retired pay cut by the amount of the disability pay. This is called an "offset." Some veterans who served 20 or more years have had that offset removed over time. But veterans who were medically retired because of injury or illness (under "chapter 61" of the law) with fewer than 20 years of service are still hit by the offset, even when their disability came from combat.

This bill would end the offset for that group. If a veteran was medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service and is eligible for combat-related special compensation (a separate payment for combat-related disabilities), their retired pay could no longer be reduced because of their VA disability pay. They would receive both in full.

The bill also cleans up the law. It changes a section title and deletes old language about a phase-in period that has already ended. The changes would start on the first day of the first month after the bill becomes law. They would apply to payments for months from that date on. The bill does not say it pays back money withheld in the past. It also does not state a cost. The House has passed it, and it now goes to the Senate Armed Services Committee.

Applies to those veterans who are eligible for combat-related special compensation.
Changes the title of section 1414 of title 10 to refer to "concurrent receipt" of retired pay and VA disability compensation.
Removes outdated phase-in language that no longer applies.
Takes effect the first day of the first month after enactment, covering payments from then on.

Families and survivors who depend on those veterans' income
The Department of Defense and the Department of Veterans Affairs, which administer the payments
Federal taxpayers, because the government would pay out more

benefits: Veterans with combat-related disabilities in this group could receive their full retired pay and full VA disability pay.
Could reduce financial strain for veterans whose retired pay was previously cut by the offset.
The bill removes an outdated phase-in provision, which may make the law easier to read.
concerns: The bill does not pay back money withheld in the past, so veterans who lost pay before the change may not get that money back.
Because the change applies only to this group, veterans with other disabilities or other service lengths may still face the offset.
The material does not describe how the change fits with other concurrent-receipt rules.

The total cost to the government and how it would be funded.
Whether the Senate will pass the bill in its current form.

The bill covers only one group: combat-related disabled veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service. Veterans with other disabilities or other service lengths would still face the offset, which some may see as an uneven result.

The summary does not explain how this change fits with other concurrent-receipt rules, and it does not state a cost, so Congress would need to review the budget impact and related rules before acting.

The offset currently applies to veterans medically retired with fewer than 20 years of service even when their disability came from combat, and this bill would end that reduction for that group.

label: H.R. 7954
title: Don Young Doug LaMalfa Indian Buffalo Management Act
short_title: Indian Buffalo Management Act
one: Directs the Interior Department to help Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations own, restore, and manage buffalo herds and habitat on Indian land, through contracts, grants, technical help, consultation, and transfer of surplus federal buffalo, for seven years.
summary: This bill would tell the Department of the Interior to work with Indian Tribes and Tribal organizations so they can own and manage buffalo (bison) and the land where buffalo live on Indian land. Interior would have to sign contracts and cooperative agreements and give grants to Tribes and qualifying Tribal groups. The money could pay for buffalo restoration or management programs, commercial activities tied to buffalo or buffalo products, mobile Tribal meat processing facilities, and other related work. Interior would also have to give technical help. Within one year, and then on an ongoing basis, Interior would have to consult with Tribes on Interior actions that affect buffalo, including efforts to contain or wipe out diseased buffalo. It would also write a policy for managing buffalo and habitat on Indian land that follows Tribal-approved plans and Tribal laws. Information that Tribes label as culturally sensitive, proprietary, or confidential could not be shared by Interior. Interior could also, but is not required to, sign agreements to move surplus buffalo from federal land onto Indian land, and could waive charges for them. The bill says it does not weaken federal or state laws on diseased buffalo or buffalo that escape Indian land, and it does not change treaty rights. The authority ends seven years after the bill becomes law. The bill does not set a dollar amount.

This bill directs the Department of the Interior to work with Indian Tribes and tribal organizations to develop and promote tribal ownership and management of buffalo and buffalo habitat on Indian lands.

label: H.R. 8483
title: Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026
short_title: Barona Tribe Land Transfer Act
one: Moves about 847 acres of federal land in San Diego County into trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians, keeps public access and fire-response access, and bans casino gaming on it.
summary:
This bill would take three pieces of federal land in San Diego County, California, totaling about 847 acres, and place them in trust for the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians. "In trust" means the United States holds the land for the Tribe, and it becomes part of the Tribe's reservation. One piece (about 164 acres) is now managed by the Bureau of Land Management. The other two (about 683 acres) are now managed by the Forest Service, and control of those would move to the Interior Department.

The transfer comes with conditions. Existing rights such as easements, leases, permits and road rights-of-way would stay in place. The public would keep access for recreation, scenery, science and conservation, including existing roads and trails, under the rules in effect when the bill is enacted. Federal employees would keep access for search and rescue, wildfire fighting, evacuations and land management. Federal agencies could still do fuel-reduction work in consultation with the Tribe. The Tribe must maintain the fuel break (a cleared strip meant to slow wildfire) on the two Forest Service parcels to Forest Service standards. The land cannot be used for casino-style gaming. Existing water rights and service agreements would not be changed. The Interior and Agriculture departments must prepare an official map available for public inspection. The bill text gives no cost estimate.

Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians Land Transfer Act of 2026
This bill takes three parcels of specified federal land (approximately 847 acres) in San Diego County, California, into trust for the benefit of the Barona Group of Capitan Grande Band of Mission Indians of the Barona Reservation, California. The land taken into trust shall be part of the Tribe's reservation.
One parcel (approximately 164 acres) is currently administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), and two parcels (approximately 683 acres) are currently administered by the Forest Service. Administrative jurisdiction over the Forest Service land must be transferred to the Department of the Interior.
Among other requirements, the bill requires the land taken into trust to remain subject to (1) existing liens, rights-of-way, reciprocal road rights-of-way agreements, licenses, leases, permits, special use permits, and easements; (2) continuing public access to the land, including roads and trails, as on the date of the bill's enactment; and (3) rights-of-way necessary for BLM and Forest Service employees to access the land for operational and emergency purposes (e.g., wildfire suppression).
The bill requires the Tribe to maintain the fuel break within two of the parcels in accordance with applicable Forest Service standards.
The bill prohibits gaming on the land taken into trust.

equality.reason: The land transfer is specific to one tribe and existing public access rights are preserved, so the bill does not clearly create unequal treatment under the law for any group.

justice.reason: The bill keeps existing rights, access and emergency-access provisions and bans gaming, but the public access guarantee is tied to rules at enactment and has no clear new remedy or accountability mechanism, so the net effect is unclear.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill mainly changes land ownership and management; public recreational access is kept, and no provision clearly expands or restricts what individuals may do with their own lives.
