label: H.R. 9237
title: Take Care of America's Veterans Act
short_title: Take Care of America's Veterans Act
one: A very large House-passed veterans package that expands benefits for retirees, survivors and caregivers. It also overhauls claims, mental health and community care, VA hiring, acquisition and construction, and adds many reporting duties, while tightening sleep apnea and tinnitus disability ratings for future claims.
summary:
H.R. 9237 is a six-title package that changes many parts of veterans law at once. It passed the House on November 11, 2026, and was received in the Senate on November 18, 2026. This summary follows the bill's structure. A few sections (parts of Secs. 303–304, 316–320 and 402–403) were cut off or only partly visible in the material I was given, so I can't describe them fully.

TITLE I, COMPENSATION. Retirees with combat-related disabilities could collect full military retired pay and VA disability pay together (the "Major Richard Star Act"). Surviving spouses who remarry would keep Dependency and Indemnity Compensation (DIC, the monthly payment to survivors of veterans who die of service-connected causes). They would also regain Survivor Benefit Plan annuities and TRICARE eligibility. The increased DIC rate would extend to survivors of veterans who died of ALS. Veterans eligible for aid and attendance would get an extra $833.33 a month starting December 1, 2026. DIC would get a cost-of-living increase plus 1 percent for three adjustments. VA home loan eligibility would expand for Guard and Reserve members. Some VA loan funding fees would rise (for example 0.50 to 1.42 percent in two categories), so some borrowers would pay more. VA could not deny a claim only because a veteran missed an exam. The bill adds claims tracking and many reports, and it creates tools to improve the Board of Veterans' Appeals. It allows grouping of similar appeals and class actions at the veterans' appeals court, and it requires better remand reasons, quality checks and training. VA must also study automation and independent reviews of its notices and forms, and report yearly on veteran causes of death. For military sexual trauma (MST) claimants, the bill requires sensitive letters, crisis and coordinator contact information, an annual accuracy review, a medical-exam working group and a public dashboard. Sleep apnea and tinnitus rating rules would be rewritten for claims filed on or after October 1, 2026. Sleep apnea ratings would depend on treatment results and organ damage, and tinnitus would usually not get its own compensable rating. Current awards could not be reduced.

TITLE II, EDUCATION AND ECONOMIC OPPORTUNITY. Provisions cover timely GI Bill contribution refunds, stricter rules for independent-study programs, and housing stipends for short online summer courses. They also cover a 100 percent first-year apprenticeship payment (up from 80), payment for more licensing and certification tests, VET-TEC expansion to emerging technologies with tougher job-outcome counting, and text and electronic messaging options. Transition Assistance Program counseling would be reworked, with a one-hour VA benefits presentation. VetSuccess on Campus would be placed in every state. Automobile-seller payments would be faster and tracked.

TITLE III, HEALTH CARE. Transportation grants grow to include tribes and counties. Family caregivers get 180 days of continued coverage, certification reimbursement up to $1,000, retirement planning and bereavement support. New or extended programs include a chronic mild traumatic brain injury grant program, a three-year mental health grant pilot ($20 million a year), the Fox suicide prevention grants ($200 million for fiscal years 2027–2029), and service dog grants ($10 million a year). The bill also covers naloxone distribution, a blast overpressure task force, and research on hyperbaric oxygen therapy, precision medicine, menopause and veterans' descendants' birth defects. Health services reach veterans in the Freely Associated States. Lactation rooms are required at VA medical centers. Annual evaluations are required for spinal cord injury. A bowel and bladder care program is created, a critical access hospital pilot is launched, and a community platform pilot is added. A VHA Policy Advisory Commission is set up. Three major construction projects are authorized: Manchester, NH ($1.18 billion), San Antonio ($30 million) and Indianapolis (about $1.64 billion). Committees get guaranteed access to project information.

TITLE IV, ORGANIZATION. It provides $500 million for VA technology, cybersecurity and supply chain through 2031. It creates an Under Secretary for Management and CFO, consolidates acquisition under one assistant secretary, and adds independent verification contracts, a cost-estimation director and acquisition intern targets. It also requires a single outbound VA phone number, call centers in six time zones, emergency management reports and updated scheduling rules for community care.

TITLE V, MEMORIAL AFFAIRS. It broadens headstone eligibility, limits duplicate burial benefits when an urn or plaque is provided, and funds a program to correct markers on Jewish servicemembers buried under crosses overseas.

TITLE VI, COMMUNITY CARE AND VA OPERATIONS. Community care access standards are written into law: 30 minutes and 20 days for primary and mental health care, 60 minutes and 28 days for specialty care. They expire after eight years unless Congress acts. Veterans get written notice of eligibility or denial within five days. Providers must file claims within one year and can be suspended for suspected fraud. A new standardized process covers admission to residential mental health programs, with 48-hour screening. It also covers fee schedules and training. Psychologists move to Title 38 status. New hiring, telework, reduction-in-force (60-day notice) and reorganization rules apply. VA must give lease cost estimates to Congress, and the VA Center for Innovation gets new cost-neutral payment pilots. VA must also give more data on workforce and education programs. Telemedicine licensing is widened, and controlled-substance prescribing by telemedicine is allowed with safeguards until 2031.

Because the bill is so large, its overall cost and Senate prospects are unclear from the material provided.
does: Sec. 101 (Major Richard Star Act): lets retirees with combat-related disabilities receive full military retired pay and VA disability compensation together. Retirees with under 20 years of service get a formula based on 20 years. It applies to months beginning on or after enactment.

Sec. 102 (Love Lives On Act): remarriage no longer cuts off DIC. It also ends the Survivor Benefit Plan age-55 remarriage rule, restores annuities (generally one year after enactment), and makes remarried widows and widowers whose later marriage ended eligible for TRICARE.
Sec. 103: treats veterans who die of ALS as qualifying for the increased DIC rate, with no minimum time having the disease. It applies to deaths on or after October 1, 2022.

Sec. 104: adds a $833.33 monthly supplement for veterans receiving aid and attendance (from December 1, 2026). It also gives DIC a COLA plus 1 percent for three adjustments. It raises certain VA loan funding fees from October 1, 2026, and expands home-loan eligibility for Guard and Reserve service since September 11, 2001, with an extra 1-point fee for some.

Sec. 105: bars denying a claim solely because the veteran missed a VA exam. It requires claim-tracking technology and annual reports. It lets the Board of Veterans' Appeals aggregate appeals with common questions, and gives the veterans' appeals court class-action and limited-remand powers. It adds Board quality assurance, training, annual performance reviews, remand explanations and notices to VBA employees who made errors. It also requires a federally funded research center (FFRDC) assessment on precedential Board decisions, plus studies on avoidable deferrals and General Counsel opinions.
Sec. 106: requires an annual report for five years on veteran deaths: primary and secondary cause, manner of death, and total-disability status.

Sec. 107: requires a plan for claims automation tools (records retrieval, evidence compilation, decision support). It also requires automatic notices when child-related benefits change and correct labeling of uploaded documents.

Sec. 108: rewrites disability ratings for sleep apnea (0/10/50/100 percent based on treatment effectiveness and end-organ damage). Tinnitus would get no separate compensable rating except 10 percent when tied to otherwise noncompensable service-connected hearing loss. It applies to claims filed on or after October 1, 2026 and may not reduce existing awards.

Secs. 109–110: extend and broaden temporary licensure for contract disability-exam clinicians to September 30, 2033, with a report. They require a rural exam access study, a review of VSR and RVSR training and second-level review, a GAO review, and quarterly sampling of inadequate or unnecessary exams.

Sec. 111: for MST claimants, requires a sensitivity review of VA letters and added crisis and coordinator contacts in notices. It also requires a training and accuracy study, an annual accuracy review with reprocessing of errors (sunset after five years), a medical-exam working group, a public MST claims dashboard updated every 30 days, and quarterly briefings.
Secs. 112–113: VA must seek an FFRDC assessment of claimant notices (to reduce paper and improve clarity) and of claimant forms, then implement compliant recommendations within one to two years.

Sec. 201 (VETS Opportunity Act): sets 60-day repayment of Post-9/11 GI Bill contributions and a lump sum for some. It tightens independent-study rules, adds oversight of Title IV institutions with a GAO report, lets service members withdraw or finish a course after receiving orders, and adjusts compliance survey notice times. These changes take effect around August 1, 2027.

Secs. 202–204: speed up and centralize VA payments to automobile sellers, with semiannual reports and a GAO review. They create a housing stipend for short online summer courses and define medically necessary vehicle adaptations as VA medical services.

Secs. 205–209: allow text and electronic messaging for Solid Start and education benefits, with opt-in. They revamp Transition Assistance Program counseling (3 or 5 days, standardized pathways, VA/DOL contact within 60 days) and add a one-hour VA benefits presentation. They also order a GAO study of SkillBridge. Contractors can provide on-campus counseling, and VetSuccess on Campus must have a counselor in every state. Licensing and certification test payments extend to more education programs.

Secs. 210–211: raise first-year apprenticeship GI Bill payments from 80 to 100 percent. They expand VET-TEC to emerging technologies such as AI and semiconductors, with stricter job-outcome calculation, public reporting and feedback collection.

Sec. 301: expands the VA transportation grant program to tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations and county veterans offices. Grants are capped at $50,000, with bonuses for off-road communities and up to $80,000 for ADA vehicles. Service to nearby rural areas is allowed.

Sec. 302: gives family caregivers 180 days of continued coverage after leaving the program, up to $1,000 in certification and relicensure reimbursement, and retirement, return-to-work and bereavement support. It also orders studies on returnships, VA hiring of former caregivers and a caregiver retirement plan.

Secs. 303–309 (Sec. 303 and part of 305 only partly visible): create chronic mild TBI grant programs and allow adaptive recreational prosthetics. They extend and expand the Fox suicide prevention grants to 2029 ($200 million) with new reporting and 24- and 72-hour referral contact rules. They also order hyperbaric oxygen therapy reviews, create a three-year nonprofit mental health grant pilot ($20 million a year), and require health services and travel pay for veterans in the Freely Associated States.

Secs. 310–312: expand Precision Medicine for Veterans to blast exposure and dementia ($5 million a year to 2032), add occupation data to suicide reports, create a VA Blast Overpressure Task Force through 2029, and strengthen VA–DoD resource sharing. These include guaranteed congressional access to unfiltered VA information and an extension of the 8111(d)(3) sunset to September 30, 2027.

Secs. 313–315: require VA clinicians to certify natural deaths within two business days. They create a five-year critical access hospital pilot in frontier states, a rural care action plan and outreach. They also create a community integration platform pilot at 5 or more sites with consent protections for social-needs data.

Secs. 321–324: order an independent comparison of VA and non-VA mental health and addiction care. They require lactation spaces at every VA medical center within three years, a report and strategic plan on menopause and mid-life women's health, and a one-year pilot giving naloxone free to any veteran, with self-attestation allowed.

Sec. 325: creates a 17-member, Comptroller General-appointed VHA Policy Advisory Commission that issues annual recommendations by March 15 and ends September 30, 2032. It is advisory only and cannot direct VA programs.

Secs. 326–329: add MST resource information to claim notices and to service academy withdrawals. They order ATSDR research and a health monitoring program on birth defects in descendants of toxic-exposed veterans (no new benefits, seven-year sunset). They require annual spinal cord injury preventive evaluations covering assistive technology and neuromodulation, and a three-year service dog grant pilot with grants up to $2 million per year ($10 million a year authorized).

Secs. 330–332: authorize major VA medical facility projects in Manchester NH ($1.18 billion), San Antonio TX land ($30 million) and Indianapolis IN (about $1.64 billion). They allow waiving rules on non-VA federal construction management, require 60-day notice of changes, and add a new section guaranteeing committees access to project and lease information.

Sec. 333: creates a bowel and bladder care program for veterans with spinal cord injury. It provides stipends to family or individually employed caregivers, pays home health agencies, and presumes lifelong need after three continuous years.

Sec. 401: authorizes and appropriates $500 million (through 2031) for VA information technology: $150 million for logistics and supply chain, $200 million for cybersecurity, and $150 million for communications and digitization. It requires implementation plans and briefings, and limits new staffing.

Secs. 401 (acquisition parts)–402: create an Under Secretary for Management and CFO. They put acquisition and logistics under the Assistant Secretary for Acquisition, with program managers, independent verification contracts with strict conflict-of-interest rules, a cost assessment director, intern hiring targets, a DoD acquisition analysis and a requirements process for large programs. Details of Sec. 403 were cut off.

Secs. 404–406: require a single recognizable VA outbound number and VHA call centers in six time zones, with reports. They also require an emergency management and FEMA fuel-sharing report and add State home and nursing home administrator members to the Geriatrics and Gerontology Advisory Committee.

Sec. 407: requires an electronic scheduling process for VA and community care appointments. It sets guidelines, training, metrics and provider outreach, and codifies the process as 38 U.S.C. 1703H, with full implementation in two years.

Secs. 501–503: remove the death-date limit for headstones for spouses and dependents. They bar duplicate burial benefits when an urn or plaque is provided (for deaths on or after January 5, 2021), and create a five-year program with $500,000 yearly nonprofit contracts to correct markers for Jewish servicemembers buried overseas under crosses.

Secs. 601–607: write community care access standards into law (30 min/20 days for primary and mental health care; 60 min/28 days for specialty care; 48-hour screening for treatment programs). The standards expire after eight years unless Congress approves new ones. They require written notice of eligibility or denial within five days, add continuity-of-care, caregiver and telehealth factors, and set a one-year claim filing deadline with fraud-based suspension procedures. They also order annual audits and wait-time and drive-time information.

Secs. 621–622 (Subchapter IX, §§1791–1795): create a standardized screening and admission process for residential mental health treatment programs, with 48-hour screening, appeals answered within 72 hours, public wait-time data and training. They also add care plans, 30-day stay approvals, a fee schedule with recoupment of overpayments, and a spinal-cord-injury access plan and pilot at three or more facilities.

Secs. 631–639: move psychologists to Title 38 and allow scarce specialist contracts. They create a voluntary mentorship program for medical center leaders (through 2030), equivalent role postings, standardized hiring approvals with e-signatures, a telework policy, and continuing education reimbursement of up to $1,000 for up to 50,000 people a year. They also add staffing transparency changes, broader cross-state telemedicine licensure, including controlled-substance prescribing, and education program data.

Secs. 641–644: require a five-year VA strategic human capital plan with GAO reviews. They require 60 days' notice before any reduction in force, with no effect until notice is given, and stronger justification and risk-mitigation for office reorganizations.

Secs. 661–664: require market-based and life-cycle cost estimates for major leases, and notice to Congress if the lowest offer exceeds the authorized rent by more than 10 percent. They also require reports on research infrastructure, fraud prevention in capital projects and long-term care infrastructure.

Secs. 671–676: allow VA clinicians to prescribe controlled substances by telemedicine without a prior in-person exam under conditions (to 2031, with limits on starting opioids). They exempt opioid antagonists from copays, create an online self-service care module plan, and replace the Center for Innovation with a new cost-neutral Center for payment models and community care pilots. They also require reports on the clinical appeals process and accessibility for spinal cord injury.

crs:
Take Care of America's Veterans Act
This bill addresses veterans’ benefits, health care, counseling, Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) personnel, VA infrastructure, and the Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP).
The bill modifies various compensation programs for veterans, including by (1) allowing concurrent receipt of disability compensation and military retired pay for certain retirees with a combat-related disability, (2) extending entitlement for various benefits and services to remarried surviving spouses, (3) increasing the rate of dependency and indemnity compensation, and (4) establishing a supplemental monthly allowance for certain disabled veterans.
The bill also addresses VA education and training benefits, including by (1) modifying which independent study programs are covered under veterans’ educational assistance benefits, (2) requiring Transition Assistance Program counseling to include a presentation about VA benefits, and (3) increasing the housing allowance rate for individuals pursuing apprenticeships.
The bill revises health care provisions, including by (1) expanding support and assistance provided to family caregivers, (2) extending the Staff Sergeant Parker Gordon Fox Suicide Prevention Grant Program, and (3) expanding the scope of VA mental health research.
Among other elements, the bill
revises VA disability ratings for sleep apnea and tinnitus;
expands eligibility for a memorial headstone or marker for the spouse, surviving spouse, child, or dependent of a veteran or member of the Armed Forces;
addresses the administration of the VCCP and codifies the eligibility standards;
establishes a standardized screening process for priority or routine admission to certain mental health care programs; and
addresses VA personnel, hiring, and infrastructure matters.

environment.reason: The bill's provisions concern veterans' benefits, health care, personnel and facilities; none addresses water, air, land or ecosystem protection in a way that materially changes them. The construction authorizations (Sec. 330-332) do not describe environmental effects.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 111 creates a public MST claims dashboard updated every 30 days, Secs. 310-312 guarantee congressional access to unfiltered VA information, Sec. 661-664 require lease cost estimates and notice to Congress, and Sec. 105 and 106 require annual reports; these expand public and congressional visibility. Sec. 111 and 113 also require sensitive letters and crisis contacts, which supports humane treatment of claimants.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mixes benefits gains for veterans and survivors with outside-contractor and third-party provisions (Secs. 601-607 community care, Sec. 671-676 cost-neutral payment pilots, Sec. 401 independent verification contracts) that could shift care and money toward private providers, and the VA loan funding fee increases in Sec. 104 raise costs on some borrowers, but the effects on corporate profit versus people are mixed and unclear overall.

local_say.reason: Sec. 302 and Sec. 301 expand grants to tribes, Native Hawaiian organizations and county veterans offices, and Sec. 315 creates a rural care action plan and frontier-state pilot, giving local and tribal entities more role; however, Sec. 601-607 and 671-676 set nationwide standards and national payment models that reduce local discretion.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide bailouts to corporations; the funding provisions are veterans' benefits and VA appropriations, and the bill has no clear ratepayer or corporate rescue component.

equality.reason: Sec. 102 restores DIC and TRICARE eligibility for remarried survivors, Sec. 501 removes death-date limits for headstones for spouses and dependents, and Sec. 326-329 add MST and descendant health provisions, expanding equal access to benefits; Sec. 108 and the sleep apnea and tinnitus rating rules apply only to claims filed after October 1, 2026, creating different treatment for claimants by filing date, which partly offsets this.

justice.reason: Sec. 105 bars denying claims solely for a missed exam and adds Board quality assurance, remand explanations and class-action powers at the veterans' appeals court; Sec. 111 requires annual accuracy review with reprocessing of MST errors; Sec. 601-607 require written notice within five days and fraud-based suspension procedures; Sec. 621-622 add appeals answered within 72 hours.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. 671 allows VA clinicians to prescribe controlled substances by telemedicine, and Sec. 201 and 205 give service members options to withdraw or finish courses and opt in to text messaging, expanding choices; Sec. 108 would restrict how claimants are rated for sleep apnea and tinnitus, which partly offsets this.

label: H.R. 9600
title: Common Sense 250 Act of 2026
short_title: Common Sense 250 Act (Thomas Paine monument location)
one: The bill approves placing the already-authorized Thomas Paine monument in Area I of the National Mall, the zone reserved for works of preeminent historical significance.
summary: Congress already authorized a monument to Thomas Paine in a 2023 spending law. Paine was the writer whose pamphlet "Common Sense" argued for American independence. This bill does one narrow thing: it decides where that monument can go. Normally, the Commemorative Works Act (the law that controls memorials in Washington, DC) sets strict rules for putting a memorial in Area I, the most prestigious part of the National Mall and its surroundings. Area I is saved for works of preeminent and lasting importance to the nation. This bill says "notwithstanding" those rules, which means it skips the normal requirements. It approves the location for the Paine monument within Area I, as shown on a 2003 National Capital Planning map, and requires the monument be built there. The bill does not say how much the monument would cost, who would pay, or exactly which spot inside Area I. It does not appear to provide federal money. Since the bill text skips the usual approval steps for Area I, the usual review by planning and design bodies and public input may be shortened. The bill text itself does not describe those review steps, so that is a possible consequence, not a stated provision.

label: H.R. 4464
title: Preventive Health Savings Act
short_title: Preventive Health Savings Act
one: Lets key congressional budget leaders ask the CBO to estimate long-term (beyond 10 years) federal savings from preventive health care in proposed bills, as a supplementary number that doesn't affect budget rules.
summary: Today, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), Congress's nonpartisan number-cruncher, usually estimates a bill's costs and savings over 10 years. That can hide savings from prevention, such as screenings or vaccines, which often pay off later. This bill would let the top leaders (chair and ranking minority member) of the House or Senate Budget Committee, together with the leaders of the committee that handles the bill's subject, ask CBO to check whether a proposed bill would cut federal spending through preventive health care in the 20 years after the first 10 years. If CBO finds net savings, it must describe and estimate them, and explain how it reached that conclusion, in any projection it prepares for that bill. CBO may extend its projections to those later years despite existing time limits. The new estimate is only supplementary. It cannot be used to decide whether Congress is following the 1974 budget law or other budget enforcement rules, such as spending caps or pay-as-you-go requirements. The bill defines preventive health care as actions that protect and promote health and prevent disease, disability, and early death. That includes effective, innovative interventions backed by credible, public evidence such as clinical trials and long-term studies. The bill spends no money and does not change any health program directly. It passed the House and is now in the Senate Budget Committee.
does: Amends Section 202 of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 to add a new "scoring of preventive health savings" subsection.
Triggers only when requested jointly by the Budget Committee chair and ranking minority member and the primary-jurisdiction committee chair and ranking minority member, in the House or the Senate.
Directs the CBO Director to determine whether proposed legislation would produce net reductions in federal outlays (spending) in the "budgetary outyears" through preventive health care.
If CBO finds net savings, it must include a description and estimate of those savings, and the basis for its conclusions, in any projection it prepares on the bill.
Allows CBO to prepare projections covering some or all of the outyears, despite the usual time periods in the budget law.
Defines "budgetary outyears" as the two consecutive 10-year periods starting 10 years after the current fiscal year.
Requires that the estimate be only supplementary and not used for budget-law compliance or any budget enforcement controls.

Defines "preventive health care" as actions to protect, promote, and maintain health and prevent disease, disability, and premature death, including interventions shown effective by credible, public evidence (epidemiological models, clinical trials, observational and longitudinal studies, meta-analyses).
who: Congressional Budget Office staff, who would do extra long-range analysis when asked
Members and committees of Congress, who would get more information when weighing health bills
Patients and the public, who could benefit indirectly if prevention-focused policies become easier to justify
Health care providers, public health agencies, and prevention-related industries (e.g., screening, vaccines, wellness programs)
Federal taxpayers, since the estimates concern long-term federal spending

benefits: Could make it easier to justify screenings, vaccines, and other prevention that saves lives and money over time.
Adds public information about long-term budget effects, helping voters and lawmakers.
The evidence standard (clinical trials, long-term studies) is meant to limit guesswork.
Does not change budget enforcement, so it carries little fiscal risk.
concerns: Projections 10 to 30 years out are very uncertain and could be overly optimistic or misused to promote favored programs.
Only savings are required to be reported; the bill does not require reporting long-term costs from prevention.
Requests need agreement of both chair and ranking member of several committees, which could limit use.
Extra CBO workload without stated added funding.
Companies selling preventive products could use favorable estimates to push for funding.
imp.cost: No spending is authorized and no cost estimate was provided. CBO would take on extra analysis work using existing resources, as far as the text shows.
unknowns: How often committees would make requests, and how CBO would model 20-year-out effects.
Whether CBO would need more staff or funding.
How the reported savings would affect actual votes and funding decisions.
Whether the Senate will take up the bill.

stage.last_action: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to let Congress see long-term federal savings from preventive health care, such as screenings and vaccines, which often pay off after the usual 10-year budget window. It would allow the Congressional Budget Office to check, when requested by key committee leaders, whether a proposed bill would reduce federal spending through prevention in the 20 years after that window, and to report any savings it finds. The estimate would be supplementary only and would not affect budget enforcement rules.

oppose: Projections 10 to 30 years into the future are highly uncertain, and a constituent could ask whether these long-range savings estimates would be reliable enough to guide spending decisions.
The bill requires CBO to report only savings from prevention, not long-term costs. A constituent could ask for balanced reporting that also shows possible added spending.
CBO has no added funding under this bill, so the extra work could take time away from its other budget analysis. A constituent could ask how Congress plans to cover that workload.
support: Prevention such as screenings and vaccines often saves money and lives over many years, and the standard 10-year budget window can miss those savings. A constituent could say this bill helps Congress see the full picture.
The bill sets an evidence standard based on clinical trials and long-term studies, which a constituent could say helps limit guesswork in these estimates.
The bill spends no money, does not change any health program directly, and its estimates cannot be used for budget enforcement. A constituent could say it adds information without adding fiscal risk.

crs:
Preventive Health Savings Act
This bill requires the Congressional Budget Office (CBO), upon receiving a request from Congress, to determine if proposed legislation would reduce spending outside of the 10-year budget window through the use of preventive health care.
Under the bill, the term 
preventive health care
 generally refers to an action that focuses on the health of the public, individuals, and defined populations in order to protect, promote, and maintain health and wellness and prevent disease, disability, and premature death.
If CBO determines that the proposed legislation would result in net reductions in budget outlays from the use of preventive health care, any CBO projection regarding the legislation must include (1) a description and estimate of the reductions in outlays, and (2) a description of the basis for these conclusions. 
Any estimate provided by CBO pursuant to this bill must be used as a supplementary estimate and may not be used to determine compliance with the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 or any other budgetary enforcement controls.

transparency_kindness.reason: Adds supplementary CBO analysis of long-term prevention savings, giving Congress and the public more information about budget effects, though the bill's scope is limited to reporting savings only.

title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
short_title: Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
one: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to review threats at the U.S.-Canada border every two years, update its northern border strategy, brief Congress in a classified setting, and set performance measures for its air and marine patrol unit.
summary:
This bill changes an existing 2016 law that told the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to study security at the U.S.-Canada border. Under the bill, DHS must do a new threat analysis by September 2, 2026, and then repeat it every two years. The analysis looks at terrorist and criminal threats, what improvements are needed, and whether "preclearance" (checking travelers before they reach the U.S. border) could help stop terrorists.

After each analysis, DHS has 90 days to update its northern border strategy. If it decides no update is needed, it must tell the relevant congressional committees. DHS must also give those committees a classified (secret) briefing within 30 days of each analysis.

Separately, within six months of the bill becoming law, DHS's Air and Marine Operations (AMO), part of Customs and Border Protection, must create performance measures. These measures would show how well AMO secures the northern border between official ports of entry, in the air and on the water. This follows recommendations from the Government Accountability Office (GAO), Congress's watchdog agency.

The bill does not appropriate new money, and it does not add new enforcement powers, barriers, or personnel. It is mainly a reporting and oversight bill. The briefings are classified, so the public would not see all of the results. The bill has passed the House and is waiting in the Senate.
does: Amends the 2016 Northern Border Security Review Act so DHS must complete a northern border threat analysis by September 2, 2026, and every two years after that.
Requires DHS to update its northern border strategy within 90 days after each threat analysis, or send the congressional committees a notice that no update is needed.
Requires a classified briefing to the appropriate congressional committees within 30 days after each threat analysis.

Per the CRS summary, the analysis covers terrorist and criminal threats, improvements needed to prevent terrorism and reduce crime, and whether preclearance and advance inspection at northern ports of entry could keep terrorists out (this content comes from the existing 2016 law, which the bill text amends but does not reprint).

Requires DHS, through the head of Air and Marine Operations at CBP, to develop performance measures within six months of enactment to assess how effective AMO is at securing the northern border between ports of entry in air and maritime settings.
Implements a GAO recommendation about AMO performance measures.
who: Department of Homeland Security and Customs and Border Protection (Air and Marine Operations) staff, who take on recurring reporting duties
Congressional committees that oversee homeland security
Communities and businesses along the U.S.-Canada border
Travelers and trade crossing the northern border, if the analyses later lead to policy changes such as preclearance
Taxpayers, who fund the agency work

benefits: Regular reviews could keep northern border policy up to date.
Performance measures for AMO could show whether its spending is effective.
Congress gets more oversight through required briefings and notices.
Responds to a GAO watchdog recommendation.
concerns: Briefings are classified, so the public may not see the findings.
DHS can decide no strategy update is needed, and only has to notify Congress.
The analysis could lead to more enforcement or preclearance measures that affect border communities, though the bill itself does not require them.
Adds recurring paperwork and staff time with no stated funding.
imp.cost: The bill provides no new funding. No cost estimate was in the material provided. Costs would come from existing DHS and CBP budgets.
unknowns: Whether public, unclassified versions of the analysis or the AMO measures would be released.
What the AMO performance measures will be.
Whether the analyses will lead to new policies like preclearance, and how these would affect local communities and trade.
The cost to DHS of the recurring work.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to strengthen oversight of security along the U.S. northern border with Canada. crs:
Northern Border Security Enhancement and Review Act
This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to regularly perform a threat analysis of the northern U.S. border.
The analysis must be performed every two years and include terroristic and criminal threats, improvements needed to prevent terrorism and reduce criminal activity, and whether preclearance and advance inspection operations at northern ports of entry could prevent terrorists from entering in the United States.
DHS must (1) update its northern border strategy after performing each threat analysis, and (2) provide a classified briefing to Congress. If DHS determines no update is required, DHS must notify Congress.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection’s Air and Marine Operations (AMO) must develop performance measures to assess the AMO’s effectiveness at securing the northern border between ports of entry in air and maritime environments.

environment.reason: The bill concerns threat analysis, strategy updates and AMO performance measures and does not directly change water, air or land protections.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on the threat analysis requires a classified briefing within 30 days of each analysis, so the public cannot see those findings, though the AMO performance measures and reporting to committees are still produced.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill has no provisions that favor or disfavor corporate profits over public interest; it is a reporting and oversight measure with no stated cost shift.

local_say.reason: The bill requires reporting to Congress but does not give border communities or state and local governments any new input into decisions affecting them.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has nothing to do with bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks.

equality.reason: The bill applies uniformly to the northern border and does not create differing rights or treatment for groups of people.

justice.reason: The AMO performance-measure requirement and recurring threat analyses with strategy updates add accountability and oversight of federal border enforcement, though the public visibility is limited.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not add or remove individual rights or choices; it only requires analysis and reporting, and any future preclearance changes would require separate action.

label: H.R. 7443
title: I&A Mission Reorientation Act of 2026
short_title: I&A Mission Reorientation Act of 2026
one: The bill directs the Department of Homeland Security's intelligence office to prioritize sharing intelligence both ways with state, local, tribal, and territorial governments and private companies, and to report to Congress on progress within 180 days.
summary: This bill changes the law that governs the Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A), the intelligence arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). It tells I&A to make its work for state, local, tribal, and territorial governments and private sector groups a real priority, and to resource it sufficiently relative to the support it gives to other federal intelligence agencies. To do that, I&A would look for new threats using "forward-deployed" staff, meaning people stationed outside Washington. It would also share information in both directions: getting information from local partners and sending useful intelligence back to them. It would keep up strong, steady work with fusion centers, which are shared hubs where federal, state, and local agencies combine information to spot crime and terrorism. The office must also make sure the intelligence it gives DHS leaders, including the Secretary, does not push aside its duties to those partners. Within 180 days of enactment, the head of I&A must report to key House and Senate committees on the steps taken, progress on two-way sharing, the measures used to judge success, and any staffing or organizational changes needed. The bill says it does not change I&A's watchlisting functions. It does not set out new spending, new surveillance powers, or new privacy rules. The bill passed the House and is now in the Senate Homeland Security committee.
does: Adds a new paragraph (24) to section 201(d) of the Homeland Security Act, requiring that I&A's mission of supporting state, local, tribal, territorial governments and private sector entities be sufficiently prioritized and resourced relative to support for other intelligence community elements.
Directs I&A to identify and address emerging threats using forward-deployed intelligence capabilities.
Directs I&A to facilitate two-way information sharing: receiving intelligence from, and sending actionable intelligence to, state, local, tribal, territorial governments and private entities.
Directs I&A to maintain robust, proficient, and sustained engagement with fusion centers.
Requires that intelligence support to DHS leadership, including the Secretary, not hinder or deprioritize I&A's duties to state, local, tribal, territorial, and private partners.

Requires a report within 180 days of enactment to House and Senate homeland security and intelligence committees covering implementation steps, progress on two-way sharing, effectiveness metrics, and any resource or organizational changes needed.
Includes findings and a sense of Congress (non-binding) favoring two-way collaboration and avoiding a one-way flow of information from field entities to the intelligence community.
States that nothing in the section changes I&A's watchlisting functions.
who: DHS Office of Intelligence and Analysis and its Under Secretary
State, local, tribal, and territorial governments and law enforcement
Fusion centers
Private sector entities such as critical infrastructure operators that receive DHS intelligence
DHS leadership, including the Secretary
Congressional homeland security and intelligence committees
The general public, whose information may be collected or shared in intelligence activity

benefits: Local, state, tribal, and territorial governments could get more timely, relevant threat information, which may help protect people from attacks and crime.
Two-way sharing could give local officials a bigger voice in what federal intelligence focuses on.
The required report to Congress gives lawmakers a way to check progress and see the metrics used.
Keeps DHS leadership needs from crowding out the office's duties to local partners.
concerns: The bill adds no new privacy, civil liberties, or data-handling protections for information collected and shared, including with private companies.
Fusion centers have drawn past criticism over civil liberties and oversight, and the bill calls for more sustained engagement with them.
Closer intelligence sharing with private sector entities could raise questions about who gets access to information about people.
'Forward-deployed intelligence capabilities' is not defined, so the scope of field activity is unclear.
The report goes to congressional committees and may not be public.
imp.cost: No spending is authorized and no cost estimate was provided. The bill requires the mission be 'sufficiently prioritized and resourced,' and the report must identify any resource changes needed, so future costs are possible but unspecified.
unknowns: How much it would cost, and whether I&A would shift resources from other work or ask for more funding.
What 'forward-deployed intelligence capabilities' would mean in practice.
How 'sufficiently prioritized' relative to the rest of the intelligence community would be measured.
Whether the report will be public or classified.
What safeguards will govern shared information about individuals.

stage.last_action: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.

crs:
I&A Mission Reorientation Act of 2026
This bill requires the Office of Intelligence and Analysis (I&A) of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to prioritize providing intelligence support to state, local, tribal, and territorial governments and private sector entities equally with providing support to other elements of the intelligence community.
To carry out this requirement, the bill directs I&A to facilitate two-way information sharing between I&A and its government and private sector partners and to identify and address threats using forward-deployed intelligence capabilities. I&A must also ensure that its provision of intelligence support to DHS leadership does not interfere with I&A’s responsibilities to government and private sector partners.
Further, the bill directs I&A to maintain robust and sustained engagement with fusion centers. (Fusion centers are collaborative efforts between federal, state, local, or tribal governments that combine resources, expertise, or information to detect, prevent, investigate, and respond to criminal or terrorist activity.)
After the bill’s enactment, I&A must report to Congress on its efforts to implement these provisions.

environment.reason: The bill does not address water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires a report to Congress within 180 days, but the summary notes it goes to committees and may not be public, and it adds no new public disclosure or privacy rules, so the effect on transparency is unclear and roughly balanced.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill concerns intelligence sharing with government and private partners and does not shift costs or favor corporate profit in a clear way; effects are unclear.

local_say.reason: Sec. 201(d)(24) and the two-way sharing directive give state, local, tribal, and territorial governments a more direct channel to feed information into and receive intelligence from federal intelligence, which gives them somewhat more input on federal intelligence priorities.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts, subsidies, or ratepayer cost shifts.

equality.reason: The bill treats partner governments and private entities under the same mission directive and does not create unequal treatment of groups of people.

justice.reason: The bill adds no new due process, remedies, or accountability mechanisms for individuals; the reporting requirement is modest and its effect on legal fairness is unclear.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may legally do, say, or choose; it governs intelligence agency mission and reporting.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage (two headlines) ties the bill's subject to Trump's intelligence chief taking on cyber policy and to a spy-agency data breach, implying a link between the two. Center coverage (six headlines) is more event-driven, covering the interim cyber appointment, several breaches, and congressional hearings on unrelated agencies, with less direct focus on the bill itself. The evidence is limited: the excerpts are truncated headlines with no article text, so the bill's provisions and any opposing views cannot be assessed from this set.

label: S. 4784
title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027
short_title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027 (NDAA)
one: The yearly Pentagon policy and spending-authorization bill sets troop levels, pay raises, weapons purchases, military construction, Department of Energy nuclear programs, and hundreds of policy rules, from PFAS cleanup and military housing mold standards to AI, China supply-chain bans, and contractor oversight.
summary:
This is the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). It does not itself pay for anything. It authorizes spending levels and sets rules, and separate appropriations bills actually provide the money. It has four divisions: Department of Defense (DoD) programs, military construction, Department of Energy (DOE) nuclear security programs, and funding tables.

Division A, Titles I–III (weapons, research, operations). Title I authorizes procurement and lets the services sign multiyear contracts for items such as Infantry Squad Vehicles, F-35s, F-15EXs, E-2D aircraft, and amphibious ships. It sets minimum inventories for Air Force fighters (1,800), MQ-9 drones, E-3 and E-7 warning aircraft, and C-130s. Title II funds research and sets up a low-cost missile and interceptor push, writes the DoD Research Security Program into law, and bars universities that do DoD research from contracting with listed foreign entities starting in 2028. Title III covers operations and maintenance. It requires DoD to revise its burn-pit policy, notify EPA, states, and local boards of PFAS dashboard updates, raise caps on technical help for communities taking part in cleanup, and start interim PFAS cleanup actions at 50 or more sites within two years. It also bans connected vehicles of concern from bases, sets deadlines for the Military Aviation and Installation Assurance Clearinghouse reviews of outside projects, and ties large amounts of travel money to Congress receiving requested documents, including civilian-harm investigations and strike videos.

Titles IV–VII (people). The bill sets active-duty and reserve strength levels and gives troops a 3.6 percent basic pay raise in January 2027. It raises hostile fire pay to $600 a month and imminent danger pay to $400, and lifts some bonuses. It removes diversity language from officer selection boards, repeals the pronoun policy, defines sex by biology for facilities, and shifts to "sex-neutral" job standards. It adds a DoD-wide hate symbol policy. It expands victim access to the military's top court, extends Special Victims' Counsel to domestic violence victims, and orders more reporting on hazing and protective orders. It adds child care, spouse fellowship, and tuition help. Health provisions include a TRICARE complaint system, provider directory accuracy tests with penalties, mental health counselor coverage, a toxic-exposure record that can cover family members, a suicide-risk notification policy, and a disease surveillance system. A waiver is also created for the limit on live-animal trauma training.

Titles VIII–X (acquisition and organization). Multiyear buys are authorized for 19 munitions. The bill makes government purpose rights the default for technical data, requires contractors to report large price increases on sole-source cost-plus contracts, and bars awarding contracts to firms that buy back stock or pay dividends after June 15, 2027, unless they have an approved investment plan (sunset 2031). It consolidates bans on buying from China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, and adds bans on Chinese optical fiber, modems, routers, and TVs. It extends printed-circuit-board rules and lowers the foreign-influence reporting threshold to $500,000. It also creates an Economic Defense Unit and lets the Office of Strategic Capital take equity stakes (up to $500 million per company, no board seats) in critical minerals and battery firms, with notice requirements. It restructures cyber leadership under a new Under Secretary starting January 2029, requires standing combatant commands, and renames DoD the "Department of War." It bans prediction-market trading on military matters by DoD staff, and bans wagers on military operations generally. It requires record retention for Caribbean and Eastern Pacific maritime strikes and protects Stars and Stripes' independence. It orders declassification of POW/MIA records, protects Afghan allies' records and Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah from forced return, and makes the Gaza Civil-Military Coordination Center official through 2027.

Titles XII–XVII (foreign policy, nuclear, missile defense, cyber, AI, space). The bill extends or raises aid and cooperation for Israel (including Iron Dome, David's Sling, and Arrow 3), Ukraine (the aid cap rises to $750 million), Taiwan and the Philippines, Lebanon's army, and AUKUS. It limits troop cuts in Europe and Korea. It requires AI protections: no AI deciding nuclear launches, no unlawful domestic surveillance with AI, and human control over lethal force. It also requires AI bills of materials, competition rules, insider-threat reporting from large AI contractors, and biosecurity testing. It authorizes contractor-run cyber access operations as a pilot. It adds Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification grants for small businesses, up to $50 million total. It requires annual reports on data center impacts, including on local communities.

Division B (military construction). It authorizes hundreds of projects, including microgrids, water treatment, flood protection, a landfill liner, child development centers, and barracks. It shifts facility maintenance money into the construction accounts, which is why totals jump. It also adds requirements for military housing: certified mold inspectors, independent inspections, tenant relocation, anti-retaliation protections, and tenants' right to withhold rent money in failed units.

Division C and D. DOE's nuclear weapons programs, environmental cleanup, and the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board ($45 million) are authorized, along with a nuclear effects testing partnership. Division D has the funding tables, which give the dollar amounts for each line.

The text I was given is a digest, so the exact total is not shown. The funding tables show large increases above the request in many accounts.
does: Authorizes FY2027 appropriations for procurement, research and development, operations and maintenance, military personnel, military construction, and DOE national security programs, as itemized in Division D funding tables.
Allows multiyear contracts for Infantry Squad Vehicles, F-35s, F-15EXs, E-2D aircraft, and 19 munitions programs, and extends amphibious ship procurement authority to 2030.
Sets minimums for Air Force fighters (1,800 total, 1,369 combat-coded), MQ-9s (180 from 2028), E-3 (16) and E-7 retention, and extends the C-130 minimum to 2028.
Writes the DoD Research Security Program into law and bars universities with DoD research funds from contracts with covered foreign nations or entities after January 1, 2028, with waivers.
Directs development of low-cost weapons (hypersonic, cruise, interceptors, air-to-air) to reach low-rate production by FY2030.

Requires interim PFAS remedial actions at 50+ covered sites within two years, prompt notice of PFAS dashboard updates to EPA, states, local authorities and restoration advisory boards, and a GAO study of PFAS contracting.

Raises caps on technical assistance grants for community participation in defense environmental restoration (up to $1,000,000 per installation combined, annual cap the lesser of $100,000 or 1% of cost-to-complete).
Requires DoD to revise its open-air burn pit policy per the DoD IG advisory and prioritize waste disposal systems where burn pits remain.

Requires grid-impact assessments for enhanced use leases, an assessment of foreign energy reliance on installations, and a plan to remove foreign-adversary equipment from the electric grid near bases.
Bars connected vehicles of concern from DoD property in two phases (July 2027 and January 2029) with waivers and notice periods.
Sets Clearinghouse deadlines: 180 days for adverse-impact reviews and 5 days if no impact, with 'unreasonable delay' defined for missed deadlines.
Withholds portions of travel funds until DoD gives Congress requested items, including civilian harm investigations, unedited strike videos, and a Ukraine support report.
Sets end strengths (Army 469,000; Navy 356,600; Marines 173,700; Air Force 330,400; Space Force 13,200) and reserve strengths.
Gives a 3.6% basic pay raise effective January 2027, raises hostile fire pay to $600 and imminent danger pay to $400, and raises aviation, ROTC, and student loan relief benefits.
Removes diversity language from selection board statutes, repeals the pronoun policy, defines sex biologically for restrooms and sleeping quarters, and moves to sex-neutral occupational standards.
Adds a DoD-wide hate symbol policy and training, with exceptions for legitimate uses.

Expands military justice victim protections: victim petitions to the top military court, Special Victims' Counsel for domestic violence, protective order notices, emergent housing policy, and a hazing analysis.

Expands family supports: child care provider eligibility, child care reporting, pay updates for child and youth programs, a 500-fellowship military spouse program, tuition assistance cap up to $350 per credit hour, and driver's license and guardianship cost help.
Puts commissary and exchange eligibility into statute, allows infrastructure spending from commissary funds, and pilots commissary access for civilian employees at up to 16 stores.
Creates a TRICARE complaint system, directory accuracy testing with penalties, mental health counselor coverage, and cranial orthotic coverage.
Expands the Individual Longitudinal Exposure Record to possibly cover family members, and creates a disease and non-battle injury surveillance system.
Waives the live-animal trauma training limit for units with a readiness impact, with notice and a no-alternative certification.

Makes government purpose rights the default for technical data, requires reporting of large price increases on sole-source cost-plus contracts, and removes the late-data defense in defective pricing cases.
Bars contracts to firms that repurchase stock or pay dividends after June 15, 2027, unless they have a Secretary-approved investment plan, until January 1, 2031.

Restricts DoD buying from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea starting 2028, and bans Chinese optical fiber, modems, routers, and TVs, plus synthetic biology data sharing with foreign entities of concern.

Lets the Office of Strategic Capital buy equity (up to $500 million per company, no board seats) in critical minerals and battery firms, with ownership reviews and congressional notice and waiting periods.
Creates an Economic Defense Unit and holds its funds until briefings and ownership reviews are delivered.

Restructures DoD: new Under Secretary for Cyber, Information, and Networks from January 2029, statutory combatant commands, optional robotic systems command, and redesignation of DoD as the Department of War.
Bans prediction-market trading on military matters by DoD staff and contractors, and bans wagers on military operations.
Requires records retention for Caribbean and Eastern Pacific maritime strikes, protects Stars and Stripes' independence, and orders POW/MIA record declassification.
Protects Afghan allies' records, bars funds for forced return of Afghans at Camp As Sayliyah, and extends the Gaza Civil-Military Coordination Center to 2027.

Extends and raises aid and cooperation for Israel, Ukraine ($750 million cap), Lebanon's army, Syria and Iraq programs, Taiwan and the Philippines ($1.5 billion cap), and AUKUS, and limits troop cuts in Europe and Korea.

Sets AI rules: no AI nuclear launch decisions, limits on AI surveillance in the U.S., human control over lethal force, AI bills of materials, anti-lock-in competition rules, insider-threat reporting for large AI contractors, and biosecurity testing.
Authorizes contractor-run cyber access operations as a pilot, adds $50 million in CMMC assessment grants for small businesses, and requires post-quantum cryptography by 2030 to 2031.
Requires annual high-performance computing and data center reporting that now covers effects on local communities and annual resource use.
Authorizes military construction projects (microgrids, water treatment, flood protection, child development centers, barracks) and shifts facility maintenance funding into construction accounts.

Sets military housing rules: certified mold personnel, independent inspections, relocation within 30 days of a failed inspection, owner responsibility for costs, anti-retaliation protections, and allowing tenants to withhold or abate housing allowance.

Authorizes DOE national security programs, a Los Alamos plutonium support building ($88.7 million), nuclear effects testing partnerships, and $45 million for the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board.
who: Active-duty, Guard, and Reserve service members and their families
Military housing tenants and privatized housing companies
Communities near military installations, including those with PFAS contamination, burn pits, or data centers
Defense contractors, including large primes, small businesses, and AI and tech firms
Universities and researchers that receive DoD funding
Veterans, retirees, and TRICARE beneficiaries
Taxpayers who fund defense spending
Allies and partners such as Israel, Ukraine, Taiwan, NATO members, and Lebanon
Afghan allies, Camp As Sayliyah residents, and POW/MIA families
DoD civilian employees and DoDEA students
Laboratory animals used in military training

benefits: Could speed PFAS cleanup and give communities faster notice and more resources to take part.
Could improve health and safety for military families through mold standards, independent inspections, and tenant protections.
Adds many reporting and records requirements (strike records, award files, POW/MIA records, price increases, foreign influence) that could improve transparency.
Could curb contractor payouts to shareholders and price gouging, and improve the government's access to technical data.
Increases pay and family supports for service members.
Sets guardrails on AI, including bars on AI nuclear launch decisions and on unlawful domestic surveillance, and requires human accountability for lethal force.
concerns: Authorizes very large spending and commits future funds through multiyear contracts, which benefit private contractors.
Equity investments by the Office of Strategic Capital put taxpayer money into private companies (up to $500 million each).
Waives limits on live-animal trauma training, which could harm animals.
Removes diversity language and sets a biological definition of sex for facilities, which could reduce inclusion.
Funding holds on travel accounts and the Department of War rename may be seen as political or costly.
Contractor-run cyber operations, equity stakes, and AI use raise accountability and oversight questions.
Clearinghouse deadlines could limit careful review of outside projects, and large data center and construction activity could affect local environments.
imp.cost: Funding tables authorize hundreds of billions of dollars, but the digest does not give the grand total. Military construction alone shows about $50 billion authorized, versus about $26 billion requested, mostly from shifting facility maintenance money into those accounts. Specific items include a $6 billion general transfer cap, $750 million for Ukraine, $1.5 billion for First Island Chain, $50 million for CMMC grants, and $45 million for the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board. The PAYGO statement of budget effects is to come from the Budget Committees.
unknowns: The total authorization amount is not shown in the text I saw.
Many reports, plans, and briefings are required, but their results and cost are unknown.
How many sites will actually qualify for PFAS interim actions, and whether appropriations will fund them.
How waivers (research contracts, procurement bans, live-animal limits, equity investments) will be used.
Several sections were summarized only in part in my digest, and a few contain apparent drafting errors.
What will survive Senate floor amendments, House negotiation, and appropriations.

purpose: The bill says it is the annual National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027. It sets policies and authorities for Department of Defense programs, military construction, and Department of Energy national security programs, including authorizing procurement, personnel levels, and military construction projects. According to its summary, it does not itself provide the money; separate appropriations bills do.

oppose: The bill authorizes very large spending and commits future funds through multiyear contracts. Funding tables show increases above the request in many accounts, so you could ask your member how these amounts were justified.

The bill lets the Office of Strategic Capital take equity stakes of up to $500 million per company in critical minerals and battery firms. You could ask whether taxpayer money in private companies carries enough oversight and risk protection.

The bill waives the limit on live-animal trauma training for units with a readiness impact. You could ask whether animal welfare protections should be weakened and whether reasonable alternatives were fully considered.
The bill removes diversity language from selection board statutes and sets a biological definition of sex for facilities. You could ask how this affects inclusion and recruiting in the force.
support: The bill raises pay and family supports, including a 3.6 percent basic pay raise in January 2027, higher hostile fire and imminent danger pay, and expanded child care and military spouse programs. You could thank your member or ask for continued support for service members and families.

The bill requires faster PFAS cleanup actions, with interim actions at 50 or more sites within two years, and more notice and resources for affected communities. You could ask that these deadlines be kept.

The bill sets military housing rules, including certified mold inspectors, independent inspections, relocation after failed inspections, and anti-retaliation protections. You could ask that these tenant protections be enforced.

The bill sets guardrails on AI, including no AI decisions on nuclear launches, limits on unlawful domestic surveillance, and human control over lethal force. You could ask your member to support these accountability measures.

cost_flag: Funding tables authorize hundreds of billions of dollars, but the digest does not give the grand total. Military construction alone shows about $50 billion authorized, versus about $26 billion requested, mostly from shifting facility maintenance money into those accounts. Specific items include a $6 billion general transfer cap, $750 million for Ukraine, $1.5 billion for First Island Chain, $50 million for CMMC grants, and $45 million for the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board. The PAYGO statement of budget effects is to come from the Budget Committees.

water.reason: PFAS interim cleanup at 50+ sites, a GAO review, public notice of PFAS data, and water treatment and flood projects advance clean water.

air.reason: Burn pit policy revisions, waste disposal systems, and mold and ventilation standards in housing improve air quality for troops and families.

transparency.reason: Numerous new public reports, records retention for strikes, award file production, POW/MIA declassification, price increase reporting, and investment notices increase openness.

people_over_profit.reason: Limits on contractor buybacks and dividends, price reporting, technical data rights, and tenant protections favor people, though large contract authorizations also benefit contractors.

local_say.reason: Larger technical-assistance grants for community participation, local community engagement in housing leases, and local community effects in data center reporting give affected people more voice.

honesty_kindness.reason: Support for victims, military families, spouses, Afghan allies, and civilian harm reporting reflect kindness and honesty.

equality.reason: Removing diversity language and adopting biological sex definitions for facilities could reduce inclusion, though disability hiring audits and victim services help some groups.

justice.reason: Expanded victim access to appellate review, Special Victims' Counsel for domestic violence, protective order notice, and anti-reprisal protections advance justice.

environmental_protection.reason: PFAS cleanup, landfill and stormwater projects, and energy resilience help, partly offset by the live-animal training waiver and military and mining-related activity.

label: H.R. 3495
title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
short_title: Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
one: Says that direct sellers (like people who sell products through home-party or network sales companies) and qualified real estate agents are not "employees" under the federal wage-and-hour law, so minimum wage and overtime rules would not apply to them.
summary:
This bill changes the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA), the main federal law that sets the minimum wage and overtime pay. It adds one sentence to the law's definition of "employee." Under that sentence, anyone who counts as a "direct seller" or a "qualified real estate agent" would not be an employee under the FLSA. Those two terms are not defined in the bill itself. Instead, it points to section 3508(b) of the tax code, which already treats these groups as independent contractors for federal tax purposes. That tax rule generally covers people paid based on sales or output, not hours worked, who work under a written contract saying they are not employees for tax purposes.

In practice, a company that works with these sellers or agents would not have to pay them the federal minimum wage or overtime under the FLSA. The bill supporters call it "harmonizing" labor law with tax law so the two match. The bill does not say what happens under state wage laws, and it does not change any other federal worker protection laws, as far as the text shows. It does not include any spending. The House Rules Committee has set it for floor debate under a closed rule, meaning no floor amendments, with one hour of debate.
does: placeholder
who: Direct sellers (people who sell consumer products person-to-person, such as through home sales or network marketing companies)
Real estate agents who meet the tax code definition of a qualified real estate agent
Direct selling companies and real estate brokerages
Workers who might be misclassified or who work under unclear arrangements

benefits: Aligns federal labor-law and tax-law treatment, which could reduce confusion and legal disputes over classification.
Could keep the flexible, commission-based work arrangements many sellers and agents say they prefer.
Could lower legal and compliance risk for direct selling companies and brokerages, which may help small independent sellers keep access to the work.
concerns: Takes away federal minimum wage and overtime coverage from these workers, even if a particular worker is in practice controlled like an employee.
Could make it harder for workers to challenge misclassification under the FLSA, and might encourage companies to push more control over workers without paying wage protections.
Could shift risk and costs onto individual workers, and the exclusion is written to be broad rather than tied to actual independence.
imp.cost: The bill has no spending or funding provisions. Any cost would fall indirectly on workers (lost wage protections) or benefit businesses (lower labor costs). I could not see a Congressional Budget Office estimate in the material provided.
unknowns: How many workers would actually lose FLSA coverage today versus those already treated as contractors.
Whether state minimum wage and overtime laws would still apply to these workers.
How the tax-code definitions, which depend on written contracts and pay based on sales, would interact with real working conditions.
The text of the amendment is short, but the committee report and any floor changes were not available to me.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to harmonize federal labor law with federal tax law. It would add a sentence to the Fair Labor Standards Act's definition of "employee" so that direct sellers and qualified real estate agents, as defined in section 3508(b) of the tax code, are not treated as employees under that law. Supporters describe this as aligning the two laws so that workers classified as independent contractors for tax purposes are treated the same way under labor law.

oppose: The bill would remove federal minimum wage and overtime protections under the Fair Labor Standards Act from direct sellers and real estate agents, even if a worker is in practice controlled by a company the way an employee would be.

The bill's exclusion relies on a tax-code definition that covers people paid by sales or output rather than hours and who sign a contract calling them non-employees. Critics say this could be broad and does not test whether a worker is actually independent.

Critics worry the bill could make it harder for workers to challenge misclassification and could let companies shift costs and risks onto workers without paying wage protections. The bill's text does not address state wage laws, so protections there would be unchanged.
support: The bill would align federal labor law with federal tax law, which could reduce confusion and legal disputes over whether these sellers and agents are employees or independent contractors.
Supporters say many direct sellers and real estate agents prefer flexible, commission-based work and want to keep control over their schedules, and this bill would keep that arrangement in place.
Supporters argue that lowering legal and compliance risk for direct selling companies and brokerages could help small independent sellers keep access to these opportunities.

crs:
Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act
This bill excludes a real estate agent or a direct seller of consumer products from the definition of an 
employee
 for the purpose of applying the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA). Workers who are considered employees under the FLSA must be paid the minimum wage and are generally eligible to receive overtime compensation for hours worked in excess of a 40-hour workweek.

environment.reason: The bill concerns wage classification under the FLSA and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill does not change public access to government information, though it removes certain worker protections; the effect on humane treatment is addressed under people_over_profit and justice rather than here.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 1 (the added sentence to the FLSA 'employee' definition) removes federal minimum wage and overtime protections from direct sellers and qualified real estate agents, shifting costs of labor protection from companies onto the workers themselves.

local_say.reason: The bill does not alter state or local authority over decisions affecting their areas; it does not address state wage laws either way.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no spending, funding, or bailout provisions.

equality.reason: Sec. 1 excludes a specific group of workers, defined by tax-code categories, from FLSA coverage that other employees keep, creating unequal treatment under the wage law.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 removes these workers from FLSA coverage, which would make it harder for them to challenge misclassification and to obtain wage-law remedies.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. 1 lets sellers and agents and the companies that engage them structure work as contractor arrangements that the workers may prefer, expanding choice over work arrangements, though it also limits the wage protections workers can claim.

news.overall: None of the six headlines or descriptions mentions the Direct Seller and Real Estate Agent Harmonization Act, so this evidence does not show how any outlet framed the bill itself. The provided coverage is thin (one to two items per group, with descriptions mostly missing), so these observations describe adjacent labor, wage, and housing topics rather than the bill. Across groups, the Lean Left and Lean Right outlets frame labor and wage issues in opposing terms of worker protection versus economic cost, while the Center items are more descriptive and do not clearly take a side.
