label: H.R. 5267
title: American Franchise Act
short_title: American Franchise Act
one: Writes into federal law a narrow test for when a franchisor (the parent brand) counts as a "joint employer" of a franchisee's workers under labor and wage laws, so brands are liable only if they directly and substantially control key job terms.
summary: This bill changes two major workplace laws: the National Labor Relations Act (which protects the right to organize and bargain collectively) and the Fair Labor Standards Act (which sets minimum wage and overtime rules). It says a franchisor, such as a national fast-food brand, can be treated as a "joint employer" with a local franchise owner only if the franchisor has and uses substantial, direct, and immediate control over at least one key job term. Those terms are wages, benefits, hours, hiring, firing, discipline, supervision, and direction of work. The bill spells out what counts as control for each term. It also lists many things that do not count, such as setting store operating hours, setting minimum staffing levels, setting brand standards, offering training materials, setting basic hiring or conduct standards, or telling a franchisee about an employee's poor performance. The bill gives the 2020 National Labor Relations Board standard the force of statute, so a future board could not easily change it. Supporters say franchise owners are independent businesses and brands should not be liable for decisions they don't make. Critics say brands can shape working conditions through contracts and standards without directly managing workers, and this could make it harder for workers to bargain with or hold the real decision-maker accountable. The bill does not apply to cases already started before it becomes law.
does: Adds a new Section 20 to the National Labor Relations Act saying a franchisor may be a joint employer of a franchisee's employees only if it possesses and exercises substantial direct and immediate control over one or more essential terms and conditions of employment.
Defines essential terms as wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction.
Defines 'substantial' control as control with a regular or continuous consequential effect; sporadic, isolated, or minor control does not count.

Spells out for each term what counts as control (e.g., actually setting pay rates, picking benefit plans, setting individual schedules, deciding who is hired, fired, or disciplined) and what does not (e.g., setting operating hours, minimum staffing levels, brand standards, training materials or minimum training requirements, minimal hiring or conduct standards, flagging misconduct to the franchisee, letting franchisees join the franchisor's benefit plan under an arm's-length contract).

Adds a matching Section 20 to the Fair Labor Standards Act applying the same joint-employer test to franchisors and franchisees for minimum wage, overtime, and related rules, using that Act's own definitions of employer and employee.
Uses the Federal Trade Commission's franchise rule definitions (16 CFR 436.1) for 'franchise,' 'franchisee,' and 'franchisor.'
Includes findings that franchisees are independent owners and that broad joint-employer views hurt franchising.
Does not apply to any proceeding that began before the date the Act becomes law.
who: Workers at franchise businesses (about 8.4 million per the bill's findings), including fast food, hotel, retail, and service workers
Franchisors (national brands)
Franchisees (local owner-operators)
Labor unions and workers trying to organize or bargain with franchise brands
The National Labor Relations Board and the Department of Labor, which enforce these laws
Consumers of franchise goods and services

benefits: Gives franchisees and franchisors clearer, more predictable rules about who is the employer.
May protect small local franchise owners from being treated as extensions of a large brand, and may encourage franchise growth and job creation.
Brands can set quality and safety standards without fear of automatic liability.
Applies one consistent test under both the labor and wage laws.
concerns: Workers could find it harder to bargain collectively with the brand that holds real economic power.
Brands could be shielded from wage-and-hour liability, leaving workers to pursue claims against franchisees who may have fewer resources.
Broad exclusions (e.g., setting staffing minimums, schedules via operating hours, brand standards, training) allow significant indirect influence over workers without being counted as control.
Putting the standard in statute makes it harder for future agencies or Congress to adjust it.
A closed rule limits amendments and debate.
imp.cost: No spending or appropriations are in the bill and no cost estimate was provided. Costs would be indirect, falling on workers or franchisees depending on how liability shifts.
unknowns: How courts would apply terms like 'regular or continuous consequential effect'.
How many workers would lose or keep bargaining or wage-claim rights against franchisors.
Whether franchisee-level enforcement would be as effective as claims against brands.
No official cost estimate was provided.

stage.stage_label: Scheduled for / under House floor consideration
stage.last_action: Rules Committee Resolution H. Res. 1665 Reported to House. Rule provides for consideration of H.R. 3495 and H.R. 5267. The resolution provides for consideration of H.R. 3495 and H.R. 5267 under a closed rule with one hour of debate and one motion to recommit on each bill.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give franchisors and franchisees clearer, more predictable rules about when a franchisor counts as a "joint employer" of a franchisee's workers under the National Labor Relations Act and the Fair Labor Standards Act. It states that franchisees are independent business owners and that broad joint-employer views harm franchising. It would write into law a 2020 National Labor Relations Board standard, which says a company is a joint employer only if it has substantial, direct, and immediate control over at least one essential term of employment.

oppose: The bill says a franchisor is a joint employer only if it directly and immediately controls a key job term, such as pay, hours, hiring, firing, or discipline. Critics say this leaves out indirect influence that brands have through contracts, staffing rules, and operating standards.

The bill lists setting operating hours and minimum staffing levels as not counting as control over hours or workers. Critics say these choices strongly shape workers' schedules and pay, so the bill may understate the brand's real role.
Putting the standard into statute would make it harder for future boards, agencies, or Congress to change it if it creates problems for workers. Critics say that limits future debate and adjustment.
support: The bill says franchisees are independent owners who make their own employment decisions. Supporters say treating brands as joint employers in these cases is unfair to them.
Supporters say the bill gives franchisors and franchisees clearer, more predictable rules, so businesses can plan ahead and know when they carry legal responsibility for workers.

The bill lets brands set quality, safety, and brand standards without automatically becoming liable for workers' employment conditions. Supporters say this protects small local owners and may help franchise growth and job creation.

crs:
American Franchise Act
This bill explicitly states that, for purposes of requirements under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA) and the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 (FLSA), franchisors are only considered to be joint employers with their franchisees if they regularly exercise direct and immediate control over the terms and conditions of employment for a franchisee's employees (e.g., directly hiring or firing employees on a regular basis). (The NLRA provides for collective bargaining rights in the private sector. The FLSA provides for a minimum wage, overtime pay, and other standards for employment.)
Specifically, the bill provides statutory authority for a 2020 
rule 
by the National Labor Relations Board, particularly in relation to franchisors and franchisees. Under this rule, an entity is considered a joint employer of a separate employer's employees under the NLRA only if the entity exercises substantial, direct, and immediate control over one or more essential terms or conditions of employment. 
Essential terms or conditions of employment
 are defined to mean wages, benefits, hours of work, hiring, discharge, discipline, supervision, and direction. (In 2026, the board reinstated the 2020 rule as the applicable standard.) 
The bill explicitly applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees and additionally specifies conduct that does and does not meet this standard (e.g., a franchisor setting a franchisee's operating hours does not sufficiently indicate direct and immediate control over the hours of work of a franchisee's employees). The bill also applies this standard to franchisors and franchisees under the FLSA.

environment.reason: The bill concerns joint-employer standards under labor and wage laws and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 20 (NLRA and FLSA) lists many activities that do not count as control, which may limit how workers can learn about and challenge who directs their conditions; the bill also gives the 2020 standard statutory force, reducing open review of the rule through agency rulemaking.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 20 excludes brand-level influence such as operating hours, staffing minimums, brand standards, and training from counting as control, which shields franchisors from joint-employer responsibility for worker conditions they shape indirectly.

local_say.reason: The bill sets a federal standard for joint-employer status and does not clearly shift decision-making power to state or local governments or community bodies.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no spending, appropriations, or ratepayer provisions, so it does not involve bailouts or shifting costs to ratepayers.

equality.reason: The joint-employer test applies the same standard to all franchisors and franchisees, and the bill does not create different treatment for protected groups.

justice.reason: Sec. 20 narrows which franchisors can be held liable as joint employers and states that the rule does not apply to pending proceedings, which limits workers' remedies against the party that shapes their terms and conditions.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill concerns legal liability between businesses and does not directly expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose about their own lives.

label: H.R. 1849
title: Disaster Mitigation and Tax Parity Act of 2025
short_title: Disaster Mitigation and Tax Parity Act of 2025
one: Makes money that homeowners get from state disaster-mitigation programs, to harden their property against wind, earthquake, or wildfire, tax-free, with the change reaching back to 2021.
summary: Some states run programs that pay or help pay for homeowners to make their property safer, such as retrofitting a house against earthquakes or clearing and hardening it against wildfire. Under current federal law, grants of this kind from federal disaster programs are not counted as taxable income, but similar grants from state programs may be. This bill would fix that gap by treating certain state-program payments the same way. The payment would not count as income if it comes from a state or local government program, a joint powers authority (a group of local governments working together), or a state-created "last resort" property insurer that a state insurance agency oversees. The money must be used only to reduce damage from a windstorm, earthquake, or wildfire. Because the payment is tax-free, it also cannot be added to the home's "basis" (the value used to figure taxable profit when the property is sold). The change would apply to tax years starting after December 31, 2020, so people could claim it for past years. The Treasury Department must give people a way to do that, including by filing an amended return. One note: the CRS summary lists floods too, but the bill text I was given lists only windstorm, earthquake, and wildfire. The cost to the federal budget is not stated in the material provided.
does: Adds a new subsection (h) to Section 139 of the tax code. Qualified payments from state-based catastrophe loss mitigation programs would not count as gross (taxable) income.

Covers programs set up by a state or local government body, a joint powers authority, or a state-created market-of-last-resort property insurer that is overseen by a state agency or insurance department.

Defines a qualified payment as money received by, or paid for the benefit of, a property owner to improve the property for the sole purpose of reducing damage from a windstorm, earthquake, or wildfire. The CRS summary also lists flood, but flood does not appear in the bill text provided.
Says these payments do not increase the property's tax basis, using rules similar to the existing federal hazard mitigation exclusion.
Makes conforming edits to other parts of Section 139 so the new payment type is included.
Applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2020.
Requires the Treasury Secretary to give individuals a chance to claim the exclusion for past years, including by amended return.
who: Homeowners and other property owners who get payments or benefits from state-run mitigation programs, such as those in wildfire- or earthquake-prone states
State and local governments, joint powers authorities, and state-created insurers of last resort that run these programs
The IRS and Treasury, which must set up a way to claim past-year exclusions
The federal Treasury, which would collect less tax revenue
Communities exposed to wildfire, earthquake, and windstorm risk

benefits: Homeowners keep the full value of mitigation grants instead of owing tax on them.
May encourage more people to retrofit or harden homes, which could reduce deaths, injuries, and property losses in disasters.
Treats state-based programs the same as federal ones, which is consistent and fair.
Retroactive claims could give relief to people who already received payments and may have been taxed on them.
concerns: Lowers federal tax revenue, and no cost estimate was provided.
Benefits only people in states or places that run such programs, and mainly property owners rather than renters.
Includes payments tied to state-created last-resort insurers, which some may view as indirectly linked to the insurance industry, though the payments go to individuals.
Retroactive claims back to 2021 could add administrative work for the IRS and for taxpayers.
The bill text omits flood even though the CRS summary lists it, which could confuse who is covered.
imp.cost: No cost estimate is given in the material provided. The bill reduces federal income tax revenue by excluding these payments from income. It creates no new spending program.
unknowns: How much revenue the federal government would lose, including from retroactive claims.
Whether flood is meant to be covered, since the text and CRS summary differ.
How many people currently get these payments, and how many were taxed on them.
How Treasury would handle the amended-return process for past years.

stage.last_action: ASSUMING FIRST SPONSORSHIP - Mr. Murphy asked unanimous consent that he may hereafter be considered as the first sponsor of H.R. 1849, a bill originally introduced by Representative LaMalfa, for the purpose of adding cosponsors and requesting reprintings pursuant to clause 7 of rule XII. Agreed to without objection.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make payments that homeowners receive from state catastrophe loss mitigation programs tax-free, the same way certain federal hazard mitigation payments already are. It aims to fix the gap where state-program payments may be taxed while similar federal payments are not, so that people can keep the full value of grants used to make their property safer from windstorms, earthquakes, and wildfires.

oppose: The bill would reduce federal tax revenue, and the material provided includes no cost estimate, so the size of the loss is unknown.
The tax break applies only to people in states or places that run these programs, so homeowners elsewhere would not benefit, which could be seen as uneven treatment.

The bill covers payments tied to state-created last-resort insurers. Some may see this as indirectly linked to the insurance industry, and the bill would also require the IRS to process retroactive claims back to 2021, adding administrative work.
support: The bill would treat state mitigation grants the same way federal hazard mitigation grants are already treated, which supports consistent and fair tax rules.

Homeowners would keep the full value of grants used to harden homes against windstorms, earthquakes, and wildfires instead of owing tax on them, which may encourage more people to make these improvements.

Retroactive claims would help people who already received state payments and may have paid tax on them, and fewer disaster-related losses could mean lower costs for families and communities over time.

crs:
Disaster Mitigation and Tax Parity Act of 2025
This bill excludes from gross income, for federal income tax purposes, payments received from a state catastrophe loss mitigation program by an individual for the purpose of making improvements to the individual’s property that mitigate the impact of certain disasters.
Under current law, individuals may exclude from gross income, for federal income tax purposes, payments received under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act or the National Flood Insurance Act (as in effect on April 15, 2005) for hazard mitigation. (Some exceptions apply.) Further, under current law, such payments do not increase the basis of the property for which the payments are made.
The bill allows a similar exclusion from gross income for certain payments received by an individual from a program established by
a state (or any political subdivision or instrumentality of the state),
a joint powers authority, or
an entity that was established by the state to provide essential or basic property insurance and is regulated by the state.
Under the bill, such payments must be for making improvements to the individual’s property for the sole purpose of reducing damage that would be done to the property by a windstorm, earthquake, flood, or wildfire.
Finally, the bill provides that such payments from a state catastrophe loss mitigation program do not increase the basis of the property for which the payments are made.

environment.reason: The bill concerns income tax treatment of mitigation payments and does not affect water, air, land, or ecosystem protection or enforcement.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill does not change public disclosure, open government, or humane treatment; it is a tax exclusion with no transparency or secrecy provisions.

people_over_profit.reason: The tax-free treatment extends to payments tied to state-created last-resort insurers, which are insurance entities, and the excluded income reduces federal tax revenue that taxpayers otherwise fund; the benefit mainly goes to property owners rather than corporations, so the effect is modest.

local_say.reason: The exclusion applies to payments from state, local, and joint powers authority programs, which supports state and local governments choosing to run their own mitigation programs with the same federal tax treatment.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill provides a tax exclusion for homeowners' mitigation payments and does not bail out corporations or insurers; the lost federal revenue is a general tax cost, not a ratepayer or corporate bailout.

equality.reason: Sec. 139(h) makes state-program mitigation payments tax-free like federal hazard mitigation payments, treating recipients of state and federal programs alike, though only residents of states running such programs benefit.

justice.reason: The retroactive claim provision for tax years beginning after December 31, 2020, with amended-return process, gives taxpayers a remedy for past taxation of these payments.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do, say, or choose about their lives; it only changes the tax treatment of certain payments.

news.overall: Only one Lean Left article (NPR) was provided, with a headline and no description, so the evidence is too thin to compare framing across perspectives. No Lean Right, center, or other perspective coverage was included in the input, so no cross-perspective comparison can be made.

label: H.R. 2323
title: Big Bend National Park Boundary Adjustment Act
short_title: Big Bend National Park Boundary Adjustment Act
one: Lets the Interior Secretary add about 6,100 acres next to Big Bend National Park in Texas, but only through donation or land swap, never by forced taking.
summary: This bill would let the Secretary of the Interior bring about 6,100 acres of land into Big Bend National Park in Texas. The land is marked on a map titled "Big Bend National Park, Proposed Boundary Adjustment," dated November 2022. The government could get the land only by donation (someone gives it) or exchange (a land swap). It could not buy the land under this bill, because the bill only authorizes donation or exchange. It also bars the government from using eminent domain or condemnation, which means forcing a landowner to sell. Once the government gets any of the land, the Secretary must move the park boundary to include it and manage it like the rest of the park under existing laws and rules. The map has to be kept on file where the public can look at it, at National Park Service offices. The bill does not say how much an exchange might cost, who the current owners are, or what the land is used for today. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. The bill text is complete, but the map itself was not included in the material I reviewed.
does: unused
who: Owners of the roughly 6,100 acres shown on the map, who could choose to donate or swap land
Visitors to Big Bend National Park
National Park Service staff who would manage the added land
Nearby communities and local businesses in the Texas Big Bend region
Wildlife and plants living on the added land

benefits: Could protect more habitat for wildlife and plants by placing the land under park management.
Because it is voluntary, landowners keep the choice to take part.
Bans eminent domain, protecting landowners from forced takings.
The map must be publicly available, which supports openness.
Could improve park management by tidying up boundaries, though the bill does not say this is the goal.
concerns: Added land could raise park upkeep and staffing costs, and the bill does not say who pays.
Land exchanges could trade away federal land; the bill does not say what land might be given up.
Neighbors or local governments may lose some local land use or tax base once land becomes federal; the bill does not address this.
Landowners may feel pressure to sell or donate even without condemnation; the bill does not discuss this.
imp.cost: The bill does not authorize any specific money and no cost estimate was provided. Donations would cost little up front, but managing the land could create future costs for the National Park Service.
unknowns: Who owns the 6,100 acres and whether they support the plan
Current uses of the land, such as grazing, and whether they would continue
Cost of managing the additional land
What federal land might be offered in exchanges
No CRS summary or cost estimate was available
I did not see the map itself

purpose: The bill says it would allow the Secretary of the Interior to bring about 6,100 acres of land into Big Bend National Park in Texas, as shown on a map dated November 2022. The land could be added only through donation or exchange, not purchase or condemnation, and once acquired it would be managed as part of the park under existing laws. The bill's text does not spell out a broader problem it is meant to solve; its stated aim is to change the park's boundary to include this land.

oppose: The bill does not say who would pay for managing the added land, so park upkeep and staffing costs could fall on the federal budget.
Land exchanges could give up federal land, but the bill does not say which federal land would be traded away.
Once land becomes federal, neighboring communities and local governments may lose some tax revenue and local land-use options, and the bill does not address this.
support: The bill would add about 6,100 acres of land that could protect more habitat for wildlife and plants inside Big Bend National Park.
The bill is voluntary: land would come into the park only by donation or exchange, and landowners keep the choice to take part.
The bill bans eminent domain and condemnation, so landowners cannot be forced to sell, and the map must be available to the public at National Park Service offices.

environment.reason: Sec. (boundary adjustment) would bring about 6,100 acres of land into Big Bend National Park under park management, which could protect habitat for wildlife and plants.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires the boundary map to be kept on file at National Park Service offices where the public can review it.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill has no provision that clearly favors or disfavors corporate profits over public interests; donations and exchanges are voluntary and the cost effects are unstated.

local_say.reason: The bill does not provide a clear mechanism for local or state input on the boundary change, and it is unclear whether local land use or tax base effects would arise; it bans condemnation, which protects owners but the net effect on community input is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks.

equality.reason: The bill treats all owners within the mapped area the same, offering donation or exchange to any willing owner with no group-specific treatment.

justice.reason: Sec. (eminent domain bar) prohibits condemnation and forced takings, giving landowners a clear protection against compelled sale.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill bars the government from using eminent domain or condemnation, so owners keep the choice of whether to donate or swap their land.

label: S. 1489
title: Anti-Racism in Public Health Act of 2025
short_title: Anti-Racism in Public Health Act of 2025
one: The bill would create a National Center on Antiracism and Health at the CDC and a CDC program to study police violence as a public health issue, with unspecified funding.
summary: This bill would set up a new National Center on Antiracism and Health inside the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The Center's director would need experience living and working in racial and ethnic minority communities. The Center would declare racism a public health crisis, study how racism affects health care and conditions like housing, jobs, and environment, and develop ways to reduce those effects. It could give grants without competition to state, local, territorial, and Tribal health groups, and fund at least three regional centers of excellence in minority communities. It would build a public data clearinghouse (a central data collection) that breaks data down by race, language, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, age, income, and disability while protecting individual privacy. It would also train public health workers, add racism measures to surveys, form an advisory committee, consult with Tribes, and publish a report at least every two years. The bill also creates a law enforcement violence prevention program inside the CDC's injury center. That program would research police use of force, collect and standardize data with the Justice Department, fund community and academic research, study alternatives to police response, and send Congress an annual report. Both parts authorize "such sums as may be necessary," so no dollar amount is set. The bill defines "antiracist" as any measure that produces or sustains racial equity between racial groups.

Directs the Center to declare racism a public health crisis and a historical and present threat to health, and to build knowledge and interventions to dismantle what the bill calls mechanisms of racism.

Requires a public report on the Center's activities at least every two years.

Creates a law enforcement violence prevention program in the CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control to research police use of force, brutality, and related deaths and injuries, and to prepare statistics and strategic plans.

Requires a study of alternatives to law enforcement response and an annual report to Congress with recommendations, including on disrupting policing processes that reinforce racial disparities.
Authorizes such sums as may be necessary for each part, with no specific dollar amount.

label: S. 2302
title: Access to Birth Control Act
short_title: Access to Birth Control Act
one: Requires pharmacies that stock birth control to provide it, refer or transfer customers, or order it without delay, bars harassment and deception, and allows fines and lawsuits for violations.
summary: This bill would add a new federal rule for pharmacies. If a customer asks for birth control, or a related medicine a medical professional says is needed with it, and the pharmacy has it in stock, the pharmacy must provide it without delay, meaning in the same time it takes for other products. If the pharmacy normally stocks birth control but is out, it must tell the customer right away and offer to send them or their prescription to another pharmacy, or to order it quickly. Pharmacies must also make sure employees do not intimidate, harass, block, or lie to customers about birth control, do not break medical privacy, and do not refuse to hand back a valid prescription. Pharmacies can still say no if there is no valid prescription where one is legally required, if the customer cannot pay, or if an employee makes a professional clinical judgment, such as a safety concern. Pharmacies that do not normally stock birth control are not required to order it. The bill says the Religious Freedom Restoration Act cannot be used as a claim or defense under it. States may keep or pass stronger customer protections. The federal government could fine a pharmacy up to $1,000 a day, capped at $100,000 per proceeding. Customers could also sue for damages, court orders, and attorney's fees within five years. It would take effect 31 days after enactment.
does: Requires pharmacies that get FDA-regulated products across state lines to give customers in-stock birth control, or related medication, without delay (the usual time for other products).

If the item is out of stock but the pharmacy normally stocks birth control, requires it to tell the customer immediately and offer a referral or prescription transfer to the customer's chosen pharmacy or the closest one confirmed to have it, or expedited ordering with notice on arrival.

Bars pharmacies from allowing intimidation, threats, or harassment, employee interference or obstruction, intentional misrepresentation about availability or how the drug works, breaches or threats of breaching medical confidentiality, and refusal to return a valid prescription.
Allows refusals when a required valid prescription is not presented, the customer cannot pay, or an employee acts on professional clinical judgment under prevailing medical standards.
Exempts pharmacies from the out-of-stock referral and ordering duties if they do not ordinarily stock birth control.

States the Religious Freedom Restoration Act gives no claim or defense related to the new section (the text refers to a 'covered title' that it does not define), and does not limit Title VII of the Civil Rights Act.
Does not override state laws or licensing rules that protect customers more than this bill does.

Sets federal civil penalties up to $1,000 per day (max $100,000 per proceeding) and lets aggrieved people sue for actual and punitive damages, injunctions, and attorney's fees, with a 5-year time limit.

Defines key terms: contraception means any FDA-approved, cleared, or authorized drug or device to prevent pregnancy; a pharmacy is a state-authorized retail seller of prescription drugs with at least one employee. Takes effect 31 days after enactment.
who: People who use birth control, including for medical conditions like endometriosis, especially in rural areas or with low incomes
Retail pharmacies, chain and independent, that stock birth control
Pharmacists and pharmacy staff, including those with religious or moral objections
State pharmacy boards and state attorneys/courts
Federal enforcement agencies and courts handling penalties and lawsuits

benefits: Could reduce delays and denials of birth control, including emergency contraception and medication needed with it.
Protects customers from harassment, deception, and breaches of medical confidentiality.
Referral, transfer, or ordering options could help people in rural areas or with few pharmacies nearby.
Penalties and private lawsuits give the rules real enforcement.
Leaves states free to adopt stronger protections.
concerns: Bars RFRA claims or defenses, which could override religious or conscience objections by pharmacy owners or employees.
Pharmacies, including small independent ones, face fines up to $100,000 per proceeding and lawsuits with punitive damages, which could raise compliance costs.
The 'professional clinical judgment' exception and the 'without delay' standard could lead to disputes over how they apply.
Does not require pharmacies that don't normally stock birth control to start, so some access gaps would remain.
Some people hold moral objections to certain contraceptives and may see the bill as conflicting with their view of protecting human life.
imp.cost: No spending is authorized in the text. Costs would fall on pharmacies for compliance and potential penalties or damages, and on federal and state courts and agencies for enforcement. No federal cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: The text refers to a 'covered title' without defining it, so the exact reach of the RFRA provision is unclear.
Which federal agency would bring penalty actions is not stated.
How courts would interpret 'without delay' and 'professional clinical judgment' is unknown.
Whether the bill would pass is uncertain; no CRS summary or cost estimate is available yet.

purpose: The bill says its goal, as shown in its title, is to improve access to birth control at pharmacies. It would require pharmacies to fill in-stock birth control and related medicine without delay, to offer referrals or transfers when an item is out of stock, and to bar intimidation, misrepresentation, breaches of privacy, and refusal to return valid prescriptions. The provided summary does not include official findings, so this description relies on the title and the plain-English summary.

oppose: The bill bars Religious Freedom Restoration Act claims or defenses under the new section, which could limit the ability of pharmacy owners or employees with religious or conscience objections to raise those objections in court.

Penalties of up to $1,000 per day, capped at $100,000 per proceeding, plus private lawsuits for punitive damages and attorney's fees, could be costly for small independent pharmacies to defend, even when they act in good faith.
Terms like 'without delay' and 'professional clinical judgment' may be open to different readings, which could lead to disputes and uncertainty for pharmacists about how to comply.
support: The bill would require pharmacies that stock birth control to fill in-stock prescriptions without unnecessary delay, which could reduce waits and denied prescriptions for patients, including for emergency contraception.
If a pharmacy is out of stock, it must tell the customer right away and offer a transfer, referral, or expedited order, which could help people in rural areas or those with few nearby pharmacies.

The bill bans harassment, intimidation, misleading statements, and breaches of medical privacy, and it lets states keep or add stronger protections, which could give patients clearer rights and real ways to enforce them.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on misrepresentation and intimidation bars pharmacies from deceiving customers about availability or how the drug works, and the duty to tell customers right away when stock is out promotes honest information; medical confidentiality protections also support humane treatment.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill imposes compliance duties and penalties on pharmacies, which constrain business but also protect customers' access; the effects on corporate margins and consumer costs are mixed and not clearly net positive or negative.

local_say.reason: The bill preempts nothing that protects customers more, so state and local protections are kept, but it adds a federal rule that sets the baseline for pharmacies nationwide without a clear change to local decision-making on land use or facilities.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts or ratepayer cost shifts; it authorizes no spending.

equality.reason: The bill applies one federal standard to all customers, and the referral and ordering duties and the bar on intimidation help equal access to contraception, particularly for people in rural areas or with low incomes; the exemption for pharmacies that do not normally stock birth control leaves some access gaps.

justice.reason: Sec. on penalties and private rights of action gives federal fines up to $1,000 per day (capped at $100,000 per proceeding), lets aggrieved people sue for actual and punitive damages, injunctions and attorney's fees within five years, and bars RFRA claims or defenses, giving customers real remedies and consistent enforcement.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill expands individuals' ability to obtain contraception without delay, referral or harassment, and bars RFRA defenses that could otherwise be used to refuse; it also restricts pharmacy owners' and employees' ability to refuse some services, though refusals remain allowed for missing prescriptions, inability to pay and clinical judgment.

No other perspective groups were supplied for comparison.

label: H.R. 2116
title: Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
short_title: Law Enforcement Support and Counter Transnational Repression Act
one: Requires the Department of Homeland Security to run a public awareness campaign about foreign governments harassing or threatening people in the U.S., and to research tools to help law enforcement counter it.
summary: This bill adds a new section to the Homeland Security Act. It tells the Secretary of Homeland Security to have the department's Office of Partnership and Engagement run a public service announcement campaign. The campaign would teach the public and U.S. international allies about "transnational repression." That term means a foreign government, or someone acting under its control, trying to scare, harass, coerce, or hurt people in the U.S. or U.S. persons abroad. It includes threats against family members, efforts to silence people's First Amendment rights, and extrajudicial killings (killings outside any legal process). The campaign must also explain what help is available to victims and how to anonymously report suspected cases to the FBI. It should be run in languages the Secretary finds relevant. Within one year, and "to the extent practicable," DHS must also research and test technologies and methods to better support federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial officials in countering this kind of repression and related terrorism threats. That work must follow constitutional, privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties protections. The bill sets no dollar amount and does not create new crimes or new police powers. It does not say where the money comes from. The bill is out of committee and on the House calendar.

The bill does not create new crimes or new police powers, according to the summary provided.

label: H.R. 143
title: Unauthorized Spending Accountability Act
short_title: Unauthorized Spending Accountability Act
one: Starting in fiscal year 2026, the bill automatically cuts the spending limits for federal programs whose congressional authorization has expired, by 10% and then 15% a year, and ends those programs after three years unless Congress reauthorizes them.
summary:
Congress usually works in two steps. First, it passes a law that "authorizes" a program, which means it permits the program to get money. Second, it passes yearly spending bills that actually fund it. Many programs keep getting money after their authorization runs out. This bill targets those programs.

Each year, the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) publishes a list of programs whose authorizations have expired or will expire that year. Under the bill, every program on that list would face automatic cuts to its share of the spending ceiling set for the House and Senate Appropriations Committees. The first year after expiration, the ceiling drops by 10% of what the program got in its last authorized year. In the second and third years, it drops by 15% each year, if the program is still unauthorized.

If a program is still unauthorized after the third year of cuts, it ends on October 1 of the following year. Only already-made commitments could still be paid off. No new money could be committed unless Congress reauthorizes it for no more than three years.

If Congress reauthorizes a program in time, with a sunset of three years or less, the cuts are cancelled and any lost funding is restored. Programs that expired before 2026 and are funded in 2026 are treated as if they expire in 2026. The cycle repeats every three years.
does: Creates a repeating three-year cut cycle for unauthorized programs, starting in fiscal year 2026.
Defines an unauthorized program as one listed in CBO's 'Expired and Expiring Authorizations of Appropriations' report.
Treats programs that expired before fiscal 2026 and are funded in 2026 as expiring in 2026.
Cuts the spending ceiling by 10% of the program's last-authorized-year funding in the first year after expiration.
Cuts it by 15% in each of the second and third years if the program is still unauthorized.
Requires the House and Senate Budget Committee chairs to send the revised levels to the Appropriations chairs.
Terminates programs after the third reduction year, with funds left only to close out valid earlier obligations.
Bars new spending on a terminated program unless Congress reauthorizes it for three years or less.
Cancels and restores cuts if a program is reauthorized in time with a sunset of three years or less.
who: Recipients and workers of federal programs with expired authorizations
Federal agencies running those programs
House and Senate Appropriations and Budget Committees
State and local governments and nonprofits that depend on federal grants
Congressional authorizing committees, which would face deadlines
Taxpayers and the public served by affected programs

benefits: May push Congress to review and renew program authorizations on a regular schedule.
Could make the link between authorization and funding more visible to lawmakers and the public.
Could reduce funding for programs that have not been reviewed in a long time.
concerns: Programs could lose funding or end even if their work is still useful, if Congress does not act in time.
Automatic cuts could create uncertainty for people and organizations that depend on these programs.
Termination after three years could disrupt services, though existing commitments could still be paid.

The exact dollar effect is not stated."]

It is not stated how the bill would treat programs whose authorization lapses for only a short time, or how it would apply to multi-year funding beyond what is described.
The bill's latest action is 'out of committee, on the House calendar'; whether it will pass is not stated.

crs:
Unauthorized Spending Accountability Act
This bill reduces budgetary levels for certain federal programs that are funded through the annual appropriations process and do not have an authorization of appropriations.
Under the bill, 
budgetary levels
 are spending allocations provided to the congressional appropriations committees by a congressional budget resolution or a deeming resolution. The allocations are provided under the Congressional Budget Act of 1974 and are often referred to as 302(a) allocations.
The bill applies to programs included in the Congressional Budget Office's (CBO's) annual report listing programs that are funded through the appropriations process and have an authorization of appropriations that has either expired or will expire during the year. 
If a program is listed in the CBO report, the bill requires specified reductions to be implemented over a three-year period and terminates the unauthorized programs at the end of the third unauthorized year.

environment.reason: The bill does not address water, air, or land protections; effects on environmental programs depend on which programs lose authorization, and the bill itself does not change environmental standards.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2 ties cuts to CBO's published 'Expired and Expiring Authorizations of Appropriations' report, making the authorization-to-funding link public and visible to lawmakers and the public.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill does not direct money toward or away from corporate profits; it adjusts appropriations ceilings for unauthorized programs, with effects on recipients being mixed and unclear.

local_say.reason: The bill shifts budget levels within Congress and does not give states or localities new decision-making authority or remove any existing say over their areas.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no provisions about bailing out corporations or shifting costs to ratepayers.

equality.reason: The cuts and termination apply uniformly to all listed programs based on the same criteria, so the bill does not create unequal treatment of groups on its face.

justice.reason: The bill sets a uniform, rule-based process for unauthorized programs, but it does not create new due process or remedies for affected people; the effects on fairness are mixed.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill governs federal program funding and does not expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose about their own lives.

label: H.R. 1640
title: HEIRS Act of 2025
short_title: HEIRS Act of 2025
one: The bill lets HUD create two grant programs, running seven years, to help families who inherited property without a will pay for the legal and paperwork costs of clearing title and keeping their homes.
summary: When someone dies without a will, their heirs often end up co-owning the home as "tenants in common." This is called heirs' property. Under old state laws, one co-owner can force a sale of the whole property, and families, often low-income and Black, rural or Tribal families, have lost land and homes this way. This bill would let the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) set up two grant programs. The first would give money to states, territories, local governments and Tribal governments that have adopted the Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (or something HUD finds equivalent), either before or after the bill passes. Those governments would use the money to help residents pay real costs of proving ownership or settling an estate, such as title reports, surveys, heir searches, estate planning, filing fees and legal fees. The second program would give yearly grants to HUD-approved housing counseling agencies, law school legal clinics and qualifying nonprofits. They would provide counseling, legal help and financial help for clearing title and keeping the home. estate planning;

recording and filing fees, notary fees, and legal fees and expenses.

label: H.R. 2613
title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
short_title: Next Generation Pipelines Research and Development Act
one: Sets up Department of Energy research, demonstration, and standards programs to develop better pipeline materials, leak sensors, and safety technology, funded by shifting money already authorized for other energy research.
summary: This bill would create several federal programs to research and test new pipeline technology. Pipelines covered include natural gas, liquid fuel, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and water lines, plus liquefied natural gas (LNG) and fuel storage sites. First, the Department of Energy (DOE) would run a demonstration program giving competitive grants to colleges, labs, nonprofits, and private companies. Projects could cover leak detection, stronger materials and coatings, sensors, robots, self-repairing pipe, cybersecurity, and tools to judge whether old pipelines can carry hydrogen or carbon dioxide. Projects that measurably reduce pipeline harm to air, water, or soil, especially in rural and underserved areas, get priority, as do projects with matching non-federal money. Second, DOE, the Department of Transportation, and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) would run a joint early-stage research program. Third, DOE would set up a National Pipeline Modernization Center with a university or similar partner, and it would help train federal and state pipeline safety inspectors. Fourth, NIST would run pipeline measurement and standards research. The bill authorizes (allows Congress to spend, but does not itself pay) $45–50 million a year for demonstrations, $20–30 million for the joint program, $10–15 million for the center, and up to $2.5 million a year for NIST. Most programs end after five years. The money would come from existing authorizations for other DOE energy research, which would be reduced.

label: H.R. 5089
title: Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
short_title: Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
one: Renews and expands federal programs at NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration) that research, forecast and warn the public about tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunamis, landslides and harmful algal blooms, while also increasing the agency's purchase of private-sector weather data.
summary:
This bill renews and widens a 2017 law that guides how the federal government studies and forecasts weather. Most of it authorizes money and sets priorities for NOAA. An "authorization" is permission to spend up to a set amount, and Congress still has to pass separate spending bills to provide the money.

Title I: Reauthorization of the 2017 Act. NOAA's weather research office is authorized at about $164 million in FY2026, rising to about $170 million in FY2030. The bill rewrites the tornado program (VORTEX) and the hurricane program. These programs aim for earlier, more useful warnings, including "warn-on-forecast," which means warning before a storm is detected and not only after. The bill also looks at updating the tornado severity rating system with local communities. The tsunami program gets $30 million a year. It adds the Atlantic, Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico, backup warning centers, and a review of alert wording with high-risk communities. The bill also: sets up a computing and artificial intelligence research effort with the Department of Energy; calls for open public access to NOAA's modeling systems and a public "data lake"; renames and restructures the interagency weather council; starts a ships-of-opportunity pilot for ocean data; and consolidates reports. It renews the National Landslide Preparedness Act through 2030 and adds Tribal and Native Hawaiian participation. It also overhauls the harmful algal bloom and low-oxygen ("hypoxia") law. That part authorizes $27.5 million a year, adds EPA freshwater work, creates a national observing network and a technology "incubator," and gives priority to harmed communities, including low-income communities, communities of color, Tribal communities and rural communities. It also treats the bloom forecasting service as an essential function during a government shutdown.

Title II: Federal forecasting and innovation. NOAA must start a program to protect weather radar from interference, such as wind turbines and buildings. It must plan to replace the NEXRAD radar network by 2040, and it may contract with private firms for "radar-as-a-service" in areas without coverage. Other sections require pilot projects to fill data gaps in underserved places and to help operators of dams and power plants use local data. They create new forecast improvement programs for atmospheric rivers and for coastal flooding and storm surge. They expand aviation weather data from commercial aircraft, including a greenhouse gas instrument pilot, with up to $10 million a year. They authorize $20 million a year for a satellite partnership program, move the National Weather Service's forecaster system (AWIPS) to a cloud-based system by 2030, and address workforce issues. The workforce section lets the Weather Service study outsourcing its hiring, requires a study of the health effects of rotating shift work, and allows a hydrologist at each forecast office.

Title III: Commercial data. NOAA must buy weather and environmental data from private companies. The bill authorizes $100 million a year, includes a pilot program to test the data, uses open competition for the pilot contracts, and creates an ombudsman to handle disputes. It also sets standards for data sharing and storage. Commercial data that is not under redistribution limits must be made available to U.S. weather-enterprise members. A $1 million study is authorized on data management costs.

Title IV: Communicating with the public. The bill rewrites how NOAA studies and improves warnings and public understanding, with attention to vulnerable people and different languages. It includes a hurricane survey on evacuation and trust, and research on elderly populations. It replaces NWSChat by October 2027, expands and modernizes NOAA Weather Radio, including in rural areas and parks, and requires post-storm survey data to be made public. Those surveys would be exempt from the Paperwork Reduction Act. It orders a GAO report on alert delays and requires methods such as digital watermarks to reduce tampering with alerts.

Title V: Agriculture and water. The bill creates pilot projects for forecasting precipitation weeks to months ahead, one for western water management and one for central-U.S. agriculture. It also authorizes $46 million a year for River Forecast Centers, orders a report on transferring weather satellites to other agencies, and creates a precipitation forecast improvement program.

Overall, the bill is mostly about public safety, and its main risks involve reliance on private vendors and the details of how funds are spent.
does: Authorizes NOAA's weather research office at $163.8 million in FY2026, rising to $170.4 million in FY2030, split among labs, the U.S. Weather Research Program, tornado/radar research and technology transfer.

Rewrites the VORTEX tornado program and the hurricane forecast program to extend warning lead times, use probabilistic guidance, fund grants and social science, and examine the tornado severity rating system with local communities.

Reauthorizes the tsunami warning program at $30 million a year (FY2026-2030), with at least 27% for State mitigation and 8% for research, expands coverage to the Atlantic, Caribbean and Gulf, requires backup centers, and reviews alert levels with high-risk communities.
Requires planning for observation gaps and a report on putting a polar-orbiting satellite in the early-morning orbit, and adjusts observing system simulation experiments to compare commercial data.

Creates a NOAA/Department of Energy computing research initiative (AI, cloud, quantum) that ends after five years, allows AI centers of excellence and multi-year contracts, and requires a report within two years.
Expands the Earth Prediction Innovation Center with public access to models, cloud use, portable Unified Forecast System models, and a publicly available NOAA Data Lake.
Updates NOAA satellite planning to use a mix of government, academic, commercial and international partners, and extends a deadline to 2030.

Restructures the interagency weather body as the Interagency Council for Advancing Meteorological Services, with stakeholder coordination, a data inventory, annual private-industry data requests for five years, and annual reports.
Starts a ships-of-opportunity ocean and atmosphere data pilot (including the Arctic) that ends by Sept. 30, 2030 or one year after a report on a global vessel-based network.

Reauthorizes the National Landslide Preparedness Act through 2030, adding atmospheric rivers and extreme precipitation, Tribal and Native Hawaiian participation, NASA, an Alaska regional partnership, and priority for regions with recent landslide deaths.

Overhauls the Harmful Algal Bloom and Hypoxia law: $27.5 million a year, a 5-year action strategy, an EPA freshwater program, a national observing network, treatment of the bloom forecast as an essential service during a funding lapse, and a technology incubator that gives priority to harmed communities.

Lets NOAA waive the non-federal cost share for algal bloom event response and fund States, Tribes and territories with $2 million, and lets the Army Corps work with water and irrigation districts on new bloom removal technologies.

Requires a radar interference research program (wind turbines, buildings) within 180 days, ending by Sept. 30, 2030, and a plan to replace NEXRAD radars by Sept. 30, 2040, with optional private radar-as-a-service contracts.
Directs data-void pilots in under-observed and vulnerable areas, including tools for dam, power plant, nuclear plant and transportation operators, and a national heat-health information effort.
Creates atmospheric river and coastal flooding/storm surge forecast improvement programs, each needing a plan within 180 days and annual budget submissions.
Expands aviation weather: commercial aircraft data (up to $10 million a year), turbulence and icing forecasts, and a greenhouse gas instrument pilot on commercial aircraft.
Authorizes $20 million a year for a NESDIS private-sector/academic satellite joint venture transition program and moves AWIPS to a cloud environment by Sept. 30, 2030.

Addresses the National Weather Service workforce: annual hiring assessment that may recommend outsourcing hiring, a study of shift-work health effects, and optional service hydrologists at forecast offices.

Replaces the Commercial Data Program with a program to buy private weather data ($100 million a year), publishes data standards within 180 days, allows hosted instruments on platforms 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' creates an ombudsman, and requires a data governance report in two years.
Creates a Commercial Data Pilot Program using open competition, with at least 15% of the program's funds, and requires NOAA to assess commercial options before designing future satellites.

Sets multi-year and multi-vendor contracting rules, requires other agencies using the data to fairly compensate NOAA or the provider, sets open data and sharing standards, a data assimilation university consortium, and a $1 million data management study.

Rewrites hazard risk communication law: social science to simplify warning terms, hurricane evacuation and language-access survey, tornado communication pilot, research on elderly populations, and measures against tampering with online alerts.

Requires NWSChat replacement by Oct. 1, 2027 (up to $3 million a year), modernizes and expands NOAA Weather Radio (rural, parks, backups), makes post-storm survey data public with an exemption from the Paperwork Reduction Act and mental health support for staff, and orders a GAO report on alert delays.

Creates subseasonal-to-seasonal precipitation pilots for western water and central agriculture, authorizes $46 million a year for River Forecast Centers, orders a satellite transfer report within 180 days, and creates a precipitation forecast improvement program.

Coastal, lakeside and freshwater communities, drinking water managers, and fishing and subsistence communities affected by algal blooms.

benefits: Could give people more warning time and clearer alerts for tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, tsunamis and landslides.
Could improve monitoring and response to harmful algal blooms that threaten drinking water, fish and health, including in freshwater lakes.
Could expand radar, NOAA Weather Radio and observations in rural, remote, Tribal and underserved areas.
Requires public access to many NOAA models and datasets and to post-storm survey data, which supports transparency.

Post-storm survey information would be exempt from the Paperwork Reduction Act, reducing standard federal review of those data collections.
Cloud-hosting, AI and high-performance computing could carry costs and energy use, and commercial data may have licensing limits on public sharing.

Radar interference research focuses on wind turbine effects, which some may see as burdening renewable energy siting, though the bill does not impose siting rules.
imp.cost: Authorizes funding through FY2030, including about $164-170 million a year for weather research, $30 million a year for tsunami programs, $27.5 million a year for algal bloom and hypoxia programs, $100 million a year for commercial data, up to $10 million a year for aviation data, $20 million a year for satellite partnerships, $46 million a year for River Forecast Centers, up to $3 million a year for NWSChat replacement, plus smaller amounts ($1 million for a data study, $2 million for algal bloom event response). These are authorizations that need later appropriations. The bill says no extra funds beyond the stated amounts are authorized for some programs; no overall cost estimate was provided.

crs:
Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Reauthorization Act of 2025 or the Weather Act Reauthorization Act of 2025
This bill reauthorizes, revises, and establishes several programs related to weather forecasting, monitoring, and research. 
For example, the bill reauthorizes through FY2030 programs that are administered by the Office of Oceanic and Atmospheric Research in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), including the U.S. Weather Research Program. It also provides statutory authority for NOAA's Verification of the Origins of Rotation in Tornadoes Experiment (known as VORTEX-USA).
The bill also requires NOAA to establish programs that support weather forecasting technology, including improvements to radar accuracy, weather forecasting in underserved areas, and coastal flooding forecasting. NOAA must also acquire weather-related data from the private sector and establish a pilot program to test the compatibility of this data with NOAA infrastructure. 
In addition, NOAA must improve weather-related communication systems, including those related to hazardous weather events, through system upgrades that use more modern technology (e.g., cloud-based services) and that allow for expanded coverage (e.g., in rural areas).
Finally, NOAA must administer programs that support weather forecasting for agricultural and water management, including pilot programs to improve precipitation forecasts in the western and central states and a soil moisture monitoring network.

label: H.R. 5276
title: Community Bank LIFT Act
short_title: Community Bank LIFT Act
one: Lowers the capital cushion required for simplified-rule community banks, raises the size cap for those banks from $10 billion to $15 billion in assets, and orders regulators to review and rewrite the rules.
summary: Banks must hold a certain amount of their own money, called capital, as a cushion against losses. Smaller "community banks" can use a simple version of this rule called the community bank leverage ratio (CBLR). Under current law, a bank can use it if it has under $10 billion in assets, and regulators must set the required ratio between 8% and 10%. This bill makes two changes. It raises the asset limit to $15 billion, so larger banks can use the simple rule. It also lowers the allowed range for the ratio to 6% to 8%, which would let regulators require less capital. The bill also tells the Federal Reserve, the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days. The report must suggest ways to get more community banks to join, especially smaller ones, and to cut paperwork. It can cover how the ratio is calculated, how certain assets are treated, who qualifies, how banks opt in or out, and any needed law changes. Within 180 days regulators must propose rules, and within one year they must finalize rules carrying out the bill and the report's recommendations. The bill does not set a specific ratio. Regulators would pick one within the new range.

Lowers the legal range for the CBLR from 8%-10% to 6%-8%.
Requires the Fed, OCC, and FDIC to review the CBLR and report to Congress within 150 days of enactment.
Requires the report to consider how to get more banks, especially smaller ones, to opt in and how to reduce compliance burdens.
Lets the report recommend changes to ratio calculation, asset risk treatment, qualifying criteria, opt-in/out procedures, and grace periods.
Requires proposed rules within 180 days and final rules within one year, implementing the bill and the report's recommendations.

Because the bill sets only a range, the actual requirement depends on later regulatory choices that are not yet made.

Community Bank Leverage Improvement and Flexibility for Transparency Act or the Community Bank LIFT Act
This bill relaxes requirements related to the community bank leverage ratio, which is a simplified capital standard applicable to qualified community banks. Community banks qualify by having less than $10 billion in assets, along with meeting other criteria.

label: H.R. 7086
title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
short_title: Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
one: Rewrites the federal charter school facilities grant program to help state entities pay up to 60% of the cost of acquiring, leasing, renovating and maintaining charter school buildings, and loosens some federal oversight tied to the money.
summary: This bill changes parts of the federal Charter Schools Program, which supports publicly funded but independently run charter schools. First, it replaces the current State Charter School Facilities Incentive Grant program with a new competitive grant program. State entities (such as state agencies or charter school financing groups) could get grants of up to 5 years to help charter schools buy, lease, renovate, and pay ongoing costs for buildings, or to set up other ownership models. Federal money could cover no more than 60% of the cost, and the rest must come from non-federal sources, including partner organizations. The Education Department must give priority to states that offer charter schools tax-exempt financing, treat charter schools like other public schools in land use rules, or bar local deed restrictions that keep charter schools from buying surplus public property. Second, in the existing State Entities grant program, states could use money to help charter schools find facilities and get one-time help meeting building codes, and could reserve up to 10% for a revolving loan fund (money lent out and repaid for reuse). The share that must go to subgrants falls from 90% to 80%. Third, the bill says these funds do not create a "federal interest" in property, which removes certain property recording and reporting requirements. Fourth, entities with Credit Enhancement grants must file annual reports for 10 years after receiving the grant. The bill does not state a dollar amount; it draws from money already set aside for the program.

Allows grant money to be used to increase funding or create financing for charter schools to acquire, lease, and renovate buildings, cover ongoing facilities costs, and create alternative ownership models; partnerships with school districts for public buildings are allowed.

Limits the federal share to 60% of total cost; partner organizations may provide any amount of the non-federal share. Funds must supplement, not replace, non-federal spending. Up to 5% may go to evaluation, technical help, and sharing information.

Requires applications to describe charter school involvement, how aid will be allocated, expertise to judge school success, and how the plan would improve access to state funds, public buildings, and facilities for low-income and rural charter schools. The Secretary may not ask for other information.

Declares that no Charter Schools Program funds create a 'federal interest' in property, exempting them from federal property recording and reporting rules.
Requires Credit Enhancement grant recipients to file annual reports for 10 years after receiving the grant, applying to past, current and future grantees.

crs:
Equitable Access to School Facilities Act
This bill expands and revises certain grant programs under the Charter Schools Program (CSP).
Currently, the CSP's State Charter School Facilities Incentive Grant (SFIG) program provides competitive grants to help states establish and enhance or administer per-pupil facilities aid for charter schools.
The bill replaces the SFIG program with a new grant program, which requires the Department of Education to (1) award competitive grants to state entities with the highest-quality applications for paying the federal share of acquiring and maintaining charter school facilities; and (2) give priority to certain state entities, such as those located in a state that has tax-exempt financing for charter schools. Further, the bill outlines program requirements (e.g., cost-sharing) and allowable uses of grants.
Currently, the CSP's State Entities (SE) program authorizes competitive grants to state entities and, through them, subgrants to eligible applicants to enable them to open and prepare for the operation of a new charter school or replicate or expand a charter school. 
The bill revises the SE program by allowing grants to be used for (1) providing assistance to charter schools with locating and accessing a facility, and (2) providing one-time assistance to ensure the facility complies with building codes. Further, state entities may reserve up to 10% of grant funds for a revolving loan fund.
The bill (1) specifies that no funds made available under the CSP create a federal interest in associated property, and (2) revises reporting requirements for the CSP's Credit Enhancement grants.

environment.reason: The bill concerns charter school facility funding and does not address water, air, land protection, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on 'federal interest' in property removes federal property recording and reporting requirements, which reduces public visibility into taxpayer-funded assets; this is partly offset by the 10-year annual reporting extension for Credit Enhancement grantees.

people_over_profit.reason: Public grant money may flow to private or nonprofit operators and financial partners, and the 80% subgrant floor shifts more funds toward state-level administration and loans rather than direct school use; the 60% federal cap with partner-funded match partly offsets this.

local_say.reason: Priority points for states that bar local deed restrictions and require equal land-use treatment for charter schools (including surplus public property purchases) reduce local communities' control over land use and property decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not bail out corporations or shift costs to ratepayers; revolving loans carry default risk but no bailout provision is present.

equality.reason: Priority for states that treat charter schools equally in land-use rules and the requirement to show how aid narrows funding gaps for low-income and rural charter schools expand access to facilities support.

justice.reason: The 10-year annual reporting requirement for Credit Enhancement grantees adds accountability, but removing the federal interest in property reduces recovery and tracking of taxpayer-funded assets, so effects roughly cancel.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill affects institutional funding and facilities for schools and does not meaningfully expand or restrict what individuals may do about their own lives.

news.overall: None of the provided headlines or descriptions mention the Equitable Access to School Facilities Act, so this analysis cannot describe how outlets framed the bill itself. The Lean Left group has two articles on Wisconsin testing and a federal gender-support investigation, and the Center group has one article on AI in special education; this evidence is thin, and both groups' coverage is only loosely related to the bill's subject, if at all.

label: H.R. 8437
title: Geo POWER Act
short_title: Geo POWER Act (Geothermal demonstration financing)
one: Directs the Department of Energy to create a program that gives milestone-based financing to next-generation geothermal power demonstration projects in at least three states.
summary: This bill would change an existing 2007 energy law to set up a new Department of Energy program for "next-generation" geothermal power. These are projects in hot rock that is hard for water to flow through (called low-permeability or impermeable reservoirs), which older geothermal methods can't easily use. Within 180 days of becoming law, the Energy Secretary would have to start the Milestone-Based Geothermal Demonstration Program. Money would be awarded through a competition, and projects would get it as they hit set technical and financial goals. The Secretary would have to favor projects in places with little or no geothermal power now (including on or near tribal land), projects that share data publicly, projects aiming for at least 30 megawatts of power, and projects likely to draw private investment. The program must fund at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, from at least 3 different sponsors. "Innovative financing" can include tools like loans or loan guarantees the Department of Energy can already use. The bill also removes one paragraph from the existing law (subsection (d), paragraph 3) and authorizes "such sums as are necessary" to be appropriated for the program. It sets no dollar cap, so total cost is unknown and would depend on later spending decisions by Congress.

label: H.R. 9468
title: STAR Act
short_title: STAR Act (Saving Today's Acute-Care Resources Act)
one: The bill would let more very sick Medicare patients in long-term care hospitals qualify for the higher Medicare payment rate, while extending a payment cut on other long-term care hospital stays through fiscal year 2032.
summary:
Long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) treat patients who are very sick and need hospital care for a long time. Medicare pays them one of two ways. Stays that meet certain rules get a higher, specialized rate. Stays that don't meet the rules get a lower "site-neutral" rate. That lower rate is based on what Medicare would pay a regular acute-care hospital, or the stay's cost if that is lower.

This bill would change who gets the higher rate. For stays ending on or after October 1, 2026, it adds a new "high acuity" test. A stay would qualify if the patient came straight from a regular hospital or a critical access hospital (a small rural hospital). The patient must also have a diagnosis group with a "relative weight" of 0.8 or more, a measure of how costly the case is. The diagnosis group must not be one assigned because of 96 or more hours on a ventilator. The LTCH must also have been enrolled, been in its qualifying period, been under construction, or had state approval before the bill became law. That limit blocks new LTCHs from using the exemption.

The bill would also count ICU and ventilator care given at a critical access hospital, or at an LTCH, toward the existing ICU and ventilator tests. Finally, it extends a payment reduction that applies to the site-neutral rate. The extension runs through fiscal year 2032 instead of ending in 2026. The text doesn't give cost estimates.

Limits the new exemption to LTCHs that were enrolled, in their qualifying period, mid-construction (with a binding contract and spending of at least 10% or $2.5 million), or had state certificate-of-need approval before enactment.
Requires mid-build hospitals to send a written certification from their CEO or COO to the Secretary within 60 days of enactment.
Lets ICU and ventilator care at a critical access hospital, or at an LTCH, count toward the existing ICU and ventilator exemptions for discharges on or after October 1, 2026.
Extends an adjustment that reduces the site-neutral payment rate by changing the end date from 2026 to 2032.
Applies the new exemptions to discharges on or after October 1, 2026.
