Securing Access to Care for Seniors in Critical Condition Act of 2025
This bill exempts additional types of hospital stays from the Medicare site-neutral payment rate for long-term care hospitals (LTCHs) and extends certain adjustments to the payment rate. (The site-neutral rate is the lower of Medicare’s acute care hospital payment rate under the inpatient prospective payment system or 100% of the cost of the stay. LTCH stays that do not qualify for the specialized LTCH payment rate under Medicare are instead paid at the lower, site-neutral rate.)
Specifically, the bill exempts discharges from LTCHs from the site-neutral payment rate if the discharge meets specified high acuity criteria. It also allows discharges to qualify for the exemption if certain intensive care or ventilator services were furnished by a critical access hospital immediately prior to the LTCH stay. These exemptions apply to discharges that occur on or after October 1, 2026.
The bill additionally extends an adjustment that reduces the site-neutral payment rate through FY2032.

environment.reason: The bill concerns Medicare payment rules for long-term care hospitals and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill has no provisions on public disclosure or open government; the CEO/COO certification in the mid-build provision goes to the Secretary, not the public, so it does not clearly add or remove transparency.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. on high-acuity exemption and extension through FY2032 of the site-neutral adjustment would pay LTCHs higher rates for more stays, shifting costs to Medicare and taxpayers to benefit facility operators.

local_say.reason: The bill sets federal Medicare payment rules and does not give states or communities new decision-making authority; the mention of state certificate-of-need approval is only a grandfathering test and does not change local input.

no_bailouts.reason: Higher Medicare payments to LTCHs under the new high-acuity exemption and the extended payment adjustment shift fiscal responsibility to taxpayers and program funds, though it is not a direct bailout of distressed corporations.

equality.reason: The new exemption and the mid-construction/enrollment limit treat LTCHs differently based on when they were enrolled or began building, so newer facilities are excluded while existing ones qualify.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal processes, due process, or remedies for harm; it changes payment eligibility rules.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may legally do or choose about their own lives.

label: S. 1254
title: A bill to amend the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act to clarify a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes.
short_title: Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act Clarification
one: The bill would let holders of existing federal land water-conveyance permits (like ditches and canals) use them to refill underground aquifers, for themselves or for public bodies, without new federal approval, after giving 30 days' notice to the Bureau of Land Management.
summary: Many ditches, canals, and pipelines cross federal land under permits, easements, or rights-of-way. A earlier law, the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, said holders could move water to refill underground water supplies (aquifers) without extra federal approval, as long as the use did not expand or change the operation. This bill would clarify and widen that rule. The holder could use the existing authorization for aquifer recharge, acting for itself or for a state, local government, Indian Tribe, or other public entity. It would not need new approval from the Interior Secretary, and this use would not count as an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation from the original permit. The holder would have to tell the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) at least 30 days ahead. The notice must name who will use it, identify the permit, describe the planned use, and include a copy of the agreement between the parties. The bill also says the law does not excuse anyone from following all other applicable federal laws and BLM policies, and it does not allow building, changing, or expanding infrastructure. The Senate committee's amended version replaced the first draft. The first draft would have had a rent exemption and named specific laws, and it would have said these uses are not "major Federal action." The amended text drops those parts. CRS has not yet published a summary, so this is based on the bill text alone.
does: items below
who: Holders of federal rights-of-way, easements, and permits for ditches and canals (irrigation districts, water companies)
States, local governments, Indian Tribes, and public entities that want to recharge aquifers
Bureau of Land Management, which would receive notices
Farmers and communities that depend on groundwater
Nearby residents, downstream water users, and wildlife that depend on affected waterways

benefits: Could speed up and lower the cost of aquifer recharge projects, helping groundwater supplies in dry regions.
The 30-day notice gives BLM and the public record some visibility into planned uses.
Clearly keeps all federal laws and BLM policies in force and bars new construction or expansion under this authority.
Public entities and Tribes can use existing infrastructure rather than building new.
concerns: Treating recharge as not an expansion or modification could bypass new federal review of local environmental effects, and the notice does not give the public a chance to comment.
The notice goes only to BLM; the bill does not require public posting or input from nearby residents, which could limit local say and transparency.
Water quality could be affected if recharged water carries pollutants; the bill relies on existing laws for this.
The text says 'acting ... on behalf of' a public entity but does not clearly bar for-profit involvement, since the rent exemption and for-profit carve-out were dropped in the amended version.
The amended 'all applicable Federal laws' language is broader than the original draft, but it is unclear how it interacts with the 'not a substantial deviation' language.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is provided in the text. BLM would have to process notices, which could add small administrative costs. No new spending is authorized.
unknowns: Whether BLM can object to or block a use after receiving notice.
How the changes affect water rights under state law.
Whether and how environmental review (like NEPA) would apply in practice, since the bill no longer states 'major Federal action' wording.
What BLM does if the notice is incomplete.
No CRS summary or cost estimate was available.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify and widen an earlier law, the Aquifer Recharge Flexibility Act, which lets holders of permits, easements, or rights-of-way on federal land move water through existing ditches, canals, and pipelines to refill underground water supplies without extra federal approval. The amended bill says this use is allowed when it is for aquifer recharge, whether the holder acts for itself or for a public entity, and that it does not need new Interior Secretary approval, as long as the holder gives BLM at least 30 days' notice. The bill states that other federal laws and BLM policies still apply and that it does not allow building or expanding infrastructure. The official title describes the bill only as clarifying a provision relating to conveyances for aquifer recharge purposes. No CRS summary is available yet, so this is based on the bill text alone.

oppose: The bill says recharge use is not an expansion, modification, or substantial deviation of an existing permit, so it may avoid new federal review of possible local environmental effects of the water movement.
The only required step is a 30-day notice to the Bureau of Land Management. The bill does not require public posting or a chance for nearby residents to comment, which could limit local input.
Water quality is not addressed in the bill itself. It depends on existing laws, and the bill does not add new safeguards if recharged water carries pollutants.
support: The bill could make aquifer recharge projects faster and less costly by using infrastructure that already exists, which may help groundwater supplies in dry regions.
The 30-day notice gives BLM a written record of who will use the water, which permit is involved, what the use is, and a copy of the agreement between the parties.

The bill keeps all other federal laws and BLM policies in force and states that it does not allow new construction or expansion of infrastructure. Public entities and Tribes could use existing facilities instead of building new ones.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 treats aquifer recharge moves as not an expansion or modification, so new federal review of local environmental effects is bypassed, though the bill keeps all other federal laws in force, which limits the harm.

transparency_kindness.reason: The 30-day notice goes only to BLM and must name users, permit, use, and agreement copy, but the bill provides no public posting or comment opportunity, so the public has limited view of the decisions.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill has no clear shift of costs onto the public or profit gain for corporations, and the for-profit carve-out was dropped, but the text does not clearly bar for-profit involvement; effects are unclear.

local_say.reason: Sec. 1 removes the need for new Interior Secretary approval for recharge uses, so local and state governments and nearby residents get less say over these uses of existing rights-of-way.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve taxpayer bailouts or ratepayer tax shifts; the rent exemption that could have touched on costs was removed in the amended text.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same rule to all holders, and public entities and Tribes are included alongside other holders, so it does not create clear unequal treatment.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 exempts these uses from new federal approval and public review, which reduces accountability and remedies, though the amended text keeps all other federal laws and BLM policies in force.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill concerns permit holders' use of existing rights-of-way and does not meaningfully expand or restrict individuals' personal choices.

label: S. 1262
title: A bill to require the Secretary of Agriculture to release a reversionary interest in certain land in the Black River State Forest in Millston, Wisconsin, and for other purposes.
short_title: Black River State Forest Land Swap (Deli, Inc.) Release Bill
one: The bill would have the federal government give up its legal claim requiring about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest in Wisconsin to stay in public use, so Wisconsin can trade that land to a moss-producing company, Deli, Inc., for about 37.27 acres that would be added to the forest.
summary: Some of the land in Wisconsin's Black River State Forest, near Millston, came with a federal strings-attached rule. Under an older farm law, the United States keeps a "reversionary interest." This means the land must always be used for public purposes. If it isn't, the federal government could claim it back. This bill would remove that rule from about 31.83 acres. The release would happen only if the State of Wisconsin offers, in a written agreement, to trade that land to Deli, Inc. Deli is a sphagnum moss (a bog plant used in gardening) business in Millston. In return, Deli would give the state about 37.27 acres in two separate parcels, and those acres would be added to the state forest. After the release, the Secretary of Agriculture (through the Forest Service) must provide a quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed is a paper that passes along whatever federal interest exists, at no charge. It must be recorded before the swap deeds. The Secretary may fix mistakes in the land descriptions, working with the state. The bill's land definition says the swap is subject to approval by the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources, the Natural Resources Board, and the Governor. The bill text does not mention appraisals, environmental review, or public comment.
does: Removes the federal 'public purposes' reversionary interest on about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest land.
Triggers the release only if Wisconsin makes a written offer to trade that land to Deli, Inc. for about 37.27 acres of Deli land.
Says the Deli land would be added to Black River State Forest after the swap.
Requires the Agriculture Secretary to provide a free quitclaim deed 'as expeditiously as practicable', to be recorded before the swap deeds.
Lets the Secretary, working with the state, correct the legal descriptions of the state land.
Describes the Deli land as subject to existing public water use or easements on Lee Lake, plus existing roads, zoning rules, and the railroad right-of-way.
who: Deli, Inc., a sphagnum moss producer in Millston, Wisconsin, which would get the state forest parcels
The State of Wisconsin, including the Department of Natural Resources, Natural Resources Board, and Governor, who must approve the exchange
Visitors and nearby residents of Jackson County and the Town of Millston who use or live near the forest
The U.S. Forest Service / Department of Agriculture, which gives up its claim and issues the deed
Wisconsin taxpayers and the public, who own the state forest

benefits: The state would gain about 37.27 acres that would be added to the state forest, if the exchange goes through.
The swap could give the state forest land in exchange for land of similar or different use, which may simplify ownership of the area.
Deli, Inc. would receive the release of the federal restriction on its trade-off parcel, which may make the land more useful to the business.
concerns: The bill text does not mention appraisals, so it is not stated whether the two parcels are of equal value.
The bill does not mention environmental review or public comment before the exchange.
Because the release depends on a state offer and state approvals, the final terms would be set outside this bill.
Removing the public-use requirement from about 31.83 acres could allow those acres to be used differently in the future, depending on later state decisions.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not state any cost, appropriation, or funding amount. The quitclaim deed is described as being provided at no charge."]
unknowns: It is not stated whether the land values in the exchange are equal.
It is not stated what environmental, appraisal, or public review steps would apply before the swap.
It is not stated how the 37.27 acres would be managed once added to the state forest.
It is not stated what uses Deli, Inc. might make of the released land, or what happens if the state does not make an offer.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to have the Secretary of Agriculture release a federal reversionary interest on about 31.83 acres of Black River State Forest land near Millston, Wisconsin, so that land can be exchanged with Deli, Inc. for about 37.27 acres that would be added to the state forest. The bill describes the release as conditional on Wisconsin offering that trade in writing. The bill's text does not state a broader problem beyond this land exchange.

crs:
This bill directs the Forest Service to release its reversionary interest in approximately 31.83 acres in the Black River State Forest if the State of Wisconsin offers to exchange those acres for approximately 37.27 acres of land owned by Deli, Inc., a sphagnum moss production business located in Millston, Wisconsin. The Forest Service's reversionary interest requires the state forest land to be used for public purposes. 
After the release, the Forest Service must provide a quitclaim deed of the release as expeditiously as practicable.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2 and the bill text do not require appraisals, environmental review, or public comment before the land exchange, so the public has less visibility into the swap terms.

people_over_profit.reason: The release of the federal public-purpose restriction on about 31.83 acres would benefit Deli, Inc., a private business, and the bill does not require an appraisal showing the parcels are of equal value.

local_say.reason: The release is triggered only by a written state offer and is subject to approval by the Wisconsin DNR, Natural Resources Board, and Governor, so state decision-makers control whether the swap proceeds.

news.overall: Evidence is limited: only four headlines with no descriptions, and none directly covers the Black River State Forest bill. The Lean Left coverage that is provided touches on federal public land policy and Wisconsin parks and recreation, so any inference about how these outlets would frame the bill itself would be speculative.

label: S. 1350
title: A bill to modify the boundaries of the Talladega National Forest, and for other purposes.
short_title: Talladega National Forest Boundary Modification
one: The bill would expand the official boundary of Alabama's Talladega National Forest to include land shown on a 2024 Forest Service map and let the Agriculture Department acquire land inside that area only from willing sellers.
summary: This bill would change the official boundary of the Talladega National Forest in Alabama so it includes additional land shown on a map dated September 6, 2024, titled "Talladega National Forest Proposed Proclamation Boundary Addition." The map must be kept on file at the appropriate Forest Service office, where the public can look at it. Once land is inside the boundary, the Secretary of Agriculture (who oversees the Forest Service) may acquire land, water, and related interests there using the usual National Forest tools, including the 1911 Weeks Law. Any private land or water must come from a willing seller. It can be donated, swapped for other land, or bought with donated or appropriated (Congress-approved) money. The bill says this should happen without undue delay where practical. Land that is acquired would be managed under the Weeks Law and all rules for the National Forest System. The bill does not force anyone to sell and does not give a dollar amount. It does not say how many acres are in the map area. I could not see the map itself, so I cannot tell where the added land is, how big it is, or who owns it now.
does: Expands the Talladega National Forest boundary to cover land on a map dated September 6, 2024.
Requires the map to be on file and open to public inspection at the Forest Service.
Lets the Agriculture Secretary acquire land, waters, and interests in the mapped area using National Forest System authorities, including the Weeks Law.
Limits acquisition of private land to willing sellers, by donation, exchange, or purchase with donated or appropriated funds.
Requires acquired land to be managed under the Weeks Law and all National Forest System laws and regulations.
Directs that acquisitions happen without undue delay, to the extent practicable.
who: Private landowners inside the mapped area who may choose to sell, donate, or swap land
The U.S. Forest Service and the Agriculture Department
Visitors, hunters, hikers, and other recreation users of the forest
Nearby communities and local governments in Alabama
Wildlife, plants, and downstream water users
Federal taxpayers, if appropriated money is used for purchases

benefits: If land is added and acquired, the national forest could grow, which may protect natural areas, wildlife habitat, and water sources.
The willing-seller requirement means landowners keep the choice to sell.
The public can review the official map on file, which may increase transparency about the boundary.
concerns: Because the map is not described in the bill text provided, it is unclear where the added land is or who owns it, which could make the effects hard to judge.
Adding land and buying it with appropriated funds could increase federal spending and federal land ownership in Alabama, which some people may see as a concern.
Changes to forest boundaries could affect nearby local uses, such as hunting, timber, or property taxes, though the material does not address these points.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not state a dollar amount or authorize a specific appropriation. Acquisitions could be made through donations, land exchanges, or purchases using donated or appropriated money. The total cost is not stated."]
unknowns: The number of acres in the expanded area is not stated.
The location, land types, and current owners of the added land cannot be determined from the bill summary, since the map was not available.
The total cost of any future purchases is not stated.
Whether any specific landowners have expressed interest in selling, donating, or exchanging land is not stated.
The bill's effects on local governments, tax revenue, and current land uses are not addressed in the material provided.
The Congressional Research Service summary was blank, so no independent summary of the bill was available.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to modify the boundaries of the Talladega National Forest in Alabama so the forest covers additional land shown on a map dated September 6, 2024. It lets the Secretary of Agriculture acquire land and related interests inside that expanded boundary, using willing sellers, donations, exchanges, or purchases, and manage that land as part of the National Forest System.

Buying land with appropriated federal funds would add to federal spending and federal land ownership in Alabama. A constituent could ask how much the purchases would cost taxpayers and whether that spending is justified.

Expanding a national forest can affect nearby residents, including hunting, timber, and property tax concerns. The summary does not address these, so a constituent could ask the member to find out how local communities would be affected.
support: The bill would expand the Talladega National Forest to cover additional land on an official map, which could help protect natural areas, wildlife habitat, and water sources over time.
Landowners keep the choice to sell. The bill requires willing sellers and does not force anyone to give up their property, so a constituent could say the approach respects private property rights.
The bill requires the boundary map to be kept on file at the Forest Service where the public can look at it, which supports transparency about where the boundary is.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 expands the Talladega National Forest boundary so the Secretary may acquire land and water in the mapped area, which could protect habitat and water sources, though no acquisition is required and the land is unidentified.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires the September 6, 2024 boundary map to be kept on file at the Forest Service where the public can inspect it, which makes the boundary change easier to review.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill's effects on corporate profit versus public interest are not clearly addressed; acquisitions are willing-seller only and no corporate tax or cost shift is described.

local_say.reason: The bill adds land to federal forest boundaries without a stated local consultation step, and it also lets landowners decide whether to sell, so the net effect on local say is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has nothing to do with bailing out corporations; it concerns federal land acquisition, and no dollar amount is specified.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same willing-seller rule and acquisition tools to all landowners within the mapped area and does not create unequal treatment.

justice.reason: The bill does not change legal processes, remedies, or due process for affected persons, so no clear effect on justice is apparent.

personal_freedom.reason: Private landowners keep the choice to sell, donate, or exchange land, and the bill does not restrict personal conduct, so the net effect on personal freedom is unclear.

news.overall: Evidence is very limited: only one Lean Left item (NPR) was provided, and its headline covers a broader national forest policy rather than the Talladega boundary bill. No other perspective groups were supplied, so cross-perspective comparison is not possible.

label: S. 140
title: Wildfire Prevention Act of 2026
short_title: Wildfire Prevention Act of 2026
one: Sets rising targets for thinning and prescribed burning on Forest Service and BLM land, speeds up some environmental reviews, adds wildfire-data reporting and a technology pilot, and lets local governments and tribes join lawsuits over certain federal projects.
summary:
This bill aims to reduce wildfire risk on national forests and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land. It orders the Forest Service and BLM to set yearly goals for mechanical thinning (cutting trees and brush) and prescribed fire (planned, controlled burns). The goals start at the 2019–2023 average and rise to at least 40% above that average by 2029. The agencies must give each region or state an acreage target and publish the data. The goals and targets would be exempt from National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) review.

The bill adds a lot of reporting. Agencies must publish annual reports on acres treated, obstacles such as lawsuits or paperwork delays, regeneration harvests, and which streamlined review tools were used. They must put a hazardous-fuels report in the President's budget materials and standardize how they track acres. They must also report on the effectiveness and cost per acre of treatments. The Forest Service must publish regional estimates of whether national forests absorb or release carbon every three years. Agencies must also report to Congress on better ways to measure wildfire risk reduction.

On forest management, the bill raises the distance for removing hazard trees near power lines from 10 to 50 feet. It lets agencies allow utilities to cut vegetation near power facilities without a separate timber sale, with sale proceeds going to the government. It raises the dollar threshold in the National Forest Management Act's timber sale provision from $10,000 to $55,000. It requires a new categorical exclusion (a shortcut that skips a full environmental study) for removing high-priority hazard trees near certain roads, trails, and developed recreation sites. Projects are capped at 3,000 acres, and it excludes wilderness and roadless areas. Local governments and tribes would be allowed to intervene in lawsuits over approved federal projects nearby that cut wildfire, insect, or disease risk or that raise money from timber sales. The agencies must also study using livestock grazing to reduce fire fuels.

Within three years, the agencies must use at least one existing streamlined review authority on each unit with land at high risk from wildfire, insects, or disease. A 7-year public-private pilot would test wildfire technologies, including AI, sensing, and mesh networks. Finally, the bill repeals a reporting requirement in the FLAME Act of 2009. The text gives no cost estimate or new funding amount.
does: Requires the Forest Service and BLM to set yearly acreage goals for mechanical thinning (commercial and pre-commercial) and prescribed fire, equal to the 2019–2023 average in FY2025–26, 20% higher in FY2027–28, and at least 40% higher from FY2029 on.
Requires regional or state acreage allotments within 90 days of enactment and yearly after that, with the goal and allotment data published online.
Exempts the setting of these goals and allotments from NEPA review, and says the section does not override the Wilderness Act or the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.

Requires annual public reports starting Sept. 30, 2025, on acres treated, whether goals were met, obstacles such as litigation or paperwork delays, regeneration harvests, high-risk areas, streamlined reviews used, and partnership agreements used.

Requires a hazardous fuels reduction report in the President's budget materials covering wildland-urban interface acres, risk levels, cost per acre, effectiveness, and a standard counting method. Each acre is counted once a year.
Requires standardized data-tracking procedures within 90 days, with accuracy checks and effectiveness analysis, plus a report to Congress with policy recommendations.
Requires the Forest Service to publish a regional forest carbon balance (carbon source or sink) for the National Forest System every 3 years.
Requires a report to Congress within 18 months on performance measures for wildfire risk reduction, including tracking outcomes, mapping updates, and new technologies.

Raises the hazard-tree clearing distance near power lines on federal land from 10 to 50 feet. Lets agencies authorize utility vegetation cutting in permits without a separate timber sale, with sale proceeds (minus transport costs) going to the government.
Raises the National Forest Management Act timber-sale dollar figure from $10,000 to $55,000.

Requires the Agriculture Secretary to develop a categorical exclusion for high-priority hazard tree work within 1 year. It covers trees near certain roads, trails, and developed recreation sites, is capped at 3,000 acres, and excludes wilderness, roadless areas, and areas where cutting is restricted.

Gives local governments and Indian tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits over approved nearby federal projects that reduce wildfire, insect, or disease risk or generate timber revenue, and full participation in settlement talks.

Requires a strategy within 18 months on using livestock grazing, including targeted grazing, invasive grass control, post-fire recovery, and temporary use of vacant allotments, without changing existing grazing programs.
Requires agencies to use at least one of six existing streamlined environmental review authorities on each unit with land at high risk from insects, disease, or wildfire within 3 years.

Creates a 7-year wildfire technology deployment and testbed pilot program with private entities, nonprofits, and universities. It prioritizes AI, quantum sensing, augmented reality, and 5G/mesh networks, and requires annual reports to Congress.
Repeals a reporting subsection of the FLAME Act of 2009.
who: Forest Service and BLM staff, who would face new goals and reporting duties
Residents and communities near federal forests and rangelands, especially in the wildland-urban interface
Local governments and Indian tribes, who would gain a right to intervene in lawsuits
Timber companies and contractors
Livestock ranchers with grazing permits
Electric utilities with rights-of-way on federal land
Environmental groups and others who sue over or comment on federal projects
Technology companies, nonprofits, and universities that join the pilot program
Wildlife, forest ecosystems, and downstream water users

benefits: Could reduce catastrophic wildfire risk near communities, protecting lives, homes, air quality, and watersheds.
Public reporting on acres treated, cost per acre, effectiveness, and carbon balance improves government transparency.
Local governments and tribes gain a stronger legal voice on nearby federal projects.
Pilot program could bring new detection and communication technology to firefighting.
Hazard tree removal near power lines and roads could reduce ignition and safety risks.
concerns: Exempting goals from NEPA, creating a new categorical exclusion, and mandating streamlined reviews could reduce environmental analysis and public comment.
Rising thinning targets and timber-revenue projects could favor commercial logging over ecological health, and could affect wildlife habitat and water quality.
Intervenor rights apply only to local governments and tribes, not to individual residents or other groups.
Reports track obstacles such as litigation and delays, which could add pressure to limit legal challenges.
Prescribed burns create smoke that can affect local air quality.
Increasing grazing on federal land could affect streams and native plants.
imp.cost: The text provides no new appropriation or cost estimate. Costs for higher treatment goals, reporting, and the 7-year pilot would depend on future funding. Utility cutting proceeds go to the government.
unknowns: How much money Congress would provide to meet the higher targets.
How many acres the new hazard-tree categorical exclusion and mandatory streamlined reviews would actually cover.
Whether the targets would focus on high-risk areas near communities.
How intervenor rights would affect the pace and outcome of lawsuits.
What the carbon accounting would show and how it would be used.
Effects of the $10,000 to $55,000 timber-sale threshold change, since the text doesn't explain it.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reduce wildfire risk on National Forest System and BLM land by setting rising yearly targets for mechanical thinning and prescribed fire, speeding certain forest management projects, and testing new wildfire technology. It also adds public reporting requirements so the public can track results.

oppose: The bill exempts the setting of acreage goals and allotments from NEPA review and creates a new categorical exclusion, which could reduce environmental analysis and public comment on projects.
Rising thinning targets and timber-revenue projects could put more weight on commercial logging, which may affect wildlife habitat, water quality, and ecological health.
Intervenor rights go only to local governments and tribes, not to individual residents or other groups, which may leave some affected people with less of a voice in court.
support: The bill sets clear, rising yearly goals for thinning and prescribed fire, reaching at least 40% above the 2019–2023 average by 2029, which could reduce catastrophic wildfire risk near communities.
The bill requires public annual reports and published data on acres treated, cost per acre, and effectiveness, which improves transparency about whether the work is getting done.
The bill creates a 7-year pilot program to test new wildfire detection and communication technology, such as AI, sensing, and mesh networks, which could help firefighters respond sooner.

crs:
This bill establishes forest management requirements for federal lands, particularly with respect to reducing wildfires. 
For example, the bill establishes annual goals to increase (1) the number of acres of Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management (BLM) land that are mechanically thinned (i.e., a management process related to the removal of trees and vegetation); and (2) the number of acres of Forest Service and BLM land treated by prescribed fire. By FY2029, the goals must be to increase the number of acres of each by at least 40% compared to the average number of acres of each in FY2019-FY2023.
The bill also directs the Forest Service and the BLM to (1) implement standardized procedures for tracking data relating to hazardous fuels reduction activities they carry out, and (2) develop a strategy to identify opportunities to use livestock grazing as a wildfire risk reduction tool on federal land. Additionally, the Forest Service and the Department of the Interior must establish a deployment and test bed pilot program for wildfire prevention, detection, communication, and mitigation technologies.
The bill mandates use of existing authorities for expedited environmental review for certain forest land at high risk from wildfire, insects, or disease.
Finally, the bill provides local governments and Indian tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits concerning certain projects on federal land that (1) reduce risks posed by wildfire, insects, or disease; or (2) generate revenue from harvesting timber.

environment.reason: Sec. on goals and categorical exclusion (NEPA exemption for goals, new 3,000-acre categorical exclusion, mandated streamlined reviews) reduces environmental analysis, while thinning and prescribed-fire targets and the carbon reporting could reduce catastrophic fire risk to watersheds and air; on balance the bill leans modestly toward weaker environmental review, with prescribed-fire smoke and grazing expansion as added concerns.

transparency_kindness.reason: Annual public reports on acres treated, cost per acre, effectiveness, carbon balance, and obstacles, plus publishing goals and regional allotments online, make agency performance more visible, though the NEPA exemption for goals and reduced environmental comment limit public review.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. raising the NFMA timber-sale threshold to $55,000 and the utility vegetation-cutting provision expand commercial timber sales, which may favor timber and utility interests over ecological and public interests, though proceeds go to the government and the bill also targets community fire protection.

local_say.reason: Sec. giving local governments and tribes the right to intervene in lawsuits and full participation in settlement talks increases their voice, though the NEPA exemption and categorical exclusion reduce local review of federal projects and individuals lack the same right.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks; the utility vegetation provision lets utilities cut vegetation without a timber sale, but no cost is shifted to ratepayers in the text.

equality.reason: Sec. granting intervenor rights only to local governments and tribes, not to individuals or other groups, creates unequal access to litigation participation.

justice.reason: Sec. on NEPA exemption and new categorical exclusion and mandated streamlined reviews reduce analysis and public challenge opportunities, while intervenor rights for local governments and tribes add some procedural standing, on balance making legal review less accessible to the public.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill regulates federal land management and agency actions and does not meaningfully expand or restrict what individuals may do with their own lives.

label: S. 1680
title: Virginia Wilderness Additions Act of 2025
short_title: Virginia Wilderness Additions Act of 2025
one: The bill would add about 1,000 acres to the Rough Mountain Wilderness and about 4,600 acres to the Rich Hole Wilderness in Virginia's George Washington National Forest, allowing temporary use of motorized equipment on the Rich Hole land for water quality work before it becomes full wilderness.
summary:
This bill would protect more public forest land in western Virginia as wilderness. Wilderness is the strongest level of federal land protection. It generally bans roads, permanent buildings, and motor vehicles or machines.

About 1,000 acres would be added to the Rough Mountain Wilderness right away. The land is in the George Washington National Forest and is shown on a 2014 Forest Service map.

About 4,600 acres would be added to the Rich Hole Wilderness in two steps. First, the land becomes "potential wilderness," and the Forest Service must manage it under the Wilderness Act. The one exception is that the Forest Service may use motorized equipment and mechanized transport (such as machines or wheeled carts) to carry out water quality and fish passage projects. Those projects are described in a 2015 Forest Service decision called the Lower Cowpasture Restoration and Management Project. While doing this work, the agency must use the least intrusive tools it practically can.

The land becomes full wilderness on the earlier of two dates. One is when the Secretary of Agriculture publishes notice in the Federal Register that the work is done. The other is five years after the bill becomes law.

The bill does not say how much money it would cost, and it does not set aside new funding.

The bill does not state whether local governments or residents were consulted. The text does not describe public input.
The bill does not describe how much of the restoration work is left or what it would cost.

label: S. 1682
title: Alex Gate Safety Act of 2025
short_title: Alex Gate Safety Act of 2025
one: Requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to make existing industry gate safety standards mandatory for large and vehicle gates within one year, and to run a national public education campaign about gate dangers.
summary: This bill would make gate safety rules mandatory. Right now, many gate safety standards are voluntary guidelines written by industry groups. The bill tells the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), the federal agency that handles dangerous consumer products, to issue a final safety rule within one year of the bill becoming law. The rule would require "covered gates" to meet certain existing standards from ASTM (a standards group) and, for gates with motors or similar operators, a standard called UL 325. Covered gates include automatic and manual vehicle gates and any other gate wider than 48 inches or 84 inches or taller. The CPSC would decide exactly which types of gates fall under the rule. If those standards groups update their standards, the update would automatically become part of the rule after 180 days unless the CPSC says within 90 days that the change does not improve safety. The CPSC could also change the rule later to reduce injury risk. Within two years, the CPSC must also launch a national campaign to teach manufacturers, contractors, owners, consumers, building officials, and school agencies about the dangers of falling or detached gates and about low-cost ways to prevent injuries. Within three years, it must report to Congress on what it did. The bill text does not state a dollar amount or any new money.

label: S. 1748
title: Kids Online Safety Act
short_title: Kids Online Safety Act
one: Requires social media, video games, messaging apps and streaming services likely used by under-17s to build in safety settings, parental tools, reporting, audits and design-care duties, and requires big platforms to offer a non-personalized feed option.
summary:
This bill would set new rules for online platforms that kids and teens under 17 are likely to use. That includes social media, online video games, messaging apps with public or community features, and video streaming services. Plain email, school, library, nonprofit, and news or sports sites are mostly left out.

Title I covers kids' safety. Platforms must use reasonable care when they design features, like infinite scroll, autoplay, push alerts, reward streaks, and in-game purchases. The goal is to prevent foreseeable harms such as eating disorders, suicidal behavior, compulsive use, severe harassment, sexual exploitation, drug, alcohol, tobacco and gambling exposure, and deceptive financial practices. Platforms must give known minors easy settings to limit who can contact them, hide their data, turn off addictive features, switch off personalized recommendations, limit location sharing, and set time limits. Those settings must default to the most protective option. Parents get tools to see and manage settings, limit purchases, and see and limit time spent. Platforms must also provide a way to report harm. They must answer within 10 days for the biggest platforms, or 21 days for smaller ones, and faster if a child is in imminent danger. The bill bans "dark patterns" (tricky design that undermines these controls), bans advertising of drugs, tobacco, gambling and alcohol to known minors, and bars market research on children under 13. Research on 13 to 16 year olds needs parental consent.

Large social media platforms (over 10 million monthly U.S. users) must publish yearly independent audit reports on risks to minors. The bill also orders a federal study of age verification at the device level. It does not require platforms to collect new age data or verify ages. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) must issue guidance. The FTC and state attorneys general enforce most of the rules. States cannot use the duty of care in section 102 as the basis for state-law suits. A temporary 11-member Kids Online Safety Council, exempt from open-meeting advisory committee rules, would advise Congress. Most of Title I starts 18 months after enactment.

Title II, "Filter Bubble Transparency," applies to all users, not just minors. One year after enactment, platforms that use "opaque" algorithms (ones that rank content using data users didn't give for that purpose) must tell users, explain in their terms how the algorithm works, and let users switch easily to a feed that doesn't use that data. They can't charge more or deny service to users who switch. Trade secrets don't have to be disclosed. The FTC enforces this title.

Title III says federal law overrides only conflicting state laws. States may pass stronger protections for minors.
does: Covers online platforms, online video games, messaging apps and video streaming services used or likely used by anyone under 17, with exceptions (email, broadband, schools, libraries, nonprofits, news/sports sites, business software, VPNs, .gov sites).

Imposes a duty of reasonable care in creating and using design features (infinite scroll, autoplay, notifications, reward badges, in-game purchases, appearance filters, personalized features) to prevent foreseeable harms: eating disorders, substance use, suicidal behavior, diagnosable anxiety/depression tied to compulsive use, severe harassment, sexual exploitation, drug/alcohol/tobacco/gambling exposure, and unfair financial practices.
Says platforms need not block minors from deliberately searching for content, and no government may enforce the duty of care based on the viewpoint of protected speech.

Requires easy-to-use safeguards for known minors: limit contacts, restrict viewing of personal data, limit addictive features by default, opt out of personalized recommendations (chronological feed), restrict location sharing, and set time limits, all defaulting to the most protective setting.

Requires parental tools: view settings (and change them for children under 13), restrict purchases, view and restrict time spent. Tools are on by default for children under 13, and users must be told when tools are active.

Requires reporting channels and a point of contact for harms to minors, with a substantive response within 10 days (platforms over 10 million U.S. monthly users) or 21 days (smaller), or faster for imminent threats.
Bans facilitating ads for narcotics, cannabis, tobacco, gambling, or alcohol to known minors, and bans dark-pattern interfaces that undermine the safeguards and parental tools.

Requires clear disclosures before registration, explanations of recommendation systems, ad labels (including paid endorsements), parental consent for children consistent with COPPA, and materials in multiple languages where practicable.

Requires large social/community platforms (over 10 million monthly U.S. users) to publish annual public reports based on independent third-party audits, with data de-identified and platforms required to give auditors full access and not misrepresent facts.
Bans market or product research on children under 13 and on 13-16 year olds without verifiable parental consent.

Orders a Commerce/FCC/FTC study within 1 year on device-level age verification; the FTC must issue guidance within 18 months, including on how it judges whether a platform 'knows' a user is a minor. The bill does not require age verification or new collection of age data.
Enforcement by the FTC (treated as a violation of an FTC rule) and by state attorneys general for sections 103-105; states can't sue under state law based on the duty of care (section 102).

Creates a temporary 11-member Kids Online Safety Council (government, academics, parents, youth, educators, platforms, games, state AGs, disadvantaged communities) that reports to Congress (interim at 1 year, final at 3 years); it is exempt from the Federal Advisory Committee Act.

Title II: one year after enactment, platforms using 'opaque' algorithms (ranking on data not expressly supplied by the user) must give notice, explain main inputs and optimization goals in their terms, and let users easily switch to an input-transparent feed with no price penalty. Trade secrets are protected, and the FTC enforces it.
Title III: federal law preempts only conflicting state laws; states may enact stronger minor protections. The bill has a severability clause.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to protect minors (users under 17) from online harms on covered platforms, such as social media, online video games, messaging apps, and video streaming services. It requires these platforms to use reasonable care in designing features that could cause foreseeable harm, and to provide safeguards and parental tools. Title II says it aims to give all users more transparency and choice about algorithms that rank content using personal data they did not provide for that purpose.

crs:
Kids Online Safety Act
This bill requires covered online platforms, including social media platforms, to implement tools and safeguards to protect users and visitors under the age of 17. 
Covered platforms
 are online platforms, video games, messaging applications, or video streaming services used or likely to be used by individuals under the age of 17, with specified exceptions. 
The bill generally requires covered platforms to exercise reasonable care in the design and use of features that increase minors’ online activity in order to prevent and mitigate harm to minors (e.g., mental health disorders and severe harassment).  
Covered platforms are also required to provide certain safeguards to minors, such as protections for minors’ data; tools for parents of minors, such as access to minors’ privacy settings; and a mechanism for account holders and visitors to report harm to minors on the platform. 
Covered platforms are prohibited from conducting market or product research on children under the age of 13, and may only conduct such research on those under the age of 17 with parental consent. 
The bill provides for enforcement through the Federal Trade Commission and states. 
The bill also requires online platforms to meet certain requirements before using algorithms that select, order, or prioritize information presented to users based on user-specific data not provided for that purpose. Specifically, such platforms must (1) provide users with notice of the use of such algorithms, and (2) permit users to switch to an algorithm that does not rely on such user-specific data.

environment.reason: The bill does not address water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: Title I requires public annual audit reports for large platforms and Title II requires disclosure of algorithm notices and explanations to users, while the bill also bans dark patterns and protects minors from harmful design and unwanted ads; offsetting concerns are the council's exemption from open-meeting rules and trade-secret carve-outs.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 102 duty of care and the default-protective settings for minors limit profit-driven addictive design, and the bans on ads for drugs, alcohol, tobacco and gambling to known minors and on research on children under 13 favor child welfare over engagement revenue; compliance costs may partly be passed to users, a modest offset.

local_say.reason: Sec. 107-type language bars states from using the duty of care as the basis for state-law suits, which limits state enforcement, though Title III lets states enact stronger minor protections, so the net effect on state and local say is somewhat negative.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide bailouts or ratepayer subsidies, and its costs are mainly FTC enforcement and platform compliance, with no dollar appropriation stated.

equality.reason: The protections apply to all known minors on covered platforms with defaults to the most protective setting, and Title II gives all users the option of a non-personalized feed without price penalty, though the weaker parental tools for 13-16 year olds create some unequal treatment by age.

justice.reason: Sec. 103-105 require a reporting channel with response deadlines (10 or 21 days, faster for imminent danger) and give the FTC and state attorneys general enforcement authority, though the bar on duty-of-care suits by states and vague standards reduce accountability.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill restricts platform design and ads for minors and adds parental controls, which limits some minors' choices, while Title II expands users' choice of feed, so the effects on individual freedom roughly offset.

news.overall: Coverage of the Kids Online Safety Act is sparse and mostly indirect: no group has more than a few headlines, and none clearly reports on the bill's content or status. Lean Left coverage centers on political pressure over social media harms, Center coverage touches on related online safety and fraud efforts, and Lean Right coverage focuses on legal challenges and skepticism toward regulation. Since only headlines and brief descriptions were provided, these characterizations are tentative and based on limited evidence.

label: S. 1759
title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
short_title: Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
one: As reported by the Senate Commerce Committee, the bill tells the FAA to write a final rule within 2 years creating a noise-based certification standard for civil supersonic (faster-than-sound) aircraft, replacing the original text that would have lifted the overland supersonic ban whenever no sonic boom reaches the ground.
summary:
This bill is about passenger and business jets that fly faster than the speed of sound (supersonic). Today, FAA rules generally ban civil aircraft from flying supersonic over U.S. land unless they get a special authorization. The bill was introduced to change that, and the CRS summary describes that original version: allow supersonic flight without special authorization as long as no sonic boom reaches the ground.

The Senate Commerce Committee rewrote the bill before sending it to the full Senate. The version now on the Senate calendar does something different. It gives the FAA two years after enactment to issue a final rule that creates a "noise-based certification standard" for civil supersonic aircraft. The FAA must consult NASA. Takeoff and landing noise for these aircraft could not exceed the levels required of subsonic aircraft now in operation. The FAA must also set up a process to review and update the standards over time. The reviews would take into account better noise-reduction technology, research on sonic booms and acceptable sound levels, and changes in other rules.

The rewritten text does not mention emissions, fuel use, or public input beyond the normal rulemaking process. It also does not say outright whether supersonic flight over land is allowed or what boom level would be acceptable. Those details would be left to the FAA's rule.
does: Requires the FAA to issue a final rule within 2 years of enactment creating a noise-based certification standard for civil supersonic aircraft.
Requires the FAA to consult with NASA while writing the rule.
Sets takeoff and landing noise limits for these aircraft at no higher than what subsonic aircraft in operation must meet at the time of enactment.
Requires a process to review and update the takeoff and landing noise standards as technology and international standards change.
Requires a process to review and update the overall standard using new research on sonic booms and acceptable sound levels.
Replaces the original text, which would have had the FAA allow supersonic flight without special authorization as long as no sonic boom reaches the ground.
who: Aircraft makers and airlines developing or planning to use supersonic jets
People living near airports and under possible supersonic flight routes
The FAA and NASA, which would write and inform the rule
Air travelers, especially premium and business travelers
Communities, wildlife, and ecosystems exposed to aircraft noise and emissions

benefits: A clear noise-based standard could give aircraft makers a defined path toward certification.
Requiring takeoff and landing noise at or below current subsonic levels may limit noise near airports.

Supersonic Aviation Modernization Act
This bill directs the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to allow civil aircraft to operate at speeds above Mach 1 (i.e., supersonic) over land in the United States under certain conditions.

title: Stratton Ridge Air Force Memorial Act

one: Lets the Forest Service allow a memorial for nine Air Force crew members killed in a 1982 crash to be moved from private land to a rest area on the Cherohala Skyway in North Carolina, at no federal cost.
summary: This bill deals with a memorial honoring nine Air Force crew members who died when a C-141B transport plane crashed over the Cherokee and Nantahala National Forests in North Carolina on August 31, 1982. The memorial now sits on private land next to the Cherohala Skyway, a scenic road. If the private landowner agrees, the bill lets the Secretary of Agriculture (who oversees the Forest Service) approve moving the memorial to the Stratton Ridge rest area at mile marker 2 of the Skyway, in Graham County, inside the Nantahala National Forest. The Secretary would do this through a "special use authorization," which is a permit for using national forest land. The exact spot must be approved by the North Carolina Department of Transportation. If the spot is next to a federal-aid highway, the Federal Highway Administration must also approve. No federal money may be used to move, install, or maintain the memorial. Whoever asks for the move must pay all costs, including the application review, any environmental review, and the moving and upkeep. The permit can include conditions, such as a ban on making the memorial bigger. The bill says "may," so it allows the move but does not require it.

who: Families, friends and fellow service members of the nine crew members

label: S. 2440
title: A bill to direct the Secretary of Agriculture to convey certain National Forest System land located in Franklin County, Mississippi, and for other purposes.
short_title: Okhissa Lake Rural Economic Development Land Conveyance
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to sell about 310 acres of surface land near Okhissa Lake in Homochitto National Forest, Mississippi, to a state agency for fair market value. The state agency would take on dam upkeep and safety duties, and the sale would be exempt from environmental review.
summary:
This bill would make the Secretary of Agriculture sell two pieces of Homochitto National Forest land in Franklin County, Mississippi, to the Scenic Rivers Development Alliance. The Alliance is an instrumentality (a body) of the State of Mississippi. The pieces are about 137.7 acres and about 173 acres, and they sit around Okhissa Lake. Only the surface of the land would transfer. The federal government would keep all minerals, oil, gas, and other underground rights.

The Alliance would pay cash equal to the land's fair market value, set by a federal-standard appraisal. It would also pay appraisal, survey, and closing costs. It would sign an agreement to pay for upkeep of the Okhissa Lake Dam and take responsibility for following federal and state dam safety laws. The sale money would go into a Forest Service fund used to buy other land for national forests.

The government would keep road and trail easements so the public can still reach the lake and nearby forest. It could take the land back if the land goes to a private (nonpublic) owner or is used for anything other than public recreation and fish and wildlife habitat. The Alliance could not split the land into home lots.

However, the bill says the Forest Service does not have to follow the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) or any other environmental law for the sale. The Forest Service would also not have to clean up any hazardous materials on the land. It would only have to disclose them. If the government takes the land back, the Alliance stays liable for cleanup.
does: Orders the Forest Service to convey about 137.7 acres and about 173 acres of surface land in Homochitto National Forest to the Scenic Rivers Development Alliance by quitclaim deed.
who: Scenic Rivers Development Alliance, the Mississippi state body that would receive the land and the dam duties

benefits: The Alliance could take over management of the lake area and dam, which may ease the federal government's upkeep duties.
Sale proceeds would go to a Forest Service fund for buying other national forest land.

Not requiring hazardous material cleanup could leave contamination for future owners or the state to address.
Transferring the dam's upkeep may raise questions about whether the Alliance has enough funding to keep it safe over time.
Selling public land out of federal ownership may reduce long-term public control over the area.

title: A bill to release a Federal reversionary interest and convey mineral interests in Chester County, Tennessee, and for other purposes.
short_title: Chester County Church Encroachment Land Release Bill
one: The bill would have the federal government give up its future claim on, and its underground mineral rights to, a 0.62-acre piece of Chickasaw State Forest in Tennessee so a church that sits about 19 inches over the property line is no longer a problem.
summary: In 1955 the U.S. Forest Service gave a small piece of land in Henderson, Tennessee, to the state. That land is now part of Chickasaw State Forest. The federal government kept a "reversionary interest," which is a right to take the land back if the state stops using it for public purposes. The government also kept the mineral rights, meaning the rights to what lies underground. A recent state survey found that Bethel Baptist Church extends about 19 inches onto this 0.62-acre parcel. This bill would fix that problem by having the Secretary of Agriculture release the federal right to take the land back, with no payment. It would also hand over the federal mineral rights to Tennessee by quitclaim deed. A quitclaim deed transfers whatever interest the seller has, with no promises about its quality. The state would have to pay the federal government's administrative costs. The bill says these steps must happen without an appraisal, a mineral survey, or an environmental review. The bill does not itself say how the church's encroachment would be resolved after that. That would be up to the state. The bill would take effect once it becomes law. The text gives no timeline.

who: Bethel Baptist Church and its members in Henderson, Tennessee

short_title: Perry County, Arkansas Forest Service Land Conveyance
one: The bill would require the Forest Service to give a small (about 0.81-acre) parcel in Perryville, Arkansas, to Perry County for free, to be used for public purposes like education and youth development.
summary: This bill would make the U.S. Forest Service hand over a small piece of land to Perry County, Arkansas. The land is about 0.81 acres at 1069 Fourche Avenue in Perryville, and it includes any buildings on it. The county has to ask for it in writing within 180 days after the bill becomes law. The county would not pay for the land itself, but it would have to pay all costs of the transfer. Those costs include a land survey, any environmental review required by federal law, and any review needed under the National Historic Preservation Act. The land would be given by quitclaim deed, which means the government passes along whatever interest it has but does not promise the title is clean. The Forest Service also would not have to provide the usual warranty or promise about environmental cleanup that normally applies when the government transfers property. The county could use the land only for public purposes, such as education and youth development. If the county stops using it that way, the Forest Service may choose to take it back. The Forest Service can also add other terms it considers necessary to protect the government's interests. The transfer is subject to any valid existing rights others have in the land.
does: Requires the Forest Service to convey about 0.81 acres (land and buildings) at 1069 Fourche Avenue, Perryville, AR to Perry County if the county asks within 180 days of enactment.
who: Perry County government and residents of Perryville, Arkansas

benefits: The county would gain a small federal parcel with buildings for public uses such as education and youth development, without paying the purchase price.
The Forest Service would no longer need to manage a small, possibly unneeded property.
concerns: Because the transfer is by quitclaim deed with no warranty, the county could face unknown title defects or environmental problems after it takes the land.
If the county stops using the land for public purposes, it could lose the property, which may affect how it plans long-term use or investment.
The material does not say whether the buildings are in good condition or what they would cost to repair or maintain.

crs:
This bill directs the Forest Service to convey approximately one acre of land to Perry County, Arkansas, upon the request of the county. The county must use the land for public purposes, such as supporting education and youth development. If it ceases to be used for such purposes, then the property must, at the discretion of the Forest Service, revert to the United States.
The exact acreage of land to be conveyed must be determined by a survey satisfactory to the Forest Service.
The conveyance must be subject to valid existing rights, made without consideration, made by quitclaim deed, and subject to other terms and conditions that the Forest Service considers to be appropriate to protect the interests of the United States.
As a condition of the conveyance, the county must pay costs associated with the conveyance, including the cost of a survey, any environmental analysis or resources survey required under federal law, and any analysis required to comply with the National Historic Preservation Act.

label: S. 3226
title: Bring Our Heroes Home Act
short_title: Bring Our Heroes Home Act
one: The bill would create a special collection of government records at the National Archives about missing U.S. military and civilian personnel since 1941, run by a five-member review board that pushes agencies to release the records unless there is a strong reason to keep them secret.
summary:
This bill is about records on Americans who went missing in service to the country. That includes service members and certain civilians and contractors who went missing from December 7, 1941 to the day the bill becomes law. Families have long said the government holds files that could tell them what happened to their loved ones. The bill would set up a "Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Collection" at the National Archives. It starts from the idea that these records should be public.

Every federal agency, the Library of Congress, the National Archives, presidential libraries and the military would have to find their relevant records. They would copy them to the Archives on a set schedule, with transmission starting about 270 days and finishing about one year after the review board gets a quorum (enough members to act). Each office must certify under penalty of perjury that it searched thoroughly. Records may not be destroyed or altered. Anything already made public cannot be pulled back or reclassified.

A new five-member Review Board, appointed by the President with Senate approval after consulting congressional leaders, would decide which records can stay secret. It could hold hearings, subpoena documents, and require agencies to explain any destroyed records. Agencies that want to withhold or heavily redact a record must publicly explain the specific harm. Secrecy is allowed only for narrow reasons, such as protecting intelligence sources, current war plans, foreign relations, or personal privacy. Older records face a tougher test. After 10 years, everything must be released unless the President personally certifies that continued secrecy is needed. The Board would end four years after its members are sworn in. It would publish regular notices and reports on what it has kept secret and why.

The bill also says the Attorney General should help unseal court and grand jury records. It says the State Department should ask Russia, China, and North Korea for their records. It keeps Freedom of Information Act rights and court review in place. It authorizes "such sums as are necessary" to fund the work.

Important caveat: in the text provided, every section appears as "struck out." That usually means a committee amendment replaced the whole text. I could not see any replacement text, so this analysis covers the original text. The final version could differ.
does: Creates the Missing Armed Forces and Civilian Personnel Records Collection at the National Archives, covering people who went missing from Dec. 7, 1941 until the law is enacted.
Declares that these records should be preserved, presumed declassified, and disclosed so families can learn what happened to loved ones.

Requires every government office (agencies, military, Library of Congress, National Archives, presidential libraries) to locate relevant records and send copies to the Archivist, starting within 270 days and finishing within one year after the Review Board has a quorum.
Requires each office to certify under penalty of perjury that it searched thoroughly and to say whether any records were not sent.
Bans destroying, altering, or mutilating covered records, and bars withholding, redacting, or reclassifying anything already public.
Requires an unclassified public report from any office wanting to withhold or heavily redact a record, showing a clearly expected harm that outweighs the public interest.

Allows postponing release only for listed reasons (military plans, intelligence sources and methods, foreign relations, nuclear and weapons security, FOIA exemptions, privacy, safety of confidential sources). Records over 25 years old need clear and convincing evidence.
Exempts the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency's active case files and casualty offices' family-support case files from the transmission requirement.

Creates a five-member independent Review Board (presidentially appointed, Senate-confirmed, nonpartisan, including a historian and an attorney) with ethics screening and removal only for cause, with court review.

Gives the Board power to direct agencies, hold hearings, issue subpoenas (including to private persons), require accounts of destroyed records, and make final disclosure decisions, subject to Presidential override on executive-branch records.
Lets the President override a Board decision, but only with a public unclassified written certification within 30 days, published in the Federal Register.

Requires full public release of all records within 10 years unless the head of the originating agency recommends continued secrecy in writing and the President certifies it with clear and convincing evidence. Postponed records get periodic review at least every 5 years after the Board ends.

Requires the Board to publish its review schedule, post postponement notices every 30 days, and report annually to Congress, with congressional committees having oversight and access to Board records.
Expresses the sense of Congress that the Attorney General should help unseal court and grand jury records and the State Department should ask Russia, China, North Korea, and others for their records.

Preserves FOIA and judicial review rights, makes the Act override conflicting laws on disclosure (except tax return privacy), ends the Board after 4 years, and authorizes 'such sums as are necessary' for funding.

Sworn certifications and the ban on destroying records could improve agency honesty.
Agencies must publicly justify secrecy, and postponed records are reviewed regularly.

Congressional oversight and public reporting add accountability.
concerns: Broad national security exceptions and a Presidential override could still keep important records secret.
Releasing records could expose personal or privacy-sensitive details about missing people or their families if safeguards fail.
Agencies may ask for extensions, and the Board could be slow or overwhelmed by the volume of records.
The Board's subpoena power over private persons could raise concerns for some people.
Costs are open-ended ('such sums as are necessary').

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help families learn what happened to Americans who went missing in military or related service, by collecting federal records on them in one place at the National Archives and making them public. It states that these records should be presumed declassified and disclosed, with secrecy allowed only for narrow reasons under an independent Review Board.

oppose: The bill lets the President override a Review Board decision on executive-branch records, so the final say on secrecy could still rest with the executive branch.
Broad national security and foreign relations exceptions could be used to keep important records hidden, and the bill gives no detailed standards for applying them.

support: The bill would gather records on missing service members and certain civilians in one place at the National Archives, so families and researchers would not have to search many agencies separately.
Agencies would have to certify under penalty of perjury that they searched thoroughly, and they could not destroy, alter, or reclassify covered records, which could improve accountability.

environment.reason: The bill concerns records about missing personnel and does not touch water, air, land, or ecosystems.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill presumes declassification, requires public written justification for any withholding or heavy redaction, requires public postponement notices every 30 days, and requires annual public reports to Congress, with sworn certifications from agencies, which strongly advances open government and truthful information for families.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill is about government records and does not involve corporate profit or shifting costs from corporations to the public.

local_say.reason: The Board must be nonpartisan and include a historian and attorney, and congressional committees gain oversight access, which expands public and legislative input, though this is about federal records rather than local decisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts or ratepayer tax breaks; its open-ended 'such sums as are necessary' funding is a general appropriation, not a corporate subsidy.

equality.reason: The Collection covers service members and certain civilians and contractors who went missing equally, and families gain equal access to records, though the national security exceptions and Presidential override apply to records in a way that may not be uniform.

justice.reason: Sec. on the Review Board provides subpoena power, requirements that agencies explain destroyed records, sworn certifications under penalty of perjury, a ban on destroying records, and court review, giving families real remedies and making agency decisions more accountable.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not expand or restrict what individuals may do in their own lives; subpoena power over private persons is a narrow government power and does not clearly restrict personal choices.

label: S. 3371
title: National Museum of the Blind People’s Movement Act
short_title: National Museum of the Blind People's Movement Act
one: The bill would give the existing Museum of the Blind People's Movement in Baltimore the official title "National Museum of the Blind People's Movement," with no new money or federal control attached.
summary: This bill is mostly a naming bill. It would officially call the Museum of the Blind People's Movement, at 200 East Wells Street in Baltimore, Maryland, the "National Museum of the Blind People's Movement." The museum sits inside the National Federation of the Blind's Jernigan Institute. The bill as first introduced included a long list of findings. These said blind people have faced discrimination and low expectations, and that the National Federation of the Blind, founded in 1940, has collected many records and artifacts about blind people's history. A Senate committee, led by Sen. Lee, removed those findings. The version now on the Senate calendar keeps only the short title and the one-sentence designation. The text we can see does not give the museum any federal money. It also doesn't create a federal agency role, change who owns or runs the museum, or add any rules. The text says nothing about costs. Because the bill only gives a title, any practical effect would likely be about recognition and public attention. The bill has not passed the Senate yet. It was placed on the Senate calendar on November 12, 2026, and would still need to pass both chambers and be signed by the President.

label: S. 3524
title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act of 2026
short_title: American Battlefield Protection Program Amendments Act
one: As introduced, this bill would extend and adjust federal grants for protecting and restoring historic battlefields and order National Park Service studies of French and Indian War and Mexican-American War sites. The version now on the Senate calendar appears to have replacement text that was not provided.
summary:
The text provided shows only the original bill, and all of it is marked "struck out." That usually means a committee replaced it with new wording, but the new wording was not included. This analysis therefore describes the original proposal. The final version may differ.

The original bill had two parts. First, it would change the American Battlefield Protection Program, which helps protect historic battlefields. It would extend the battlefield land acquisition grant program from 2028 to 2035. It would change a number from 50 to 75 in the rules for two other grant programs, one for interpretation (telling a site's story to visitors) and one for restoration. The text doesn't say what that number measures. It would remove one subsection of the interpretation grant law. It would also authorize $2 million per year through 2035 for the interpretation and restoration grants. "Authorize" means Congress allows the spending, but a separate vote must actually provide the money.

Second, it would have the National Park Service study sites tied to the French and Indian War (1754–1763) and the Mexican-American War (1846–1848). The studies would rank the sites by importance, identify threats to them, and suggest ways to preserve them. One option would be making some of them national park units. The Park Service would consult governors, Tribes, local governments, and preservation groups. It would report to Congress within 2 years after funding is provided.

Changes a figure from 50 to 75 in the interpretation and restoration grant sections; the text doesn't say what it measures.
