label: S. 3527
title: Montana Sportsmen Conservation Act
short_title: Montana Sportsmen Conservation Act
one: The bill would remove "wilderness study area" protection from about 104,000 acres of federal land in Montana across three areas and require them to be managed under existing agency land plans instead.
summary: This bill would end the "wilderness study area" status of three pieces of public land in Montana. These are the Middle Fork Judith area (about 81,000 acres), the Hoodoo Mountain area (about 11,380 acres), and the Wales Creek area (about 11,580 acres). A wilderness study area is land that is kept in its natural state while Congress decides whether to make it permanent wilderness. Right now, these areas are managed to protect their wilderness qualities. Under the bill, they would be "released." That means Congress would no longer treat them as possible wilderness. The Forest Service would manage Middle Fork Judith under its national forest plan. The Bureau of Land Management would manage Hoodoo Mountain and Wales Creek under its resource management plans. The version reported by the Senate committee is short. It dropped the long list of findings from the original bill. Those findings said the agencies had found these lands unsuitable for wilderness and that release would allow more hunting and fishing access, wildlife habitat projects, and wildfire work. The bill text does not list the specific rules in those plans. It does not set aside new land or add new funding. The effects depend on what the current plans allow, such as roads, logging, motorized use, or other development.
does: Ends wilderness study area status for the roughly 81,000-acre Middle Fork Judith area under the Montana Wilderness Study Act of 1977.
Ends wilderness study area status for the roughly 11,380-acre Hoodoo Mountain and 11,580-acre Wales Creek areas under the Federal Land Policy and Management Act.
Requires the Middle Fork Judith land to be managed under the applicable Forest Service land management plan.
Requires Hoodoo Mountain and Wales Creek to be managed under the applicable Bureau of Land Management resource management plans.
The committee amendment removed the original findings and the language that referred to the 'most recently adopted' plan and to 'resource' plans for the Forest Service area.

label: S. 3597
title: National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: National Quantum Initiative Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Renews and expands the federal quantum technology research program through 2034, adding new research centers, testbeds, workforce programs, supply chain studies, and security rules, while ending the National Nanotechnology Program.
summary: This bill renews a federal program that coordinates research on quantum technology. Quantum technology uses the laws of physics at the tiniest scales to build new kinds of computers, sensors, and communication networks. The bill extends the program's authority to the end of 2034 and sets spending levels for 2026 through 2030. It adds up to three new quantum centers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), doubles the National Science Foundation (NSF) research centers from 5 to 10, and creates testbeds where new quantum uses can be tried out. It also creates a national workforce hub with community colleges, new student training and fellowship options, and a NASA quantum program. It directs studies of quantum supply chains, a plan for working with allies, and a review of regulations that may slow quantum work. It pushes the government and businesses toward "post-quantum" encryption, which is designed to stay secure against future quantum computers. It bars certain funds from going to Confucius Institute–linked schools or to research with countries and groups of concern, and adds research-security screening. It requires yearly outside evaluations of the program, with a public summary. Finally, it shuts down the National Nanotechnology Program 180 days after enactment. Most dollar amounts are "authorizations," meaning limits on what Congress may later fund, not actual spending.

label: S. 388
title: Promoting Resilient Buildings Act
short_title: Promoting Resilient Buildings Act
one: Changes FEMA disaster-mitigation rules so building code upgrades can use the two latest code editions, removes building code activities from a mitigation loan fund, and creates a pilot program (through 2030) giving grants to low-income homeowners for disaster-proofing homes.
summary: This bill changes how the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) helps communities get ready for disasters before they happen. First, it says that when FEMA helps governments adopt modern building codes, the codes can be either of the two most recently published editions, not only the very newest. That gives local governments more flexibility. Second, it removes a rule that lets states and tribes lend money from FEMA's Safeguarding Tomorrow revolving loan fund (a pool of money that is repaid and lent out again) to local governments for setting up and enforcing building codes. Third, it creates a pilot program, which is a temporary test project. FEMA would give money to state and local governments, which would give grants to individuals for retrofits that make existing homes safer from local hazards. Examples include raising homes, floodproofing, tornado safe rooms, earthquake retrofits, wildfire protection, and stronger roofs and hurricane straps. People getting grants must show financial need. FEMA could use up to 10% of its yearly predisaster mitigation money for this, must set the program up within a year, and must end it on September 30, 2030. FEMA must report to Congress within four years on the results, including the number of homes retrofitted, costs, participant demographics, and whether it saved disaster costs. It applies only to money appropriated after the bill becomes law and does not affect other programs.

Promoting Resilient Buildings Act
This bill increases flexibility for predisaster mitigation assistance for building code activities, prohibits using certain loan funds for building code activities, and establishes a pilot program to fund residential resilience retrofits.
Under current law, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) may provide predisaster hazard mitigation assistance to government entities for implementing the latest published editions of relevant building codes and standards. Also, FEMA must consider a government entity’s adoption of such building codes when determining whether to award it predisaster hazard mitigation assistance. The bill specifies that the building codes applicable in such instances are the two most recently published editions (i.e., either the current edition or the previous one).
Also, currently, under FEMA's Safeguarding Tomorrow Revolving Loan Fund (STRLF) program, states and Indian tribal governments may provide loans to local governments for establishing and carrying out building codes and standards. The bill removes this authority, so STRLF loans may not be used for such building code-related activities.
Additionally, the bill establishes a pilot program for FEMA to provide grants to government entities that then provide the funding to individuals for residential resilience retrofits. The retrofit projects must reduce risk to homes from local natural hazards and individuals must demonstrate financial need. To implement the pilot program, FEMA may use up to 10% of the funds FEMA provides annually for predisaster hazard mitigation assistance. The pilot program terminates at the end of FY2030.

people_over_profit.reason: Provides grants directly to households to protect homes and safety rather than to corporations.

local_say.reason: Lets local governments choose between two code editions and run grants based on local hazards, though removing loan use for codes narrows one tool.

honesty_kindness.reason: Helps financially strained households protect themselves from disasters.

equality.reason: Directs retrofit grants to individuals who show financial need.

summary: This bill tells the Department of Energy (DOE) to set up a new program within 180 days of becoming law. The program would help pay for experimental geothermal power projects. Geothermal power uses heat from underground to make electricity. These projects would be in rock that water does not flow through easily, which needs newer drilling methods. Money would be awarded in stages, as a project hits technical and money-related goals. DOE would give priority to projects in places that have little or no geothermal power now, including on or near Indian land. It would also favor projects that share data publicly, projects aimed at 30 megawatts or more of power, and projects likely to attract private investment. DOE must fund at least 3 proposals, in at least 3 states, from at least 3 different sponsors. The Senate committee changed the bill to authorize $800 million, with up to $750 million for projects and up to $50 million for running and overseeing the program. An authorization only allows spending. Congress must still pass a separate law to provide the money. The bill also removes an existing part of the law, paragraph (3) of subsection (d) of section 615, and the text does not say what that paragraph covers. The bill text has no new environmental, water, or local-input rules. Existing laws would still apply.

title: A bill to amend the Mineral Leasing Act to provide for the payment of bonus payments of certain coal leases issued under that Act.
short_title: Coal Lease Bonus Payment Installments Bill
one: The bill would let companies that win federal coal leases under a deferred-payment system pay their upfront "bonus" bid in 10 equal yearly installments, with the first paid when they bid.
summary: When the federal government leases public land for coal mining, the winning company pays a "bonus bid." That is a one-time amount offered to win the lease, on top of later royalties (a share of the coal's value). The Mineral Leasing Act already allows a "deferred bonus payment" system, where the bonus can be paid over time. This bill sets the terms for that system. If a coal lease is issued under it, the bonus must be paid in 10 equal annual installments. The first installment is due with the bid, and the other nine come over the following years. The bill is one short paragraph added to the law. It doesn't change royalties, environmental rules, or how leases are offered. It doesn't say what happens if a company stops paying, and it doesn't say whether interest is charged. It also doesn't say whether the system is required or only allowed. The effect would be that coal companies pay less up front and the government gets its money later. The text has no cost estimate, and no Congressional Research Service summary is available yet. The bill was reported out of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee without changes. It is on the Senate calendar, and no vote has been scheduled.

label: S. 465
title: GRID Power Act
short_title: GRID Power Act
one: Directs FERC to write rules letting grid operators move "dispatchable" power plants (like gas, coal, nuclear, hydro-type plants that can be turned up on demand) ahead in the line to connect to the electric grid, with FERC deciding on each request within 60 days.
summary:
New power plants must wait in a line, called the interconnection queue, to get hooked up to the high-voltage grid. This bill tells the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), the federal agency that oversees the interstate power grid, to rewrite its rules so that grid operators can ask to move "dispatchable" plants higher in that line. Dispatchable means a power source that can reliably supply known, forecastable amounts of electricity when needed. The bill does not list fuels, but the Congressional Research Service says it generally covers things like fossil fuel plants. Solar and wind are generally not dispatchable on their own, so they could end up lower in line.

Before asking, a grid operator would have to show why moving these projects up is needed and explain how it would improve grid reliability or resilience. It would also have to hold a public comment and stakeholder process before submitting the request, and report regularly to FERC on grid reliability. FERC would have 60 days to approve or deny each request. FERC must start the rulemaking within 90 days of enactment and finish the final rule within 180 days. It must review the rule at least every 5 years. The bill does not add spending or say how it would be paid for, and it does not set any environmental standards for the plants that are moved up.
does: Requires FERC to start a rulemaking within 90 days of enactment and finish a final rule within 180 days.
Directs FERC to address inefficiencies in the interconnection process so new dispatchable plants that improve reliability and resource adequacy can connect quickly, cost-effectively, and reliably.

ispatchable power

label: S. 4709
title: UNLOCK AUKUS Act
short_title: UNLOCK AUKUS Act
one: The bill makes a one-line change to the Arms Export Control Act so that three specific exclusions no longer limit the license-free export of certain defense items to Australia and the United Kingdom under the AUKUS security partnership.
summary:
AUKUS is a security partnership among Australia, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Under current law, some U.S. defense items and services can be sent to Australia and the UK without the usual individual export license. That shortcut has limits. This bill changes one of those limits.

The limit sits in Section 38(l)(4)(B) of the Arms Export Control Act. It refers to another part of the law, subsection (j)(1)(C)(ii). The bill adds the words "excluding subclauses (I), (II), and (III)" after that reference. In effect, three listed items in that other part would no longer count toward the limit.

The bill text does not say what those three items are. It also doesn't say how much easier or harder exports would become. The Congressional Research Service has not yet published a summary. I could not see the text of the section being referenced, so I can't say exactly which items or technologies are affected. The bill's title suggests the goal is to speed up licensing and technology sharing among the three countries. That is an inference from the name, not something the text says.

The bill has 10 cosponsors from both parties. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee reported it without changes, and it is now on the Senate calendar. The text sets no start date, no new spending, and no new reporting rules.

label: S. 4846
title: TAAP Act
short_title: TAAP Act (Transboundary Aquifer Assessment Program Act)
one: Renews and extends a federal program that studies groundwater shared between the U.S. and Mexico, adds Arizona aquifers to the study list (with one exception), and authorizes funding through fiscal year 2036.
summary:
Some underground water supplies, called aquifers, sit under both the United States and Mexico. A 2006 law set up a program to study these shared aquifers, working with states, universities, and Mexico. The program's funding permission ran out after 2016. This bill would renew it.

The bill does three things. First, it widens the list of states where "priority" aquifers can be picked for study. The current law covers New Mexico and Texas. The bill would add Arizona, but not the shared aquifer that is partly in the Yuma groundwater basin, which is excluded. Second, it says Congress may spend money on the program for fiscal years 2026 through 2036. Third, it resets the program's end date so the clock starts from when this new law is enacted instead of from 2006.

The bill does not set a dollar amount or change the other parts of the 2006 law. "Authorizing" funding only allows Congress to pay for the program. A separate spending bill would still have to provide the money. The bill text does not say why the Yuma-area aquifer is left out. The bill text does not give the new end date, because it refers to the existing law's timeline, which I could not see.

label: S. 4870
title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Earth MRI Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends the federal Earth Mapping Resources Initiative (a USGS-led effort to map underground resources) for five more years (2027–2031), adds newer mapping technologies, and links it to the 3D Hydrography Program.
summary:
This bill would keep alive a federal program called the Earth Mapping Resources Initiative, or Earth MRI. It was created in the 2021 infrastructure law and is run through the U.S. Geological Survey. The program collects maps and data about what is under the ground, with a focus on critical minerals, which are materials used in things like batteries and electronics. Its current authorization runs from 2022 through 2026. The bill changes that to 2027 through 2031.

The bill also updates the program's mapping purpose. It says the data may come from newer tools, such as airborne gravity gradiometry (measuring tiny changes in gravity from aircraft), digital geochemistry, real-time data collection, and data-driven analysis. These could help describe critical minerals, geothermal energy, geologic hydrogen, and other underground resources.

Finally, the bill adds the 3D Hydrography Program, a federal water-mapping effort, to the list of data sources the Earth MRI must combine with its own data.

The bill text we have does not give a dollar amount. It only extends the time period. Any money would depend on later spending decisions by Congress. The bill also does not add rules on environmental review, public input, or mining permits.

label: S. 4950
title: ITS Codification Act
short_title: ITS Codification Act
one: The bill writes the Commerce Department's Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (a federal radio and wireless test lab) into law and creates an initiative to develop technology for locating people trapped in mines, collapsed buildings, and similar places where radios don't work well.
summary: The Institute for Telecommunication Sciences (ITS) is a federal lab that already exists inside the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the part of the Commerce Department that advises on telecom and manages federal use of radio airwaves. This bill would put ITS into permanent law instead of leaving it to agency decisions alone. The law would say ITS serves as a lab for the executive branch. It would study radio signals, how they travel, and how they cause interference. It would also test technology that lets federal and non-federal users share airwaves, and it would study how well federal systems tolerate interference. ITS could also take on other tasks the NTIA head assigns. The bill lets ITS make agreements with companies, universities, and other agencies under existing laws on technology partnerships, interagency work, and patents and licensing. The second part requires ITS to start an initiative for emergency communication and tracking tools. These would help find people trapped in places such as underground mines, tall buildings, or collapsed structures. ITS would work with private companies and federal agencies to assess needs and help develop technical standards. Within 18 months, NTIA must send Congress a public report on that needs assessment. The bill does not state a dollar amount or new funding.

one: Extends and adjusts federal programs that help fund and research turning seawater, salty groundwater, and wastewater into usable water, including a new pilot-project research track and a higher university grant cap.
summary:
This bill renews and updates federal desalination programs. Desalination means removing salt and other minerals from ocean water, salty groundwater, or wastewater so people can use it. The bill restarts the clock on the authority for these programs from the date the bill becomes law. It sets the Bureau of Reclamation's desalination project program to expire 15 years after enactment.

For construction projects, the bill defines which projects can get help. They must be in a western "Reclamation State" or mainly benefit one, and they must involve an ocean or brackish water plant run or backed by a state, Tribe, or water district. It lets the Interior Secretary pay up to 25 percent of a project's total cost, with no dollar limit.

The bill also adds "advanced pilots" to the research program. These are real-world tests of new or first-of-a-kind technologies, including ways to treat or dispose of brine, the very salty leftover waste. Pilot projects fall under the existing cost-sharing rules. Finally, it raises the cap on grants to colleges and universities from $1 million to $2.5 million.

The text I was given does not include a new dollar amount of funding, and no CRS summary was available. The Senate committee replaced the original text with a version that adds the university grant increase and changes how the pilot program is defined.

label: S. 5359
title: Pennington County Land Conveyance Act
short_title: Pennington County Land Conveyance Act
one: The bill would give about 9 acres of Black Hills National Forest land, plus any buildings on it, to Pennington County, South Dakota, for public uses such as a highway maintenance and public works facility, with the land returning to the federal government if it is misused.
summary: This bill would require the U.S. Department of Agriculture, through the Forest Service, to hand over a small piece of the Black Hills National Forest to Pennington County, South Dakota. The parcel is about 8.97 acres, and any buildings or other improvements on it go along with it. The map title, "Pennington County (SD) Highway Maintenance Facility Land Conveyance," suggests the land is tied to a county highway maintenance site. The county would not pay anything for the land. The Forest Service may attach any conditions it considers appropriate. The county must use the land for public purposes, including a public works facility. After the transfer, the national forest boundary would be redrawn to leave out the parcel. The Senate committee changed the bill's wording so the land may be used for "public purposes, including a public works facility." The original version said "a public works facility or any other uses determined to be necessary by the County." The committee version also adds a reversion rule. If the Forest Service, after consulting South Dakota, finds the county is using the land in a way the bill does not allow, the land could go back to the United States. Before that, the Forest Service must notify the county, hold a hearing if the county asks, and take public comment. It must also give the county a reasonable chance to fix the problem. The bill text does not say how much the land is worth, and I could not see the map or any environmental review.

label: S. 5526
title: Agricultural Act of 2026
short_title: Agricultural Act of 2026 (Farm Bill)
one: A very large five-year farm bill that renews and changes USDA programs for crops, dairy, conservation, food aid, SNAP and nutrition, rural development, research, forestry, energy, crop insurance, foreign farmland ownership and fuel rules such as year-round E15.
summary:
This is the 2026 farm bill. It renews most USDA programs through fiscal year 2031, and it changes many of them along the way. It is a mixed package. Parts of it line up closely with your values, and other parts raise real concerns.

Commodities (Title I): The bill pushes back the date when old "permanent" farm price-support law would take effect. It lets farm-stored fertilizer and propane qualify for storage loans. It requires the Commodity Credit Corporation (CCC, USDA's funding arm) to send Congress a public, searchable twice-yearly budget book. It allows more "base acres" (the acres tied to farm payments). Dairy farmers would pay no fee for Dairy Margin Coverage, and they would get premium-free coverage on their first 6 million pounds of milk. Disaster aid grows for livestock, honey bees, fish, trees and specialty crops. It also sets up a framework for specialty-crop emergency aid if money is provided later.

Conservation (Title II): The bill adds a Forest Conservation Easement Program and replaces the Healthy Forests Reserve. It raises the federal share of farmland easements, lets trusted land trusts act with more independence, and creates a wetland easement stewardship program. It reworks the Regional Conservation Partnership Program, with advance payments and a $15 million per-project cap. It adds a state conservation grant program ($50 million a year), a feral swine program ($150 million), and a white oak initiative. It also caps CRP and wetland easements at 25 percent of a county's cropland. It waives some public comment and speeds some environmental reviews for emergency conservation work on BLM land.

Trade (Title III): It reauthorizes Food for Peace and related food aid programs through 2031. It would move Food for Peace administration from USAID/State to USDA under a transfer plan. It raises market-promotion funding to $515–$533 million a year. It also directs USDA to help protect the right to use "common names" like feta or parmesan abroad.

Nutrition (Title IV): SNAP gets stronger EBT card protections. That means free, faster replacement of stolen or damaged cards, chip-enabled retailer terminals, and a GAO study. Online-only and inventory-less sellers face tougher rules. States may hire contractors for some SNAP office tasks. The bill adds payment-error reporting and extends the food bank programs (TEFAP), the senior farmers' market program and GusNIP. It also expands a dairy nutrition incentive to cheese and yogurt at $80 million a year, and requires 95 percent domestic purchases for school food. Dietary guidelines would move to every 10 years, with formal public rulemaking.

Credit (Title V) and Rural Development (Title VI): It updates farm loan law and extends many programs. The ReConnect rural broadband program is retooled ($100 million a year), and a "Last Acre" broadband program is created. Rural water, solid waste, business, cooperative and childcare programs get more funding or priority. It adds zero-interest loans for small rural hospitals, new rural health technical assistance, and meat processing grants of up to $500,000.

Research (Title VII): It extends dozens of research programs. These include new work on PFAS in farmland, biochar, pests, AI, aquaculture and wildfire grazing. It raises funding for 1890 institutions. It also sends $200 million of CCC money to the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research.

Forestry (Title VIII): It renews and widens Good Neighbor Authority, including new permanent roads. It updates wood-products grants and wildland firefighter workforce, housing and smoke-safety measures. It also makes several land conveyances and designations. Two of them stand out: Okhissa Lake land is conveyed in Mississippi without environmental review, and wilderness is designated in Virginia and Illinois.

Energy, horticulture and regulation (Titles IX–X): Biofuel, biobased products and rural energy programs are extended and in some cases expanded. Organic and local food programs get more funding. New organic import testing and a mandatory-reporting program for local food buying are added. The bill also loosens pesticide law. It exempts certain "biostimulants" and certain gene-edited plant-incorporated protectants from regulation under the federal pesticide law (FIFRA). It increases USDA's role in EPA pesticide decisions, and it moves some Endangered Species Act deadlines to 2031.

Crop insurance (Title XI): Specialty crop growers get an advisory committee and a coordinator. Insurers' administrative reimbursement rates are frozen at 2026 levels. USDA interpretations of crop insurance rules would be binding and could not be reviewed by courts.

Miscellaneous (Title XII): Foreign ownership of U.S. farmland would face stronger reporting. That includes civil penalties of up to 25 percent of the land's value, audits, public datasets and a USDA intelligence role. The bill adds fertilizer market studies and mandatory weekly fertilizer price reporting, with a bar on FOIA release of the data. Grain inspection laws are extended to 2033. Year-round E15 gas is allowed, and small refinery exemptions from renewable fuel rules end after 2027. Other provisions create a Commission on Rural Maternal Health, rollover-protection grants for tractors, whole milk in school breakfasts, and stronger whistleblower protections at the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

Overall, the bill spends a great deal of public money and affects very many people. Much of its content is extension of existing programs, and some of it aims at transparency, rural health, clean water and conservation. Other parts cut environmental review, relax pesticide oversight, or favor industry interests.
does: Title I: Pushes the suspension of permanent price-support law from 2023 to 2031 and treats marketing assistance and sugar loan servicing as emergency work during a government funding lapse.
Allows enrolled agents to certify farm income for payment-limit purposes.
Requires the CCC to report directly to Congress, publish a searchable twice-yearly Commodity Estimate Book, and raise a quarterly reporting threshold from $10,000 to $25,000.
Expands farm storage facility loans to cover propane and fertilizer storage, with rules due within 180 days.
Orders a study of adding dry edible beans to commodity programs and changes the cap on additional base acres to the lesser of eligible acres or 31.5 million.

Dairy: repeals the forward pricing program, extends dairy indemnity and promotion programs to 2031, requires new processing cost and yield reporting, eliminates the Dairy Margin Coverage fee, and gives premium-free coverage on the first 6 million pounds of milk.

Disaster aid: covers community ditch irrigators, adds wolf and panther predators, broadens livestock, bee and fish emergency losses, expands the Tree Assistance Program with advance payments, and creates a framework for specialty-crop emergency payments if funds are later provided.

Title II conservation: caps CRP plus wetland easements at 25 percent of county cropland, expands third-party technical service providers (with a 60-business-day approval clock and public reporting), and creates farmer-to-farmer mentoring networks.

Lets USDA bar conservation payments that directly benefit entities tied to a foreign country of concern (optional, not required) and sets a 270-day interim period to run changed conservation programs without new regulations.

Raises the federal share of farmland easements to 60 percent, creates certified-entity and lower-cost-share options, allows minor easement adjustments, requires wetland easement stewardship plans and a 2028 backlog report, and exempts easement income from the adjusted gross income limit.

Reworks the Regional Conservation Partnership Program: adds emergency watershed work, agricultural retailers as partners, advance payments, a $15 million project cap, indirect-cost payments, and a focus on big game migration corridors.
Creates a Forest Conservation Easement Program (replacing the Healthy Forests Reserve), with forest land and forest reserve easements.

Expands emergency watershed floodplain easements and emergency forest restoration (including to industrial owners and grazing permit holders), and waives the 30-day NEPA comment period and lets USDA-led reviews be used on BLM land during disasters.
Creates a $150 million feral swine program, a $50 million-a-year state and tribal conservation grant program, a white oak initiative, and extends private grazing land conservation to 2031.

Title III trade: extends Food for Peace and related food aid programs to 2031, adds child wasting, repeals minimum aid levels, sets aside $15 million a year for the international food relief partnership, adds reporting on waste and on women and girls, and moves Food for Peace administration to USDA under a 180-day transfer plan.

Directs USDA to support U.S. negotiators in protecting use of common food names such as feta and parmesan abroad, and adds foreign-market infrastructure help and a specialty crop export barriers report.
Sets market access and trade promotion funding at $515 million (FY2027) and $533 million (FY2028 onward), and creates a fruit and vegetable import monitoring working group.

Extends or changes Food for Progress, McGovern-Dole (adds lower-middle-income countries), Global Crop Diversity Trust (federal share capped at 33 percent), and creates a $10 million-a-year agricultural exchange program.

Title IV nutrition: requires free and faster SNAP EBT card replacement (5 business days), bars replacement fees for theft or fraud, requires chip-enabled retailer terminals, and orders GAO and Puerto Rico card security reports.

Tightens SNAP retailer approval so stores must own food inventory and limits online-only and aggregator participants, and streamlines farmer applications across SNAP, WIC and farmers' market programs.

Allows states to hire contractors for some SNAP certification work (not eligibility decisions) with transparency rules, adds supplemental reporting of all payment errors, and adds animal protein to incentive foods.

Extends nutrition programs to 2031, sets TEFAP commodity funding at $525 million indexed to the Thrifty Food Plan, expands the dairy nutrition incentive (cheese and yogurt; $80 million a year), and creates a $10 million-a-year rural senior home-delivery pilot.
Requires 95 percent domestic purchasing by school food authorities per food category, and changes dietary guidelines to every 10 years starting 2030 with public rulemaking.
Title V credit: modernizes farm loan law (agency names, appeals, interest rate caps of 5 percent for certain loans, longer property disposal periods).

Title VI rural development: retools ReConnect broadband (25/3 Mbps minimum, $100 million a year, simplified applications, challenge process, no rate regulation), creates the Last Acre precision agriculture broadband program, and funds water testing ($10 million a year).

Increases rural solid waste grants to $20 million a year, expands rural business, cooperative, microentrepreneur and technology transfer (Armed to Farm) programs, adds a Rural Development Innovation Center, and caps guarantee fees at 3 percent initial and 0.75 percent annual.

Prohibits rural development loans and grants for wetland draining and filling (with permitted exceptions) and sets rural hospital zero-interest loans, rural health facility refinancing and technical assistance, childcare priorities, and $25 million a year for meat and poultry processing grants.

Title VII research: extends dozens of programs to 2031, adds research on PFAS, biochar, pests, AI, aquaculture, white oak, grazing for wildfire and tick-borne diseases, and raises funding for 1890 centers ($50 million a year) and specialty crop automation ($30 million a year).

Restores the 4-H name authority, adds a veterans farming grant program, sets a national biochar research network, and requires a $200 million CCC transfer to the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research within 30 days.

Title VIII forestry: updates forest inventory, expands Good Neighbor Authority (including new permanent roads) to 2031, raises funding for collaborative forest landscape restoration, expands wood product grants, and sets up a forest carbon data tracker.

Includes several land actions: releasing reversionary interests in Tennessee and Wisconsin, a Perry County (Arkansas) conveyance, an Okhissa Lake (Mississippi) sale to a state group with NEPA waived, a Minnesota land exchange, Rough Mountain and Rich Hole wilderness in Virginia, and Camp Hutchins wilderness in Illinois.

Adds wildland firefighter workforce hiring goals, housing pilots, smoke respirator standards, utility vegetation clearing authority, and NEPA exemptions for communications equipment on already-analyzed Forest Service land.

Title IX energy: extends biobased, biorefinery, Rural Energy for America and related programs to 2031 (raises the REAP cap to $50 million, rescinds $15 million of biorefinery funds), and adds sustainable aviation fuel and pumping efficiency efforts.

Title X horticulture and regulation: expands local food, organic and urban agriculture programs, adds organic import testing and risk-based inspections, and creates a $200 million-a-year local food purchasing program.

Rewrites pesticide rules: exempts certain biostimulants and certain plant-incorporated protectants from FIFRA, gives USDA more say in EPA decisions, sets registration review deadline to 2031, and creates a USDA Office of Biotechnology Policy.

Title XI crop insurance: adds specialty crop advisory committee and board seats, raises the substantial-interest threshold from 5 to 10 percent, makes USDA interpretations final and unreviewable by courts, adds market price decline coverage, extends veteran farmer status to 10 years, and freezes insurer reimbursement rates at 2026 levels.

Title XII: toughens foreign farmland ownership reporting (penalties up to 25 percent of land value, audits, public datasets, intelligence and cybersecurity roles), orders fertilizer market studies and mandatory weekly fertilizer price reporting (FOIA-exempt), and reauthorizes grain inspection to 2033.
Allows year-round E15, ends small refinery exemptions after 2027 (with volume reallocation), and orders an EPA rule on E15 infrastructure and labeling.

Adds a Commission on Rural Maternal Health, tractor rollover protection grants ($500 per grant), whole milk in school breakfast, drought monitor extension, and stronger Commodity Futures Trading Commission whistleblower protections and faster award decisions.
who: Farmers, ranchers and dairy producers, including specialty crop, beginning and veteran producers
Rural communities, hospitals, broadband providers and childcare providers
SNAP recipients, food banks, schools and WIC and senior nutrition participants
Landowners, land trusts, conservation districts and Tribes
Fertilizer, pesticide, biotech, biofuel and refinery companies
Crop insurers and agents
Foreign owners of U.S. farmland
Wildland firefighters and Forest Service land users
International food aid recipients and relief organizations
Consumers of gasoline, dairy, organic products and school meals

Better rural health access (zero-interest hospital loans, technical help, maternal health study) and rural broadband and childcare support.
Fertilizer price reporting, CCC data and farmland ownership disclosure increase transparency.
SNAP recipients get faster, free card replacement and stronger fraud protection.
Whistleblower protections and veterans, beginning-farmer and tribal-institution support.
concerns: Waived public comment and environmental review in some emergency measures, communications sites and the Okhissa Lake sale.

Year-round E15 waiver of summer vapor pressure limits could add smog; small refinery exemption changes carry costs for some.
Crop insurance rule interpretations would be unreviewable by courts and insurer reimbursement is frozen at 2026 rates.
Large public spending, including $200 million to one foundation, plus subsidy expansions that mostly benefit larger operations.
FOIA exemption for fertilizer price data and the 25 percent county cap on conservation enrollment.
imp.cost: No total cost is given in the digest. Named amounts include $150 million for feral swine (FY2027–31), $50 million a year for state conservation grants, $200 million to the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research, $515–$533 million a year for trade promotion, $100 million a year for ReConnect, $200 million a year for local food purchasing, $80 million a year for dairy nutrition incentives, and many smaller authorizations. Much comes from CCC mandatory funds, and some from appropriations that Congress must still approve.
unknowns: The total ten-year cost and offsets are not stated in the digest.
How USDA would define 'good source of protein' and 'limited added sugars' for dairy incentives.
How many entities and farms the pesticide and biotech exemptions would affect.
What the 25 percent county conservation cap would remove from current enrollment.
Whether discretionary programs would actually receive appropriations.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Original measure reported to Senate by Senator Boozman. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reauthorize and modify USDA programs through fiscal year 2031, covering areas such as commodity support, conservation, trade, nutrition, rural development, research, forestry, energy, crop insurance, and foreign ownership of farmland. The bill's own summary describes it as the 2026 farm bill, a renewal of most USDA programs that also changes many of them.

oppose: The bill would waive some public comment and environmental review requirements, including for emergency conservation work on BLM land, communications equipment on Forest Service land, and the Okhissa Lake land sale in Mississippi. Opponents could ask why these steps are being skipped.

The bill would loosen some pesticide oversight by exempting certain biostimulants and plant-incorporated protectants from FIFRA, increase USDA's role in EPA pesticide decisions, and move some Endangered Species Act review deadlines to 2031.

The bill would make USDA crop insurance rule interpretations final and not reviewable by courts, and would freeze insurer reimbursement rates at 2026 levels. Opponents could ask for judicial review and a fair, updated rate process.
support: The bill would add conservation tools, including a Forest Conservation Easement Program, a $50 million-a-year state conservation grant program, a $150 million feral swine program, and a higher federal share for farmland easements. Supporters could say these help farmers and protect land and water.

The bill would give SNAP recipients free, faster replacement of stolen or damaged EBT cards within 5 business days, bar replacement fees for theft or fraud, and require chip-enabled retailer terminals. Supporters could say this protects families who depend on these benefits.

The bill would improve rural health and infrastructure, including zero-interest loans for small rural hospitals, rural health technical assistance, expanded ReConnect broadband funding of $100 million a year, and a Commission on Rural Maternal Health. Supporters could say this helps rural communities get care and connectivity.

cost_flag: No total cost is given in the digest. Named amounts include $150 million for feral swine (FY2027–31), $50 million a year for state conservation grants, $200 million to the Foundation for Food and Agriculture Research, $515–$533 million a year for trade promotion, $100 million a year for ReConnect, $200 million a year for local food purchasing, $80 million a year for dairy nutrition incentives, and many smaller authorizations. Much comes from CCC mandatory funds, and some from appropriations that Congress must still approve.
crs:
Agricultural Act of 2026
This bill (commonly known as the farm bill) reauthorizes through FY2031 and modifies Department of Agriculture programs that address
commodity support,
conservation,
trade and international food aid,
nutrition assistance,
farm credit,
rural development,
research and extension activities,
forestry,
energy,
horticulture,
crop insurance,
livestock, 
foreign investments in U.S. agricultural land, and
the year-round sale of E15 (an ethanol and gasoline fuel blend) and the Renewable Fuel Standard.

water.reason: Water testing, watershed and floodplain easements, RCPP water goals and a wetland-draining ban in rural loans help, though looser pesticide rules offset some of the gain.

air.reason: Allowing year-round E15 by waiving summer vapor pressure limits could add smog-forming emissions, with only limited offsetting air benefits.

transparency.reason: Public CCC data, farmland ownership datasets, fertilizer price reporting and trade, ReConnect and trail project reports add openness, though a FOIA bar on fertilizer data and unreviewable crop insurance rulings cut the other way.

people_over_profit.reason: Rural hospital loans, fertilizer price reporting, food aid and SNAP card protections favor people, while pesticide and insurer provisions favor industry.

no_bailouts.reason: Large subsidy and disaster aid expansions, a frozen insurer reimbursement rate, and a $200 million CCC transfer to one foundation use public money to support private interests.

honesty_kindness.reason: Food aid, SNAP card protection, rural maternal health study, farmer stress support and veteran programs reflect care for vulnerable people.

label: S. 632
title: IHS Workforce Parity Act of 2025
short_title: IHS Workforce Parity Act of 2025
one: Lets health workers who got Indian Health Service scholarships or loan repayment help pay back their service commitment by working half-time, for twice as long.
summary: Today, doctors, nurses and other health workers who accept Indian Health Service (IHS) scholarships or loan repayment help must "pay back" that help by working full-time in Native health care settings. This bill adds a half-time option. Scholarship recipients could work half-time if they agree in writing to serve twice as long. For the loan repayment program, a participant could choose full-time service for 2 years, half-time service for 4 years, or half-time service for 2 years with loan payments cut to 50 percent of the full-time amount. The bill also says what happens if someone breaks the contract. Half-time service would be converted to its full-time equivalent when figuring out how much money the person owes back. The places where people can serve stay the same. They include IHS facilities, tribal programs, urban Indian programs, and some private practices in shortage areas that serve many Native patients. The bill doesn't add new money in its text. It was reported out of the Senate Indian Affairs Committee without changes and is waiting for a Senate floor vote.

Lets loan repayment participants choose full-time (2 years), half-time (4 years), or half-time for 2 years with 50 percent loan payments.
Keeps approved service sites the same: IHS, tribal programs, urban Indian programs, and qualifying private practice in shortage areas serving many Native patients.
Requires half-time service to be converted to full-time equivalents when calculating damages owed for breaking a contract.
Requires half-time participants to agree in writing to the terms (for scholarships).
who: Health professionals with IHS scholarships or loan repayment contracts
Native patients and communities served by IHS, tribal, and urban Indian health programs
IHS and tribal health facilities that struggle to recruit and keep staff
Health professionals who want part-time work for family, caregiving, or other reasons
Federal taxpayers, as the program's administrators

Could help Native health facilities keep or recruit clinicians who might otherwise not join a full-time commitment.
Could expand the number of clinicians available to serve Native communities, though the bill text does not provide an estimate.
concerns: Half-time service over a longer period could mean fewer clinical hours per year at a given site than full-time service would provide.
Participants who choose half-time options may take longer to finish their service obligations, which could affect their career timelines.
Allowing half-time service could reduce the total hours of care provided per commitment, depending on how many people choose it.

The material does not say whether IHS can meet staffing needs under the new options or how the change would affect recruitment.

label: S. 638
title: A bill to amend the Act of June 22, 1948.
short_title: Boundary Waters County Payments Appraisal Fix (Thye-Blatnik Act amendment)
one: The bill changes how federal payments to three Minnesota counties for Boundary Waters wilderness land are calculated, so the payments are based on the highest appraised value, including past values, instead of the current appraised value, preventing payment decreases.
summary:
Much of the land in Minnesota's Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness is owned by the federal government, so it doesn't pay local property taxes. To make up for that, the federal government makes yearly payments to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties. Under a 1948 law called the Thye-Blatnik Act, the size of those payments depends on the "fair appraised value" of the land, as figured by the Department of Agriculture.

This bill makes a one-line change to that law. Instead of using the current fair appraised value, payments would be based on the highest fair appraised value, including past (historical) values. In practice, that means that if land appraisals drop, the counties' payments would not drop with them. The Congressional Research Service says the goal is to prevent decreases in these annual payments.

The bill does not change the size of the wilderness, add new land protections, or change rules about recreation, mining, or logging. It does not say how much extra money, if any, the change would cost. The Senate committee reported it without changes, and it is waiting on the Senate calendar for a floor vote.
does: Amends Section 5 of the Thye-Blatnik Act (16 U.S.C. 577g).
Replaces 'fair appraised value' with 'highest fair appraised value, including historical fair appraised values' as the basis for payments.
Keeps the Secretary of Agriculture as the one who determines the appraised value under that section.
Prevents annual payments to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties from falling if appraisals go down.
Does not change land boundaries, wilderness protections, or land-use rules.
who: Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in Minnesota, which would get steadier or possibly higher payments
Local residents and local governments that rely on these payments for schools, roads, and services
Federal taxpayers, who fund the payments
The U.S. Forest Service / Department of Agriculture, which determines appraised values
Visitors and communities near the Boundary Waters, indirectly, because the payments help offset the tax-free federal land

benefits: Counties may receive more stable payments, since a drop in current land appraisals would not automatically reduce payments.
Local budgets that rely on these payments may be easier to plan for if payment amounts stay steady.
concerns: Because payments would be based on the highest past value, counties could receive more than the current land value would support, which some may see as unfair to other taxpayers or programs.
Federal spending could rise if appraisal values fall, since payments would not decline with them.
imp.cost: ["The bill does not say how much extra money, if any, the change would cost. The material does not provide a cost estimate."]
unknowns: The material does not state how much the payments would change under the new formula.
It is not stated how many past appraisal years would be considered or how far back the 'highest' value would reach.
It is not stated whether the change would affect other counties or payment programs.
The material does not say whether the bill is likely to pass the full Senate or the House.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry. Reported by Senator Boozman without amendment. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to prevent decreases in the annual payments made to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in Minnesota for national forest land within the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. It does this by changing the Thye-Blatnik Act formula so payments are based on the highest fair appraised value, including historical values, instead of the current fair appraised value.

oppose: The bill changes the payment formula so counties are paid based on the highest past appraised value, not the current value. Payments could be higher than today's land values would normally support.

Federal payments could rise over time if appraisals fall, because the bill is designed so payments do not go down. This could add to federal spending, and the bill does not state how much it would cost.
The payments come from federal funds that support other taxpayers and programs. You may want to ask your member of Congress whether this change is fair to other places that receive similar payments.
support: The bill helps Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties plan their budgets. Because the federal government owns much of the Boundary Waters land, these counties cannot collect local property taxes on it, and the payments help make up the difference.
Under the bill, a drop in land appraisals would not automatically lower the counties' payments. This gives local governments more predictable funding year to year.
The bill makes only a narrow change to the Thye-Blatnik Act. It does not change the wilderness boundaries, protections, or rules for recreation, mining, or logging.

crs: This bill prevents decreases in annual payments provided to Cook, Lake, and Saint Louis Counties in Minnesota for national forest lands in the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. Specifically, the bill modifies the formula created under the Thye-Blatnik Act that the Department of the Treasury uses to determine the amount of the payments. Treasury must base the payments on the highest fair appraised value, including historical fair appraised values, rather than on the fair appraised value of the land.

no_bailouts.reason: It locks in federal payments to three counties at the highest historical appraisal, so they cannot decline even when land values fall, which is a federal payment guarantee that is not tied to current conditions and has no stated cost estimate.

news.overall: Evidence is limited: each perspective group has only one headline-level article, and neither mentions the bill itself or the Act of June 22, 1948. The Lean Left piece frames the story around a state's federal funding dispute, while the Center piece frames it around mining development versus wilderness protection, so the two groups are covering different aspects of Minnesota with no visible overlap. Without full article text, these descriptions reflect only the headlines and cannot show how either outlet treats the bill.

label: S. 769
title: United States Research Protection Act of 2025
short_title: United States Research Protection Act of 2025
one: Narrows and clarifies a federal ban on researchers taking part in "malign foreign talent recruitment programs" so it applies to programs tied to foreign countries of concern (such as China, Iran, North Korea and Russia), whether the benefits come directly or indirectly.
summary: Under current law (part of the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act), researchers who get federal research money cannot take part in "malign foreign talent recruitment programs." These are programs where a foreign government offers pay or other perks in exchange for activities that create a conflict of interest or that aren't authorized, such as sharing sensitive information without permission. This bill changes the wording of that definition in two main ways. First, it ties the definition to a "foreign country of concern," a term already defined in federal law that includes China, Iran, North Korea and Russia. The older text said just "foreign country," and the bill removes a separate part of the definition (subparagraph B) that I could not see in full because the bill only lists the edits. Second, it says the pay or benefits can be given "directly or indirectly." That could cover money sent through a university, company, or middleman. The bill adds no new money, penalties or agencies. It only edits the definition. The result is that the ban would more clearly target programs backed by the named countries, and would also reach programs that route benefits through other parties. Researchers working with allied or other countries could be less likely to be caught by the rule.
does: Adds 'of concern' after 'foreign country' in the definition of a malign foreign talent recruitment program.
Removes an older part of the definition (subparagraph B), whose content is not shown in the bill text provided.
Says the compensation or incentive can be provided 'directly or indirectly.'
Reorganizes the list of qualifying activities (nine items) into lettered subparagraphs.
Adds no new funding, penalties, or reporting rules on its face.
who: University and national lab researchers who receive federal grants
Universities and research institutions that must comply with the ban
Federal research funding agencies
Foreign-born and international researchers, especially those with ties to China, Iran, North Korea or Russia
Researchers collaborating with allied countries

benefits: Could make the ban more clearly focused on programs backed by named countries of concern.
The "directly or indirectly" wording could cover payments routed through universities, companies, or middlemen, which may make the rule harder to get around.
concerns: Narrowing the definition to countries of concern could leave some programs from other countries outside the rule, which may matter if those programs raise similar research-security risks.
Removing subparagraph B could change which programs are covered in ways the summary does not explain.
Researchers may find it harder to tell which arrangements are covered, especially with indirect payments, which could lead to uncertainty or unintended violations.
imp.cost: ["The material does not state any cost or funding amounts. The bill is described as adding no new money, penalties, or agencies."]
unknowns: The full text of subparagraph B, which the bill removes, is not included in the material, so its exact effect is unclear.
It is not stated how "directly or indirectly" would be applied in practice or how agencies would enforce it.
It is not stated whether the change would affect how many researchers or programs are covered.
The bill's current status is listed only as out of committee and on the Senate calendar; no vote timing is given.

stage.last_action: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Reported by Senator Cruz without amendment. With written report No. 119-45.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to clarify the definition of a "malign foreign talent recruitment program" in the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which is part of the CHIPS and Science Act. It states that the research-funding ban on these programs should apply to programs sponsored by a "foreign country of concern" (such as China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia) and that compensation or incentives may be provided directly or indirectly.

oppose: The bill narrows the ban to programs sponsored by countries of concern. Programs from other countries that raise similar research-security risks could fall outside the rule, so a constituent could ask whether that gap is intended.

The bill removes subparagraph (B) of the existing definition, and the bill text provided does not show what that subparagraph covered. A constituent could ask the member to explain which programs would no longer be covered and why.

Adding 'directly or indirectly' may make it harder for researchers to know whether a particular arrangement is covered. Constituents could ask for clear guidance so honest researchers do not face accidental violations.
support: The bill ties the ban to 'foreign countries of concern,' a term already defined in federal law, which may focus enforcement on the countries that research-security officials see as the greatest risk.

The 'directly or indirectly' wording could stop foreign governments from avoiding the ban by routing payments through universities, companies, or middlemen, which may better protect federally funded research.
The bill adds no new spending, penalties, or agencies. It only edits an existing definition, so it could clarify current rules without creating a large new burden.

crs:
United States Research Protection Act of 2025
This bill clarifies the definition of a 
malign foreign talent recruitment program
 under the Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act.

The Research and Development, Competition, and Innovation Act, which was included in the CHIPS and Science Act, prohibits researchers who receive federal funds from participating in malign foreign talent recruitment programs, in which foreign countries incentivize or compensate researchers for activities that present a conflict of interest for the researcher or that are otherwise unauthorized (e.g., sharing proprietary information without proper authorization).
The bill clarifies that these restrictions apply to programs that are sponsored by a foreign country of concern, including China, Iran, North Korea, and Russia. The bill also clarifies that malign foreign talent recruitment programs may involve direct or indirect compensation or incentives from such countries.

equality.reason: Narrowing the rule to countries of concern and tying it to foreign-born researchers' national ties could mean applying research-security restrictions unevenly by national origin, though the bill also applies a uniform rule to named countries.

personal_freedom.reason: Researchers with ties to named countries face broader restrictions on their outside collaborations and compensation, and indirect payments make it harder to know what is prohibited.

transparency.reason: The bill edits a research-security definition without adding any disclosure, reporting, or public-access requirements.

honesty_kindness.reason: The bill does not address honesty or kindness; it narrows the ban's coverage to certain countries and adds indirect compensation, which is a security-policy change with no clear bearing on these values.

label: S. 789
title: Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
short_title: Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
one: Directs the Interior Department to study who owns the world's critical mineral and rare earth supplies, help U.S. owners sell foreign mining stakes to buyers outside adversary control, and plan technology and intellectual property sharing with allies.
summary: This bill is mostly about gathering information and making plans. It does not fund new mines, create new mining permits, or change environmental rules. It tells the Interior Department to do three things. First, within one year and every two years after, it must send Congress a report on critical minerals and rare earth elements around the world. These are materials used in electronics, batteries, and defense equipment. The report would cover who controls each supply, mine-by-mine output and remaining reserves, who the real owners are, and which companies are involved. It must also list cases where companies were forced to sell mining stakes to governments or firms tied to "covered nations" such as China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran. Second, within one year, Interior must set up a process for U.S. citizens, permanent residents, and U.S. companies to tell the government they plan to sell stock in foreign mining, processing, or recycling operations. Interior may then help find a buyer not controlled by a covered nation. Third, within one year, Interior must develop a strategy to work with allies on advanced mining, refining, and recycling technology. It must also develop a way to share the resulting intellectual property with allied governments so they can license it. It must report progress each year. The text provided is shown as struck out, so the version actually reported out of committee may differ.
does: Requires Interior, working with Energy and other agencies, to report to Congress within 1 year and every 2 years after on global critical mineral and rare earth resources, including recycled materials.
The report must assess which resources are controlled by foreign entities of concern, which by the U.S. or allies, and which by neither, and explain why some are not being commercially mined.

For each significant mine, the report must estimate yearly output and remaining reserves, name the operating country and company, and identify the ultimate beneficial owners and their ownership percentages.
The report must list key adversary-linked, U.S., and allied mining entities and assess whether they could technically mine and process unclaimed resources.

The report must assess ways to work with countries hosting mines or processing sites operated by other countries, and list forced divestments and takeovers of mining operations tied to covered nations.
Reports must be unclassified but may have a classified annex.

Within 1 year, Interior and State must create a process for U.S. persons to notify the government of plans to sell foreign mining, processing, or recycling stock, and Interior may help them find a buyer not controlled by a covered nation.
Within 1 year, Interior must develop a strategy to work with allies on advanced mining, refining, separation, processing, and recycling technologies.

Interior must also develop a method to share intellectual property from those technologies with allied governments so they can license it and develop their own resources, with annual progress reports to Congress.
who: Department of the Interior and other agencies that must prepare reports and plans
U.S. companies and individuals holding stock in foreign mining, processing, or recycling operations
Mining, battery, electronics, and defense industries that rely on critical minerals
Allied and partner governments that could license shared technology
Members of Congress and the public who rely on the reports
Communities near existing or future mining sites, indirectly

benefits: Public, unclassified reports could show who really owns and controls critical mineral supplies.
Could help policymakers spot supply risks and reduce dependence on a few adversary-linked sources.
Includes recycling in its scope, which could support reuse of materials.
Little direct cost to taxpayers, since it mainly requires reports and planning.
concerns: It does not address environmental, water, air, or worker protections tied to expanded mining.
Helping private owners find buyers could be seen as government assistance to companies.
Sharing intellectual property with allied governments could benefit private licensees, and the bill does not say how taxpayers would be compensated.
No requirement for community or tribal input on mining developments.
imp.cost: No funding amount is stated. The costs are staff time for Interior and other agencies to produce reports and plans. A formal cost estimate was not provided.
unknowns: The provided text is shown as struck out, so the committee-reported version may differ.
How the IP-sharing method would work and who would own or profit from the technology.
Whether the reports could lead to later laws that expand mining and what protections would come with them.
How much the reports would cost to produce.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Energy and Natural Resources. Reported by Senator Lee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help secure U.S. access to critical minerals and rare earth elements. It does this by requiring the Department of the Interior to report on global supplies and ownership, to help U.S. owners of foreign mining stock find buyers not controlled by covered nations (North Korea, China, Russia, or Iran), and to develop a strategy with allies on advanced mining and recycling technology, including a way to share related intellectual property.

oppose: The bill mainly requires reports and planning, but it does not address environmental, water, air, or worker protections tied to expanded mining, which some constituents may want considered.

Helping U.S. owners find buyers for foreign mining stock could be seen as government assistance to private companies, and a constituent could ask whether that is an appropriate use of federal staff time.
Sharing intellectual property with allied governments could benefit private licensees, and the bill does not say how taxpayers would be compensated for this.
The bill does not require community or tribal input on mining developments, which a constituent may see as a gap in how new projects would be reviewed.
support: The bill requires public, unclassified reports that could show who really owns and controls critical mineral supplies, helping Congress spot supply risks.
Reducing reliance on a few adversary-linked sources of critical minerals could strengthen supply chains for electronics, batteries, and defense equipment.
The bill includes recycling in its scope, which could support reuse of materials and reduce the need for new mining.
The bill mainly requires reports and planning rather than new spending, so it carries little direct cost to taxpayers.

crs:
Critical Minerals Security Act of 2025
This bill establishes requirements for the Department of the Interior related to securing U.S. access to critical minerals and rare earth element (REE) resources. 
Critical minerals
 mean any mineral, element, substance, or material designated as critical by the U.S. Geological Survey. 
REEs
 mean cerium, dysprosium, erbium, europium, gadolinium, holmium, lanthanum, lutetium, neodymium, praseodymium, promethium, samarium, scandium, terbium, thulium, ytterbium, and yttrium. 
First, Interior must report on the critical mineral and REE resources, including recyclable or recycled materials containing those resources, around the world. Among other information, the report must include an assessment of the global ownership and supply of critical mineral and REE resources. Interior must submit the report within a year and every two years thereafter.
Next, Interior must establish a process to assist a U.S. person—a U.S. citizen, a non-U.S. National (alien under federal law) lawfully admitted for permanent residence, or an entity organized under U.S. laws—seeking to divest stock in mining, processing, or recycling operations for critical minerals and REEs in a foreign country with finding a purchaser that is not under the control of North Korea, China, Russia, or Iran.
Finally, Interior must develop (1) a strategy to collaborate with U.S. allies and partners to develop advanced mining, refining, separation, processing, and recycling technologies; and (2) a method for sharing related intellectual property with U.S. allies and partners to enable those countries to license those technologies and develop their resources.

transparency.reason: It requires recurring, unclassified reports to Congress that identify mine owners and ownership percentages.

news.overall: Coverage here is thin and mostly does not name the Critical Minerals Security Act directly. The Lean Left headlines focus on China supply-chain risk, legal challenges to federal seabed mining, and political scandal, while the Center and Lean Right groups each have only one article, so their framing is limited to the single piece. Across groups, the bill's own provisions and rationale are largely absent, so the comparison is about adjacent energy and security topics rather than the legislation itself.

label: S. 81
title: Guidance Clarity Act of 2025
short_title: Guidance Clarity Act of 2025
one: Requires federal agencies to put a standard notice on the first page of their guidance documents saying the document is not law and doesn't bind the public or the agency.
summary: Federal agencies often publish "guidance" documents. These explain how an agency reads a law or how it plans to handle something. They aren't formal rules, and they skip the public comment process that formal rules go through. This bill would make agencies put a set statement on the first page of that kind of guidance. The statement says the document does not have the force and effect of law, does not by itself bind the public or the agency, and is meant only to give the public clarity about existing legal requirements or agency policies. The Office of Management and Budget (OMB, the White House office that oversees agency management) would have 90 days after enactment to write instructions for carrying out the law. Agencies would have to start using the statement 30 days after OMB issues those instructions. The Senate committee rewrote the bill and changed which part of the Administrative Procedure Act (the main law on how agencies make rules) it points to. The text does not describe any penalty for agencies that skip the statement. It also doesn't say how the statement would be enforced or how it would be handled in court. The bill doesn't change what guidance can legally do. It only requires the label.
does: Requires every federal agency to put a "guidance clarity statement" on guidance documents covered by the bill.
Requires the statement to appear prominently on the first page.
Sets exact wording: the document lacks the force and effect of law, does not by itself bind the public or the agency, and is only meant to clarify existing legal requirements or agency policies.
Directs OMB to issue implementing guidance within 90 days of enactment.
Starts the requirement 30 days after OMB issues that guidance.

Applies to guidance under a specific part of the Administrative Procedure Act, apparently the section that exempts certain documents from public notice and comment. The committee amendment changed the cross-reference from 553(b)(3)(A) to 553(b)(4)(A).
who: Federal agencies, such as the EPA and the Department of Agriculture, that issue guidance documents
OMB, which must write the implementing instructions
Businesses and industries that follow agency guidance
Members of the public, communities, and advocacy groups that read or rely on agency guidance

benefits: A standard label could make it clearer to the public that guidance is not a formal rule with the force of law.
The bill may help readers tell apart guidance documents from binding regulations.
Because the bill changes only the labeling requirement, it would not directly add new burdens on the public's rights.
concerns: The bill text does not describe any penalty for agencies that skip the required statement, so compliance may be uneven.
The bill does not say how the statement would be enforced or how courts would treat it, leaving open questions.
Some readers may find that a disclaimer on guidance could reduce how much weight agencies or the public give to guidance, though the bill does not say this directly.

label: S. 90
title: Historic Roadways Protection Act
short_title: Historic Roadways Protection Act
one: The bill would bar the Bureau of Land Management from spending money to carry out or finish certain Utah road and trail (travel management) plans until Utah's long-running "historic road" lawsuits are resolved, and in six areas it would put older pre-2017 plans back in force.
summary:
This bill deals with which roads and trails are open on federal land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) in Utah. Utah and many of its counties have sued the federal government for years. They say they own old rights-of-way (legal claims to use old roads across federal land) under a law from 1866 called R.S. 2477. Congress repealed that law in 1976 but kept rights that already existed.

While those lawsuits are pending, the bill would stop BLM from spending federal money on certain travel management plans. These are plans that decide which routes stay open to vehicles. The bill covers 11 named areas, including the San Rafael Swell, Nine Mile Canyon, Dolores River, Book Cliffs and Henry Mountains. In all 11 areas, BLM could not carry out plans finished after a January 2017 legal settlement with conservation groups. In six of them, BLM could not finish new plans. Those six areas would go back to the plans in effect before the settlement.

The ban would last until the Interior Secretary tells Congress that every listed lawsuit has been decided or otherwise resolved. It applies "notwithstanding any other law," meaning it overrides other laws that might conflict. The Senate committee rewrote the bill. The summary from the Congressional Research Service (CRS, Congress's neutral research office) describes the earlier version, so some details here differ from it.

Historic Roadways Protection Act
This bill prohibits the Bureau for Land Management (BLM) from closing historical roads on public lands in certain areas of Utah until the Federal District Court for Utah makes a decision on each of the R.S. 2477 cases, which are cases brought by Utah and counties to keep historical roads on BLM land in Utah open for public use.
By way of background, a provision of the Mining Law of 1866, commonly known as R.S. 2477, granted rights-of-way to states and counties across public lands for the construction of roads for public use in order to promote settlement of the American West. In 1976, Congress repealed R.S. 2477 when it enacted the Federal Land Policy and Management Act (FLPMA), but FLPMA preserved rights-of-way that had been established under R.S. 2477. After the BLM released travel management plans that closed some historical roads, Utah and 22 counties filed lawsuits about their rights-of-way across public lands for historical roads.
Until the BLM certifies that those cases have been decided, the bill prohibits the BLM from obligating or expending federal funds to (1) finalize or implement a new travel management plan for certain travel management areas in Utah; or (2) implement, with respect to land within the boundary of Utah, the Indian Creek (Canyon Rims) Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Desert Travel Management Plan, the San Rafael Swell Travel Management Plan, or the Labyrinth/Gemini Bridges Travel Management Plan.

transparency.reason: The bill overrides a negotiated settlement and public planning process and applies 'notwithstanding any other law,' which reduces public visibility into and input on land decisions.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill favors state and county claims and some user groups over the broader public interest in land protection, though it does not directly involve corporate profits.
