label: S. 2586
title: MARA Act of 2025
short_title: MARA Act of 2025 (Marine Aquaculture Research for America Act)
one: Sets up a NOAA office and a permit-based demonstration program for fish and seafood farming in federal ocean waters, plus grants, workforce training, and required studies.
summary: This bill would let the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) create a program to test large-scale seafood farming in federal ocean waters (from the state boundary out to 200 nautical miles). It creates an Office of Aquaculture inside NOAA's fisheries service, with a coordinator in each regional office. Within 180 days, NOAA must start an assessment program. NOAA would then issue 10-year, renewable permits for "demonstration projects." These projects may raise only native or historically naturalized species. They must limit escapes, whale and sea turtle entanglement, pollution, and antibiotic use. They must follow the Clean Water Act, Endangered Species Act, Marine Mammal Protection Act, and National Environmental Policy Act, and partner with a university. The public can comment, and affected Governors and Tribal leaders can object. If NOAA misses its deadline and no one objects, a permit can be treated as approved. NOAA can modify, end, or remove projects for violations or safety harms after a warning. The bill also funds grants: $25 million a year for Aquaculture Centers of Excellence at minority-serving and Tribal colleges, and $20 million a year for working waterfront grants, both for 2026–2030. It sets up marketing grants, workforce grants, and a database. NOAA must also run outreach promoting offshore aquaculture. Finally, the National Academies must study offshore aquaculture and the Government Accountability Office must report on it, each within 5 years.

label: S. 5718
title: Trucker Bathroom Access Act
short_title: Trucker Bathroom Access Act
one: Requires many businesses to let delivering or waiting truck drivers use their restrooms, and requires port terminal operators to provide restrooms and parking for port truck drivers.
summary: This bill would make businesses let truck drivers use the bathroom. First, if a commercial truck driver delivers goods to a business, or is waiting there to be loaded, that business would have to let the driver use a restroom meant for its customers or employees. This covers stores open to the public and also shippers, receivers, factories, warehouses, and distribution centers. There are limits. The restroom can be refused if letting the driver in would create an obvious health, safety, or security risk. Very small structures of 800 square feet or less (such as a small filling station or restaurant) with an employee-only restroom are excluded. Businesses would not have to remodel a restroom to comply. Second, the bill deals with "drayage" drivers, who haul cargo in large trucks (over 33,000 pounds) at ports and rail yards. Marine terminal operators, including port authorities that run terminals, would have to provide enough restrooms or portable toilets where these drivers usually go. They would let drivers use existing restrooms when it is safe, add more where the need is greatest, and provide parking near the restrooms. The text does not name a penalty, an enforcement agency, or a start date, and no cost estimate or CRS summary was available. The Senate Commerce Committee has approved the bill with a substitute amendment, which I could not see, so the final wording may differ.

label: H.R. 5167
title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
short_title: Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026
one: This yearly bill sets spending and rules for U.S. spy agencies, creates a new National Counterintelligence Center, adds AI, open-source data and China-related requirements, gives the CIA limited domestic drone-defense powers, and repeals a number of older reporting requirements.
summary:
This is the yearly bill that authorizes money and sets ground rules for the 18 U.S. intelligence agencies. Most dollar amounts are in a secret (classified) schedule. Only two figures are public: $674.5 million for the Director of National Intelligence's management account and $514 million for the CIA retirement fund.

Counterintelligence (Title III, the "SECURE Act"). The bill turns the current counterintelligence office into a new National Counterintelligence Center inside the Director of National Intelligence's office. Its director would be picked by the President and confirmed by the Senate. The Center would lead efforts to detect, disrupt and investigate foreign spying and influence operations. It would run a task force, keep a threat-actor database, run a polygraph program, and set its own budget. Agencies would have to tell it about counterintelligence cases and any planned arrests, and report leaks of classified information within 7 days. The bill also sets up regular strategy and threat reports to Congress.

General intelligence matters (Title IV). The bill says that funding does not by itself authorize any activity that is otherwise unlawful. It raises one acquisition threshold for the National Reconnaissance Office from $75 million to $500 million, with 14 days' notice to Congress. Agencies must name senior biotechnology officials and remove the Chinese AI app DeepSeek from intelligence systems, with exceptions. The bill also directs sharing of cartel and terrorism data and requires notice when overseas embassies or consulates close. Several sections push faster and more consistent adoption of AI, including policies for training AI on classified data, faster approvals, and shared measurements. The NSA must write an "AI Security Playbook" on protecting advanced AI from theft.

Specific agencies (Title V). The CIA must define "novel and significant expenditures" that require telling Congress. Until the end of 2029, the CIA could detect, take over, or destroy drones that threaten certain high-risk CIA or ODNI sites in the U.S. This would apply even where wiretap and similar laws would normally restrict it. The bill adds notice, record-keeping limits and FAA coordination. Defense intelligence components must avoid buying duplicate commercial data, and DOD must track vendors that support clandestine work. The NGA and NRO advisory boards are shut down. The FBI must tell congressional leaders within 5 days when it opens a counterintelligence case on a federal candidate, officeholder or congressional staffer. Department of Energy staff must report travel to "countries of risk" and may not take work devices there without approval.

Open-source intelligence (Title VI). Agencies would coordinate their use of public and commercially purchased data, with a designated official, budget controls, separate budget exhibits, audits, quarterly briefings, standard training, and updated rules on analysis. Agencies must purge incidentally collected public or commercial data about U.S. persons, though the bill gives no deadline or exceptions.

Workforce (Title VII). The DIA must provide unclassified performance appraisals. Intelligence agencies may not require or reward political or ideological activism. They may not base personnel actions on a desire to remedy societal discrimination, to provide role models, or on assumptions tied to race, sex, religion and similar traits, with exceptions for job-related needs and cover. A change to the DNI's recruitment authority removes language on recruitment and training. Some CIA veterans' injuries would count as active-duty service for VA benefits.

Foreign countries (Title VIII). The DNI must produce China net assessments, name a China intelligence manager, and prepare a National Intelligence Estimate on Chinese biotechnology. The Russian atrocities coordinator is extended through 2028 and must cover deported Ukrainian children. The bill also orders a study of atrocity intelligence and requires intelligence support to Ukraine, unless the DNI finds a compelling reason not to.

Reports and other matters (Title IX). The bill changes rules on access to nuclear "restricted data" for the President, Vice President, Members of Congress and judges, and requires the Energy Secretary and DNI to verify their access. It changes NSA notice rules for collection changes and adds drug-control budget reporting. It requires FBI notice of watchlist changes and annual counts of U.S. persons on the terrorist watchlist. It also repeals or trims more than 20 older reports and requirements. These include ones on minority hiring, Chinese Americans' civil rights, global water insecurity and pandemics, and terrorist financing. Finally, it requires a plan for using a proposed "web of biological data."

The bill is a mix. It adds some congressional oversight and privacy protections. It also reduces some reporting, adds new domestic powers, and keeps most spending secret.
does: Authorizes fiscal 2026 intelligence spending, mostly through a classified schedule; publicly sets $674.5 million for the DNI's Intelligence Community Management Account and $514 million for the CIA Retirement and Disability Fund.

Creates a Senate-confirmed National Counterintelligence Center within ODNI, replacing the National Counterintelligence and Security Center, and broadens the definition of counterintelligence to include deterring, disrupting, investigating and exploiting.

Gives the Center authority to direct counterintelligence activities, require concurrence on actions, access all counterintelligence information, transfer funds, and receive notice of investigations and planned arrests; the Attorney General's prosecutorial authority is unaffected.

Creates a National Counterintelligence Task Force, a National Counterintelligence Program budget, and recurring strategy, threat assessment and outlook reports (every 3 to 5 years), annual and quarterly task force reports, and adds the Center director to the National Security Council.

Requires agencies to notify the Center within 7 days of significant unauthorized disclosures of classified intelligence and provide information within 30 days; the Center must report noncompliance and send semiannual reports to Congress.

Sets transition steps: 90 days to move ODNI counterintelligence staff and functions, 180 days of transfer and reprogramming authority, and a one-year review of whether security functions should move to the Center.
States that authorization of funds does not authorize unlawful activity, and allows appropriations for already-authorized pay and benefit increases.
Raises the NRO acquisition authority threshold from $75 million to $500 million, with 14 days' prior notice and a national-security certification.

Requires senior biotechnology officials at major intelligence elements and bans the DeepSeek app (and High Flyer successors) from intelligence national security systems, with exceptions and standards due in 60 days.

Requires use of the Transnational Organized Crime Identity Intelligence Platform to share cartel and terrorism information, with twice-yearly briefings through 2028, and notice to Congress when diplomatic post closures of 60 days or more affect intelligence activities.

Directs AI measures: a presidential policy on using classified data to train AI (180 days), faster authority-to-operate reviews with notice after 60 days, shared technology-adoption metrics (270 days), and an NSA AI Security Playbook to defend advanced AI from theft, with a public version.
Requires CIA guidance on which expenditures are 'novel and significant' for congressional notice, within 180 days.

Gives the CIA, until December 31, 2029, authority to detect, track, take over, seize or destroy drones threatening designated CIA/ODNI sites in the U.S., overriding certain wiretap laws, with FAA coordination, Attorney General notice in 15 days, Congress notice in 90 days, and 30-day record limits.

Blocks defense intelligence components from buying commercial data already held by another component, and requires DOD to build a secure system to deconflict and assess vendor support to clandestine activities.
Terminates the NGA and NRO advisory boards within 30 days, and lets the NRO use commercial remote-sensing funds for imagery and data for defense, intelligence and some civil partners.

Requires the FBI to notify congressional leaders and committees within 5 days of opening counterintelligence assessments or investigations of federal candidates, officeholders or congressional staff, with a carve-out where the recipient is the target.
Requires Energy Department personnel to report travel to countries of risk, take briefings on request, and not carry department devices there without approval.

Creates governance of open-source and commercially available information: an oversight official, budget control by the DNI, separate budget exhibits through FY2029, standardized training, updated directives with 2% of Management Account funds withheld until compliance, audits through 2031, and quarterly purchase briefings.
Requires intelligence elements to purge incidentally collected publicly or commercially available information about U.S. persons, with no stated deadline or exceptions.

Workforce changes: unclassified DIA appraisals; bans requiring or rewarding political or ideological activism; bars personnel actions motivated by remedying societal discrimination or by race, sex, religion and similar traits (with job-related exceptions); changes DNI recruitment language; and treats some CIA service as active-duty for VA benefits.

China and Russia/Ukraine: requires China net assessments (first in 180 days), a China intelligence manager, a biotechnology National Intelligence Estimate, extends the Russian atrocities coordinator to 2028 including Ukrainian children, orders an atrocity-intelligence study, and requires intelligence support to Ukraine unless the DNI finds a compelling reason.
Changes the Atomic Energy Act so the restricted-data access limit does not apply to the President, Vice President, Members of Congress and federal judges, with lists and verification within 90 days.

Revises NSA notices on collection or sharing changes, adds an annual intelligence drug-control budget summary, requires FBI notice of watchlist policy changes and annual counts of U.S. persons on the terrorist watchlist for three years, and orders a plan on a proposed 'web of biological data.'

Repeals or trims more than 20 older reporting requirements, including annual terrorist financial intelligence reports, minority hiring reports, best practices to protect Chinese Americans' civil rights, global water insecurity and pandemics assessments, and Open Skies and Belt and Road mineral-monitoring reports.

imp.cost: Public figures: $674.5 million for the ODNI Intelligence Community Management Account and $514 million for the CIA Retirement and Disability Fund. Remaining amounts are in a classified schedule, so total cost can't be determined from the text provided. 2% of FY2026 Management Account funds are withheld until open-source directive updates are done.

label: H.R. 5470
title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
short_title: Route 66 National Historic Trail Designation Act
one: Designates the roughly 2,400-mile path of historic U.S. Route 66 from Chicago to Santa Monica as a National Historic Trail run by the National Park Service, with strong limits on land acquisition, eminent domain, and new permit requirements.
summary:
This bill would add Route 66 to the National Trails System as the Route 66 National Historic Trail. The trail would cover all the paths U.S. Highway 66 followed between 1926 and 1985, about 2,400 miles from Chicago, Illinois, to Santa Monica, California. The National Park Service would run it, in a way that respects the road's quirky, one-of-a-kind character. Before taking actions that would heavily affect Native American Tribes, the Interior Secretary must consult with those Tribes.

The bill puts many limits on federal power. The government could not take private land by eminent domain (forced purchase) or condemnation. It could not buy land outside federal areas without the owner's consent, and any land it acquires could not stretch more than an average of a quarter mile on either side of the trail. The bill bars "buffer zones" around the trail. It also says the designation cannot block or slow energy development or transport, including pipelines, power lines, and renewable projects. The designation would not add new federal permit requirements, and it would not change the power of federal, state, or local agencies to grant easements or rights-of-way (permissions to cross or use land). The trail would not count as National Park System land for a specific Mineral Leasing Act rule on pipeline rights-of-way. The text does not give a cost or funding amount. A copy of the map would be available for public viewing at National Park Service offices.
does: Adds the Route 66 National Historic Trail to the National Trails System Act, covering all alignments of U.S. 66 that existed from 1926 to 1985, about 2,400 miles from Chicago to Santa Monica, per a map dated December 2017.
Requires the map to be on file and open to public inspection at National Park Service offices.
Puts the trail under the Interior Secretary and National Park Service, to be managed in a way that respects the road's 'idiosyncratic' nature.
Requires active, meaningful, and timely consultation with affected Indian Tribes before activities with substantial direct impacts on them.
Limits land acquisition: no acquiring land outside federally managed areas without the owner's consent, and none extending more than an average of one-quarter mile on either side of the trail.
Bars buffer zones around the trail and says activities seen, heard, or detected from the trail cannot be restricted for that reason.
States that nothing in the Act can prohibit, hinder, or disrupt current or future energy development, production, transport, or transmission, including pipelines and renewable energy projects.
Bans use of eminent domain or condemnation to carry out the Act.
Says the designation does not make the trail National Park System land for the Mineral Leasing Act pipeline right-of-way provision.
Preserves existing authority of federal, state, and local officials to grant easements and rights-of-way, and says the designation adds no new federal permit or authorization requirements.
who: Communities, small businesses, museums, and tourism operators along Route 66 in Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, and California
Private landowners along the route, who gain protections against forced acquisition
Affected Native American Tribes, who get consultation rights
National Park Service and Department of the Interior
Energy and pipeline companies, whose activities are protected from restriction under the Act
Travelers, history enthusiasts, and the public

benefits: Could boost heritage tourism and the economies of small towns along the route.
Helps preserve historic road segments, signs, and landmarks.
Protects private landowners through the ban on eminent domain and consent-only acquisition.
Guarantees consultation with affected Tribes.
The map must be publicly available.
concerns: The energy provision says the Act cannot hinder pipelines or other energy projects, which could limit the trail's protection against nearby development.
The bill says no new federal permit requirements arise from designation, which could reduce some environmental review.
No buffer zones could mean the trail's setting is less protected from nearby visual or noise intrusions.
The acquisition limits could make it harder to protect some historic sites.
imp.cost: The bill text gives no funding amount or cost estimate. Costs would depend on later appropriations for National Park Service administration and any land purchases from willing owners.
unknowns: How much the National Park Service would spend and where the money would come from.
How the trail would be managed day to day given the many state and local owners along the route.
How the energy and permit language would work in practice.
What the committee's substitute amendment changed, since the version reported may differ from this text.

label: H.R. 7031
title: Making National Parks Safer Act
short_title: Making National Parks Safer Act
one: Requires the National Park Service to assess and then plan for installing modern, internet-based Next Generation 911 systems at emergency communications centers in national parks.
summary: This bill tells the National Park Service (NPS) to study and plan for upgrading 911 emergency call systems in national parks. Within one year of becoming law, NPS must finish an assessment of the emergency communications centers (dispatch centers) located in park units. The assessment must find out where Next Generation 911 (NG911) is already in use, what it would cost to buy NG911 for centers that haven't started, and what it would cost to run and maintain it everywhere. NG911 is a digital, internet-based 911 system that can better share calls, locations, and callback numbers across agencies. NPS must then send a report to the House and Senate natural resources committees and post it on the Interior Department website. The report must flag problems that could slow the upgrade, such as jurisdiction, technology, legal authority, and legal agreements. Within one year after that report, NPS must create a plan to install NG911 at the identified centers. In making the plan, NPS must talk with state and local emergency officials, other local stakeholders chosen by park superintendents, and the Departments of Commerce and Transportation and the FCC. Parks whose superintendent decides they already have, or are installing, enough NG911 do not have to be covered. The bill does not itself pay for or order installation, and it does not provide any new money.
does: Requires the Interior Secretary, through NPS, to complete an assessment within 1 year of enactment of emergency communications centers in national park units.

The assessment must identify the current status of NG911 at existing centers, estimated purchase costs for centers that haven't started, and estimated operating and maintenance costs across all centers.
Requires a report on the results to the House Natural Resources and Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committees, and public posting on the Interior Department website.
The report must identify obstacles to implementation: jurisdictional, technological, legal authority, and legal agreement issues.
Requires NPS to develop a plan to install NG911 at identified centers within 1 year after the report is submitted.

Requires consultation with state and local emergency operations officials (to ensure interoperability), appropriate state and local stakeholders, and the Commerce Department, Transportation Department, and FCC.
Exempts units from the plan where the superintendent decides sufficient NG911 is already installed or being installed.
Defines key terms, including emergency communications center, interoperability, and NG911.
who: Visitors, hikers, campers, and staff in national parks who may need to call 911
National Park Service dispatch and emergency communications staff
Park rangers and other first responders
State and local emergency operations officials and nearby communities that share emergency response with parks
Department of the Interior, Commerce, Transportation, and the FCC
Congressional natural resources committees

benefits: Could lead to faster, more accurate emergency response in parks, including better location data and call transfers between agencies.
Public report increases transparency about costs and obstacles.
Requires consultation with state and local emergency officials and stakeholders.
Gives Congress cost information for future funding decisions.
concerns: Only requires an assessment and plan; it does not require or fund installation, so safety gains may be delayed.
The timeline (up to about 2 years before a plan exists) is slow.
Superintendents can exempt units from the plan based on their own determination of 'sufficient' systems, with no outside check specified.
The consultation requirement for local stakeholders depends on superintendent discretion.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to make national parks safer by upgrading 911 emergency communications in park units to Next Generation 911 (NG911), a digital, internet-based system that can better share calls, locations, and callback numbers across agencies. label: S. 4577
title: Reassessing the United States-Tanzania Bilateral Relationship Act
short_title: Reassessing the U.S.-Tanzania Bilateral Relationship Act
one: The bill, as introduced, would order a review of U.S.-Tanzania relations, require a list of Tanzanian officials tied to abuses, allow sanctions on some of them, and pause certain U.S. security aid, development-finance support and Millennium Challenge Corporation funds until Tanzania makes democratic reforms.
summary:
Important note first: the copy of the bill I was given shows every section as "struck out." That usually means the Senate committee replaced the original text with a different version, and I could not see the replacement. This analysis covers the original text as introduced. The version that moves forward may differ.

The bill responds to Tanzania's October 29, 2025 elections. Its findings say the elections involved ballot manipulation, that security forces killed hundreds of protesters, that the government shut down the internet, and that opposition figures were abducted or prosecuted for political reasons. They also cite attacks on religious freedom.

The bill would do five main things. First, it would have the Secretary of State, working with the Defense Department, the Trade Representative and other agencies, review the whole U.S.-Tanzania relationship. That review would cover Tanzania's democratic direction, a reform strategy, whether U.S.-supported police and military are reliable partners, the effect of the unrest and internet shutdown on U.S. business, and Tanzania's ties to China. A report would be due to Congress within 90 days.

Second, within 180 days the State Department would report a list of senior Tanzanian officials it finds responsible for abuses. These include abductions, attacks on journalists, internet shutdowns, religious persecution, cross-border repression and killings.

Third, the President "may" (not must) freeze U.S. assets and ban visas for people on the list who are tied to abductions, disappearances or arbitrary detention of opponents, journalists or activists. The sanctions have exceptions for food, medicine and humanitarian aid, UN obligations, law enforcement and intelligence activities. The President can lift them if the person stops the conduct.

Fourth, U.S. security assistance and support from the Development Finance Corporation, the Export-Import Bank and the Trade and Development Agency would be barred for entities in Tanzania. The bar would end 30 days after the Secretary of State certifies that Tanzania has made election reforms, released political prisoners, held abusers accountable and stopped intimidating the media. Humanitarian aid, health aid and aid for democracy and civil society would still be allowed.

Fifth, Millennium Challenge Corporation money for Tanzania would be blocked until its board certifies that Tanzania is committed to just and democratic governance.

The bill also expresses support for ending Tanzania's MCC threshold program and for an independent international investigation. No cost estimate is available.

Requires reporting to Congress, adding oversight of U.S. aid and security cooperation.

Examines how Chinese financing affects debt and U.S. competitiveness.

Sanctions are discretionary, so they may not be used consistently.
Restricting security assistance could reduce U.S. influence and cooperation on regional security, and could push Tanzania closer to China.
Sanctions and asset freezes can affect people through broader economic impacts, though humanitarian exceptions exist.
Findings use strong language ('fraudulent', 'illegitimate') that may complicate diplomacy.

label: H.R. 4449
title: Advocating for Small Business Act
short_title: Advocating for Small Business Act
one: Requires the SEC to create an Office of Small Business inside each of its rule-writing divisions to work with the SEC's small business capital formation advocate.
summary:
This bill changes the law that governs the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the federal agency that oversees stock markets and the sale of investments. It would require the SEC to set up an "Office of Small Business" inside every division that writes rules. Each of these offices would have to work with the SEC's existing Office of the Advocate for Small Business Capital Formation. They would coordinate on rules and policy priorities that affect "capital formation," which means how businesses raise money from investors, such as by selling stock or other securities.

The bill is short. It does not give the new offices any power to block or approve rules. It also does not set a budget, staffing level, deadline, or reporting requirement. It does not change investor protection or disclosure rules directly. In practice, the main effect would be that small business concerns get considered earlier within the SEC's rule-writing process. The bill also does not say how the offices would be staffed or paid for, so the cost and the real impact are unclear. Supporters would likely say it helps small firms be heard. Critics could worry that it adds bureaucracy or leans the agency toward easing rules, depending on how it is used. As written, the bill only sets up internal coordination.

concerns: Could add bureaucracy or cost without clear results.
Could tilt rule writing toward easing disclosure rules, which could reduce protections for investors.
No requirement for public reporting, so the offices' influence might not be visible to the public.

one: Renames the Secret Service's Uniformed Division as the "U.S. Secret Service Police" and updates federal law to match, with no other changes shown in the text.
summary: This bill changes the name of the Secret Service's Uniformed Division to the "U.S. Secret Service Police." The Uniformed Division is the uniformed branch that guards the White House, the Vice President's residence, foreign embassies in Washington, and other protected sites. The bill does not create new powers, change who works there, or set new rules. It goes through several parts of federal law (Titles 2, 5, 10, 18, 28 and 31 of the U.S. Code) and swaps the words "Uniformed Division" for "Police" wherever they appear in the listed sections. The bill's title honors Officer Leslie Coffelt, a White House police officer killed in 1950 while defending President Truman during an assassination attempt. That background comes from general history, not the bill text. The bill text does not say what the change would cost. It appears to be a name and wording change only, so any cost would likely be small, such as new uniforms, badges, or signs. That is my inference, not something the bill states. The House committee approved an amended version by voice vote on September 16, 2026. I could only see the original text, not the amendment.

label: S. 2883
title: Quantifying Uncertainty and Action to Help Optimize Growth of Shellfish Act of 2025
short_title: QUAHOGS Act of 2025 (East Coast Shellfish Research Task Force)
one: The bill would create a federal task force to study why clam, oyster, mussel and scallop harvests are declining or becoming unpredictable along the East Coast, and to recommend what research is needed. The copy provided shows all of its text as struck out.
summary: This bill is about shellfish such as quahogs (hard clams), oysters, mussels and scallops, which are called bivalves. Harvests of some of them along the East Coast have become less predictable or have fallen. The bill would have the Secretary of Commerce set up an East Coast Bivalve Research Task Force within 90 days of becoming law. The task force would have 16 to 21 members. They would come from federal agencies, regional fishery councils, state wildlife agencies, Native American tribes, the shellfish industry, and university scientists. The task force would review the existing research. It would look at water quality, erosion, climate change, ocean acidification, disease, habitat restoration, and shellfish farming. It would then name the biggest gaps in knowledge and recommend research to fill them. It would set up work groups, including one on quahogs in Rhode Island and one on climate change. It would send Congress a progress report after 1 year and a final public report after 2 years. Members would not be paid but could get travel costs covered. The bill does not set a dollar amount. It allows "such sums as may be necessary" to be spent. One important caveat is that the text provided shows every section as "struck out." This usually means a committee replaced the original text with a substitute. I could not see the replacement text, so the final version may differ from what is described here.

The NOAA representative chairs the group.

Directs the task force to review existing science on traditional ecological knowledge, habitat and water quality, erosion and sedimentation, climate change and ocean acidification, restoration, assisted migration, breeding and genomic techniques, life cycles, range shifts, disease, aquaculture management, and the economics of aquaculture, including barriers for small operators.
Tells the task force to identify gaps in research and possible solutions to declining harvests, and to evaluate economic impacts of wild populations, fisheries and aquaculture.

Requires work groups within 30 days: one on quahog research needs (including Rhode Island) and one on climate change effects. Other regional or species work groups are optional. Each has at least 5 people and balanced stakeholder representation. Work groups report to the task force within 2 years.
Requires an interim public report at 1 year and a final public report at 2 years, sent to the relevant Senate and House committees and the Secretaries of Commerce and Agriculture.
Members serve without pay but receive travel expenses and per diem. Commerce provides administrative support, including virtual participation.

label: S. 3301
title: Chip Equipment Quality, Usefulness, and Integrity Protection Act of 2026
short_title: Chip EQUIP Act (Chip Equipment Quality, Usefulness, and Integrity Protection Act)
one: Companies that take CHIPS Act money would be barred for 10 years from buying fully assembled chipmaking machines made, assembled, or refurbished by firms tied to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea, unless the Commerce Department grants a waiver.
summary:
This bill adds a rule to the CHIPS Act programs, which give federal money to help build semiconductor (computer chip) factories and fund chip research. Under the bill, the Commerce Department must write into every funding agreement a ban on using that project to buy, install, or use certain chipmaking equipment from "foreign entities of concern." That term mainly means companies owned or controlled by China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia, and their subsidiaries. The ban lasts 10 years from the day the agreement is signed.

The ban covers complete, ready-to-use machines such as deposition, etching, and lithography tools, testing and inspection gear, wafer cutting tools, and similar equipment. It does not cover individual parts, chambers, or subcomponents that go into such machines.

Commerce could waive the ban in three cases. First, the equipment isn't made in the U.S. or an allied country in enough quantity or good enough quality. Second, the machine was built by a non-concern company and only refurbished by a concern company. Third, the use follows export control rules and Commerce, after consulting the Director of National Intelligence or the Secretary of Defense, decides a waiver serves U.S. national security. The bill says it does not weaken the existing section 9907 restrictions on foreign entities of concern.

Note: the text provided shows most provisions marked as "struck out," which looks like a formatting artifact. I used the CRS summary and the provision language to describe the bill's content. I could not see any cost estimate.
does: Adds definitions to the CHIPS provisions of the FY2021 National Defense Authorization Act: 'completed, fully assembled' equipment and 'ineligible semiconductor manufacturing equipment.'

Defines ineligible equipment as complete machines made, assembled, or refurbished by a foreign entity of concern (such as firms controlled by China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea) or its subsidiary, used for chip fabrication, assembly, testing, packaging, or research.

Lists covered equipment types, including deposition, etching, lithography, inspection/measuring/test gear, wafer slicing and dicing, wire bonders, ion implantation, chemical mechanical polishing, furnaces, thermal processing, and automated material handling systems.
Excludes individual parts, chambers, subsystems, and subcomponents from the definition.

Requires Commerce to put a 10-year ban on buying, installing, or using this equipment into each funding agreement under CHIPS manufacturing incentives (section 9902) and research awards (section 9906).

Lets Commerce waive the ban if equipment isn't available in enough quantity or quality from the U.S. or allies, if a non-concern maker built it and a concern company only refurbished it, or if export rules are met and Commerce, consulting intelligence or defense officials, finds a waiver is in the national security interest.
States that nothing in the new subsection waives the existing section 9907 restrictions on foreign entities of concern.
who: Semiconductor companies receiving CHIPS Act incentives or research awards
The Commerce Department, which must write and enforce the terms and decide waivers
Chip equipment makers in China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and their subsidiaries
Equipment makers in the U.S. and allied countries that could gain sales
Workers and communities near federally supported chip plants
Taxpayers whose money funds CHIPS programs

benefits: Could keep federally funded projects from relying on equipment from firms tied to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea.
Could reduce national security and supply-chain risks, such as hidden access or forced dependence.
Could boost demand for U.S. and allied equipment makers.
Adds conditions to how public money is used.
concerns: Waivers are decided by Commerce, and the bill has no public reporting requirement for them.
Parts and subcomponents from foreign entities of concern are not covered, so the ban could be sidestepped.
Could raise costs or delay projects if substitute equipment is scarce.
Does not address worker, environmental, or community protections around chip plants.
Does not reduce subsidies to companies.
imp.cost: No new spending is authorized in the text provided. It adds conditions to existing CHIPS funding. No cost estimate was available to me; compliance could raise costs for recipients and administrative work for Commerce.
unknowns: How often Commerce would grant waivers and whether they would be made public.
Whether the 'fully assembled' limit would let restricted firms' parts into U.S. fabs.
How much it would raise costs or slow chip projects.
Why the provided text shows provisions as struck out, and what the final text is.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep federal CHIPS Act money from being used to buy, install, or use complete chipmaking machines made or refurbished by foreign entities of concern, such as firms owned or controlled by China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia, and their subsidiaries. It aims to address national security and supply-chain risks tied to these companies by adding a 10-year ban to every CHIPS funding agreement, with limited waiver options.

support: The bill says its goal is to keep federally funded chip projects from relying on equipment from firms tied to China, Russia, Iran, or North Korea, which could reduce national security risks.

Chip Equipment Quality, Usefulness, and Integrity Protection Act of 2025 or the Chip EQUIP Act
This bill prohibits companies that receive certain federal funds from purchasing specified semiconductor manufacturing equipment made by foreign entities of concern (e.g., companies owned or controlled by China, Iran, North Korea, or Russia) or their subsidiaries for the federally funded project.
The CHIPS Act of 2022, which became law in August 2022, appropriated funding for the Department of Commerce to carry out the CHIPS for America provisions enacted in the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. These provisions included appropriations for financial incentives to expand domestic manufacturing capacities across the semiconductor supply chain, as well as for research and development programs.
Under the bill, Commerce must include in the terms of each agreement with a covered entity (e.g., companies receiving CHIPS funds) prohibitions with respect to a project relating to the procurement, installation, or use of the specified semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The prohibitions must be effective for 10 years beginning on the date on which the agreement is signed.
The bill authorizes Commerce to waive these prohibitions under certain circumstances, such as if the specified semiconductor manufacturing equipment is not produced in the United States or an allied or partner country in sufficient and reasonably available quantities or of a satisfactory quality to support established or expected production capabilities.

environment.reason: The bill concerns equipment purchasing conditions for CHIPS-funded projects and does not address air, water, or land protections.

transparency_kindness.reason: Waiver decisions by Commerce under the new subsection carry no public reporting requirement, so the public would have limited view of how exemptions are granted.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill restricts equipment sourcing and adds conditions to funding without clearly shifting costs to consumers or taxpayers; the cost effects are uncertain.

local_say.reason: The bill sets federal Commerce-level conditions with no change to state or local decision-making over land use, permits, or facilities.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill adds conditions to existing CHIPS funding but does not authorize new subsidies or shift losses to taxpayers or ratepayers.

equality.reason: The ban applies by ownership category of equipment makers and does not create unequal treatment of people.

justice.reason: The bill creates an enforceable contract term with a clear rule, but the waiver process lacks public accountability, so the net effect on legal fairness is unclear.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill restricts companies' purchasing choices under federal agreements, not individuals' personal choices about their own lives.

label: S. 3741
title: Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026
short_title: Biosecurity Modernization and Innovation Act of 2026
one: As introduced, the bill would require companies that make synthetic DNA/RNA or the machines that make it to screen orders and customers for dangerous sequences, create a testing "sandbox" for biotech governance, and order a review to streamline federal biosecurity oversight.
summary:
Important note first: in the text provided, every section is marked "struck out." This usually means a committee replaced the original text with a new version, but the replacement text was not included. So this analysis covers the bill as originally introduced, and the version now on the Senate calendar may differ.

The bill is about biosecurity, meaning protection against the deliberate or accidental creation of dangerous germs. Gene synthesis (making custom DNA or RNA) is getting cheaper and more powerful, and Congress says this could let bad actors build new pathogens. The bill treats screening as a short-term stopgap while the government builds a broader strategy.

First, within one year the Secretary of Commerce would write rules. Companies that sell synthetic DNA/RNA, or the equipment to make it (including benchtop synthesizers), would have to screen orders against a government list of "sequences of concern" and check who their customers are and whether they are legitimate. A privacy-protecting system would help catch people who split a dangerous order into smaller pieces across companies. The list would be updated regularly, with a public docket for suggestions and a fast track for adding new threats. Companies would be audited, including by surprise "red team" tests, and could lose their compliance status. Anyone getting federal money could only buy synthetic DNA from compliant companies. Safeguards would let trusted institutions like universities get faster reviews and would exempt clearly harmless sequences. The government would offer technical help. Customer information in these submissions would be shielded from public records requests. Rules would be reviewed at least every two years.

Second, the Attorney General could sue violators, including those giving false information. Penalties could reach $500,000 for an individual and $750,000 for a company, adjusted yearly for inflation. Commerce would report yearly to Congress.

Third, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) would build a "biotechnology governance sandbox," a secure space where experts from industry, universities and civil society test tools and methods for biosecurity.

Fourth, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy would, within 90 days, review all federal biosecurity and biosafety authorities, find overlaps and gaps, and make a plan to streamline them. It would report to Congress and start carrying out the plan by administrative action. It could recommend creating a new agency.

No cost estimate or funding amount appears in the text. A Congressional Research Service summary was not available.
does: Defines 'covered providers' as sellers of synthetic nucleic acids to people in the U.S. and makers or sellers (including resellers) of nucleic acid synthesis equipment such as benchtop synthesizers.

Directs Commerce to issue rules within 1 year requiring covered providers to screen orders against a list of 'sequences of concern,' prioritizing sequences that could create pandemic-potential pathogens.
Requires providers to verify customer identity and legitimacy, and to use a privacy-preserving way to detect orders split across multiple providers.
Has Commerce build and regularly update the sequence list with expert input, a public docket for privacy-preserving suggestions, a fast provisional-add process, and strong data security.
Creates a conformity assessment system: audits, random adversarial ('red team') tests, and a process to revoke compliance status after a grace period to fix failures.
Adds burden-reducing safeguards: expedited review for trusted institutions like accredited universities, exemptions for clearly non-hazardous sequences, and regular expert consultation.
Requires anyone receiving federal funds to buy synthetic nucleic acids only from compliant providers, and offers providers technical help with ambiguous screening results.
Has NIST develop best practices, standards, testing of screening tools, and prototype sequence-to-function models; rules must be reviewed at least every 2 years.
Exempts customer information in these screening submissions from public records disclosure (FOIA trade-secret exemption) and replaces earlier voluntary federal screening guidance.

Lets the Attorney General sue violators, including for false or misleading information, seeking injunctions and damages up to $500,000 (individuals) or $750,000 (others), adjusted yearly for inflation.
Requires an annual Commerce report to Congress, including how many providers have been verified.
Orders NIST to set up a biotechnology governance 'sandbox' within 1 year to test biosecurity tools and governance approaches with outside experts, and report annually.

Orders the OSTP Director to assess all federal biosecurity and biosafety authorities within 90 days, develop a streamlining plan, report to Congress (including whether a new agency is needed), and begin implementing the plan administratively.
who: Companies that make or sell synthetic DNA/RNA and gene synthesis equipment
Universities, labs and researchers who order synthetic genes, especially federally funded ones
Biotechnology industry and startups
The general public, who could face lower risk of engineered pandemics
Federal agencies (Commerce, NIST, OSTP, Justice Department)
Customers whose identity and orders would be screened

benefits: Could lower the risk that bad actors obtain synthetic genes to build dangerous pathogens.
Replaces voluntary guidance with enforceable, uniform rules and real penalties.
Includes audits, red-team tests, and annual reports to Congress for accountability.
Includes safeguards that may limit burdens on universities and legitimate research.
Review of overlapping federal authorities could make oversight clearer and more consistent.
concerns: Customer information in screening submissions would be shielded from public records requests, limiting public visibility.
Identity and legitimacy checks and purchase limits could burden or slow some researchers and small companies.
Streamlining or consolidating authorities by administrative action, possibly via a new agency, could weaken some existing oversight if done poorly.
The sequence list is set by the Commerce Secretary, so its accuracy and fairness depend on agency choices.
Penalties are large and could hit small providers hard.
imp.cost: No funding amount or cost estimate is given in the text provided. Costs would come from Commerce, NIST, OSTP and Justice Department activities, plus compliance costs for providers.
unknowns: What replacement text the committee adopted, since all provided text is struck out.
The cost to taxpayers and to providers, and whether new money would be appropriated.
What will be on the sequences-of-concern list and how often it changes.
Whether the OSTP plan would create a new agency or move authorities.
How foreign providers selling into the U.S. would be handled in practice.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Reported by Senator Cruz with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. Without written report.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to reduce biosecurity risks from the deliberate or accidental creation of dangerous germs, citing concern that cheaper, more powerful gene synthesis could let bad actors build new pathogens. It sets up interim screening rules for synthetic DNA/RNA providers as a stopgap while a broader federal strategy is developed, and it aims to streamline overlapping federal biosecurity and biosafety authorities. Note: the text provided marks every section as "struck out," and no CRS summary was available, so this reflects the bill as originally introduced and the current version may differ.

oppose: Customer information submitted for screening would be exempt from public records requests, which could limit public oversight of how the system works.
Identity checks, legitimacy reviews, and purchase limits could slow research and add costs for smaller companies and labs that lack compliance staff.
Penalties of up to $500,000 for individuals and $750,000 for companies could hit small providers hard, and the bill does not include a cost estimate or funding amount.

The Commerce Secretary would set the list of sequences of concern, so its accuracy and fairness would depend on agency decisions. Asking whether these decisions will be open to public input could be a useful question.
support: The bill would replace voluntary federal screening guidance with enforceable, uniform rules for companies that sell synthetic DNA/RNA and benchtop synthesizers, which could lower the risk of bad actors obtaining genes for dangerous pathogens.
Audits, surprise red-team tests, and annual reports to Congress would provide accountability and show whether the rules are working.
Safeguards such as faster reviews for trusted institutions like accredited universities and exemptions for clearly harmless sequences aim to limit burdens on legitimate research.
A review of overlapping federal biosecurity and biosafety authorities could make oversight clearer and more consistent, and a NIST sandbox would let experts test tools before they are widely used.

transparency.reason: Public docket for list suggestions and annual reports to Congress add openness, though customer information would be shielded from public records requests.

people_over_profit.reason: It imposes enforceable safety screening on synthetic DNA sellers and equipment makers to protect public safety, though it includes safeguards to limit industry burden.

honesty_kindness.reason: It penalizes false or misleading information and deceptive practices in screening and compliance.

justice.reason: It sets clear rules, audits, a grace period to fix failures, and court-based enforcement rather than relying on voluntary guidance.

personal_freedom.reason: Customers would face identity and legitimacy checks and could be blocked from buying certain sequences, which limits individual access and privacy somewhat.

label: S. 3954
title: No Lifeline for Dead People Act
short_title: No Lifeline for Dead People Act
one: Would bar phone and internet companies from giving Lifeline discounts to anyone unless the company first checked their eligibility through the federal National Verifier system.
summary: Lifeline is a federal program that helps low-income households pay for phone or internet service. It is paid for through the Universal Service Fund, which is supported by fees on telecommunications services. This bill would make one rule: a company that is approved to offer Lifeline (an "eligible telecommunications carrier") could not give Lifeline service to a customer unless it had used the National Verifier to confirm that customer qualifies. The National Verifier is the federal database and process that checks eligibility, for example by matching records. The bill's title points to a concern about people who have died still being enrolled and having benefits billed on their behalf. The text I was given shows every section, including the short title, as struck out. This usually means the committee removed or replaced the original language. The replacement text, if there is any, was not included. So I can only describe the introduced language, and the version on the Senate calendar may differ. The bill has no stated cost, no new spending, and no start date in the text I could see. It could cut fraud and improper payments. It could also add paperwork hurdles for eligible low-income people if the verification process wrongly rejects them or is slow.
does: Defines key terms: eligible telecommunications carrier, Lifeline service (voice or broadband under the FCC's Lifeline rules), and National Verifier (as defined in FCC rules).
Says a Lifeline-approved carrier may not provide Lifeline service to a consumer unless the carrier has used the National Verifier to verify that person's eligibility.
The text provided shows all sections as struck out, so the final committee version may differ or be replaced. The replacement text was not shown.
Contains no new funding, penalties, deadlines, or appeals process in the text I could see.

Taxpayers and ratepayers concerned about fraud and waste

Could make carriers more accountable for who they enroll, reducing the chance of carriers enrolling people just to collect payments.
Uses an existing federal system rather than creating a new one.
concerns: Eligible low-income people could be delayed or denied if the verifier has data errors or hard paperwork.
No appeals process or help for applicants is described.
Many carriers may already use the National Verifier, so the real-world effect may be small.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or new spending is stated. Lifeline is funded through the Universal Service Fund, which is supported by fees on telecom services. The bill could reduce improper payments, but the amount is unknown.

How verification failures would be handled for eligible applicants

label: S. 4691
title: Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
short_title: Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
one: Directs the FCC to review how it notifies phone and internet providers about disaster reporting, publish plain-language guides for state, local, and tribal officials, and study a clearer contact point for communications status during disasters.
summary: This bill asks the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to improve how it coordinates with local officials and phone and internet companies during disasters like hurricanes, floods, and wildfires. It does three main things. First, within 180 days, the FCC must review and, if needed, update how it tells providers when the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS) is turned on or off. DIRS is the system providers use to report outages and service problems. The FCC must talk with providers and with state, local, tribal, and territorial emergency officials where practicable. Second, within 18 months, the FCC must study whether it could expand its existing public safety liaison functions, such as its 24-hour operations center, into a clear point of contact for local officials who want to know the status of communications and coordinate with providers. Third, within one year, the FCC must publish plain-language materials explaining DIRS, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative (rules requiring cell providers to share resources during emergencies), available FCC contacts, and other tools. The bill states that it does not require new regulations, new reporting duties for providers, or any action following the study. It does not provide new money, and the text gives no cost estimate.
does: Within 180 days, requires the FCC to review and, as appropriate, update how it notifies providers when DIRS is activated or deactivated, including whether the notice format or content could be more usable.
Requires the FCC, where practicable, to consult with providers that report in DIRS and with state, local, tribal, and territorial emergency and public safety authorities during that review.

Within 18 months, requires the FCC to evaluate the feasibility of strengthening its public safety liaison functions, including expanded use of its 24-hour operations center, as a clear entry point for officials seeking communications status and a way to coordinate with providers before, during, and after disasters.

Within 1 year, requires the FCC to publish plain-language materials for state, local, tribal, and territorial officials about DIRS, the types and limits of information available (including protections for confidential information), how to access public DIRS-derived reports, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative, FCC contacts and 24-hour capabilities, and other public safety communications services.
Allows the FCC to reuse and consolidate existing outreach materials and guidance.

Includes rules of construction: no new regulations required, no change to the FCC's discretion over when to activate DIRS, no new reporting or operational mandates on providers, and no requirement to act on the feasibility study.
who: Federal Communications Commission staff, who must do the review, study, and materials
State, local, tribal, and territorial emergency management and public safety officials
Phone, cellular, and internet providers that report in DIRS or fall under the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative
Residents of disaster-prone areas, who may benefit indirectly from better coordination and faster restoration

benefits: Local, state, and tribal officials may get clearer, faster information about outages when lives are at stake.
A single clear point of contact could reduce confusion during emergencies.
Plain-language public materials improve transparency about how disaster communications systems work.
Providers may get more usable activation notices, which could improve their outage reporting.
The bill adds no new burdens or mandates on providers and no new taxes or bailouts.
concerns: The bill is mostly studies and guidance; the FCC does not have to act on the feasibility study, so real change is not guaranteed.
It does not add any new requirements for providers, such as better outage reporting or restoration standards, so it may not change provider behavior.
The FCC may have to do the work without extra funding, which could strain its resources.
Much of the work is only required "to the extent practicable," which weakens the requirements.
imp.cost: No funding is provided and no cost estimate was given in the material. Work would presumably be done with existing FCC resources.
unknowns: The cost to the FCC and whether it needs more staff or money.
Whether the FCC will actually expand its liaison functions after the study.
How much outage detail will be publicly available versus protected as confidential.
Whether the changes would measurably improve disaster response.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to improve how the Federal Communications Commission coordinates with state, local, tribal, and territorial officials and communications providers during disasters and emergencies that disrupt communications service. It addresses the problem of officials and providers needing clear, timely information about outages and how to work together during events like hurricanes, floods, and wildfires. It aims to do this by updating how providers are notified about the Disaster Information Reporting System, studying a clearer FCC point of contact for officials, and publishing plain-language guidance.

oppose: The bill mainly asks the FCC to study and publish materials. It does not require the FCC to act on its feasibility study, so you may want to ask what concrete results are expected.

The bill does not add new rules or reporting duties for phone and internet companies. If you think providers should face stronger outage reporting or restoration standards, this bill does not address that.

The FCC would have to do this work within its existing budget, since the bill provides no new funding and no cost estimate. You could ask how the agency would pay for the added tasks without pulling from other priorities.
Several requirements apply only "to the extent practicable" or "where practicable," which gives the FCC flexibility and may limit how much the bill changes current practice.
support: The bill targets a real gap: local and tribal officials often need clear, fast information about which communications services are down during disasters, and this bill asks the FCC to improve that flow.
A possible single point of contact for officials, built on the FCC's existing 24-hour operations center, could cut confusion when lives are at stake.

The bill requires plain-language public materials explaining DIRS, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative, and FCC contacts, which would make disaster communications systems easier for officials to understand and use.
The bill adds no new mandates on providers, no new taxes, and no bailouts, and it leaves the FCC's discretion over when to activate DIRS unchanged, so it is a low-cost, narrowly focused step.

crs:
Disaster Communications Coordination and Preparedness Act
This bill directs the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to assess its procedures for disasters and emergencies affecting communications service and consider measures to improve coordination with officials and service providers during such events.
Specifically, the FCC must review and update, as appropriate, its procedures for notifying communications service providers about activations and deactivations of the Disaster Information Reporting System (DIRS). (DIRS is activated during severe weather and other events to enable providers to report outages and other service issues.)
Further, the FCC must provide plain-language resources for state, local, tribal, and territorial officials on federal communications and emergency coordination mechanisms available during disasters and emergencies. To the extent practicable, these materials must include information on DIRS, the Mandatory Disaster Response Initiative (MDRI), and services that may be available to support public safety communications during such events, among other topics. (MDRI requires cell service providers to coordinate and share resources during emergencies.)
Finally, the FCC must consider enhancing its functions related to (1) informing state, local, tribal, and territorial officials of the status of communications services during disasters and emergencies; and (2) facilitating coordination between these officials and communications providers before, during, and after such events.

transparency.reason: It requires public plain-language materials and describes how to access public communications status reports, though it does not mandate new disclosures.

people_over_profit.reason: It focuses on public safety and communications during disasters without adding provider mandates or benefits, modestly favoring people's safety.

local_say.reason: It requires FCC consultation with state, local, and tribal officials and gives them better information and a point of contact.

equality.reason: It explicitly includes tribal and territorial governments and may help smaller or rural jurisdictions that lack technical expertise.

label: S. 4802
title: Hurricane Hunter Aircraft Recapitalization Act
short_title: Hurricane Hunter Aircraft Recapitalization Act
one: Directs NOAA to replace and maintain its fleet of 6 to 9 crewed hurricane-hunter aircraft, keep storm-penetrating flights and radar capability going, and raises the authorized spending to $2.5 billion for fiscal years 2027–2031.
summary: This bill updates a 2022 law so the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) can replace its aging "hurricane hunter" planes, which fly into and around storms to collect data used in forecasts and warnings. NOAA would have to keep between 6 and 9 crewed aircraft (the old law said "up to 6"). It would have to gather weather, ocean, and atmospheric data and share it in near real time. It would also have to keep the ability to fly directly into hurricanes, keep backup aircraft so there is no single point of failure while planes are being replaced, and maintain or replace the onboard radar, including Tail Doppler Radar. NOAA could sign long multiyear contracts for buying and maintaining aircraft, with some limits removed, as long as the contracts include protections against unfunded cancellation costs. NOAA must also keep enough qualified NOAA Corps pilots (uniformed officers) to fly these missions. The bill authorizes up to $2.5 billion (up from $800 million) for aircraft over fiscal years 2027–2031, plus $45 million per year for aviation operations. "Authorized" means Congress allows the spending; a separate appropriations law must actually provide the money. Finally, the bill moves this section into the Weather Research and Forecasting Innovation Act of 2017 and removes an older section 413. Note: the supplied text shows much of the language as "struck out" in bracketed form, so I read the bracketed language as the bill's operative content.
does: Requires NOAA to acquire and maintain aircraft that meet its air reconnaissance and research needs, and to carry out hurricane-hunter airborne missions with them.
Sets the fleet at no fewer than 6 and no more than 9 crewed aircraft (previously up to 6).
Requires real-time collection of weather, ocean, and atmospheric observations, made available in near real time for research and operations such as forecasting and warnings.

Requires NOAA to keep the ability to safely fly directly into hurricanes and tropical cyclones, and to keep continuity of that capability during aircraft replacement, including backup aircraft to avoid a single point of failure.
Requires NOAA to maintain and replace airborne radar and remote sensing equipment, including Tail Doppler Radar or successors.

Allows multiyear contracts for buying and maintaining aircraft, lifting the usual contract-length limit, provided the contracts follow applicable law and protect against unfunded liability if cancelled.

label: S. 5332
title: Cooperative Institute Act of 2026
short_title: Cooperative Institute Act of 2026
one: As introduced, the bill would put into law NOAA's existing program of research partnerships with universities and nonprofits, including how they are chosen, funded, reviewed and ended. The text provided is entirely struck out because the committee replaced it with a substitute we could not see.
summary:
Important limit: all of the text given to me is marked "struck out." The Senate committee reported the bill with an "amendment in the nature of a substitute," which replaces the whole original bill. I could not see the replacement, so this summary describes the bill as first introduced. The final version could differ.

As introduced, the bill would require the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the agency that studies weather, oceans and climate, to keep a "Cooperative Institute" program. These are partnerships between NOAA and non-federal universities or nonprofit research groups. They would do long-term research, train students and young scientists, and add research capacity NOAA does not have in-house.

New institutes would usually be picked through open, merit-based competition with peer review. NOAA could limit the pool of applicants only if it explained why. Each institute could get a five-year grant, and a second five-year grant after an outside peer review. NOAA would have to check every two years whether new institutes are needed. To end or not renew an institute, NOAA would have to send Congress a timeline and a detailed report at least 60 days ahead. NOAA would also keep a handbook on managing the institutes and would keep existing institutes running unless they are ended by that process. The bill does not set a dollar amount.
does: Requires NOAA's Under Secretary to maintain a Cooperative Institute program for research, education, training and outreach tied to NOAA's mission (as introduced).

Defines eligible partners as non-federal academic or nonprofit research institutions with relevant research programs that involve students and postdoctoral scientists and cooperate with other institutes.
Requires open, merit-based, peer-reviewed competition for new institutes; a limited pool is allowed only with a written justification under Commerce and NOAA policy.
Encourages consolidating management among institutes that join together, if benefits outweigh costs, and allows NOAA and partner staff to work at each other's facilities.

Allows five-year financial assistance awards, with a second award of up to five more years after an outside peer review (supported by NOAA's Science Advisory Board) using agreed performance measures, with funding tied to the review rating.
Requires NOAA to assess every two years whether new institutes are needed for emerging research.
Lets NOAA end or not renew an institute only after sending Congress a timeline and a detailed report (reasons, performance, staff plans, how the research will continue) at least 60 days beforehand.
Requires a Cooperative Institute Handbook, updated in consultation with institute directors, and requires existing institutes to be maintained unless terminated through the above process.
The committee's substitute amendment text was not available, so final provisions may differ.

label: S. 5663
title: PROOF Act
short_title: PROOF Act (Promoting Reproducibility and Oversight of Federal Research Act)
one: As introduced, the bill would have the National Science Foundation fund universities to repeat (replicate) federally funded studies and check whether their results hold up, but the text shown is entirely struck out, so the version that may advance is unclear.
summary:
Every section of the text I was given is marked "struck out." That usually means a committee replaced the original language with a new version, but the replacement text is not included here. So I can only describe the original, introduced version, and the bill that actually moves forward could differ.

As introduced, the bill would have told the director of the National Science Foundation (NSF) to give competitive grants to colleges and universities. The money would pay for repeating studies that the federal government had already funded, to test whether the results can be reproduced. Schools would apply by naming the study they want to repeat, explaining how the work would improve the reliability and transparency of science, showing they can do it with existing equipment, disclosing conflicts of interest, and giving a timeline and measures of reproducibility.

Grant money could cover tuition, stipends, materials, equipment, travel, and analysis costs. Support for students would go to U.S. citizens, U.S. nationals, and lawful permanent residents who are in, or entering, a research-based STEM master's program. The NSF could not require or favor discrimination based on race, sex, religion, national origin, or other protected traits. Starting 18 months after the first award, and then every year, NSF would report to Congress on the number of awards, students supported, fields, and how the repeated results compared with the originals. No dollar amount appears in the text I saw.

label: S. 69
title: COLLUDE Act
short_title: COLLUDE Act (Section 230 and government censorship requests)
one: Would strip online platforms of Section 230 legal protection when they suppress political speech because of a private government request (other than for law enforcement or national security), and would make platforms prove they didn't create the content in question when sued.
summary: Section 230 is a federal law that generally keeps websites and apps from being sued over what their users post, and lets them moderate content in good faith. This bill would change that in two ways. First, if a platform limits or removes content that looks like political speech (including a particular viewpoint) because a government agency, or a private group acting at a government's request, sent it a message, the platform would lose Section 230 protection. This applies only when the message was sent just to that platform and not to anyone else. Requests made for a legitimate law enforcement investigation or for national security purposes (such as intelligence work or military missions) would not trigger the loss of protection. Second, in lawsuits that treat a platform or user as the publisher of information, the bill says the platform or user must prove it did not help create or develop that information. The CRS summary describes this more broadly as turning Section 230 into an "affirmative defense" that must be proven before a case is dismissed. The bill text I was given is marked "struck out" throughout, so I could not confirm the final wording in the version now on the Senate calendar. The bill has no spending and no start date in the text I saw.
does: Adds a new rule (Section 230(c)(3)) saying platforms lose Section 230(c) protection if they restrict access to, or reduce the visibility of, material that reasonably appears to be legitimate political speech, including a discernible viewpoint.

That loss of protection applies only when the restriction results from a communication from a government entity, or from a non-government entity acting at a government's request, that was sent only to the platform and not to any other entity.
Creates an exception: communications for a 'legitimate law enforcement purpose' or a 'national security purpose' do not trigger the loss of protection.
Defines 'legitimate law enforcement purpose' as a law enforcement agency acting within its lawful authority to investigate a criminal offense.

Defines 'national security purpose' as relating to intelligence activities, national-security-related cryptologic activities, command and control of the Armed Forces, weapons equipment, or direct fulfillment of a military or intelligence mission.

Adds an 'affirmative defense' provision: in criminal or civil cases that treat a provider or user as the publisher or speaker of information, the provider or user must prove it is not an 'information content provider' (a creator or developer of the content) to claim protection.
Makes conforming wording changes so the existing good-faith moderation protection (paragraph (2)(B)) refers to the revised paragraph.
who: Social media companies and other websites or apps that host user content
Ordinary internet users who post or share content, who are also covered by Section 230
Federal, state, and local government agencies that send content removal requests to platforms
People whose political speech is removed or down-ranked
Law enforcement and national security agencies (their requests are exempt)
Smaller platforms and startups that could face more lawsuit costs

benefits: Could discourage government agencies from quietly pressuring platforms to suppress political viewpoints.
May increase public awareness and accountability about government involvement in content moderation.
Exceptions for real law enforcement and national security needs keep legitimate requests possible.
Could protect the ability of people to express political views online.
concerns: Making platforms prove they did not create the content could increase lawsuit costs, especially for small sites and ordinary users.
Platforms might remove more content, or moderate less, to avoid legal risk, which could include harmful content like harassment or misinformation.
The rule only covers requests sent solely to the platform, so a request copied to others might fall outside it.
Losing all protection under subsection (c) for one type of removal may be a broad penalty and could expose platforms to unrelated lawsuits.
Terms like 'legitimate political speech' and 'reasonably appears' are vague and could lead to court fights.
The bill does not require governments to disclose their requests; it only penalizes platforms.
imp.cost: No spending or funding is in the bill text. Indirect costs could fall on platforms and courts through more litigation. No CBO estimate was provided.
unknowns: The bill text I received was marked 'struck out' throughout, so the version on the Senate calendar may be different.
How courts would interpret 'legitimate political speech' and 'at the behest of' a government.
Whether platforms would be exposed to lawsuits on all content or only the content they restricted.
How the new burden of proof would work in practice and how often early dismissals would be lost.
Whether there is a companion House bill or a date for a Senate vote.
