label: H.R. 8957
title: American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026
short_title: American Reserve Modernization Act (Strategic Bitcoin Reserve)
one: The bill would have the Treasury Department set up a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a Digital Asset Stockpile to hold the federal government's existing Bitcoin and other crypto, lock the Bitcoin away for 20 years, and study ways to buy more without adding to the national debt.
summary:
This bill would create two new storage and management accounts inside the Treasury Department within 180 days of becoming law. The first, the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, would hold Bitcoin the federal government already owns, mostly coins taken in criminal or civil forfeiture cases or collected as penalties, that no other law requires be used another way. The second, the Digital Asset Stockpile, would hold all other crypto the government owns.

Federal agencies would have 60 days to report what crypto they hold. Until the new accounts exist, they would generally have to stop selling it. Exceptions cover national security, court orders, returning assets to crime victims, and other legal requirements. After the accounts are set up, agencies would have 30 days to transfer their holdings to Treasury.

Bitcoin in the Reserve could not be sold, swapped, or pledged as collateral for 20 years. Treasury would send Congress a study within one year on when early sales might make sense, such as for national security or financial stability. Two years before the 20 years end, Treasury would make recommendations on whether to keep holding. After that, it could recommend selling up to 10 percent per two-year period. The Stockpile's other assets could be sold under a public rule. Any sale proceeds would first cover the costs of managing the accounts. Anything left over would go to reducing the national debt.

The bill sets rules for assets created by "forks" and "airdrops." These are new coins that appear from changes to a blockchain or from free distributions. Such coins would be held for one year. Treasury would then keep the most valuable one and could sell the rest, with an exception for coins that have special strategic value.

The bill also requires several transparency and safety measures. These include security standards developed with Defense and Homeland Security, annual public "proof of reserve" reports checked by an independent auditor, Government Accountability Office oversight, and annual reports to Congress.

States could voluntarily store their own Bitcoin in the Reserve in separate accounts. They would pay fees, keep ownership, be able to withdraw, and accept all custody risks.

Treasury and Commerce would study whether the government could buy more Bitcoin without new spending, borrowing, taxes, or deficit increases. The bill does not authorize any such purchase. Finally, it says nothing in it allows seizing private crypto or limits people's rights to own or self-custody it.
does: Requires Treasury to create a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a Digital Asset Stockpile within 180 days of enactment.

Defines 'qualifying Bitcoin' and 'qualifying digital assets' as government-owned crypto, including forfeited assets and civil penalties, that is not legally required for other uses such as forfeiture-fund rules.

Requires every federal agency to report all its crypto holdings to Treasury within 60 days and annually after that, and to transfer qualifying holdings to Treasury (within 30 days once the Reserve and Stockpile exist).
Freezes sales, swaps, and encumbrances of agency-held crypto before the accounts are set up, except for national security, legal requirements, court orders, or returning assets to crime victims.

Bars selling, swapping, auctioning, or pledging Reserve Bitcoin for 20 years, with a study within one year on conditions or exceptions for early sale, and recommendations to Congress two years before the period ends.
After 20 years, allows Treasury to recommend selling up to 10 percent of the Reserve in any 2-year period, after weighing deficit, market, and diversification effects.

Lets Treasury sell, exchange, or convert Stockpile assets under a public rule that prioritizes transparency and limits market disruption. Proceeds first cover management costs and the remainder goes to reducing the national debt.
Lets Treasury use special purpose entities to manage digital assets, and gives it broad rulemaking power over custody, accounting, and reporting.
Requires fork and airdrop assets to be kept one year, then keeps the one with the highest market value and allows sale of the others, with an exception for assets with novel strategic value.
Requires physical and cybersecurity protections, developed with Defense, Homeland Security, and industry experts.
Creates a Proof of Reserve system with annual public reports on holdings, transactions, and private-key control, verified by an independent auditor and overseen by the Comptroller General (GAO).
Requires annual reports to the House Financial Services and Senate Banking Committees starting 360 days after setup.
Sets up a voluntary program within one year for states to store their Bitcoin in segregated Reserve accounts. States keep title, pay fees, can withdraw, and bear all custody risk.

Orders a joint Treasury-Commerce study within 180 days on whether more Bitcoin could be acquired in a budget-neutral way. The bill does not authorize borrowing, taxes, deficit spending, or collateral pledges for purchases.
States that the Act does not authorize seizing private crypto or restrict people's rights to buy, hold, or self-custody it, and includes a sense of Congress supporting private self-custody.
who: Treasury Department, which would build and run the Reserve and Stockpile
Federal agencies that hold seized or forfeited crypto, such as law enforcement agencies
Taxpayers, who bear any management costs and market risk and could see any gains applied to the debt
State governments that hold Bitcoin and may choose to participate
Crime victims and forfeiture programs that depend on the proceeds of seized assets
Crypto holders and markets
Congress and the Government Accountability Office, which would receive reports and carry out oversight

benefits: Creates public annual audits of holdings, transactions, and key control by an independent auditor, plus GAO oversight.
Requires public rules, with disclosure of sale methodology, before any sales.
Bars borrowing, new taxes, or deficit spending to acquire Bitcoin, and any excess proceeds reduce the national debt.
Centralizes tracking of crypto agencies hold, which could reduce loss or mismanagement.
State participation is voluntary, with states keeping ownership and the right to withdraw.
Protects crime victims and court-ordered returns during the interim freeze.
Affirms private property rights and self-custody.
concerns: Locking up an asset with volatile prices for 20 years could expose taxpayers to losses.
Treasury would have wide discretion, including special purpose entities and sales rules not yet written.
The 20-year hold and the later cap of 10 percent per two years could limit flexibility in a crisis, though a study of exceptions is required.
Treasury could sell Stockpile assets (non-Bitcoin) and keep fork assets by its own rules, which gives it market influence.
Holding government-held Bitcoin could lend legitimacy to or encourage a market whose mining uses large amounts of energy. The bill does not address this.
States bear all risk and pay fees for custody.
The acquisition study could pave the way for later purchases that use public money.
imp.cost: No appropriation is stated. Management costs are paid from asset-sale proceeds. Any leftover proceeds go to reduce the national debt. The bill bars borrowing, new taxes, or deficit spending to buy Bitcoin. States would pay fees for custody services. Cost of the studies, audits, and security are not estimated and no CBO score was provided.
unknowns: How much Bitcoin and other crypto the government actually holds and could be put into the Reserve.
Whether the management and security costs would be covered by the Stockpile's sale proceeds.
How the exemption for forfeiture-fund laws would play out in practice, and how it would affect law enforcement budgets and victims' payments.
What the early-sale study and acquisition study would find.
What Treasury's final rules on sales and fork assets would look like.
Environmental and energy effects, which the bill does not address.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the House calendar
stage.last_action: Reported (Amended) by the Committee on Financial Services. H. Rept. 119-894.

purpose: The bill says it would create a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve and a Digital Asset Stockpile inside the Treasury Department to hold cryptocurrency the federal government already owns, mostly coins from forfeiture cases or penalties. It sets rules for how that crypto is held, reported, audited, and in some cases sold, and it aims to bring tracking and oversight to government crypto holdings.

oppose: Holding Bitcoin for 20 years with no sales could expose taxpayers to large losses, since crypto prices are very volatile.
Treasury would have wide discretion over special purpose entities, custody, and sale rules that have not been written yet, which could limit public input on key decisions.

The 20-year hold and the later cap of 10 percent per two years could limit flexibility in a financial crisis, and the bill does not address the energy use of the Bitcoin mining that a government-held reserve could help legitimize.
support: The bill requires annual public proof-of-reserve reports checked by an independent auditor, with GAO oversight, which gives Congress and the public clear information about government crypto.
The bill bars government purchases of Bitcoin using new borrowing, taxes, or deficit spending, and sends any sale proceeds from other digital assets toward reducing the national debt.

The bill says it does not allow seizing private crypto or limiting people's rights to hold or self-custody it, and it makes state participation voluntary with states keeping ownership and the right to withdraw.

environment.reason: The bill does not change water, air, or land protections; it does not address mining energy use, which the bill itself notes it leaves unaddressed.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on Proof of Reserve requires annual public reports on holdings, transactions, and key control verified by an independent auditor, and public rules before stockpile sales; annual reports go to Congress. Some Treasury discretion over special purpose entities and unwritten rules limits this somewhat.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly governs government-held crypto; it neither clearly favors people over corporate profit nor shifts costs onto the public beyond the market-risk exposure of holding assets, which is offset by the debt-reduction and no-purchase provisions.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill has no provision directing taxpayer money to corporations or ratepayer cost shifts; the 20-year hold creates market-risk exposure for taxpayers but is not a bailout.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same rules to agencies and states and does not create unequal treatment of groups; it is unclear or neutral on equal access.

justice.reason: Sec. on interim freeze protects court-ordered returns and crime-victim restitution, and GAO oversight plus independent audits add accountability; Treasury's broad rulemaking and special purpose entity authority reduces some predictability.

label: S. 2378
title: SAFEGUARDS Act of 2026
short_title: SAFEGUARDS Act (Aviation Security Fee Funding)
one: The bill would direct more of the existing 9/11 passenger security fee to airport baggage-screening equipment and a new fund for checkpoint technology, instead of letting that money go to the general Treasury.
summary:
When you buy an airline ticket, you pay a passenger security fee, often called the 9/11 fee. Today, part of that money goes to the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) for aviation security. The rest generally goes into the Treasury's general fund and is used to reduce debt. This bill would send more of the fee money to aviation security equipment.

First, it would raise the amount set aside each year for the Aviation Security Capital Fund from $250 million to $500 million, starting in fiscal year 2026. That fund pays for things like in-line baggage screening systems, which are conveyor-based machines that scan checked bags for explosives, and some other airport security upgrades. Second, it would create a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund. The next $250 million collected each year, after the first $500 million, would go into it. It would pay for buying, installing and maintaining checkpoint and exit-lane technology. TSA could also approve payment for projects already started on or after January 1, 2023.

An earlier version also included a "sense of Congress" statement. It said the fee should be used only for aviation security and that diverting it to other purposes should end by 2027. In the text provided, all sections appear struck out, which usually means the bill was amended or replaced in committee. I could not see any replacement text, so the final wording may differ. The bill does not clearly say it creates a new tax. It redirects fee revenue that already exists, and that could leave less money for the general fund.
does: Raises the yearly amount of 9/11 passenger security fee money available for the Aviation Security Capital Fund from $250 million to $500 million, starting in fiscal year 2026.

Directs TSA to set the fee so that it collects at least $500 million per year for that Capital Fund, which pays for in-line checked-baggage explosives screening systems and certain other airport security improvements, through grants.

Creates a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund. After the first $500 million goes to the Capital Fund, the next $250 million of fee revenue each year would go into it, and the money would stay available until spent.
Directs TSA to set the fee so that it collects at least $250 million per year for the new fund.
Lets TSA use the new fund to buy, deploy and maintain checkpoint and exit-lane security technology, including through grants.
Lets TSA retroactively approve grant funds for checkpoint and exit-lane projects carried out on or after January 1, 2023.
The struck-out text also included a nonbinding 'sense of Congress' that 9/11 fee revenue should be used only for aviation security and that diversion of the fee to other purposes should end by 2027.
In the text provided, every section is marked as struck out, so I could not see any replacement language or confirm the final form of the bill.
who: Air travelers who pay the 9/11 passenger security fee
Airports and airlines that receive or use security screening equipment
The Transportation Security Administration and its screening workforce
Federal taxpayers, because the money would no longer go to the general fund and debt reduction
Security equipment manufacturers and contractors

benefits: Could speed up upgrades to explosives-detection and checkpoint technology, which may improve traveler safety.
Would tie a passenger-paid fee more closely to the security purpose it was created for.
Could cut wait times and help airports that need costly screening equipment.
The retroactive provision could reimburse airports and others who already paid for checkpoint technology since 2023.
concerns: Redirecting fee revenue away from the general fund could reduce money for deficit reduction or other programs.
Retroactive reimbursement could favor projects already completed and gives TSA wide discretion.
The bill sets no explicit reporting or oversight rules for how grants are chosen, and no privacy rules for new screening technology.
Equipment contractors and well-connected airports could benefit disproportionately without competitive-bidding requirements being stated.
imp.cost: Redirects existing 9/11 passenger security fee revenue: about $250 million more per year to the Capital Fund (from $250 million to $500 million) plus a new $250 million per year for the Checkpoint Technology Fund, so roughly $500 million more per year in total. This would reduce the amount deposited in the general fund. No new fee rate is stated in the text I saw. No official cost estimate was provided.
unknowns: What replacement or amended text, if any, the committee adopted, since all sections appear struck out.
Whether the redirection would be offset elsewhere in the budget.
Whether the fee rate itself would change.
What oversight, reporting or privacy protections would apply to the new funds.
How the 'sense of Congress' about ending fee diversion by 2027 fits in the final bill.

stage.stage_label: Out of committee — on the Senate calendar
stage.last_action: Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation. Reported by Senator Cruz with an amendment in the nature of a substitute. With written report No. 119-157.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to increase funding for TSA aviation security, mainly for checked-baggage explosives detection equipment and checkpoint and exit-lane technology. It would do this by directing more of the passenger security fee to two funds: the Aviation Security Capital Fund (raised from $250 million to $500 million per year) and a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund ($250 million per year). The bill's title describes its purpose as spending aviation fees on equipment and upgraded risk detection and safety.

oppose: The bill would move $250 million more per year of passenger security fee money away from the Treasury general fund, which is used for debt reduction, so it could leave less money for other federal priorities.
The bill gives TSA wide discretion over which grants are chosen and sets no clear reporting or oversight rules, so taxpayers may have limited ability to check how the money is spent.
The bill sets no privacy rules for new screening technology, which may matter to travelers as checkpoint equipment is upgraded.

The retroactive provision could reimburse projects already completed since January 1, 2023, and the bill does not state competitive-bidding requirements, so equipment contractors or well-connected airports could benefit more than others.
support: The bill would tie a fee that passengers already pay to the aviation security purpose it was created for, instead of sending much of it to the general fund.
Dedicating $500 million a year to in-line checked-baggage explosives screening and $250 million a year to checkpoint technology could speed up upgrades that may improve traveler safety.
Better screening equipment could help reduce long checkpoint waits and help airports that need costly screening systems.
The retroactive provision would let TSA reimburse airports and others who already paid for checkpoint technology projects started on or after January 1, 2023.

cost_flag: Redirects existing 9/11 passenger security fee revenue: about $250 million more per year to the Capital Fund (from $250 million to $500 million) plus a new $250 million per year for the Checkpoint Technology Fund, so roughly $500 million more per year in total. This would reduce the amount deposited in the general fund. No new fee rate is stated in the text I saw. No official cost estimate was provided.
crs:
Spending Aviation Fees for Equipment, Guaranteeing Upgraded and Advanced Risk Detection and Safety Act of 2025 or the SAFEGUARDS Act of 2025
This bill allocates additional funding for the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) for aviation security, including checked baggage explosives detection equipment and security checkpoint technology.
As background, TSA collects passenger civil aviation security service fees (often referred to as the 9/11 security fee or passenger security fee) on air carrier passengers originating at airports in the United States. In general, these fees are deposited into the Department of the Treasury general fund and applied towards debt reduction. A portion of these fees are allocated to TSA for aviation security.
The bill requires that the first $500 million collected in each fiscal year from passenger security fees be deposited into the Aviation Security Capital Fund. This is an increase from the currently required $250 million. This fund provides for the costs associated with acquiring and installing in-line baggage screening systems (i.e., systems that use a conveyor belt infrastructure to automatically screen, sort, and track baggage) to accommodate checked baggage explosives detection equipment and for certain other airport security improvements.
The bill also requires that the next $250 million collected in each fiscal year from passenger security fees be deposited into a new Aviation Security Checkpoint Technology Fund for the costs associated with acquiring, deploying, and sustaining aviation security checkpoint and exit lane technology. TSA may use these funds retroactively for projects implemented on or after January 1, 2023.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill's text is struck out and it sets no explicit reporting or public-disclosure rules for grant selection, but it does not clearly add secrecy or harm either.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. 1 redirects about $250 million more per year of passenger fee revenue away from the general fund to airport and equipment grants, and the bill sets no competitive-bidding rules, so the benefit leans toward equipment buyers and contractors rather than the public purse.

local_say.reason: The bill does not clearly change how states or communities get a say over decisions about their own areas.

no_bailouts.reason: Sec. 1 retroactively allows TSA to fund checkpoint projects started on or after January 1, 2023, which could reimburse airports and others for costs they already bore, shifting costs onto the fee pool and taxpayers.

equality.reason: The bill treats travelers, airports and vendors under the same rules and does not create group-based unequal treatment.

justice.reason: The bill gives TSA wide discretion over grant selection and retroactive approvals and sets no explicit oversight or reporting rules, which makes accountability weaker.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill does not change what individuals may legally do, say or choose; it only affects fee allocation and equipment funding.

label: S. 4256
title: Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act
short_title: Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act
one: Lets pilots show FAA inspectors a digital copy of their pilot or medical certificate instead of only a paper one, and orders the FAA to update its rules by November 30, 2028.
summary: Right now, pilots must carry a physical copy of their airman certificate (their pilot license) and medical certificate, and show it when the FAA or certain other officials ask. This bill would let a pilot show an FAA inspector either a physical certificate or a digital certificate issued by the FAA. The digital version could be stored on an electronic device or, where internet connection is good enough, in a cloud-based system. It would have to be shown following authentication and verification rules (ways to prove it is real) that the FAA sets. The bill changes federal law (Title 49, section 44703) and directs the FAA Administrator to issue a final rule by November 30, 2028. That rule would update FAA regulations in parts 61, 63, 65, 67, and 107 of Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations, plus related guidance and policies. Those parts cover pilots, mechanics and other crew, medical standards, and small drone operators. The bill does not spell out costs. The text provided shows some sections marked as struck out, which likely reflects a legislative formatting of a reported or passed version; the substance described here follows the text and CRS summary. Note that the CRS summary mentions only FAA inspectors in the new provision, not police, TSA, or NTSB requests. The bill is a small, practical change that mainly affects convenience for pilots and FAA staff.
does: Adds a new subsection (m) to 49 U.S.C. 44703 saying a person issued an airman certificate (including a medical certificate) may present it to an FAA inspector in either physical or digital form.
Physical option: a physical certificate issued by the FAA Administrator or a designee.
Digital option: a digital certificate issued by the FAA, stored on an electronic device or, where connectivity is sufficient, in a cloud-based system.
Digital certificates must be presented following authentication and verification requirements set by the FAA Administrator.
Requires the FAA to issue a final rule by November 30, 2028, updating 14 CFR parts 61, 63, 65, 67, and 107, along with related guidance and policies.
The bill's text covers presentation to FAA inspectors only; it does not itself change rules for police, TSA, or NTSB requests.
who: Pilots and other certificated airmen, including medical certificate holders and drone operators covered by part 107
FAA inspectors and the FAA, which must build verification systems and update rules
Pilots in areas with poor internet connectivity (device storage allowed)

benefits: Pilots could avoid problems if a paper certificate is lost, damaged, or left behind.
Keeps the paper option, so no one is forced to go digital.
Allows device storage where connectivity is poor.
Could reduce paperwork for the FAA.
concerns: Digital certificates could raise data security and privacy questions.
Pilots with dead batteries or broken devices could face trouble if they have no paper copy.
Applies only to FAA inspectors in the bill text, so pilots may still need paper for police, TSA, or NTSB requests.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is given in the material provided. The FAA would bear costs of building digital certificates, verification systems, and rulemaking.
unknowns: Exact authentication and verification requirements the FAA will set.
Cost to the FAA and any fees to pilots.
Whether other officials (law enforcement, TSA, NTSB) will accept digital copies.
How data would be stored and protected.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to let pilots show a digital copy of certain FAA certificates, such as an airman certificate or medical certificate, to an FAA inspector, in addition to a physical copy. The CRS summary describes the problem as current rules requiring a physical certificate to be presented on request. The bill would also require the FAA to update its regulations by November 30, 2028.

A pilot whose device has a dead battery, is broken, or has no signal could have trouble showing a valid certificate if no paper copy is carried.
The bill applies only to FAA inspectors. Pilots would still need paper or other documents for police, TSA, and NTSB requests, so the change may not reduce carrying paper overall.
support: Pilots could avoid trouble if a paper certificate is lost, damaged, or left at home, since a digital copy would be an option.
The bill keeps the paper option, so pilots who prefer physical certificates can still carry them.
Storing certificates on a device, including where connectivity is poor, could be more convenient, and the change may reduce paperwork for the FAA.

crs:
Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act
This bill allows a pilot to present a digital copy of certain certificates (e.g., an airman certificate or a medical certificate) when required to present such documentation by a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) inspector.
Under current FAA regulations, a pilot must present for inspection a physical copy of an airman certificate and other paperwork upon a request from the FAA; a federal, state, or local law enforcement officer; or an authorized representative of the Transportation Security Administration or the National Transportation Safety Board. This bill allows a pilot to present a certificate such as an airman certificate or a medical certificate to an FAA inspector as (1) a physical certificate, or (2) a digital copy stored on an electronic device or cloud storage platform.
The FAA must update current regulations to implement this change.

personal_freedom.reason: Gives pilots a choice between paper and digital certificates, easing a small burden.

news.overall: Coverage from both groups focuses on the FAA ground stop and aviation infrastructure rather than the Airmen Certificate Accessibility Act, which none of the headlines name. The evidence is limited to headlines only, so no article-level claims about the bill can be made.

label: S. 5251
title: ACPAC Modernization Act
short_title: ACPAC Modernization Act
one: Makes ticket agents (such as travel booking companies) full, voting-type members of the federal Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee instead of non-member participants.
summary: The Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee (ACPAC) is a panel created in 2012 that advises the U.S. Department of Transportation on airline passenger protections. Under current law, the committee's membership list includes representatives of airlines, airports, state and local governments, and consumer groups. Ticket agents, the travel booking companies that sell airline tickets, are listed in a different part of the law, in what appears to be a section about who is excluded from or treated differently under the committee's rules. This bill would add "ticket agents" to the official list of groups that must be represented on the committee. It would also delete the reference to ticket agents in subsection (i). I could not see the full text of subsection (i), so I can't say exactly what that reference currently does. The bill is short and makes only these two edits. It does not add money, create new rules for airlines or ticket sellers, or change consumer protections directly. Its effect would be to give the travel-booking industry a formal seat in an advisory group. The group can only make recommendations. Possible effects include a more complete view of how tickets are sold and refunded. There is also a chance that industry voices gain more weight relative to consumers.
does: Adds 'ticket agents' as a fifth category in the list of groups that make up the Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee (Section 411(b) of the FAA Modernization and Reform Act of 2012).
Fixes the punctuation of the existing list so the new item fits (changes the 'and' and period in paragraphs 3 and 4).
Strikes the words 'ticket agents,' from subsection (i) of the same section. The full text of that subsection was not provided, so its exact effect is unclear.
Creates no new funding, penalties, or regulations; it only changes who is formally named on the advisory committee.
who: Ticket agents and online travel companies, who would get formal representation on the committee
Airline passengers, whose protections the committee advises on
Airlines and airports, who share the committee with ticket agents
The Department of Transportation, which runs the committee
Consumer advocacy groups on the committee

benefits: Could give the committee a fuller picture of how tickets are sold, changed, and refunded.
Ticket agents, which handle many consumer transactions, could help find problems that passengers face.
Clarifies the committee's membership categories.
concerns: Could increase industry representation on a consumer protection panel without adding consumer seats.
Removing the ticket agent reference from subsection (i) may have effects that can't be judged without seeing that text.
imp.cost: No funding is provided or authorized. No cost estimate was given; costs appear negligible.
unknowns: What subsection (i) currently says about ticket agents and how deleting the reference changes it.
Whether the committee's total size is limited, and whether adding ticket agents displaces other members.
Why the sponsor proposed this and who supports or opposes it.
Whether the committee is currently active.

purpose: The bill says it would add ticket agents to the official list of groups that must be represented on the Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee, which advises the Department of Transportation on airline passenger protections. It also removes a reference to ticket agents in subsection (i) of the same section. The committee only makes recommendations, but advisory input can still shape the Department of Transportation's policy direction, so a member's viewpoint matters even without new rules or penalties.
support: Ticket agents handle many airline ticket sales, changes, and refunds, so having them on the committee could give it a more complete picture of problems passengers face when buying tickets.
The bill is short and makes only two edits. It adds no new funding, penalties, or regulations, and it simply clarifies who is named in the committee's membership list.

label: H.R. 1390
title: Ocean Pollution Reduction Act II
short_title: Ocean Pollution Reduction Act II
one: Lets EPA issue San Diego's Point Loma sewage plant a conditional permit with firm pollution caps and a water-recycling target, instead of requiring full secondary treatment or repeated waivers.
summary: San Diego's Point Loma Wastewater Treatment Plant dumps treated sewage into the Pacific through a deep pipe. It now operates under a temporary waiver from the Clean Water Act's "secondary treatment" standard, and the city has asked for a new waiver. If that is denied, the city would have to build a full secondary treatment system. This bill creates a third path. It lets the EPA issue a permit that applies despite other parts of the Clean Water Act. The permit would require the plant to keep its deep ocean pipe (at least 300 feet deep and 4 miles from shore). It would also cap solids discharged each year, in three steps: 12,000 metric tons now, 11,500 from the end of 2029, and 9,942 from the end of 2031. The permit would cap solids at 60 mg per liter on a 30-day average. It would require at least 80% solids removal monthly and 58% removal of biochemical oxygen demand (a measure of oxygen-depleting waste) annually. The plant would still have to meet other secondary treatment limits, pretreatment rules, state concurrence, and ocean discharge review. San Diego must supply 10 years of ocean monitoring data and keep a monitoring program. Where state and federal regulators allow, it must show that it will produce 83 million gallons a day of water suitable for drinking-water reuse by the end of 2039. EPA sets milestones. The city can still choose to apply for full secondary treatment. The bill does not say how much it would cost.
does: Allows the EPA Administrator to issue a Clean Water Act section 402 discharge permit for the Point Loma Plant that applies notwithstanding other provisions of the Act, if the listed conditions are met.
Requires the plant to keep its deep ocean outfall at least 300 feet deep and at least 4 miles from shore.
Caps total suspended solids discharge at 12,000 metric tons per year at enactment, 11,500 from December 31, 2029, and 9,942 from December 31, 2031, plus a 60 mg/L 30-day average limit.
Requires at least 80% monthly removal of suspended solids and 58% annual removal of biochemical oxygen demand, counting treatment upstream and at the plant.
Requires meeting all other secondary treatment effluent limits, pretreatment program requirements, California concurrence (section 401), and ocean discharge criteria review (section 403).
Requires the applicant to provide 10 consecutive years of ocean monitoring data before each application and to maintain a monitoring program that meets or exceeds federal standards.

Where federal and state regulators permit potable reuse, requires the city to show it will produce at least 83 million gallons per day (annual average) of water suitable for potable reuse by December 31, 2039.
Directs EPA to set development milestones and include them as permit conditions in each permit issued before December 31, 2039.
Preserves the city's option to apply instead for a permit that meets full secondary treatment.
who: City of San Diego and its wastewater ratepayers
Residents and coastal users near Point Loma and the San Diego coastline
Marine life and ocean ecosystems off San Diego
EPA and California regulators (the state water boards and Coastal Commission)
Communities that may receive recycled drinking water
Fishers and recreational ocean users

benefits: Sets enforceable, declining annual caps on solids discharged to the ocean.
Requires 10 years of monitoring data and an ongoing ocean monitoring program.
Pushes large-scale water recycling (83 million gallons per day), which could increase local drinking water supply and reduce ocean discharge.
Keeps California's concurrence and ocean discharge review, preserving state oversight.
May avoid a very costly full secondary treatment build-out for ratepayers, and avoid repeated waiver cycles.
concerns: Allows a permit that departs from standard secondary treatment through a congressional exception ('notwithstanding' the Clean Water Act).
Removal targets (80% solids, 58% oxygen-demand waste) are lower than usual secondary treatment standards, so more pollution may reach the ocean than under full compliance.
Potable reuse requirement applies only 'to the extent' regulators allow it, so it may not be met.
A special law for one plant could set a precedent for other cities seeking relief from Clean Water Act standards.
Discharge could continue for years before the 2031 and 2039 targets take effect.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding is stated in the bill. Costs for new recycling facilities would likely fall on the City of San Diego and its ratepayers, with possible state or federal funding that the bill does not address.
unknowns: How much recycling infrastructure would cost and who would pay.
Whether the permit would protect marine ecosystems as well as full secondary treatment.
Whether California regulators would concur and whether potable reuse will be approved in time.
Which 'other' secondary treatment limits would apply and how EPA would set milestones.
Whether this approach will be copied by other cities.

stage.last_action: Introduced in House

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give San Diego's Point Loma Wastewater Treatment Plant an alternative path to comply with the Clean Water Act's discharge permit program, so the city does not have to keep applying for temporary waivers or build a full secondary treatment system. It sets conditions the plant must meet, including declining solids caps, monitoring requirements, and a goal of producing 83 million gallons per day of water suitable for potable reuse by the end of 2039.

title: PIGS Act of 2025
short_title: PIGS Act of 2025 (Pigs In Gestation Stalls Act)
one: The bill would make it illegal under federal law to keep breeding pigs in gestation crates or other spaces where they can't move freely, with limited exceptions, and would set up grant money for pig farmers to comply.
summary: This bill would change the Animal Welfare Act to ban the use of gestation crates (small cages where mother pigs are kept during pregnancy). It would be illegal to confine a breeding pig in a way that stops her from lying down, standing up, or turning around in a full circle without touching the sides of the enclosure or another animal. Starting December 31, 2025, each pig would also need at least 24 square feet of usable floor space. Space is figured by dividing an enclosure's total floor space by the number of animals in it. There are exceptions for transport, veterinary care done by or under a licensed vet, slaughter under the Humane Methods of Slaughter Act, and the five days before a sow is due to give birth. Violators would face the penalties used in the Animal Health Protection Act, enforced by the Agriculture Department. States and cities could still pass identical or stricter rules. The bill also directs USDA to create a financial help program for pig farmers, with priority for independent farmers who own their own pigs. It would be paid for by requiring the National Pork Board to set aside at least $10 million of its industry-collected fees in each of two fiscal years. The ban would apply one year after the bill becomes law. (The bill text lists a December 31, 2025 date for the space rule, which may conflict with that one-year delay.)

title: Train EATS Act
short_title: Train EATS Act
one: Requires Amtrak to offer sit-down dining (when practicable) and a cheaper alternative food service on overnight routes, with open seats offered to coach passengers and healthy and dietary-restriction meal options.
summary:
This bill would add a new rule for Amtrak's overnight routes, meaning trains that leave and arrive on different dates. On those routes, Amtrak would have to offer traditional dining "to the extent practicable." Traditional dining means sitting at a table in a dining car and being served by wait staff. Amtrak would also have to offer all passengers a second food and beverage option that costs less than the sit-down meal.

If a train has a dining car, any seats not used by first-class or business-class passengers would have to be offered to coach passengers for a fee, first come, first served. Sit-down dining would also have to include at least one healthy meal that fits the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans. Passengers could pre-order meals that meet their dietary restrictions. The bill does not say what counts as a dietary restriction.

The Secretary of Transportation would write any rules needed to carry this out. The bill gives no start date and no dollar amount. It does not say how Amtrak would pay for the requirements or how they would be enforced. It was introduced in January 2025 and sent to a House subcommittee. It has not moved beyond that.

title: Department of Homeland Security Climate Change Research Act
short_title: DHS Climate Change Research Act
one: Directs the Department of Homeland Security's science chief to review existing research on how climate change threatens homeland security and, if funded, to research ways to reduce those threats, with yearly reports to Congress.
summary: This bill adds a new section to the Homeland Security Act of 2002. It requires the Under Secretary for Science and Technology at the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to review existing federal research on ways to reduce the harm climate change could do to homeland security. The review must look at how climate change affects emergency planning and disaster preparedness, response and recovery. It must also look at whether the way the federal government pays for major disaster and emergency declarations fits those effects. After that review, the Under Secretary may do new research and development on ways to reduce these effects, but only if Congress provides the money. Any such work must put first the problems that hurt DHS's ability to carry out its own operations. While doing this work, the Under Secretary must consult with other federal agencies, state, local, Tribal and territorial governments, and owners and operators of critical infrastructure (like power, water and transport systems). The Under Secretary may also coordinate with them. The bill defines climate change as detectable changes in the climate system that are directly or indirectly caused by human activity and that change the makeup of the global atmosphere. One year after enactment, and then every year for three more years, DHS must send Congress a report on any research it carries out.

label: H.R. 4892
title: Seedlings for Sustainable Habitat Restoration Act of 2025
short_title: Seedlings for Sustainable Habitat Restoration Act
one: The bill lets the Forest Service sign contracts, grants, and agreements with states, tribes, nonprofits, colleges, and others to collect native seeds and grow seedlings for restoring damaged forests and habitats.
summary:
This bill changes two existing laws to make it clearer that the U.S. Forest Service can pay partners to collect native seeds and grow seedlings. These seedlings would be used to replant damaged land, such as areas hurt by wildfire or other disturbances.

The first change adds to a section of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act on ecosystem restoration. It says the Forest Service may enter into contracts, grants, or agreements with state forestry agencies, local private or nonprofit groups, colleges and universities, Indian Tribes, and groups of several states. The work covered is collecting and maintaining native seeds, including from managed seed orchards, and producing seedlings for revegetation (replanting).

The second change updates the Collaborative Forest Landscape Restoration Program, an existing program from a 2009 law. It adds seed collection and seedling production to the work that can be done through contracts and agreements under that program. It also adds colleges and universities to the list of groups the Forest Service can work with.

The bill does not set a dollar amount or create new money. It only widens what the Forest Service is allowed to do and who it can work with. The text does not say how much would be spent, so that would depend on separate funding decisions.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill neither adds nor removes public disclosure, comment, or humane-treatment requirements; it only widens partner eligibility and allowed activities.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill expands contracting with private and nonprofit seed and nursery businesses but sets no cost shifts or profit terms, so its effect on corporate versus public interest is unclear.

local_say.reason: The amendments add state forestry agencies, local nonprofits, Tribes, and multistate coalitions as partners, which gives state, local, and Tribal entities a formal role in restoration agreements.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill sets no dollar amount, creates no new money, and includes no bailout or ratepayer provisions.

equality.reason: Eligible partners are broadened to include several groups, but the bill does not treat people differently under law and does not restrict anyone's access.

justice.reason: The bill does not change due process, remedies, or accountability mechanisms for any party.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill regulates agency authority to contract for seeds and seedlings and does not change what individuals may do or choose.

news.overall: Only one Lean Left group was provided, with eight headlines and no article descriptions, so the evidence is limited to headlines. The coverage largely treats the bill through the lens of energy permitting, intra-environmental-movement disagreement, and criticism of Trump-related projects, while the bill's named subject of seedlings and habitat restoration is absent from the headlines. Without descriptions or other perspective groups, a comparison across outlets is not possible.

label: H.R. 5017
title: Greyhound Protection Act of 2025
short_title: Greyhound Protection Act of 2025
one: Would add a federal ban on commercial greyhound racing (with betting), live-bait training, and open field coursing, with penalties of up to 7 years in prison, starting October 1, 2027.
summary: This bill would change the Animal Welfare Act to make greyhound racing for betting illegal across the country. It would also ban "live lure" training, where live animals such as rabbits are used as bait for dogs to chase, and "open field coursing," where dogs chase and kill live bait animals. It would ban betting on greyhound races, including online and TV-broadcast (simulcast) betting across state or national lines. It would also make it illegal to buy, sell, own, train, or move greyhounds for these purposes. The Secretary of Agriculture would investigate violations and could get help from the FBI, the Treasury Department, and state and local agencies. People who break the law could face fines, up to 7 years in prison, or both, for each violation. The bill adds "hare" to the law's definition of "animal." The rules would apply only to conduct on or after October 1, 2027. The bill says it does not override state laws on gambling or animal welfare. It also does not change how horse racing is treated under federal law. The bill's findings say only two tracks, both in West Virginia, remain, and that they get subsidies of nearly $20 million a year. They also cite state records of thousands of injuries and hundreds of deaths of dogs there.

Bans betting on greyhound races, including online and simulcast (TV-broadcast) betting that crosses state or national lines.

Adds "hare" to the Animal Welfare Act's definition of "animal."

purpose: The bill says its goal is to end greyhound racing for betting nationwide, citing the bill's findings that only two tracks in West Virginia remain, that they receive subsidies of nearly $20 million a year, and that state records show thousands of dog injuries and hundreds of deaths there. It also aims to ban live-lure training and open field coursing, which use live animals as bait, and to stop interstate and online betting on greyhound races.

The bill says it does not override state laws on gambling or animal welfare, so you could ask how federal and state rules would work together in practice.

The bill says the two remaining tracks receive subsidies of nearly $20 million a year, and supporters may argue that public money should not support an activity with these welfare concerns.
The bill would stop betting on greyhound races, including online and simulcast betting across state or national lines, which supporters say would reduce the activity overall.

cost_flag: The material does not state the cost of enforcement or any specific appropriation for the Department of Agriculture or other agencies. The bill's findings say the two remaining West Virginia tracks receive subsidies of nearly $20 million a year. The material does not say whether these subsidies would end under the bill.

transparency_kindness.reason: Bans live-lure training and open field coursing, which end the practice of using live rabbits and hares as bait and so reduce needless animal harm; the findings also cite injury and death records.

people_over_profit.reason: Ending nationwide betting on greyhound racing and the subsidized West Virginia tracks shifts activity away from betting operators and tracks toward animal welfare, though it also costs workers and operators income.

local_say.reason: Sec. on criminal and USDA enforcement sets a single federal rule that overrides local and state choices on greyhound racing, although the bill states it does not override state gambling or animal welfare laws.

personal_freedom.reason: Makes it a federal crime to buy, sell, own, train, or move greyhounds for racing or coursing and bans betting on those races, restricting what individuals may do, with up to 7 years in prison per violation.

label: H.R. 5020
title: Supporting Our Shelters Act
short_title: Supporting Our Shelters Act
one: Would create a federal grant program, run by the Agriculture Secretary, to help animal shelters pay for animal care and staff, with yearly reporting on how the money is spent.
summary: This bill would change a part of the Animal Welfare Act so the Secretary of Agriculture sets up a grant program for animal shelters. The money could be used for feeding, housing, veterinary care, recreation for animals, and hiring, training and keeping staff. Grants would last up to three years, and a shelter could renew its grant if it turns in the required report. Each shelter getting a grant would have to report to the Secretary every year, starting about 180 days after the first grant is awarded. The report must say how many animals of each species came in, what happened to each one (the "outcome"), and how the grant money was spent. The Secretary would also report to the House and Senate Agriculture Committees each year on how grant money was used to improve animal care. The Secretary would have 180 days after enactment to write the rules for the program. The bill does not state a dollar amount or say where the money would come from. It also replaces (strikes) the current subsection (d) of Section 28, and the bill text does not show what that subsection says now, so what is lost or kept is unclear from the text alone. Which shelters can apply depends on a definition in subsection (a)(2) of that section, which is also not shown here.
does: Requires the Agriculture Secretary to set up a grant program for eligible animal shelters.
Lets grant money pay for food, shelter, vet care, recreation, and hiring, training and keeping staff.
Limits each grant to 3 years, renewable if the shelter files its required report.
Requires grantees to report yearly on animals taken in by species, outcomes for each species, and how funds were used.
Requires the Secretary to report yearly to the House and Senate Agriculture Committees on how funds improved animal care.
Requires the Secretary to write regulations within 180 days of enactment.
Strikes and replaces the existing subsection (d) of Section 28 of the Animal Welfare Act.
who: Animal shelters that qualify under the Animal Welfare Act section being amended
Animals in shelter care
Shelter staff and volunteers
U.S. Department of Agriculture, which would run the program and write rules
Taxpayers, who would fund any grants
House and Senate Agriculture Committees, which would receive reports

benefits: Could help under-resourced shelters afford food, vet care and staff.
Staff hiring and retention funding could improve the quality of care.
Annual reports on intake and outcomes by species could give the public and Congress data on how shelters and grants perform.
Renewal tied to reporting encourages accountability.
concerns: No dollar amount or funding authorization is stated, so the program might not get funded.
Reporting requirements could be a burden for small shelters with little administrative staff.
Striking the existing subsection (d) could remove existing provisions, which can't be checked from the text provided.
Outcome reporting alone does not set standards (such as limits on euthanasia), so it is unclear how results would affect grants.
imp.cost: The bill gives no dollar amount and does not name a funding source in the text provided. Any costs would depend on later appropriations (money set by Congress) and the USDA rules.
unknowns: Which entities qualify as eligible shelters (defined in subsection (a)(2), not shown).
What the current subsection (d) says and what is lost by striking it.
How much money would be available and how grants would be awarded or ranked.
What the USDA rules would require and whether any outcome standards would be set.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help animal shelters pay for food, housing, veterinary care, recreation for animals, and hiring, training and keeping staff, through a grant program run by the Secretary of Agriculture. It also requires grant recipients to report yearly on animal intake, outcomes, and how funds were used, so Congress and the public can see how grant money improves animal care.

oppose: The bill does not state a dollar amount or say where the money would come from, so it is unclear whether the grant program would be funded at all. Asking how it would be paid for is a fair question to raise.
Yearly reporting on intake, outcomes by species, and spending could be a heavy paperwork load for small shelters that have little administrative staff.

The bill strikes the current subsection (d) of Section 28 of the Animal Welfare Act, but the bill text does not show what that subsection says. Constituents may want to ask what existing protections, if any, would be lost.
support: The bill would give shelters a dedicated source of grant money for food, housing, veterinary care, and enrichment, which could help shelters that are short on resources.
Funding for hiring, training, and keeping staff could help shelters retain experienced workers, which may improve the quality of animal care.

Yearly reports on animals taken in and their outcomes by species would give the public and Congress better data on how shelters and grants perform, and renewal tied to reporting encourages accountability.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 28 reporting requirements (annual grantee reports on intake, species outcomes and spending, plus Secretary's annual report to the Agriculture Committees) make shelter care and grant use more visible to the public and Congress, though the stricken subsection (d) is unclear and standards for humane treatment are not set.

justice.reason: Renewal of grants tied to filing the required report and the annual reporting requirements add accountability for how grant money is used, though no enforcement or remedy provisions are stated.

news.overall: Evidence is very limited: each perspective group has one headline, and neither mentions the Supporting Our Shelters Act, so no comparison of how the bill itself is framed is possible. The two items are about animal welfare topics (retired research chimpanzees and a stray dog) rather than legislation, which suggests the grouped coverage may not actually be about this bill. Coverage of the bill itself would need to be gathered to assess framing across perspectives.

label: H.R. 5068
title: MORE Act
short_title: MORE Act (Marijuana Opportunity Reinvestment and Expungement Act)
one: The bill ends federal criminal penalties for marijuana, clears past federal marijuana convictions, taxes legal cannabis, and uses the money for grants and loans in communities hurt by the war on drugs.
summary:
This bill would end the federal ban on marijuana. It removes marijuana and THC from the federal list of controlled substances and ends federal criminal penalties for growing, selling, or having it. The Attorney General must finish the formal rule change within 180 days. The change applies to past offenses and pending cases too. The bill also replaces the words "marijuana" and "marihuana" with "cannabis" throughout federal law. Hemp is already handled separately and is not covered by the new tax. The bill leaves FDA authority over cannabis-containing products in place. The FDA must hold at least one public meeting within a year on safety, labeling, marketing, and sale. Federal employee drug testing for marijuana can continue. Transportation agencies (trucking, aviation, rail, transit, Coast Guard) can keep testing and screening for marijuana.

Taxes and the Opportunity Trust Fund: The bill creates a federal excise tax (a tax on a specific product) on cannabis products made in or imported into the U.S. The rate starts at 5% of the removal price (roughly the sale price at the producer level) for two years. It rises to 6%, 7%, and then 8% by the fifth year. After that, the tax becomes a flat amount tied to 8% of the prevailing market price per ounce of flower, or per gram of THC for concentrated products. Producers and export warehouses also pay a $1,000 yearly occupational tax per location. Cannabis businesses must post bonds, get federal permits, keep records, follow packaging and labeling rules, and face civil and criminal penalties for tax evasion. Personal or family use growing that is not for sale is exempt. Tax revenue goes into a new Opportunity Trust Fund. Half goes to a community reinvestment grant program. Ten percent goes to substance use disorder services. Twenty percent goes to SBA loans and technical help for disadvantaged-owned cannabis businesses. Twenty percent goes to grants to states and localities for fair licensing programs.

Programs funded: A new Cannabis Justice Office in the Justice Department would give grants to nonprofits. They would provide job training, reentry help, legal aid including expungement, literacy, youth programs, health education, and substance use treatment. The SBA would run a Cannabis Restorative Opportunity Program for loans and a grant program for equitable state licensing. Grantees must adopt at least four of several fairness steps, such as waiving fees for low-income first-time applicants and limiting criminal record bars. Each year the GAO must study who receives the aid.

Small business access: SBA programs could not turn away otherwise eligible businesses just because they work in state-legal cannabis or serve those businesses. This covers loans, disaster loans, microloans, development centers, women's business centers, SCORE, and veteran outreach centers.

Benefits, immigration and clearances: People could not be denied federal public benefits because of cannabis use, possession, or a cannabis conviction. Agencies could not use past or present cannabis use to grant, deny, or revoke a security clearance. Under immigration law, cannabis would not count as a controlled substance. Immigrants could not be denied benefits or protections for cannabis-related conduct or convictions.

Expungement and resentencing: Within one year, each federal district must review and expunge nonviolent federal cannabis convictions back to May 1, 1971, along with related arrests. Courts must notify people where practical. People can also petition, with a lawyer appointed if they cannot afford one. People still serving sentences get a resentencing review and the sentence is redone as if the offense had not been criminal. Records are sealed. People whose records are expunged do not have to disclose them. Anyone who received a leadership-role sentencing enhancement is not eligible.

Data and studies: The Bureau of Labor Statistics must publish demographic data on cannabis owners and workers, keeping identities confidential. Treasury must study the industry, with updates every 5 years. Several studies would also be done: GAO on the societal effects of legalization, DOT/NHTSA on marijuana driving impairment ($10 million authorized), NIOSH on workplace effects, and Education on school effects. Agencies have a year to write the rules the bill requires.
does: Removes marijuana and THC (other than hemp) from the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules, with a final Attorney General rule due within 180 days.
Eliminates federal criminal penalties for making, distributing, or possessing marijuana, and applies this retroactively to past offenses, pending cases, convictions, and juvenile adjudications.
Replaces 'marijuana' and 'marihuana' with 'cannabis' across federal statutes, rules, and agency interpretations.
Keeps FDA and HHS authority over cannabis-containing products, and requires at least one public FDA meeting within a year on regulation, safety, labeling, marketing, and sale.
Lets federal employee drug testing continue to include marijuana, and preserves DOT and Coast Guard authority to regulate and screen for it (trucking, aviation, rail, transit, maritime).
Requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to regularly publish demographic data on cannabis business owners and workers, keeping individual identities confidential.

Creates a federal excise tax on cannabis products: 5% of removal price in years 1-2, rising to 6%, 7%, then 8% by year 5; after that, a flat amount based on 8% of the market price per ounce of flower or per gram of THC.
Excludes FDA-approved drugs and industrial hemp (0.3% THC or less) from the tax, and exempts personal or family use growing not for sale.
Imposes a $1,000 per year per location occupational tax on producers and export warehouses, with fines up to $5,000 or 2 years in prison for willful nonpayment.

Requires cannabis producers and export warehouses to post bonds and get federal permits, keep inventories and records open to IRS inspection, and follow packaging and labeling rules. Packaging bans lottery features and indecent material.

Sets civil penalties (such as $10,000 for willful noncompliance and 10% for late tax) and criminal penalties (up to $10,000 and 5 years) for tax fraud or evasion. Export-labeled products that are relanded for sale are forfeited.

Creates an Opportunity Trust Fund fed by the cannabis taxes: 50% to community reinvestment grants, 10% to substance use disorder services, 20% to SBA loans for disadvantaged-owned cannabis businesses, 20% to equitable licensing grants.

Creates a Cannabis Justice Office in the DOJ Office of Justice Programs to run the Community Reinvestment Grant Program for nonprofits. The grants cover job training, reentry, legal aid and expungement, literacy, youth programs, health education, and substance use treatment.

Creates the SBA Cannabis Restorative Opportunity Program (loans and technical help) and Equitable Licensing Grant Program. Eligible states and localities must have automatic expungement processes and must adopt at least four fairness steps, including fee waivers, limits on record-based license denials, a ban on suspicionless employee drug testing, and a representative licensing board.
Requires an annual GAO study on who receives assistance under the SBA programs, with a first report within one year.

Bars SBA programs (7(a), disaster, microloans, SBICs, development company loans, small business development centers, women's business centers, SCORE, veteran outreach centers) from refusing eligible businesses solely for being state-legal cannabis businesses or service providers.
Bars denial of federal public benefits based on cannabis use, possession, or conviction, and bars agencies from using cannabis use to grant, deny, or revoke security clearances.

Under immigration law, cannabis is no longer a controlled substance, and immigrants cannot be denied benefits or protections based on past or present cannabis-related events. Related exceptions are removed from the Immigration and Nationality Act.

Requires federal courts to expunge nonviolent federal cannabis convictions and related arrests (since May 1, 1971) within one year, notify people where practicable, and seal records. People can petition any time, with appointed counsel for those who cannot afford one.

Gives people still under sentence a resentencing review with appointed counsel. Their sentence is vacated or redone as if the offense had not been a crime. People with a leadership-role sentencing enhancement are excluded.

Mandates studies: GAO on the demographics of those convicted and on the societal impact of state legalization (21 topics, including crime, health, schools, and driving). Also DOT/NHTSA on marijuana impairment detection ($10 million authorized), NIOSH on workplace effects and employer best practices, and Education on school impacts with best practices.
Requires Treasury to study the industry within 2 years and then every 5 years, and to publish its rate-setting methodology 6 months before the flat-rate period.

Requires Treasury, DOJ, and SBA to write the rules needed within 1 year, and requires 60-day notice to congressional committees before issuing new sub-regulatory guidance after that. Severability clause included.
who: People with federal marijuana arrests, convictions, or sentences
Communities that were disproportionately policed for marijuana, especially Black and Latino communities
State-legal cannabis growers, processors, sellers, and importers, who would face new federal taxes, permits, and bonds
Small businesses and service providers that work with cannabis
Nonprofits that serve people affected by the war on drugs
Immigrants with cannabis-related records
Federal benefit applicants and security clearance holders
Federal employees and transportation workers subject to drug testing
Consumers of cannabis products
IRS, DOJ, SBA, FDA, HHS, DOT, BLS, GAO, and courts
States and localities that apply for equitable licensing grants
Employers and schools, who will be studied and given best practices

benefits: Could end federal arrests and prosecutions for marijuana, reducing racial disparities in enforcement.
Could clear records for many people, improving access to jobs, housing, and benefits.
Could protect immigrants from deportation and benefit denials over past cannabis conduct.
Could direct industry tax revenue to legal aid, job training, treatment, and disadvantaged business owners.
Could improve public understanding through BLS data, GAO studies, and FDA public meetings.
Could open SBA programs to small cannabis businesses that have trouble getting loans.
Requires states to have fair licensing practices to get equitable licensing grants.
concerns: Would let SBA-backed loans and services flow to cannabis businesses, which some may see as a public subsidy to the industry.
Taxes could be passed to consumers or push some businesses toward the illicit market if they are too high.
Federal permits, bonds, and recordkeeping could burden small and disadvantaged operators.
The bill preserves workplace and federal employee drug testing, so some people could still face job consequences.
Public health, impaired driving, youth use, and environmental effects are only studied, not directly addressed.
The bill does not address pesticide, water, energy, or other environmental impacts of cannabis cultivation.
Expungement excludes anyone with a leadership-role sentencing enhancement and is limited to nonviolent federal offenses.
imp.cost: No cost estimate was provided. The bill creates new federal excise and occupational taxes whose net revenue goes into the Opportunity Trust Fund, which spends without further appropriation. It also authorizes $10 million for the marijuana impairment study. Other costs, like courts handling expungements, new offices, and lost enforcement, are not quantified. The bill's findings cite ACLU's estimate that prohibition enforcement costs about $3.6 billion a year.
unknowns: How much tax revenue the fund would actually collect, given market prices and the illicit market.
How courts would handle the one-year expungement deadline across all federal districts.
Whether states would qualify for equitable licensing grants.
How the FDA and DOT would regulate products and impairment after decriminalization.
How tax-and-permit rules would work for businesses that cross state lines, given state laws differ.
The bill's chance of passing; it is in a House subcommittee with 75 cosponsors.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to end federal criminal penalties for marijuana and remove it from the federal Controlled Substances Act, while using tax revenue and other programs to reinvest in communities affected by the war on drugs. It also aims to clear past federal cannabis convictions, protect people from benefit denials and immigration consequences tied to cannabis, and collect data and studies on the cannabis industry and its effects.

oppose: The bill removes marijuana from the federal Controlled Substances Act and ends federal criminal penalties, which some constituents may feel sends the wrong message about public health and youth access.
The bill creates new federal excise and occupational taxes, along with bonds, permits, and recordkeeping rules, which some small operators may find costly to meet.

The bill's health, impaired driving, and workplace effects are mainly studied rather than directly addressed, so some constituents may want stronger safeguards before federal legalization takes effect.
The bill makes SBA loans and services available to state-legal cannabis businesses, which some constituents may see as a federal subsidy to an industry they oppose.
support: The bill ends federal arrests and prosecutions for marijuana, which supporters say would reduce racial disparities in enforcement.
The bill requires expungement of nonviolent federal cannabis convictions and related arrests, which supporters say could help people access jobs, housing, and benefits.

The bill directs excise tax revenue into a Trust Fund for community reinvestment, substance use treatment, disadvantaged business owners, and fair state licensing programs, which supporters say would help communities harmed by the war on drugs.
The bill protects people from federal benefit denials, security clearance decisions, and immigration consequences based on past cannabis conduct, which supporters say treats people more fairly.

cost_flag: No cost estimate was provided. The bill creates new federal excise and occupational taxes whose net revenue goes into the Opportunity Trust Fund, which spends without further appropriation. It also authorizes $10 million for the marijuana impairment study. Other costs, like courts handling expungements, new offices, and lost enforcement, are not quantified. The bill's findings cite ACLU's estimate that prohibition enforcement costs about $3.6 billion a year.
crs:
Marijuana Opportunity Reinvestment and Expungement Act or the MORE Act
This bill decriminalizes marijuana.
Specifically, it removes marijuana from the list of scheduled substances under the Controlled Substances Act and eliminates criminal penalties for an individual who manufactures, distributes, or possesses marijuana.
The bill replaces statutory references to 
marijuana 
and 
marihuana 
with 
cannabis
.
The bill also makes changes related to the economic impact of decriminalization, including the following:
requires the Bureau of Labor Statistics to regularly publish demographic data on cannabis business owners and employees,
establishes a trust fund to support various programs and services for individuals and businesses in communities impacted by the war on drugs,
imposes an excise tax on cannabis products produced in or imported into the United States and an occupational tax on cannabis production facilities and export warehouses, and
makes Small Business Administration loans and services available to entities that are cannabis-related legitimate businesses or service providers.
The bill also makes changes to other federal programs and legal processes to account for decriminalization, including the following: 
prohibits the denial of federal public benefits to a person on the basis of certain cannabis-related conduct or convictions,
prohibits the denial of benefits and protections under immigration laws on the basis of an event (e.g., conduct or conviction) relating to possession or use of cannabis that is no longer prohibited under the bill, and
establishes a process to expunge convictions and conduct sentencing review hearings related to federal cannabis offenses.

environment.reason: The bill does not directly address cultivation impacts such as water, pesticide, or energy use; it only mandates studies, so the effect on environmental protection is unclear.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on BLS data and FDA public meeting require public release of demographic data and a public FDA meeting, though records sealing and expungement limit some public visibility.

people_over_profit.reason: Sec. on SBA programs opens loans and services to cannabis businesses, and the tax is a cost on producers, but the Opportunity Trust Fund and reinvestment grants direct revenue to communities, so the net effect leans toward industry support with some offsetting public benefit.

local_say.reason: Equitable Licensing Grant requires states and localities to adopt a representative licensing board and fairness steps, while leaving licensing authority with states and localities that already regulate cannabis.

no_bailouts.reason: Sec. on SBA loans and services for cannabis businesses, funded through the Opportunity Trust Fund outside annual appropriations, can be seen as taxpayer-supported assistance to the industry.

equality.reason: Sec. on expungement, benefit denial bans, and clearance protections end cannabis-based unequal treatment, and the disadvantaged-owner set-asides and fairness steps target equal access, though the leadership-enhancement exclusion and set-asides create some distinctions.

justice.reason: Sec. on automatic expungement, resentencing review with appointed counsel, and retroactive application to pending cases and convictions give real remedies and due process to people with federal cannabis records.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. ending federal criminal penalties for making, distributing, or possessing marijuana, plus the personal-use growing exemption, expands what individuals may legally do with cannabis.

news.overall: The provided coverage barely addresses the MORE Act directly. Lean Left headlines touch on cannabis and related policy areas (prices, search rules, crime labs, taxation) without naming the bill, and the Lean Right group has only one thin article on criminal justice history. Any comparison of framing between perspectives is therefore limited, and conclusions about how each side views the MORE Act would need more directly relevant coverage.
