label: H.R. 5468
title: Community College Agriculture Advancement Act of 2025
short_title: Community College Agriculture Advancement Act of 2025
one: The bill would let USDA give competitive grants to community colleges (and groups of them) to build up farm and natural resources training, education, research, and outreach, with up to $20 million a year authorized for 2026–2031.
summary: This bill would create a new grant program at the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) for community colleges and groups of two-year public colleges that support agriculture. Colleges would compete for the money. The grants would help them keep and grow their ability to offer job training, classes, research, and outreach on agriculture and similar fields. USDA must give priority to colleges that team up with a local farm or agriculture business to give students hands-on training. Colleges could use the money to buy equipment, pay for faculty development, set up apprenticeships and work-based learning, teach about farm jobs (including business subjects like accounting, paralegal studies, and finance), share information with the public, and improve their odds of winning other grants. Grant money could not be used to build, renovate, or repair buildings. Colleges could also apply to be named a "Center of Excellence for Agriculture Advancement," with money used to show best practices and lead capacity building regionally or nationally. Within three years, USDA must evaluate the program and report to Congress. The bill authorizes up to $20 million per year from fiscal year 2026 through 2031. "Authorizes" means Congress would still need to pass a separate spending bill to actually provide the money.
does: Creates competitive USDA grants for community colleges and consortia of 2-year public colleges supporting agriculture.
who: Community and junior colleges and 2-year public college consortia

benefits: Colleges could get money for equipment, faculty training, and apprenticeships, which may help them expand agriculture training.
Priority for partnerships with local agriculture businesses may give students more hands-on and job-connected learning.
Centers of Excellence could share best practices with other colleges across a region or the nation.
concerns: Because grants cannot pay for buildings, colleges may still struggle to fund facility repairs or expansion needed for programs.
Including business subjects like paralegal studies and finance under an agriculture grant may raise questions about whether the program stays focused on farming.
imp.cost: "The bill authorizes up to $20 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2031. An authorization does not itself provide money; Congress would need to pass a separate appropriations bill to fund the program. The bill text summary does not state how the money would be divided among grants or Centers of Excellence."
unknowns: The materials do not say how many grants would be awarded or how large each would be.
The materials do not state how USDA would define a 'local agriculture industry operator' or how it would rank applications beyond the priority rule.
It is not stated whether Congress will fund the program at the authorized level.
The materials do not describe what the three-year evaluation must measure.
The bill's current status is only listed as being in House committee (hearing or markup); the material does not say whether it will advance.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to help community colleges and groups of two-year public colleges keep and grow their ability to offer agriculture-related job training, education, research, and outreach. It creates a competitive USDA grant program for this purpose, gives priority to colleges that partner with local agriculture businesses, and lets colleges apply to be named Centers of Excellence for Agriculture Advancement. The bill authorizes up to $20 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2031, but Congress would still need to pass a separate spending bill to provide the funds.

oppose: The bill authorizes up to $20 million per year for six years, which adds to federal spending. Those costs would need to be weighed against other priorities.
Grant money can be used for business subjects such as accounting, paralegal studies, and finance. Some people may feel this moves the program away from its focus on agriculture.
The grants cannot pay for buildings, renovation, or repairs. Colleges may still need other funding sources for facilities, so the benefit may be limited for some schools.
The program is competitive, so only some colleges would receive grants. Some people may ask whether existing USDA or state programs already cover this need.
support: The bill would help community colleges buy equipment, train faculty, and set up apprenticeships, which can prepare students for agriculture jobs.
Priority for colleges that work with local farms and agriculture businesses means students can get hands-on, job-connected experience.
Centers of Excellence could share best practices across a region or the nation, which could help more colleges improve their agriculture programs.
The bill requires USDA to evaluate the program and report to Congress within three years, so lawmakers can check whether it is working.

cost_flag: The bill authorizes up to $20 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2031. An authorization does not itself provide money; Congress would need to pass a separate appropriations bill to fund the program. The bill text summary does not state how the money would be divided among grants or Centers of Excellence.
crs:
Community College Agriculture Advancement Act of 2025
This bill allows the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make competitive grants to assist eligible entities (i.e., a junior or community college, or a consortium or alliance of two-year public colleges, supporting agriculture advancement) in maintaining and expanding their capacity to conduct workforce training, education, research, and outreach activities related to agriculture and similar disciplines
In awarding grants, USDA must give priority to entities coordinating with a local agriculture industry operator to provide experiential training and other opportunities for students.
Grant funds may be used to expand and maintain the capacity of the eligible entity, including through the purchase or other acquisition of equipment and other infrastructure, the professional growth and development of faculty, and the development of apprenticeships and other work-based learning opportunities.
An eligible entity may submit to USDA an application for designation and funding as a Center of Excellence for Agriculture Advancement. Funding received as a result of such a designation must be used to demonstrate agriculture best practices and to provide leadership in capacity building at a regional or national level.

local_say.reason: Priority for colleges coordinating with local agriculture operators and funding for regional Centers of Excellence gives local colleges and regions a somewhat larger role in agricultural training decisions.

label: H.R. 598
title: FIR Act
short_title: FIR Act (Forest Information Reform Act)
one: The bill says the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management do not have to redo Endangered Species Act reviews of their long-term land plans when a new species is listed, new critical habitat is set, or new information shows harm not previously considered.
summary:
Federal agencies that manage public land, mainly the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), write long-term plans for how each forest or area will be used. Under the Endangered Species Act (ESA), they must consult with wildlife agencies to check that those plans won't harm protected species. Current rules say that this consultation must be reopened ("reinitiated") in certain cases. Those cases include a new species being listed, new critical habitat being designated, or new information showing the plan may harm a protected species in a way that wasn't looked at before.

This bill would change the laws that govern Forest Service and BLM planning. It would say that the agencies are not required to reopen consultation in those situations. The language begins "notwithstanding any other provision of law," so it would override the ESA and its regulation (50 CFR 402.16) on this point. The bill does not ban reconsultation. It only removes the requirement. It does not say what, if anything, would replace it, and it does not cover individual projects approved under the plans. The bill has no listed cost. It has been referred to a House subcommittee, and I could not see any further action.
does: Amends the Forest and Rangeland Renewable Resources Planning Act so the Forest Service need not reinitiate ESA consultation on forest plans when a new species is listed or critical habitat is designated.
Also removes the requirement when new information shows a plan may affect a listed species or critical habitat in a way or to an extent not previously considered.
Amends the Federal Land Policy and Management Act to give BLM the same exemption for its land use plans.
Uses 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' wording, so it would override ESA section 7(a)(2) and the regulation at 50 CFR 402.16 for these plans.
Makes no mention of funding, new monitoring, or other safeguards.
who: Forest Service and BLM planners and staff
Threatened and endangered species and their habitat on national forests and BLM land
Timber, grazing, mining, energy and recreation users of public lands
Local communities, tribes and the public who rely on or live near federal lands
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and NOAA Fisheries (consulting agencies)
Conservation groups and others who bring lawsuits over land plans

benefits: Agencies could avoid repeating consultation when new species listings or habitat designations occur, which may save time and staff effort.
Land management plans may be easier to keep on schedule, since reopening consultation can take a long time.
Land managers may have more certainty about plans they have already approved.
concerns: Species listed or habitat designated after a plan is approved might not get a fresh review of the plan's effects, which could leave protected species less protected.
New scientific information about harm to a listed species might not lead to a new review, which could delay or prevent changes to the plan.
Because the bill overrides the Endangered Species Act on this point, it could weaken a standard set in federal law.
Because the bill does not replace the requirement, there may be no required check at all in these situations.
imp.cost: >The bill has no listed cost, and the material does not state any budget or funding effects.
unknowns: The material does not say what, if anything, would replace reconsultation.
It is not stated how the bill would affect individual projects approved under the plans, since the bill does not cover them.
It is not stated how often these situations arise or how many plans might be affected.
The material does not say whether the agencies or wildlife agencies would still be able to reconsult voluntarily.
The bill has been referred to a House subcommittee, and no further action was found, so its final form and chance of passage are unknown.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Forestry and Horticulture.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to relieve the Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management of a requirement to reopen Endangered Species Act consultation on their land management plans when a new species is listed, new critical habitat is designated, or new information shows a plan may affect a listed species in a way not previously considered. The bill's title is the Forest Information Reform Act (FIR Act).

oppose: The bill overrides the Endangered Species Act on this point, so a standard set in federal law would no longer require a new review of forest and land plans when a species is newly listed or its habitat is newly designated.
Species listed or habitat designated after a plan is approved might not get a fresh look at how the plan affects them, which could leave protected wildlife with less protection.
New scientific information showing a plan may harm a listed species might not trigger a review, and the bill does not replace that check with any other safeguard, monitoring, or funding requirement.
support: Reopening consultation can take a long time, and this bill would let the Forest Service and BLM avoid repeating it, which may save agency time and staff effort.
Land management plans may be easier to keep on schedule, and land managers would have more certainty about plans they have already approved.
The bill does not ban consultation or stop protections for species. It only removes one required step for forest and land plans, so agencies could focus resources on other work.

crs:
Forest Information Reform Act or the FIR Act
This bill specifies that neither the Forest Service nor the Bureau of Land Management are required to reinitiate consultation on a land management plan when a new species is listed as threatened or endangered, critical habitat is designated, or new information reveals effects of the plan may affect a listed species or critical habitat in a manner or to an extent not previously considered.

environment.reason: Sec. 1 (as summarized) removes the requirement to reinitiate ESA consultation on Forest Service and BLM land plans when new species are listed, critical habitat is designated, or new effects emerge, so plans may go unchecked against harm to listed species and their habitat, with no replacement safeguard.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill removes a required federal check on whether plans harm protected species, and the summary notes it adds no replacement review or public-facing safeguard, which reduces the openness of decisions affecting wildlife.

people_over_profit.reason: By relieving land managers of reconsultation duties, the bill makes it easier for timber, grazing, mining, and energy uses already approved under plans to continue without fresh review, which tends to favor those commercial interests over broader public and ecological interests.

local_say.reason: Removing the reconsultation requirement reduces the procedural points at which wildlife agencies and the public can revisit approved land plans affecting local areas.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not involve bailouts or ratepayer cost shifts, and no funding is listed.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same exemption to all plans on Forest Service and BLM land and does not create differing treatment among people or groups.

justice.reason: Sec. 1 (as summarized) overrides ESA section 7(a)(2) and 50 CFR 402.16 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' for these plans, weakening a legal check and the remedy it provided without substituting any accountability mechanism.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill concerns agency planning duties and does not expand or restrict what individuals may do or choose about their own lives.

news.overall: Only three headlines from two outlets (NPR and Politico) were provided, with no article descriptions, so this assessment is based on limited evidence. The Lean Left coverage centers on environmental impacts and concerns about how the bill could be used, while its headlines say little about the bill's substance or its supporters' views.

label: H.R. 6192
title: Fertilizer Research Act of 2025
short_title: Fertilizer Research Act of 2025
one: Requires the USDA to publish, within one year, a public report on the U.S. fertilizer industry covering prices, imports, market concentration, regulation, new fertilizer technologies, and price transparency.
summary: This bill would make the Secretary of Agriculture, working with the USDA's Economic Research Service, write and post a public report about the U.S. fertilizer industry. The report would be due one year after the bill becomes law. It would look at how the fertilizer industry affects the prices farmers get for their crops, and how big the fertilizer market has been over the last 25 years. It would also cover price patterns and where fertilizer comes from, including lists of imported fertilizer types, importing companies, and source countries. It would explain how anti-dumping and countervailing duties (extra taxes on unfairly cheap or subsidized imports) affect retail prices. The report would study whether a few companies control too much of the market and whether that has hurt competition. It would compare newer products, such as biological fertilizers, with conventional ones on price, efficiency, and yield. It would review the rules on making, distributing, and using fertilizer, including where they are seen as hurting domestic production. It would also judge whether public fertilizer price reporting is transparent enough. It would evaluate, and recommend to Congress on, a possible rule making industry report prices daily, weekly, or monthly. It would also look at expected market growth and risks. Confidential business information would be left out. The bill itself creates no new rules, fees, or programs.
does: Requires USDA to publish a fertilizer industry report on its website within one year of enactment.
Requires the report to cover market size, value, and price patterns over 25 years, including by fertilizer type.
Requires lists of imported fertilizer types, importing companies (foreign and domestic) with quantities, and source countries.
Requires a description of how anti-dumping and countervailing duties affect retail fertilizer prices.
Requires a study of industry concentration and whether it has caused anticompetitive effects.
Requires a comparison of emerging fertilizers (including biological ones) with conventional ones on price, efficiency, and yield.
Requires an assessment of regulations, including where regulatory burden is hampering production, distribution, and use.
Requires an evaluation of price reporting transparency and a recommendation to Congress on whether to require industry price reporting.
Requires a look at projected market growth and economic and political risks.
Bars the report from including confidential business information.
who: Farmers and ranchers who buy fertilizer
Fertilizer manufacturers, importers, distributors, and retailers
USDA and its Economic Research Service
Congress and policymakers who weigh fertilizer rules, trade duties, and competition policy
Consumers and communities indirectly, through food prices and fertilizer's environmental effects

benefits: A public, government-written study could give farmers, buyers, and lawmakers clearer information about how the fertilizer market works.
Reviewing price reporting could show whether market information is open enough for people who buy and sell fertilizer.
Comparing newer products with conventional ones could give farmers information about options such as biological fertilizers.
Recommendations on price reporting frequency could inform future decisions by Congress.
concerns: The report would be a study only, so it may not lead to any direct change in fertilizer prices or competition.
Listing importers and source countries could reveal business relationships, although the bill says confidential business information would be left out.
imp.cost: ["The material does not state a cost or funding amount for the report. The bill itself creates no new rules, fees, or programs, according to the plain-English summary."]
unknowns: The material does not say how much the study would cost or how USDA would pay for it.
It is not stated what findings the report would reach, or whether its recommendations would lead to new laws.
The material does not say whether the bill has passed either chamber; its latest action is listed as House committee hearing or markup.
It is not stated how the report's recommendations on price reporting would be carried out if Congress acts.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to give the public a government-written report on the U.S. fertilizer industry. According to the CRS summary, the report would cover how the industry affects prices farmers receive, market size and value over 25 years, imports and the effects of antidumping and countervailing duties, market concentration, regulations, and how transparent public fertilizer price reporting is. The bill itself creates no new rules, fees, or programs.

oppose: The bill creates a new government study that costs federal staff time and resources, and it may not lead to any change in fertilizer prices or competition, so you could ask whether it is the best use of USDA's time.

Listing importing companies, both foreign and domestic, along with quantities and source countries could expose business relationships. Although the bill excludes confidential business information, you could ask how the line will be drawn in practice.

The report's regulatory section looks at rules where they may be hurting domestic production. You could ask that the review be balanced, covering the health, safety, and environmental purposes these rules serve, not only their costs to industry.
support: A public USDA report would give farmers, buyers, and lawmakers clearer, government-backed information about how the fertilizer market works over 25 years of data, which is useful when input costs are a major concern.

Reviewing price reporting transparency and recommending whether Congress should require daily, weekly, or monthly industry price reporting could help market participants make better-informed decisions.
Comparing newer products, such as biological fertilizers, with conventional ones on price, efficiency, and yield could give farmers objective information about more options for their operations.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill requires USDA to publish a public report on its website covering fertilizer prices, imports, and market concentration, and to assess price reporting transparency; confidential business information is excluded.

justice.reason: The report would examine market concentration and anticompetitive effects, and recommend whether industry price reporting is needed, which could inform future accountability measures; the bill itself creates no enforcement tools.

news.overall: Evidence is very limited: only three Lean Left headlines were provided, with no descriptions, and none of them clearly addresses the Fertilizer Research Act of 2025. No other perspective groups were supplied, so a cross-perspective comparison cannot be made. Coverage of the bill itself would need to be gathered to assess framing.

label: H.R. 665
title: Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act
short_title: Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act
one: Lifts Jones Act ship-build, ownership and crew rules on shipping routes to Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and U.S. territories unless at least three unaffiliated U.S.-qualified carriers each move at least 20% of the cargo on that route.
summary: The Jones Act says that goods or passengers moving by ship between two U.S. ports must use a ship that was built in the U.S., is at least 75% owned by U.S. citizens, and is mostly crewed by U.S. citizens. This bill adds an exemption for "noncontiguous" routes, meaning shipping to or from Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and U.S. territories or possessions. On those routes the Jones Act rules would be lifted unless there is real competition. Competition is defined as at least three companies regularly running Jones Act-qualified ships on the route, each carrying at least 20% of the goods on that route, and none of the three sharing common ownership. If a route does not meet all three tests, any ship, including foreign-built and foreign-crewed ones, could carry cargo or passengers on it. If a route does meet them, the Jones Act rules stay in place. The bill is short and one-sided in what it changes: it only edits the exemption list in the Jones Act. It does not say how the competition tests would be measured or checked, who would decide, or how fast changes would happen. The bill's sponsor is from Hawaii, where many goods arrive by ship. Supporters of changes like this point to high shipping costs in island and remote places. Defenders of the Jones Act point to U.S. jobs, shipyards and national security.
does: Adds a new exemption (paragraph 4) to the Jones Act's coastwise rules at 46 U.S.C. 55101(b).
Exempts shipping on noncontiguous routes (to or from Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and U.S. territories/possessions) from U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed requirements.
Keeps the Jones Act in force on a route only if at least three owners/operators of qualified vessels regularly serve it.
Requires that each of those operators carries at least 20% of the goods by volume on the route.
Requires that none of those operators be under common ownership.
Does not set up a process for measuring market share or deciding which routes qualify.
who: Consumers and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, Guam and other territories that depend on ships for goods
U.S. shipping companies that operate Jones Act vessels on these routes
U.S. mariners and maritime unions
U.S. shipyards
Foreign-flag shipping operators who could gain access to some routes
Federal agencies (e.g., Maritime Administration, Customs and Border Protection) that would have to apply the rules

benefits: Could lower shipping costs and consumer prices in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico and territories where few carriers operate.
Could reduce the power of a small number of or commonly owned carriers on thin routes.
Keeps the Jones Act protections where real competition already exists.
Could give isolated communities more reliable or more varied shipping options.
concerns: Could cut demand for U.S.-built ships and U.S. crews, affecting jobs in shipyards and the merchant marine.
Foreign-flag vessels may be held to different labor, safety and environmental rules than U.S.-flag vessels, which could affect worker welfare and the risk of spills or pollution.
Could weaken the pool of U.S. ships and mariners available for national security needs.
Because most routes have fewer than three qualified carriers, the exemption could apply broadly, and savings are not guaranteed to reach consumers.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding provided in the bill text. It does not appropriate money or create a program, though agencies would need resources to determine which routes meet the competition tests.
unknowns: Which agency would decide whether a route meets the three-carrier, 20% and no-common-ownership tests, and how often.
How many current routes would actually be exempted.
How much shipping prices would fall, and whether savings would reach consumers.
How foreign-flag ships would be held to U.S. safety, pollution and labor laws on these routes.
Effective date and transition rules; the bill text does not give any.
Effects on national defense sealift capacity.

stage.last_action: Sponsor introductory remarks on measure. (CR E90-91)

purpose: The bill says its goal is to promote competition in shipping on noncontiguous routes (to or from Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and U.S. territories or possessions). It would exempt those routes from Jones Act requirements unless there is real competition, defined as at least three qualified carriers regularly serving the route, each carrying at least 20% of the goods by volume, and none under common ownership. The official title, the Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act, reflects this focus. The bill does not say how competition would be measured or who would decide.

oppose: The Jones Act helps keep U.S.-built, U.S.-owned, and U.S.-crewed ships in service. Removing those rules on some routes could reduce demand for American shipyards and merchant mariners.
Foreign-flag ships may follow different labor, safety, and environmental rules. Please ask whether the bill would protect workers and reduce the risk of spills or pollution on these routes.

A strong U.S. merchant fleet and trained U.S. mariners are often cited as important for national security. Please ask how the bill would protect the availability of U.S. ships and crews in an emergency.
support: Many goods to Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and U.S. territories arrive by ship, and the bill aims to lower shipping costs where few carriers compete. Lower costs could mean lower prices for families and businesses.

The bill keeps Jones Act rules in place on any route that already has real competition, defined as at least three unaffiliated carriers each carrying at least 20% of the cargo. It targets only routes where competition is thin.
Isolated communities may gain more reliable or varied shipping options if more carriers can serve their routes. Please ask your member how the competition tests would be measured and enforced.

crs:
Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act 
This bill revises coastwise laws, commonly known as the Jones Act, that govern domestic transportation of merchandise or passengers by vessels.
The Jones Act generally requires that a vessel transporting merchandise or passengers from one U.S. point to another U.S. point be (1) built in the United States, (2) at least 75% owned by U.S. citizens, and (3) mostly crewed by U.S. citizens. The act also includes several exemptions and exceptions.
The bill exempts carriage on a route in noncontiguous trade from Jones Act requirements unless (1) at least three owners or operators of coastwise qualified vessels regularly operate such a vessel on the route, (2) each of such owners or operators transports at least 20% of the volume of goods on that route, and (3) none of such owners or operators are under common ownership. (Generally, 
noncontiguous trade
 is trade between two U.S. points where at least one of the points is in Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, or an insular territory or U.S. possession.)

environment.reason: Sec. 2 (new paragraph 4 at 46 U.S.C. 55101(b)) lets foreign-flag ships serve noncontiguous routes without Jones Act requirements, and the bill sets no environmental standards or enforcement for them, which could raise spill and pollution risk in Alaska, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico waters.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill neither adds nor removes public disclosure, and it leaves measurement and decision-making unspecified, which is neutral rather than a clear transparency gain or loss.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill could lower shipping costs for island consumers, but it also could reduce U.S. shipping jobs, and savings are not guaranteed to reach consumers, so effects on the balance are unclear.

local_say.reason: The bill does not give local or state governments a formal role; it sets a federal competition test that federal agencies would apply, with no provision for community input, so the effect on local say is unclear.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill involves no taxpayer subsidies, bailouts, or ratepayer cost shifts.

equality.reason: Sec. 2 would let carriers serving Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico and territories use any ship on routes that fail the competition tests, which could expand access to shipping for residents of those places compared with the current Jones Act rule applied uniformly.

justice.reason: The bill sets no process for measuring market share, deciding which routes qualify, or enforcing the tests, leaving the rules less clear and less accountable for affected parties.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill changes which carriers businesses may use on certain routes, which affects commercial choice more than individuals' personal freedoms, so the effect is marginal and unclear.

news.overall: None of the provided headlines or descriptions mention the Noncontiguous Shipping Competition Act, so this set of coverage cannot show how outlets frame the bill itself. The Lean Left group has seven articles, but they cover unrelated topics such as Alaska politics, Puerto Rico's grid, and inflation, which only loosely connect to noncontiguous regions. The Center group has just one article, so the evidence there is very limited; it touches on Hawaii but not on the bill. Coverage specifically about the bill would be needed for a meaningful framing comparison.

label: S. 764
title: Colorado Outdoor Recreation and Economy Act
short_title: Colorado Outdoor Recreation and Economy Act
one: The bill would protect large areas of Colorado public land as wilderness, wildlife conservation areas, special management areas, and a new national recreation area. It would also block new oil and gas leasing in the Thompson Divide, pay existing leaseholders who give up their leases with credits, and start a pilot program to capture coal mine methane.
summary: This bill covers four areas of Colorado. In the Continental Divide area, it adds about 30,000 acres to wilderness (Ptarmigan Peak, Holy Cross, Eagles Nest, and the new Hoosier Ridge and Tenmile wilderness areas). It sets aside about 8,000 acres of the Williams Fork Mountains as potential wilderness, with a delay tied to a decision on livestock grazing. It also creates three wildlife conservation areas, including a wildlife corridor over Interstate 70. In the San Juan Mountains, it adds wilderness to Lizard Head, Mount Sneffels, and the new McKenna Peak Wilderness. It creates two special management areas and releases some leftover study lands from further wilderness consideration. In the Thompson Divide, it bars new mineral leasing and mining on federal land. Companies that give up existing oil and gas leases there can get credits, which they can use against bids, royalties, or rent on other federal oil and gas leases in Colorado. It also starts a pilot program to inventory, lease, capture, or destroy methane leaking from coal mines. In the Curecanti area, it creates a roughly 50,300-acre National Park Service recreation area. That area keeps hunting, fishing, boating, and most existing grazing, and it keeps dam and water operations in place. Across the bill, existing grazing and water rights are mostly protected, tribal treaty rights and traditional uses are kept, and military overflights stay allowed. The bill creates no protective buffer zones around the new areas.
does: Adds roughly 30,000 acres to the White River National Forest wilderness system, including the new Hoosier Ridge and Tenmile Wilderness areas.
Designates the Williams Fork Mountains as potential wilderness. It becomes full wilderness after a grazing decision and any range improvements, or after a set period.
Creates the Porcupine Gulch, Williams Fork Mountains, and Spraddle Creek Wildlife Conservation Areas, with limits on motor vehicles, new roads, and commercial logging.
Allows the Interstate 70 and Eisenhower-Johnson Tunnels projects to use the subsurface under the Porcupine Gulch area. It also lets the Secretary make minor boundary changes for highway work.
Adds wilderness to Lizard Head and Mount Sneffels and creates the McKenna Peak Wilderness (BLM land) in the San Juan Mountains.

Creates the Sheep Mountain and Liberty Bell East Special Management Areas, with no permanent roads and limited motor use. Existing permitted activities, such as helicopter access and a running event, may continue.
Releases the rest of the Dominguez Canyon and McKenna Peak Wilderness Study Areas from wilderness study status, so they are no longer protected as study areas.
Withdraws the new protected areas, a 6,590-acre Naturita Canyon area, and the Thompson Divide from new mining claims, mineral leasing, and geothermal leasing, subject to valid existing rights.

Lets leaseholders give up Thompson Divide oil and gas leases in exchange for credits. The credits equal bonus bids, rentals paid, and certain permit-preparation expenses. They can be applied to other federal oil and gas payments in Colorado, and the surrendered leases are permanently cancelled.
Sets up a pilot program to inventory coal mine methane leaks, lease or authorize capture or destruction of that methane, cap or destroy what remains, and report to Congress within 4 years.

Establishes the Curecanti National Recreation Area (about 50,300 acres) as a National Park System unit. It transfers some Forest Service, BLM, and Reclamation land to the Park Service, protects water rights, and keeps hunting, fishing, and boating.
Requires the Secretary to fulfill a 26-mile public fishing easement obligation in the Upper Gunnison Basin within 10 years.
Protects tribal treaty rights and traditional ceremonial and plant-gathering uses on the covered lands.
States that military overflights and airspace use are not restricted, and expresses the sense of Congress that military aviation training is critical.
who: Colorado residents and communities near the affected public lands, including Summit, Eagle, Grand, San Miguel, Gunnison, Pitkin, Garfield, and Delta counties
Hikers, hunters, anglers, boaters, skiers, and other outdoor recreation users
Wildlife, including migratory animals that cross Interstate 70, and the plants, forests, and watersheds in the protected areas
Ranchers and livestock grazing permit holders

one: The bill orders a Government Accountability Office-led study of how the federal "similarity of appearance" protection for American alligators, common caimans and brown caimans has affected their populations and removal of nuisance or invasive animals.
summary: This bill does not change any law or loosen any protection. It only asks for a study. The Comptroller General, who leads the Government Accountability Office (a nonpartisan congressional watchdog), would work with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and wildlife agencies in states that have American alligators, common caimans or brown caimans. The study would look at a federal rule under the Endangered Species Act. Under that rule, some reptiles are treated as "threatened" only because they look like a protected species. This is called "similarity of appearance." The goal is to prevent confusion and illegal trade in protected look-alikes. The study would ask how this treatment has affected the animals' populations and state management programs. It would also ask whether the treatment led to the American alligator recovering more than fully, and whether it led the caiman to become invasive in Florida. Finally, it would ask whether the treatment has made it harder to remove nuisance alligators or invasive caimans from waterways near homes and businesses. The bill sets no deadline, no dollar amount, and no new rules. Any later changes would need separate action by Congress or the agency. The bill's wording assumes some of these effects happened, and the study is meant to test that.

title: 9–8–8 Implementation Act of 2026
short_title: 9-8-8 Implementation Act of 2026
one: The bill would fund and expand the 9-8-8 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and related crisis care by paying for call centers, facilities, workforce training, and a media campaign, and by requiring insurers, Medicare, Medicaid and other programs to cover crisis response services.
summary: This bill aims to strengthen the 9-8-8 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline and the care that people get after they call. It would authorize new grants for local and regional crisis call centers, for hiring, training, and technology. It would raise funding for a pilot program that pairs mental health responders with emergency calls. It would also create a national suicide prevention media campaign and authorize $1 billion for building and renovating crisis facilities, such as health centers, crisis stabilization units, and call centers. Workforce programs would be expanded to train more crisis workers, including a fellowship for minority students. The bill would require Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, TRICARE, federal employee health plans, VA reimbursement, and private insurers to cover "crisis response services," with cost-sharing no stricter than for medical and surgical care. Most coverage rules start 3 years after enactment. It would set up a federal panel to recommend training and protocols for 9-1-1 dispatchers, including when to send callers to crisis care instead of police, and to set data standards with privacy protections. It would make Medicaid enhanced funding for mobile crisis and other crisis services permanent, and it would change the Medicaid "IMD exclusion" (a rule that limits Medicaid payment to some large mental health facilities) so that certain crisis facilities and clinics are not covered by it. Most spending is "authorized," meaning Congress must still vote to actually fund it.

label: H.R. 10543
title: PREP Act
short_title: PREP Act (Promoting Reentry through Education in Prisons Act of 2026)
one: Creates an Office of Prison Education in the Bureau of Prisons to run education partnerships in federal prisons, share best practices with states, and help incarcerated veterans use education benefits.
summary: This bill would set up a new Office of Prison Education inside the federal Bureau of Prisons. The office would run a Federal Prison Education Program. Through it, schools, nonprofits, community groups, faith-based groups, and employer partnerships could team up with federal prisons to teach reading, high school equivalency, college courses, job training, and apprenticeships. Providers would be picked based on their track record, including completion rates, jobs, and lower repeat-offense rates. Diploma mills (fake or low-quality schools) would be barred. Providers must tell students how a program could affect later job licensing, help them continue studies after release, and offer career and financial aid counseling. The program would be independently evaluated, with results published. The federal share of program costs could not exceed 75 percent, and $170 million of Bureau of Prisons funds would be set aside over fiscal years 2027–2033. The office would also build a public clearinghouse of research and best practices and give training and technical assistance to state prisons. Finally, the Department of Veterans Affairs would reach out to incarcerated veterans in federal and state prisons about education benefits and connect them to programs. Veterans with felony convictions could not receive housing stipends while incarcerated, and their benefits would be reduced by costs that other programs already cover.

one: The bill would require the military to give an honorable discharge, and would protect veterans benefit eligibility, to service members separated solely because of pseudofolliculitis barbae, a painful skin condition caused by shaving.
summary:
Pseudofolliculitis barbae (PFB) is a skin condition, often called razor bumps. It happens when shaved hairs curl back into the skin and cause pain and inflammation. It is more common in people with coarse, curly hair, and it affects Black men at especially high rates. Military grooming rules usually require a clean-shaven face, and some service members have been discharged because they could not meet those rules because of PFB.

This bill deals with what happens after such a discharge. It says the military branch's Secretary must label the separation as "honorable" when the only reason for the discharge is PFB. It also says a person separated solely because of PFB cannot be denied Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) benefits just because they did not serve the minimum amount of active duty time normally required by section 5303A of title 38 of the U.S. Code.

The bill does not change grooming rules, does not say whether shaving waivers must be granted, and does not set up a new benefits program. It only fixes the discharge label and waives the minimum-service rule for these cases. The text does not say whether it applies to past discharges or only to future ones, and it does not give a start date. It also does not give a cost estimate.

label: H.R. 177
title: Yosemite National Park Equal Access and Fairness Act
short_title: Yosemite Equal Access and Fairness Act (Hetch Hetchy)
one: Raises the rent San Francisco pays for its Hetch Hetchy dam and reservoir in Yosemite from $30,000 to $2 million a year, bars passing that cost to wholesale customers, and directs the Park Service to open the reservoir and Lake Eleanor areas to recreation such as swimming, boating, and camping.
summary:
In 1913, Congress passed the Raker Act, which let San Francisco dam the Hetch Hetchy Valley inside Yosemite National Park for water and power. San Francisco pays $30,000 a year in rent for this. This bill would raise the rent to $2 million a year and adjust it each year for inflation. San Francisco's utility could not recover that money from the wholesale water or power customers it sells to. The bill also lets the rent money be used for wildfire mitigation (reducing fire risk), as well as other improvements.

The bill also adds a new section telling the National Park Service to manage the Hetch Hetchy Reservoir and Lake Eleanor Basin for public recreation. It says the agency should preserve scenic, historic, and scientific features. Swimming, non-motorized boating, camping above the high-water mark, picnicking, and other approved activities would be allowed. The Secretary of the Interior could set limits and rules. These activities must not conflict with each area's primary use. Vehicles could use the access roads as long as they do not harm dam operations.

Within one year, the Park Service must report to Congress. The report would cover whether the 1913 access intent has been followed. It would also look at how to fund access, including changing water and power prices, treating San Francisco as a concessioner (a business operating in a park), and adding the value of lost recreation and flood control to the rent.

Yosemite National Park Equal Access and Fairness Act
This bill modifies the Raker Act, which allowed San Francisco to dam the Hetch Hetchy Valley within Yosemite National Park, to (1) increase the annual rent San Francisco pays to the National Park Service (NPS), and (2) direct the NPS to expand public access to the reservoir and lake created by the dam.
Specifically, the bill increases rent paid by the San Francisco Public Utilities Commission for the use of the park from $30,000 to $2 million per year. That amount must be adjusted annually to reflect increases in the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers. The commission may not recoup such sums from wholesale water or power customers. The bill allows collected rent to be used by the Department of the Interior for wildfire mitigation activities in the park and other national parks in California.
The bill also requires the NPS to administer the Hetch Hetchy Reservoir and Lake Eleanor Basin areas for public recreation, benefit, and use in a manner that will preserve scenic, historic, scientific, or otherwise important features.

label: H.R. 2086
title: Rights for the TSA Workforce Act
short_title: Rights for the TSA Workforce Act
one: Moves Transportation Security Administration (TSA) employees onto the standard federal personnel system (Title 5), giving screeners collective bargaining and appeal rights, protecting current pay, and ordering several reports on workplace safety and morale.
summary: Today, TSA runs its own personnel system, set by the agency head. Airport screeners, air marshals and other TSA staff do not get the same job protections and bargaining rights as most other federal workers. This bill would end that special system and place TSA employees under Title 5 of the U.S. Code, the main law covering federal workers. The change would happen no later than December 31, 2025. Within 90 days, screeners would get collective bargaining rights and the right to appeal firings and discipline through the regular federal process. The union certified in 2011 would be treated as their representative, though workers could choose a different one. Bargaining would be mainly national. Strikes would stay illegal. Pay cannot be cut in the switch, and years of service would count toward pay steps. Leave, split-shift pay, and some other benefits would be kept. Federal air marshals would keep availability pay and overtime protections. The bill also requires several reports and briefings. They cover recruitment, diversity in leadership, harassment and assault, threats from the public against screeners, worker morale and retention, and air marshal concerns such as mental health and suicide rates. It also asks for a plan to align background-check rules. It authorizes "such sums as may be necessary" to carry it out, with no dollar figure.

Bars any pay cut in the conversion and credits past service for pay steps.
Preserves accrued leave, part-time screener health premium parity, emergency leave, split-shift pay, and retention incentives.
Keeps law enforcement availability pay and FLSA-level overtime for Federal air marshals.
Keeps the existing ban on strikes.
Orders Government Accountability Office (GAO) reports on recruitment, promotion and leadership diversity, harassment and assault, and implementation.
Requires a TSA briefing on assaults and threats against screeners since 2019 and annual workforce reports on job satisfaction and retention.
Directs TSA to talk with air marshal groups about mental health, suicide, morale, training, and rest schedules.
Authorizes whatever money is needed to carry out the Act.

label: H.R. 3708
title: No Place for LGBTQ+ Hate Act
short_title: No Place for LGBTQ+ Hate Act
one: The bill would cancel five 2025 executive orders on sex and gender identity (covering federal definitions of sex, military service, youth gender-related health care, school sports, and school instruction) and bar federal money from being used to carry them out.
summary:
This bill would wipe out five executive orders (directives from the President) signed in early 2025 that deal with transgender, nonbinary, and intersex people. It says those orders, plus any "related or successor" orders that "similarly harm or limit the rights" of LGBTQI+ people, would have no legal force. It also says no federal money could be used to put them into effect.

The five orders are: EO 14168, which sets the federal government's definition of sex and limits identity markers such as those on IDs; EO 14183, which reinstates and expands a military ban on transgender service members; EO 14187, which directs agencies to act to stop gender-related medical care for people under 19; EO 14201, which bars transgender girls and women from school sports teams matching their gender identity; and EO 14190, which deals with schools and how they address gender identity. The bill's own wording describes these orders in strongly critical terms.

The bill has a savings clause saying it does not reduce any constitutional power of the President. The bill was referred to the Judiciary Committee and several others. It would take effect only if passed by both chambers and signed, or if a veto were overridden. Its text does not include a start date or an estimate of cost.

Includes findings-style language describing the orders as discriminatory and as refusing federal identity markers to some people.
States that the Act does not impair the President's constitutional authority.

Opponents could say the bill's wording about the orders is one-sided, since it describes them in strongly critical terms.
Some could argue that the savings clause does not fully resolve questions about the limits of presidential power.
Schools, sports groups, and agencies could face uncertainty about which rules still apply if the bill passes.

label: H.R. 3717
title: Golden Mussel Eradication and Control Act of 2025
short_title: Golden Mussel Eradication and Control Act of 2025
one: The bill sets up a five-year federal program, led by the Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force, to research, monitor, control and wipe out the invasive golden mussel, starting in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, with $15 million a year authorized.
summary:
The golden mussel is a small invasive shellfish that has shown up in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta. It can clog water pipes, pumps and fish screens, and it can harm native fish and water quality. This bill would change an existing law on aquatic invasive species to create a demonstration (pilot) program aimed at the golden mussel. The federal Aquatic Nuisance Species Task Force would run it, working with state and local governments, port authorities, industry, universities and local nonprofits.

The program would fund research on the mussel's biology, how it affects fish and water quality, and how well different control tools work. It would build an early warning system to predict where the mussel will spread next. It would also develop plans to remove it from boats, abandoned boats, public works, fish screens and waterways, including boat hull inspections. Within one year, the Task Force would write guidelines for controlling the mussel, which could include boat inspection stations.

The bill also creates a competitive grant program for projects that find better ways to remove mussels from water intakes, pipes, screens, boats and waterways. The Task Force could make agreements for the use or sale of new technology developed under the grants. It could hand parts of the work to other agencies if that would work better. Congress would authorize $15 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. Authorizing money does not guarantee it is spent. A separate spending bill would still be needed.

Authorizes $15 million per year for fiscal years 2026-2030.

label: H.R. 4837
title: Written Informed Consent Act
short_title: Written Informed Consent Act
one: The bill would require the VA to extend its written informed-consent rules for long-term opioid pain therapy to also cover antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anxiety medications, and narcotics.
summary: This bill would change how the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) handles certain prescriptions. Right now, a VA Health Administration rule called Directive 1005 (dated May 13, 2020) sets out how doctors must get a patient's informed consent before starting long-term opioid treatment for pain. Informed consent means the patient is told about the benefits, risks, and alternatives and agrees to the treatment. The bill orders the VA Secretary to update that directive so the same kind of consent process applies to five more types of drugs: antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines (anxiolytics), and narcotics. The bill is very short. It does not say what the written consent must contain, how long the update must take, how it will be enforced, or whether any money is provided. Those details would be left to the VA when it rewrites the directive. The bill does not say whether the rules would apply to short-term prescriptions or only long-term use, since the existing directive is about long-term therapy. It also does not spell out which specific drugs count within each category. The bill has been referred to a House subcommittee and has not advanced further.
does: Requires the VA Secretary to update VHA Directive 1005 (May 13, 2020, 'Informed Consent For Long-term Opioid Therapy For Pain').
Extends the directive to antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anxiolytics, and narcotics.
Gives no deadline, funding, or detailed consent requirements in the bill text.
Leaves the details of the new consent process to the VA.

VA doctors, psychiatrists, nurse practitioners, and pharmacists

Applying one consent process across several drug types could make informed consent practices more consistent across VA care.
Written consent may help patients and doctors talk through treatment choices and side effects.
concerns: Because the bill leaves key details to the VA, the actual requirements could differ from what lawmakers expect.
Adding extra consent steps for antipsychotics, antidepressants, and other drugs could add paperwork and may slow access to care, though the size of this effect is not stated.
The bill does not say whether short-term prescriptions are covered, so the reach of the rule is unclear.
Without defined drug lists, it may be hard to know which medicines are covered in each category.
The bill does not describe enforcement, so it is unclear how compliance would be checked.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to extend the VA's existing informed consent rule for long-term opioid therapy (VHA Directive 1005, May 13, 2020) to five more drug types: antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anxiolytics, and narcotics. It aims to have patients receive a written explanation of benefits, risks, and alternatives before starting these medicines. The bill is very short and leaves most details to the VA Secretary.

oppose: The bill leaves key details to the VA, so the actual consent rules could be different from what Congress expects. Lawmakers would have little say over the final requirements.
Adding consent steps for antipsychotics, antidepressants, and other medicines could add paperwork for VA staff and may slow access to care. The bill does not estimate how big this effect would be.

The bill does not say whether short-term prescriptions are covered or which specific drugs fall in each category, so it is unclear how far the rule would reach. Without a timeline, funding, or enforcement plan, it is hard to judge its real effect.
support: The bill would give patients a written explanation of the benefits, risks, and alternatives before they start these medicines, helping them make more informed choices about their care.
Using one consent process across several drug types could make VA informed consent practices more consistent and easier to follow for patients and staff.
Written consent may help patients and doctors talk through treatment options and side effects, which could improve communication about medicines with serious risks.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 1 requires patients to receive written information on benefits, risks, and alternatives before starting these medications, which promotes truthful information for patients, though the bill leaves the content of the consent to the VA.

justice.reason: The bill sets no enforcement mechanism or remedy, so it neither clearly improves nor clearly weakens accountability.

personal_freedom.reason: Sec. 1 adds a required consent step before veterans can begin antipsychotics, stimulants, antidepressants, anxiolytics, and narcotics, which adds a condition on how veterans may obtain these medications.

news.overall: Lean Left coverage links the bill's subject, psychedelic treatment for veterans, to criticism of the Trump administration, VA staffing and care failures, and post-treatment patient harms. Center coverage is more procedural, focusing on veterans' promises and competing congressional benefits bills, and does not mention the psychedelic subject directly. Evidence is limited: each group has only two or three headlines with truncated descriptions, and none of the headlines explicitly names the Written Informed Consent Act, so the framing of the bill itself is inferred rather than confirmed.

label: H.R. 4987
title: Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
short_title: Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
one: Sets one national standard for the wording of voluntary "best by" and "use by" dates on food labels, and blocks states and localities from requiring different wording.
summary: Today, food makers use many different phrases for dates on packages, such as "sell by," "best before," "use by," and "expires on." Shoppers often don't know which ones mean the food is unsafe and which only mean the quality may slip. This bill would create two standard phrases. If a company chooses to print a quality date, it must put "BEST If Used By" in front of it. If it chooses to print a date after which the food should be thrown away, it must use "USE By." Short forms, "BB" and "UB," are allowed only when the package is too small. Companies may add "or freeze by." Dates must be easy to read and easy to find. Putting a date on a package stays optional. The bill covers foods overseen by the FDA and the USDA (meat, poultry, and eggs), but not infant formula. Within two years, the agencies must write rules and start a consumer education campaign. The rules would apply to foods labeled two years after the bill becomes law. The agencies could later pick different standard phrases. Labels that break the rules would count as "misbranded" under federal food laws. The bill also overrides state and local rules about date wording. It bars states and cities from banning the sale or donation of food after its quality date. States may still ban sales or donations after a discard date. People's ability to sue under existing state or federal law is preserved.
does: Requires 'BEST If Used By' (or 'BB' on tiny packages) before any quality date.
Requires 'USE By' (or 'UB' on tiny packages) before any discard date.
Keeps printing a date optional; the company decides whether and on which foods.
Requires dates in an easy-to-read type style and in a prominent place, in month/year or month/day/year form.
Lets companies add 'or freeze by' and use QR codes or smart labels in addition.
Has HHS and USDA write final rules and run consumer education within two years.
Treats noncompliant labels as misbranded under FDA, meat, poultry, and egg laws.
Blocks state and local rules that differ on date wording or ban sale or donation after the quality date, but allows bans after the discard date.
Excludes infant formula and keeps existing rights to sue under other laws.
Applies only to foods labeled two years after enactment.
who: Food manufacturers, grocers, and others who put date labels on food
Shoppers and households
Food banks and food donors
State and local governments with their own date-label or sale/donation rules
FDA, USDA, and the Federal Trade Commission

benefits: Shoppers may more easily tell whether a date means quality or safety.
A single set of phrases may reduce confusion and the cost of meeting many different state rules.
Clear, easy-to-find dates may help people make decisions about food use and waste.
Standard wording may make it easier for businesses that sell in many states to follow one set of rules.
concerns: Because dates stay optional, the bill may not reduce confusion for foods that carry no date.
Preempting state and local rules may limit states' ability to set their own date or food-donation policies.
Allowing states to ban sales after a discard date but not after a quality date may affect how food banks and retailers handle food near its quality date.
Short forms "BB" and "UB" may still be unclear to some shoppers.

unknowns: The material does not say how much the rules or consumer education campaign would cost, or how they would be funded.
It is not stated what the final rules will say, including any alternative phrases the agencies might choose later.
It is not stated how many companies currently use date labels or how many would need to change their packaging.
It is not stated whether the bill will pass the House or Senate, since it is currently in committee.
The material does not explain how the bill's preemption language would interact with specific state laws.

stage.last_action: Referred to the Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to create uniform, standard phrases for voluntary food date labels so shoppers can tell whether a date refers to food quality or to safety. Under the bill, a quality date must be marked "BEST If Used By" (or "BB"), and a discard date must be marked "USE By" (or "UB"). The bill also aims to reduce confusion from the many different date phrases used today and to simplify compliance for businesses that sell in multiple states.

oppose: Putting a date on food stays optional under the bill, so many foods may still carry no date and the confusion may remain for those products.
The bill would block states and cities from setting their own rules on date wording and from banning sale or donation of food after its quality date, which could limit local policy choices.
The bill allows states to ban sales or donations after a discard date but not after a quality date, which could affect how food banks and retailers handle food near its quality date.
The short forms "BB" and "UB" may still be unclear to some shoppers, which could weaken the goal of clearer labels.
support: The bill would create two standard phrases, so shoppers could more easily tell whether a date refers to food quality or to a discard point.
A single national set of phrases could reduce confusion and the cost of meeting many different state labeling rules, especially for businesses that sell across state lines.
Requiring dates to be easy to read and placed prominently could help people make better decisions about using food and reduce food waste.
The bill requires HHS and USDA to write rules and run a consumer education campaign, which could help people learn what the new phrases mean.

crs:
Food Date Labeling Act of 2025
This bill establishes uniform requirements for quality and discard date phrases (e.g., 
best by
 and 
use by
) placed voluntarily on food labels.
Specifically, if a food is labeled with a quality date (i.e., the date after which the quality of the item may deteriorate), the label must include the phrase 
BEST If Used By
 or the abbreviation 
BB
. Similarly, if a food is labeled with a discard date (i.e., the date after which the item should not be consumed), the label must include the phrase 
USE By
 or the abbreviation 
UB
. Abbreviations may be used only if an item’s packaging is too small to fit the full phrase.
Quality and discard dates must be written in a single, easy-to-read font and placed in a prominent location on an item’s label or package. The phrase 
or freeze by
 may be added after a quality or discard date phrase where appropriate.
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Department of Agriculture (USDA) must promulgate regulations to carry out these provisions and ensure that the uniform phrases are standardized across all food products. HHS and USDA may specify alternative quality and discard date phrases through regulations.
The bill specifies that no state or local government may enforce a requirement related to quality and discard date phrases that differs from the requirements of the bill. The bill does not apply to infant formula, which is subject to separate labeling requirements under current law.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. 2 standardizes date wording and requires dates to be easy to read and prominent, so shoppers get clearer information about whether a date signals quality or safety.

local_say.reason: The bill blocks state and local rules that differ on date wording and bars states and cities from banning sale or donation of food after its quality date, removing their ability to set those policies.

justice.reason: The bill states that existing rights to sue under other state or federal law are preserved, so it neither adds nor removes remedies; labels that break the rules are treated as misbranded under federal food law.

label: H.R. 5935
title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
short_title: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act
one: Ratifies a settlement of long-running water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band, two Coachella Valley water agencies, and the U.S., confirming a 20,000 acre-feet-per-year groundwater right, spending $500 million in federal money, and moving about 2,700 acres of federal land into trust for the Tribe.
summary:
This bill would approve a deal, signed May 19, 2025, that ends water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians and two local water agencies, the Coachella Valley Water District (CVWD) and the Desert Water Agency (DWA). The Tribe's right to pump up to 20,000 acre-feet of groundwater a year from the Indio Subbasin (the aquifer under the Palm Springs area) would be confirmed. That right dates to 1876–77 and would take priority over the agencies' claims to native groundwater. The Tribe would also keep its rights to certain creeks.

The federal government would put $500 million into a trust fund for the Tribe: $300 million for water projects, $100 million to reimburse the water agencies for groundwater-recharge projects, $50 million for water management, and $50 million for operations and upkeep. Amounts would be adjusted for construction cost inflation. In exchange, the Tribe and the U.S. would give up many past and some future water claims. They keep claims under the Clean Water Act, the Safe Drinking Water Act and the Superfund law (CERCLA), and claims over misconduct.

The bill moves about 2,700 acres of Bureau of Land Management land into trust for the Tribe, bars gaming on it, and lets CVWD buy about 842 acres at fair market value. It sets up a Tribal possessory-interest tax that replaces the county property tax on those interests, with payments to other local agencies. It also adds protections for Native cultural resources. It takes effect only after several conditions are met, and expires if they aren't met by the end of 2035.
does: placeholder
who: Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians and its members and allottees (individual trust landholders)
Coachella Valley Water District and Desert Water Agency and their ratepayers
Riverside County and other local taxing agencies
Residents and businesses on Agua Caliente reservation land
U.S. taxpayers who fund the $500 million
Users of the Indio Subbasin aquifer in the Palm Springs/Coachella Valley area

benefits: Could end more than a decade of costly litigation (cases filed 2013 and 2020) and give all parties certainty about groundwater use.
Funds recycling, infrastructure, and groundwater-recharge projects that may improve water supply and reliability in a drought-prone aquifer.

Keeps Tribal, federal, and citizen-style water quality claims under the Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act and Superfund, and requires the Interior Secretary to follow NEPA and the Endangered Species Act for projects.
Honors a senior Tribal water right and adds cultural resource and burial protections at the CVWD facility; bars gaming on transferred land.
Allottees get a tribal process with appeals, then federal recourse; the tax deal requires the Tribe to pay other local agencies at least what they would have received, enforceable in federal court.
Public notice: the Secretary must publish findings in the Federal Register before the deal takes effect, and the Tribe must file annual expenditure reports.
concerns: Costs U.S. taxpayers $500 million in mandatory spending, with automatic inflation adjustments that could raise the total.
Waives many damage claims, including past overdraft, subsidence, and water-quality claims where water meets standards; some of these releases are broad and cover unknown claims.
The Tribal water right is not subject to state law or the replenishment charge, and can't be lost through non-use. This could shift aquifer management costs to other pumpers or ratepayers.
The $100 million to reimburse water agencies could be seen as taxpayer money subsidizing local utilities.
Executing the Agreement is declared not a major federal action under NEPA, which limits environmental review of that step; the Tribe prepares environmental documents for later projects.
Land transfers override protections tied to the Santa Rosa and San Jacinto Mountains National Monument and the California Desert Protection Act, and withdraw the land from mining and other uses.
The Tribal tax preempts county property tax, which could reduce local government oversight; the Tribe need not pay other agencies more than they'd otherwise get.
Off-reservation leasing of water for up to 99 years, with Secretary approval, could affect neighboring communities.
Some expenditure details and tribal rate-setting for reservation customers are in the Agreement, which I could not see.

The Facility Land sale would bring in fair-market-value proceeds, paid by CVWD. The antideficiency clause says the U.S. isn't liable if Congress doesn't appropriate the funds. No CBO estimate was provided.
unknowns: The full Settlement Agreement and its exhibits were not provided, so many details (fees, forbearance, recycled water projects) can't be checked.
No CRS summary or cost estimate is available.
Exact effect on water rates for Coachella Valley customers is unclear.
How the aquifer will fare under 20,000 AFY of Tribal pumping rights plus recharge projects is unclear.
Whether the mandatory appropriation will be paid for with offsets is unclear.

purpose: The bill says its goal is to approve a settlement, signed May 19, 2025, that ends water lawsuits between the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians and the Coachella Valley Water District and Desert Water Agency, and to confirm the Tribe's groundwater and creek rights in the Indio Subbasin. It also provides $500 million in federal funding for water projects and related purposes, along with land transfers into trust for the Tribe. The summary provided does not include an official CRS summary, so this description relies on the bill's title and the plain-English summary provided.

oppose: The bill would commit $500 million in mandatory federal spending, and its inflation adjustments could raise the total over time. You may want to ask how this cost compares with other priorities.

The settlement waives many past and some future water claims, including some damage claims such as overdraft, subsidence, and certain water-quality claims, and some of these releases cover unknown claims. You may want to ask whether ratepayers and other pumpers have been fully protected.

The Tribal water right would not be subject to state law or the replenishment charge and could not be lost through non-use, which could shift aquifer management costs onto other groundwater users or ratepayers. You may want to ask how these costs would be shared.
support: The bill would end litigation that was filed in 2013 and 2020, giving the Tribe, the water agencies, and other parties more certainty about groundwater use in the Indio Subbasin.
The $500 million trust fund would support recycling, infrastructure, and groundwater-recharge projects that could improve water supply and reliability in a drought-prone aquifer.

The bill honors a Tribal water right dating to 1876-77 and adds cultural resource and burial protections, while keeping Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act, and Superfund claims and requiring NEPA and Endangered Species Act review for projects.

cost_flag: $500 million in mandatory federal spending from the Treasury ($300M development projects, $100M groundwater augmentation, $50M water management, $50M operations and maintenance), adjusted upward or downward for construction costs from May 19, 2025. $50 million of it is available right away; the rest after the Enforceability Date. The Facility Land sale would bring in fair-market-value proceeds, paid by CVWD. The antideficiency clause says the U.S. isn't liable if Congress doesn't appropriate the funds. No CBO estimate was provided.

transparency_kindness.reason: Sec. on Executing the Agreement declares it not a major federal action under NEPA, limiting public environmental review of that step, though the Secretary must publish findings in the Federal Register and the Tribe must file annual expenditure reports.

people_over_profit.reason: The $100M reimbursement to water agencies and the Tribal water right that is not subject to the replenishment charge could shift aquifer management costs from pumpers and ratepayers to the public and other users.

local_say.reason: The Tribal possessory-interest tax preempts county property tax, and the federal confirmation of the water right and land transfers override state law and local land-use protections such as the Monument protections.

no_bailouts.reason: Sec. on the $500M trust fund includes $100 million to reimburse the water agencies for groundwater-recharge projects, using Treasury funds to support local utilities, and the Tribal water right is exempt from the replenishment charge, shifting costs to other ratepayers.

equality.reason: The bill's tribal-specific provisions (water right, tax and gaming bar) apply to one tribe under a settlement; the effects on equal treatment are mixed and not clearly unequal in the sense of this definition.

justice.reason: The bill ends litigation and adds appeals for allottees and enforceability in federal court, but it also waives many claims, including unknown ones, and keeps Clean Water Act, Safe Drinking Water Act and CERCLA claims, so the net effect on fairness is mixed.

news.overall: None of the provided headlines or descriptions mention the Agua Caliente Band of Cahuilla Indians Water Rights Settlement Act, so this set of coverage cannot show how outlets frame the bill itself. The Lean Left group has six articles, but they cover El Niño, coastal flooding, groundwater, and wildfire insurance rather than the bill, and the descriptions are empty so only headlines were available. The Center group has one article, about Napa Valley wine history, which is unrelated; the evidence for that perspective is too thin to characterize at all. Coverage specific to this bill would need to be gathered to make a meaningful comparison.
