crs:
Washington, D.C. Admission Act
This bill provides for the establishment of the State of Washington, Douglass Commonwealth, and its admission into the United States.
The state is composed of most of the territory of the District of Columbia (DC), excluding a specified area that encompasses the U.S. Capitol, the White House, the U.S. Supreme Court building, federal monuments, and federal office buildings adjacent to the National Mall and the U.S. Capitol. The excluded territory shall be known as the Capital and serve as the seat of the government of the United States, as provided for in Article I of the Constitution. The state may not impose taxes on federal property except as Congress permits.
The bill provides for the DC Mayor to issue a proclamation for the first elections to Congress of two Senators and one Representative of the state. The bill eliminates the office of Delegate to the House of Representatives.
The bill applies current DC laws to the state. DC judicial proceedings and contractual obligations shall continue under the state’s authority. The bill also provides for specified federal obligations to transfer to the state upon its certification that it has funds and laws in place to assume the obligations. These include maintaining a retirement fund for judges and operating public defender services. 
The bill establishes a commission that is generally comprised of members who are appointed by DC and federal government officials to advise on an orderly transition to statehood.

environment.reason: The bill does not change environmental protection rules; it mainly addresses governance, boundaries, and federal functions, with water supply role of the Army Corps kept unchanged.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill includes a Transition Commission and public election procedures, but it also has drafting oddities and no cost estimate, which roughly offset each other.

people_over_profit.reason: The bill mainly shifts federal costs during transition to taxpayers, but its primary effect is on residents' representation and self-rule rather than corporate profit margins.

local_say.reason: Sec. on admission and Title I give about 700,000 DC residents two Senators and a voting Representative and let the state govern itself with its own constitution and budget, free of congressional override.

no_bailouts.reason: Title III continues federal funding for courts, pensions, Medicaid matching at the current rate, and loaned prosecutors without reimbursement, which shifts some fiscal responsibility to federal taxpayers during transition.

equality.reason: Title I admits DC on equal footing with the states, giving its residents full voting representation in Congress that they currently lack.

justice.reason: The bill includes a severability and nonseverability structure and absentee voting enforceable by the Attorney General, but it also limits amendment and debate on the 23rd Amendment resolution, so effects on fairness are mixed.

personal_freedom.reason: Title I and Title II let residents vote for full congressional representation and absentee voting in their last state of residence for Capital residents, expanding their say over their own governance.

news.overall: Only five headlines were provided, and only two (The Economist and Roll Call) touch on D.C. or the broader political landscape in a way tied to the bill's subject. The Lean Left evidence rests on a single article that does not mention statehood. The Center group has more coverage, but most of it is about midterm results and party dynamics rather than the D.C. Admission Act itself. The sample is too thin to say how perspectives differ on the bill's merits. Descriptions were not included, so these readings rely on headlines alone.

label: H.R. 510
title: Regulatory Cooling Off Act of 2025
short_title: Regulatory Cooling Off Act of 2025
one: Requires most final federal agency rules to wait 6 months (instead of 30 days) before taking effect, lengthens public comment to at least 60 days, adds posting and notice requirements, and makes it easier to sue agencies in more courts.
summary:
When a federal agency, such as the EPA or the FDA, writes a new rule, it usually must let the public comment first. After the rule is final, it normally can't take effect for at least 30 days. This bill would change that in several ways.

First, the public would get at least 60 days to comment on a proposed rule. Second, the waiting period before a final rule takes effect would grow from 30 days to 6 months. Third, agencies would have to send each final rule to the congressional committees that oversee the issue at least 6 months before it takes effect. They would also have to post final and proposed rules on their own websites at least 24 hours before publishing them in the Federal Register (the government's daily journal of rules), and publish a notice on the day a rule actually takes effect.

The bill also changes where people can sue an agency over a rule. A lawsuit could be filed in the plaintiff's home district or in any district where the agency has an office. Finally, it changes the Congressional Review Act, the law that lets Congress cancel new rules. Big rules that now wait 60 days would wait 6 months, unless Congress passes a measure approving them.

The bill does not say whether existing exceptions to the waiting period, such as emergencies, would still apply. It does not edit those parts of the law.

who: Federal agencies that write rules (for example, environmental, health, safety, and consumer agencies)
Members of the public who comment on proposed rules

Congress and its committees, which would get rules earlier

benefits: A 60-day minimum comment period gives the public, local groups, and small organizations more time to review and respond to proposals.
Posting rules on agency websites 24 hours before publication, and publishing a notice on the effective date, adds some transparency.
Sending rules to Congress earlier could improve oversight of agencies by elected officials.
Letting people sue in their home district could make court challenges cheaper and easier for ordinary people and local communities.
A longer runway could give businesses, small businesses, and local governments more time to prepare for compliance.
concerns: A 6-month delay on rules could slow protections for clean air, clean water, food and workplace safety, and public health.
The longer delay and the Congress-approval condition for major rules could give regulated industries more time to lobby against or block rules, which could favor corporate interests over the public.
Broader court venue could also let industry groups choose favorable courts to challenge rules, and could encourage forum shopping (picking a court expected to rule a certain way).

The requirement to send a rule to Congress 6 months before it takes effect, combined with the 6-month delay, could make it hard for agencies to act quickly in emergencies, unless existing exceptions still apply.
Longer delays may raise agency workload and costs and slow changes that relieve burdens on people (such as rules that loosen restrictions), if those are not exempt.
imp.cost: No cost estimate or funding provisions are in the text. Costs could come from agency administrative work and more litigation. The delayed benefits or savings from rules could also have economic effects, but none are quantified here.
unknowns: Whether existing exceptions in section 553(d) (such as good cause or interpretive rules) would still apply. The bill does not change them, but I could not see the full existing statute in the material provided.
How the Congressional Review Act changes would work in practice, especially the phrase 'unless the Congress enacts a joint resolution or other measure explicitly approving the rule.'
How emergency or deadline-driven rules set by other laws would be handled.
The number of cosponsors and whether a committee will take up the bill.
No Congressional Research Service summary or cost estimate was available.

It would require at least 60 days for public comment on proposed rules, lengthen the wait before final rules take effect from 30 days to 6 months, and require earlier notice to Congress and public posting of rules. The bill's own summary describes these changes as adding transparency and oversight of agency rulemaking.

oppose: A 6-month waiting period before final rules take effect could delay protections for clean air, clean water, food safety, workplace safety, and public health.
The bill does not say whether emergency exceptions would still apply, so agencies could have trouble acting quickly when urgent problems arise.
Allowing lawsuits in any district where an agency has an office could let industry groups pick favorable courts, which could encourage forum shopping.
support: A 60-day minimum comment period gives the public, local groups, and small organizations more time to review proposed rules and respond.

transparency_kindness.reason: The 60-day minimum comment period and the 24-hour advance website posting plus effective-date notice give the public more time to review and see rules before publication.

people_over_profit.reason: The longer delays and the Congress-approval condition for major rules give regulated industries more time and more avenues to block public-protection rules, while the longer compliance runway benefits businesses.

no_bailouts.reason: The bill does not provide bailouts, subsidies, or ratepayer cost shifts.

equality.reason: The bill applies the same procedures to all parties and does not create differing treatment by group.

justice.reason: The home-district venue provision makes it easier for ordinary people to bring suit, and the agency posting and notice requirements add accountability, though the delays and forum choice for industry cut the other way.

label: H.R. 5112
title: Tipped Worker Protection Act
short_title: Tipped Worker Protection Act
one: The bill would phase out the lower "tipped" minimum wage so tipped workers get the full federal minimum wage, and it adds new rules to stop employers from keeping tips, hiding service charges, or imposing tip pools without worker votes.
summary:
Right now, employers can pay tipped workers a lower cash wage (the federal floor is $2.13 an hour) as long as tips bring them up to the regular minimum wage. This bill would end that system in steps. In the first year after enactment, the minimum cash wage for tipped workers would be $3.60 an hour. Each year after, it would rise by $1.50 until it reaches the regular federal minimum wage (currently $7.25). At that point, tipped workers would be paid the full minimum wage by the employer, and tips would be extra.

The bill also sets new tip rules. Employers could not keep tips, and managers and supervisors could not take any part of them. Employers could not use tips to pay credit card processing fees. Tip pools (where tips are shared) would only be allowed if at least 51 percent of non-supervisory workers vote for them, after at least 30 percent ask for a vote. Joining a pool would have to be voluntary, and workers could not be punished for how they vote.

Mandatory service charges would have to be explained to customers and workers, including how much goes directly to workers. Any part promised to workers must be paid to them promptly. A charge described as optional could not be added unless the customer asks. Those worker-directed charges would also count as tips for an employer Social Security tax credit. Penalties for misusing tips would be expanded. The bill's text does not include cost estimates.

label: H.R. 5122
title: NASA Talent Exchange Program Act
short_title: NASA Talent Exchange Program Act
one: Lets NASA swap employees with private companies for 3 months to 3 years, with ethics, conflict-of-interest, and reporting rules attached.
summary:
This bill would let NASA set up a program to temporarily trade workers with private companies. A NASA employee could work at a company, or a company's employee could work at NASA. Both the company and the worker must agree. Each assignment would last at least three months and normally no more than two years. It could run up to three years if NASA decides the mission needs it. A single NASA employee could not spend more than three years total on these assignments.

A written agreement would cover each assignment. NASA employees would have to return to government service for twice as long as their assignment, or repay the costs. Company workers sent to NASA would stay on their company's payroll. They would be treated as federal employees for many ethics, conflict-of-interest, and liability laws. They could not see the home company's trade secrets. They also could not do "inherently governmental" work, meaning core decisions that only the government should make. The company could not bill the government for those workers' pay. No more than 2% of NASA's civil service workforce could be on assignment at once.

NASA would have to build a system to manage conflicts of interest. It would also have to send Congress yearly reports. These would name the companies, positions, and pay grades involved. The Government Accountability Office (GAO, Congress's watchdog) would review the program within three years. The bill does not say who pays the salary of NASA workers sent to a company.

label: H.R. 5147
title: WIRELESS Leadership Act
short_title: WIRELESS Leadership Act (cell tower and small cell approval deadlines)
one: Sets firm deadlines for state and local governments to approve or deny cell tower and small-cell requests, treats missed deadlines as approvals, caps fees, and bars local regulation based on radio-frequency health or environmental concerns when FCC limits are met.
summary: This bill rewrites part of federal communications law that now preserves local control over where cell towers and other wireless equipment go. Under the bill, cities, counties, and states would have to approve or deny a complete request within set deadlines: 60 to 150 days, depending on whether the equipment is a "small cell" (antennas of 3 cubic feet or less) and whether it uses an existing structure. If a government misses the deadline, the applicant can send written notice and the request is automatically treated as approved. Deadlines could not be paused by a local moratorium (a temporary ban on new applications). Any denial must be in writing, backed by evidence in a written record, and made public the same day. Local governments could not discriminate among providers, and could not block service. They could still set objective, reasonable engineering, safety, and appearance rules, unless those rules effectively block installations. Fees would have to be set in advance, made public, and based on actual, reasonable costs. The bill also bars local governments from regulating wireless facilities based on the environmental effects of radio-frequency emissions, as long as the equipment meets Federal Communications Commission (FCC) limits. Anyone harmed by a violation could sue within 30 days or petition the FCC, which must rule within 120 days. The bill does not include new federal spending. It cuts local review time and the community's ability to slow or reject projects, while aiming to speed wireless service.

Allows objective, reasonable, nondiscriminatory structural engineering standards, safety requirements, and aesthetic or concealment rules, unless they effectively prohibit installation.

Sets decision deadlines for complete requests: 90 days (existing structure) or 150 days (other) for larger facilities; 60 days (existing structure) or 90 days (other) for small facilities with antennas of 3 cubic feet or less. Batched requests get the longest applicable deadline. The deadline covers all required local proceedings, and a moratorium does not pause it.

Bars states and localities from regulating wireless facilities based on environmental effects of radio-frequency emissions, as long as the facilities meet FCC emission rules.

Limits fees (for request review and for right-of-way use) to those that are competitively and technology neutral, set in advance and public, based on actual, direct, objectively reasonable costs (review, processing, and repairs), and described by recurring versus nonrecurring and by whether the facility is already located there.
Lets anyone adversely affected sue in court within 30 days (expedited) or petition the FCC, which must grant or deny within 120 days.

Defines when a request is 'complete': the applicant takes the first procedural step, and the government gives no written notice of missing information within 10 days (small facilities) or 30 days (others) that cites a specific public rule. Excludes eligible facilities requests under existing section 6409(a) of the 2012 law, which keeps its own rules.
Adds definitions, such as personal wireless service, small facility, antenna, and wireline backhaul.

Winning the International Race for Economic Leadership and Expanding Service to Support Leadership Act or the WIRELESS Leadership Act
This bill imposes limits on state and local review and regulation of requests to construct wireless telecommunication facilities.
Specifically, states and localities must grant or deny requests to place, modify, or construct personal wireless service (PWS) facilities by a specified deadline. This deadline varies based on the nature of the request and the proposed facility. If a state or locality fails to act on a request within that timeframe, the request is deemed granted. On the day a decision to deny a request is made, the state or locality must publish the decision and provide it to the requesting party.
Further, the bill expands an existing prohibition on unreasonable discrimination in the regulation of such requests. Under the bill, any discrimination among PWS facilities or communications service providers is prohibited. For example, a state or locality may not grant preferential or exclusive use of facilities to a particular provider or class of providers. However, states and localities may establish objective, reasonable, and nondiscriminatory engineering standards, safety requirements, or aesthetic requirements.
Finally, the bill establishes requirements for fees imposed by states and localities for consideration of a request. For example, such fees must be (1) competitively neutral, technology neutral, and nondiscriminatory; (2) established in advance and publicly disclosed; and (3) based on actual and direct costs to the state or locality.

justice.reason: The 30-day expedited suit window and FCC petition path favor well-resourced applicants, and the requirement to cite a specific public rule for incompleteness notices narrows local recourse; the written-denial requirement and private right of action partly offset this.

personal_freedom.reason: The bill governs government permitting of facilities and does not directly expand or restrict what individuals may do about their own lives.

label: H.R. 5151
title: Quiet Communities Act of 2025
short_title: Quiet Communities Act of 2025
one: The bill would bring back the EPA's Office of Noise Abatement and Control to research noise pollution, help states and towns fight it, and study aircraft noise, with $25 million a year authorized for five years.
summary:
This bill would restart an office inside the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that deals with noise pollution. That office, called the Office of Noise Abatement and Control, has not had funding since 1982. Congress says that has left noise programs across the country dormant, even though the EPA is still legally responsible for enforcing the noise rules already on the books.

The restarted office would give states technical help and grants to build noise control programs. Those grants could cover equipment for local communities. The office would also research how noise affects mental and physical health, track noise levels over time, and create public education materials, training, and workshops. It would set up regional help centers that work with colleges and private groups. It would also review how well the 1972 Noise Control Act has worked.

The EPA would also run a special study of aircraft noise. Outside scientists would look at how the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) measures noise, at what noise level health problems begin, and at whether airport noise programs work. A report with recommendations would be due to Congress within 2 years.

The bill also updates the grant section of the 1972 Noise Control Act and repeals a 1970 noise law. It says the office should favor approaches that rely on state and local action, market incentives, and teamwork with other agencies. It authorizes $25 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. "Authorizes" means Congress would still have to actually provide the money in a separate spending bill.

transparency_kindness.reason: The bill creates public education materials, training, workshops, and a noise-level tracking function, and requires an aircraft noise study report to Congress, which makes information about noise and health more available to the public.

label: H.R. 5152
title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
short_title: BOP Release Card ID Act of 2025
one: Requires the federal Bureau of Prisons to give departing U.S.-citizen prisoners a REAL ID-standard photo ID card valid at least 18 months, to be accepted for many federal benefit programs and to help them get state IDs.
summary:
This bill would require the Bureau of Prisons (BOP), which runs federal prisons, to hand a photo ID card to each U.S. citizen leaving federal custody. The card would have to meet the federal REAL ID security standards. The BOP would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to start issuing the cards. Each card would stay valid for at least 18 months after the person is released.

The bill would also make many federal agencies and programs accept the card as proof of identity. These include Social Security, Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP (food assistance), TANF (cash assistance), and programs at the Education, Housing and Urban Development, and Veterans Affairs departments. It would also cover federal probation and pretrial services, the D.C. offender supervision agency, and entry into federal buildings.

The BOP director would have to negotiate with each state so the card can be used to get a state ID. The director would report on that progress to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees each year, starting one year after enactment. Within one year, the Attorney General would also issue guidance to states that want to issue similar release cards to people leaving state prisons. The bill does not say how much this would cost, and it does not replace the BOP's existing duty to plan for prisoners' release. It does not cover non-citizens.

one: Changes how often the Manufacturing USA program must update its strategic plan from every 3 years to every 4 years, so it lines up with the National Strategy for Advanced Manufacturing.
summary:
Manufacturing USA is a network of institutes where government, companies, and universities work together on new manufacturing technology. Under current law, the program's strategic plan (a planning document that sets goals and priorities) must be updated at least every 3 years. A separate document, the National Strategy for Advanced Manufacturing, must be updated every 4 years. Because the two cycles do not match, the timing can be awkward.

This bill changes the program's update schedule to at least once every 4 years. The goal stated in the bill is to match the national strategy's cycle so the program better reflects national priorities. The bill does not create new programs, give out money, or change who can take part in Manufacturing USA. It also makes small wording changes in nearby paragraphs so that references to the plan include the new update requirement. The bill was introduced on September 4, 2025, by Rep. Luz Rivas (D-CA) with one cosponsor, Rep. David Rouzer (R-NC), and was sent to the House Science, Space, and Technology Committee. It has not moved further. The text does not say when the change would take effect beyond becoming law.

title: Nationwide Right to Unionize Act
short_title: Nationwide Right to Unionize Act
one: The bill would repeal the part of federal labor law that lets states ban contracts requiring workers to join or pay a union, which would end state "right-to-work" laws.
summary: Federal labor law lets employers and unions agree to a contract rule that workers covered by the union contract must support the union, usually by paying dues or fees, to keep their jobs. These are called "union security" agreements. Right now, Section 14(b) of the National Labor Relations Act lets each state ban those agreements. About half the states have used that power to pass "right-to-work" laws. This bill is just one operative sentence. It repeals Section 14(b). If it became law, states could no longer ban union security agreements for workplaces covered by that Act, which covers most private-sector employers. Employers and unions in those states could then negotiate these agreements, as they already can in other states. The bill does not force any employer or union to adopt such an agreement. It only removes the state ban. The bill text does not say when it would start, and it does not add other rules, funding, or penalties. The title talks about a "right to unionize," but the bill does not change the right to form or join a union. It only changes whether states can bar union-security clauses. Outside the bill text, existing court rulings limit what unions can require of workers who object to joining. Those rulings are not changed by this bill. Because there is no CRS summary yet, this reading relies on the short bill text.

one: Lets TV subscribers in 13 northwestern Wisconsin counties, who now get Minnesota-market stations, choose to receive Wisconsin network stations instead of, or in addition to, their assigned local stations.
summary: Some Wisconsin counties near the Minnesota border are placed in TV markets based in another state, so cable and satellite customers there often see Minnesota news, weather, and sports instead of Wisconsin programming. This bill would let customers in 13 named Wisconsin counties (Ashland, Barron, Bayfield, Burnett, Douglas, Dunn, Florence, Iron, Pierce, Polk, Sawyer, St. Croix, and Washburn) pick what they get for each TV network. They could choose the local-market station their provider must already carry, a Wisconsin station from a neighboring TV market, or both. The bill applies to counties that have no same-network station of their own in Wisconsin. If a customer picks only the Wisconsin station, that counts as meeting the provider's duty to carry a local station. The bill also changes some copyright and broadcast-rule details so these Wisconsin signals do not use up satellite limits, do not need the usual cable permission deal, and are treated as "significantly viewed" (a rule that lets certain out-of-market stations be carried). Satellite companies only have to do this where it is technically feasible, as decided by the FCC. The bill does not say when it would start or what it would cost, and the text does not describe how it affects local stations' finances.

Go Pack Go Act of 2025
This bill requires cable and satellite television providers to make Wisconsin-based television programming available to subscribers in counties assigned to out-of-state television markets.
U.S. counties are assigned to geographic television markets, and television providers are generally required to provide subscribers with programming local to their assigned market. Counties on state borders are sometimes assigned to out-of-state markets; subscribers in those counties often receive out-of-state programming (e.g., out-of-state news and sports).
Under the bill, a cable or satellite television provider must offer subscribers in specified Wisconsin counties with the choice of (1) programming local to the subscriber's assigned market that the provider is currently required to retransmit, (2) Wisconsin-based adjacent-market programming, or (3) both.
The bill also establishes that the provision of Wisconsin-based programming to subscribers who have elected it fulfills certain statutory coverage obligations applicable to providers.

label: H.R. 5170
title: CABLE Leadership Act
short_title: CABLE Leadership Act
one: Requires local cable franchising authorities to approve or deny a new cable franchise request within 120 days, or the request is automatically approved.
summary: Today, a cable company that wants to offer service in a town or county usually needs a "franchise," which is a permission agreement from the local government (the "franchising authority"). This bill would put a strict clock on that process for new franchise requests (not renewals). The local government would have 120 days after getting a complete request to say yes or no. If it misses the deadline, the request is automatically treated as approved. The clock covers all local steps combined, and a local moratorium (a pause on considering requests), whether official or informal, cannot stop the clock. If a local government says no, it must do so in writing, back the decision with substantial evidence in a written record, and release it publicly and to the applicant the same day. The bill also defines a "complete" request. A request counts as complete once the applicant takes the first step the locality requires, unless the locality sends a written notice within 30 days naming the missing information and citing a public rule that requires it. If no such notice arrives, the request is treated as complete and received the day after that 30-day period ends. The bill does not mention broadband build-out terms, community service requirements, or fees, so how those would interact with automatic approval is not addressed in the text.

label: H.R. 663
title: To oppose the permitting of deep seabed mining and exploration for deep seabed mining, and for other purposes.
short_title: Oppose Deep Seabed Mining Permitting Act
one: The bill would direct the President to have U.S. representatives at international bodies push for a pause on deep seabed mining permits and exploration, and oppose funding for it, until international rules are in place and certified as protective of the ocean.
summary: This bill is about mining the deep ocean floor for minerals. It starts with a list of findings from Congress. These say scientists think deep seabed mining poses major risks, such as killing unique species, creating large clouds of sediment, adding noise pollution, possibly contaminating food fish, and harming the ocean's ability to store carbon. It also says we don't yet know enough about the deep sea to judge the full risks. The bill then states the "sense of Congress," which is a non-binding opinion. That opinion is that no deep seabed mining should happen in international waters until the International Seabed Authority (the UN-linked body that oversees the international seabed) adopts a full, binding set of rules based on solid science. The one binding part is an instruction to the President. The President must tell U.S. representatives at international organizations the U.S. belongs to or observes to use the country's voice, vote, and influence to call for a moratorium (a pause) on permitting deep seabed mining and exploration. They must also oppose investment, financing, or other support for it. This continues until the President certifies to Congress that the International Seabed Authority has issued regulations that are based on scientific consensus and effectively protect the marine environment. The President must also send Congress a report describing those regulations. The bill does not create a domestic ban or change U.S. law on permits.

label: H.R. 664
title: American Seabed Protection Act
short_title: American Seabed Protection Act
one: Bans new federal permits for deep seabed mining and for hardrock mining on the Outer Continental Shelf (except scientific research) and orders a National Academies study of the environmental effects of such mining.
summary:
This bill would stop the U.S. government from issuing licenses, permits, or other approvals for two kinds of ocean mining. The first is exploring for or commercially recovering minerals from the deep seabed, which is the ocean floor beyond national boundaries that current law lets U.S. companies seek permits for. The second is exploring for, developing, or producing hardrock minerals (such as metals) on the Outer Continental Shelf, the underwater lands off U.S. coasts that the federal government manages. Permits for scientific research would still be allowed.

The bill also tells the Commerce Secretary, working through NOAA, to try to make a deal within 90 days with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. The Academies would do a broad study of how this mining could affect ocean life, habitats, sediment clouds, the ocean's ability to store greenhouse gases, fishing, recreation, fish farms, undersea cables, and Indigenous peoples and cultures. The study would also estimate greenhouse gas emissions from mining and look at alternatives, like recycling, substitute materials, and cleaner land-based mining. NOAA would send a report on the findings to key House and Senate committees.

The bill begins with findings that say scientists have raised serious concerns about deep seabed mining and that there is not enough information to judge its risks. It does not set a deadline for the study or give a dollar amount.

Requires the study to assess alternatives such as recycling, substitute materials, and less harmful land-based mining.

title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
short_title: Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
one: Directs USDA to create a single application (or shared-information system) and standard technology so small direct-selling farmers and ranchers can more easily accept SNAP, WIC, senior farmers market, and GusNIP benefits.
summary:
Farmers who sell directly to shoppers, such as at farmers markets, often have to fill out separate applications for each federal food assistance program they want to accept. They also may need different equipment for each one. This bill would tell the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to make that easier.

First, USDA would build either a single application farmers and ranchers could use to apply to SNAP (food stamps), WIC (nutrition aid for women, infants, and children), the Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program, and the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program (which helps people buy more fruits and vegetables). Or, USDA would build a system that shares a farmer's information between programs, so approval in one program automatically counts as pre-qualified for the others.

Second, USDA would set up a streamlined way for these farmers to process benefits with standard technology, such as one device or one mobile app.

Third, the bill changes the SNAP law so USDA must make sure equipment and systems that states or their partners provide are right for the seller. For farmers markets and other direct-to-consumer markets, that includes wireless or mobile equipment.

USDA must report to Congress on progress within one year. The bill gives no dollar amounts for funding.

Promoting Access to Local Agriculture Act of 2026
This bill directs the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to establish a streamlined process for farmers and ranchers to provide benefits under certain federal nutrition programs. These programs include the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP); the Senior Farmers Market Nutrition Program (SFMNP); the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC); and the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program (GusNIP).
Specifically, USDA must establish a streamlined application process for farmers and ranchers to apply to be vendors under the nutrition programs, including by developing a single application for the programs or an information sharing system. USDA must also develop a streamlined process for these vendors to use standardized technology to process program benefits (such as a single piece of equipment or a mobile application).

For example, this includes ensuring wireless or mobile processing equipment and technology systems are appropriate for farmers markets and other direct-to-consumer markets.

label: H.R. 9968
title: Opening Programs to Organic Farms Act
short_title: Opening Programs to Organic Farms Act
one: Requires the USDA to study and publicly report on barriers that organic and organic-transitioning farms face in USDA programs, then give three yearly progress updates.
summary: This bill does not create new programs or hand out money. It orders the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to study why certified organic farms, and farms thinking about switching to organic, have trouble using USDA programs. The USDA would have 180 days after the bill becomes law to send a report to the House and Senate agriculture committees and post it on its website. The report would look at programs for conservation, loans, disaster aid, crop insurance, exports, marketing, technical help, rural development, data collection, buying food for government use, and organic certification cost-sharing. It would include data where possible on how many organic farms apply, are approved or denied, how much funding they get, where they are, and why they are denied or don't take part. It would also look at specific problems such as eligibility rules, payment rates, paperwork, crop insurance prices, how disaster losses are valued, and whether USDA staff know enough about organic farming. It would assess the need for organic training for field staff. The USDA must describe the steps it plans to take and suggest any law changes Congress should consider. For three years after, it must post yearly updates on progress and remaining barriers.

short_title: Ahmad Butler Pediatric Cancer Hope for a Cure Act
one: The bill would put $2 billion over 10 years into childhood cancer research and help families pay for clinical trial costs, and it would create a voluntary donation fund, including a tax-return checkoff, for the same work.
summary: This bill aims to fight childhood cancer. It tells the Department of Health and Human Services to step up research, especially on rare and high-risk tumors, brain cancers, cancers that come back or resist treatment, and the long-term health of survivors. It also tells the National Institutes of Health to start a research effort on holistic, nutritional, and alternative therapies. That research must be evidence-based and focused on safety and effectiveness. The bill creates grants for families in pediatric cancer clinical trials. These can cover travel, lodging, meals, childcare, and unpaid leave. Other grants go to groups that run trials, to open sites in underserved areas. Congress would appropriate $2 billion for fiscal years 2027 through 2036. That money could not be shifted to adult cancer programs. The bill also sets up the "One Lunch 4 Cure" fund at the Treasury. People, employers, and groups could donate voluntarily, including by payroll deduction and by a line on federal tax returns that lets filers send an overpayment to the fund. The fund could not pay agency administrative costs, and the Government Accountability Office (GAO) would audit it every year. HHS would send Congress yearly reports on spending, results, trial enrollment, and gaps. The bill says it should not reduce existing pediatric cancer programs.

title: Public Shipyard Workforce Protection Act of 2026
short_title: Public Shipyard Workforce Protection Act of 2026
one: Bars the Defense Department from using fiscal year 2027 funds to freeze hiring, cut staff through layoffs, or needlessly delay filling civilian jobs at public (government-owned) shipyards.
summary: This bill is short. It says that for fiscal year 2027, money given to the Department of Defense cannot be used to do three things at a public shipyard. A public shipyard is a government-owned yard, such as the Navy yards that repair ships and submarines. First, the department cannot freeze hiring there. Second, it cannot carry out a "reduction in force," which is the formal name for layoffs or job cuts. Third, it cannot delay filling an open federal civilian job there without a good reason. The bill does not define "public shipyard" or "without cause," and the text we have doesn't say who decides what counts as a good reason. It does not add new money, create new jobs, or set hiring targets. It only limits how existing funds may be used for one year. The bill was introduced November 17, 2026, and sent to the House Armed Services Committee and the Oversight and Government Reform Committee. It has not yet had a vote or hearing. There is no Congressional Research Service summary yet.

one: Requires companies seeking or holding Defense Department aerospace contracts to disclose ties to Chinese entities on U.S. government military-concern lists, and requires the Pentagon to assess those ties, without banning them.
summary: This bill would make companies that bid on or hold certain Defense Department (DoD) aerospace contracts tell the Pentagon about business ties to Chinese companies the U.S. government has already flagged as helping China's military. Covered contracts, grants, and other agreements involve software, technology, or intellectual property used to design, build, or maintain military aircraft, spacecraft, launch vehicles, propulsion, avionics, and related systems. Ties that must be reported include joint ventures, technology or intellectual property licenses, co-production deals, any stock ownership (even partial), and other arrangements that give recurring access to the company's controlled technology, people, or facilities. Parent companies and affiliates count. The Defense Secretary would issue guidance within 90 days. Current contractors would have 180 days after that guidance to report existing ties. New ties and ties with newly listed entities would have to be reported within 90 days. The Pentagon must review each disclosure for security, supply chain, and technology-transfer risks. It may require fixes or weigh the disclosure, or a failure to disclose, when deciding whether to renew a contract. It is not required to act, and the bill does not ban any relationship. The Pentagon would also send Congress an annual report, unclassified but possibly with a classified annex, giving the number and general nature of disclosed ties and actions taken.

label: S. 5608
title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2026
short_title: Secure Rural Schools Reauthorization Act of 2026
one: Extends by three years the federal program that sends payments to rural counties and schools near national forests and other federal land, and fixes a few typos.
summary: Many rural counties contain large amounts of national forest land that cannot be taxed. Since 2000, the Secure Rural Schools program has sent these counties payments to help pay for schools, roads, and other services. The program's authority is set to run out after 2026. This bill pushes the key dates back three years, from 2026 to 2029, so the payments can continue. It also moves back by three years the dates for the local advisory committees and for the special projects they can recommend on federal land. These projects are paid for with a share of the payments. Counties would also get three more years to spend certain project money, with the dates moving from 2028 and 2029 to 2031 and 2032. A pilot program for the advisory committees is also extended to 2029. Finally, the bill makes three tiny wording fixes, such as adding the word "of" before "acres" and removing stray commas. The bill does not set a dollar amount itself. It changes dates in the existing law, so payment amounts would follow the formulas already in that law. We could not see those formulas in the text provided, so the cost is not stated here.
does: Extends the Secure Rural Schools payment authority from 2026 to 2029.
Extends the deadline for distributing payments to eligible counties to 2029.
Extends the committee composition waiver authority to 2029.
Extends authority for special projects on federal land by three years (to 2031 and 2032).
Extends the time counties may spend project funds by three years (to 2031 and 2032).
Extends the resource advisory committee pilot program to 2029.
Makes three minor wording corrections to the existing law.
who: Rural counties and school districts containing national forest or other federal land
Residents who rely on county-funded schools, roads and services in those areas
Local resource advisory committee members who review project proposals
The Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management, which work with the committees
Federal taxpayers, who fund the payments

benefits: Gives rural counties and schools predictable funding for three more years.
Keeps local advisory committees active so residents can weigh in on projects.
Corrects small typos for clarity.
concerns: Adds federal spending, but the amount is not stated in the bill.
Special projects on federal land could affect forests, water or wildlife depending on how they are chosen.
Continues a payment system that is not tied to how much timber is harvested, which some may see as a long-term subsidy.
imp.cost: The bill gives no dollar figure. It changes dates in existing law, so costs depend on the existing payment formulas, which are not shown. No Congressional Budget Office estimate was provided.
unknowns: Total cost to taxpayers over the three years.
Which counties would receive how much.
What kinds of special projects will be approved and their environmental effects.
Whether the bill will be changed in committee or pass.

stage.last_action: Introduced in Senate

purpose: The bill says its goal is to keep the Secure Rural Schools program running by extending its key deadlines from 2026 to 2029, so rural counties with large amounts of untaxable national forest land can keep receiving payments for schools, roads, and other services. It also extends related deadlines for local advisory committees, special projects on federal land, and the time counties have to spend project funds, and makes three small wording corrections. The bill does not set a dollar amount; payments would follow the formulas already in existing law.

oppose: The bill adds federal spending for three more years, yet it does not state a total cost, so taxpayers cannot see the full price from the bill text alone.
Payments under this program are not tied to how much timber is harvested, so you could argue it is a long-term subsidy that should be reviewed rather than simply extended.
Special projects on federal land are funded by these payments; you could ask that project selection include strong safeguards for forests, water, and wildlife.
support: The bill gives rural counties and schools three more years of predictable funding, which helps them plan budgets for schools, roads, and services.
Counties with large amounts of national forest land cannot collect property tax on that land, and these payments help make up for that lost revenue.
Local advisory committees stay active for three more years, so residents keep a voice in choosing special projects on federal land.

equality.reason: Continues payments to rural counties that cannot tax federal land, helping fund schools and roads in those areas on a formula basis.

justice.reason: Maintains predictable funding for rural schools and services in counties that host untaxable federal land.

environmental_protection.reason: Special projects on federal land could help or harm the environment depending on selection; the bill itself does not set environmental standards, so the effect is unclear.

people_over_profit.reason: It directs public money to rural schools, roads and community services rather than to private companies.

local_say.reason: It extends local advisory committees that let residents recommend projects on nearby federal land.
